const ADMIN_USER = "admin";
const ADMIN_PASS_DEFAULT = "aya123";
// Admin password stored in persistent storage under key "hub-admin-pass" (shared)
async function getAdminPass() {
  try {
    const stored = await storeGet("hub-admin-pass", true);
    return stored || ADMIN_PASS_DEFAULT;
  } catch { return ADMIN_PASS_DEFAULT; }
}
// Test gate threshold stored under "hub-gate-threshold" (shared)
async function getGateThreshold() {
  try {
    const stored = await storeGet("hub-gate-threshold", true);
    return typeof stored === "number" ? stored : 25;
  } catch { return 25; }
}

// â”€â”€â”€ LESSONS â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
const LESSONS = {
  java:{
    Beginner:[
      {id:"jb1",title:"Welcome to Java",est:"10 min",content:`## Why Java for Robotics?
Java is the primary language for both FTC and FRC. It runs on the Control Hub (Android) for FTC and the roboRIO for FRC.

## Your First Variables
\`\`\`java
int speed = 75;           // whole numbers
double angle = 90.5;      // decimals
String teamName = "1234"; // text
boolean isRunning = true; // true or false
\`\`\`

## Rules to Remember
- Every statement ends with **;**
- Java is case-sensitive -- speed != Speed
- Code lives inside classes and methods
- Curly braces { } group blocks of code

## Data Types Quick Reference
| Type    | Example       | Use For        |
|---------|--------------|----------------|
| int     | 42           | Whole numbers  |
| double  | 3.14         | Decimals       |
| boolean | true / false | Flags          |
| String  | "hello"      | Text           |`},
      {id:"jb2",title:"If/Else & Comparisons",est:"12 min",content:`## Making Decisions
Your robot constantly decides -- when to stop, turn, or score.

\`\`\`java
if (distance < 10) {
    robot.stop();
} else if (distance < 30) {
    robot.slowDown();
} else {
    robot.driveForward(0.8);
}
\`\`\`

## Comparison Operators
- == equal to
- != not equal to
- > greater than  / < less than
- >= greater or equal / <= less or equal

## Logical Operators
\`\`\`java
if (hasBlock && armIsUp) { deposit(); }    // AND
if (touchSensor || distance < 5) { emergencyStop(); } // OR
if (!isRunning) { startMotors(); }         // NOT
\`\`\`

## Ternary (shorthand if/else)
\`\`\`java
double power = isAuto ? 0.5 : gamepad1.left_stick_y;
\`\`\``},
      {id:"jb3",title:"Loops",est:"12 min",content:`## Repeating Actions

### For Loop -- known number of repetitions
\`\`\`java
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    robot.rotate(45);
    sleep(500);
}
\`\`\`

### While Loop -- repeat while condition is true
\`\`\`java
while (opModeIsActive()) {
    double power = gamepad1.left_stick_y;
    leftMotor.setPower(power);
    telemetry.update();
}
\`\`\`

### Do-While -- always runs at least once
\`\`\`java
do {
    collectSample();
} while (!hasSample());
\`\`\`

### For-Each -- loop through a collection
\`\`\`java
String[] sensors = {"front", "back", "left"};
for (String s : sensors) {
    telemetry.addData("Sensor", s);
}
\`\`\`

## Loop Control
- break -- exit the loop immediately
- continue -- skip to next iteration`},
      {id:"jb4",title:"Methods & Functions",est:"15 min",content:`## Why Use Methods?
Methods let you reuse code without copy-pasting. Makes OpModes easier to read and debug.

## Void Methods (no return value)
\`\`\`java
public void driveForward(double speed, int ms) {
    leftMotor.setPower(speed);
    rightMotor.setPower(speed);
    sleep(ms);
    leftMotor.setPower(0);
    rightMotor.setPower(0);
}

driveForward(0.5, 2000); // 50% power for 2 seconds
\`\`\`

## Methods That Return Values
\`\`\`java
public double getDistanceCM() {
    return distanceSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM);
}

public boolean isClose() {
    return getDistanceCM() < 20;
}

if (isClose()) { stopDriving(); }
\`\`\`

## Multiple Parameters
\`\`\`java
public void turn(double power, String direction) {
    double sign = direction.equals("left") ? -1 : 1;
    leftMotor.setPower(-power * sign);
    rightMotor.setPower(power * sign);
    sleep(500);
    leftMotor.setPower(0);
    rightMotor.setPower(0);
}

turn(0.5, "left");
turn(0.7, "right");
\`\`\``},
      {id:"jb5",title:"Arrays & ArrayLists",est:"15 min",content:`## Arrays -- Fixed Size
\`\`\`java
double[] motorPowers = {0.5, 0.5, -0.5, -0.5};
String[] sensorNames = {"front","back","left","right"};

double front = motorPowers[0]; // index starts at 0!
int len = motorPowers.length;  // 4
motorPowers[2] = 0.8;          // modify element
\`\`\`

## ArrayList -- Dynamic (resizable)
\`\`\`java
import java.util.ArrayList;

ArrayList<String> log = new ArrayList<>();
log.add("Auto started");
log.add("Drove 30cm");
log.add("Scored sample");

String first = log.get(0);      // "Auto started"
int size = log.size();          // 3
log.remove(1);                  // removes "Drove 30cm"
boolean found = log.contains("Auto started"); // true
\`\`\`

## Looping
\`\`\`java
// Traditional for loop
for (int i = 0; i < motorPowers.length; i++) {
    telemetry.addData("Motor " + i, motorPowers[i]);
}

// Enhanced for-each
for (String name : sensorNames) {
    telemetry.addData("Sensor", name);
}
\`\`\``},
      {id:"jb6",title:"FTC OpMode Structure",est:"18 min",content:`## LinearOpMode -- The FTC Programming Model
\`\`\`java
@TeleOp(name = "MyTeleOp", group = "Linear Opmode")
public class MyTeleOp extends LinearOpMode {

    DcMotor leftDrive, rightDrive;
    Servo clawServo;

    @Override
    public void runOpMode() {
        // INIT -- runs when Init button pressed
        leftDrive  = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "left_drive");
        rightDrive = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "right_drive");
        clawServo  = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "claw");
        rightDrive.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE);

        telemetry.addData("Status", "Ready!");
        telemetry.update();

        waitForStart(); // pause until driver presses Start

        // RUN LOOP
        while (opModeIsActive()) {
            double drive = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;
            double turn  =  gamepad1.right_stick_x;
            leftDrive.setPower(drive + turn);
            rightDrive.setPower(drive - turn);

            if (gamepad1.a) clawServo.setPosition(0.8);
            if (gamepad1.b) clawServo.setPosition(0.2);

            telemetry.addData("Drive", drive);
            telemetry.update();
        }
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Key Annotations
- @TeleOp -- shows in Driver Hub as teleop program
- @Autonomous -- shows as autonomous program
- The name parameter appears on the Driver Hub screen`},
      {id:"jb7",title:"Gamepad Controls",est:"12 min",content:`## Reading Gamepad Input
FTC uses two gamepads: gamepad1 (driver) and gamepad2 (operator).

## Buttons -- boolean (true/false)
\`\`\`java
if (gamepad1.a)           { /* A button */ }
if (gamepad1.b)           { /* B button */ }
if (gamepad1.x)           { /* X button */ }
if (gamepad1.y)           { /* Y button */ }
if (gamepad1.dpad_up)     { intake.setPower(1.0); }
if (gamepad1.dpad_down)   { intake.setPower(-1.0); }
if (gamepad1.left_bumper) { /* Left bumper */ }
\`\`\`

## Analog Sticks and Triggers -- float values
\`\`\`java
double drive   = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;  // -1.0 to 1.0
double strafe  =  gamepad1.left_stick_x;  // for mecanum
double rotate  =  gamepad1.right_stick_x; // turning
double leftTrig  = gamepad1.left_trigger;  // 0.0 to 1.0
double rightTrig = gamepad1.right_trigger; // 0.0 to 1.0
\`\`\`

## Toggle (Press vs Hold)
\`\`\`java
boolean prevA = false;
boolean clawOpen = false;

// Inside loop:
if (gamepad1.a && !prevA) {
    clawOpen = !clawOpen; // toggle on press
}
prevA = gamepad1.a;
clawServo.setPosition(clawOpen ? 0.8 : 0.2);

      {id:"jb8",title:"Telemetry & Debugging",est:"12 min",content:`## Why Telemetry Matters
Telemetry sends data from the robot to your Driver Hub screen. Good telemetry turns a 2-hour debug session into 5 minutes.

\`\`\`java
telemetry.addData("Status", "Running");
telemetry.addData("Left Power", leftMotor.getPower());
telemetry.addData("Heading", imu.getHeading());
telemetry.addData("Distance", distSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM));
telemetry.addData("Encoder", leftMotor.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.update(); // MUST call this to send data!
\`\`\`

## Formatted Numbers
\`\`\`java
telemetry.addData("LF", "%.2f", leftFront.getPower()); // 2 decimal places
telemetry.addData("Angle", "%.1f deg", heading);
\`\`\`

## Section Headers
\`\`\`java
telemetry.addLine("=== Drive System ===");
telemetry.addData("LF", leftFront.getPower());
telemetry.addData("RF", rightFront.getPower());
telemetry.addLine("=== Arm ===");
telemetry.addData("Position", arm.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("State", currentState.name());
\`\`\`

## Telemetry Tips
- Always call telemetry.update() at the END of your loop
- Add state machine states to telemetry for debugging
- Use FTC Dashboard for live graphs in a browser`},

      {id:"ji1",title:"Object-Oriented Programming",est:"20 min",content:`## Classes and Objects
OOP organizes robot code into reusable, logical units instead of one giant file.

\`\`\`java
public class DriveSystem {
    private DcMotor leftFront, rightFront, leftBack, rightBack;
    private double maxSpeed;

    public DriveSystem(HardwareMap hwMap, double maxSpeed) {
        leftFront  = hwMap.get(DcMotor.class, "leftFront");
        rightFront = hwMap.get(DcMotor.class, "rightFront");
        leftBack   = hwMap.get(DcMotor.class, "leftBack");
        rightBack  = hwMap.get(DcMotor.class, "rightBack");
        rightFront.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE);
        rightBack.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE);
        this.maxSpeed = maxSpeed;
    }

    public void drive(double x, double y, double rotate) {
        double lf = (y + x + rotate) * maxSpeed;
        double rf = (y - x - rotate) * maxSpeed;
        double lb = (y - x + rotate) * maxSpeed;
        double rb = (y + x - rotate) * maxSpeed;
        leftFront.setPower(lf);  rightFront.setPower(rf);
        leftBack.setPower(lb);   rightBack.setPower(rb);
    }

    public void stop() { drive(0, 0, 0); }
}
\`\`\`

## Using It in Your OpMode
\`\`\`java
DriveSystem drive = new DriveSystem(hardwareMap, 0.8);
// In loop:
drive.drive(gamepad1.left_stick_x, gamepad1.left_stick_y, gamepad1.right_stick_x);
if (gamepad1.a) drive.stop();
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ji2",title:"PID Control",est:"25 min",content:`## What is PID?
PID is a feedback control algorithm that makes your robot reach a target accurately and smoothly.

## The Three Terms
- P (Proportional) -- Output proportional to current error
- I (Integral) -- Sums error over time; fixes persistent offset
- D (Derivative) -- Rate of change of error; prevents overshoot

\`\`\`
output = (kP x error) + (kI x integral) + (kD x derivative)
\`\`\`

## Java Implementation -- Heading Control
\`\`\`java
double kP = 0.01, kI = 0.0001, kD = 0.005;
double integral = 0, lastError = 0;
double targetAngle = 90.0;

while (opModeIsActive()) {
    double error = targetAngle - imu.getHeading();
    while (error > 180)  error -= 360;
    while (error < -180) error += 360;

    integral  += error * 0.02;
    double derivative = (error - lastError) / 0.02;
    double output = kP*error + kI*integral + kD*derivative;

    leftMotor.setPower(basePower + output);
    rightMotor.setPower(basePower - output);
    lastError = error;
    sleep(20);
}
\`\`\`

## Tuning Steps
1. kI = kD = 0. Increase kP until oscillating
2. Add kD to damp oscillation (try kP/10)
3. Add small kI only if there is steady-state error`},

      {id:"ji4",title:"State Machines",est:"22 min",content:`## Why State Machines?
Complex sequences -- intake, lift, score, reset -- are hard to manage with if/else chains.

\`\`\`java
enum RobotState { IDLE, INTAKING, LIFTING, SCORING, RESETTING }
RobotState state = RobotState.IDLE;

while (opModeIsActive()) {
    switch (state) {
        case IDLE:
            if (gamepad1.a) state = RobotState.INTAKING;
            break;
        case INTAKING:
            intake.setPower(1.0);
            if (colorSensor.alpha() > 500) {
                intake.setPower(0);
                state = RobotState.LIFTING;
            }
            if (gamepad1.b) { intake.setPower(0); state = RobotState.IDLE; }
            break;
        case LIFTING:
            lift.setTargetPosition(LIFT_HIGH);
            lift.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
            lift.setPower(0.8);
            if (!lift.isBusy()) state = RobotState.SCORING;
            break;
        case SCORING:
            claw.setPosition(0.0);
            sleep(300);
            state = RobotState.RESETTING;
            break;
        case RESETTING:
            lift.setTargetPosition(0);
            if (!lift.isBusy()) state = RobotState.IDLE;
            break;
    }
    telemetry.addData("State", state);
    telemetry.update();
}
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ji5",title:"Autonomous Programming",est:"25 min",content:`## Encoder-Based Movement (Accurate)
\`\`\`java
static final double TICKS_PER_REV  = 537.7;
static final double WHEEL_DIAM_CM  = 9.6;
static final double TICKS_PER_CM   = TICKS_PER_REV / (WHEEL_DIAM_CM * Math.PI);

public void driveInches(double inches, double power) {
    int ticks = (int)(inches * 2.54 * TICKS_PER_CM);
    leftMotor.setTargetPosition(leftMotor.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);
    rightMotor.setTargetPosition(rightMotor.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);
    leftMotor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
    rightMotor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
    leftMotor.setPower(Math.abs(power));
    rightMotor.setPower(Math.abs(power));
    while (opModeIsActive() && (leftMotor.isBusy() || rightMotor.isBusy())) {
        telemetry.addData("Target", leftMotor.getTargetPosition());
        telemetry.update();
    }
    leftMotor.setPower(0); rightMotor.setPower(0);
}
\`\`\`

## Gyro Turn
\`\`\`java
public void turnToHeading(double target, double power) {
    double error = target - imu.getHeading();
    while (Math.abs(error) > 2 && opModeIsActive()) {
        double p = Range.clip(error * 0.01, -power, power);
        leftMotor.setPower(p);
        rightMotor.setPower(-p);
        error = target - imu.getHeading();
    }
    leftMotor.setPower(0); rightMotor.setPower(0);
}
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ji6",title:"Mecanum Drive Math",est:"20 min",content:`## Why Mecanum?
Mecanum wheels have 45-degree rollers that allow strafing sideways, forward, backward, and diagonal movement.

## The Formula
\`\`\`java
double y  = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;  // forward/back (negated)
double x  =  gamepad1.left_stick_x;  // strafe
double rx =  gamepad1.right_stick_x; // rotate

double frontLeft  = y + x + rx;
double frontRight = y - x - rx;
double backLeft   = y - x + rx;
double backRight  = y + x - rx;

// Normalize so no value exceeds 1.0
double maxPower = Math.max(Math.abs(frontLeft),
    Math.max(Math.abs(frontRight),
    Math.max(Math.abs(backLeft), Math.abs(backRight))));
if (maxPower > 1.0) {
    frontLeft /= maxPower; frontRight /= maxPower;
    backLeft  /= maxPower; backRight  /= maxPower;
}

leftFront.setPower(frontLeft);   rightFront.setPower(frontRight);
leftBack.setPower(backLeft);     rightBack.setPower(backRight);
\`\`\`

## Field-Centric Drive
\`\`\`java
double heading = imu.getHeading();
double rotX = x * Math.cos(-heading) - y * Math.sin(-heading);
double rotY = x * Math.sin(-heading) + y * Math.cos(-heading);
// Use rotX and rotY in the formula above
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ji7",title:"Motor Run Modes",est:"15 min",content:`## The Four Run Modes in FTC
Understanding run modes is critical for both autonomous and teleop.

\`\`\`java
// 1. RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER -- raw power, no encoder feedback
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.5);

// 2. RUN_USING_ENCODER -- velocity-controlled (more consistent speed)
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.5); // power = fraction of max velocity

// 3. RUN_TO_POSITION -- encoder-based position control
motor.setTargetPosition(1000); // ticks
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
motor.setPower(0.8);           // speed (always positive)
while (motor.isBusy()) {
    telemetry.addData("Current", motor.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.update();
}

// 4. STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER -- zero the encoder count
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);
\`\`\`

## ZeroPowerBehavior
\`\`\`java
motor.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE);  // holds position
motor.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.FLOAT);  // coasts
// Always use BRAKE for lifts!
\`\`\``},

      {id:"ja1",title:"Road Runner & Path Planning",est:"30 min",content:`## What is Road Runner?
Road Runner follows time-optimal trajectories using a mathematical model of your robot. No more sleep() timing!

\`\`\`java
TrajectorySequence traj = drive.trajectorySequenceBuilder(startPose)
    .forward(30)
    .turn(Math.toRadians(90))
    .strafeLeft(15)
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(48, -12), Math.toRadians(0))
    .waitSeconds(0.5)
    .back(10)
    .build();

drive.followTrajectorySequence(traj);
\`\`\`

## Localization with Odometry
\`\`\`java
// Dead-wheel odometry: position even when wheels slip
Pose2d pose = drive.getPoseEstimate();
double x = pose.getX(), y = pose.getY();
double heading = pose.getHeading();
\`\`\`

## FRC PathPlanner
\`\`\`java
return new SequentialCommandGroup(
    AutoBuilder.followPath(PathPlannerPath.fromPathFile("ScoreThenPickup")),
    new ScoreCommand(shooter),
    new IntakeCommand(intake)
);
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ja2",title:"Computer Vision & AprilTags",est:"30 min",content:`## AprilTag Setup
\`\`\`java
aprilTag = new AprilTagProcessor.Builder()
    .setDrawTagOutline(true)
    .setLensIntrinsics(578.272, 578.272, 402.145, 221.506)
    .build();

visionPortal = new VisionPortal.Builder()
    .setCamera(hardwareMap.get(WebcamName.class, "Webcam 1"))
    .addProcessor(aprilTag)

\`\`\`

## Reading Tag Data
\`\`\`java
for (AprilTagDetection d : aprilTag.getDetections()) {
    if (d.metadata != null) {
        telemetry.addData("Tag ID", d.id);
        telemetry.addData("X offset cm", d.ftcPose.x);
        telemetry.addData("Y offset cm", d.ftcPose.y);
        telemetry.addData("Yaw deg", d.ftcPose.yaw);
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Auto-Align to a Tag
\`\`\`java
double kP = 0.02;
while (opModeIsActive()) {
    List<AprilTagDetection> tags = aprilTag.getDetections();
    if (!tags.isEmpty()) {
        double xError = tags.get(0).ftcPose.x;
        double power = kP * xError;
        leftMotor.setPower(power);
        rightMotor.setPower(-power);
        if (Math.abs(xError) < 1.0) break;
    }
}
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ja3",title:"Command-Based FRC",est:"35 min",content:`## Subsystem -- Hardware Abstraction
\`\`\`java
public class Shooter extends SubsystemBase {
    private final TalonFX motor = new TalonFX(1);
    private double targetRPM = 0;

    public void setVelocity(double rpm) {
        targetRPM = rpm;
        motor.setControl(new VelocityVoltage(rpm / 60.0));
    }
    public boolean atSpeed() {
        return Math.abs(motor.getVelocity().getValue() * 60 - targetRPM) < 50;
    }
    public void stop() { motor.setControl(new NeutralOut()); }
}
\`\`\`

## Sequential Command
\`\`\`java
public class SpinUpAndShoot extends SequentialCommandGroup {
    public SpinUpAndShoot(Shooter shooter, Indexer indexer, double rpm) {
        addCommands(
            new RunCommand(() -> shooter.setVelocity(rpm), shooter)
                .until(shooter::atSpeed),
            new InstantCommand(indexer::feed),
            new WaitCommand(0.5),
            new InstantCommand(shooter::stop)
        );
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Binding to Controller
\`\`\`java
new JoystickButton(driver, Button.kA.value)
    .onTrue(new SpinUpAndShoot(shooter, indexer, 5000));
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ja4",title:"Advanced PID & Feedforward",est:"30 min",content:`## Beyond Basic PID

## Feedforward -- Predictive Control
\`\`\`java
// Flywheel: kS=static, kV=velocity, kA=acceleration
double ff = kS * Math.signum(targetVel) + kV * targetVel + kA * targetAccel;
double pidOut = pid.calculate(currentVel, targetVel);
motor.setVoltage(ff + pidOut);
\`\`\`

## Arm with Gravity Compensation
\`\`\`java
double gravityFF = kG * Math.cos(Math.toRadians(currentAngle));
double totalOutput = pidOutput + gravityFF;
armMotor.setPower(totalOutput);
\`\`\`

## WPILib SysId (FRC) -- Auto-Find Motor Constants
\`\`\`java
// Deploy SysId, run quasistatic and dynamic tests,
// then analyze with SysId app to get kS, kV, kA automatically.
SimpleMotorFeedforward ff = new SimpleMotorFeedforward(kS, kV, kA);
double ffOut = ff.calculate(targetVelocity, targetAcceleration);
\`\`\`

## Elevator Motion Profile
\`\`\`java
TrapezoidProfile.Constraints c = new TrapezoidProfile.Constraints(MAX_V, MAX_A);
TrapezoidProfile profile = new TrapezoidProfile(c);
TrapezoidProfile.State setpoint = profile.calculate(0.02, currentState, goal);
double out = kG + kV * setpoint.velocity + pid.calculate(pos, setpoint.position);
motor.setVoltage(out);
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ja5",title:"Multi-Threading & Async",est:"35 min",content:`## Why Multi-Threading?
Vision processing and complex math take longer than 20ms. Threading lets them run in parallel without blocking driving.

## Vision Thread in FTC
\`\`\`java
AtomicReference<Pose2d> latestPose = new AtomicReference<>(new Pose2d());
volatile boolean stopRequested = false;

Thread visionThread = new Thread(() -> {
    while (!stopRequested && !isStopRequested()) {
        List<AprilTagDetection> tags = aprilTag.getDetections();
        if (!tags.isEmpty()) {
            latestPose.set(calculatePoseFromTags(tags));
        }
        try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
    }
});
visionThread.setDaemon(true);
visionThread.start();

while (opModeIsActive()) {
    Pose2d pose = latestPose.get();
    drive.update(pose);
    telemetry.update();
}
stopRequested = true;
\`\`\`

## Thread Safety Rules
- Never write to hardware from a background thread
- Use volatile for simple primitives shared between threads
- Use AtomicReference for complex objects
- Use synchronized blocks when multiple threads modify shared state`},
      {id:"ja6",title:"FRC Swerve Drive",est:"35 min",content:`## Swerve Drive Overview
Each wheel has independent steering AND driving. Full maneuverability + full traction.

## Popular Modules
- MK4/MK4i (SDS) -- most used in FRC
- REV MAXSwerve -- great value, easy setup
- WCP SwerveX -- high quality

## WPILib Swerve Setup
\`\`\`java
SwerveDriveKinematics kinematics = new SwerveDriveKinematics(
    new Translation2d( TRACK/2,  WHEEL_BASE/2), // frontLeft
    new Translation2d( TRACK/2, -WHEEL_BASE/2), // frontRight
    new Translation2d(-TRACK/2,  WHEEL_BASE/2), // backLeft
    new Translation2d(-TRACK/2, -WHEEL_BASE/2)  // backRight
);

// Field-relative drive
ChassisSpeeds fieldSpeeds = ChassisSpeeds.fromFieldRelativeSpeeds(
    vx, vy, omega, gyro.getRotation2d());
SwerveModuleState[] states = kinematics.toSwerveModuleStates(fieldSpeeds);
SwerveDriveKinematics.desaturateWheelSpeeds(states, MAX_SPEED);

frontLeft.setDesiredState(states[0]);
frontRight.setDesiredState(states[1]);
\`\`\`

## Odometry
\`\`\`java
SwerveDriveOdometry odometry = new SwerveDriveOdometry(
    kinematics, gyro.getRotation2d(), getModulePositions(), startPose);
// Update each loop:
Pose2d pose = odometry.update(gyro.getRotation2d(), getModulePositions());
\`\`\``},

      {id:"pb1",title:"Python Basics",est:"10 min",content:`## Why Learn Python?
Python is used in FRC (via RobotPy), scouting data analysis, automation scripts, and web apps. It is easier to learn than Java and great for data work.

## Variables -- No Type Declaration!

speed = 75           # integer
angle = 90.5         # float
team_name = "1234"   # string
is_running = True    # boolean (capital T/F)
\`\`\`

## Print Output
\`\`\`python
print("Hello, FIRST!")
print(f"Speed: {speed}, Angle: {angle}")  # f-string
print("Team:", team_name)
\`\`\`

## Basic Math
\`\`\`python
result = 10 + 5     # 15   addition
result = 10 - 3     # 7    subtraction
result = 4 * 2.5    # 10.0 multiplication
result = 10 / 3     # 3.333 true division
result = 10 // 3    # 3    integer division
result = 10 % 3     # 1    remainder
result = 2 ** 8     # 256  power

      {id:"pb2",title:"If/Else & Comparisons",est:"12 min",content:`## Decisions in Python
Python uses indentation instead of curly braces. Indentation IS the code structure!

\`\`\`python
distance = 25

if distance < 10:
    print("Stop!")
elif distance < 30:
    print("Slow down")
else:
    print("Full speed ahead")

## Comparison Operators
- == equal / != not equal
- > greater / < less
- >= greater or equal / <= less or equal

## Logical Operators

if has_block and arm_up:
    print("Deposit!")

if touch_sensor or distance < 5:
    print("Stop!")

if not is_running:
    print("Robot stopped")

## Chained Comparisons (Python only!)

      {id:"pb6",title:"RobotPy Basics (FRC)",est:"18 min",content:`## What is RobotPy?
RobotPy lets you write FRC robot code in Python using the same WPILib hardware classes as Java.

\`\`\`python
import wpilib
import wpilib.drive

class MyRobot(wpilib.TimedRobot):

    def robotInit(self):
        self.left_motor  = wpilib.PWMSparkMax(0)
        self.right_motor = wpilib.PWMSparkMax(1)
        self.drive = wpilib.drive.DifferentialDrive(
            self.left_motor, self.right_motor)
        self.gamepad = wpilib.Joystick(0)

    def teleopPeriodic(self):
        speed  = -self.gamepad.getY()
        rotate =  self.gamepad.getX()
        self.drive.arcadeDrive(speed, rotate)

    def autonomousInit(self):
        self.timer = wpilib.Timer()
        self.timer.start()

    def autonomousPeriodic(self):
        if self.timer.get() < 2.0:
            self.drive.arcadeDrive(0.5, 0)
        else:
            self.drive.arcadeDrive(0, 0)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    wpilib.run(MyRobot)

      {id:"pi1",title:"Classes & OOP in Python",est:"20 min",content:`## Python Classes
\`\`\`python
class DriveSystem:
    def __init__(self, hardware_map, max_speed=1.0):
        self.left_front  = hardware_map.get("leftFront")
        self.right_front = hardware_map.get("rightFront")
        self.left_back   = hardware_map.get("leftBack")
        self.right_back  = hardware_map.get("rightBack")
        self.max_speed   = max_speed

    def drive(self, x, y, rotate):
        lf = (y + x + rotate) * self.max_speed
        rf = (y - x - rotate) * self.max_speed
        lb = (y - x + rotate) * self.max_speed
        rb = (y + x - rotate) * self.max_speed
        self.left_front.set(lf)
        self.right_front.set(rf)
        self.left_back.set(lb)
        self.right_back.set(rb)

    def stop(self):
        self.drive(0, 0, 0)

      {id:"pi5",title:"State Machines in Python",est:"18 min",content:`## Python State Machines with Enum
\`\`\`python
from enum import Enum, auto
import wpilib

class RobotState(Enum):
    IDLE     = auto()
    INTAKING = auto()
    LIFTING  = auto()
    SCORING  = auto()
    RESET    = auto()

class Robot(wpilib.TimedRobot):
    def robotInit(self):
        self.state  = RobotState.IDLE
        self.intake = wpilib.PWMSparkMax(2)
        self.pad    = wpilib.Joystick(0)

    def teleopPeriodic(self):
        if self.state == RobotState.IDLE:
            if self.pad.getRawButton(1):
                self.state = RobotState.INTAKING

        elif self.state == RobotState.INTAKING:
            self.intake.set(1.0)
            if self.color_sensor.proximity > 500:
                self.intake.set(0)
                self.state = RobotState.LIFTING

        elif self.state == RobotState.LIFTING:
            self.lift.setTarget(self.LIFT_HIGH)
            if self.lift.at_target:
                self.state = RobotState.SCORING

        elif self.state == RobotState.SCORING:
            self.claw.set(0.0)
            self.state = RobotState.RESET

        elif self.state == RobotState.RESET:
            self.lift.setTarget(0)
            if self.lift.at_target:
                self.state = RobotState.IDLE

        wpilib.SmartDashboard.putString("State", self.state.name)

\`\`\`python
from wpimath.controller import PIDController
import wpilib

class Robot(wpilib.TimedRobot):
    def robotInit(self):
        self.pid = PIDController(kP=0.01, kI=0.0001, kD=0.005)
        self.pid.setTolerance(2.0)  # degrees
        self.imu = ...

    def teleopPeriodic(self):
        target = 90.0  # degrees
        current = self.imu.getAngle()
        output = self.pid.calculate(current, target)

        self.left_motor.set(output)
        self.right_motor.set(-output)

        if self.pid.atSetpoint():
            self.left_motor.set(0)
            self.right_motor.set(0)
\`\`\`

## Manual PID (for understanding)
\`\`\`python
kP, kI, kD = 0.01, 0.0001, 0.005
integral = 0
last_error = 0
dt = 0.02  # 20ms loop

def pid_step(target, current):
    global integral, last_error
    error = target - current
    integral += error * dt
    derivative = (error - last_error) / dt
    output = kP*error + kI*integral + kD*derivative
    last_error = error
    return output

      {id:"pa1",title:"OPR Calculation in Python",est:"30 min",content:`## Computing OPR from Scratch
OPR uses linear algebra: given alliance scores, find each robot's individual contribution.

\`\`\`python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests

def calculate_opr(event_key, tba_key):
    headers = {"X-TBA-Auth-Key": tba_key}
    base = "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3"

    matches = requests.get(f"{base}/event/{event_key}/matches", headers=headers).json()
    teams   = requests.get(f"{base}/event/{event_key}/teams/simple", headers=headers).json()

    team_list = sorted([t["key"] for t in teams])
    idx = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(team_list)}
    n = len(team_list)

    A_rows, b_rows = [], []
    for m in matches:
        if m["comp_level"] != "qm": continue
        for color in ["red", "blue"]:
            score = m["alliances"][color]["score"]
            if score < 0: continue
            row = [0.0] * n
            for t in m["alliances"][color]["team_keys"]:
                if t in idx: row[idx[t]] = 1.0
            A_rows.append(row)
            b_rows.append(float(score))

    A = np.array(A_rows)
    b = np.array(b_rows)
    opr, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
    return pd.Series(opr, index=team_list).sort_values(ascending=False)

oprs = calculate_opr("2024casd", "YOUR_KEY")
print(oprs.head(10))

      {id:"pa2",title:"Scouting App with Flask",est:"35 min",content:`## Build a Web Scouting App
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import json, os

app = Flask(__name__)
DATA_FILE = "scouting_data.json"

def load_data():
    if os.path.exists(DATA_FILE):
        with open(DATA_FILE) as f: return json.load(f)
    return []

def save_data(data):
    with open(DATA_FILE, "w") as f: json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

@app.route("/api/submit", methods=["POST"])
def submit():
    entry = request.json
    data = load_data()
    data.append(entry)
    save_data(data)
    return jsonify({"status": "ok", "total": len(data)})

@app.route("/api/stats/<int:team>")
def team_stats(team):
    data = [d for d in load_data() if d.get("team") == team]
    if not data:
        return jsonify({"error": "Not found"}), 404
    return jsonify({
        "team": team,
        "matches": len(data),
        "avg_auto":   round(sum(d["auto"]   for d in data) / len(data), 1),
        "avg_teleop": round(sum(d["teleop"] for d in data) / len(data), 1),
        "climb_rate": f"{sum(d.get('climbed',0) for d in data)/len(data)*100:.0f}%"
    })

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)

import asyncio

async def read_sensors():
    while True:
        distance = await sensor.read_async()
        pose_queue.put_nowait(distance)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)   # 20Hz

async def drive_loop():
    while True:
        dist = pose_queue.get_nowait() if not pose_queue.empty() else None
        if dist and dist < 15:
            motors.stop()
        else:
            motors.drive(speed, rotate)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.02)   # 50Hz

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(read_sensors(), drive_loop())

asyncio.run(main())

      {id:"pa5",title:"Full Data Pipeline",est:"30 min",content:`## Automated Scouting Pipeline
\`\`\`python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import requests
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

class ScoutingPipeline:
    def __init__(self, tba_key, event_key):
        self.headers   = {"X-TBA-Auth-Key": tba_key}
        self.event_key = event_key
        self.base      = "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3"

    def fetch(self, endpoint):
        return requests.get(self.base + endpoint, headers=self.headers).json()

    def get_team_stats(self):
        oprs    = self.fetch(f"/event/{self.event_key}/oprs")
        matches = self.fetch(f"/event/{self.event_key}/matches")
        teams   = self.fetch(f"/event/{self.event_key}/teams/simple")

        data = []
        for team in teams:
            key = team["key"]
            opr = oprs["oprs"].get(key, 0)
            scores = []
            for m in matches:
                if m["comp_level"] != "qm": continue
                for color in ["red", "blue"]:
                    if key in m["alliances"][color]["team_keys"]:
                        scores.append(m["alliances"][color]["score"])
            data.append({
                "number": team["team_number"],
                "name":   team["nickname"],
                "opr":    round(opr, 1),
                "ccwm":   round(opr - oprs["dprs"].get(key, 0), 1),
                "avg":    round(np.mean(scores) if scores else 0, 1),
                "std":    round(np.std(scores)  if scores else 0, 1),
            })
        return pd.DataFrame(data).sort_values("opr", ascending=False)

    def generate_picklist(self, my_team):
        df = self.get_team_stats()
        df = df[df["number"] != my_team]
        df["pick_score"] = df["opr"]*0.6 + (-df["std"])*0.2 + df["ccwm"]*0.2
        return df.sort_values("pick_score", ascending=False)

pipeline = ScoutingPipeline("YOUR_TBA_KEY", "2024casd")
picklist = pipeline.generate_picklist(my_team=1234)

      {id:"mb1",title:"Types of Drivetrains",est:"12 min",content:`## Choosing a Drivetrain

## Tank / Differential Drive
- Simple to build and program
- Very strong pushing force
- Forward, backward, and turning only

## Mecanum Drive
- Angled rollers allow **strafing** (sideways movement)
- Much more maneuverable â€” FTC favorite
- Slightly weaker traction sideways

## Swerve Drive
- Each wheel steers AND drives independently
- Full maneuverability + full traction
- Very complex â€” high-level FRC teams

## Key Trade-offs
- **Speed vs Torque** â€” Faster is harder to control
- **Complexity vs Reliability** â€” Simpler drivetrains break less`},
      {id:"mb2",title:"Gears, Belts & Chains",est:"15 min",content:`## Gear Ratios
\`\`\`
Gear Ratio = Driven Teeth Ã· Driving Teeth
3:1 reduction â†’ 3Ã— more torque, â…“ speed
1:2 increase  â†’ 2Ã— more speed, Â½ torque
\`\`\`

| Type  | Backlash | Slip | Noise |
|-------|----------|------|-------|
| Gears | Some     | None | High  |
| Belt  | None     | Rare | Low   |
| Chain | Some     | None | Med   |

## Tips
- Belt drives for precision, light loads
- Chains for heavy loads (drivetrains)
- Always tension properly â€” loose chains skip teeth`},
      {id:"mb3",title:"Motors & Servos",est:"14 min",content:`## DC Motors
- Continuous rotation, -1.0 to 1.0 speed
- Common FTC: REV HD Hex, goBILDA Yellow Jacket
- Common FRC: Falcon 500, NEO, Kraken X60

## Servos
- Precise angular position (0.0 to 1.0 in FTC)
- Use for: claws, wrist joints, small actuators

\`\`\`java
clawServo.setPosition(0.5);  // midpoint
armMotor.setPower(0.5);       // half speed
\`\`\`

## Key Specs
- **Stall Torque** â€” max torque at 0 RPM
- **Free Speed** â€” max RPM at 0 torque
- **Stall Current** â€” avoid prolonged stalling!`},
      {id:"mb4",title:"Structural Materials",est:"12 min",content:`## Common Robot Materials

### Aluminum Extrusion
- Lightweight, strong, versatile
- Easy to attach with brackets
- Most common for FTC robot structure

### 3D Printed Plastics
- PLA: easy to print, brittle under impact
- PETG: more flexible, better for stress
- Nylon/Onyx: high strength, expensive

### Polycarbonate (Lexan)
- Very tough, flexible, transparent
- Great for bumpers (FRC) and panels

## Tips
- Minimize weight everywhere possible
- Triangulate members for rigidity
- Over-engineer high-stress joints`},
      {id:"mb5",title:"Bearings & Axles",est:"10 min",content:`## Why Bearings Matter
Bearings allow wheels and shafts to rotate with minimal friction.

## Types
- **Ball Bearings** â€” most common, handles radial loads
- **Pillow Block** â€” self-contained housing, easy to mount

## Axle Types
- **Hex shaft** â€” FTC standard 5mm, easy attachments
- **D-shaft** â€” reliable gear attachment
- **Round shaft** â€” needs set screws

## Tips
- Use bearings at BOTH ends of every rotating shaft
- Check for binding after assembly
- Grease drivetrain wheel bearings under high load`},

      {id:"mi1",title:"Lift & Elevator Mechanisms",est:"18 min",content:`## Types of Lifts

### Single-Stage Linear Slide
- Simple, reliable, 1x height extension

### Cascade Lift
- Multiple stages extend simultaneously
- 2-3x height from same motor travel

### Four-Bar Linkage
- End effector maintains constant orientation
- Great for intakes that need to stay level

\`\`\`java
// Gravity feedforward to hold lift position
double ff = 0.1;
liftMotor.setPower(targetPower + ff);
\`\`\`

## Design Rules
- Add hard stops to prevent over-extension
- String lifts need consistent tensioning`},
      {id:"mi2",title:"Intake Mechanisms",est:"16 min",content:`## Roller Intakes
- Spinning rollers grab and pull in game pieces
- Use compliant (flex) wheels for best grip

\`\`\`java
if (gamepad1.right_trigger > 0.1) {
    intakeMotor.setPower(gamepad1.right_trigger);
} else if (gamepad1.left_trigger > 0.1) {
    intakeMotor.setPower(-gamepad1.left_trigger);
} else {
    intakeMotor.setPower(0);
}
\`\`\`

## Common Problems
- **Pieces jam**: Add dividers or wider channels
- **Pieces spit out**: Reverse roller or add stopper
- **Motor stalls**: Gear down the intake motor`},
      {id:"mi3",title:"Pneumatics (FRC)",est:"20 min",content:`## Key Components
- **Compressor** â€” fills tank automatically
- **Storage Tank** â€” holds pressurized air (max 120 PSI)
- **Solenoid Valve** â€” switches airflow electronically
- **Cylinder** â€” converts air to linear force

\`\`\`java
DoubleSolenoid clawSolenoid = new DoubleSolenoid(
    PneumaticsModuleType.CTREPCM, 0, 1);
clawSolenoid.set(DoubleSolenoid.Value.kForward); // extend
clawSolenoid.set(DoubleSolenoid.Value.kReverse); // retract
\`\`\`

## When to Use Pneumatics
- Fast, repeatable binary actions (< 0.3 sec)
- High-force requirements
- Limitation: can't hold precise intermediate positions`},
      {id:"mi4",title:"Claw & End Effector Design",est:"15 min",content:`## Claw Types
- **Parallel Gripper** â€” consistent force at any width, needs linkage
- **Pivoting Gripper** â€” simpler, force varies with opening

## End Effector Checklist
âœ… Picks up game piece reliably at speed?
âœ… Holds piece while driving over bumps?
âœ… Scores without getting stuck?
âœ… Releases fully without jamming?
âœ… Has a backup release method?

\`\`\`java
double CLAW_OPEN = 0.8;
double CLAW_CLOSED = 0.2;
if (gamepad1.a) clawServo.setPosition(CLAW_OPEN);
if (gamepad1.b) clawServo.setPosition(CLAW_CLOSED);
\`\`\``},
      {id:"mi5",title:"CAD & Design Software",est:"18 min",content:`## Popular CAD Tools
- **Onshape** â€” browser-based, free for students, real-time collaboration
- **Fusion 360** â€” free for students, powerful, offline
- **SolidWorks** â€” industry standard, free via FIRST

## Design Workflow
1. Sketch 2D profile with constraints
2. Extrude into 3D solid
3. Add features (holes, fillets, chamfers)
4. Assembly: combine parts, add mates
5. Check for interference (collision detection)

## Best Practices
- Model every bolt hole accurately
- Store files with version history (Onshape does this automatically)
- Use configurations for different variants`},

    Advanced:[
      {id:"ma1",title:"FEA & Structural Analysis",est:"25 min",content:`## Finite Element Analysis
FEA simulates how forces affect parts â€” finding stress concentrations before they fail.

## In Fusion 360 (Free)
1. Apply material (aluminum 6061-T6)
2. Define constraints (fixed mounting points)
3. Apply loads (forces in Newtons)
4. Run simulation â†’ view stress heatmap

## Interpreting Results
- **Von Mises Stress** â€” combined stress at each point
- Compare to yield strength (6061-T6: ~276 MPa)
- Safety factor = yield strength Ã· max stress
- Target: **Safety factor â‰¥ 2.0**`},
      {id:"ma2",title:"Advanced Drivetrain Design",est:"30 min",content:`## Swerve Drive Deep Dive

### Popular Modules
- **MK4/MK4i (SDS)** â€” most used in FRC
- **REV MAXSwerve** â€” great value
- **WCP Swerve** â€” high quality, expensive

### Field-Oriented Control
\`\`\`java
ChassisSpeeds fieldRelative = ChassisSpeeds.fromFieldRelativeSpeeds(
    vx, vy, omega, gyro.getRotation2d());
\`\`\`

## Weight Distribution
- Keep center of mass low and centered
- Mount battery centrally â€” it's heavy!`},
      {id:"ma3",title:"Manufacturing Techniques",est:"22 min",content:`## CNC Routing / Laser Cutting
- Cut aluminum plate and polycarbonate precisely
- Export DXF from CAD â†’ cut at 1:1 scale

## 3D Printing for Competition
- Use 20-40% infill for structural parts
- Increase perimeters for strength
- Orient print to avoid layer lines along main stress axis
- Use PETG or ASA for outdoor/high-temp exposure

## Fastener Tips
- Use **nylocs** for rotating joints
- Apply **Loctite Blue** on vibrating bolts
- Never rely on friction alone for critical joints`},
      {id:"ma4",title:"Scouting-Informed Design",est:"20 min",content:`## Build to the Game, Not Your Imagination

## Pre-Season Research
1. Watch every reveal video from past 2-3 years
2. Study Worlds recaps â€” what mechanisms won?
3. Analyze scoring â€” where are the most points per cycle?
4. Survey your team's actual build capabilities

## The 80/20 Rule
Often 80% of match points come from 20% of mechanisms. Build that 20% excellently before adding complexity.

## Prototyping Checklist
âœ… Built cardboard/wood prototype first?
âœ… Proof of concept before investing in aluminum?
âœ… Tested with actual game pieces?
âœ… Driver tested before locking in design?`},
      {id:"ma5",title:"Robot Reliability Engineering",est:"25 min",content:`## Reliability Wins Competitions
An 80%-effective robot that works 100% of the time beats a perfect robot that works 70% of the time.

## Failure Mode Analysis
For every critical mechanism:
1. How can this fail?
2. How likely in 10 matches?
3. Can we detect failure early?
4. What's the recovery procedure?

## Pre-Match Checklist
\`\`\`
â–¡ All motor connections seated?
â–¡ All encoder connections seated?
â–¡ Wires secured and not pinching?
â–¡ Servos responding to controller?
â–¡ Auto path verified on this field?
â–¡ Battery charged â‰¥ 13.5V?
â–¡ Driver station paired?
\`\`\``},

      {id:"eb1",title:"Basic Electricity Concepts",est:"12 min",content:`## The Three Basics

| Quantity   | Unit  | Symbol | What it means           |
|------------|-------|--------|--------------------------|
| Voltage    | Volts | V      | Electrical pressure       |
| Current    | Amps  | A      | Flow rate of electrons    |
| Resistance | Ohms  | Î©      | Opposition to current     |

## Ohm's Law
\`\`\`
V = I Ã— R    (Voltage = Current Ã— Resistance)
P = V Ã— I    (Watts = Volts Ã— Amps)
\`\`\`

## What This Means for Robots
- Higher voltage = more motor speed
- Higher current = more torque (but more heat)
- Short circuits = near-zero resistance = massive current = fire risk`},
      {id:"eb2",title:"Robot Batteries",est:"10 min",content:`## FTC Battery
- **12V NiMH** (Nickel-Metal Hydride)
- ~3000-4000 mAh capacity
- Fully charged: ~13.2V; Replace when below ~12V under load

## FRC Battery
- **12V Lead-Acid** (like a car battery)
- ~18 Ah capacity
- Never discharge below ~11V under load

## Battery Safety
- Never short circuit a battery
- Inspect for bulging, cracking, or corrosion
- Never charge an unattended battery overnight`},
      {id:"eb3",title:"Wiring Basics",est:"14 min",content:`## Wire Gauge

| AWG | Max Current | Common Use          |
|-----|------------|---------------------|
| 12  | 20A        | Main power, motors  |
| 18  | 10A        | Light loads, sensors|
| 22  | 5A         | Signal wires         |
| 26  | 1A         | Data (I2C, SPI)     |

## Color Standards
- **Red** = positive (+)
- **Black** = negative (-)

## Wiring Tips
- Secure all wires with zip ties â€” vibration kills connections
- Leave service loops near hinges and rotating joints
- Use correct gauge for current load`},
      {id:"eb4",title:"Control Hub & Driver Hub (FTC)",est:"15 min",content:`## REV Control Hub
- 4Ã— motor ports, 6Ã— servo ports
- Multiple I2C, analog, digital ports
- Wi-Fi for Driver Station connection

## Port Assignment
\`\`\`java
// In your OpMode's init():
leftDrive  = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "left_drive");
rightDrive = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "right_drive");
claw       = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "claw");
color      = hardwareMap.get(ColorSensor.class, "color");
\`\`\`
Names must match the **configuration file** on the Control Hub exactly!`},
      {id:"eb5",title:"Fuses & Circuit Protection",est:"10 min",content:`## Why Protection Matters
Without protection, a short circuit can melt wires, destroy motor controllers, and damage the battery.

## FTC Protection
- 20A fuse on main power lead (required by rules)
- Motor controllers have internal overcurrent protection

## FRC Protection
- 120A main breaker (robot master power switch)
- Individual PDH breakers for each branch

## Signs of Overcurrent Issues
- Fuses blowing repeatedly â†’ wire too small OR short circuit
- Motor controllers very hot â†’ motor stalling too long
- Voltage sag under load â†’ battery old or connections poor`},

      {id:"ei1",title:"Motor Controllers Deep Dive",est:"20 min",content:`## FRC Motor Controllers
- **SPARK MAX** (REV) â€” brushed or brushless, CAN or PWM
- **Talon FX** (CTRE) â€” integrated Falcon 500/Kraken motor
- **Victor SPX** â€” budget option, brushed only

## CAN Bus vs PWM
- **PWM**: Simple, one wire per controller, limited feedback
- **CAN**: Network bus, advanced features, full diagnostic data

\`\`\`java
// SPARK MAX via CAN
CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
motor.set(0.5);
double velocity = motor.getEncoder().getVelocity(); // RPM
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ei2",title:"Sensors & Signal Types",est:"18 min",content:`## Analog vs Digital

### Analog â€” varies continuously (0V to 3.3V/5V)
- Potentiometers, analog distance sensors

### Digital â€” only HIGH or LOW
- Limit switches, beam break sensors

### I2C â€” multiple devices on 2 wires
\`\`\`java
// FTC: Reading a digital limit switch
DigitalChannel limit = hardwareMap.get(DigitalChannel.class, "limit");
limit.setMode(DigitalChannel.Mode.INPUT);
boolean isPressed = !limit.getState(); // usually inverted
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ei3",title:"PWM & Servo Signals",est:"15 min",content:`## PWM Standard
- Frequency: 50 Hz (one pulse every 20ms)
- Pulse width: 1000Âµs = full reverse, 1500Âµs = center, 2000Âµs = full forward

\`\`\`java
// FTC SDK abstracts this to 0.0â€“1.0
servo.setPosition(0.0); // 1000Âµs â†’ one extreme
servo.setPosition(0.5); // 1500Âµs â†’ center
servo.setPosition(1.0); // 2000Âµs â†’ other extreme
\`\`\`

## Issues to Watch
- **Jitter**: Radio interference â†’ separate signal from power wires
- **Range mismatch**: Not all servos respond to full 1000-2000Âµs`},
      {id:"ei4",title:"Power Distribution",est:"18 min",content:`## FTC Power Chain
\`\`\`
Battery (12V NiMH)
  â†’ Main Power Switch
  â†’ REV Control Hub
  â†’ Motor Ports (12V, up to 20A per port)
  â†’ Servo Ports (5V regulated)
\`\`\`

## FRC Power Chain
\`\`\`
Battery (12V Lead-Acid)
  â†’ 120A Main Breaker
  â†’ Power Distribution Hub (PDH)
  â†’ Motor Controllers (breaker-protected)
  â†’ roboRIO (10A breaker)
\`\`\`

## Voltage Sag
Under heavy load, voltage drops â€” causing slower motors, sensor errors, and control issues. Fresh batteries and clean connections prevent this.`},
      {id:"ei5",title:"Troubleshooting Electrical Problems",est:"18 min",content:`## Systematic Diagnosis

### Step 1: Visual Inspection
- Check all connectors are fully seated
- Look for burnt marks, melted insulation, corrosion
- Check for wires pinched in mechanisms

### Step 2: Multimeter Checks
- DC Voltage mode: battery should read 12.6-13.2V charged
- Continuity mode: check each wire end-to-end

| Problem | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Motor not running | Loose connector | Reseat connections |
| Servo jittering | RFI | Separate signal from power wires |
| Random reboots | Low voltage | Charge/replace battery |
| Fuse blowing | Short circuit | Find and fix the short |`},

      {id:"ea1",title:"Brushless Motor Theory",est:"25 min",content:`## Brushed vs Brushless
- **Brushed**: physical contact to commutate, simple control, wears out
- **Brushless**: electronic commutation, higher efficiency, longer life

## FOC (Field-Oriented Control)
Advanced control that maximizes torque at any speed.

\`\`\`java
// Kraken X60 with Phoenix 6 FOC
TalonFX kraken = new TalonFX(1);
kraken.setControl(new TorqueCurrentFOC(targetCurrent));
\`\`\`

## Key Specs
- **Kv rating**: RPM per volt (lower = more torque)
- **Motor constant (Km)**: Torque per amp`},
      {id:"ea2",title:"CAN Bus & Advanced Communication",est:"22 min",content:`## CAN Bus Architecture
- Two-wire differential (CANH and CANL)
- Multiple devices share one bus with unique node IDs
- 1 Mbps in FRC typical configuration

\`\`\`java
// Every device needs a unique CAN ID (1-62 in FRC)
TalonFX leftDrive  = new TalonFX(1);
TalonFX rightDrive = new TalonFX(2);
CANSparkMax intake = new CANSparkMax(3, MotorType.kBrushless);
\`\`\`

## Reducing CAN Latency
\`\`\`java
// Reduce status frame rate for less-critical devices
motor.setPeriodicFramePeriod(PeriodicFrame.kStatus0, 100);
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ea3",title:"Signal Filtering & Noise",est:"20 min",content:`## Moving Average Filter
\`\`\`java
double[] buffer = new double[5];
int idx = 0;

double filteredValue(double raw) {
    buffer[idx++ % buffer.length] = raw;
    double sum = 0;
    for (double v : buffer) sum += v;
    return sum / buffer.length;
}
\`\`\`

## Exponential Low-Pass Filter
\`\`\`java
double alpha = 0.2; // 0=very smooth, 1=no filter
filtered = alpha * raw + (1 - alpha) * lastFiltered;
\`\`\`

## Hardware Solutions
- Shielded cable for sensitive sensors
- Ferrite beads on motor power leads
- Keep signal wires away from motor wires`},
      {id:"ea4",title:"Battery Management & Power Budget",est:"22 min",content:`## Power Budget Example

| System | Current |
|--------|---------|
| 4 drive motors (avg) | 24A |
| 2 arm motors | 8A |
| 2 servos | 1A |
| Control Hub | 0.5A |
| Sensors | 0.3A |
| **Total** | **~34A** |

FTC battery: 3500 mAh Ã· 34A â‰ˆ **6 min** (plenty for a 2-min match)

## Extending Battery Life
- Avoid stalling motors â€” add current limits
- Use efficient motors
- Monitor voltage in telemetry`},
      {id:"ea5",title:"PCB Design for Robots",est:"30 min",content:`## Why Custom PCBs?
- Eliminate unreliable breadboard connections
- Reduce wiring mess and weight
- Professional, repeatable assemblies

## Tools
- **KiCad** â€” free, professional, widely used
- **EasyEDA** â€” browser-based, integrates with JLCPCB

## Workflow
1. Draw schematic
2. Assign footprints
3. Layout and route traces
4. Design rule check (DRC)
5. Export Gerbers â†’ Order from JLCPCB (~$5 for 5 boards)

## Robot-Specific Tips
- Use 2oz copper for power traces
- Add TVS diodes on motor power inputs
- Include test points on every important net`},

  strategy:{
    Beginner:[
      {id:"sb1",title:"Understanding FIRST Games",est:"12 min",content:`## Game Structure

### Autonomous Period
- First 15 seconds â€” robot acts without driver input
- Pre-programmed movements
- Usually worth bonus points

### Teleop Period
- Drivers control robots via gamepads
- FTC: 2 minutes | FRC: 2 min 15 sec
- Most of your score comes from here

### Endgame
- Last 30 seconds â€” high-value actions (climbing, parking)
- Often the deciding factor in close matches

## Ranking
- Top 8 seeds select alliance partners for eliminations`},
      {id:"sb2",title:"Intro to Scouting",est:"12 min",content:`## What is Scouting?
Observing and recording other teams' capabilities to make smart alliance decisions.

## Basic Scouting Sheet
\`\`\`
Team #: ___    Match #: ___
Autonomous: Did/Didn't run  Points: ___
Main action: ___  Cycles: ___
Endgame: Climb / Park / Nothing   Points: ___
Issues: ___
Overall (1-5): ___
\`\`\`

## Getting Started
- Each team member scouts 1-2 robots per match
- Use a spreadsheet to collect data
- Share notes at end of each round`},
      {id:"sb3",title:"Game Piece Strategy",est:"14 min",content:`## Cycle Time â€” The Most Important Metric
A "cycle" = picking up a game piece and scoring it.

\`\`\`
Points per match â‰ˆ Points per cycle Ã— Cycles per match

4 pts/cycle Ã— 15 cycles = 60 pts
6 pts/cycle Ã— 8 cycles  = 48 pts
\`\`\`

Faster cycles often beat fewer high-value cycles!

## Prioritizing Scoring Zones
- High zones score more but are harder to reach
- Low zones are reliable but score less
- Maximize **consistent** scoring, not max per-cycle scoring`},
      {id:"sb4",title:"Alliance Coordination Basics",est:"12 min",content:`## Pre-Match Meeting
Always meet your alliance 5-10 minutes before queue.

Discuss:
1. **Autonomous paths** â€” Do our autos conflict?
2. **Field zones** â€” Who goes where?
3. **Endgame plan** â€” Who climbs where?
4. **Signals** â€” How do we communicate mid-match?

## Being a Good Alliance Partner
- Share your scouting data
- Be honest about your robot's capabilities and limitations
- Always show up on time for queuing`},
      {id:"sb5",title:"Basic Match Analysis",est:"12 min",content:`## Watching Matches Effectively
Don't just watch the scoreboard â€” **watch robots**.

## What to Track Per Robot
- **Auto**: Did it run? Points? Path taken?
- **Teleop**: Where does it score? How fast?
- **Endgame**: Attempt? Succeed?
- **Issues**: Breakdowns, penalties

## Red Flags
- Robots that frequently break down mid-match
- Autonomous that consistently fails
- Drivers who struggle with precision tasks`},
    ],
    Intermediate:[
      {id:"si1",title:"Advanced Scouting Systems",est:"18 min",content:`## Moving Beyond Paper

## Key Metrics to Track

### Per-Match Data
- Auto routine + points
- Teleop: pieces per zone
- Cycles completed
- Endgame: result + time taken

### Derived Metrics
- **Average score**: Sum Ã· matches played
- **Consistency**: Standard deviation (lower = more consistent)
- **Peak performance**: 90th percentile score

## Tools
- Google Forms â†’ Sheets: Simple, free, no dev needed
- Statbotics / TBA Scout: Pre-built apps
- Custom PWA: Full control, best for advanced teams`},
      {id:"si2",title:"Autonomous Strategy",est:"16 min",content:`## Reliability > Maximum Points

| Routine | Points | Reliability | Expected |
|---------|--------|-------------|----------|
| Simple  | 8      | 95%         | 7.6      |
| Complex | 12     | 60%         | 7.2      |

The simple routine has a **higher expected value**!

## Multiple Autonomous Options
1. **Safe/reliable**: Works >90% of the time
2. **Aggressive**: Higher points when confident

Switch based on alliance partner's auto and match situation.`},
      {id:"si3",title:"OPR & Statistical Analysis",est:"20 min",content:`## OPR â€” Offensive Power Rating
OPR estimates each robot's individual contribution to alliance scores.

## Accessing OPR
The Blue Alliance (thebluealliance.com) shows OPR for every team at every event.

## Other Metrics
- **DPR** â€” Defensive Power Rating (points prevented)
- **CCWM** â€” Calculated Contribution to Winning Margin (OPR - DPR)

## Limitations
- Small sample sizes mean high uncertainty
- Doesn't capture driver skill, reliability, or defense capability

## Best Practice
OPR for initial ranking â†’ scouting notes for your top 20 candidates`},
      {id:"si4",title:"Pit Scouting",est:"15 min",content:`## When to Do It
- During practice matches
- During lunch breaks
- Never during a team's match

## What to Ask
\`\`\`
1. "Walk me through your robot's capabilities?"
2. "What's your strongest scoring action?"
3. "How reliable is your autonomous?"
4. "Do you have an endgame mechanism?"
5. "Any known issues we should know as partners?"
\`\`\`

## Etiquette
- Introduce yourself (name and team number)
- Respect their time
- Offer to share your data in return
- Thank them!`},
      {id:"si5",title:"Endgame & Climbing Strategy",est:"18 min",content:`## Timing Your Endgame
- If climbing takes 15 seconds, start at 25-30 seconds remaining
- Practice your endgame in every practice match
- Set a rule: at X seconds left, all scoring stops â€” go for endgame

## Alliance Coordination
\`\`\`
Questions before every match:
1. Where does each robot climb? (Do we conflict?)
2. What's each robot's climbing success rate?
3. Is defense more valuable than a 3rd climb?
\`\`\`

## Common Mistakes
- Starting too late (most common)
- Two robots competing for same position
- Not practicing endgame enough`},

    Advanced:[
      {id:"sa1",title:"Building a Championship Picklist",est:"30 min",content:`## Five-Phase Picklist Process

## Phase 1 â€” Mathematical Pre-Ranking
\`\`\`python
teams.sort(key=lambda t: (
    t.opr * 0.4 +
    t.auto_avg * 0.3 +
    t.endgame_avg * 0.2 +
    t.consistency * 0.1
), reverse=True)
\`\`\`

## Phase 2 â€” Event Scouting Refinement
Update after every match round. Flag "unknown" teams.

## Phase 3 â€” Pit Scouting Spot Checks
Visit top 20 candidates during downtime.

## Phase 4 â€” Human Review (Night Before Selection)
Full team reviews list â€” does the order feel right?

## Phase 5 â€” Real-Time Updates During Selection
Cross off taken teams instantly. Know your next pick before they call your name.`},
      {id:"sa2",title:"Autonomous Coordination in Eliminations",est:"28 min",content:`## Why Auto Matters More in Elims
A failed auto can cost you the entire tournament.

## Pre-Selection Prep
\`\`\`
â–¡ Starting positions available
â–¡ Average points per routine (not best case)
â–¡ Your auto's conflict zones
â–¡ Backup auto if primary fails
\`\`\`

## Alliance Auto Meeting (After Selection)
1. Each team diagrams their auto paths
2. Check for path conflicts
3. Assign positions to minimize conflict
4. Decide if anyone should delay start

## Trust Your Data
If data shows 60% auto reliability, plan for the 40% failure case too.`},
      {id:"sa3",title:"Live Match Coaching",est:"25 min",content:`## The Drive Coach's Mental Model
1. **Robot status** â€” what's our robot doing?
2. **Scoreboard** â€” are we winning? trajectory?
3. **Alliance coordination** â€” are partners on plan?

## In-Match Scoreboard Math
\`\`\`
Gap: +12   Time left: 45s
Their rate: 3 pts/10s = 13.5 total
Our rate:   4 pts/10s = 18 total
Projected: +12 + 4.5 = +16.5 â†’ HOLD COURSE
\`\`\`

## Endgame Calls
- "Endgame in 10" â€” warning
- "ENDGAME NOW" â€” drop everything, climb
- Pre-agreed hand signals beat voice in loud arenas`},

      {id:"sa5",title:"Championship Strategy",est:"30 min",content:`## Pre-Event Research (1 Week Before)
1. Pull TBA data for all attending teams
2. Watch reveal videos and regional recaps
3. Build initial mathematical ranking
4. Identify top 40 teams to watch closely

## Choosing Alliance Partners at Worlds
- Consider **defensive potential** â€” defense wins close brackets
- Evaluate **drive team skill** â€” you'll face equally-capable robots
- Chemistry matters â€” pick teams who communicate and adapt

## Elimination Mindset
\`\`\`
For each opponent: Ask what would beat us?
Then: How do we prevent that?
\`\`\`
Don't assume lower seeds are easy â€” they've scouted you extensively.`},

      {id:"wb1",title:"HTML Basics",est:"12 min",content:`## What is HTML?
HTML is the skeleton of every webpage. Your team website, scouting app, and pit display all use it.

## Block vs Inline
- Block elements (div, p, h1-h6) take full width

- main: main content area
- section: grouped related content
- footer: bottom of page

Using semantic tags makes your site accessible and SEO-friendly.`},

      {id:"wi1",title:"Fetch API & The Blue Alliance",est:"18 min",content:`## Getting Live Data with Fetch
Your scouting app can pull real match data from The Blue Alliance API.

\`\`\`js
const API_KEY = "your_tba_api_key_here";
const team = "frc1234";

async function getTeamEvents() {
  const response = await fetch(
    "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/" + team + "/events/2024/simple",
    { headers: { "X-TBA-Auth-Key": API_KEY } }
  );
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("API call failed");
  const events = await response.json();
  return events;
}

getTeamEvents().then(events => {
  events.forEach(event => {
    console.log(event.name, event.start_date);
  });
});

      {id:"wi2",title:"Build a Scouting Form",est:"20 min",content:`## HTML Form for Match Scouting
\`\`\`html
<form id="scoutForm">
  <label>Team Number</label>
  <input type="number" id="teamNum" required />
  
  <label>Auto Points</label>
  <input type="number" id="autoPoints" value="0" min="0" />
  
  <label>Teleop Notes</label>
  <textarea id="notes"></textarea>
  
  <label>Rating (1-5)</label>
  <select id="rating">
    <option value="1">1 - Struggled</option>
    <option value="3">3 - Average</option>
    <option value="5">5 - Excellent</option>
  </select>
  
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>
\`\`\`

## Saving Data
\`\`\`js
document.getElementById("scoutForm").addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const entry = {
    team: document.getElementById("teamNum").value,
    auto: document.getElementById("autoPoints").value,
    notes: document.getElementById("notes").value,
    rating: document.getElementById("rating").value,
    ts: new Date().toISOString()
  };
  const existing = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("scoutData") || "[]");
  existing.push(entry);
  localStorage.setItem("scoutData", JSON.stringify(existing));
  alert("Scout entry saved!");
});
\`\`\``},

      {id:"wa1",title:"Full Scouting App with Analytics",est:"30 min",content:`## Building a Complete Scouting System
A production scouting app has three layers: data entry, storage, and analytics.

## Architecture
- ScoutForm.jsx â€” match data entry
- TeamDashboard.jsx â€” per-team analytics
- MatchList.jsx â€” browsable match history
- utils/storage.js â€” data persistence
- utils/analytics.js â€” OPR calculations

## Simple OPR in JavaScript
\`\`\`js
function calculateOPR(matchData) {
  const scores = {};
  const counts = {};
  
  matchData.forEach(match => {
    match.redAlliance.forEach(team => {
      scores[team] = (scores[team] || 0) + match.redScore;
      counts[team] = (counts[team] || 0) + 1;
    });
    match.blueAlliance.forEach(team => {
      scores[team] = (scores[team] || 0) + match.blueScore;
      counts[team] = (counts[team] || 0) + 1;
    });
  });
  
  const opr = {};
  Object.keys(scores).forEach(t => { opr[t] = scores[t] / counts[t]; });
  return opr;
}
\`\`\`

## Export to CSV
\`\`\`js
function exportCSV(data) {
  const rows = data.map(d => [d.team,d.match,d.auto,d.teleop,d.rating].join(","));
  const csv = ["Team,Match,Auto,Teleop,Rating", ...rows].join("\\n");
  const a = document.createElement("a");
  a.href = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([csv], {type:"text/csv"}));
  a.download = "scout_data.csv";
  a.click();
}
\`\`\``},

      {id:"fb1",title:"Fundraising Basics",est:"10 min",content:`## Why Fundraising Matters
A competitive FTC/FRC season costs $3,000-$25,000+. Fundraising is a core team skill â€” it determines what parts you buy and events you attend.

## Typical FRC Budget
- Registration and Events: $5,000-$10,000
- Parts and Materials: $3,000-$8,000
- Travel and Hotel: $2,000-$10,000
- Pit Supplies and Tools: $500-$2,000
- Total: $10,000-$30,000

## Three Pillars of Fundraising
1. Corporate Sponsors â€” local businesses and large companies
2. Grants â€” foundations, FIRST grants, school district funds
3. Community Events â€” car washes, bake sales, demonstrations

## The 20% Rule
Focus 20% of effort on opportunities that return 80% of money. One corporate sponsor often outperforms 50 bake sales.`},
      {id:"fb2",title:"Writing a Sponsor Letter",est:"12 min",content:`## The Perfect Sponsor Letter
A strong sponsor letter is short (one page), specific, and shows value to the business.

## Template Structure
Opening: Who you are and what FIRST is (2 sentences).
"Team 1234 is a student robotics team competing in FIRST Robotics. FIRST is a 501c3 nonprofit impacting 680,000+ students worldwide."

Impact: Why it matters to THEM.
"Your $500 sponsorship puts your logo on our robot, seen by 5,000+ attendees at our regional tournament, and featured on our website and social media."

The Ask: Be specific.
"We are asking for a $500 Gold Sponsor contribution."

Sponsor Levels:
- Bronze $100: Website mention
- Silver $250: Logo on robot
- Gold $500: Logo + social media posts
- Platinum $1000: All above + visit build season

## Key Rules
- Address a real person by name â€” never "To Whom It May Concern"
- Follow up with a phone call 5-7 days later
- Send a thank-you note within 48 hours of any donation`},
      {id:"fb3",title:"Grant Writing 101",est:"14 min",content:`## What is a Grant?
A grant is free money from a foundation, government, or company. FIRST teams can win $500-$10,000+ per grant.

## FIRST-Specific Grants
- FIRST Dean's List Scholarship â€” outstanding students
- Motorola Solutions Foundation â€” engineering-focused teams
- Boeing Higher Education â€” teams with STEM programs
- Google.org â€” tech-focused nonprofit grants

## Grant Answer Formula
1. PROBLEM: What challenge does this solve?
2. SOLUTION: How does your team address it?
3. IMPACT: How many people benefit? Use data.
4. SUSTAINABILITY: How will the program continue?
5. BUDGET: Specific line items, not vague totals

## Tips
- Apply for multiple small grants ($500-$2,000) â€” higher success rate
- Track all deadlines in a spreadsheet
- Reuse strong answers across applications (tailor the opening)
- Show community impact with numbers: "We taught 200 students at 5 schools"
- Thank funders publicly on social media`},
      {id:"fb4",title:"Running Community Events",est:"12 min",content:`## Events = Money + Relationships
Events raise funds AND build team reputation, which attracts more sponsors.

## High-ROI Event Ideas
Robot Demonstrations:
- Set up at school events, fairs, libraries
- Let kids drive the robot â€” they go home and tell parents
- Collect email sign-ups for future sponsor contact

STEM Night Hosting:
- Partner with a local elementary school
- Teach basic coding or build simple machines
- 2-hour event, charge the school $200-$500

Trivia or Game Night:
- Rent a space or use the school cafeteria
- $10-$15 per ticket, sell food and drinks
- Goal: 100 attendees = $1,000+ net

## Planning Checklist
- Reserve location 6+ weeks out
- Create flyers and social media posts
- Assign team roles: setup, sales, demo, cleanup
- Prepare a short robot demo or presentation
- Bring a sign-up sheet for mailing list
- Send follow-up thank-you emails to attendees`},

      {id:"fi1",title:"Corporate Partnership Strategy",est:"16 min",content:`## Beyond One-Time Donations
The best teams build long-term corporate partnerships. A partner gives year after year and provides mentors, space, and equipment.

## Target Company Types
- Local manufacturers: workforce pipeline, $500-$5,000
- Engineering firms: STEM brand, $1,000-$10,000
- Tech companies: community relations, $500-$25,000
- Hospitals/Healthcare: STEM outreach, $500-$3,000

## The Partnership Pitch (5 slides)
1. Cover: Team number, logo, season year
2. Who We Are: Team stats, record, awards
3. Why FIRST: Impact data (67% of alumni enter STEM)
4. What We Offer: Visibility package with photos
5. The Ask: Tiered sponsor levels with clear prices

## Maintaining Relationships
- Send monthly update emails with robot progress photos
- Invite sponsors to practice open house
- Give them a framed team photo after the season
- Ask for a quote for your award submissions
- Always report back on how their money was used`},
      {id:"fi2",title:"Social Media for Fundraising",est:"14 min",content:`## Social Media = Free Marketing + Donor Visibility
Good social media attracts sponsors who want exposure and builds community trust.

## Platform Strategy
Instagram: Best for visual content
- Behind-the-scenes build photos
- Robot reveal videos
- Team culture and milestones

LinkedIn: Best for corporate sponsors
- Professional milestone posts
- Tag sponsor companies in achievement posts
- Student profiles with team experience

YouTube: Best for showcasing work
- Robot reveal videos
- Tutorial series
- Event recaps

## Content Calendar
- Monday: Build update photo
- Wednesday: Team member spotlight
- Friday: Robot mechanism video
- During events: Live match updates

## Sponsor Visibility Post Formula
"We are grateful to [Sponsor] for their [Level] sponsorship! Their contribution helps us [specific thing it paid for]. Check them out at [website]. #FIRST #FRC #STEM"`},
      {id:"fi3",title:"Budget Planning and Tracking",est:"15 min",content:`## Why Teams Fail at Finance
Most teams underspend on events and overspend on parts, or vice versa. A solid budget prevents both.

## Budget Spreadsheet Structure
Income columns: Budget, Actual, Difference
- Corporate Sponsors: $5,000 / $4,200 / -$800
- Grants: $2,000 / $2,500 / +$500
- Community Events: $1,000 / $750 / -$250
- School District: $1,500 / $1,500 / $0
- TOTAL INCOME: $9,500 / $8,950 / -$550

Expenses columns: Budget, Actual, Difference
- Parts and Materials: $3,000 / $3,400 / +$400
- Registration Fees: $2,000 / $2,000 / $0
- Travel: $2,500 / $1,800 / -$700
- TOTAL EXPENSES: $8,500 / $8,150 / -$350

NET: $1,000 / $800

## Budget Rules
- Keep a 15% contingency buffer â€” robots break at events
- Never spend more than 50% of income by week 4 of build season
- Get approval for purchases over $100
- Save all receipts (required for some grants)
- Report to sponsors with a budget summary at end of season`},

      {id:"fa1",title:"Winning the FIRST Impact Award",est:"20 min",content:`## What is the Impact Award?
The Impact Award is the highest honor in FIRST â€” it recognizes the team with the greatest community impact. Winners advance to World Championship.

## Submission Components
1. Essay: narrative of your team's story and impact
2. Executive Summary: 10,000 characters max
3. Video: 4 minutes max
4. Presentation: 7 minutes plus Q&A to judges

## The Award Formula
Judges look for SPREAD + DEPTH + SUSTAINABILITY

- Spread: How many people did you reach? (Hundreds beats dozens)
- Depth: How meaningful was the impact? (Changed lives beats entertained)
- Sustainability: Does it continue after your team graduates?

## Essay Structure
1. Opening hook: a student story or moment of impact
2. Team Mission: your unique approach to spreading FIRST
3. Signature Programs: 2-3 flagship programs with data
4. Partnerships: lasting relationships built
5. Sustainability: how you are building for the future
6. The Ask: why YOUR team best represents FIRST's mission

## Data Makes Winners
"We ran a workshop" loses to "We taught 347 students across 12 schools, resulting in 3 new FLL teams still active 2 years later."

Always attach measurable outcomes to every program you describe.`},

      {id:"jb9",title:"Classes & Objects",est:"15 min",content:`## What Is a Class?
A class is a blueprint. An object is a built thing from that blueprint.

\`\`\`java
public class Motor {
    String name;
    double power;

    // Constructor
    public Motor(String name) {
        this.name = name;
        this.power = 0.0;
    }

    public void setPower(double p) {
        this.power = Math.max(-1.0, Math.min(1.0, p));
    }
    public double getPower() { return power; }
}
\`\`\`

## Creating Objects
\`\`\`java
Motor left  = new Motor("left_drive");
Motor right = new Motor("right_drive");

left.setPower(0.8);
right.setPower(-0.8); // negative = reverse
\`\`\`

## Why This Matters for FTC/FRC
WPILib and the FTC SDK are built entirely on classes. \`DcMotor\`, \`Servo\`, \`LinearOpMode\` â€” all classes you instantiate as objects.`},
      {id:"jb10",title:"Autonomous with Encoders",est:"18 min",content:`## What Are Encoders?
Encoders count shaft rotations (ticks). The FTC SDK reads them to know how far wheels have turned.

\`\`\`java
// Reset encoders
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);

// Drive by target ticks
int TARGET_TICKS = 1440; // ~1 full wheel rotation for typical goBILDA
motor.setTargetPosition(TARGET_TICKS);
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
motor.setPower(0.5);

while (motor.isBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {
    telemetry.addData("Position", motor.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.update();
}
motor.setPower(0);
\`\`\`

## Conversion Formula
\`\`\`java
// Ticks per inch for a 4" wheel with 1440 ticks/rev encoder
double TICKS_PER_INCH = 1440 / (Math.PI * 4.0);

int ticksForDistance(double inches) {
    return (int)(inches * TICKS_PER_INCH);
}
\`\`\`

## Pro Tips
- Always reset encoders before every auto run
- Use \`RUN_TO_POSITION\` for precise movements
- Add a timeout in case the target is never reached`},

      {id:"ji8",title:"Vision & AprilTags (FTC)",est:"20 min",content:`## Vision Portal Setup

VisionPortal visionPortal = new VisionPortal.Builder()
    .setCamera(hardwareMap.get(WebcamName.class, "Webcam 1"))
    .addProcessor(aprilTagProcessor)

## Reading AprilTag Data
\`\`\`java
List<AprilTagDetection> detections = aprilTagProcessor.getDetections();
for (AprilTagDetection d : detections) {
    int id = d.id;                    // tag number
    double range  = d.ftcPose.range;  // distance in inches
    double bearing = d.ftcPose.bearing; // angle to target
    double yaw    = d.ftcPose.yaw;    // tag rotation

    telemetry.addData("Tag ID", id);
    telemetry.addData("Range (in)", range);
    telemetry.addData("Bearing (deg)", bearing);
}
\`\`\`

## Auto-Align to Tag
\`\`\`java
double driveError = -d.ftcPose.y + TARGET_Y;
double strafeError = d.ftcPose.x - TARGET_X;
double yawError   = d.ftcPose.yaw;

double drive  = driveError  * DRIVE_GAIN;
double strafe = strafeError * STRAFE_GAIN;
double turn   = yawError    * TURN_GAIN;
\`\`\``},
      {id:"ji9",title:"State Machines in Depth",est:"16 min",content:`## Why State Machines?
Sequential behaviors (pick up, drive, score) can get messy with if/else chains. State machines keep it clean.

\`\`\`java
enum State { IDLE, EXTENDING, GRABBING, RETRACTING, SCORING }
State currentState = State.IDLE;

// In your loop:
switch (currentState) {
    case IDLE:
        if (gamepad1.a) currentState = State.EXTENDING;
        break;
    case EXTENDING:
        arm.setTargetPosition(ARM_EXTENDED);
        if (arm.getCurrentPosition() > ARM_EXTENDED - 50)
            currentState = State.GRABBING;
        break;
    case GRABBING:
        claw.setPosition(CLAW_CLOSED);
        timer.reset();
        currentState = State.RETRACTING;
        break;
    case RETRACTING:
        arm.setTargetPosition(ARM_HOME);
        if (timer.seconds() > 1.5)
            currentState = State.SCORING;
        break;
    case SCORING:
        // deposit game piece
        claw.setPosition(CLAW_OPEN);
        currentState = State.IDLE;
        break;
}
\`\`\``},

      {id:"ja7",title:"Road Runner Trajectories",est:"25 min",content:`## Road Runner v1 (FTC)
Road Runner generates smooth, time-optimal paths using motion profiles.

\`\`\`java
// Build a trajectory
Action trajectory = drive.actionBuilder(startPose)
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(24, 0), Math.toRadians(0))
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(48, 24), Math.toRadians(90))
    .build();

// Run it (FTC Actions API)
Actions.runBlocking(trajectory);
\`\`\`

## Pose Estimation
\`\`\`java
// Localization updates every loop tick automatically
Pose2d currentPose = drive.localizer.getPose();
double x = currentPose.position.x;
double y = currentPose.position.y;
double heading = currentPose.heading.log();
\`\`\`

## Combining Actions
\`\`\`java
// Run intake while driving
Actions.runBlocking(
    new ParallelAction(
        trajectory,
        new SequentialAction(
            intake.setOn(),
            new SleepAction(2.0),
            intake.setOff()
        )
    )
);
\`\`\``},

      {id:"pi9",title:"Match Data Analytics",est:"20 min",content:`## Pulling Data from The Blue Alliance API
\`\`\`python
import requests

API_KEY = "your_tba_key_here"

      {id:"mb6",title:"Timing Belts & Pulleys",est:"14 min",content:`## Belt Drive Advantages
- Quieter than chains
- No lubrication needed
- Precise power transfer with HTD/GT2 profile belts

## Gear Ratio with Pulleys
\`\`\`
Ratio = Driven Pulley Teeth / Driver Pulley Teeth

Example: 60T driven / 20T driver = 3:1 reduction
Output speed = Motor RPM / 3
Output torque = Motor Torque Ã— 3
\`\`\`

## Choosing Belt Width
| Width   | Max Torque | Use Case |
|---------|-----------|---------|
| 9mm     | Low       | Servo linkages |
| 15mm    | Medium    | Arm pivots |
| 25mm    | High      | Drivetrains |

## Common Mistakes
- Over-tensioning snaps belts and destroys bearings
- Under-tensioning causes skipping under load
- **Rule**: Belt should deflect ~2mm under light finger pressure
- Always use an idler pulley to maintain tension on long runs`},
      {id:"mb7",title:"Pneumatics for FTC/FRC",est:"16 min",content:`## How Robot Pneumatics Work
Compressor â†’ Storage Tank (120 PSI max) â†’ Pressure Regulator (60 PSI working) â†’ Solenoid â†’ Cylinder

## FRC Pneumatics Components
- **Compressor**: REVPH or CTRE PCM required in FRC
- **Tanks**: Store compressed air (120 PSI max)
- **Regulator**: Steps down to 60 PSI working pressure
- **Solenoids**: 24V digital valves controlled by robot code
- **Cylinders**: Double-acting (push and pull) or single-acting

## FTC Pneumatics (limited)
FTC allows only pre-charged CO2 canisters or air reservoirs, no onboard compressors.

piston.set(true);  // extend
piston.set(false); // retract

// DoubleSolenoid (more reliable)
DoubleSolenoid ds = new DoubleSolenoid(PneumaticsModuleType.REVPH, 1, 2);
ds.set(DoubleSolenoid.Value.kForward); // extend
ds.set(DoubleSolenoid.Value.kReverse); // retract
