      {id:"mi6",title:"Wrist & Pivot Mechanisms",est:"18 min",content:`## Wrist Design Goals
A wrist rotates the end-effector (claw/intake) independently of the arm.

## Four-Bar Linkage Wrist
The four-bar keeps the end-effector at a constant angle as the arm sweeps up/down.

\`\`\`
Parallelogram four-bar:
- Link 1: Robot frame (fixed)
- Link 2: Arm (driven)
- Link 3: Coupler (parallel to Link 1)
- Link 4: End-effector mount (stays level)
Result: End-effector orientation is constant regardless of arm angle
\`\`\`

## Servo-Driven Wrist
\`\`\`java
// Servo at 0.5 = center (90Â°)
// Servo at 0.0 = full back
// Servo at 1.0 = full forward

double ARM_ANGLE_DEG = encoder.getCurrentPosition() / TICKS_PER_DEG;
// Counteract arm angle to keep wrist level
double wristCompensation = ARM_ANGLE_DEG / 180.0; // map to servo range
wristServo.setPosition(0.5 + wristCompensation);
\`\`\`

## Material Choices
- Aluminum: light, strong, standard
- 3D printed (Nylon/PETG): custom geometry, lighter
- Use gussets at joints to prevent flex`},

Free, browser-based, cloud-synced â€” the standard for FTC teams.

## Document Structure

Team Document
â”œâ”€â”€ Part Studios (design individual parts)
â”œâ”€â”€ Assemblies (put parts together)
â””â”€â”€ Drawings (2D prints for manufacturing)
\`\`\`

## Key Modeling Workflows
1. **Sketch** on a plane â†’ add dimensions â†’ constrain fully
2. **Extrude** (add material) or **cut** (remove material)
3. **Mirror** and **pattern** for symmetric parts
4. **Import** goBILDA/REV part libraries from Onshape public documents

## Design for Manufacturing
- Add 0.2mm clearance on press-fit features
- Chamfer drill entry holes (easier to start)
- Keep wall thickness â‰¥ 1.5mm for FDM 3D printing
- Use standard hole sizes (M3, M4, #10-32) so stock hardware fits

## Version Control
Onshape auto-versions every save. Right-click â†’ History to restore old versions. Branches let you explore designs without breaking the main model.`},

      {id:"eb6",title:"Crimping & Connectors",est:"14 min",content:`## Why Proper Crimping Matters
Bad crimp connections fail at competitions. A loose wire during a match can disable your robot instantly.

## Common FTC/FRC Connectors
| Connector | Used For | Tool Needed |
|-----------|---------|------------|
| Anderson SB50 | Main battery | SB50 crimper |
| XT30/XT60 | Secondary power | Soldering iron |
| Dupont (2.54mm) | Sensors/signals | Dupont crimper |
| JST-PH/XH | REV sensors | JST crimper |
| Wago 221 | Quick wire joins | Hand snap |

## Crimp Quality Test
After crimping, tug-test every connection. A proper crimp holds 15+ lbs of pull force. If it slips â€” re-crimp.

## Strip Length Guide
- Too short â†’ no copper in the crimp barrel (weak)
- Too long â†’ copper sticks out past the barrel (shorts)
- **Correct**: Strip exactly to barrel length (usually 4-6mm)

## Solder vs Crimp
For high-vibration robot environments, **crimp > solder** for power connections. Solder joints can crack from vibration. For signal lines (sensors), solder is fine with heat shrink tubing.`},

      {id:"ei6",title:"CAN Bus Deep Dive",est:"20 min",content:`## What is CAN Bus?
Controller Area Network â€” a 2-wire differential serial bus (CAN H + CAN L) that connects smart devices on FRC robots.

## FRC CAN Network
\`\`\`
roboRIO â†’ PDH â†’ TalonFX â†’ SparkMax â†’ SparkMax â†’ ...
         â†‘ 120Î© terminator at each end of bus
\`\`\`

## CAN IDs
Every device must have a unique ID (0â€“62). Set via:
- REV Hardware Client (Spark MAX, PDH)
- Phoenix Tuner X (Talon FX/SRX)
- CAN Configurator (other devices)

## Troubleshooting CAN Errors
\`\`\`
Common error patterns:
"CAN Bus Off" â†’ wiring short or termination missing
"Receive Error" â†’ bad cable, wrong ID, interference
"Bus Usage > 90%" â†’ too many devices, reduce update rates
\`\`\`

## Wiring Best Practices
- Use twisted-pair wire (reduces EMI)
- Maximum run: 40m total, though keep under 5m on robots
- 120Î© termination resistors at BOTH ends â€” critical!
- Keep CAN wires away from motor power cables`},

- Need to break out many sensor connections in one place

1. **Schematic Editor**: Draw circuit logic with symbols

## FTC/FRC-Safe Design Rules
- 5V logic: keep traces â‰¥ 6 mil wide
- 12V power: â‰¥ 40 mil traces (up to 2A), wider for more current
- Add 100nF decoupling caps on every IC power pin
- Use mounting holes matching M3 screws

- Sensor breakout (I2C hub with 4Ã— JST connectors)
- LED controller board

- Raspberry Pi power management board`},

      {id:"sa6",title:"Drive Team Roles & Practice",est:"22 min",content:`## The Drive Team Structure
Typically 3-4 people: Driver, Operator, Human Player, Drive Coach

### Driver
- Controls robot movement only
- Practices 30+ hours before competition
- Builds muscle memory for field-relative movement

### Operator
- Controls all mechanisms (arm, intake, shooter)
- Calls out mechanism state to driver
- Practices specific game piece sequences

### Drive Coach
- Does NOT touch controls during match
- Watches score, time, alliance partner status
- Makes macro decisions: "defend now", "go for climb"

## Practice Drills
\`\`\`
Drill 1: Cycle timing
- Time every cycle start-to-score
- Goal: consistent cycles, not fastest single run

Drill 2: Pressure scenarios  
- Play with opponent defense robot actively blocking
- Simulates real match stress

Drill 3: Communication
- Operator calls all state changes verbally
- Driver repeats back to confirm
- Eliminates confusion from ambiguous gamepad presses
\`\`\``},

      {id:"ja8",title:"Vision & Camera Pipelines",est:"25 min",content:`## Computer Vision in FTC/FRC
Vision lets your robot detect targets, game pieces, and field landmarks automatically.

## AprilTags (FTC/FRC)
AprilTags are like QR codes the field posts on key scoring zones.

Steps to use AprilTags in FTC:
1. Initialize VisionPortal with your camera
2. Enable AprilTagProcessor
3. In loop: call processor.getDetections()
4. Use detection.ftcPose.x/y/z for position

Key data from a detection:
- id: which tag (1-10 for typical game)
- ftcPose.range: distance in inches
- ftcPose.bearing: left/right angle in degrees
- ftcPose.yaw: rotation

## TFOD (TensorFlow Object Detection)
For detecting game pieces like rings, cones, or cubes.
- Train or use provided model
- Get recognition list each loop
- Check recognition.getLabel() == "Target"
- Use getBoundingBox() for position on screen

## Color Sensor Tricks
Use a REV Color Sensor for reliable close-up detection:
- getDistance() to detect nearby objects
- getNormalizedColors() for color matching
- Great for line following and alliance-color detection`},

      {id:"pa6",title:"Computer Vision with OpenCV",est:"22 min",content:`## OpenCV for Robotics
OpenCV is the most popular computer vision library. Use it for scouting analysis, game piece detection, and field localization.

Install: pip install opencv-python numpy

## Basic Image Operations
import cv2
import numpy as np

# Load and show an image
img = cv2.imread("field.jpg")
cv2.imshow("Field", img)

# Convert to grayscale
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)

# Resize
small = cv2.resize(img, (640, 360))

## Detect Colored Game Pieces
# Convert to HSV for better color detection
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)

# Define color range (example: orange cone)
lower_orange = np.array([5, 100, 100])
upper_orange = np.array([25, 255, 255])

mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, lower_orange, upper_orange)
contours, _ = cv2.findContours(mask, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)

for cnt in contours:
    area = cv2.contourArea(cnt)
    if area > 500:  # ignore small noise
        x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(cnt)
        cv2.rectangle(img, (x,y), (x+w,y+h), (0,255,0), 2)
        print(f"Found piece at ({x},{y}), size {w}x{h}")`},

      {id:"ma2b",title:"Swerve Drive Deep Dive",est:"28 min",content:`## What Makes Swerve Special
Swerve drive has steered, independently powered modules â€” each wheel can face any direction. The result: full holonomic movement with traction-wheel grip.

## Module Anatomy
Each swerve module has:
- Drive motor: spins the wheel for propulsion
- Steer motor: rotates the wheel direction (0-360 degrees)
- Absolute encoder: knows wheel angle at startup (usually CANCoder or MA3)
- Gear stages: ~6-7:1 steering, ~6-8:1 driving typical

## Coordinate System
Swerve math uses a field-oriented coordinate system:
- X: left/right on the field
- Y: forward/back on the field
- Rotation: counterclockwise positive

## Inverse Kinematics
To drive at angle A with speed S and rotation R, each module calculates:
wheelSpeed[i] = magnitude of (translationVector + rotationVector[i])
wheelAngle[i] = direction of (translationVector + rotationVector[i])

WPILib provides SwerveDriveKinematics to handle all this math.

## Odometry
Track robot position using:
SwerveDriveOdometry odometry = new SwerveDriveOdometry(
    kinematics, gyro.getRotation2d(), getModulePositions());

Update every loop: odometry.update(gyro.getRotation2d(), getModulePositions());`},

      {id:"sa6b",title:"Data-Driven Alliance Selection",est:"22 min",content:`## Why Data Wins Alliance Selection
At high-level events, alliance captains spend 40+ hours analyzing data before selection. Here is how to build a data-driven selection process.

## Your Data Stack
1. Blue Alliance API: official match scores
2. Statbotics: OPR, EPA, win probabilities
3. Your scouting app: qualitative notes, reliability
4. Video: rewatch specific matches

## EPA vs OPR
EPA (Expected Points Added) from Statbotics is more accurate than raw OPR:
- Accounts for score inflation in different years
- Normalized across events
- Use EPA for inter-event comparisons

## The Picklist Algorithm
Score = (0.4 x EPA) + (0.3 x Reliability) + (0.2 x Auto) + (0.1 x Defense)

Weights depend on your game and strategy. Adjust based on:
- What scoring elements are you weakest at?
- Does the game reward defense this year?
- What does your ideal alliance look like?

## Red Flags to Check
- Does their score drop significantly in quals vs elims? (Sandbagging or inconsistency)
- Do they have mechanical failures? (Check match history for no-shows)
- Can they work with your drive team? (Pit conversation quality matters)
- Are they already committed to another alliance captain?`},

      {id:"ea2b",title:"REV Control Hub Deep Dive",est:"20 min",content:`## REV Control Hub Architecture
The Control Hub is the brain of every FTC robot. It runs Android 8 and communicates with motors, servos, and sensors over a single cable.

## Port Reference
- Motor ports 0-3: DC motors (12V, 40A max combined)
- Servo ports 0-5: Standard servo signal (3.3V signal)
- I2C ports 0-3: Distance, color, IMU sensors
- Digital 0-7: Touch sensors, magnetic limit switches
- Analog 0-3: Potentiometers, custom sensors
- USB: Webcam or USB devices

## Bulk Reads (Critical for Performance)
Without bulk reads, each sensor query takes ~3ms. With them, all data is fetched once per loop.

expansionHub.setBulkCachingMode(LynxModule.BulkCachingMode.AUTO);
// or MANUAL for precise timing control

## Motor Encoders
- Default ticks per revolution varies by motor
  - goBILDA 5202: 537.7 PPR
  - REV Core Hex: 288 PPR
  - AndyMark NeveRest 20: 537.6 PPR
- setMode(RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER) for velocity control
- setMode(RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION) for position control

## The IMU
Built-in BNO055 or BHI260AP IMU:
- Access via imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles()
- YawAngle.getDegrees() for field-centric driving
- Must initialize with correct hub mounting orientation`},

      {id:"ji10",title:"Generics & Type Safety",est:"16 min",content:`## What Are Generics?
Generics let you write code that works with any type while keeping compile-time safety.

\`\`\`java
// Without generics â€” unsafe
ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
list.add("hello");
String s = (String) list.get(0);  // runtime cast â€” could crash

// With generics â€” safe
ArrayList<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add("Alpha");
String n = names.get(0);  // no cast needed, compiler checks type
\`\`\`

## Common Generic Collections
\`\`\`java
List<DcMotor> driveMotors = new ArrayList<>();
Map<String, Double> pidMap = new HashMap<>();
Queue<Pose2d> waypointQueue = new LinkedList<>();

pidMap.put("kP", 0.01);
pidMap.put("kI", 0.0);
pidMap.put("kD", 0.005);
double kP = pidMap.get("kP");
\`\`\`

## Generic Methods
\`\`\`java
// Works with any Comparable type
public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T clamp(T val, T min, T max) {
    if (val.compareTo(min) < 0) return min;
    if (val.compareTo(max) > 0) return max;
    return val;
}
// Usage:
double power = clamp(rawPower, -1.0, 1.0);
int ticks = clamp(targetTicks, 0, 4000);
\`\`\``},

      {id:"ja9",title:"Road Runner Path Planning",est:"30 min",content:`## Road Runner: Smooth Autonomous Paths
Road Runner is the most widely used FTC autonomous library. It generates spline paths and handles odometry automatically.

## Core Concepts
- **Drive train localizer**: tracks robot position using encoders/IMU
- **Trajectory**: a time-parameterized path with velocity constraints
- **Action**: executes commands at specific trajectory points

## Basic Drive Setup
\`\`\`java
// In MecanumDrive.java (Road Runner quickstart)
public final class MecanumDrive {
    public static final DriveConstants params = new DriveConstants.Builder()
        .setTicksPerRev(537.7)   // goBILDA 5202 encoder
        .setMaxRPM(312)
        .setWheelRadius(1.8898)  // inches
        .setTrackWidth(14.0)     // inches between wheel centers
        .build();
}
\`\`\`

## Building a Trajectory
\`\`\`java
Pose2d startPose = new Pose2d(0, 0, Math.toRadians(0));
drive.pose = startPose;

TrajectoryActionBuilder tab = drive.actionBuilder(startPose)
    .lineToX(24)                          // drive 24 inches forward
    .strafeToLinearHeading(
        new Vector2d(24, -24),
        Math.toRadians(90))               // strafe and rotate
    .splineTo(
        new Vector2d(48, 0),
        Math.toRadians(0));               // smooth spline curve

Action traj = tab.build();
// Run with: Actions.runBlocking(traj);
\`\`\`

## Parallel Actions (Do two things at once)
\`\`\`java
Action sequence = new ParallelAction(
    traj,              // drive the path
    new SequentialAction(
        new SleepAction(0.5),
        new InstantAction(() -> arm.extend())
    )
);
\`\`\``},

      {id:"ja10",title:"Custom FRC Subsystems",est:"26 min",content:`## Command-Based Architecture
Every modern FRC robot uses command-based. Subsystems own hardware. Commands operate subsystems.

## Writing a Subsystem
\`\`\`java
public class Shooter extends SubsystemBase {
    private final CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(5, kBrushless);
    private final SparkMaxPIDController pid = motor.getPIDController();
    private double targetRPM = 0;

    public Shooter() {
        motor.restoreFactoryDefaults();
        motor.setIdleMode(kCoast);
        pid.setP(0.0003); pid.setFF(0.000175);
    }

    public void setRPM(double rpm) {
        targetRPM = rpm;
        pid.setReference(rpm, kVelocity);
    }

    public boolean atSpeed() {
        return Math.abs(motor.getEncoder().getVelocity() - targetRPM) < 50;
    }

    @Override public void periodic() {
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Shooter RPM",
            motor.getEncoder().getVelocity());
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Writing a Command
\`\`\`java
public class SpinUpAndShoot extends SequentialCommandGroup {
    public SpinUpAndShoot(Shooter shooter, Indexer indexer) {
        addCommands(
            new RunCommand(() -> shooter.setRPM(3000), shooter)
                .until(shooter::atSpeed),
            new InstantCommand(() -> indexer.feed()),
            new WaitCommand(0.5),
            new InstantCommand(() -> {
                shooter.setRPM(0);
                indexer.stop();
            })
        );
    }
}
\`\`\``},

      {id:"pb11",title:"Error Handling",est:"11 min",content:`## Why Handle Errors?
Robotics code runs during a match. A crash from an unhandled error = match loss.

\`\`\`python
# Basic try/except
try:
    power = desired_velocity / max_velocity
    motor.set(power)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    motor.set(0)
    print("Warning: max_velocity is zero")

# Catch multiple types
try:
    data = load_config("robot.json")
except FileNotFoundError:
    data = default_config()
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print(f"Bad config file: {e}")
    data = default_config()
finally:
    # Always runs â€” good for cleanup
    print("Config loading complete")
\`\`\`

## Raising Exceptions
\`\`\`python
def set_speed(speed: float) -> None:
    if not -1.0 <= speed <= 1.0:
        raise ValueError(f"Speed {speed} out of range [-1, 1]")
    motor.set(speed)

class RobotFaultException(Exception):

        super().__init__(f"[{subsystem}] {message}")
        self.subsystem = subsystem

raise RobotFaultException("Drivetrain", "Encoder disconnected")

      {id:"pa7",title:"Robot State Machines",est:"24 min",content:`## Finite State Machines in Python
State machines make complex robot behavior readable and testable. Instead of tangled if/else chains, each state is clear and transitions are explicit.

\`\`\`python
from enum import Enum, auto
import time

class ArmState(Enum):
    STOWED     = auto()
    EXTENDING  = auto()
    EXTENDED   = auto()
    RETRACTING = auto()

class ArmSubsystem:
    def __init__(self, motor, encoder, limit_switch):
        self.motor = motor
        self.encoder = encoder
        self.limit = limit_switch
        self.state = ArmState.STOWED
        self._state_start = time.time()

    @property
    def state_time(self) -> float:
        return time.time() - self._state_start

    def _set_state(self, new_state: ArmState):
        print(f"Arm: {self.state.name} â†’ {new_state.name}")
        self.state = new_state
        self._state_start = time.time()

    def update(self):
        match self.state:
            case ArmState.STOWED:
                self.motor.set(0)

            case ArmState.EXTENDING:
                self.motor.set(0.6)
                if self.encoder.position >= 1000:
                    self._set_state(ArmState.EXTENDED)
                elif self.state_time > 3.0:  # timeout safety
                    self._set_state(ArmState.STOWED)

            case ArmState.EXTENDED:
                self.motor.set(0.05)  # hold

            case ArmState.RETRACTING:
                self.motor.set(-0.5)
                if self.limit.get():
                    self._set_state(ArmState.STOWED)

    def extend(self):
        if self.state == ArmState.STOWED:
            self._set_state(ArmState.EXTENDING)

    def retract(self):
        if self.state == ArmState.EXTENDED:
            self._set_state(ArmState.RETRACTING)
\`\`\``},

      {id:"mb8",title:"Fasteners & Thread Locking",est:"11 min",content:`## Fasteners: Small Parts, Big Consequences
Loose bolts cause more robot failures than broken motors. Knowing fasteners is a core build skill.

## Types in FTC/FRC
- **Socket Head Cap Screw (SHCS)**: most common, hex driver
- **Button Head**: low-profile, same hex driver
- **Set Screw**: locks shaft collars â€” must use Loctite
- **Standoff**: creates precise spacing between plates
- **Rivet**: permanent, fast, blind fastening

## Thread Engagement Rule
Bolt should engage at least **1Ã— its diameter** in threads.
M3 bolt â†’ 3mm minimum thread depth in aluminum
Under-engaged threads strip under shock loads.

## Loctite Guide
| Color | Strength | When to Use |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Blue 243 | Removable | All structural bolts, mechanism pivots |
| Red 271 | Permanent | Bolts you'll never remove |
| None | â€” | Bolts removed frequently (battery, inspection panels) |

âš ï¸ Never Loctite into plastic â€” it dissolves the threads.

## Anti-Vibration Tricks
- Use Loctite + proper torque (don't over-tighten)
- Nylock nuts on high-vibration pivot points
- Split lock washers on motor mounts
- Thread inserts (Helicoil) for aluminum you remove often`},

      {id:"mi7",title:"Elevator & Lift Systems",est:"19 min",content:`## The Vertical Challenge
Lifts move game pieces up. They're mechanically challenging but strategically essential in most FTC/FRC games.

## Lift Types
**Single-stage linear slide**: Simple, low height gain (1:1 extension)
**Continuous rigging**: Rope/cable systems, 2:1 or 3:1 extension ratio
**Cascade (stacked)**: Stages extend sequentially, highest extension per stage
**Scissor lift**: Compact when folded, expands to significant height

## Rigging Patterns
Most FTC teams use 2-stage or 3-stage continuous slides.
- String path: spool â†’ fixed pulley â†’ moving carriage â†’ fixed anchor
- Each stage doubles height: 4" travel â†’ 8" with 2 stages, 12" with 3
- Use Dyneema or spectra line â€” doesn't stretch under load

## Counterbalancing (critical)
Without counterbalance: motor fights gravity the entire way up.
With a constant-force spring matched to arm weight: motor only accelerates/decelerates.
Result: 50% less current draw, faster movement, less heating.

## Common Problems & Fixes
| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Slides bind | Misalignment | Check carriage squareness, adjust bearing preload |
| String slips | Wrong anchor | Use cable clamp, not just a knot |
| Oscillates at top | No D-term | Add kD to PID, reduce kP |
| Drops on power loss | No brake | Enable brake mode, add mechanical stop |`},

      {id:"eb7",title:"Multimeter Basics",est:"12 min",content:`## The Multimeter: Fastest Debugging Tool
A multimeter diagnoses almost every electrical problem in minutes. Learn five measurements and you can fix most faults.

## DC Voltage (most used)
Set dial to DC Voltage (20V range).
Red probe to +, black to ground.
Read battery: 12.6V+ (full) Â· 11V (low) Â· < 10V (replace now)

## Continuity Test (beep mode)
Tells you if electricity can flow between two points.
Beep = connected path. No beep = broken wire or blown fuse.
Uses: check fuses, test crimped connectors, trace broken wires.

## Resistance (Î©)
Disconnect from circuit first!
Motor winding resistance: 0.5â€“5Î© (if âˆž, coil is broken)

## Diagnosing Common Problems
| Symptom | Test | Result Meaning |
|---------|------|---------------|
| Motor dead | Continuity at motor terminals | No beep = bad motor or wiring |
| Fuse blown? | Continuity across fuse | No beep = blown, replace it |
| Battery dead? | Voltage at battery terminals | < 10V = replace battery |
| Servo doesn't respond | Voltage at servo power rail | Should read ~5V |
| Encoder skips | Voltage at encoder power | Should be 3.3V or 5V |

## Pro Tips
- Always check connections at both ends of a wire
- Wiggle connectors while testing â€” intermittent faults only show when moving
- Label your probes (some cheap meters are wrong colors)`},

      {id:"ei7",title:"CAN Bus & Network Communication",est:"20 min",content:`## What Is CAN Bus?
Controller Area Network (CAN) is a serial bus that lets every device share a single two-wire network instead of individual signal wires. FRC robots use CAN for Talon SRX, Spark MAX, Falcon 500, and many sensors.

## CAN vs PWM
| Feature | CAN | PWM |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Wires per device | 2 (shared bus) | 3 (per device) |
| Status feedback | Full telemetry | None |
| Fault detection | Yes | No |
| Configuration | Software | Hardware jumper |
| Max devices | 62 | ~20 practical |

## CAN Wiring
- Yellow wire = CAN-High, Green wire = CAN-Low
- Daisy-chain from roboRIO CAN port through all devices
- Terminate with 120Î© resistor at each END of chain
- Missing termination = intermittent CAN faults

## CAN ID Assignment
Each device needs a unique ID (1â€“62).
In Phoenix Tuner X (Talons) or REV Hardware Client (Spark MAX):
1. Connect via USB
2. Set CAN ID â€” start at 1 for drivetrains
3. Confirm it appears on CAN bus before disconnecting
4. Label the physical motor controller with its ID

## Diagnosing CAN Problems
- Driver Station shows "CAN Utilization" â€” should be < 70%
- Devices blinking alternating colors = CAN fault
- Check termination resistors first, then connections, then IDs`},
    ],

      {id:"ea3b",title:"FRC Power Distribution Hub",est:"22 min",content:`## REV Power Distribution Hub (PDH)
The PDH replaced the PDP in 2022. It has 20 high-current channels and full CAN telemetry.

## Channel Map
- Channels 0â€“15: High current (40A breakers)
- Channels 16â€“19: High current (40A breakers)  
- Channels 20â€“21: Low current (15A or 20A)
- Switchable channel: software-controlled 12V output (great for cameras, lights)

## Breaker Selection Guide
| Motor/Device | Breaker |
|--------------|---------|
| CIM, NEO, Falcon 500 | 40A |
| Mini CIM, NEO 550, 775pro | 30A |
| Servo, sensor rail | 10â€“20A via VRM |
| Radio, roboRIO | 10A via VRM |

## CAN Telemetry (Java)
\`\`\`java
PowerDistribution pdh = new PowerDistribution(1, kRev);

// In periodic:
double totalCurrent = pdh.getTotalCurrent();
double ch0Current   = pdh.getCurrent(0);
double voltage      = pdh.getVoltage();
double temperature  = pdh.getTemperature();

SmartDashboard.putNumber("Battery V", voltage);
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Total A", totalCurrent);
\`\`\`

## Brownout Prevention
roboRIO brownout occurs at 6.8V â€” robot becomes disabled.
Prevention:
- Monitor getTotalCurrent() â€” alert if > 200A
- Limit peak current per motor with setSmartCurrentLimit()
- Use ramp rate on drivetrain motors (0.1â€“0.3 sec)
- Keep battery in good condition (test with load tester)`},

      {id:"sb6",title:"Reading the Game Manual",est:"13 min",content:`## The Most Important Document Each Season
Every January FIRST releases a new game. Teams that master the manual in week 1 start build season with a huge advantage.

## What to Read First
1. The scoring summary table â€” what scores the most points?
2. Ranking Points â€” what earns bonus RP beyond wins?
3. Auto period rules â€” early game is high-value with less competition
4. Endgame â€” often a disproportionately large point source
5. Penalties â€” what can lose you a match immediately?

## The 5 Build-Priority Questions
After reading, answer:
1. What single action has the highest point value?
2. What can EVERY team do at minimum? (Your floor)
3. What separates good robots from great robots?
4. What does a complete 3-robot alliance need?
5. What's achievable in 6 weeks for your team?

## Scoring Prioritization Matrix
Plot every game element on:
(Point value) Ã— (Match frequency) = Priority score

High Ã— High: Build this FIRST
High Ã— Low: Build if you have time
Low Ã— High: Skip â€” return not worth cost
Low Ã— Low: Never build this

## Rules Pitfalls to Watch
- Contact rules: what touching is legal?
- Zone restrictions: where can you go?
- Game piece possession limits
- Auto/teleop transitions rules`},

      {id:"si7",title:"Scouting System Design",est:"17 min",content:`## Building a Scouting System from Scratch
Great scouting systems have three layers: collection, storage, and analysis.

## Collection Layer
**What data matters?**
- Auto: specific actions completed (not just score)
- Teleop: cycles per minute, scoring locations used
- Endgame: attempted, succeeded, time taken
- Defense: did they play it, were they effective?
- Reliability: 1â€“5 scale, mechanical issues noted

**Collection tools:**
- Paper forms (low-tech, reliable, offline)
- Google Forms â†’ Sheets (free, easy analysis)
- Custom app (most powerful, your web dev skills apply here)

## Storage Layer
6 scouts Ã— 12 quals = 72 scouting records minimum.
At a regional: 6 scouts Ã— 72 matches Ã— 3 robots = ~200 entries needed.

Store: team, match, scout name, all metrics, timestamp

## Analysis Layer
\`\`\`
Per-team stats:
  avg_auto = mean(auto_score)
  consistency = 1 - std(total)/mean(total)
  weighted_score = (auto * 1.5) + teleop + (endgame * 2)
  combined_score = weighted_score * consistency
\`\`\`
Combined score rewards both high performance AND reliability.

## Red Flags in Data
- Team has > 30% variance in score = unreliable
- Score drops significantly in later matches = battery/mechanical issues
- Big gap between scouted and official score = data quality problem`},

      {id:"sa7",title:"Eliminations Strategy",est:"19 min",content:`## Quals vs Elims: Different Games
Everything changes in eliminations. Winning matches is the only goal â€” ranking points and experimentation are irrelevant.

## Alliance Selection Psychology
Captains select based on: your robot's capabilities, your reliability, and how well you complement their robot.

Be ready to answer in the pit:
- "What can your robot do reliably?" (not what it does sometimes)
- "Do you have any known mechanical issues?"
- "What do you need from alliance partners?"

## Pre-Elim Alliance Strategy Meeting (7 minutes)
1. Starting positions (agree who goes where) â€” 1 min
2. Auto routines â€” what does each robot run, can any combine? â€” 2 min
3. Teleop zones â€” who owns which field area? â€” 1 min
4. Endgame timing â€” countdown, abort signal â€” 1 min
5. Emergency plan â€” if a robot dies, what changes? â€” 1 min
6. Questions from drive teams â€” 1 min

## Score Differential Decisions (Last 30 Seconds)
- Up 15+: protect lead, early endgame
- Up 5â€“14: one offensive robot, two protect
- Down 1â€“14: max offense AND endgame, need both
- Down 15+: only way back is opponent penalty â€” clean play, hope

## Drive Team Communication
Simple codewords agreed before match:
- "Park" = go to endgame position now
- "Chase" = go for high-value scoring
- "Box" = play defense on [color][number]
- "Clear" = stop defending, return to offense`},

      {id:"wb5",title:"CSS Grid Layout",est:"13 min",content:`## CSS Grid: Two-Dimensional Layout
Flexbox is one-dimensional (row OR column). Grid is two-dimensional (rows AND columns simultaneously). Perfect for dashboards and match displays.

\`\`\`css
/* 3-column responsive dashboard */
.dashboard {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); /* 3 equal columns */
  gap: 16px;
  padding: 20px;
}

/* Specific template */
.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 250px 1fr; /* sidebar + main */
  grid-template-rows: 60px 1fr 40px; /* header + content + footer */
  height: 100vh;
}
.sidebar { grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1 / 3; }
.header  { grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; }
.main    { grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; }
.footer  { grid-column: 1 / 3; grid-row: 3; }
\`\`\`

## Auto-Fit Responsive Grid (Most Useful)
\`\`\`css
.team-cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr));
  gap: 12px;
}
/* Cards are automatically 280px+ wide, wrap to next row as needed */
/* No media queries needed! */
\`\`\`

## Grid vs Flexbox: When to Use Each
- **Flexbox**: nav bars, button groups, centering single items
- **Grid**: page layouts, card grids, any 2D arrangement`},

      {id:"wb6",title:"JavaScript DOM Events",est:"14 min",content:`## Events Make Pages Interactive
Every click, keypress, scroll, and form input fires an event. You listen for events to run your code.

\`\`\`javascript
// Click events
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log("Clicked!", event.target);
});

// Keyboard events
document.addEventListener("keydown", (e) => {
  if (e.key === "Enter") submitForm();
  if (e.ctrlKey && e.key === "s") saveData();
});

// Input events (fires on every keystroke)
searchInput.addEventListener("input", (e) => {
  filterTeams(e.target.value);
});

// Form submission (prevent default refresh)
form.addEventListener("submit", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault(); // IMPORTANT: stops page reload
  const data = new FormData(form);
  saveScoutData(Object.fromEntries(data));
});
\`\`\`

## Event Delegation (One Listener for Many Elements)
\`\`\`javascript
// BAD: adds listener to every card
cards.forEach(card => card.addEventListener("click", handler));

// GOOD: one listener on parent, check which child was clicked
teamList.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
  const card = e.target.closest(".team-card");
  if (card) selectTeam(card.dataset.teamNumber);
});
\`\`\``},

      {id:"wi4",title:"TypeScript Basics",est:"17 min",content:`## Why TypeScript?
TypeScript adds types to JavaScript. It catches bugs before you run the code â€” huge in production scouting apps.

\`\`\`typescript
// JavaScript â€” no safety
function getScore(team) {
  return team.auto + team.teleop; // team could be anything!
}

// TypeScript â€” compiler catches mistakes
interface TeamData {
  number: number;
  name: string;
  auto: number;
  teleop: number;
  reliability?: number; // ? means optional
}

function getScore(team: TeamData): number {
  return team.auto + team.teleop; // IDE helps you here
}
\`\`\`

## Type Annotations
\`\`\`typescript
// Variables
let teamNumber: number = 1234;
let teamName: string = "Gear Grinders";
let isEliminated: boolean = false;
let scores: number[] = [45, 52, 61, 38];

// Functions
function average(nums: number[]): number {
  return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b) / nums.length;
}

// Generics
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined {
  return arr[0];
}
const topTeam = first<TeamData>(rankedTeams);
\`\`\`

## React + TypeScript
\`\`\`tsx
interface TeamCardProps {
  team: TeamData;
  onSelect: (number: number) => void;
}
function TeamCard({ team, onSelect }: TeamCardProps) {
  return <div onClick={() => onSelect(team.number)}>{team.name}</div>;
}
\`\`\``},

      {id:"wi5",title:"Local Storage & IndexedDB",est:"15 min",content:`## Persisting Data in the Browser
Scouting apps need to save data even when offline. The browser has two storage options.

## localStorage â€” Simple Key/Value
\`\`\`javascript
// Save
localStorage.setItem("scoutData", JSON.stringify(scoutEntries));

// Load
const raw = localStorage.getItem("scoutData");
const entries = raw ? JSON.parse(raw) : [];

// Delete
localStorage.removeItem("scoutData");
localStorage.clear(); // nuclear option

// Limits: ~5MB, strings only, synchronous
\`\`\`

## When localStorage Isn't Enough
For large datasets (1000+ scouting entries), use IndexedDB.

\`\`\`javascript
// Using the idb library (much simpler API)
import { openDB } from "idb";

const db = await openDB("scoutApp", 1, {
  upgrade(db) {
    db.createObjectStore("entries", { keyPath: "id", autoIncrement: true });
  }
});

// Add entry
await db.add("entries", { team: 1234, match: 5, auto: 15, teleop: 32 });

// Get all entries
const all = await db.getAll("entries");

// Query by team
const tx = db.transaction("entries");
// (use IDB cursor for filtering)
\`\`\`

## Offline Sync Strategy
1. Save all scout entries to IndexedDB immediately
2. When online: batch-sync to Firebase/Supabase
3. Show sync status indicator in UI`},
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"wa2",title:"Real-Time Scouting with Firebase",est:"28 min",content:`## Firebase: Instant Multi-Device Sync\nFirebase Realtime Database lets multiple scouts enter data on their phones and everyone sees updates instantly â€” perfect for competition.\n\n## Setup\n\\\`\\\`\\\`bash\nnpm install firebase\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// firebase.js\nimport { initializeApp } from "firebase/app";\nimport { getDatabase, ref, push, onValue } from "firebase/database";\n\nconst app = initializeApp({\n  apiKey: "your-key",\n  databaseURL: "https://your-app.firebaseio.com",\n  projectId: "your-project",\n});\nexport const db = getDatabase(app);\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Writing Scout Data\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\nimport { db } from "./firebase";\nimport { ref, push, set } from "firebase/database";\n\nasync function saveScoutEntry(entry) {\n  const entriesRef = ref(db, "scouting/2024casj");\n  await push(entriesRef, {\n    ...entry,\n    timestamp: Date.now(),\n    scoutName: currentUser.name,\n  });\n  console.log("Entry saved to Firebase!");\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Real-Time Listening\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\nimport { ref, onValue } from "firebase/database";\n\nfunction subscribeToEntries(eventKey, callback) {\n  const entriesRef = ref(db, \\\`scouting/\\" + (eventKey) + "\\\`);\n  return onValue(entriesRef, (snapshot) => {\n    const data = snapshot.val() || {};\n    const entries = Object.values(data);\n    callback(entries);\n  });\n  // Returns unsubscribe function â€” call it to stop listening\n}\n\n// In React component:\nuseEffect(() => {\n  const unsub = subscribeToEntries("2024casj", setEntries);\n  return unsub; // cleanup on unmount\n}, []);\n\\\`\\\`\\\``},
    ],
  },
  fundraising: {
    Intermediate: [
      {id:"fi4",title:"Corporate Outreach Campaigns",est:"15 min",content:`## Running a Systematic Outreach Campaign
One sponsor letter sent to one company is an ask. Fifty letters sent to fifty companies with follow-up is a campaign.

## Building Your Target List
Start with 50â€“100 companies. Prioritize:
1. Companies within 10 miles (local connection matters)
2. Companies in STEM/manufacturing sectors
3. Companies where team members' parents work (warm leads)
4. Companies that sponsor other local nonprofits (proven givers)

## The 5-Touch Outreach Sequence
\`\`\`
Day 0:  Send personalized email/letter
Day 7:  Follow-up call ("Did you receive our letter?")
Day 14: Second email with a specific ask and deadline
Day 21: Call decision maker directly (not front desk)
Day 30: Final email â€” "We're finalizing sponsors this week"
\`\`\`
Most sponsors say yes between touches 2 and 4.

## Call Script
"Hi, this is [Name] from Team 1234, a FIRST Robotics team at [School].
We sent you a letter last week about our sponsorship program.
I'm calling to see if [Company] might be interested in supporting
our team this season. We're looking for a [Bronze/Silver/Gold] sponsor.
Do you have two minutes to discuss?"

Keep it under 90 seconds. Be confident â€” you're offering them value, not begging.

## Tracking Your Pipeline
Use a spreadsheet with columns:
Company | Contact | Date Sent | Date Called | Response | Status | Amount
Color-code by status: Not contacted, Contacted, Interested, Committed, Declined`},
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"fa2",title:"Year-Round Fundraising Program",est:"17 min",content:`## Fundraising Is a System, Not an Event
Teams that treat fundraising as a year-round program consistently raise 3â€“5Ã— more than teams that only fundraise in build season.

## The Fundraising Calendar
- **Septemberâ€“October**: Sponsor renewals, fall grant applications
- **November**: Holiday appeal letter campaign (highest open rates of year)
- **December**: Year-end tax-deadline push for business donations
- **January**: Kickoff event, invite sponsors to game reveal
- **Februaryâ€“March**: Competition visibility â€” robots carry sponsor logos to events
- **April**: End-of-season report sent to all sponsors
- **Mayâ€“August**: Community events, new grant research, sponsor prospecting

## The 5 Key Roles
Assign these to students, not mentors:
1. **Sponsor Relations Lead**: manages all corporate contacts
2. **Grants Lead**: researches and writes grant applications
3. **Events Lead**: plans and executes community events
4. **Social Media Lead**: creates content, tags sponsors
5. **Finance Lead**: tracks budget, receipts, reports to mentors

## Sponsor Retention Formula
80% of next year's funding comes from this year's sponsors â€” if you treat them right.
- End-of-season impact report (photos, results, student thank-you letter)
- Invite to build season open house in January
- Personal call from a STUDENT (not mentor) in October
- First right of refusal for same sponsorship level next year

## KPIs to Track Annually
- Total raised vs goal
- Sponsor retention rate (target > 75%)
- New sponsors acquired
- Grants applied vs grants won (industry average: ~25% win rate)`},
    ],
  },
};

      {id:"ji11b",title:"Debug Challenge: Fix the PID Loop",est:"18 min",type:"challenge",
       buggedCode:`// Arm position control - something is wrong!
double kP = 0.01;
double kI = 0.001;
double kD = 0.1;

double targetPos = 1500; // ticks
double integral = 0;
double lastError = 0;

while (opModeIsActive()) {

       hint:"Check the error sign and the derivative calculation. Also think about output clamping.",
       fixedCode:`double kP = 0.01;
double kI = 0.001;
double kD = 0.1;

double targetPos = 1500;
double integral = 0;
double lastError = 0;

while (opModeIsActive()) {
    double currentPos = armMotor.getCurrentPosition();
    double error = targetPos - currentPos;  // FIX: target MINUS current (not current minus target)

    integral = integral + error;
    // Optional: integral windup guard
    integral = Math.max(-500, Math.min(500, integral));

    double derivative = (error - lastError);  // FIX: same direction as error
    
    double output = kP * error + kI * integral + kD * derivative;
    // FIX: clamp output to valid motor power range
    output = Math.max(-1.0, Math.min(1.0, output));
    
    armMotor.setPower(output);
    lastError = error;
    telemetry.update();
}`,
       explanation:"Two critical bugs: (1) Error must be target MINUS current â€” this way positive error means we need to go up, and positive power goes up. Reversed sign makes the arm run away from the target. (2) The output must be clamped to [-1.0, 1.0] â€” motors accept only this range. Bonus: integral windup guard prevents accumulation when the mechanism is stuck."},

    LESSONS[subject][level] = [...LESSONS[subject][level], ...LESSONS_EXTRA2[subject][level]];

});

      {id:"jb13",title:"Writing Your First TeleOp",est:"20 min",content:`## Your First TeleOp Program

TeleOp (Tele-Operated) is the 2-minute driver-controlled period in FTC. Here's the bare minimum to drive a robot:

\`\`\`java
@TeleOp(name = "BasicDrive", group = "Iterative")
public class BasicDrive extends OpMode {
    DcMotor leftDrive, rightDrive;

    @Override
    public void init() {
        leftDrive  = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "left_drive");
        rightDrive = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "right_drive");
        leftDrive.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE);
    }

    @Override
    public void loop() {
        double drive = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;
        double turn  =  gamepad1.right_stick_x;

        leftDrive.setPower(drive + turn);
        rightDrive.setPower(drive - turn);
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Key Points
- **@TeleOp** registers your class in the Driver Hub app list
- **init()** runs once when you press INIT
- **loop()** runs continuously during the match
- **gamepad1** gives access to the driver's controller inputs
- Left stick Y is negated because pushing up returns negative values

### Gamepad Inputs Available
| Input | Value Range |
|-------|-------------|
| left_stick_y | -1.0 to 1.0 |
| right_stick_x | -1.0 to 1.0 |
| a, b, x, y (buttons) | true / false |
| left_bumper | true / false |
| left_trigger | 0.0 to 1.0 |

      {id:"ji13",title:"Finite State Machines for Autonomous",est:"25 min",content:`## Finite State Machines (FSM)

Instead of one long sequence of if-statements, FSMs make autonomous code readable and robust.

### The Problem with Simple Sequences
\`\`\`java
// BAD: hard to modify, breaks if one step fails
drive(30);
turn(90);
drop();
drive(20);
\`\`\`

### FSM Approach
\`\`\`java
enum State { DRIVE_TO_SPIKE, TURN_TO_BACKDROP, PLACE_PIXEL, PARK, IDLE }

State currentState = State.DRIVE_TO_SPIKE;
ElapsedTime timer = new ElapsedTime();

@Override
public void loop() {
    switch (currentState) {
        case DRIVE_TO_SPIKE:
            if (robot.driveToPosition(30, 0.6)) {
                currentState = State.TURN_TO_BACKDROP;
                timer.reset();
            }
            break;
        case TURN_TO_BACKDROP:
            if (robot.turnToHeading(90, 0.4)) {
                currentState = State.PLACE_PIXEL;
            }
            break;
        case PLACE_PIXEL:
            robot.openClaw();
            if (timer.seconds() > 0.5) {
                currentState = State.PARK;
            }
            break;
        case PARK:
            robot.driveToPosition(60, 0.4);
            currentState = State.IDLE;
            break;
        case IDLE:
            break;
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Benefits
- **Easy to add states** â€” just add a new enum value and case
- **Easy to debug** â€” you can log which state you're in
- **Non-blocking** â€” the loop keeps running even while waiting
- **Reusable** â€” states can be reused across auto routines
`,
        quiz:[
          {q:"What is the main benefit of FSMs over sequential autonomous code?",opts:["They run faster","They're non-blocking and easy to modify","They use less memory","They don't need encoders"],ans:1},
          {q:"In an FSM, where do you transition to the next state?",opts:["In init()","Inside each state's case when the condition is met","At the top of loop()","In a separate method"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"ja10b",title:"Road Runner Trajectory Building",est:"30 min",content:`## Road Runner Trajectories

Road Runner is a motion planning library that generates smooth, mathematically optimal paths for FTC robots.

### Basic Trajectory
\`\`\`java
TrajectorySequence traj = drive.trajectorySequenceBuilder(startPose)
    .forward(24)
    .turn(Math.toRadians(90))
    .forward(12)
    .waitSeconds(0.5)
    .back(6)
    .build();

drive.followTrajectorySequence(traj);
\`\`\`

### Spline Paths (Smooth Curves)
\`\`\`java
TrajectorySequence traj = drive.trajectorySequenceBuilder(startPose)
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(36, 12), Math.toRadians(0))
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(60, 24), Math.toRadians(45))
    .build();
\`\`\`

### Marker Actions (Run code mid-trajectory)
\`\`\`java
TrajectorySequence traj = drive.trajectorySequenceBuilder(startPose)
    .forward(20)
    .addTemporalMarker(0.5, () -> {     // after 0.5 sec
        intake.setPower(1.0);
    })
    .addDisplacementMarker(30, () -> {   // after 30 inches
        intake.setPower(0);
    })
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(50, 0), 0)
    .build();
\`\`\`

### Coordinate System
- (0, 0) is typically the robot's starting position
- X is forward, Y is left
- Heading is in radians (use Math.toRadians() to convert degrees)
`,

      {id:"mb11",title:"How Robot Intakes Work",est:"18 min",content:`## Robot Intake Systems

The intake collects game pieces from the field. Good intakes are fast, reliable, and forgiving.

### Types of Intakes

**Roller Intake**
- Spinning rollers or wheels grab pieces
- Best for flat game pieces (rings, discs)
- Simple and reliable

**Claw / Gripper**
- Opens and closes to grab specific objects
- Best for 3D objects (cones, cubes, balls)
- Needs precise positioning

**Sushi Belt / Conveyor**
- Moving belt pulls pieces in
- Good for fast cycling
- Can hold multiple pieces

### Key Design Principles
1. **Passive alignment** â€” guide rails help funnel pieces in even if the robot isn't perfectly aligned
2. **Over-extension protection** â€” use compliant wheels or rubber that flex instead of jamming
3. **Reverse-ability** â€” always be able to spit pieces out if you intake the wrong one
4. **Speed** â€” a fast intake can double your scoring rate

### Compliance
Compliant (flexible) materials like Stealth Wheels or surgical tubing grip game pieces without breaking them. This is better than rigid materials for most intakes.
`,

      {id:"mi10",title:"Linear Slides and Lifting Mechanisms",est:"22 min",content:`## Linear Slides

Linear slides allow robots to extend vertically or horizontally â€” critical for scoring in high goals.

### Types of Linear Slides
- **Cascade (continuous rigged)**: Stages extend together, efficient use of motor power
- **Parallel rigged**: All stages move at same rate, simpler rigging
- **Single stage**: Simple but limited extension

### Key Concepts

**Rigging String**
String (or cord) connects the stages. When the bottom stage moves, the top stage extends proportionally.

\`\`\`
Stage 1 moves 12" â†’ Stage 2 moves 24" (cascade, 2-stage)
\`\`\`

**Motor + Spool**
A spool winds the string to extend or retract. Size the spool so:
- Full extension in ~2 seconds
- Motor doesn't stall at full load

**Counterbalancing**
A rubber band or constant force spring reduces the load on the motor when holding the slide up. This:
- Uses less battery
- Reduces motor heat
- Allows holding position with less current

### Extension Limits
FTC robots have an 18" cube limit at start, but can extend during the match. Always check the specific game manual for extension rules.
`,

      {id:"si7b",title:"Match Scouting Systems",est:"20 min",content:`## Building a Scouting System

Good scouting data wins alliance selection. Here's how to build one.

### What to Track Per Match
| Metric | Why It Matters |
|--------|---------------|
| Auto points | Reliability in autonomous |
| Tele-op cycles | Scoring rate per minute |
| Endgame points | Consistency on climbs/parking |
| Defense played | Are they a threat or asset? |
| Penalties | Do they play clean? |
| Robot breakdown | Reliability score |

### Quantitative vs Qualitative
- **Quantitative**: Numbers you can average (cycles, points scored)
- **Qualitative**: Observations ("struggles with tight spaces", "fast intake")

Both matter. Numbers show what â€” observations explain why.

### The Scouting Rotation
Assign each scout 1-2 robots per match. Rotate assignments so every robot gets scouted by multiple people. This catches outliers and reduces bias.

### Red Flags to Watch For
- Inconsistent auto (ran it once perfectly, failed 3 times)
- Only scores when not defended
- Slow cycling (< 4 cycles/match)
- Mechanical issues each match

### Alliance Selection Strategy
In elims you want three robots that complement each other:
- **Scorer**: High OPR, reliable auto
- **Defender**: Mobile, sturdy
- **Support**: Consistent, no penalties
`,

        ]
      },

      {id:"sa7b",title:"Autonomous Path Planning Strategy",est:"25 min",content:`## Autonomous Strategy

The first 30 seconds of a match are worth disproportionately more than teleop because:
1. Autonomous points often have multipliers
2. Field is uncrowded â€” no defense
3. Consistency separates elite teams

### Picking Your Auto Routine

**Conservative (High Consistency)**
- Score 1-2 guaranteed elements
- Park in a safe zone
- 90%+ success rate
- Good for unreliable robots or new drivers

**Aggressive (High Ceiling)**
- Score 3+ elements
- Multi-zone paths
- 60-70% success rate
- Only worth it if your robot is reliable

### The 70% Rule
An aggressive auto that scores 2x points but only works 60% of the time is worth less than a conservative auto that works 90% of the time.

Expected value = success rate Ã— points scored

Example:
- Conservative: 0.90 Ã— 20 = **18 expected points**
- Aggressive: 0.65 Ã— 40 = **26 expected points**

In this case, aggressive is worth it. But if success drops to 40%: 0.40 Ã— 40 = 16 â€” now conservative wins.

### Path Redundancy
Build in fallbacks. If vision fails to detect a target, default to a safe scoring position instead of doing nothing. 

Something > Nothing in autonomous.
`,
        quiz:[
          {q:"How do you calculate the 'expected value' of an auto routine?",opts:["Max points possible","Success rate Ã— points scored","Points scored minus penalties","Average of all runs"],ans:1},
          {q:"What should your robot do if vision detection fails during autonomous?",opts:["Stop immediately","Default to a safe fallback routine","Try again indefinitely","Drive off the field"],ans:1},
        ]
      },

      {id:"ei7b",title:"Motor Controllers and REV Hub Wiring",est:"20 min",content:`## REV Control Hub Wiring

The REV Control Hub is the brain of your FTC robot. Here's what every port does.

### Motor Ports (0-3)
- 4 motor ports, each drives one DC motor
- Power comes from the 12V battery through the main switch
- Each port can output up to ~20A peak

\`\`\`
Port 0: Left Front Motor
Port 1: Right Front Motor  
Port 2: Left Back Motor
Port 3: Right Back Motor
\`\`\`

### Servo Ports (0-5)
- 6 servo ports at 5V
- Each port handles one servo
- DO NOT plug DC motors into servo ports (will fry the hub)

### I2C Ports (0-3)
- For sensors using I2C protocol: color sensors, distance sensors, IMU
- Each device needs a unique I2C address
- REV Color/Distance sensor default address: 0x52

### Digital Ports (0-7)
- For digital sensors: limit switches, magnetic sensors
- Returns 0 or 1 (off/on)

### Analog Ports (0-3)  
- For analog sensors: potentiometers, some distance sensors
- Returns 0-3.3V mapped to 0-1023

### Common Wiring Mistakes
1. Reversed motor polarity (robot drives backward â€” fix in code with .setDirection())
2. Wrong I2C address conflict (two sensors fighting each other)
3. Servo on motor port (will damage the hub)
4. Loose XT30 connector (robot cuts out mid-match)
`,

        ]
      },
    ],

};

      {id:"ji14",title:"PID Control Deep Dive",est:"28 min",content:`## PID Controllers

PID makes motors go exactly where you want â€” it's the most important control algorithm in robotics.

### The PID Formula
\`\`\`
output = (Kp Ã— error) + (Ki Ã— integral) + (Kd Ã— derivative)
\`\`\`

| Term | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| P (Proportional) | Power proportional to error |
| I (Integral) | Fixes steady offset P alone can't fix |
| D (Derivative) | Damps oscillation |

### Simple P Controller
\`\`\`java
double Kp = 0.005;
double target = 1000; // encoder ticks

public void loop() {
    double error = target - motor.getCurrentPosition();
    double power = Math.max(-1.0, Math.min(1.0, Kp * error));
    motor.setPower(power);
}
\`\`\`

### Tuning Steps
1. Start with Kp only (Ki=Kd=0)
2. Raise Kp until it oscillates
3. Back off Kp 30%
4. Add Kd slowly to reduce bounce
5. Add Ki only if there's a steady offset
`,

          {q:"When should you add the I term?",opts:["Always","Only if there's a steady offset P can't fix","Before tuning P","Never"],ans:1},

      {id:"ja11",title:"Command-Based Programming (FRC)",est:"30 min",content:`## Command-Based Architecture

Command-Based separates robot behavior into Subsystems and Commands.

### Subsystem
\`\`\`java
public class ShooterSubsystem extends SubsystemBase {
    private final CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
    public void shoot(double speed) { motor.set(speed); }
    public void stop() { motor.set(0); }
    @Override public void periodic() {
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("RPM", motor.getEncoder().getVelocity());
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Command
\`\`\`java
public class ShootCommand extends Command {
    private final ShooterSubsystem shooter;
    private final double speed;
    public ShootCommand(ShooterSubsystem shooter, double speed) {
        this.shooter = shooter; this.speed = speed;
        addRequirements(shooter);
    }
    @Override public void initialize() { shooter.shoot(speed); }
    @Override public void end(boolean i) { shooter.stop(); }
    @Override public boolean isFinished() { return false; }
}
\`\`\`

### Button Bindings
\`\`\`java
new JoystickButton(controller, Button.kA.value)
    .whileTrue(new ShootCommand(shooter, 0.8));
\`\`\`

### Command Groups
\`\`\`java
new SequentialCommandGroup(
    new DriveForward(drive, 30),
    new TurnToAngle(drive, 90),
    new ShootCommand(shooter, 0.8).withTimeout(1.5)
)
\`\`\`
`,

      {id:"mb12",title:"Fasteners and Structural Connections",est:"18 min",content:`## Fasteners for Robots

### Common Types
| Fastener | Best For | Removable? |

3. **Double nuts** â€” jam two nuts against each other

      {id:"mi11",title:"Shooter and Launcher Mechanisms",est:"25 min",content:`## Shooter Design

### Flywheel Shooter
Two counter-rotating wheels fling game pieces. Key variables:
- **Wheel RPM** â€” exit velocity
- **Compression** â€” grip and spin
- **Hood angle** â€” launch angle (30-45Â° typical)

**Velocity Drop Problem**: When a piece enters, it steals RPM from the flywheel.
Solutions: heavier flywheel, more motor power, wait between shots.

### Catapult
Elastic energy (tubing/springs) releases instantly.
- âœ… No velocity drop, simple, reliable
- âŒ Slower cycle time, harder angle adjustment

### Indexer
Feeds pieces into the shooter at a controlled rate:
\`\`\`java
if (gamepad1.right_bumper && shooterReady()) {

} else { indexer.setPower(0); }

      {id:"ma3x2",title:"Chassis Design Tradeoffs",est:"28 min",content:`## Choosing Your Chassis

### Material Comparison
| Material | Weight | Machinability | Best For |
|----------|--------|---------------|---------|

| Steel | Heavy | Hard | High-impact areas |
| Polycarbonate | Light | Easy | Panels, guards |
| Carbon Fiber | Lightest | Difficult | Weight-critical parts |

### Frame Types
- **Tube frame**: 1Ã—1 or 2Ã—1 aluminum tube + gussets. Most common, repairable.
- **Plate frame**: Single large plate as structure. Rigid, harder to modify.
- **Kit frame**: Pre-made (VEX, REV). Fast to build, less customizable.

- **FTC size**: 18"Ã—18"Ã—18" cube at start
- **FRC bumpers**: Must be 4.5" â€“ 7.5" from ground
- **COG**: Keep heavy parts (battery, hubs) low to prevent tipping

      {id:"eb10",title:"Robot Power Systems",est:"18 min",content:`## How Power Flows in Your Robot

### FRC Power Chain
\`\`\`
12V Battery â†’ Main Breaker â†’ PDH â†’ Motor Controllers â†’ Motors
                                  â†’ RoboRIO â†’ Sensors/Radio
\`\`\`

### FTC Power Chain
\`\`\`
12V Battery â†’ Main Switch â†’ Control Hub â†’ Motors, Servos, Sensors
\`\`\`

### Brown-Outs
When motors draw too much current, battery voltage drops and the robot reboots.
**Prevention**: Don't run all motors at full simultaneously. Keep connections tight. Replace old batteries.

### Wire Gauge (AWG)
Lower AWG = thicker wire = more current capacity:
| Circuit | AWG |
|---------|-----|
| Battery cables | 6 AWG |
| Motor power | 12-14 AWG |
| Signal/sensor | 22-26 AWG |

### Fuse Tips
If a breaker trips â†’ check for a jammed (stalled) motor first.
`,

      {id:"ea3x2",title:"AprilTag Vision and Field Localization",est:"30 min",content:`## AprilTag Vision

AprilTags are QR-like markers on the field. Your camera detects them to know exactly where the robot is.

### FTC Setup
\`\`\`java
VisionPortal visionPortal = new VisionPortal.Builder()
    .setCamera(hardwareMap.get(WebcamName.class, "Webcam 1"))
    .addProcessor(aprilTagProcessor)
    .build();

// In loop():
for (AprilTagDetection d : aprilTagProcessor.getDetections()) {
    telemetry.addData("Tag ID", d.id);
    telemetry.addData("Range (in)", d.ftcPose.range);
    telemetry.addData("Bearing (deg)", d.ftcPose.bearing);
}
\`\`\`

### Auto Alignment to Tag
\`\`\`java
double rangeError   = detection.ftcPose.range   - 12.0;
double bearingError = detection.ftcPose.bearing;
double drive  = 0.015 * rangeError;
double strafe = -0.015 * bearingError;
leftFront.setPower(drive + strafe);
rightFront.setPower(drive - strafe);
leftBack.setPower(drive - strafe);
rightBack.setPower(drive + strafe);
\`\`\`

### Camera Placement Tips
- Fixed, known position on robot
- Slight upward tilt to see tags from distance
- Not blocked by mechanisms during normal operation
- USB 3.0 = higher framerate = better tracking

      {id:"sa8b",title:"Playoff Alliance Strategy",est:"25 min",content:`## Playoff Strategy

Playoffs use double-elimination (FRC) or single-elimination (FTC). Every match is critical.

### Alliance Selection (FRC)
- Top 8 ranked teams each pick 2 partners (serpentine order)
- Teams can decline to be picked (must then be a captain)
- Build a complementary alliance: scorer + defender + support

### Double Elimination
- Lose once â†’ losers bracket
- Lose twice â†’ eliminated
- **Strategy**: Take risks in first match (you have a second chance). Play conservatively in elimination matches.

### Pre-Match Checklist
\`\`\`
Before every playoff match:
1. Did their auto change from quals?
2. Which robot can we defend most effectively?
3. Set a cycle target (e.g. "We need 8 cycles to win")
4. Assign clear roles: scorer / defender / feeder
5. Set endgame timing: when do we stop cycling and climb?
\`\`\`

### Score Reading Mid-Match
- **+20 pts**: Protect your lead, play conservatively
- **-10 to -20**: Push harder on cycles
- **Within 10**: Stick to the plan â€” consistency beats heroics
`,

      {id:"pi10b",title:"Match Data Analysis with Python",est:"25 min",content:`## Analyzing Match Data

After scouting 50 matches, Python turns your spreadsheet into winning insights.

### Load and Prepare Data
\`\`\`python
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv('scouting_data.csv')
df['total_score'] = df['auto_score'] + df['teleop_score']
df['climb_val'] = df['climb'].map({'success':1, 'attempted':0.5, 'no':0})
\`\`\`

### Average Performance Per Team
\`\`\`python
team_stats = df.groupby('team').agg({
    'total_score': ['mean', 'std', 'max'],
    'auto_score': 'mean',
    'climb_val': 'mean',
}).round(2)
team_stats.columns = ['avg','std','max','avg_auto','climb_rate']
team_stats = team_stats.sort_values('avg', ascending=False)
print(team_stats.head(10))
\`\`\`

### Find Consistent Teams
\`\`\`python
# Consistency = mean / std (higher = more predictable)
team_stats['consistency'] = team_stats['avg'] / (team_stats['std'] + 1)
top = team_stats[team_stats['avg'] > 30].nlargest(10, 'consistency')
print(top)

### Visualize

top10 = team_stats.head(10)
plt.bar(top10.index.astype(str), top10['avg'])
plt.xlabel('Team'); plt.ylabel('Avg Score')

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

      {id:"jb15",title:"Loops and Arrays for Robotics",est:"20 min",content:`## Loops and Arrays in Robot Code

Loops and arrays let you control multiple motors and sensors without repeating code.

### Arrays â€” Store Multiple Values
\`\`\`java
// Instead of: DcMotor m0, m1, m2, m3;
DcMotor[] motors = new DcMotor[4];
String[] motorNames = {"lf","rf","lb","rb"};

// Initialize all motors in one loop
for (int i = 0; i < motors.length; i++) {
    motors[i] = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, motorNames[i]);
    motors[i].setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE);
}
\`\`\`

### For Loop â€” Repeat Known Number of Times
\`\`\`java
// Set all motors to zero
for (DcMotor motor : motors) {
    motor.setPower(0);
}
\`\`\`

### While Loop â€” Repeat Until Condition Met
\`\`\`java
// Drive forward until limit switch pressed
while (!limitSwitch.isPressed() && opModeIsActive()) {
    leftDrive.setPower(0.5);
    rightDrive.setPower(0.5);
    telemetry.addData("Driving", "forward");
    telemetry.update();
}
// Stop
leftDrive.setPower(0);
rightDrive.setPower(0);
\`\`\`

### ArrayList â€” Dynamic Lists
\`\`\`java
ArrayList<String> autonSteps = new ArrayList<>();
autonSteps.add("Drive forward 24 inches");
autonSteps.add("Turn right 90 degrees");
autonSteps.add("Drop game piece");

for (String step : autonSteps) {
    telemetry.addData("Step", step);
    telemetry.update();
    sleep(500);
}
\`\`\`

      {id:"ji15",title:"Writing Reusable Robot Utility Classes",est:"25 min",content:`## Utility Classes â€” Clean Robot Code

As your code grows, utility classes keep things organized and reusable across autonomous routines.

### DriveTrain Utility Class
\`\`\`java
public class DriveTrain {
    private DcMotor lf, rf, lb, rb;
    private double ticksPerInch;

    public DriveTrain(HardwareMap hMap, double ticksPerInch) {
        lf = hMap.get(DcMotor.class, "lf");
        rf = hMap.get(DcMotor.class, "rf");
        lb = hMap.get(DcMotor.class, "lb");
        rb = hMap.get(DcMotor.class, "rb");
        lf.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE);
        lb.setDirection(DcMotor.Direction.REVERSE);
        this.ticksPerInch = ticksPerInch;
    }

    public void setPowers(double lPow, double rPow) {
        lf.setPower(lPow); lb.setPower(lPow);
        rf.setPower(rPow); rb.setPower(rPow);
    }

    public void driveInches(double inches, double power, LinearOpMode opMode) {
        int target = (int)(inches * ticksPerInch);
        setAllRunToPosition(target);
        setPowers(power, power);
        while (lf.isBusy() && opMode.opModeIsActive()) {
            opMode.telemetry.addData("Target", target);
            opMode.telemetry.addData("Current", lf.getCurrentPosition());
            opMode.telemetry.update();
        }
        setPowers(0, 0);
        setAllRunUsingEncoder();
    }

    private void setAllRunToPosition(int ticks) { /* set all motors */ }
    private void setAllRunUsingEncoder() { /* reset mode */ }
}
\`\`\`

### Using It in Autonomous
\`\`\`java
public class MyAuto extends LinearOpMode {
    @Override
    public void runOpMode() {
        DriveTrain drive = new DriveTrain(hardwareMap, 44.5);
        waitForStart();
        drive.driveInches(24, 0.6, this); // Drive 24 inches
        drive.driveInches(-12, 0.4, this); // Back up 12 inches
    }
}
\`\`\`

      {id:"ja12",title:"Odometry and Dead Wheel Tracking",est:"35 min",content:`## Odometry â€” Know Exactly Where You Are

Odometry tracks your robot's position using passive encoder wheels (dead wheels) that always touch the floor.

### Why Dead Wheels?
Regular motor encoders measure motor rotation â€” but wheels slip. Dead wheels are unpowered, always contacting the floor, so they measure actual travel.

### Two-Wheel Odometry Setup
\`\`\`
Two perpendicular wheels:
- Forward wheel: measures forward/backward movement
- Strafe wheel: measures left/right movement
\`\`\`

### Math â€” Pose Tracking
\`\`\`java
// Track position as (x, y, heading)
double x = 0, y = 0, heading = 0;

// Each loop:
double deltaForward = (forwardEncoder.getCurrentPosition() - prevForward) / TICKS_PER_INCH;
double deltaStrafe  = (strafeEncoder.getCurrentPosition()  - prevStrafe)  / TICKS_PER_INCH;
double deltaHeading = imu.getAngularOrientation().firstAngle - prevHeading;

// Field-centric update
x += deltaForward * Math.cos(heading) - deltaStrafe * Math.sin(heading);
y += deltaForward * Math.sin(heading) + deltaStrafe * Math.cos(heading);
heading += deltaHeading;

prevForward = forwardEncoder.getCurrentPosition();
prevStrafe  = strafeEncoder.getCurrentPosition();
prevHeading = imu.getAngularOrientation().firstAngle;

telemetry.addData("X", x);
telemetry.addData("Y", y);
telemetry.addData("Heading", Math.toDegrees(heading));
\`\`\`

### Drive to Point
\`\`\`java
public void driveToPoint(double targetX, double targetY, double targetH) {
    while (distance(x, y, targetX, targetY) > 1.0 && opModeIsActive()) {
        updateOdometry();
        double dx = targetX - x;
        double dy = targetY - y;
        double drive  = dy * 0.05;
        double strafe = dx * 0.05;
        double turn   = (targetH - heading) * 0.03;
        setMecanumPowers(drive, strafe, turn);
    }
}
\`\`\`
`,

          {q:"In field-centric odometry, why multiply by cos(heading) and sin(heading)?",opts:["To convert units","To rotate the robot-relative movement into field-relative coordinates","To reduce drift","To measure heading"],ans:1},

      {id:"sfb2",title:"Electrical Safety on the Robot",est:"15 min",content:`## Electrical Safety

A 12V robot battery stores a LOT of energy. Mishandled, it can cause fires, burns, or permanent eye damage.

### The Golden Rules
1. **Always disconnect the battery before working on electrical components**
2. **Never short-circuit the battery** (touch + and - together â€” it will arc and can cause fires)
3. **Keep wires away from moving parts** â€” a spinning gear can strip insulation and short
4. **Secure all connections** â€” loose wires = arcing = fire risk
5. **Never use a battery that is damaged, swollen, or leaking**

### Pinch Points
Every rotating mechanism is a pinch point. Keep fingers, hair, and loose clothing away when the robot is powered.

### Safe Power-Up Sequence
1. Check all connections are secure
2. Ensure no one is touching moving parts
3. Clear the area and announce "powering up"
4. Connect battery
5. Arm main switch LAST

### Safe Power-Down Sequence
1. Arm switch OFF first
2. Wait for all motors to stop
3. Disconnect battery
4. NOW it's safe to work on the robot

### PPE at Build Meetings
- Safety glasses when cutting, grinding, or drilling
- No loose jewelry near machinery
- Closed-toe shoes always
`,

          {q:"What should you ALWAYS do before working on electrical components?",opts:["Put on gloves","Disconnect the battery","Turn off the lights","Wear safety glasses"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why are pinch points dangerous?",opts:["They cause electrical shorts","Rotating parts can catch fingers, hair, or clothing","They drain battery faster","They void the warranty"],ans:1},
          {q:"What is the correct LAST step when powering down the robot?",opts:["Turn off the arm switch","Disconnect the battery","Wait for motors to stop","Remove the camera"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
      {id:"sfb3",title:"Safe Robot Lifting and Transport",est:"12 min",content:`## Safe Handling of Heavy Robots

FRC robots can weigh up to 125 lbs. FTC robots up to 42 lbs. Improper lifting causes back injuries.

### Lifting Technique
1. **Bend at the knees, not the waist**
2. **Keep the robot close to your body**
3. **Lift with your legs, not your back**
4. **Use at least 2 people for any robot over 30 lbs**
5. **Communicate**: "Lifting in 3â€¦2â€¦1â€¦lift"

### Safe Transport
- Use a cart with straps â€” never carry a robot across a venue unstrapped
- Robot should be powered OFF during transport
- Protect fragile mechanisms with foam or padding
- Know where your robot's sharp edges are â€” warn others

### At Competition
- Pit crews: max 3 people in the pit at once (check event rules)
- When the robot is on the field, keep hands clear of all mechanisms
- Never reach into a running robot
- If something jams during a match, let the operators handle it â€” don't run onto the field

### Pre-Match Safety Check
Run through this mentally before every match:
- â˜ Battery fully charged and secure
- â˜ All fasteners tight
- â˜ No loose wires near mechanisms
- â˜ Camera/sensors in place
- â˜ Drive team briefed and ready
`,

        ]

      {id:"sfi2",title:"Competition Day Safety Protocols",est:"18 min",content:`## Safety at a FIRST Event

Competitions are busy, loud, and fast-paced. Safety becomes even more important when you're stressed.

### Pit Safety
- Max people in pit area (check event rules â€” usually 3-5)
- Safety glasses required when robot is powered
- Never run in the pit â€” walk, always
- Keep your pit area clean â€” cables on the floor are trip hazards

### Field Safety
- When the field is active, stay behind the protective barrier
- Only enter the field when instructed by field staff
- Never reach into the robot during a match â€” call for a timeout if needed
- Report any field damage or unsafe conditions immediately

### Robot Transport to the Field
- Use a cart, never carry the robot without control
- Battery must be connected and main switch accessible for field reset
- Have a drive team member at each end of the cart

### Electrical Safety Checks Before Every Match
\`\`\`
â˜ Battery voltage > 12.5V (FRC) or > 13V (FTC)
â˜ Battery connector fully seated
â˜ Main switch accessible (you'll need to reset quickly)
â˜ No exposed bare wire visible
â˜ All motor controller LEDs showing expected state
\`\`\`

### If Something Goes Wrong
- Robot catches fire: Activate main breaker immediately, alert field staff
- Someone gets hurt: Stop everything, call for help, don't move injured person
- Robot is tipping: Let it fall â€” don't try to catch a 125 lb robot
- Mechanism jams mid-match: Operators should try reverse â€” never reach in

      {id:"pya4",title:"Building a Scouting Dashboard with Flask",est:"35 min",content:`## Scouting Dashboard with Flask

Build a live web dashboard your whole team can view during competition â€” runs on a laptop on the pit WiFi.

### Setup
\`\`\`bash
pip install flask pandas
\`\`\`

### app.py â€” The Server
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, render_template, jsonify, request
import pandas as pd, json, os

app = Flask(__name__)
DATA_FILE = "scouting.json"

def load_data():
    if os.path.exists(DATA_FILE):
        with open(DATA_FILE) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    return []

def save_data(data):
    with open(DATA_FILE, "w") as f:
        json.dump(data, f)

@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template("index.html")

@app.route("/api/entries", methods=["GET"])
def get_entries():
    return jsonify(load_data())

@app.route("/api/submit", methods=["POST"])
def submit():
    entry = request.json
    data = load_data()
    data.append(entry)
    save_data(data)
    return jsonify({"ok": True})

@app.route("/api/stats")
def stats():
    data = load_data()
    if not data:
        return jsonify({})
    df = pd.DataFrame(data)
    df["total"] = df["auto"].fillna(0) + df["teleop"].fillna(0)
    result = df.groupby("team")["total"].agg(["mean","max","count"]).round(2)
    return jsonify(result.reset_index().to_dict(orient="records"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)
\`\`\`

### Run It
\`\`\`bash
python app.py
# Open http://YOUR_LAPTOP_IP:5000 on any device on the same WiFi
\`\`\`

### What Your Scouts See
Each scout opens the dashboard on their phone, submits match data via a form, and the stats page auto-updates with team averages.

      {id:"jb16",title:"If Statements and Logic in Robot Code",est:"18 min",content:`## Decisions in Robot Code

Robots need to make decisions â€” if statements let your code react to the world.

### Basic If Statement
\`\`\`java
double power = gamepad1.left_stick_y;

if (power > 0.1) {
    telemetry.addData("Moving", "Forward");
} else if (power < -0.1) {
    telemetry.addData("Moving", "Backward");
} else {
    telemetry.addData("Moving", "Stopped");
    power = 0; // deadzone â€” ignore tiny stick values
}
\`\`\`

### Boolean Logic (AND, OR, NOT)
\`\`\`java
boolean aPressed = gamepad1.a;
boolean bPressed = gamepad1.b;

// AND: both must be true
if (aPressed && bPressed) {
    robot.activateSpecialMode();
}

// OR: at least one must be true
if (aPressed || bPressed) {
    intake.setPower(1.0);
}

// NOT: reverse a boolean
if (!limitSwitch.isPressed()) {
    lift.setPower(0.8); // only run if NOT at limit
}
\`\`\`

### Deadzone â€” Stop Joystick Drift
\`\`\`java
// Joysticks never perfectly return to 0.0
// Always apply a deadzone to prevent robot creep
double raw = gamepad1.left_stick_y;
double deadzoned = Math.abs(raw) > 0.05 ? raw : 0.0;
motor.setPower(deadzoned);
\`\`\`

### Toggle with Button
\`\`\`java
boolean clawOpen = false;
boolean lastA = false; // track previous state

// In loop():
boolean currentA = gamepad1.a;
if (currentA && !lastA) { // rising edge â€” button just pressed
    clawOpen = !clawOpen;  // toggle
    claw.setPosition(clawOpen ? 1.0 : 0.0);
}
lastA = currentA;
\`\`\`

      {id:"ji16",title:"Encoders and Precise Movement",est:"25 min",content:`## Encoder-Based Driving

Encoders measure exactly how far your motors have turned, enabling precise autonomous movement.

### What is an Encoder?
A small sensor attached to the motor shaft that counts electrical pulses as it rotates. More ticks = more rotation.

\`\`\`
Typical FTC motor: 537.7 ticks per revolution (goBILDA 5202)
If wheel diameter = 4 inches:
  Circumference = Ï€ Ã— 4 = 12.57 inches
  Ticks per inch = 537.7 / 12.57 = 42.8 ticks/inch
\`\`\`

### Setting Up Encoders
\`\`\`java
// In init():
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
\`\`\`

### Drive a Specific Distance
\`\`\`java
public void driveInches(double inches, double power) {
    int ticks = (int)(inches * TICKS_PER_INCH); // e.g. 42.8

    leftDrive.setTargetPosition(leftDrive.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);
    rightDrive.setTargetPosition(rightDrive.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);

    leftDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
    rightDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);

    leftDrive.setPower(power);
    rightDrive.setPower(power);

    while (leftDrive.isBusy() && rightDrive.isBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {
        telemetry.addData("Left ticks", leftDrive.getCurrentPosition());
        telemetry.addData("Right ticks", rightDrive.getCurrentPosition());
        telemetry.update();
    }

    leftDrive.setPower(0);
    rightDrive.setPower(0);
    leftDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
    rightDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
}
\`\`\`

### Turning with Encoders
Turn by driving one side forward and the other backward:
\`\`\`java
public void turnDegrees(double degrees, double power) {
    // Robot width Ã— Ï€ Ã— (degrees/360) = arc length to travel
    double arcInches = ROBOT_WIDTH_INCHES * Math.PI * (degrees / 360.0);
    int ticks = (int)(arcInches * TICKS_PER_INCH);

    leftDrive.setTargetPosition(leftDrive.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);
    rightDrive.setTargetPosition(rightDrive.getCurrentPosition() - ticks);
    // ... run to position same as above
}
\`\`\`

      {id:"ja13",title:"Multithreading in FTC",est:"30 min",content:`## Multithreading â€” Do Two Things at Once

In FTC, multithreading lets your robot update sensors or run background tasks without blocking the main loop.

### The Problem
\`\`\`java
// This BLOCKS the whole loop for 500ms:
sleep(500);
// Nothing else can happen during this time!
\`\`\`

### Solution: Background Thread
\`\`\`java
public class SensorThread extends Thread {
    volatile double distance = 0;
    DistanceSensor sensor;
    volatile boolean running = true;

    public SensorThread(DistanceSensor sensor) {
        this.sensor = sensor;
    }

    @Override
    public void run() {
        while (running) {
            distance = sensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM);
            try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
        }
    }

    public void stopThread() { running = false; }
}
\`\`\`

### Using It in OpMode
\`\`\`java
SensorThread sensorThread;

@Override public void init() {
    DistanceSensor ds = hardwareMap.get(DistanceSensor.class, "dist");
    sensorThread = new SensorThread(ds);
    sensorThread.start(); // Runs in background
}

@Override public void loop() {
    // Main loop still runs freely
    double dist = sensorThread.distance; // Read latest value
    if (dist < 10) { intake.setPower(0); }

    leftDrive.setPower(-gamepad1.left_stick_y);
}

@Override public void stop() {
    sensorThread.stopThread(); // Always clean up!
}
\`\`\`

### volatile Keyword
\`\`\`java
volatile double distance = 0;
\`\`\`
**volatile** tells Java this variable can change from another thread. Without it, Java might cache a stale value.

### Thread Safety Rules
1. Use **volatile** for simple values shared between threads
2. Use **synchronized** blocks for complex data structures
3. Always call **stopThread()** in stop() to prevent memory leaks
4. Keep threads simple â€” no UI updates or hardware calls from background threads

        ]
