      {id:"mb13",title:"Reading Engineering Drawings",est:"18 min",content:`## Reading Engineering Drawings (Technical Drawings)

Every manufactured part comes with a drawing. Learning to read them lets you order the right parts and build correctly.

### The Three Views
Engineering drawings show three orthogonal views:
\`\`\`
      Top View
         â†‘
Left â† [Part] â†’ Right View
         â†“
      Front View
\`\`\`

### Dimensions
Numbers on drawings show size in inches or millimeters:
- **2.500** = 2.5 inches (trailing zeros mean precision)
- **Ã˜0.500** = hole diameter of 0.5 inches (Ã˜ means diameter)
- **4Ã—** = feature repeated 4 times

### Title Block (Bottom Right Corner)
Every drawing has a title block showing:
- Part name and number
- Material (e.g., 6061-T6 Aluminum)
- Scale (e.g., 1:2 means drawing is half real size)
- Tolerance (e.g., Â±0.010 means Â±10 thousandths allowed)
- Revision (A, B, C â€” newer revisions fix errors)

### Tolerances â€” How Precise?
| Tolerance | What It Means |
|-----------|---------------|
| Â±0.100 | Low precision â€” rough cut OK |
| Â±0.010 | Medium â€” CNC or careful hand work |
| Â±0.001 | High â€” requires precision machining |

### Bill of Materials (BOM)
Many drawings include a parts list:
- Part number, description, quantity, material
- Use this to order everything needed before building

**Pro tip**: When in doubt, measure twice, cut once. A misread drawing wastes expensive material.

      {id:"mi12",title:"CAD Design Principles for FIRST",est:"25 min",content:`## CAD for Robot Design

Computer-Aided Design (CAD) lets you design your robot digitally before cutting any metal. Most FIRST teams use Onshape (free, browser-based) or Fusion 360.

### Why CAD First?
- Catch design problems before wasting materials
- Measure exact dimensions for ordering parts
- Create technical drawings for manufacturing
- Document your design for future seasons
- Share with mentors and team members remotely

### Onshape Basics (Free for FIRST Teams)
1. **Part Studio** â€” design individual parts
2. **Assembly** â€” combine parts into the full robot
3. **Drawing** â€” create manufacturing drawings

### Key Operations
| Operation | What It Does |
|-----------|-------------|
| Sketch | Draw 2D shapes on a plane |
| Extrude | Pull a 2D sketch into 3D |
| Revolve | Rotate a sketch around an axis |
| Fillet | Round sharp corners |
| Mirror | Copy across a plane |
| Pattern | Repeat a feature N times |

### Design for Manufacture
Always ask: **"Can we actually build this?"**
- Minimum feature size for 3D print: 1mm walls
- Minimum hole size for hand drill: 3mm
- Aluminum sheet: cut with bandsaw or CNC router
- Don't design features that require 5-axis machining if you only have a drill

### Version Control in CAD
Use branches or versions in Onshape to try designs without losing your previous work. Label versions before major changes: "V1-working", "V2-lighter-frame".

### FIRST CAD Resources
- Onshape FIRST tech challenge app: pre-made FTC parts
- GrabCAD: free models of motors, servos, REV parts
- Chief Delphi: FRC community with shared CAD
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What does 'design for manufacture' mean?",opts:["Make the robot look good","Design parts that can actually be built with available tools","Use standard parts only","Minimize cost"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"ma4b",title:"Swerve Drive Kinematics",est:"35 min",content:`## Swerve Drive â€” The Most Advanced Drivetrain

Swerve drive lets every wheel both drive AND steer independently, enabling movement in any direction while facing any direction.

### Why Swerve?
- Move sideways, diagonally, or rotate while translating
- No need to turn before driving somewhere
- Maximum field coverage and agility
- Used by most top FRC teams today

### How One Module Works
Each swerve module has:
1. **Drive motor** â€” controls wheel speed
2. **Steer motor** â€” controls wheel angle (0Â°â€“360Â°)
3. **Absolute encoder** â€” knows exact wheel angle at all times

### Inverse Kinematics â€” The Math
Given robot translation (vx, vy) and rotation (omega):
\`\`\`java
// For each of 4 modules (front-left, front-right, back-left, back-right):
// L = half wheelbase, W = half trackwidth

double fl_vx = vx - omega * L;    double fl_vy = vy + omega * W;
double fr_vx = vx - omega * L;    double fr_vy = vy - omega * W;
double bl_vx = vx + omega * L;    double bl_vy = vy + omega * W;
double br_vx = vx + omega * L;    double br_vy = vy - omega * W;

// Speed and angle for each module:
double fl_speed = Math.hypot(fl_vx, fl_vy);
double fl_angle = Math.atan2(fl_vy, fl_vx); // radians
\`\`\`

### Field-Centric Control
Rotate driver inputs by robot's current heading so "forward" is always away from driver:
\`\`\`java
double heading = imu.getYaw(); // degrees

// Rotate joystick vector by -heading
double fieldX = vx * Math.cos(-heading) - vy * Math.sin(-heading);
double fieldY = vx * Math.sin(-heading) + vy * Math.cos(-heading);
\`\`\`

### Wheel Angle Optimization
Never rotate a wheel more than 90Â° â€” instead, flip direction:
\`\`\`java
double delta = targetAngle - currentAngle;
if (Math.abs(delta) > 90) {
    targetAngle += 180; // flip direction
    speed *= -1;
}
\`\`\`

### WPILib Swerve (FRC)
FRC teams use WPILib's built-in swerve classes:
\`\`\`java
ChassisSpeeds speeds = ChassisSpeeds.fromFieldRelativeSpeeds(vx, vy, omega, heading);
SwerveModuleState[] states = kinematics.toSwerveModuleStates(speeds);
SwerveDriveKinematics.desaturateWheelSpeeds(states, MAX_SPEED);
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What is field-centric control?",opts:["Robot always faces forward","Joystick forward always means away from the driver regardless of robot heading","Robot is locked to the field","Control from the field side"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why flip wheel direction instead of rotating more than 90 degrees?",opts:["Saves battery","Reaches target angle faster â€” never rotate more than 90Â°","Required by kinematics","Prevents motor damage"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"ei8",title:"Servo Control and PWM Signals",est:"20 min",content:`## Servos and PWM

Servos are motors with built-in position control. They're used for claws, arms, hoods, and anything needing precise position.

### Standard Servo vs Continuous Rotation
| Type | setPosition() | What Happens |
|------|---------------|-------------|
| Standard | 0.0 â€“ 1.0 | Moves to angle (0Â° â€“ 180Â°) |
| Continuous | 0.0 â€“ 1.0 | Controls SPEED (0.5 = stop) |
| Axon MAX | 0.0 â€“ 1.0 | 355Â° range, very strong |

### Basic Servo Code
\`\`\`java
Servo claw = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "claw");

// Open and close with buttons
if (gamepad1.a) {
    claw.setPosition(1.0); // Fully open
}
if (gamepad1.b) {
    claw.setPosition(0.0); // Fully closed
}

// Intermediate position
claw.setPosition(0.5); // Halfway
\`\`\`

### PWM â€” How Servos Get Their Signal
PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) sends pulses to the servo:
- 1ms pulse = 0Â° position
- 1.5ms pulse = 90Â° position
- 2ms pulse = 180Â° position
- Repeats every 20ms (50Hz)

The Control Hub handles PWM timing automatically â€” you just use setPosition().

### Servo Range Extension
Some servos can be reprogrammed with a servo programmer to extend their range beyond 180Â°.

### Linkage Design
Servo rotation (0Â°â€“180Â°) becomes linear motion through a linkage:
\`\`\`
Servo arm 25mm â†’ pushrod â†’ output moves 25mm linearly
\`\`\`
Use CAD to design linkages and check for binding at all positions.

### Multiple Servos Moving Together
\`\`\`java
Servo left = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "left_arm");
Servo right = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "right_arm");
right.setDirection(Servo.Direction.REVERSE); // Mirror

// Now both servos move in sync when you set the same position
left.setPosition(pos);
right.setPosition(pos);
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What PWM pulse width corresponds to the 90Â° (center) position?",opts:["1ms","1.5ms","2ms","2.5ms"],ans:1},
          {q:"How do you make two mirrored servos move in sync?",opts:["Set different positions","Reverse one servo's direction, then set same position on both","Connect them physically","Use separate programs"],ans:1},
        ]
      },

      {id:"ea4x2",title:"CAN Bus and Smart Motor Controllers",est:"28 min",content:`## CAN Bus â€” The FRC Electrical Backbone

CAN (Controller Area Network) is a communication protocol that lets motor controllers, sensors, and the roboRIO share data on a two-wire bus.

### Why CAN Over PWM?
| Feature | PWM | CAN |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Wires needed | 3 per device | 2 shared bus |
| Feedback | None | Full telemetry |
| Velocity control | External | Built-in |
| Current limiting | External | Built-in |
| Addresses | None | Each device has ID |

### Wiring CAN Bus
\`\`\`
roboRIO â†’ [CAN H / CAN L] â†’ SPARK MAX â†’ SPARK MAX â†’ SPARK MAX â†’ PDH
                              (ID: 1)      (ID: 2)      (ID: 3)
\`\`\`
Daisy-chain all devices. Terminate the last device with a 120Î© resistor.

### REV SPARK MAX Configuration
\`\`\`java
// Set CAN ID via REV Hardware Client (USB)
// Then use in code:
CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless); // ID 1

// Velocity control (RPM) â€” built-in closed loop
SparkMaxPIDController pid = motor.getPIDController();
RelativeEncoder encoder = motor.getEncoder();

pid.setP(0.0001);
pid.setI(0);
pid.setD(0);
pid.setFF(0.000175); // Feedforward for NEO

// Set target: 3000 RPM
pid.setReference(3000, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kVelocity);

// Read actual RPM
double currentRPM = encoder.getVelocity();
\`\`\`

### Current Limiting (Very Important!)
\`\`\`java
motor.setSmartCurrentLimit(40); // Amps â€” prevents brownouts and motor damage
// Drivetrain: 40A each
// Mechanism motors: 20-30A
// Small mechanisms: 10-15A
\`\`\`

### Status Frames â€” Reduce CAN Bus Load
\`\`\`java
// Only request data you need â€” reduces 50% of bus traffic
motor.setPeriodicFramePeriod(CANSparkMax.PeriodicFrame.kStatus0, 10);  // Applied output, faults
motor.setPeriodicFramePeriod(CANSparkMax.PeriodicFrame.kStatus1, 20);  // Velocity, current
motor.setPeriodicFramePeriod(CANSparkMax.PeriodicFrame.kStatus2, 100); // Position (slower is fine)
\`\`\`

      {id:"si8",title:"Alliance Communication During Matches",est:"18 min",content:`## In-Match Alliance Communication

The 2:30 of a match is chaotic. Good communication is the difference between a coordinated alliance and three robots getting in each other's way.

### Pre-Match Alliance Meeting (5 minutes)
Before every match, your alliance gets 5 minutes together. Use ALL of it:
1. **Introduce yourselves and your robot's capabilities**
2. **Assign explicit roles**: Who scores where? Who runs defense? Who feeds?
3. **Set auto strategy**: Do your autos conflict? Who goes where?
4. **Agree on signals**: What does thumbs-up mean? Thumbs-down?
5. **Set a cycle target**: "We need 10 cycles to win"
6. **Endgame timing**: "We all stop at :30 and go for climb"

### During the Match â€” Driver Communication
Your alliance has 2-way radio communication between driver stations.
- Keep calls SHORT: "I'm blocked", "Open on left", "Go for climb"
- Use team numbers: "254, your side is open"
- Never talk over each other â€” designate one person as communicator

### Human Player Communication
Your human player on the field can signal your robot team:
- Thumbs up = execute plan A
- Point = direct robot to that zone
- Wave = come to my side

### When Plans Break Down
Plan A rarely survives contact with reality. Practice Plan B:
- Auto fails â†’ default to driving to safe zone
- Alliance partner breaks down â†’ redistribute their scoring role
- Opponent plays defense â†’ switch to opposite side

### Post-Match Debrief (2 minutes)
After every match:
- What worked? What didn't?
- Did the alliance stick to the plan?
- Any robot issues to fix before next match?
- Update scouting notes on opponents you just played against
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What should you do when Plan A fails mid-match?",opts:["Panic","Stop playing","Execute a pre-planned Plan B â€” redistribute roles as needed","Call for a timeout"],ans:2},
        ]
      },

      {id:"sa9",title:"OPR, DPR, and CCWM Explained",est:"22 min",content:`## Advanced Match Statistics

### OPR â€” Offensive Power Rating
OPR estimates how many points a team contributes per match, calculated by solving a system of linear equations across all match results.

\`\`\`
If Team A + Team B + Team C = 85 points (match 1)
And Team A + Team D + Team E = 72 points (match 2)
...
OPR solves for each team's individual contribution
\`\`\`

**Interpretation:**
- High OPR = high scoring contribution
- OPR is an ESTIMATE â€” solo testing or defense affect it
- Useful for initial alliance selection sorting

### DPR â€” Defensive Power Rating
DPR estimates how many points a team's opponents score LESS when that team is in the match.

- High DPR = effective defense player
- Low DPR (negative) = opponents score more â€” avoid this team on defense

### CCWM â€” Calculated Contribution to Winning Margin
CCWM = OPR âˆ’ DPR

The most complete single metric. A team with high CCWM both scores a lot AND prevents opponents from scoring.

### Auto OPR (Auto Points Contribution)
Some scouting platforms calculate Auto OPR separately â€” crucial because:
- Auto points often have multipliers
- Consistent auto = reliable points even when teleop is inconsistent
- Helps identify teams who are great scorers but have no auto

### Using Stats Wisely
\`\`\`
Don't: rank teams purely by OPR and pick in order
Do: combine OPR with:
  - Consistency (std deviation)
  - Climb rate (% of matches)
  - Auto reliability
  - Your own scouting observations
\`\`\`

Stats describe the past â€” your scouts observe the present. A team that fixed a bug between events won't show it in stats yet.
`,quiz:[

          {q:"Why shouldn't you rely solely on OPR for alliance selection?",opts:["OPR is inaccurate","Stats describe the past â€” recent changes and scouting observations are also critical","OPR is too complex","It's not available at events"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],

      {id:"pi11b",title:"Web Scraping The Blue Alliance",est:"25 min",content:`## Getting Match Data from The Blue Alliance

The Blue Alliance (TBA) has an API that gives you real FRC match data. No manual data entry needed.

### Get Your API Key
1. Go to **thebluealliance.com**
2. Create an account
3. Go to Account â†’ Read API Keys
4. Create a key named "scouting tool"

### Basic API Call
\`\`\`python
import requests

API_KEY = "your_key_here"
HEADERS = {"X-TBA-Auth-Key": API_KEY}
BASE = "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3"

def get_event_teams(event_code):
    # event_code like "2024ctwat" or "2024micmp"
    url = f"{BASE}/event/{event_code}/teams/simple"
    r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

teams = get_event_teams("2024micmp")
for team in teams[:5]:
    print(f"Team {team['team_number']}: {team['nickname']}")
\`\`\`

### Get Match Results
\`\`\`python
def get_event_matches(event_code):
    url = f"{BASE}/event/{event_code}/matches/simple"
    r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS)
    return r.json()

matches = get_event_matches("2024micmp")
for match in matches[:3]:
    red_score = match['alliances']['red']['score']
    blue_score = match['alliances']['blue']['score']
    print(f"{match['key']}: Red {red_score} - Blue {blue_score}")
\`\`\`

### Get Team OPR
\`\`\`python
def get_event_oprs(event_code):
    url = f"{BASE}/event/{event_code}/oprs"
    r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS)
    data = r.json()
    # Returns: {"oprs": {"frc254": 45.2, ...}, "dprs": {...}, "ccwms": {...}}
    return data

oprs = get_event_oprs("2024micmp")
# Sort teams by OPR
sorted_teams = sorted(oprs["oprs"].items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("Top 5 by OPR:")
for team, opr in sorted_teams[:5]:
    print(f"  {team}: {opr:.1f}")
\`\`\`

      {id:"sfa2",title:"Pneumatics Safety (FRC)",est:"20 min",content:`## Pneumatics Safety in FRC

Pneumatic systems use compressed air (up to 120 PSI working pressure) to power cylinders and actuators. High pressure means serious safety risks if mishandled.

### FRC Pneumatics Rules
- Max storage pressure: **120 PSI** (stored in tanks)
- Max working pressure: **60 PSI** (after the regulator)
- Relief valve must be set to release at 125 PSI

### Safe Pressure-Up Procedure
1. Ensure all fittings are connected and secure
2. Keep everyone clear of cylinders (they WILL move when pressurized)
3. Turn on compressor gradually â€” monitor pressure gauge
4. Listen for hissing (air leaks) â€” shut down if you hear any
5. Verify relief valve pops at correct pressure

### Safe Pressure-Down Procedure
**Before working on pneumatics, ALWAYS bleed the system:**
\`\`\`
1. Disable robot
2. Manually actuate each solenoid valve to exhaust air
3. Verify pressure gauge reads 0 PSI
4. Open the manual bleed valve if available
5. Confirm all cylinders are fully retracted or in safe position
NEVER disconnect a fitting under pressure!
\`\`\`

### Leak Detection
- Use soapy water on fittings â€” bubbles = leak
- Common leak points: push-to-connect fittings, solenoid valves, cylinder ports
- Never use your hand to feel for leaks (high-pressure air can penetrate skin)

### Cylinder Safety
- Cylinders extend with force â€” keep fingers, eyes, and faces clear
- Know the cylinder's max force: Force = Pressure Ã— Area
- A 1" bore cylinder at 60 PSI = 47 lbs of force
- Add physical hard stops in CAD so cylinders can't slam mechanisms into the robot

### Solenoid Valves
- Single-acting: spring return when unenergized (safer â€” returns to known state)
- Double-acting: holds position when unenergized (must account for this in code)

      {id:"sb10",title:"Understanding the Ranking System",est:"15 min",content:`## How FIRST Rankings Work

Understanding rankings helps you make smart decisions during qualifications.

### FRC Ranking Points (RP)
Teams earn Ranking Points (RP) each match â€” it's not about wins alone.

**Standard RP:**
- Win = 2 RP Â· Tie = 1 RP Â· Loss = 0 RP

**Bonus RP:** Awarded for hitting game-specific thresholds
- Usually 1-2 bonus RP per match (e.g., "Score 25 points in auto")
- You can earn bonus RP even if you LOSE

**Why this matters:**
A team that wins 60% of matches with bonus RP every time often ranks HIGHER than a team that wins 80% but rarely earns bonus RP.

### FTC Ranking Points
FTC uses actual alliance score as the ranking point â€” simpler:
- Qualification Points (QP) = your alliance's final score
- Ties in QP: use Ranking Points (RP) = opponent's score
- Win big â†’ high QP â†’ high rank

### Seeding â€” Why It Matters
- Seeds 1â€“8 become Alliance Captains
- Seed 1 picks first and has the strongest negotiating position
- Seeds 9+ are picked â€” they don't choose

**Strategy implication:** Late in qualifications, if you're safely in seeds 1â€“8, focus on keeping your robot healthy. If you're seed 9â€“12, you need big performances to move up.

### Win-Loss Record vs. Ranking
In FRC, two teams with the same win-loss record can be ranked very differently based on RP. Always know:
1. How many RP do you have?
2. What RP are available in your next match?
3. What bonus can you realistically hit?
`,quiz:[
          {q:"In FRC, how many RP does a WIN give?",opts:["1","2","3","4"],ans:1},
          {q:"What is the advantage of being seeded 1-8 in FRC playoffs?",opts:["Automatic win","You become an Alliance Captain and choose your partners","You get extra RP","You skip to finals"],ans:1},
          {q:"Can you earn bonus RP even if your alliance loses?",opts:["No â€” only winners earn bonus RP","Yes â€” bonus RP are earned by hitting game thresholds regardless of win/loss","Only if both alliances agree","Only captains earn bonus RP"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"si9",title:"Reading Your Opponents",est:"20 min",content:`## Opponent Analysis During Competition

The teams you'll face in playoffs are still competing in qualifications. Every match is a scouting opportunity.

### What to Watch For
**Autonomous:**
- Does their auto work consistently? (Watch 3+ matches)
- Do they leave the starting zone?
- Which field elements do they target?
- Do they interfere with alliance partners?

**Teleop:**
- How fast is their cycle? Count game piece deliveries per minute.
- Where do they score? High goal only? Low too?
- Do they drive defensively when losing?
- Any patterns in their movement?

**Endgame:**
- Do they always attempt climb?
- What's their climb success rate?
- How early do they start climbing?

### The Red Flag List
These patterns indicate unreliable robots to avoid in alliance selection:
- âŒ Auto works 1 in 3 matches
- âŒ They break down mid-match
- âŒ Their cycle time varies wildly (5 cycles one match, 2 the next)
- âŒ They take penalties every match
- âŒ They never climb despite attempting

### Building Your Scouting Database
Track for every team:
\`\`\`
Team # | Auto âœ“/âœ— | Avg Cycles | Best Score | Climb% | Notes
---------|-----------|------------|------------|--------|------
4512    | 9/10 âœ“   | 7.2/match  | 52 pts     | 90%    | Strong auto, reliable
1234    | 3/9 âœ—    | 4.1/match  | 31 pts     | 40%    | Inconsistent auto
\`\`\`

### Trust Your Scouts Over Stats
Stats are averages. Your scouts see what actually happened:
- That team's OPR looks high because they had easy opponents
- That team fixed their auto after match 5 â€” stats don't show that
- That team plays dirty defense when losing â€” you need to know

**The goal:** Enter alliance selection knowing the strengths, weaknesses, and reliability of every top-20 team.

double targetHeading = 90.0;  // 90 degrees left

while (opModeIsActive()) {
    double current = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles()
                        .getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES);
    double error = targetHeading - current;
    
    // Wrap error to -180 to +180
    if (error > 180)  error -= 360;
    if (error < -180) error += 360;
    
    double turnPower = error * 0.015;  // P controller
    turnPower = Math.max(-0.5, Math.min(0.5, turnPower));
    
    leftDrive.setPower(-turnPower);
    rightDrive.setPower(turnPower);
    
    if (Math.abs(error) < 2.0) break;  // Close enough!
}`,explanation:"Error wrapping handles the -180/+180 boundary. Without it, trying to turn from 170Â° to -170Â° would spin the long way around (340Â°) instead of the short way (20Â°). The P gain of 0.015 gives smooth, stable turns."},

                    .getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES);
double radians = Math.toRadians(heading);

double driveX = gamepad1.left_stick_x;
double driveY = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;

double fieldY = driveX*Math.sin(radians) + driveY*Math.cos(radians);`,explanation:"Field-centric drive means joystick 'forward' always moves the robot away from the driver regardless of which way the robot is facing.       {id:"pya5",title:"OPR Calculator in Python",est:"30 min",content:`## Calculate OPR from Match Data

OPR (Offensive Power Rating) solves a system of equations to estimate each team's contribution.

### The Math
Given N matches, for each match:
\`\`\`
team_A_OPR + team_B_OPR + team_C_OPR = alliance_score
\`\`\`
Across all matches this forms a system Ax = b where:
- A = match participation matrix (1 if team played, 0 if not)
- x = OPR vector we want to solve for
- b = alliance scores

### Implementation
\`\`\`python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def calculate_opr(matches_df):
    """
    matches_df columns: team1, team2, team3, score
    """
    teams = sorted(set(
        matches_df['team1'].tolist() +
        matches_df['team2'].tolist() +
        matches_df['team3'].tolist()
    ))
    team_idx = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(teams)}
    n = len(teams)
    m = len(matches_df)
    
    # Build participation matrix
    A = np.zeros((m, n))
    b = np.zeros(m)
    
    for i, row in matches_df.iterrows():
        A[i, team_idx[row['team1']]] = 1
        A[i, team_idx[row['team2']]] = 1
        A[i, team_idx[row['team3']]] = 1
        b[i] = row['score']
    
    # Least squares solution: A^T A x = A^T b
    x, _, _, _ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)
    
    return {team: round(float(opr), 2) for team, opr in zip(teams, x)}

# Example usage
data = {
    'team1': [254, 118, 971],
    'team2': [1678, 254, 118],
    'team3': [148, 330, 1678],
    'score': [85, 72, 91]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
oprs = calculate_opr(df)
for team, opr in sorted(oprs.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"Team {team}: {opr:.1f}")
\`\`\`

### Interpreting Results
- OPR is an ESTIMATE â€” small sample sizes (< 6 matches) have high uncertainty
- Calculate DPR by running the same algorithm on opponent scores
- CCWM = OPR - DPR (net contribution to winning margin)
- High OPR teams should be your first alliance picks
`,quiz:[
          {q:"What mathematical method does OPR use?",opts:["Simple averaging","Least squares regression solving Ax=b","Maximum likelihood","Monte Carlo simulation"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why is OPR unreliable with few matches?",opts:["The math breaks down","Small sample sizes have high uncertainty â€” outliers skew the estimate","Teams play differently early on","The API doesn't report early match data"],ans:1},
          {q:"What does np.linalg.lstsq() solve?",opts:["Finds the maximum value","Solves an overdetermined system of linear equations by least squares","Calculates averages","Sorts data"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },
};

      {id:"jb20",title:"Robot Telemetry and Debugging",est:"16 min",content:`## Telemetry â€” Your Robot's Debug Console

Telemetry sends data from the robot to the Driver Hub screen. Without it, debugging is guesswork.

### Basic Telemetry
\`\`\`java
// In loop():
telemetry.addData("Motor Power", leftDrive.getPower());
telemetry.addData("Encoder Pos", leftDrive.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("Heading", imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles().getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES));
telemetry.addData("Claw State", clawOpen ? "OPEN" : "CLOSED");
telemetry.update(); // MUST call this â€” sends data to screen
\`\`\`

### Format Numbers Cleanly
\`\`\`java
// Basic: shows many decimal places
telemetry.addData("Power", leftDrive.getPower()); // e.g. 0.6000003814697266

// Formatted: 2 decimal places
telemetry.addData("Power", String.format("%.2f", leftDrive.getPower())); // e.g. 0.60
\`\`\`

### Categories with Lines
\`\`\`java
telemetry.addLine("=== DRIVE ===");
telemetry.addData("Left", leftPow);
telemetry.addData("Right", rightPow);
telemetry.addLine("=== ARM ===");
telemetry.addData("Arm Pos", arm.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("Arm Target", armTarget);
telemetry.update();
\`\`\`

### Debug Mode Toggle
\`\`\`java
boolean debugMode = false;

// In loop():
if (gamepad1.back) debugMode = !debugMode;

if (debugMode) {
    // Detailed telemetry that might slow things down
    telemetry.addData("Encoder L", leftDrive.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.addData("Encoder R", rightDrive.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.addData("IMU Yaw", heading);
    telemetry.addData("Loop Time", loopTimer.milliseconds());
}
\`\`\`

### Log vs Data
\`\`\`java
// .addData() â€” shown on screen, refreshes each update
telemetry.addData("Live", sensorValue);

// .log() â€” persistent log that stays on screen (max 9 entries)
telemetry.log().add("Auto started at " + System.currentTimeMillis());
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

VisionPortal visionPortal;
ColorBlobLocatorProcessor colorProcessor;

// Detect yellow game elements

    .setTargetColorRange(ColorRange.YELLOW)
    .setRoi(ImageRegion.asUnityCenterCoordinates(-1,1,1,-1))
    .build();

visionPortal = new VisionPortal.Builder()
    .addProcessor(colorProcessor)
    .setCameraResolution(new Size(640, 480))
    .build();`,explanation:"VisionPortal is the FTC SDK's unified camera framework. ColorBlobLocatorProcessor finds blobs of a specific color. You choose a Region of Interest (ROI) â€” often just the full image but can be restricted to avoid false detections."},
          {type:"sensor",label:"Find Largest Blob",code:`List<ColorBlobLocatorProcessor.Blob> blobs =
    colorProcessor.getBlobs();

if (blobs.isEmpty()) {
    telemetry.addData("Game Piece", "NOT FOUND");
} else {
    // Sort by area â€” biggest first
    ColorBlobLocatorProcessor.Util.filterByArea(200, Integer.MAX_VALUE, blobs);

    ColorBlobLocatorProcessor.Blob target = blobs.get(0);
    Rect box = target.getBoxFit();
    double centerX = box.x + box.width  / 2.0;
    double centerY = box.y + box.height / 2.0;
    telemetry.addData("Target X", centerX); // 0-640 pixels
    telemetry.addData("Target Y", centerY); // 0-480 pixels
}`,explanation:"getBlobs() returns all detected color regions. filterByArea() removes tiny noise blobs. The largest remaining blob is almost always the actual game piece. Center coordinates tell you where in the camera frame the piece is."},
          {type:"control",label:"Drive Toward Target",code:`// Image center X is ~320 pixels
double imageCenter = 320.0;
double error = centerX - imageCenter; // + means piece is to the right

// Proportional steer toward piece
double steer = error * 0.005; // tune this gain
double drive = 0.3;           // slow approach speed

leftDrive.setPower(drive - steer);
rightDrive.setPower(drive + steer);

// Stop when piece is centered AND close
if (Math.abs(error) < 20 && centerY > 350) {
    leftDrive.setPower(0);
    rightDrive.setPower(0);
    intake.setPower(1.0); // Grab it!
}`,explanation:"This is proportional visual servoing â€” drive toward the piece using camera error as feedback. Large error = big correction. Small error = gentle correction. Stop when centered (error < 20px) and close (high Y value = low in frame = near robot)."},
          {type:"action",label:"April Tag Navigation",code:`AprilTagProcessor aprilTag = new AprilTagProcessor.Builder()
    .setDrawTagOutline(true)
    .build();

// In auto loop:
List<AprilTagDetection> detections = aprilTag.getDetections();
for (AprilTagDetection det : detections) {
    if (det.id == 2) { // Target tag ID
        double range   = det.ftcPose.range;   // distance in inches
        double bearing = det.ftcPose.bearing; // angle to tag, degrees
        double yaw     = det.ftcPose.yaw;     // tag rotation

        // Drive to 6" in front of tag
        double driveErr  = range - 6.0;
        double steerErr  = bearing;
        leftDrive.setPower(driveErr*0.04 - steerErr*0.02);
        rightDrive.setPower(driveErr*0.04 + steerErr*0.02);
    }
}`,explanation:"AprilTag detection gives you precise field position. det.ftcPose.range is distance in inches, bearing is left/right angle in degrees. A simple P controller on both values drives you to exactly the right spot â€” very reliable for scoring positions."},

        ]

      {id:"ji19",title:"Linear OpMode vs Iterative OpMode",est:"20 min",content:`## Two Ways to Write FTC OpModes

FTC offers two base classes for OpModes. Choosing the right one matters.

### LinearOpMode â€” Sequential Programming
\`\`\`java
@TeleOp
public class MyLinear extends LinearOpMode {
    @Override
    public void runOpMode() {
        // Setup
        DcMotor motor = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "motor");
        waitForStart();

        // Runs once â€” you control the loop
        while (opModeIsActive()) {
            motor.setPower(-gamepad1.left_stick_y);
            telemetry.update();
        }
    }
}
\`\`\`
**Best for:** Autonomous (sequential steps), beginners learning flow control

### OpMode (Iterative) â€” Callback-Based
\`\`\`java
@TeleOp
public class MyIterative extends OpMode {
    DcMotor motor;

    @Override
    public void init() {
        motor = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "motor");
    }

    @Override
    public void loop() {
        // Called ~100 times/sec automatically
        motor.setPower(-gamepad1.left_stick_y);
        telemetry.update();
    }

    @Override
    public void stop() {
        motor.setPower(0); // Called once when STOP pressed
    }
}
\`\`\`
**Best for:** TeleOp, experienced programmers, time-sensitive loops

### Key Differences
| Feature | LinearOpMode | OpMode (Iterative) |
|---------|-------------|-------------------|
| Loop control | You write while() | SDK calls loop() for you |
| sleep() | âœ… Available | âŒ Never use (freezes) |
| Blocking | OK in auto | Never block |
| Best for | Autonomous | TeleOp |

### When to Use Each
- **Just starting out?** â†’ LinearOpMode for everything
- **Complex TeleOp?** â†’ Consider OpMode (Iterative)
- **Autonomous always** â†’ LinearOpMode (sequential steps make sense)
`,quiz:[
          {q:"Which OpMode type gives you direct control over the loop with while()?",opts:["OpMode (Iterative)","LinearOpMode","Both","Neither â€” the SDK controls all loops"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why should you NEVER use sleep() in an OpMode (Iterative) loop() method?",opts:["It wastes battery","It freezes the loop() callback â€” the robot becomes unresponsive","It's slower","Required by FTC rules"],ans:1},
          {q:"Which base class is generally better for autonomous routines?",opts:["OpMode (Iterative) â€” faster","LinearOpMode â€” sequential steps match auto logic naturally","They're identical","Neither â€” use CommandBased only"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
      {id:"ji20",title:"Finite State Machine â€” Deep Dive",est:"25 min",content:`## FSM Architecture for Complex Robots

A well-designed FSM lets your robot handle complex behaviors without spaghetti code.

### Why FSM?
Compare these two approaches for scoring a game piece:

**Sequential (breaks easily):**
\`\`\`java
driveToPosition(60);  // blocks â€” nothing else runs
sleep(200);
arm.setTarget(HIGH);
sleep(500);
intake.setPower(-1);
sleep(300);
\`\`\`

**FSM (robust, concurrent):**
\`\`\`java
// Each state is a small, focused task
enum State { DRIVE, RAISE_ARM, SCORE, RETRACT }
\`\`\`

### Multi-System FSM
\`\`\`java
enum DriveState { IDLE, DRIVE_TO_GOAL, ALIGN }
enum ArmState   { STOWED, RAISING, HIGH, SCORING, LOWERING }

DriveState driveState = DriveState.IDLE;
ArmState   armState   = ArmState.STOWED;

// Both FSMs run in the same loop â€” they're independent
switch (driveState) {
    case DRIVE_TO_GOAL:
        // Drive code
        break;
}
switch (armState) {
    case RAISING:
        // Arm code
        break;
}
\`\`\`

### Transition Triggers
States can transition based on:
| Trigger Type | Example |
|-------------|---------|
| Position reached | isBusy() == false |
| Sensor trip | distance < 5cm |
| Time elapsed | elapsed > 500ms |
| Button pressed | gamepad1.a |
| Score complete | colorSensor.red() > 200 |

### State History for Debugging
\`\`\`java
// Keep a log of state transitions for post-match debugging
List<String> stateLog = new ArrayList<>();

void transition(State newState) {
    stateLog.add(currentState + " â†’ " + newState + " at " + timer.seconds());
    currentState = newState;
}

// After match: print log
for (String entry : stateLog) {
    telemetry.log().add(entry);
}
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

      {id:"ja14",title:"Road Runner 1.0 â€” Trajectories",est:"35 min",content:`## Road Runner 1.0 â€” Modern FTC Pathing

Road Runner 1.0 (not legacy 0.5) uses a different API that's cleaner and more powerful.

### Setup in MecanumDrive
\`\`\`java
// Road Runner 1.0 uses a different pose representation
// Pose2d uses (x, y, heading) in inches and radians
Pose2d startPose = new Pose2d(0, 0, Math.toRadians(0));
MecanumDrive drive = new MecanumDrive(hardwareMap, startPose);
\`\`\`

### Building a Trajectory Action
\`\`\`java
// Trajectories are built as "Action" objects (RR 1.0)
Action trajectoryAction = drive.actionBuilder(startPose)
    .lineToX(24)           // Move 24" in current direction
    .waitSeconds(0.5)
    .lineToY(12)
    .turn(Math.toRadians(-90))
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(48, -12), Math.toRadians(0))
    .build();
\`\`\`

### Running Actions
\`\`\`java
// Actions run as a linear sequence
@Override
public void runOpMode() {
    MecanumDrive drive = new MecanumDrive(hardwareMap, startPose);

    Action auto = drive.actionBuilder(startPose)
        .lineToX(24)
        .build();

    waitForStart();

    // Run the action â€” blocks until complete
    Actions.runBlocking(auto);
}
\`\`\`

### Sequential + Parallel Actions
\`\`\`java
// SequentialAction: runs one after another
// ParallelAction: runs simultaneously
Action auto = new SequentialAction(
    drive.actionBuilder(startPose).lineToX(24).build(),
    new ParallelAction(
        arm.raiseAction(),           // Arm goes up
        drive.actionBuilder(...)     // While driving next segment
            .lineToY(12)
            .build()
    ),
    new InstantAction(() -> intake.setPower(-1))
);
\`\`\`

### Tuning (Critical!)
1. **DriveConstants**: Measure your wheel radius, track width, ticks per rev
2. **StraightTest**: Tune kV and kA feedforward
3. **TurnTest**: Tune kStatic and angular kV
4. **SplineTest**: Full path test
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What does ParallelAction allow you to do?",opts:["Run actions sequentially","Run multiple actions simultaneously (e.g., drive + arm at the same time)","Cancel other actions","Loop an action"],ans:1},
        ]
      },

          {type:"sensor",label:"REV Control Hub â€” Status LEDs",code:`// LED colors and what they mean:

// SOLID BLUE â€” Idle, no program running
// SOLID GREEN â€” Program running, everything OK
// BLINKING YELLOW â€” Waiting for OpMode selection
// SOLID RED â€” Low battery or hardware error

    .voltageSensor.iterator().next().getVoltage();

// BREATHING MAGENTA â€” Brushless, no signal
// YELLOW/MAGENTA ALTERNATE â€” Follower mode
// SOLID RED â€” Fault (overcurrent, sensor error)

      {id:"ea5b",title:"Closed-Loop Arm Control with Gravity Compensation",est:"30 min",content:`## Arm Control â€” The Hard Problem

Arms that lift against gravity require more than just PID â€” they need feedforward to hold position without oscillating.

### Why Pure PID Fails for Arms
\`\`\`
Problem: When arm is at 90Â° (horizontal), gravity pulls it down hard.
         At 0Â° (vertical up), gravity has no effect.
         Pure PID can't know this â€” it just sees position error.
\`\`\`

### Gravity Feedforward
\`\`\`java
// Arm angle in radians (0 = vertical, Ï€/2 = horizontal)
double armAngle = (encoder.getCurrentPosition() / TICKS_PER_REV) * 2 * Math.PI;

// Gravity compensation term â€” cosine because:
// At horizontal (90Â°): cos(90Â°) = 1.0 â€” maximum compensation needed
// At vertical (0Â°): cos(0Â°) = 1.0 â€” wait, vertical UP means no gravity pull...
// Use sin for arms where 0 = stowed, 90 = horizontal:
double kG = 0.15; // Tune this for your arm weight
double gravityFF = kG * Math.cos(armAngle); // cos for horizontal = max gravity

// Combined PIDF output:
double pidOutput = pid.calculate(encoder.getCurrentPosition(), targetTicks);
double totalOutput = pidOutput + gravityFF;
arm.set(totalOutput);
\`\`\`

### Anti-Windup for I Term
\`\`\`java
// Integrator windup: if arm is stuck at limit, I term builds forever
// When you finally move, the arm slams past target
pid.setIntegratorRange(-0.15, 0.15); // SPARK MAX / WPILib
\`\`\`

### Trapezoidal Motion Profile
\`\`\`java
// Instead of jumping to target, ramp velocity smoothly
// WPILib TrapezoidProfile:
TrapezoidProfile.Constraints constraints =
    new TrapezoidProfile.Constraints(300, 200); // max vel, max accel (ticks/s)

TrapezoidProfile profile = new TrapezoidProfile(constraints);
TrapezoidProfile.State goal = new TrapezoidProfile.State(targetTicks, 0);
TrapezoidProfile.State current = new TrapezoidProfile.State(encoder.getPosition(), encoder.getVelocity());

TrapezoidProfile.State setpoint = profile.calculate(0.02, current, goal); // 20ms dt
pid.setReference(setpoint.position, ControlType.kPosition);
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What does kG * cos(armAngle) compute?",opts:["Motor velocity","Gravity feedforward â€” the power needed to hold the arm against gravity at its current angle","Position error","Integral windup"],ans:1},
          {q:"What problem does anti-windup (setIntegratorRange) prevent?",opts:["Overheating","Integrator accumulating too large a value, causing the arm to slam past target when finally moving","Encoder noise","Speed limit"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"mi13",title:"Linear Slides â€” Design and Build",est:"25 min",content:`## Linear Slides for Vertical Extension

Linear slides let your robot reach far beyond its frame â€” essential for high-goal scoring and hanging.

### Slide Types
**V-Rail / C-Channel Cascade:**
- Each stage extends as the previous reaches limit
- Single motor can extend multiple stages (cascade)
- Used by: goBILDA, REV, Misumi

**Drawer Slides:**
- Commercial or custom
- Smooth, low friction
- Good load capacity

**Belt/String Cascade:**
- String connects stages â€” extending one extends all
- Faster than rack-and-pinion for same motor speed
- Complex rigging, string can break

### Extension Math
\`\`\`
3-stage cascade slide:
Stage 1 length: 24"
Stage 2 length: 22"
Stage 3 length: 20"

Maximum extension = 24 + 22 + 20 = 66"
Starting length (collapsed) = 24"
Net extension = 66 - 24 = 42"

FTC max height: 18" starting, allowed to extend!
FRC frame perimeter rules may limit extension depending on game
\`\`\`

### Rigging for Speed
String cascade doubles the output speed:
\`\`\`
Motor moves Stage 1 up 12"
Stage 2 moves 24" (2Ã— motor travel)
Stage 3 moves 36" (3Ã— motor travel)
\`\`\`

### Common Failure Modes
| Problem | Cause | Fix |
|---------|-------|-----|
| Slides bind | Misaligned stages | Square up the carriage, add spacers |
| String slips | Wrap not secure | More wraps, add tape, use proper cleat |
| Stages fall | No hard stop | Add physical limit or limit switch |
| Slow extension | Too much friction | Clean channels, add PTFE lubricant |

### Motor Recommendations
- **REV HD Hex 40:1 + string cascade:** Good all-around
- **goBILDA 5202 19.2:1:** Fast, strong
- **REV Core Hex 72:1:** Very strong, slower

Stage 3 moves 3 Ã— 10 = 30 inches."},
          {q:"What does PTFE lubricant do for linear slides?",opts:["Adds friction for grip","Reduces friction between slide stages for smoother, faster extension","Increases motor power","Prevents corrosion only"],ans:1},
          {q:"Slides are binding during extension. What is the most likely cause?",opts:["Motor too weak","Misaligned stages â€” carriage not square","String too tight","Wrong motor direction"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"ma5b",title:"Stress Analysis for Robot Structures",est:"28 min",content:`## Basic Structural Analysis for Robots

Understanding stress and failure modes prevents broken robots at competition.

### Types of Stress
| Stress Type | Caused By | Example |
|-------------|-----------|---------|
| Tension | Pulling apart | String under load |
| Compression | Squeezing | Column supporting weight |
| Shear | Sliding layers | Bolted joint under lateral load |
| Bending | Eccentic load | Arm extending away from pivot |
| Torsion | Twisting | Drive shaft under torque |

### Bending Moment â€” The Most Common Problem
\`\`\`
Long arm + heavy load = large bending moment at pivot

Bending Moment = Force Ã— Distance
M = F Ã— L

Example: 2 kg game piece on 0.5m arm
M = (2 kg Ã— 9.8 m/sÂ²) Ã— 0.5m = 9.8 NÂ·m

This is the torque your pivot bearing and shaft must handle.
\`\`\`

### Factor of Safety
\`\`\`
Safety Factor = Material Strength / Actual Load

Use at least 2Ã— safety factor for static loads
Use 3-4Ã— for dynamic/impact loads (robot hitting walls, dropping)

6061 aluminum yield strength â‰ˆ 276 MPa
If calculated stress = 100 MPa â†’ Safety factor = 2.76 âœ…
If calculated stress = 200 MPa â†’ Safety factor = 1.38 âš ï¸ Too low!
\`\`\`

### Stiffening Techniques
- **Gussets:** Right-angle brackets at joints â€” huge stiffness increase
- **Triangulation:** Three points can't flex (triangles are rigid)
- **Tube vs plate:** Square tube has much higher stiffness than flat plate same weight
- **Cross-bracing:** Diagonal members prevent parallelogram deflection

### Failure Mode Analysis
Before building, ask:
1. What is the highest-stress point?
2. What happens if it fails?
3. Is the failure safe (gradual) or dangerous (sudden)?
4. Can the robot continue the match if this fails?
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What minimum factor of safety should you use for dynamic/impact loads?",opts:["1.0","1.5","2.0","3-4"],ans:3,explanation:"Dynamic and impact loads (robot hitting walls, dropping game pieces) need 3-4Ã— safety factor. Static loads need at least 2Ã—."},
          {q:"Why do triangles make structures more rigid?",opts:["Triangles are lighter","Three points cannot change shape without changing side length â€” they resist deformation","Triangles distribute weight evenly","Triangles are easier to machine"],ans:1},

      {id:"si10",title:"Endgame Optimization",est:"18 min",content:`## Maximizing Endgame Points

Endgame often has the highest point-per-second value in FIRST games. Planning it precisely wins matches.

### Timing Calculation
\`\`\`
Endgame = last 30 seconds of teleop
Climb attempt: typically takes 10-20 seconds

Optimal start time = 30s mark
Leave 5s margin = start at 35s remaining

Trigger: Set a timer or watch the field clock
Your human player can signal you with 30s left
\`\`\`

### The Endgame Decision Tree
\`\`\`
With 35 seconds remaining:

Are we winning by > 15 points?
  YES â†’ Defend the win: park/attempt climb, avoid penalties
  NO  â†’ Can we realistically swing the score?
          YES â†’ Full endgame push
          NO  â†’ Focus on last teleop cycles, attempt climb

Is our climb reliable (>80% success rate)?
  YES â†’ Always attempt
  NO  â†’ Consider park points instead of risking 0
\`\`\`

### Pre-Positioning
The fastest climbs start from the correct position:
- Drive to climb zone BEFORE endgame triggers
- Face the correct direction
- Clear any obstacles beforehand
- Your drive team calls "PREP" at 45 seconds

### Alliance Coordination
Never have two robots trying to climb the same mechanism:
\`\`\`
Example 3-robot plan (FRC chain/stage):
Robot 1: Center climb (fastest, most reliable) â†’ 30s remaining
Robot 2: Right climb â†’ 28s remaining
Robot 3: Backup â€” park if 1 and 2 succeed, climb if needed

Failure plan: Robot 3 always parks minimum
\`\`\`

### Point Math
Always know the math for your current game:
| Action | Points | Time to complete |
|--------|--------|-----------------|
| Park | 3 | 5s |
| Low climb | 5 | 10s |
| High climb | 15 | 20s |
| Trap | 5 | 8s |
`,quiz:[
          {q:"When should you start preparing for endgame in a 2:30 match?",opts:["At the buzzer","At 30 seconds remaining","At 45 seconds â€” move to climb zone early","In the last 10 seconds"],ans:2,explanation:"Prepare at 45s, execute at 35s. This gives a 5s margin for mistakes while ensuring you have time to complete the climb."},
          {q:"If your climb succeeds only 50% of the time, what should you consider instead?",opts:["Practice more","Always attempt climb","Consider parking for guaranteed points instead of risking 0","Ask alliance to cover you"],ans:2,explanation:"50% success means you score 0 half the time. Park points (if available) might be guaranteed and worth more in expectation."},
          {q:"In FRC, what is the primary role of Robot 3 in a 3-robot endgame plan?",opts:["First to climb","Score the most points","Backup â€” guaranteed park, climb only if needed","Play defense"],ans:2},
        ]

      {id:"sa10",title:"Scouting System Design",est:"22 min",content:`## Building a Full Scouting System

A good scouting system is the difference between alliance selection based on gut feelings vs real data.

### What Data to Collect
**Per Match (Quantitative):**
- Auto points / did auto work
- Teleop cycles (game pieces per minute)
- Scoring zone(s) used
- Penalties taken
- Climb result (and time)
- Did robot break down?

**Per Match (Qualitative):**
- Defense style and effectiveness
- Driver skill rating
- Robot speed
- Notes on anything unusual

### Minimum Viable Scout Sheet
For busy competitions, collect only:
\`\`\`
Team # | Auto âœ“/âœ— | Cycles | Climb | Rating | Notes
\`\`\`
(This can be done on paper in 30 seconds per match)

### Sample Size Requirements
| Matches scouted | Confidence level |
|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1 | Very low â€” could be atypical |
| 2-3 | Low â€” small sample |
| 4-5 | Medium â€” reasonable estimate |
| 6+ | High â€” strong data |

Always scout every team at least 3 times before alliance selection.

### Aggregation and Analysis
\`\`\`python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('scout_data.csv')

# Per-team aggregates
summary = df.groupby('team').agg({
    'auto': 'mean',
    'cycles': 'mean',
    'climb_success': 'mean',  # % success
    'rating': 'mean',
    'broke_down': 'sum',  # total breakdowns
}).round(2)

summary['consistency'] = df.groupby('team')['cycles'].std().fillna(0)
print(summary.sort_values('rating', ascending=False).head(20))
\`\`\`

### Red Flags for Alliance Selection
1. **High mean, high variance**: Sometimes amazing, sometimes terrible â€” risky
2. **Broke down 2+ times in quals**: Will likely break in playoffs pressure
3. **All auto attempts failed**: May hurt alliance RP
4. **Pattern of penalties**: Will give RP to opponents in playoffs
`,quiz:[
          {q:"How many matches must you scout a team before having 'medium' confidence in their data?",opts:["1","2","4-5","10"],ans:2},
          {q:"What does 'high mean, high variance' indicate about a team?",opts:["Reliable top performer","Sometimes amazing, sometimes terrible â€” high risk","Consistent average performer","Unreliable data"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why is breaking down 2+ times in qualifications a red flag for playoff alliance selection?",opts:["Bad drivers","If it breaks under lower qual pressure, it's likely to break under playoff intensity","They won't accept a pick","Rules disqualify teams with breakdowns"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },

      {id:"pyb6",title:"Python for Scouting â€” Reading CSV Data",est:"18 min",content:`## Working with CSV Scouting Files in Python

Your exported scout CSV can be analyzed in Python for powerful insights.

### Reading the CSV
\`\`\`python
import csv

with open('scout_data.csv', 'r') as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)  # Each row = a dictionary
    data = list(reader)

# data[0] = first match
print(data[0])
# {'Team': '4512', 'Match': 'Qual 12', 'Overall': '8.2', ...}
\`\`\`

### Basic Analysis
\`\`\`python
# Group by team
from collections import defaultdict

teams = defaultdict(list)
for row in data:
    teams[row['Team']].append(row)

# Average overall rating per team
for team, matches in sorted(teams.items()):
    ratings = [float(m['Overall']) for m in matches if m['Overall']]
    if ratings:
        avg = sum(ratings) / len(ratings)
        print(f"Team {team}: {avg:.1f} avg ({len(ratings)} matches)")
\`\`\`

### Find Top Picks
\`\`\`python
# Sort teams by average rating
team_stats = {}
for team, matches in teams.items():
    ratings = [float(m['Overall']) for m in matches if m['Overall']]
    offense = [float(m['Offense']) for m in matches if m.get('Offense')]
    climbs = [m['Climb'] for m in matches]

    team_stats[team] = {
        'avg_rating': sum(ratings)/len(ratings) if ratings else 0,
        'avg_offense': sum(offense)/len(offense) if offense else 0,
        'climb_pct': climbs.count('success')/len(climbs)*100,
        'matches': len(matches)
    }

# Sort by rating
top = sorted(team_stats.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]['avg_rating'])
print("Top Alliance Picks:")
for team, stats in top[:5]:
    print(f"  Team {team}: {stats['avg_rating']:.1f} | Climb: {stats['climb_pct']:.0f}% | {stats['matches']} matches")
\`\`\`

### Export Summary
\`\`\`python
import csv

with open('summary.csv', 'w', newline='') as f:
    writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=['team','avg_rating','avg_offense','climb_pct','matches'])
    writer.writeheader()
    for team, stats in top:
        writer.writerow({'team': team, **stats})
print("Summary saved!")
\`\`\`

      {id:"pi12",title:"Graphing Robot Performance with matplotlib",est:"22 min",content:`## Visualizing Team Data

Charts help you communicate scouting findings to your alliance selection committee.

### Install Libraries
\`\`\`bash
pip install matplotlib pandas numpy
\`\`\`

### Bar Chart â€” Team Comparison
\`\`\`python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('summary.csv')
df = df.sort_values('avg_rating', ascending=False).head(10)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
bars = plt.bar(df['team'].astype(str), df['avg_rating'],
               color=['#1d4ed8' if r >= 7 else '#f59e0b' if r >= 5 else '#dc2626'
                      for r in df['avg_rating']])

plt.xlabel('Team Number')
plt.ylabel('Average Rating (0-10)')
plt.title('Top 10 Teams â€” Overall Rating')
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('team_ratings.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()
\`\`\`

### Scatter Plot â€” Offense vs Consistency
\`\`\`python
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))
plt.scatter(df['avg_offense'], df['consistency_score'],
            c=df['avg_rating'], cmap='RdYlGn',
            s=100, alpha=0.7)

# Label each dot with team number
for _, row in df.iterrows():
    plt.annotate(str(row['team']),
                (row['avg_offense'], row['consistency_score']),
                textcoords="offset points", xytext=(5, 5), fontsize=9)

plt.colorbar(label='Overall Rating')
plt.xlabel('Average Offense Rating')
plt.ylabel('Consistency Score')
plt.title('Offense vs Consistency â€” Best picks: top-right')
plt.savefig('scatter.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()
\`\`\`

### Radar Chart â€” Team Profile
\`\`\`python
import numpy as np

categories = ['Offense', 'Defense', 'Reliability', 'Climb%', 'Auto']
N = len(categories)
angles = [n / N * 2 * np.pi for n in range(N)]
angles += angles[:1]  # Close the polygon

fig, ax = plt.subplots(subplot_kw=dict(polar=True), figsize=(6,6))

for team in ['4512', '1678']:
    values = get_team_values(team, categories)  # Your data
    values += values[:1]
    ax.plot(angles, values, linewidth=2, label=f'Team {team}')
    ax.fill(angles, values, alpha=0.15)

ax.set_xticks(angles[:-1])
ax.set_xticklabels(categories)
ax.legend(loc='upper right')

      {id:"sfi3",title:"Tool Safety â€” Drills, Saws, and Grinders",est:"18 min",content:`## Power Tool Safety for Robot Building

Every year, FIRST teams have preventable shop accidents. This lesson covers the tools you'll use most.

### Universal Power Tool Rules
1. **Safety glasses ALWAYS** â€” no exceptions, even as observer
2. **No loose clothing or jewelry** â€” gets caught in spinning tools
3. **Secure the workpiece** â€” never hold stock free-hand while cutting
4. **One person, one tool** â€” never crowd or assist without asking
5. **Know where the power switch is** before starting
6. **Inspect before using** â€” damaged tools = dangerous

### Drill Safety
\`\`\`
âœ… DO: Clamp aluminum stock to table or vise
âœ… DO: Use correct bit for material (twist for metal, brad-point for wood)
âœ… DO: Start slow, increase speed gradually
âœ… DO: Use cutting fluid (WD-40) for aluminum
âœ… DO: Deburr holes after drilling â€” sharp edges cut hands

âŒ DON'T: Hold thin aluminum with your fingers while drilling
âŒ DON'T: Drill into materials that can spin (round stock)
âŒ DON'T: Force the drill â€” let it cut
âŒ DON'T: Change bits without unplugging/removing battery
\`\`\`

### Bandsaw Safety
- Keep blade guard set 3mm above material
- Never back out of a cut while blade is moving
- Minimum stock width = half the blade radius
- If blade breaks: stop, back away, tell a mentor immediately
- Never cut round stock without a V-block

### Angle Grinder Safety (High Risk Tool)
- Requires separate mentor approval
- Full face shield required (not just glasses)
- Check disc for cracks before every use
- Never use a cutting disc for grinding or vice versa
- Disc failure = projectile at 10,000 RPM

### Emergency Stop Procedures
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Material caught in tool | Release grip, step back â€” let it spin free |
| Tool drops | Let it fall, don't catch |
| Injury | Stop tool, apply pressure, call for mentor |
| Fire | Use extinguisher (ABC type), call for help |

          {q:"What additional PPE is required for angle grinders beyond safety glasses?",opts:["Gloves","Ear protection","Full face shield â€” glasses alone are insufficient","Steel-toed shoes"],ans:2},
        ]

      {id:"jb19b",title:"Working with Servos",est:"18 min",content:`## Servo Motors in FTC

Servos are position-controlled motors â€” perfect for claws, arms, and mechanisms that need precise angles.

### Basic Servo Control
\`\`\`java
Servo claw = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "claw");

// setPosition(0.0 â€“ 1.0)
// 0.0 = 0Â°  |  0.5 = 90Â°  |  1.0 = 180Â°

// Open claw
if (gamepad1.a) claw.setPosition(1.0);

// Close claw  
if (gamepad1.b) claw.setPosition(0.0);

// Read current position
double pos = claw.getPosition();
telemetry.addData("Claw position", pos);
\`\`\`

### Servo Presets â€” Named Positions
\`\`\`java
// Define named positions as constants
static final double CLAW_OPEN   = 0.85;
static final double CLAW_CLOSED = 0.20;
static final double CLAW_GRAB   = 0.50; // partial grip

if (gamepad1.right_bumper) claw.setPosition(CLAW_OPEN);
if (gamepad1.left_bumper)  claw.setPosition(CLAW_CLOSED);
\`\`\`

### Mirrored Servos (left + right)
\`\`\`java
Servo leftArm  = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "left_arm");
Servo rightArm = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "right_arm");

// Reverse one servo so they mirror
rightArm.setDirection(Servo.Direction.REVERSE);

// Now both servos move symmetrically
leftArm.setPosition(pos);
rightArm.setPosition(pos);
\`\`\`

### Servo Sweep (slow movement)
\`\`\`java
// Move gradually instead of instantly
double currentPos = 0.0;
double targetPos  = 1.0;
double stepSize   = 0.01; // per loop iteration

// In loop():
if (Math.abs(currentPos - targetPos) > stepSize) {
    currentPos += (targetPos > currentPos) ? stepSize : -stepSize;
    claw.setPosition(currentPos);
}
\`\`\`

      {id:"jb20b",title:"Motor Modes Explained",est:"20 min",content:`## Four Motor Modes in FTC

The FTC SDK gives you four ways to run a motor. Choosing the right mode is essential.

### RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER
\`\`\`java
// Raw power control â€” no encoder feedback
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.8); // just spin at 80% duty cycle
\`\`\`
Use when: You don't care about exact speed or distance. Simplest mode.

### RUN_USING_ENCODER
\`\`\`java
// Encoder-regulated speed control
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.8); // now 80% of MAX_SPEED in ticks/sec
\`\`\`
Use when: You want consistent speed regardless of battery level. Good for shooter flywheels.

### STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER
\`\`\`java
// Zeros the encoder counter
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);
// Always do this at init to start from a known position
\`\`\`
Use at start of autonomous to reset position tracking.

### RUN_TO_POSITION â† Most Useful for Auto
\`\`\`java
// Set target, run to it, stop automatically
motor.setTargetPosition(1500); // encoder ticks
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
motor.setPower(0.6);           // speed (positive always!)

// Wait for completion
while (motor.isBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {
    telemetry.addData("Current", motor.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.addData("Target",  motor.getTargetPosition());
    telemetry.update();
}
motor.setPower(0); // Stop when done
\`\`\`

### Mode Sequence for Auto
\`\`\`java
// Correct order every time:
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);  // 1. Zero
motor.setTargetPosition(2000);                           // 2. Set target
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);          // 3. Enable mode
motor.setPower(0.7);                                     // 4. Start moving
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

          {q:"When should you use STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER?",opts:["During matches","At the start of a program to zero the encoder counter","Only if the encoder is broken","Before every setPower() call"],ans:1},
          {q:"In RUN_TO_POSITION, what should setPower() always be?",opts:["Negative","Zero","Positive (direction is handled by target position)","Doesn't matter"],ans:2},
        ]

      {id:"ji18b",title:"Vision with TFOD (TensorFlow Object Detection)",est:"25 min",content:`## TensorFlow Object Detection in FTC

TFOD lets your robot recognize game elements (rings, cones, cubes) using a camera and machine learning.

### How It Works
1. Camera captures video frames
2. TensorFlow model analyzes each frame
3. Returns list of detected objects with confidence and position

### Setup
\`\`\`java
// In init():
VisionPortal visionPortal = new VisionPortal.Builder()
    .setCamera(hardwareMap.get(WebcamName.class, "Webcam 1"))
    .addProcessor(tfod)
    .setAutoStopLiveView(true)
    .build();

// Configure detection threshold
tfod.setMinResultConfidence(0.75f); // 75% confidence minimum
\`\`\`

### Reading Detections
\`\`\`java
List<Recognition> detections = tfod.getRecognitions();

if (!detections.isEmpty()) {
    Recognition best = detections.get(0); // Highest confidence first
    
    String label      = best.getLabel();       // "Yellow Pixel", "Team Prop"
    float  confidence = best.getConfidence();  // 0.0 â€“ 1.0
    float  left       = best.getLeft();        // pixel X of left edge
    float  top        = best.getTop();         // pixel Y of top edge
    float  width      = best.getWidth();
    float  height     = best.getHeight();
    
    // Center X of detected object (0 = left edge, 640 = right edge)
    float centerX = left + width / 2;
    
    telemetry.addData("Detected", label + " at X=" + centerX);
}
\`\`\`

### Using Detection for Autonomous Decision
\`\`\`java
// Detect spike mark position in CENTERSTAGE autonomous
String spikeSide = "center"; // default

List<Recognition> detections = tfod.getRecognitions();
if (!detections.isEmpty()) {
    float cx = detections.get(0).getLeft() + detections.get(0).getWidth()/2;
    if      (cx < 213) spikeSide = "left";
    else if (cx < 427) spikeSide = "center";
    else               spikeSide = "right";
}

// Execute different auto based on result
switch (spikeSide) {
    case "left":   drive.driveToLeftSpike();   break;
    case "center": drive.driveToCenterSpike(); break;
    case "right":  drive.driveToRightSpike();  break;
}
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

      {id:"ja14b",title:"Custom PID Class and Feedforward",est:"30 min",content:`## Building a Reusable PID Controller

Instead of copy-pasting PID code everywhere, build a clean reusable class.

### PIDController Class
\`\`\`java
public class PIDController {
    private double Kp, Ki, Kd, Kf;
    private double integralSum = 0;
    private double lastError   = 0;
    private double lastTime    = 0;
    private double integralMax = 1.0; // Anti-windup limit

    public PIDController(double Kp, double Ki, double Kd, double Kf) {
        this.Kp = Kp; this.Ki = Ki; this.Kd = Kd; this.Kf = Kf;
        lastTime = System.currentTimeMillis() / 1000.0;
    }

    public double calculate(double target, double measured) {
        double now = System.currentTimeMillis() / 1000.0;
        double dt  = now - lastTime;
        if (dt <= 0) dt = 0.02; // Safety: prevent divide-by-zero

        double error      = target - measured;
        integralSum      += error * dt;
        // Anti-windup: clamp integral
        integralSum       = Math.max(-integralMax, Math.min(integralMax, integralSum));
        double derivative = (error - lastError) / dt;

        lastError = error;
        lastTime  = now;

        return Kp*error + Ki*integralSum + Kd*derivative + Kf*Math.signum(target);
    }

    public void reset() { integralSum = 0; lastError = 0; }
    
    // Live tuning setters
    public void setKp(double kp) { Kp = kp; }
    public void setKi(double ki) { Ki = ki; }
    public void setKd(double kd) { Kd = kd; }
}
\`\`\`

### Using the Controller
\`\`\`java
// In OpMode:
PIDController liftPID = new PIDController(0.008, 0.0001, 0.0003, 0.05);
PIDController turnPID = new PIDController(0.015, 0, 0.001, 0);

// Lift control
int liftTarget = 1500; // ticks
double liftPower = liftPID.calculate(liftTarget, lift.getCurrentPosition());
liftPower = Math.max(-1.0, Math.min(1.0, liftPower)); // Clamp
lift.setPower(liftPower);

// Turn control
double targetHeading = 90.0;
double currentHeading = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles().getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES);
double turnPower = turnPID.calculate(targetHeading, currentHeading);
\`\`\`

### Anti-Windup
Without anti-windup, the integral accumulates infinitely when the motor is at a limit, causing overshoot when it's finally free to move. Clamping integralSum to [-1, 1] prevents this.

### Live Tuning via Telemetry
\`\`\`java
// Change gains mid-match for testing
if (gamepad2.dpad_up)   liftPID.setKp(liftPID.Kp + 0.001);
if (gamepad2.dpad_down) liftPID.setKp(liftPID.Kp - 0.001);
telemetry.addData("Kp", liftPID.Kp);
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[
          {q:"What is anti-windup in a PID controller?",opts:["A hardware protection feature","Clamping the integral term to prevent it from accumulating infinitely","A method of tuning Kd","A way to increase response speed"],ans:1},
          {q:"What does the Kf (feedforward) term add?",opts:["More oscillation","A constant output based on direction â€” overcomes gravity and static friction","Derivative response","Integral correction"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why calculate dt (delta time) in the PID loop?",opts:["Required by FTC SDK","The derivative and integral terms depend on how much time passed between updates","To measure loop speed","To synchronize with the IMU"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },

      {id:"mb15",title:"Wheels and Traction",est:"18 min",content:`## Choosing the Right Wheels

Your choice of wheels determines how your robot moves, its top speed, and how well it pushes.

### Wheel Types

**Traction Wheels (solid rubber)**
- Maximum grip â€” won't slip sideways
- Used for tank drive outer wheels
- Great for pushing and climbing obstacles

**Omni Wheels**
- Rollers on the outside allow sideways sliding
- Used in tank drive for turning (reduce scrub)
- Required for holonomic (mecanum/H-drive) support wheels

**Mecanum Wheels**
- Rollers at 45Â° angles enable strafing
- Four-wheel config enables full holonomic movement
- Less pushing force than traction wheels
- Keep rollers clean â€” debris kills performance

**Compliant Wheels (noodle wheels)**
- Soft, grippy foam â€” excellent for intakes
- Game pieces don't bounce off
- Compress around objects

### Traction Formula
\`\`\`
Max traction force = coefficient of friction Ã— robot weight

Rubber on carpet: Î¼ â‰ˆ 1.0
Rubber on tile:   Î¼ â‰ˆ 0.7

Example: 15kg robot on carpet
  Max force = 1.0 Ã— (15 Ã— 9.81) = 147 N
  In lbs: â‰ˆ 33 lbs of push before slipping
\`\`\`

### Wheel Diameter Effects
- Larger diameter â†’ faster top speed, less torque
- Smaller diameter â†’ more torque, slower top speed
- Common FTC: 3.75" or 4" mecanum, 90mm omni
- Common FRC: 4", 6" colson/traction, 3" omni

### Wheel Maintenance
- Inspect before every match
- Clean mecanum rollers with compressed air
- Replace cracked or worn wheels immediately
- Check set screws tightness â€” they vibrate loose

      {id:"ma5x2",title:"Mechanism Stress Analysis",est:"28 min",content:`## Will Your Mechanism Break?

Before fabricating, calculate whether your design can handle the forces it will experience.

### Factor of Safety (FoS)
\`\`\`
FoS = Material Strength / Applied Load

FoS â‰¥ 2.0 â†’ Safe for competition
FoS â‰¥ 3.0 â†’ Safe with impacts/shock loads
FoS < 1.5 â†’ Likely to fail
\`\`\`

### Bolt Shear Strength
An M4 bolt (grade 8.8) has:
- Tensile strength: ~2,500 N
- Shear strength: ~1,500 N (60% of tensile)

If your pivot sees 800 N of force, FoS = 1500/800 = 1.875 âœ… (borderline â€” add a second bolt)

### Beam Bending
A 1Ã—1 aluminum tube acting as a beam:
\`\`\`
Max bending stress = (Force Ã— Length) / Section Modulus

For 1Ã—1" 1/16" wall tube:
Section Modulus â‰ˆ 0.048 inÂ³
6061 Yield Strength = 35,000 psi

Max load at 12" span:
  35000 = (F Ã— 12) / 0.048
  F = 35000 Ã— 0.048 / 12 = 140 lbs
\`\`\`

### Common Failure Modes to Design Against
1. **Bolt shear** â€” pivot points under heavy load â†’ use larger bolts or two bolts
2. **Tube bending** â€” long unsupported spans â†’ add gusset or cross-brace
3. **Shaft torsion** â€” motors twisting thin shafts â†’ use hex shaft (3Ã— stronger than round)
4. **Fatigue** â€” repeated load cycles â†’ increase FoS to 3.0 for cyclic loads
5. **Stress concentration** â€” holes weaken material â†’ avoid holes near bends

### Quick Check Before Cutting Metal
Ask these questions:
- What is the maximum force this part will see? (motor stall torque, robot weight, impact)
- What is the weakest point? (smallest cross-section, longest unsupported span)
- What's the FoS? Is it â‰¥ 2?
- Have I accounted for shock loads? (multiply static load by 2â€“3 for impacts)

      {id:"si10b",title:"Drive Team Psychology and Performance",est:"18 min",content:`## The Mental Game â€” Drive Team Performance

Robotics competitions are high-pressure. Mental preparation is as important as robot preparation.

### The Five Drive Team Roles
**1. Driver** â€” Robot movement, field awareness, real-time decisions
**2. Operator** â€” Mechanisms (intake, shooter, climber), focused on their subsystems  
**3. Human Player** â€” Game piece feeding, communication signals
**4. Coach** â€” Reads the field, calls strategy, communicates with alliance, keeps team calm
**5. Technician** â€” Robot fixes between matches, does NOT speak during matches

### Coach's Mental Framework
\`\`\`
Before match: Set the plan
During match: BRIEF calls only ("left side open", "go for climb")  
After match: "What happened? What do we fix?"
\`\`\`

### Handling Mistakes During Matches
**Don't:** "You missed that shot!" / "Why did you do that?" / panic
**Do:** "Focus on next action" / "What's our score?" / stay calm

The match is still running. Every second spent on regret is a second not scoring.

### Pre-Match Routine (30 minutes before)
1. Robot inspection complete âœ“
2. Battery at full voltage âœ“
3. Drive team meeting â€” roles confirmed âœ“
4. Walk through auto and teleop plan âœ“
5. 10 minutes before: zone out â€” quiet focus

### Post-Loss Recovery
1. Debrief within 10 minutes (memories fade)
2. Identify ROOT CAUSE â€” not "we lost" but "auto failed at step 2 because..."
3. Fix it if possible, else develop a workaround
4. Move on â€” every match is independent

### Stress Signals to Watch For
- Driver making rapid, jerky stick movements â†’ too tense â†’ "breathe, slow down"
- Coach talking too much â†’ drivers tuning out â†’ be silent and let them focus
- Team arguing about what happened â†’ cut it off â†’ debrief later with the full team
`,quiz:[

          {q:"Why should the technician NOT speak during matches?",opts:["Against FIRST rules","Their focus is robot repair â€” speaking during matches distracts the drive team","Technicians aren't allowed at matches","Only drivers can speak"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"sa10b",title:"Data-Driven Strategy at Events",est:"25 min",content:`## Using Data to Win

Teams that use data systematically outperform equally skilled teams that rely on gut feelings.

### Build Your Data Pipeline Before the Event
\`\`\`
Pre-event â†’ TBA API pulls team history + average OPR
Quals 1-4 â†’ Scouts calibrate on real match observation  
Quals 5+  â†’ Merge observed data + stats
Alliance selection â†’ Combine: OPR + consistency + climb% + scout notes
\`\`\`

### The Five Metrics That Matter
| Metric | Why It Matters |
|--------|---------------|
| Avg auto pts | Reliable early pts, often has RP implications |
| Avg teleop cycles | Best predictor of teleop contribution |
| Climb success % | Endgame often determines close matches |
| Consistency (std dev) | A team with Ïƒ=5 beats Ïƒ=15 in high-stakes matches |
| Penalty rate | Penalties directly give opponent points |

### When Stats Lie
**Small sample**: 2-match OPR is meaningless â€” need â‰¥ 5 matches
**Opponent quality**: A team scoring 50 against weak alliances may only score 30 vs strong
**Recent changes**: A team that fixed their auto after match 3 will have artificially low stats
**Defense affects OPR**: Teams played against good defenses have lower stats despite being good

### Alliance Selection Data Sheet Format
\`\`\`
Rank | Team | Avg Auto | Avg Cycles | Climb% | Ïƒ (std dev) | Scout Note
-----|------|----------|------------|--------|-------------|----------
  1  | 254  |   18.2   |    11.4    |  98%   |     3.1     | Strongest bot
  2  | 1678 |   12.5   |     9.8    |  90%   |     4.2     | Fast cycles
  3  | 971  |    8.0   |     7.2    |  85%   |     6.8     | High variance
\`\`\`

### Live Adjustment During Playoffs
Track alliance scores in real time. At playoff break:
- If losing by >15: increase risk (push harder, attempt harder cycles)
- If winning by >15: play conservatively (protect lead, avoid penalties)
- If within 10: execute the plan exactly as practiced
`,quiz:[

      {id:"eb11b",title:"Wiring Your First Robot",est:"20 min",content:`## Step-by-Step Robot Wiring Guide

Good wiring prevents 80% of electronic failures at competition. Follow this order every time.

### Step 1 â€” Plan Before You Wire
Sketch or write out:
- How many motors? Where are they? Which ports?
- How many servos? Ports?
- What sensors? I2C addresses?
- Where will the battery and hubs mount?

### Step 2 â€” Mount Electronics First
Secure before wiring:
- Control Hub in an accessible location (you'll need to connect a phone)
- Battery in the lowest possible position (lowers center of gravity)
- Expansion Hub if needed â€” daisy chain with 3-pin cable

### Step 3 â€” Power Wiring
\`\`\`
Battery XT30 â†’ Main Switch â†’ Control Hub "Battery" port
\`\`\`
- Use provided XT30 connectors
- Red = positive, Black = negative â€” NEVER swap these
- Keep power wires short and routed away from moving parts

### Step 4 â€” Motor Wiring
- Control Hub motor ports: 0, 1, 2, 3 (4 total)
- Each motor connects with red/black Anderson PowerPole connectors
- Label each motor with tape: "FL", "FR", "BL", "BR"

### Step 5 â€” Servo Wiring
- Servo headers: white=signal, red=power, black=ground
- Signal pin faces inward (toward hub center)
- PWM ports: 0â€“5 on Control Hub

### Step 6 â€” Sensor Wiring
- I2C sensors: connect to I2C ports (0â€“3)
- Be careful of I2C address conflicts â€” same address = conflict!
- Digital sensors: digital ports (0â€“7)

### Step 7 â€” Cable Management
- Zip tie bundles every 6â€“8 inches
- Route cables AWAY from wheels, gears, chains
- Leave service loops â€” slack for mechanisms that move
- Label every connector: "LF Motor", "Intake Servo"

### The Wiring Inspection Checklist
- â˜ No exposed bare wire anywhere
- â˜ All connectors fully seated (click/snap in)
- â˜ No wires near moving parts
- â˜ All cables zip-tied and secure
- â˜ Battery connector not cracked or damaged

          {q:"What causes an I2C address conflict?",opts:["Too many motors","Two I2C sensors with the same address on the same bus","Wrong wire color","Outdated firmware"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"ea5x2",title:"Custom Circuit Design for Robots",est:"30 min",content:`## Basic Custom Electronics for FIRST

Sometimes you need something the Control Hub doesn't provide â€” a custom board solves it.

### LED Control with Blinkin Driver
\`\`\`java
// REV Blinkin LED Driver (servo port output)
RevBlinkinLedDriver blinkin = hardwareMap.get(
    RevBlinkinLedDriver.class, "blinkin");

// Set pattern
blinkin.setPattern(RevBlinkinLedDriver.BlinkinPattern.HEARTBEAT_RED);
blinkin.setPattern(RevBlinkinLedDriver.BlinkinPattern.RAINBOW_RAINBOW_PALETTE);
blinkin.setPattern(RevBlinkinLedDriver.BlinkinPattern.SOLID_RED);
\`\`\`

### Reading Analog Sensors
\`\`\`java
// Potentiometer on analog port 0
AnalogInput pot = hardwareMap.get(AnalogInput.class, "pot");

double voltage = pot.getVoltage();  // 0.0 â€“ 3.3V
double angle = (voltage / 3.3) * 270.0; // Map to 270Â° range
telemetry.addData("Arm angle", angle);
\`\`\`

### Digital I/O
\`\`\`java
// Magnetic limit switch on digital port 0
DigitalChannel magSwitch = hardwareMap.get(DigitalChannel.class, "mag");
magSwitch.setMode(DigitalChannel.Mode.INPUT);

boolean atHome = !magSwitch.getState(); // Inverted â€” false = triggered
if (atHome) lift.setPower(0);
\`\`\`

### Voltage Monitoring
\`\`\`java
// Read battery voltage from control hub
VoltageSensor volts = hardwareMap.voltageSensor.iterator().next();
double batteryV = volts.getVoltage();
if (batteryV < 11.5) {
    telemetry.addData("âš ï¸ LOW BATTERY", batteryV + "V");
}
\`\`\`

### Custom Breadboard Circuits
For teams wanting more: use Arduino/Raspberry Pi connected via:
- Serial (UART) to Control Hub digital ports  
- I2C with a custom I2C address
- USB to Control Hub USB port (advanced)

Always prototype on breadboard before soldering. Use ESD protection when handling microcontrollers.

      {id:"pyb6b",title:"Python for Scouting: Basic Stats",est:"20 min",content:`## Quick Team Stats with Python

You don't need pandas to start analyzing scouting data. Pure Python handles small datasets well.

### Storing Scouting Data
\`\`\`python
# List of dicts â€” one per match observation
scouting = [
    {"team": 4512, "auto": 15, "teleop": 32, "climb": True,  "cycles": 8},
    {"team": 4512, "auto": 12, "teleop": 28, "climb": True,  "cycles": 7},
    {"team": 4512, "auto":  0, "teleop": 22, "climb": False, "cycles": 5},
    {"team": 1678, "auto": 18, "teleop": 40, "climb": True,  "cycles": 11},
    {"team": 1678, "auto": 18, "teleop": 38, "climb": True,  "cycles": 10},
]
\`\`\`

### Filter by Team
\`\`\`python
def get_team(data, team_number):
    return [e for e in data if e["team"] == team_number]

team_4512 = get_team(scouting, 4512)
print(f"Matches scouted: {len(team_4512)}")
\`\`\`

### Calculate Statistics
\`\`\`python
def team_stats(entries):
    autos   = [e["auto"]   for e in entries]
    teleops = [e["teleop"] for e in entries]
    totals  = [a + t for a, t in zip(autos, teleops)]
    climbs  = [e["climb"]  for e in entries]
    
    return {
        "avg_auto":   round(sum(autos)   / len(autos),   1),
        "avg_teleop": round(sum(teleops) / len(teleops), 1),
        "avg_total":  round(sum(totals)  / len(totals),  1),
        "max_total":  max(totals),
        "climb_rate": round(sum(climbs)  / len(climbs) * 100, 1),
        "matches":    len(entries),
    }

stats = team_stats(team_4512)
print(f"Avg total: {stats['avg_total']} | Climb: {stats['climb_rate']}%")
\`\`\`

### Rank All Teams
\`\`\`python
teams = set(e["team"] for e in scouting)
rankings = []
for team in teams:
    entries = get_team(scouting, team)
    stats = team_stats(entries)
    rankings.append((team, stats["avg_total"]))

rankings.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("\\nTeam Rankings by Avg Total Score:")
for rank, (team, avg) in enumerate(rankings, 1):
    print(f"  #{rank} â€” Team {team}: {avg} pts avg")
\`\`\`
