      {id:"sfb4",title:"Eye and Hand Safety in the Shop",est:"12 min",content:`## Protecting Yourself While Building

Most robotics injuries happen at the workbench â€” not on the field. These habits prevent them.

### Eye Safety
- **Always wear safety glasses when cutting, drilling, grinding, or using compressed air**
- Prescription glasses are NOT safety glasses â€” wear safety glasses OVER them
- Flying metal shavings travel at 100+ mph â€” they cause permanent eye damage in milliseconds
- When in doubt, put them on â€” they only help when you're wearing them

### Hand Safety
**Cutting**
- Always cut AWAY from your body and other people
- Use a cutting guide or clamp for straight cuts â€” not your hand
- Deburr sharp edges immediately after cutting (file or deburr tool)
- Never use a file without a handle â€” the tang will pierce your palm

**Drilling**
- Clamp your workpiece â€” never hold it by hand while drilling
- Use proper drill speeds: slow for large bits, fast for small bits
- Clear chips away from your hand before touching near a drill bit

**3D Printer / Soldering**
- Soldering iron tip: 350Â°C â€” causes third-degree burns instantly
- Always return iron to holder when not in hand
- Let 3D printed parts cool before handling (nozzle = 200Â°C)
- Wash hands after handling solder (contains flux chemicals)

### The Most Common Injuries in Robotics
1. Cuts from deburring or handling sharp metal edges
2. Eye injuries from flying chips when drilling aluminum
3. Burns from soldering iron left on workbench
4. Pinch injuries from spinning mechanisms (gears, wheels)
5. Back strain from lifting the robot without proper technique

**Remember:** A 10-second safety step prevents a 3-month recovery.

        blocks:[
          {type:"comment",label:"Autonomous Overview",code:`// This auto routine does:
// 1. Drive forward 24 inches
// 2. Turn right 90 degrees
// 3. Run intake to score
// 4. Back up 12 inches to park
//
// All distances use encoder ticks
// TICKS_PER_INCH = 42.8 (goBILDA 5202 + 4" wheel)`,explanation:"Always comment your autonomous routine with what it does in plain English. When something breaks at competition, your scout notes and comments are how you debug fast."},
          {type:"action",label:"Drive Forward Function",code:`void driveInches(double inches, double power) {
    int ticks = (int)(inches * TICKS_PER_INCH);
    setAllTargets(ticks);           // +ticks for forward
    setRunToPosition();
    setAllPower(power);
    while (anyBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {
        telemetry.addData("Driving", inches + "\"");
        telemetry.update();
    }
    stopAll();
    resetEncoders();
}`,explanation:"Wrapping drive commands into functions makes your main routine readable: driveInches(24, 0.6) vs 40 lines of raw encoder code. Also, if you change TICKS_PER_INCH, the fix applies everywhere at once."},
          {type:"action",label:"Turn Function",code:`void turnDegrees(double degrees, double power) {
    // Arc length = robot width Ã— Ï€ Ã— (degrees/360)
    double arcInches = ROBOT_WIDTH_IN * Math.PI * (degrees/360.0);
    int ticks = (int)(arcInches * TICKS_PER_INCH);
    
    // Turn right: left forward, right backward
    leftFront.setTargetPosition(leftFront.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);
    rightFront.setTargetPosition(rightFront.getCurrentPosition() - ticks);
    leftBack.setTargetPosition(leftBack.getCurrentPosition() + ticks);
    rightBack.setTargetPosition(rightBack.getCurrentPosition() - ticks);
    
    setRunToPosition();
    setAllPower(power);
    while (anyBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {}
    stopAll(); resetEncoders();
}`,explanation:"To turn, the left side drives forward and the right side drives backward (or vice versa). The arc length formula converts degrees into a wheel travel distance, which you then convert to encoder ticks."},

      {id:"ji19b",title:"ðŸ§© Blocks: Mecanum Drive Math",est:"25 min",type:"blocks",
        intro:"Understand the math that makes mecanum wheels work â€” then implement it correctly.",
        blocks:[
          {type:"comment",label:"Mecanum Overview",code:`// Mecanum wheels have 45Â° rollers
// Combining power across 4 wheels enables:
// - Forward / Backward
// - Left / Right strafe
// - Rotation
// - Any combination simultaneously
//
// Each wheel power = drive Â± strafe Â± turn
// Wheel layout (looking down at robot):
//   FL  FR
//   BL  BR`,explanation:"The magic of mecanum is that each wheel contributes differently to drive, strafe, and turn. The math combines all three inputs into four motor powers using simple addition and subtraction."},
          {type:"math",label:"The Mecanum Equation",code:`// Read driver inputs
double drive  = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;  // Forward/back
double strafe =  gamepad1.left_stick_x;  // Left/right
double turn   =  gamepad1.right_stick_x; // Rotation

// Calculate wheel powers
double fl = drive + strafe + turn;  // Front-Left
double fr = drive - strafe - turn;  // Front-Right
double bl = drive - strafe + turn;  // Back-Left
double br = drive + strafe - turn;  // Back-Right`,explanation:"The signs follow from the 45Â° roller directions. FL and BR share the same strafe sign (+). FR and BL share the opposite (-). The turn term adds to left wheels and subtracts from right wheels (or vice versa for left turn). Memorize this table!"},
          {type:"math",label:"Normalize to [-1, 1]",code:`// If any power > 1.0, scale ALL wheels down proportionally
// This preserves the intended drive direction
double maxPower = Math.max(1.0,
    Math.max(
        Math.max(Math.abs(fl), Math.abs(fr)),
        Math.max(Math.abs(bl), Math.abs(br))
    )
);

fl /= maxPower;
fr /= maxPower;
bl /= maxPower;
br /= maxPower;`,explanation:"Without normalization, a motor power of 1.4 would be clipped to 1.0, changing the ratio between wheels and making the robot drift. Dividing by the largest absolute value scales the whole set down while preserving the direction ratios."},
          {type:"action",label:"Apply Powers + Telemetry",code:`// Send calculated powers to motors
leftFront.setPower(fl);
rightFront.setPower(fr);
leftBack.setPower(bl);
rightBack.setPower(br);

// Debug telemetry
telemetry.addData("FL|FR", String.format("%.2f | %.2f", fl, fr));
telemetry.addData("BL|BR", String.format("%.2f | %.2f", bl, br));
telemetry.addData("Drive|Strafe|Turn", 
    String.format("%.2f | %.2f | %.2f", drive, strafe, turn));
telemetry.update();`,explanation:"Always log all four wheel powers during testing. If the robot doesn't strafe correctly, this immediately tells you which motor has the wrong sign. String.format() prints cleanly aligned columns."},

      {id:"ja15",title:"ðŸ§© Blocks: Motion Profiling",est:"30 min",type:"blocks",
        intro:"Motion profiling controls acceleration and deceleration â€” making autonomous smoother, faster, and more accurate than constant-speed code.",
        blocks:[
          {type:"comment",label:"Why Motion Profiles?",code:`// Problem with constant-speed auto:
//   Start at 0 â†’ instantly command 0.8 â†’ wheels slip
//   Approach target â†’ still at 0.8 â†’ overshoot
//
// Motion profile solution:
//   Ramp up speed from 0 â†’ max (acceleration phase)
//   Cruise at max speed (cruise phase)
//   Ramp down speed to 0 â†’ target (deceleration phase)
//
// Result: Less wheel slip, more accurate stops`,explanation:"Constant-speed auto commands full power immediately, causing wheel slip that corrupts your encoder tracking. Motion profiles control acceleration, making the robot move more like a car than a rocket."},
          {type:"math",label:"Trapezoidal Profile",code:`// Trapezoidal velocity profile
// Three phases: ramp up, cruise, ramp down
double maxVelocity    = 0.8;  // max power level
double acceleration   = 0.05; // power change per loop
double decelDistance  = 200;  // ticks before target to start slowing

double currentVelocity = 0.0;

// In loop:
double distanceToTarget = Math.abs(target - current);

if (distanceToTarget < decelDistance) {
    // Deceleration phase â€” ramp down
    double decelFraction = distanceToTarget / decelDistance;
    double decelTarget   = maxVelocity * decelFraction;
    currentVelocity = Math.max(0.15, decelTarget); // min power = 0.15
} else if (currentVelocity < maxVelocity) {
    // Acceleration phase â€” ramp up
    currentVelocity = Math.min(maxVelocity, currentVelocity + acceleration);
}`,explanation:"The trapezoidal profile has three phases. Acceleration: increase velocity each loop until max. Cruise: hold max velocity. Deceleration: as distance to target shrinks, scale velocity proportionally. Keep a minimum power to avoid stalling."},
          {type:"action",label:"Applying the Profile",code:`// Apply profiled velocity to motors
double profiledPower = currentVelocity;

// Direction: move toward target
if (current > target) profiledPower = -profiledPower;

leftFront.setPower(profiledPower);
leftBack.setPower(profiledPower);
rightFront.setPower(profiledPower);
rightBack.setPower(profiledPower);

// Completion check with tolerance
if (distanceToTarget < 30) { // Within 30 ticks = done
    stopAll();
    break; // Exit motion profile loop
}`,explanation:"Direction is determined by comparing current position to target â€” negative power if we've gone past it. The tolerance (30 ticks â‰ˆ 0.7 inches) determines when we declare arrival. Too tight = oscillates. Too loose = inaccurate."},
          {type:"control",label:"S-Curve Enhancement",code:`// S-curve: smooth the velocity transitions further
// Apply jerk limiting (limit rate of change of acceleration)
double maxJerk         = 0.002; // acceleration change per loop
double targetAccel;
if (distanceToTarget < decelDistance) {
    targetAccel = -acceleration; // Slowing
} else if (currentVelocity < maxVelocity) {
    targetAccel = acceleration;  // Speeding up
} else {
    targetAccel = 0;             // Cruising
}

// Limit how fast acceleration can change (S-curve smoothing)
currentAcceleration = Math.max(currentAcceleration - maxJerk,
                      Math.min(currentAcceleration + maxJerk, targetAccel));
currentVelocity += currentAcceleration;`,explanation:"S-curves go one step further than trapezoids â€” they also smooth the acceleration transitions, producing a true S-shaped velocity curve. This reduces mechanical stress and wheel slip even further. Road Runner uses S-curve motion profiles internally."},
        ],

        ]
      },

      {id:"mi13b",title:"Belt and Chain Drive Systems",est:"22 min",content:`## Belt vs Chain Drive

Both transmit power between shafts. Each has strengths that make it better for certain applications.

### Belt Drive

**Advantages:**
- Quiet operation
- No lubrication needed
- Lightweight
- Slightly elastic â€” absorbs shock loads
- Can run at higher speeds

**Disadvantages:**
- Can slip under very high load
- Must be tensioned correctly
- Can break if misaligned

**Best uses:** High-speed mechanisms (shooters, elevators), anything where noise matters, precise ratio drives

### Chain Drive

**Advantages:**
- Higher load capacity (doesn't slip)
- Forgiving of minor misalignment
- Easy to adjust length (remove/add links)
- Available everywhere (bicycle, hardware store)

**Disadvantages:**
- Noisy
- Requires lubrication (chain lube spray)
- Heavier than belt
- Stretches over time

**Best uses:** Drivetrain, heavy lifts, anywhere slip is unacceptable

### Tension â€” The Critical Setting
\`\`\`
Belt: 2-3mm deflection at center under light finger pressure
Chain: 3-5mm total slack (too tight = bearing wear, too loose = skip)
\`\`\`

### Sprocket/Pulley Alignment
Misalignment causes:
- Belt: tracking to one side, premature wear, jumping
- Chain: side loading on bearings, skipping, wear

Always use a straightedge across pulleys/sprockets to verify alignment.

### Calculating Belt Length
\`\`\`
Belt links = 2Ã—(center distance/pitch) + (T1+T2)/2
Round UP to nearest even number
\`\`\`

### Calculating Chain Links
Same formula, pitch = 6.35mm (#25 chain) or 9.525mm (#35)
`,quiz:[
          {q:"When would you choose chain over belt drive?",opts:["High speed mechanisms","When noise doesn't matter and slip cannot be tolerated","Lightweight designs","When you need precise ratios"],ans:1},
          {q:"What is the correct belt tension check?",opts:["Belt should be tight as guitar string","2-3mm deflection at center under light finger pressure","Belt should flap freely","No tension needed"],ans:1},
          {q:"What does misaligned belt/chain cause?",opts:["Nothing â€” it self-adjusts","Tracking to one side, premature wear, jumping off pulleys/sprockets","Lower speed","More torque"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },
};

      {id:"ji20b",title:"Road Runner Basics",est:"28 min",content:`## Road Runner â€” Smooth Autonomous Trajectories

Road Runner is a motion planning library used by advanced FTC teams. Instead of writing encoder math by hand, you describe paths geometrically.

### What Road Runner Does
- Generates smooth curves (splines) between waypoints
- Runs velocity + acceleration profiles automatically
- Tracks robot position using odometry
- Handles heading continuously during movement

### Setup (FTC Dashboard + Road Runner)
\`\`\`java
// Build a trajectory
Trajectory traj = drive.trajectoryBuilder(new Pose2d(0, 0, 0))
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(30, 15), Math.toRadians(45))  // Curve to (30,15) facing 45Â°
    .lineTo(new Vector2d(48, 15))                          // Straight to x=48
    .build();

// Execute the trajectory
drive.followTrajectory(traj);
\`\`\`

### Pose2d â€” Robot Position and Heading
\`\`\`java
// Pose2d(x, y, heading in radians)
// x: inches right from start
// y: inches forward from start
// heading: radians (0 = facing right, Ï€/2 = facing forward)

Pose2d startPose = new Pose2d(-36, -60, Math.toRadians(90)); // Left alliance start
drive.setPoseEstimate(startPose);
\`\`\`

### Trajectory Sequences (Multiple Segments)
\`\`\`java
TrajectorySequence seq = drive.trajectorySequenceBuilder(startPose)
    .forward(24)
    .turn(Math.toRadians(90))
    .waitSeconds(0.5)     // Pause for mechanism
    .strafeLeft(12)
    .forward(6)
    .addTemporalMarker(2.0, () -> { // At T=2 seconds
        lift.setTargetPosition(1200);
        lift.setMode(RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
        lift.setPower(0.8);
    })
    .build();

drive.followTrajectorySequence(seq);
\`\`\`

### Tuning â€” The Most Important Step
Road Runner requires tuning several constants before it works:
1. **TICKS_PER_REV** â€” motor encoder ticks per revolution
2. **MAX_RPM** â€” motor maximum RPM
3. **WHEEL_RADIUS** â€” drive wheel radius (inches)
4. **GEAR_RATIO** â€” drive gearing
5. **TRACK_WIDTH** â€” distance between left/right wheels (tuned empirically)
6. **kV, kA, kStatic** â€” motor feedforward constants

Use the **Road Runner Quickstart** repo which includes built-in tuning OpModes.
`,quiz:[
          {q:"What does a Pose2d represent in Road Runner?",opts:["Motor powers","Robot position (x, y) and heading â€” its location and orientation on the field","Trajectory speed","Encoder values"],ans:1},
          {q:"What is a TrajectorySequence used for?",opts:["Single straight movements","Chaining multiple trajectory segments and actions (like mechanism timing) together","Replacing PID controllers","Reading sensors"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why is tuning TRACK_WIDTH critical for Road Runner accuracy?",opts:["It sets motor speed","It determines how the robot calculates turn radius â€” wrong value = incorrect heading tracking","It sets encoder resolution","It controls the speed profile"],ans:1},
        ]
      },

      {id:"ja16",title:"Advanced Auto Paths with Spline Math",est:"35 min",content:`## Cubic Hermite Splines for Smooth Paths

Understanding the math behind Road Runner's paths helps you design better autonomous routines.

### Why Splines?
Straight lines connected by point turns are inefficient. Splines create smooth curves that the robot follows at full speed, without stopping to reorient.

### Cubic Hermite Spline Definition
A cubic Hermite spline between two points is defined by:
- Start position and tangent (direction + magnitude)
- End position and tangent

\`\`\`java
// Math representation
// p(t) = h00(t)*p0 + h10(t)*m0 + h01(t)*p1 + h11(t)*m1
// where t goes 0â†’1, h00/h10/h01/h11 are basis functions
// p0, p1 = endpoints (x,y)
// m0, m1 = tangent vectors at each endpoint

// Hermite basis functions:
// h00(t) = 2tÂ³ - 3tÂ² + 1
// h10(t) = tÂ³ - 2tÂ² + t
// h01(t) = -2tÂ³ + 3tÂ²
// h11(t) = tÂ³ - tÂ²
\`\`\`

### Practical Spline Use in Road Runner
\`\`\`java
// splineTo(endPos, endTangent)
// endTangent = direction the robot is heading when it arrives
drive.trajectoryBuilder(new Pose2d(0, 0, 0))
    // Curve from (0,0) facing 0Â° to (30,20) facing 90Â°
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(30, 20), Math.toRadians(90))
    // Continue curve to (50, 30) facing 0Â°
    .splineTo(new Vector2d(50, 30), Math.toRadians(0))
    .build();
\`\`\`

### Tangent Tuning Strategy
\`\`\`
Problem: Path goes wide and hits field element
Fix:     Adjust tangent at the waypoint to change curve shape

Sharper curve â†’ lower tangent magnitude
Wider curve   â†’ higher tangent magnitude
\`\`\`

### Path vs. Trajectory
| Type | Speed Profile | Use When |
|------|-------------|---------|
| Path | Normalized (unit speed) | Shape definition only |
| Trajectory | Time-parameterized | Actual robot execution |
| TrajectorySequence | Multi-segment + actions | Full auto routine |

### Constraint Tuning for Speed
\`\`\`java
TrajectoryVelocityConstraint velConstraint = 
    SampleMecanumDrive.getVelocityConstraint(
        40,  // Max velocity (in/s) â€” increase for faster auto
        Math.toRadians(180), // Max angular velocity
        DriveConstants.TRACK_WIDTH
    );

TrajectoryAccelerationConstraint accelConstraint =
    SampleMecanumDrive.getAccelerationConstraint(30); // in/sÂ²
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[
          {q:"What is the main advantage of splines over straight-line segments with point turns?",opts:["Less code","Robot follows smooth curves at full speed without stopping to reorient â€” faster auto","More accurate","Required by FTC"],ans:1},
          {q:"What does the tangent parameter in splineTo() control?",opts:["Robot speed at that point","The direction the robot is heading when it reaches the endpoint â€” controls curve shape","The X position","The acceleration"],ans:1},
          {q:"What is the difference between a Path and a Trajectory?",opts:["Paths are straight, trajectories are curved","A path defines shape only; a trajectory is time-parameterized with real velocity and acceleration","Paths are faster","Trajectories don't use encoders"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },

      {id:"mi14",title:"Linear Motion Systems",est:"24 min",content:`## Linear Actuators and Slides

Linear motion (extending up, out, or sideways) is one of the most common robot functions â€” lifts, slides, and arms.

### Types of Linear Systems

**Linear Slides (Cascade/Continuous)**
- Nested aluminum extrusion sections
- Driven by string, cable, or belt
- REV 15mm, Misumi, GoBILDA slides are common in FTC
- Cascade: all stages extend simultaneously (fast, one motor)
- Continuous: stages extend sequentially (slower, more stages possible)

**Lead Screw**
- Motor turns threaded rod, nut translates rotation to linear
- Very high mechanical advantage
- Self-locking (holds position without power)
- Slow â€” good for precise positioning
- FTC use: arm rotation, slow precise lifts

**Rack and Pinion**
- Gear (pinion) rolls along toothed bar (rack)
- Linear, fast, backdrivable
- FTC use: horizontal extension

### Rigging String/Cable Systems
\`\`\`
Motor spool â†’ string â†’ redirect pulley â†’ slide end

Key rules:
1. String parallel to slide = no side load on bearings
2. Equal string length on both sides (if dual-strung)
3. Knot or knotless ferrule â€” never rely on tape
4. Travel limiter (hard stop) prevents over-extension
\`\`\`

### Speed vs Extension Length
\`\`\`
Motor: 312 RPM, spool diameter = 1"
Spool circumference = Ï€ Ã— 1 = 3.14"
Extension rate = 312 Ã— 3.14" / 60 = 16.3 inches/second

For a 4-stage cascade slide:
  Each stage extends 8" â†’ 32" total travel
  At 16.3"/s â†’ full extension in ~0.5 seconds âœ“ Fast!
\`\`\`

### Common Failure Points
- **String breaks** â†’ use 80+ lb braided fishing line or Spectra cord
- **String slips off spool** â†’ add string guide or flanged spool
- **Slide binds** â†’ check alignment, reduce preload, add lubrication (dry PTFE spray)
- **Over-extends** â†’ add magnetic limit switch or encoder limit in code
`,quiz:[
          {q:"What is the main advantage of a lead screw over a string-driven slide?",opts:["Faster extension","Self-locking â€” holds position without power, very high mechanical advantage","Lighter weight","Easier to build"],ans:1},
          {q:"In a cascade linear slide, how does extension work?",opts:["Stages extend one at a time","All stages extend simultaneously â€” one motor extends all stages at once","Motor extends each stage separately","Servos control each stage"],ans:1},
          {q:"What does a travel limiter prevent?",opts:["String from fraying","Over-extension that can break the slide or wiring","Motor burnout","Encoder drift"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],

      {id:"ma6",title:"Prototyping and Iteration Strategy",est:"25 min",content:`## How Top Teams Prototype

The teams that win are rarely the ones with the best initial design â€” they're the ones that iterate fastest.

### The Prototype Loop
\`\`\`
Identify requirement â†’ Rough prototype â†’ Test â†’ Measure â†’ Improve â†’ Repeat
               â†‘___________________________________|
\`\`\`

### Stage 1 â€” Cardboard/Foam Prototype (Day 1-2)
- Build at full scale using cardboard, foam, PVC
- Validates geometry and layout â€” does it fit? Does it reach?
- Tests human-robot interface â€” is it comfortable to operate?
- Costs nothing, takes hours not days
- Kill bad ideas before you cut aluminum

### Stage 2 â€” Functional Prototype (Day 3-5)
- Build in real materials but without polishing
- Test the actual mechanism physics
- Measure: cycle time, success rate, consistency
- Find failure modes BEFORE competition robot

### Stage 3 â€” Refined Mechanism (Day 5-10)
- CAD the final design based on prototype learnings
- Optimize weight, compactness, serviceability
- Build to competition quality (proper hardware, clean wiring)

### What to Measure When Testing
\`\`\`python
# Track these per prototype iteration
{
  "cycle_time": 3.8,        # seconds per game piece
  "success_rate": 0.87,     # 87% successful cycles
  "failure_modes": [
    "jams when piece is tilted",
    "drops during transit at speed"
  ],
  "best_case_time": 2.9,   # Best possible cycle
  "worst_case_time": 6.2   # Worst observed
}
\`\`\`

### The 2-Hour Rule
If a prototype doesn't work after 2 hours of debugging: **kill it and try a different approach.**
Sunk cost bias kills more robots than bad designs.

### Failure Mode Analysis Before Building
Ask for every mechanism:
1. What happens if the string breaks?
2. What happens if the motor stalls?
3. What happens if the game piece is in the wrong orientation?
4. What does the mechanism do when power cuts out?

Robots that handle failures gracefully score more than fragile robots that score when perfect.
`,quiz:[

        ]

      {id:"sb11",title:"Understanding Field Elements",est:"15 min",content:`## Know Your Field

Every FIRST game has unique field elements â€” goals, game pieces, barriers, charge stations. Learning them thoroughly gives you a huge advantage.

### Why Field Knowledge Matters
- Auto paths depend on exact element positions
- Alliance strategy requires knowing every scoring option
- Defense players need to know where they can and can't go
- Human players must understand their feeding zones

### How to Learn a New Game (Kickoff Day)
**First 30 minutes:**
1. Read the Game Manual overview (Section 1-3)
2. Watch the kickoff reveal animation twice
3. Write down every scoring opportunity and its point value

**Next 2 hours:**
4. Study the field layout diagram
5. Walk through every scoring zone mentally
6. Calculate maximum theoretical score (defines the "ceiling")

**Days 2-7:**
7. Watch reveal videos from top teams
8. Attend or watch Q&A sessions
9. Play the field at kickoff events if available

### Maximum Score Analysis
\`\`\`
Example (hypothetical game):
  High Goal:     5 pts Ã— max 12/match = 60 pts
  Low Goal:      2 pts Ã— max 8/match  = 16 pts
  Endgame Climb: 20 pts
  Auto Bonus:    10 pts
  â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
  Theoretical max = 106 pts per alliance

  Realistic target (3 good robots): ~65 pts
  Win condition: score more than opponent's 3 robots
\`\`\`

### Zone Rules to Memorize
Every game has zone restrictions:
- Where can defense be played?
- What are the protected zones?
- When can human players interact with game pieces?
- What are the robot size restrictions in each zone?

Missing a zone rule in a match = penalty points for your opponent.
`,quiz:[

      {id:"ei10",title:"Debugging Electronics Problems",est:"20 min",content:`## Systematic Electronics Debugging

When your robot doesn't work, a systematic approach finds the problem 10Ã— faster than random guessing.

### The Debugging Mindset
Stop assuming. Start measuring.

A motor that "doesn't work" could be:
- Dead motor
- Dead motor controller  
- Broken wire
- Loose connector
- Wrong port in config
- Wrong name in code
- Wrong RunMode

Test each possibility in order from easiest to hardest.

### The FTC Diagnostic Flow
\`\`\`
Symptom: Motor not responding
â”‚
â”œâ”€ Check Driver Hub: any errors? â†’ Fix the error shown
â”œâ”€ Check LED on motor controller â†’ blinking = no signal, solid = fault
â”œâ”€ Check Robot Config: is motor name correct?
â”‚   â””â”€ Rename in config to match code
â”œâ”€ Test in Driver Hub "Manage" â†’ Motor Test
â”‚   â”œâ”€ Motor responds â†’ problem is in your code
â”‚   â””â”€ Motor silent â†’ problem is hardware
â”‚       â”œâ”€ Swap motor port on hub â†’ still dead? Hub is bad
â”‚       â””â”€ Works on other port â†’ original port is dead
â””â”€ Swap motor itself â†’ motor is dead if still silent
\`\`\`

### Common FTC Error Messages
| Error | Cause | Fix |
|-------|-------|-----|
| "Unable to find hardware device" | Config name doesn't match code | Match config name exactly |
| "Failed to open servo controller" | Servo port mismatch | Check port number |
| "EMERGENCY STOP" | Java exception in code | Check logcat for stack trace |
| LED blinks red fast | Hardware fault / short circuit | Disconnect, inspect wiring |

### Using Telemetry as a Debugger
\`\`\`java
// Add debug output at key points
telemetry.addData("=== MOTOR TEST ===", "");
telemetry.addData("Power commanded", motor.getPower());
telemetry.addData("Encoder position", motor.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("Motor controller", motor.getController().toString());
telemetry.update();
\`\`\`

### Wire Continuity Test
If you suspect a broken wire:
1. Power OFF the robot completely
2. Use a multimeter in continuity mode
3. Touch probes to both ends of the wire
4. Beep = connected âœ“ | Silence = break in wire âœ—
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What does a fast-blinking red LED on a motor controller indicate?",opts:["Normal operation","Hardware fault or short circuit â€” inspect wiring","Low battery","Firmware update needed"],ans:1},
          {q:"Why is telemetry useful for debugging?",opts:["Required by FTC SDK","Shows real-time values (power, position, state) so you can verify your code is doing what you think it is","Faster than print statements","Saves to a log file"],ans:1},
        ]

      {id:"pi12b",title:"Match Simulation with Python",est:"28 min",content:`## Simulate Matches Before Playing Them

Simulation lets you answer questions like "what if we focus on cycles instead of climbing?" before you're on the field.

### Simple Match Simulator
\`\`\`python
import random

def simulate_match(team_a, team_b, team_c, team_d, team_e, team_f, n=1000):
    """
    Alliance 1: team_a, team_b, team_c
    Alliance 2: team_d, team_e, team_f
    n = number of simulations
    Returns: win probability for Alliance 1
    """
    wins = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        score1 = sum(simulate_robot(t) for t in [team_a, team_b, team_c])
        score2 = sum(simulate_robot(t) for t in [team_d, team_e, team_f])
        if score1 > score2:
            wins += 1
    return wins / n

def simulate_robot(team_stats):
    """Simulate one robot's score with variance"""
    # Base score Â± std deviation (normal distribution)
    auto   = max(0, random.gauss(team_stats['avg_auto'],   team_stats['std_auto']))
    teleop = max(0, random.gauss(team_stats['avg_teleop'], team_stats['std_teleop']))
    climb  = team_stats['climb_pts'] if random.random() < team_stats['climb_pct'] else 0
    return auto + teleop + climb
\`\`\`

### Run a Simulation
\`\`\`python
# Define team stats
team_4512 = {"avg_auto": 15, "std_auto": 3, "avg_teleop": 28, "std_teleop": 5, "climb_pts": 10, "climb_pct": 0.85}
team_1678 = {"avg_auto": 18, "std_auto": 2, "avg_teleop": 35, "std_teleop": 4, "climb_pts": 10, "climb_pct": 0.95}
team_971  = {"avg_auto":  8, "std_auto": 5, "avg_teleop": 20, "std_teleop": 8, "climb_pts": 10, "climb_pct": 0.60}
team_254  = {"avg_auto": 20, "std_auto": 2, "avg_teleop": 40, "std_teleop": 3, "climb_pts": 10, "climb_pct": 0.98}
team_118  = {"avg_auto": 12, "std_auto": 4, "avg_teleop": 25, "std_teleop": 6, "climb_pts": 10, "climb_pct": 0.75}
team_3478 = {"avg_auto": 10, "std_auto": 6, "avg_teleop": 18, "std_teleop": 9, "climb_pts": 10, "climb_pct": 0.50}

win_prob = simulate_match(team_4512, team_1678, team_971,
                          team_254,  team_118,  team_3478, n=10000)
print(f"Alliance 1 wins {win_prob*100:.1f}% of simulated matches")
\`\`\`

### What-If Analysis
\`\`\`python
# What if we improve our climb rate from 60% to 90%?
team_971_improved = {**team_971, "climb_pct": 0.90}
new_prob = simulate_match(team_4512, team_1678, team_971_improved,
                          team_254, team_118, team_3478)
print(f"With better climb: {new_prob*100:.1f}% win rate")
print(f"Improvement: +{(new_prob - win_prob)*100:.1f}%")
\`\`\`

      {id:"pya6",title:"Building a Live Scouting API",est:"35 min",content:`## Flask + WebSockets for Real-Time Scouting

Build a system where scouts on phones submit data that instantly appears on a strategy screen.

### Architecture
\`\`\`
Phone Scout â†’ POST /api/submit â†’ Flask Server â†’ Push to Strategy Screen
                                              â†’ Store to JSON file
\`\`\`

### Flask Server with Real-Time Updates
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, render_template_string
from flask_socketio import SocketIO, emit
import json, os

app = Flask(__name__)
socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*")

DATA_FILE = "scouting_data.json"

def load_data():
    if os.path.exists(DATA_FILE):
        with open(DATA_FILE) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    return []

def save_data(data):
    with open(DATA_FILE, "w") as f:
        json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

@app.route("/api/submit", methods=["POST"])
def submit_entry():
    entry = request.json
    data = load_data()
    data.append(entry)
    save_data(data)
    # Broadcast to all connected strategy screens
    socketio.emit("new_entry", entry)
    return jsonify({"status": "ok", "total": len(data)})

@app.route("/api/data")
def get_data():
    return jsonify(load_data())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    socketio.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=5000, debug=True)
\`\`\`

### Scout Phone Form (HTML)
\`\`\`html
<form id="scoutForm">
  <input name="team" placeholder="Team #" required>
  <input name="auto" type="number" placeholder="Auto score">
  <input name="teleop" type="number" placeholder="Teleop score">
  <select name="climb">
    <option value="none">No Climb</option>
    <option value="success">Climbed</option>
  </select>
  <button onclick="submitForm(event)">Submit</button>
</form>
<script>
async function submitForm(e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(document.getElementById("scoutForm")));
  await fetch("/api/submit", {
    method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
    body: JSON.stringify(data)
  });
  alert("Submitted!");
}
</script>

      {id:"sfi3b",title:"Robot Power-Up and Power-Down Safety",est:"15 min",content:`## Safe Power Procedures â€” Every Time, No Exceptions

More robots are damaged during power-up and power-down than during actual operation. These procedures prevent that.

### Pre-Power-Up Checklist
Before connecting the battery or flipping the power switch:
\`\`\`
â–¡ Is everyone's hands clear of all mechanisms?
â–¡ Is the robot on the ground or secured on a stand?
â–¡ Are all covers/guards in place?
â–¡ Have you announced "POWERING UP" to the workspace?
â–¡ Is the area around the robot clear (3-foot radius)?
â–¡ Are wheels blocked if on an inclined surface?
â–¡ Is the battery connector in good condition (no cracks, burns)?
\`\`\`

### Power-Up Sequence (FTC)
1. Place robot in known safe position (not aimed at people)
2. Announce: **"Powering up â€” stand clear!"**
3. Connect battery cable (XT30 connector)
4. Flip main power switch
5. Wait 3 seconds before sending any commands
6. Test communications: verify Driver Hub shows green connection
7. Only then: slowly test each mechanism at low power

### Power-Down Sequence
1. Stop all motors and servos (set power to 0)
2. Flip main power switch OFF
3. Disconnect battery cable
4. Confirm robot is fully de-energized (check for any motion)
5. **Only then**: reach into or handle mechanisms

### Why Wait After Powering Up
Motor controllers and the Control Hub take 2-3 seconds to initialize. If you send commands before they're ready, the robot may behave unpredictably â€” jerking, full-speed movement, or ignoring commands entirely.

### Emergency Stop Procedures
**Robot moves unexpectedly:**
â†’ IMMEDIATELY flip main power switch
â†’ Stay AWAY from moving mechanisms
â†’ Do not try to grab or stop moving parts by hand

**Wire smokes or sparks:**
â†’ Flip power switch â†’ disconnect battery
â†’ Do not use water â€” use CO2 or dry chemical extinguisher
â†’ Alert all team members and mentors

**Someone is caught in mechanism:**
â†’ Cut power immediately (switch or battery disconnect)
â†’ Do NOT reverse the mechanism â€” stop first, assess, then carefully reverse
`,quiz:[

          {q:"Why wait 3 seconds after power-up before commanding motors?",opts:["Safety regulation","Motor controllers and Control Hub need 2-3 seconds to initialize â€” early commands cause unpredictable behavior","Battery needs time to charge","FTC requirement"],ans:1},
          {q:"If someone is caught in a mechanism, what is the FIRST action?",opts:["Reverse the mechanism to free them","Cut power immediately, then carefully assess","Call 911 first","Try to pull them free"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],

};

const LESSONS_PACK13 = {

    Beginner: [
      {id:"jb23",title:"ðŸ§© Blocks: FRC Command-Based Intro",est:"22 min",type:"blocks",
        intro:"See how FRC's Command-Based framework organizes code â€” subsystems, commands, and button bindings visualized as connected blocks.",
        blocks:[
          {type:"variable",label:"Subsystem Class",code:`// A Subsystem represents a physical part of the robot
// It owns hardware and exposes methods to use it

public class ShooterSubsystem extends SubsystemBase {
    private final CANSparkMax motor = 
        new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
    private final RelativeEncoder encoder = motor.getEncoder();

    // Called repeatedly when robot is active
    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        // Log current speed every loop
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Shooter RPM", encoder.getVelocity());
    }

    // Public methods for Commands to call
    public void spinUp(double rpm) { 
        motor.set(rpm / 5600.0);  // Normalize to [-1,1]
    }
    public void stop() { motor.set(0); }
    public double getRPM() { return encoder.getVelocity(); }
}`,explanation:"The Subsystem owns hardware. No other code touches that hardware directly â€” everything goes through the Subsystem's public methods. This prevents two commands from fighting over the same motor, which was a major source of bugs in older code."},
          {type:"action",label:"Command Class",code:`// A Command describes what to DO with a Subsystem
// Commands have 4 phases: initialize, execute, end, isFinished

public class SpinUpCommand extends Command {
    private final ShooterSubsystem shooter;
    private final double targetRPM;

    public SpinUpCommand(ShooterSubsystem shooter, double rpm) {
        this.shooter   = shooter;
        this.targetRPM = rpm;
        // Tell scheduler which subsystem this needs
        addRequirements(shooter);
    }

    @Override public void initialize() { shooter.spinUp(targetRPM); }
    @Override public void execute()    { /* Monitor RPM */ }
    @Override public void end(boolean interrupted) { shooter.stop(); }
    @Override public boolean isFinished() {
        return Math.abs(shooter.getRPM() - targetRPM) < 50;
    }
}`,explanation:"addRequirements(shooter) is the key â€” it tells the Command Scheduler that this command exclusively uses the shooter. If another command also requires the shooter, the scheduler cancels the old one. No more accidental simultaneous motor commands!"},
          {type:"control",label:"Button Binding",code:`// In RobotContainer.java â€” the 'wiring' class
// Connect physical buttons to Commands

XboxController driverController = new XboxController(0);

// While right bumper held: spin shooter to 3000 RPM
new JoystickButton(driverController, XboxController.Button.kRightBumper.value)
    .whileTrue(new SpinUpCommand(shooter, 3000));

// When A pressed: run intake sequence
new JoystickButton(driverController, XboxController.Button.kA.value)
    .onTrue(new IntakeCommand(intake).withTimeout(2.0));

// Alternatively â€” inline command (no separate class needed)
new JoystickButton(driverController, XboxController.Button.kB.value)
    .onTrue(Commands.runOnce(() -> shooter.stop(), shooter));`,explanation:"whileTrue runs the command while the button is held and cancels it on release. onTrue starts the command on button press and doesn't cancel when released. Commands.runOnce() creates a one-shot command inline â€” no separate class needed for simple actions."},
          {type:"control",label:"Autonomous Command",code:`// Auto routines are just Commands too!
// Compose complex autos from simple sub-commands

public Command getAutonomousCommand() {
    return new SequentialCommandGroup(
        // Step 1: Run shooter up to speed
        new SpinUpCommand(shooter, 3000),
        // Step 2: Feed ball for 1 second
        new RunCommand(() -> feeder.run(), feeder)
            .withTimeout(1.0),
        // Step 3: Drive backward 2 meters
        new DriveDistanceCommand(drive, -2.0),
        // Step 4: Stop
        Commands.runOnce(() -> { shooter.stop(); drive.stop(); })
    );
}`,explanation:"SequentialCommandGroup chains commands so each waits for the previous to finish (isFinished() returns true). ParallelCommandGroup runs them simultaneously. This lets you build complex autonomous routines from small, tested, reusable pieces."},
        ],

      {id:"ji21",title:"FRC PathPlanner Integration",est:"28 min",content:`## PathPlanner â€” GUI-Based Auto Path Design

PathPlanner is an FRC app that lets you draw autonomous paths visually and export them to WPILib code.

### What PathPlanner Provides
- Visual path editor with field image background
- Auto-generates follower code for swerve and tank drives
- Built-in event markers for trigger commands at waypoints
- Path constraints (max velocity, acceleration)
- Hot-reload during testing â€” change path without redeploying

### Setup
\`\`\`java
// build.gradle dependency
implementation "com.pathplanner.lib:PathPlannerLib:2024.1.6"
\`\`\`

### Basic Path Following (Swerve)
\`\`\`java
// Load path created in PathPlanner app
PathPlannerPath path = PathPlannerPath.fromPathFile("MyPath");

// Configure AutoBuilder (one time in DriveSubsystem)
AutoBuilder.configureHolonomic(
    this::getPose,            // Pose supplier
    this::resetOdometry,      // Reset odometry
    this::getChassisSpeeds,   // Current chassis speeds
    this::driveRobotRelative, // Drive method
    new HolonomicPathFollowerConfig(
        new PIDConstants(5.0, 0, 0),  // Translation PID
        new PIDConstants(5.0, 0, 0),  // Rotation PID
        4.5,                           // Max module speed (m/s)
        0.4                            // Drive base radius (m)
    ),
    this  // Reference to this subsystem
);

// Create command
Command followPath = AutoBuilder.followPath(path);
\`\`\`

### Named Commands â€” Trigger Actions at Waypoints
\`\`\`java
// Register commands by name in Robot.java
NamedCommands.registerCommand("IntakeOn",
    Commands.runOnce(() -> intake.run(), intake));
NamedCommands.registerCommand("Shoot",
    new ShootCommand(shooter, feeder));
NamedCommands.registerCommand("IntakeOff",
    Commands.runOnce(() -> intake.stop(), intake));

// Then in PathPlanner app: add event marker at waypoint
// Type: "IntakeOn" â€” automatically triggers at that point
\`\`\`

### Auto Chooser on Dashboard
\`\`\`java
// Auto-detects all paths/autos in deploy/pathplanner/autos folder
SendableChooser<Command> autoChooser = AutoBuilder.buildAutoChooser();
SmartDashboard.putData("Auto Chooser", autoChooser);

// In autonomousInit:
m_autonomousCommand = autoChooser.getSelected();
\`\`\`

      {id:"sa11",title:"Building a Season-Long Strategy System",est:"25 min",content:`## Strategy from Kickoff to Championship

Top teams treat strategy like software â€” versioned, documented, and continuously updated.

### Season Phases and Strategy Focus

**Kickoff (Week 1)**
- Game analysis: what is the highest-value consistent scoring?
- Robot concept: what capabilities maximize point contribution?
- Game piece analysis: cycle time, intake difficulty, scoring location

**Build Season (Weeks 2-6)**
- Define target auto routine (must be working by Week 4)
- Teleop role: primary scorer? defender? both?
- Endgame decision: attempt always? only when winning?

**Pre-Competition (Week 7)**
- Finalize all autonomous routines
- Drive team practice: minimum 20 hours recommended
- Scouting app and sheet ready
- Pre-scout using TBA data from previous events

**At Competition (Day 1 Qualifiers)**
- Calibrate scouts: first 3 matches = calibration round
- Identify top performers early
- Build alliance target list by match 6

**Alliance Selection**
- Present your target list ranked 1â€“30
- Know which teams would accept captain vs pick roles
- Identify "sleeper" teams stats may have missed

### The Living Strategy Document
\`\`\`markdown
# [Team Name] Strategy Doc â€” [Season Name]
Version: 1.4 (updated [date])

## Current Auto Routine
Scoring: 15 pts (3 high + 2 mid + leave)
Consistency: 8/10 test runs

## Teleop Strategy
Primary role: High scorer
Cycle time: 6.2 sec average
Target: 8 cycles/match

## Endgame
Climb: Always attempt if within :35 of end
Harmony: Coordinate with alliance in pre-match meeting

## Known Weaknesses
- Auto fails if pushed in first 2 seconds
- Intake struggles with game pieces against wall
\`\`\`

Update the document after every significant test or competition. Version control it. Share with the whole team.

        intro:"FTC motors have four run modes â€” choosing the right one is crucial for predictable movement.",
        blocks:[
          {type:"variable",label:"The Four Motor Modes",code:`// Mode 1: Raw power control (simplest)
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.8); // Just spins at 80% power

// Mode 2: Consistent speed (SDK compensates for load)
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.8); // Tries to maintain consistent velocity`,explanation:"RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER is the simplest â€” just raw voltage. RUN_USING_ENCODER uses a PID loop to maintain consistent speed even when the load changes (like going uphill)."},
          {type:"action",label:"RUN_TO_POSITION â€” Precise Moves",code:`// Step 1: Reset encoder to zero
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);

// Step 2: Set the target (in encoder ticks)
int TARGET_TICKS = 1400; // â‰ˆ 1 full rev for goBILDA 5202
motor.setTargetPosition(TARGET_TICKS);

// Step 3: Set mode THEN power
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
motor.setPower(0.6); // Power while running to target

// Step 4: Wait for it to arrive
while (motor.isBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {
    telemetry.addData("Position", motor.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.update();
}
motor.setPower(0); // Stop`,explanation:"RUN_TO_POSITION is the key mode for autonomous. It handles all speed control automatically â€” you just set a target and power, and it stops when it arrives. Always STOP_AND_RESET first to zero the encoder."},
          {type:"sensor",label:"Reading Encoder Position",code:`// Get current encoder tick count
int pos = motor.getCurrentPosition();

// Useful calculations:
double TICKS_PER_REV = 537.7;   // goBILDA 5202 19.2:1
double WHEEL_CIRCUM_IN = 4.0 * Math.PI; // 4-inch wheel

// Convert ticks â†’ inches
double inches = (pos / TICKS_PER_REV) * WHEEL_CIRCUM_IN;

// Convert ticks â†’ degrees rotated  
double degrees = (pos / TICKS_PER_REV) * 360.0;

telemetry.addData("Pos (ticks)", pos);
telemetry.addData("Pos (inches)", String.format("%.1f\"", inches));`,explanation:"Encoder ticks are raw counts from the encoder disk. Convert them to meaningful units (inches or degrees) for logging and debugging. goBILDA 5202 at 19.2:1 has 537.7 ticks per output revolution."},

// TELEOP: use RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER for responsive driving
leftDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);
rightDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);

// AUTO: switch to encoder mode for precise movements
void driveToPosition(int targetTicks) {
    leftDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);
    leftDrive.setTargetPosition(targetTicks);
    leftDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
    leftDrive.setPower(0.5);
    while (leftDrive.isBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {}
    leftDrive.setPower(0);
    leftDrive.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);
}`,explanation:"A helper function wraps the full encode-drive-reset sequence so you can call driveToPosition(1400) cleanly. After finishing, switch back to RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER so teleop still works normally."},

      {id:"ji21b",title:"Command-Based Programming (FTC)",est:"28 min",content:`## Command-Based Architecture for Complex Robots

Command-based is the professional way to organize complex FTC code â€” used by top teams worldwide.

### The Core Concepts
- **Subsystem**: A hardware group (drive, arm, intake) with state and actions
- **Command**: An action to perform on one or more subsystems
- **Scheduler**: Runs commands each loop iteration, handles dependencies

### Subsystem Example
\`\`\`java
public class ArmSubsystem {
    private DcMotor armMotor;
    private int targetPosition = 0;

    public ArmSubsystem(HardwareMap hwMap) {
        armMotor = hwMap.get(DcMotor.class, "arm");
        armMotor.setMode(RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
    }

    // State methods
    public void setTarget(int ticks) {
        targetPosition = ticks;
        armMotor.setTargetPosition(ticks);
        armMotor.setMode(RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
        armMotor.setPower(0.6);
    }

    public boolean atTarget() {
        return !armMotor.isBusy();
    }

    // Called every loop
    public void periodic() {
        // Could update telemetry, run safety checks, etc.
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Command Example
\`\`\`java
public class ScoreCommand {
    ArmSubsystem arm;
    IntakeSubsystem intake;
    int phase = 0;

    public ScoreCommand(ArmSubsystem arm, IntakeSubsystem intake) {
        this.arm = arm;
        this.intake = intake;
    }

    public void execute() {
        switch (phase) {
            case 0:
                arm.setTarget(ArmSubsystem.HIGH_POS);
                phase = 1; break;
            case 1:
                if (arm.atTarget()) {
                    intake.setPower(-1.0); // Eject
                    phase = 2; break;
                }
            case 2:
                // Wait 0.5s then finish...
        }
    }

    public boolean isFinished() { return phase >= 3; }
}
\`\`\`

### Why Use Command-Based?
| Traditional | Command-Based |
|-------------|--------------|
| One giant OpMode | Separate subsystem files |
| Hard to test parts | Test each subsystem solo |
| Adding features = rewrite | Add command, done |
| Bugs hidden in long code | Bugs isolated to one command |
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What does the isFinished() method on a command return?",opts:["Motor speed","true when the command should stop executing","false always","The current state number"],ans:1},
        ]
      },

      {id:"mb15b",title:"Fasteners â€” Choosing the Right Bolt",est:"15 min",content:`## Bolts, Screws, and Nuts for Robots

Choosing wrong fasteners causes field failures. Here's what every builder needs to know.

### Bolt Size Notation
\`\`\`
M3 Ã— 10mm SHCS
â”‚    â”‚     â””â”€â”€ Thread type (Socket Head Cap Screw)
â”‚    â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Length in mm  
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Diameter (metric: M2â€“M10 for robots)

#10-32 Ã— 1/2" BHCS
â”‚   â”‚    â”‚     â””â”€â”€ Button Head Cap Screw
â”‚   â”‚    â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Length in inches
â”‚   â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Threads per inch
â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€ Size (#4=3.18mm, #10=4.83mm)
\`\`\`

### When to Use Each Head Type
| Head Type | Best For | Tool |
|-----------|----------|------|
| Socket Head Cap (SHCS) | Structural joints, high tension | Hex key (Allen) |
| Button Head (BHCS) | Panels, low-profile areas | Hex key |
| Flat Head (FHCS) | Flush mounting, hinges | Hex key |
| Pan Head | Sheet metal, electronics | Phillips/hex |

### Locking Fasteners
- **Nyloc nut**: Nylon ring grips thread â€” won't vibrate loose. Use for anything that moves.
- **Thread locker (Loctite Blue/242)**: Drop on thread before assembling. Removable with tools. Use on motors, bearing mounts.
- **Split washer**: Old design, not as reliable as nyloc. Avoid.

### Common Mistakes
- âŒ Using smooth-bore holes (no thread) without a nut â€” bolt will pull right through
- âŒ Over-torquing aluminum â€” you'll strip the hole
- âŒ Using steel bolts in aluminum without a washer â€” galvanic corrosion weakens joint over time
- âŒ Not using nyloc on drivetrain â€” vibration loosens everything

### FTC/FRC Common Sizes
| Use | FTC | FRC |
|-----|-----|-----|
| Motors | M4 Ã— 8mm | #10-32 Ã— 1/2" |
| Structure | M5 Ã— 12mm | 1/4-20 Ã— 3/4" |
| Electronics | M3 Ã— 8mm | #6-32 Ã— 3/8" |

          {q:"Why use a Nyloc nut instead of a regular nut on drivetrain parts?",opts:["Nyloc is lighter","Nyloc won't vibrate loose â€” the nylon insert grips the thread","Nyloc is cheaper","Nyloc is required by FTC rules"],ans:1},

      {id:"ma6b",title:"Mecanum Kinematics & Field-Centric Drive",est:"30 min",content:`## Mecanum Wheel Mathematics

Mecanum wheels let robots strafe in any direction â€” but only if the math is right.

### Mecanum Wheel Orientation (FTC Standard)
\`\`\`
    FL (//)   FR (\\\\)
    BL (\\\\)   BR (//)

The roller angle creates 45Â° force vectors.
\`\`\`

### Inverse Kinematics (Joystick â†’ Wheel Powers)
\`\`\`java
double axial   = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;   // Forward/back
double lateral = gamepad1.left_stick_x;    // Strafe left/right
double yaw     = gamepad1.right_stick_x;   // Rotation

// Mecanum equations
double frontLeft  = axial + lateral + yaw;
double frontRight = axial - lateral - yaw;
double backLeft   = axial - lateral + yaw;
double backRight  = axial + lateral - yaw;

// Normalize to [-1, 1] â€” don't clip!
double maxMag = Math.max(1.0, Math.max(
    Math.max(Math.abs(frontLeft), Math.abs(frontRight)),
    Math.max(Math.abs(backLeft), Math.abs(backRight))));

frontLeft  /= maxMag;
frontRight /= maxMag;
backLeft   /= maxMag;
backRight  /= maxMag;
\`\`\`

### Field-Centric Control
\`\`\`java
// Rotate joystick vector by robot heading
// So "forward" always means field-forward, not robot-forward
double heading = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles().getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES);
double rad = Math.toRadians(heading);

// Rotate the lateral/axial vector
double rotLateral = lateral * Math.cos(rad) - axial * Math.sin(rad);
double rotAxial   = lateral * Math.sin(rad) + axial * Math.cos(rad);

// Then apply mecanum equations with rotated inputs
double frontLeft  = rotAxial + rotLateral + yaw;
// ... same as before
\`\`\`

### Tuning Checklist
1. Verify all 4 wheels spin forward when setPower(+0.5) is called
2. Test strafe â€” robot should move sideways without turning
3. Test rotation â€” robot spins in place
4. Enable field-centric, verify "forward" on joystick = field forward
5. Test diagonal movement â€” should be smooth and straight
`,quiz:[

The signs follow the 45Â° force vector geometry of each wheel's roller angle."},
          {q:"Why normalize wheel powers by dividing by maxMag instead of clipping to [-1,1]?",opts:["It's faster","Clipping changes the direction of movement â€” normalization preserves the intended drive ratio","Required by FTC SDK","Normalization prevents motor damage"],ans:1},

        ]

      {id:"sb11b",title:"Reading the Game Manual",est:"20 min",content:`## How to Read a FIRST Game Manual

Every FIRST season starts with a game manual. Reading it correctly saves hours of penalty trouble.

### Manual Structure (FRC)
\`\`\`
Section 1: Introduction & Dates
Section 2: Game Overview (READ THIS FIRST)
Section 3: Robot Specifications (size, weight, rules)
Section 4: Game Rules (scoring, penalties)
Section 5: Tournament Structure
Appendices: Definitions, diagrams, Q&A process
\`\`\`

### Reading Strategy
**First pass (30 min):** Read Section 2 completely. Get the big picture.
- What is the main game action?
- What are the point values?
- What are the endgame actions?
- What does auto look like?

**Second pass (1 hour):** Read robot rules very carefully.
- Maximum size (FRAME PERIMETER, HEIGHT)
- Maximum weight
- Prohibited mechanisms (spinning hazards, etc.)
- Bumper requirements

**Third pass (ongoing):** Q&A and game updates.
- Official Q&A answers clarify rule intent
- Check Q&A before every build decision that seems borderline

### Red Flag Phrases
| Phrase | Means |
|--------|-------|
| "shall not" | Mandatory rule â€” violation = penalty |
| "may" | Optional â€” you choose |
| "during Teleop" | Not in Auto â€” timing matters |
| "Alliance-colored" | Must match your alliance, not just any |
| "per match" | Cap on how many times |

### Rule Violation Categories
- **Yellow Card**: Warning â€” accumulate 2 = red card
- **Red Card**: Match DQ, may affect playoff alliance
- **Foul Point**: Points awarded to opponent alliance
- **Tech Foul**: More opponent points (worse than regular foul)

### Free Points Strategy
Every game has "easy" points that most teams miss:
1. Auto leave bonus â€” just cross the line!
2. Park points â€” just be in the zone at the end
3. Coopertition bonus â€” coordinate with opponent alliance
`,quiz:[
          {q:"In FIRST rules, what does 'shall not' mean?",opts:["Optional prohibition","Strongly recommended against","Mandatory prohibition â€” violation = penalty","Advisory note"],ans:2},
          {q:"Where should you look for official clarifications on borderline rules?",opts:["Chief Delphi forums","The official Q&A on the FIRST website","Team mentor opinions","YouTube videos"],ans:1},
          {q:"What is the easiest category of points most teams miss?",opts:["Trap/endgame points","Auto leave and park â€” just be in the right place","High goal scoring","Defense"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },

      {id:"pi13",title:"Discord Bot for FRC Scouting Alerts",est:"30 min",content:`## Build a Discord Bot for Your Team

A Discord bot can auto-post match schedules, TBA updates, and scouting alerts to your team channel.

### Setup
\`\`\`bash
pip install discord.py requests python-dotenv
\`\`\`

Create a \`.env\` file:
\`\`\`
DISCORD_TOKEN=your_bot_token_here
TBA_KEY=your_tba_api_key
CHANNEL_ID=your_channel_id_number
\`\`\`

### Basic Bot Structure
\`\`\`python
import discord
from discord.ext import commands, tasks
import requests
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()
bot = commands.Bot(command_prefix="!")

@bot.event
async def on_ready():
    print(f"Bot ready as {bot.user}")
    check_matches.start()  # Start background task

@bot.command()
async def team(ctx, team_number: int):
    """!team 254 â€” Get team info"""
    r = requests.get(
        f"https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/frc{team_number}",
        headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": os.getenv("TBA_KEY")}
    )
    if r.status_code == 200:
        data = r.json()
        await ctx.send(f"**Team {team_number}: {data.get('nickname')}**\\n"
                      f"Location: {data.get('city')}, {data.get('state_prov')}\\n"
                      f"Rookie Year: {data.get('rookie_year')}")
    else:
        await ctx.send("Team not found.")

bot.run(os.getenv("DISCORD_TOKEN"))
\`\`\`

### Auto-Post Match Alerts
\`\`\`python
@tasks.loop(minutes=15)
async def check_matches():
    """Runs every 15 minutes â€” checks for upcoming matches"""
    channel = bot.get_channel(int(os.getenv("CHANNEL_ID")))
    
    r = requests.get(
        "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/frc4512/events/2025/matches",
        headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": os.getenv("TBA_KEY")}
    )
    
    if r.status_code == 200:
        matches = r.json()
        upcoming = [m for m in matches if m.get("actual_time") is None]
        
        if upcoming:
            next_match = min(upcoming, key=lambda m: m.get("predicted_time", 0))
            await channel.send(
                f"âš¡ Next match: **{next_match['key']}** "
                f"in {calculate_time_until(next_match)} minutes!"
            )
\`\`\`

### Safety Notes
- Never commit .env files to GitHub â€” add to .gitignore
- Use a test server first before adding to main team server
- Discord rate limits: don't send more than 5 messages/second
`,quiz:[

      {id:"sfb2b",title:"Electrical Safety Basics",est:"14 min",content:`## Electrical Safety for FIRST Robots

Robots run on 12V batteries â€” that's enough to cause serious burns and fire. Take it seriously.

### Battery Safety
\`\`\`
FTC: 12V LiPo (3 cells)
FRC: 12V SLA (Sealed Lead Acid)

Danger levels:
â€¢ Short circuit (direct + to -): FIRE, explosion risk
â€¢ Overcharge: Battery swells, vents toxic gas
â€¢ Physical damage: LiPo WILL catch fire if punctured
â€¢ Wrong charger: LiPo REQUIRES LiPo-specific charger
\`\`\`

### Non-Negotiable Rules
- **Always** connect battery to robot before turning on robot
- **Never** reverse battery polarity (swap + and -) â€” destroys electronics instantly
- **Never** leave charging batteries unattended
- **Never** charge a puffy/swollen LiPo â€” it must be disposed of properly
- **Always** use the main switch to cut power before working on robot
- **Always** have a fire extinguisher accessible when using LiPo batteries

### Wiring Best Practices
| Rule | Why |
|------|-----|
| Fuse or breaker on every positive wire | Prevents overload fire |
| No bare wire ends exposed | Short circuit risk |
| Secure all wiring away from moving parts | Abrasion causes shorts |
| Use wire of correct gauge | Undersized wire overheats |
| Red = positive, Black = ground | Universal convention, prevents mistakes |

### What to Do If a LiPo Catches Fire
1. **Do NOT use water** â€” makes lithium fires worse
2. Use a Class D fire extinguisher OR smother with sand
3. Move away â€” burning LiPo releases toxic fumes
4. Call for help immediately
5. Do NOT breathe the smoke

### Inspection Tips
Before every session, check:
- Battery connector for cracks, corrosion, or heat marks
- All wire connections secure (no loose crimp terminals)
- No exposed copper anywhere in the wiring
- Battery voltage before use (FTC LiPo: 12.6V full, warn at 11.0V)

          {q:"A LiPo battery looks puffy and swollen. What should you do?",opts:["Charge it back up","Use it carefully","Do NOT charge or use it â€” dispose of properly following LiPo disposal guidelines","It's fine, normal appearance"],ans:1},
        ]
      },
    ],
  },

      {id:"jbN1",title:"ðŸ§© Blocks: Understanding OpMode Lifecycle",est:"16 min",type:"blocks",
        intro:"Every FTC program goes through the same lifecycle â€” learn each phase and what code belongs where.",
        blocks:[
          {type:"comment",label:"The Four Lifecycle Phases",code:`// Every OpMode has four lifecycle phases:
// 1. init()     â€” runs once when INIT pressed
// 2. init_loop() â€” runs repeatedly until START pressed  
// 3. start()    â€” runs once when START pressed
// 4. loop()     â€” runs repeatedly until STOP pressed
// (LinearOpMode combines these into runOpMode())`,explanation:"Understanding the lifecycle prevents common bugs like servos twitching during init or motors not stopping properly. Each phase has a specific job."},
          {type:"action",label:"init() â€” Setup Phase",code:`@Override
public void init() {
    // Connect to hardware â€” happens ONCE
    motor = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "motor");
    servo = hardwareMap.get(Servo.class, "servo");
    
    // Set initial states
    motor.setZeroPowerBehavior(ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE);
    servo.setPosition(0.0);
    
    // Tell driver we're ready
    telemetry.addData("Status", "Initialized âœ…");
    telemetry.update();
}`,explanation:"init() is for setup only â€” no motors should move here. Set initial positions, configure hardware, and signal that you're ready. Runs once when the driver presses INIT."},

    telemetry.addData("Target found?", visionReady ? "YES âœ…" : "NO âŒ");
    telemetry.addData("Heading", imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles()
        .getYaw(AngleUnit.DEGREES));
    telemetry.update();
}`,explanation:"init_loop() is perfect for showing live sensor data to help drivers align the robot before the match starts â€” camera status, IMU heading, sensor readings. Many teams skip this, but it's very useful."},

        blocks:[
          {type:"comment",label:"Why Classes?",code:`// BAD: Everything in one giant OpMode
public void loop() {
    // 300 lines of spaghetti...

}

// GOOD: Separate classes for each subsystem
ArmSubsystem arm = new ArmSubsystem(hardwareMap);

          {type:"variable",label:"Writing a Subsystem Class",code:`// File: ArmSubsystem.java
public class ArmSubsystem {
    private DcMotor armMotor;
    private Servo wrist;
    
    // Positions (tune these for your robot)
    public static final int POS_STOWED  = 0;
    public static final int POS_PICKUP  = 350;
    public static final int POS_HIGH    = 1200;
    
    private int targetPos = POS_STOWED;
    
    // Constructor â€” receives hardwareMap from OpMode
    public ArmSubsystem(HardwareMap hwMap) {
        armMotor = hwMap.get(DcMotor.class, "arm_motor");
        wrist = hwMap.get(Servo.class, "wrist");
        armMotor.setMode(RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
    }
}`,explanation:"The constructor takes HardwareMap from the OpMode â€” the subsystem doesn't know it's in a class, it just sets up hardware normally. Public static final constants let other code reference positions by name instead of magic numbers."},
          {type:"action",label:"Subsystem Methods",code:`// Methods that teleop OR auto can call
public void setTarget(int position) {
    targetPos = position;
    armMotor.setTargetPosition(position);
    armMotor.setMode(RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
    armMotor.setPower(0.7);
}

public boolean isAtTarget() {
    return !armMotor.isBusy() ||
           Math.abs(armMotor.getCurrentPosition()-targetPos) < 20;
}

public void update(Gamepad gamepad) {
    // Called from teleop loop()
    if (gamepad.y) setTarget(POS_HIGH);
    if (gamepad.a) setTarget(POS_STOWED);
    
    // Update wrist proportionally to arm angle
    double armPct = (double)armMotor.getCurrentPosition() / POS_HIGH;
    wrist.setPosition(armPct * 0.6 + 0.2);
}`,explanation:"setTarget() and isAtTarget() can be called from both teleop AND autonomous. update() is called from the teleop loop every iteration. This means your auto can do the same arm movements as teleop with zero code duplication."},

// Sequential auto using subsystem methods

// Wait for arm to reach position
while (opModeIsActive() && !arm.isAtTarget()) {
    telemetry.addData("Arm", arm.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.update();
}

// Score
intake.setPower(-1.0); // release game piece
sleep(300);
arm.setTarget(ArmSubsystem.POS_STOWED);`,explanation:"Using the subsystem in auto is clean and readable â€” arm.setTarget(POS_HIGH) is much clearer than repeated motor configuration code. isAtTarget() makes waiting for movement completion simple and reusable."},

      {id:"jaN1",title:"Command-Based Programming (FRC WPILib)",est:"32 min",content:`## Command-Based Architecture

Command-based programming is WPILib's recommended framework for FRC robots. It separates **what the robot can do** (Subsystems) from **when to do it** (Commands).

### Core Concepts
\`\`\`
Subsystem = A robot mechanism (drivetrain, shooter, intake)
Command   = An action that uses one or more subsystems
Trigger   = Something that causes a command to run
Scheduler = Runs all active commands, handles conflicts
\`\`\`

### Creating a Subsystem
\`\`\`java
public class ShooterSubsystem extends SubsystemBase {
    private final CANSparkMax flywheelMotor;
    private final RelativeEncoder encoder;
    private final PIDController pid;
    private double targetRPM = 0;

    public ShooterSubsystem() {
        flywheelMotor = new CANSparkMax(5, MotorType.kBrushless);
        encoder = flywheelMotor.getEncoder();
        pid = new PIDController(0.0002, 0.0001, 0);
    }

    public void setTargetRPM(double rpm) { targetRPM = rpm; }
    public double getRPM() { return encoder.getVelocity(); }
    public boolean atTarget() { return Math.abs(getRPM()-targetRPM) < 50; }

    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        // periodic() runs every loop â€” like loop() for subsystems
        double output = pid.calculate(getRPM(), targetRPM);
        flywheelMotor.set(output);
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Shooter RPM", getRPM());
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Creating Commands
\`\`\`java
// InstantCommand â€” runs once immediately
new InstantCommand(() -> shooter.setTargetRPM(3000), shooter);

// RunCommand â€” runs every loop until interrupted
new RunCommand(() -> {
    shooter.setTargetRPM(3000);
}, shooter);

// Full command class for complex logic:
public class SpinUpCommand extends Command {
    private final ShooterSubsystem shooter;
    private final double targetRPM;

    public SpinUpCommand(ShooterSubsystem shooter, double rpm) {
        this.shooter = shooter;
        this.targetRPM = rpm;
        addRequirements(shooter); // Declares ownership
    }

    @Override public void initialize() { shooter.setTargetRPM(targetRPM); }
    @Override public boolean isFinished() { return shooter.atTarget(); }
    @Override public void end(boolean interrupted) {
        if (interrupted) shooter.setTargetRPM(0);
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Button Bindings in RobotContainer
\`\`\`java
// RobotContainer.java â€” bind buttons to commands
JoystickButton shootButton = new JoystickButton(gamepad, 1);

// While held: spin up. When released: stop.
shootButton.whileTrue(new SpinUpCommand(shooter, 3500));

// On press only:
shootButton.onTrue(new InstantCommand(()->intake.toggle()));

// Composed commands:
shootButton.onTrue(
    new SpinUpCommand(shooter, 3500)
        .andThen(new FeedCommand(feeder, 0.5))
        .withTimeout(2.0)
);
\`\`\`
`,quiz:[

          {q:"What does .andThen() do when chaining commands?",opts:["Runs both commands at the same time","Runs the second command after the first finishes","Cancels the first command","Reverses the command"],ans:1},
        ]
      },

      {id:"mbN1",title:"3D Printing for Robots",est:"20 min",content:`## FDM 3D Printing for FIRST Robots

3D printing is a superpower for FIRST teams â€” make custom brackets in hours, not days.

### Common Materials
| Material | Strength | Flex | Heat | Best For |
|----------|----------|------|------|----------|
| PLA | Medium | Low | Low (60Â°C) | Prototypes, covers |
| PETG | Good | Some | Medium (80Â°C) | Functional parts |
| TPU | Low | High | Medium | Bumpers, grips |
| ASA/ABS | Good | Low | High | Outdoor, heat areas |
| Nylon PA12 | Excellent | Some | High | Gears, load-bearing |

**FTC/FRC Rule:** Printed parts are legal if they don't violate other rules (sharp edges, weight limits, etc.)

### Print Settings That Matter
\`\`\`
Layer Height: 0.2mm â€” good balance of strength and speed
             0.1mm â€” stronger, much slower
Infill:       20% â€” covers/aesthetics
             40% â€” most functional parts
             60%+ â€” gears, high-stress brackets
Walls:        2 shells â€” light parts
              4 shells â€” structural parts
              6+ shells â€” critical load-bearing
Orientation:  CRITICAL â€” layers are weak in tension perpendicular to them
\`\`\`

### Designing for Printing
\`\`\`
âœ… DO:
- Orient so loads run parallel to layers (not perpendicular)
- Add fillets (0.5-2mm) to reduce stress concentrations
- Use hex nuts + heat inserts for threaded connections
- Design 0.2mm clearance for press-fit holes
- Wall thickness: minimum 1.5mm for FDM

âŒ DON'T:
- Print gears in PLA (use Nylon or buy metal)
- Use supports if you can avoid with good design
- Trust prints near motors (heat!)
- Print holes smaller than 3mm without drilling
\`\`\`

### Key Robotics Applications
- **Custom brackets:** Mount cameras, sensors at any angle
- **Cable guides:** Route wires cleanly through the robot
- **Intake wheels:** TPU for compliant surface (soft on game pieces)
- **Gear covers:** Protect drivetrain gears from debris
- **Jigs and fixtures:** Consistency when drilling or bending
`,quiz:[
          {q:"Why is print orientation critical for structural parts?",opts:["Aesthetics only","Layers are weak in tension perpendicular to them â€” load should run parallel to layers for maximum strength","Faster printing","Color accuracy"],ans:1},
          {q:"Which material is best for printed gears under load?",opts:["PLA â€” most common","TPU â€” flexible","Nylon PA12 â€” excellent strength and some flex","ABS â€” outdated"],ans:2},
          {q:"What infill percentage is recommended for high-stress brackets?",opts:["10%","20-30%","40-60%+","100% always"],ans:2},
        ]
      },
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"maN1",title:"Drivetrain Selection Deep Dive",est:"28 min",content:`## Choosing the Right Drivetrain

Your drivetrain choice fundamentally shapes your robot's capabilities. This is the most important mechanical decision of build season.

### Comparison Matrix
| Drivetrain | Agility | Pushing | Speed | Complexity | Cost |
|------------|---------|---------|-------|------------|------|
| Tank | Low | â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜…â˜… | Low | Low |
| West Coast | Medium | â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜… | Medium | Medium |
| Mecanum | â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜…â˜… | Medium | Medium |
| Swerve | â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜…â˜… | Very High | High |
| H-Drive | â˜…â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜… | â˜…â˜…â˜… | Medium | Medium |

### When to Choose Each
**Tank Drive:**
- Best for: Defense-heavy games, pushing matches, beginners
- Weakness: Can't strafe â€” must turn to realign

**Mecanum (FTC/FRC):**
- Best for: Games requiring precise lateral movement, tight spaces
- Weakness: Less pushing force, wheels wear fast, slips on carpet
- Math: All 4 wheels run simultaneously at different speeds

**Swerve (FRC mostly):**
- Best for: Highest-level competition, speed + agility
- Weakness: Complex maintenance, expensive, requires great programmers
- Avoid if: First year, small team, limited programming experience

### Gear Ratio Selection
\`\`\`
Target speed calculation:
Free speed of motor (RPM) Ã· Gear ratio = Wheel RPM
Wheel RPM Ã— Wheel circumference = Robot speed

Example (NEO motor on FRC mecanum):
5880 RPM Ã· 8.46:1 gear ratio = 695 wheel RPM
695 RPM Ã— (4" wheel Ã— Ï€ / 12) = 14.5 ft/s â‰ˆ 4.4 m/s

FRC typical target: 10-16 ft/s (3-5 m/s)
FTC typical target: 2-4 ft/s (0.6-1.2 m/s)
\`\`\`

### Wheel Selection
- **6" colson/plaction (FRC):** Durable, good traction, standard
- **4" mecanum (FRC/FTC):** Lateral movement, less traction
- **4" omni + 2" standard (FTC):** Dead-wheel odometry setup
- **90mm goBILDA mecanum (FTC):** Easy mounting, proven design

### Build Quality Factors
A well-built simple drivetrain beats a poorly-built complex one every time:
1. Parallel wheel alignment (< 1mm variance)
2. Chain/belt tension (not too tight, not loose)
3. Proper bearing press-fits
4. Ground clearance > 0.5" to avoid carpet drag

      {id:"sbN1",title:"Reading the Game Manual Like a Pro",est:"18 min",content:`## Game Manual Deep Dive

The game manual is your rulebook, scoring guide, and strategy bible all in one. Most teams don't read it carefully enough.

### Manual Structure (FRC/FTC)
\`\`\`
Section 1: Introduction â€” season theme, overview
Section 2: Arena â€” field dimensions, elements
Section 3: The Game â€” scoring, period rules
Section 4: The Robot â€” build rules, allowed materials
Section 5: Tournament â€” event structure, ranking
Section 6: Inspection â€” what referees check
Appendices â€” forms, legal parts lists, Q&A
\`\`\`

### First Read: 30-Minute Strategy Sprint
Do this within 24 hours of kickoff:

**Step 1 â€” Scoring:** Read Section 3 end-to-end. Circle every point value. Calculate maximum possible score.

**Step 2 â€” Ranking:** Find what earns Ranking Points. These shape your qualification strategy.

**Step 3 â€” Red flags:** Note any rules that could disqualify you or give opponents RP.

**Step 4 â€” Constraints:** What robot rules most limit your design? Height? Weight? Extension?

### Annotated Reading Example
\`\`\`
Rule G401: "Robots may not extend beyond their FRAME PERIMETER..."
â†³ Mark: Maximum extension = ___ inches
â†³ Strategy impact: High-goal scoring may require extension mechanism

Rule S203: "Contact with the opponent's LOADING ZONE is a FOUL..."
â†³ Mark: Keep away from loading zone during teleop
â†³ Driver training: Add bumper tape marking the zone boundary
\`\`\`

### Q&A â€” The Hidden Rulebook
The official Q&A answers referee questions:
- Check it weekly â€” answers change rulings
- Search past Q&As before submitting your own
- Print relevant Q&As to bring to events

### Rule Categories
| Category | Impact | Action |
|----------|--------|--------|
| Robot rules | Design constraints | Read before designing |
| Scoring rules | Strategy | Read immediately at kickoff |
| Safety rules | Inspection | Must comply 100% |
| Gameplay rules | Driver training | Practice avoiding penalties |

      {id:"saN1",title:"Alliance Selection Negotiation",est:"20 min",content:`## The Art of Alliance Selection

Alliance selection is a high-stakes negotiation. Being good at it wins championships even when your robot is average.

### The Offer Process (FRC)
\`\`\`
Round 1: Seeds 1-8 make first picks (in order)
Round 2: Seeds 1-8 make second picks (in reverse order)
Result: 8 alliances of 3 teams
Optional: Seeds may decline to captain â€” rare but legal
\`\`\`

### If You're an Alliance Captain
**Your goal:** Build the strongest complementary alliance.

Before selection:
1. Rank top 24 teams by YOUR specific needs (not just OPR)
2. Know which teams have already been picked
3. Have backup picks for every choice

Questions to ask a potential partner:
- "What was your most reliable auto this event?"
- "What's your cycle time on average?"
- "Does your robot play defense well?"
- "Any mechanical issues we should know about?"

**Red flags in their answer:**
- Vague or uncertain about their own performance
- "We're fixing that tonight" (for anything major)
- Claims that don't match your scouting data

### If You're Being Picked
**You have power:** You can decline any offer.
- Consider: Do they complement your weaknesses?
- Consider: Are you better off with alliance 2 vs alliance 1?
- Rarely smart to decline top-3 alliances

**Declining strategically:** If seed 3 picks you but you'd rather wait for seed 5, you can decline â€” risky but sometimes correct.

### Counter-picking (Second Pick)
Often more impactful than first pick:
- First pick fills your biggest weakness
- Second pick blocks your opponents' best options
- Consider: Who would seed 2 want? Pick them first.

### Negotiation Scripts
**As captain:** "We really liked your auto performance this weekend. Would you join our alliance?"

**If uncertain:** "Can I have 30 seconds?" â€” Always acceptable to pause and consult scouts.

**If you want to decline politely:** "Thank you for the offer â€” we're going to continue to the next round."

      {id:"ebN1",title:"FRC Electrical System Walkthrough",est:"22 min",content:`## FRC Electrical System: Every Component

FRC robots have strict electrical rules. Understanding every component prevents inspection failures and fires.

### Power Flow
\`\`\`
Battery (12V, 18Ah)
  â†“ (main breaker â€” master power switch)
Power Distribution Hub (PDH) or PDP
  â†“ (fused outputs â€” each circuit has its own breaker)
Motor Controllers, Radio, roboRIO
  â†“
Motors, Solenoids, Sensors
\`\`\`

### Required Components
| Component | Purpose | Rule |
|-----------|---------|------|
| Main Breaker | Emergency power cutoff | Must be accessible, red/button type |
| PDH/PDP | Distributes power, fuses circuits | One per robot |
| roboRIO | Main computer | FRC2 only for competition |
| RSL (Robot Signal Light) | Shows robot state | Blinking = enabled |
| Radio | WiFi link to driver station | Must use FRC radio |
| Battery | 12V, 18Ah minimum | NPC/MK or approved brands |

### Motor Controller Rules
- Each motor needs its own motor controller
- FRC-approved: Victor SPX, SPARK MAX, Talon SRX, Falcon 500 built-in
- All controllers to CAN bus OR PWM (not mixed on same controller)
- Current limit: set in software to protect motors

### Wiring Best Practices
\`\`\`
âœ… Power wires: red=positive, black=negative (ALWAYS)
âœ… Fuse every circuit appropriately (40A drivetrain, 20-30A arm, 10A small)
âœ… Strain relief: never let wires pull on connectors
âœ… Separate power and signal wires (noise reduction)
âœ… Anderson Powerpole connectors for main power
âœ… Label every wire â€” saves hours at competition

âŒ Never: bare wire exposed anywhere
âŒ Never: wire gauges too small (20A circuit â†’ minimum 18AWG)
âŒ Never: skip the main breaker
\`\`\`

### The RSL Signal Light
Rapid blink = robot enabled and receiving commands âš¡
Slow blink = robot on, not enabled
Solid = communications error or e-stop
