      {id:"eiN1",title:"Sensor Fusion â€” Combining Multiple Sensors",est:"24 min",content:`## Sensor Fusion: Better Together

No single sensor is perfect. Combining multiple sensors gives you more reliable measurements than any one alone.

### Why Fuse Sensors?
\`\`\`
IMU (gyro) alone:
  âœ… Fast, no drift over short time
  âŒ Drifts over long matches, affected by vibration

Odometry (encoders) alone:
  âœ… Accurate for straight movement
  âŒ Wheel slip causes drift in turns

Vision (camera) alone:
  âœ… Absolute position from field markers
  âŒ Can lose target, slow update rate

FUSED: IMU + Encoders + Vision = 
  Continuous tracking + drift correction + absolute reset
\`\`\`

### Dead Reckoning + IMU Correction
\`\`\`java
// Track position using encoders
double x = 0, y = 0;

// Each loop:
double deltaLeft = leftEncoder.getPositionInches();
double deltaRight = rightEncoder.getPositionInches();
double avgDelta = (deltaLeft + deltaRight) / 2.0;

// Use IMU heading (more reliable than encoder turning)
double heading = imu.getRobotYawPitchRollAngles()
                    .getYaw(AngleUnit.RADIANS);

// Update position using heading for direction
x += avgDelta * Math.cos(heading);
y += avgDelta * Math.sin(heading);
\`\`\`

### Vision Reset (AprilTag Correction)
\`\`\`java
// When AprilTag detected: trust vision over dead reckoning
if (!aprilTagDetections.isEmpty()) {
    AprilTagDetection det = aprilTagDetections.get(0);
    if (det.ftcPose.range < 36) { // Only trust close readings
        // Reset estimated position to vision measurement
        // (Much more accurate than accumulated odometry error)
        poseX = fieldPoseFromTag(det);
        poseY = fieldPoseFromTag(det);
    }
}
\`\`\`

### Simple Complementary Filter
\`\`\`java
// Complementary filter: trust gyro for fast changes,
// trust accelerometer for slow changes
// alpha = 0.98 means 98% gyro, 2% accel
double alpha = 0.98;
fusedAngle = alpha * (fusedAngle + gyroRate * dt)
           + (1-alpha) * accelAngle;
\`\`\`

### When to Use Each
- **Short auto (< 5 sec):** Dead reckoning + IMU usually sufficient
- **Long auto or complex paths:** Add vision resets at scoring positions
- **Teleop field-centric:** IMU only (fast, simple, accurate enough)

Build a live dashboard that displays real-time match data during competitions.

### Setup

from tkinter import ttk

### Basic Dashboard Window
\`\`\`python
class MatchDashboard:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = tk.Tk()
        self.root.title("âš¡ FIRST Match Dashboard")
        self.root.configure(bg="#0f172a")
        self.root.geometry("800x600")
        
        # Score display
        self.score_var = tk.StringVar(value="0")
        tk.Label(self.root, textvariable=self.score_var,
                 font=("Arial", 72, "bold"),
                 bg="#0f172a", fg="#1d4ed8").pack(pady=20)
        
        # Live data frame
        self.data_frame = tk.Frame(self.root, bg="#1e293b")
        self.data_frame.pack(fill="both", expand=True, padx=20)
        
        # Team stats grid
        self.labels = {}
        for i, key in enumerate(["Team", "Auto", "Cycles", "Climb", "Rating"]):
            tk.Label(self.data_frame, text=key, font=("Arial", 11, "bold"),
                    bg="#1e293b", fg="#64748b").grid(row=0, column=i, padx=10, pady=5)
\`\`\`

### Real-Time Update Loop
\`\`\`python
def update_loop(self):
    """Runs in background thread â€” reads CSV, updates display"""
    while self.running:
        if os.path.exists("scout_data.csv"):
            df = pd.read_csv("scout_data.csv")
            # Update UI from data (must use root.after for thread safety)
            self.root.after(0, self.refresh_display, df)
        time.sleep(2)  # Update every 2 seconds

def refresh_display(self, df):
    """Called on main thread â€” safe to update tkinter widgets"""
    for i, (_, row) in enumerate(df.tail(10).iterrows()):
        # Update or create label for each row
        key = f"team_{i}"
        text = f"{row['team']} | Auto:{row['auto']} | {row['climb']}"
        if key not in self.labels:
            self.labels[key] = tk.Label(self.data_frame, 
                bg="#0f172a", fg="#e2e8f0", font=("Arial",11))
            self.labels[key].grid(row=i+1, column=0, columnspan=5, sticky="w")
        self.labels[key].config(text=text)

def run(self):
    self.running = True
    t = threading.Thread(target=self.update_loop, daemon=True)
    t.start()
    self.root.mainloop()
    self.running = False
\`\`\`

def draw_comparison(self, canvas, teams, scores):
    canvas.delete("all")
    max_score = max(scores) if scores else 1
    
    for i, (team, score) in enumerate(zip(teams, scores)):
        x = 50 + i * 120
        bar_height = (score / max_score) * 200
        # Color based on score
        color = "#10b981" if score > 7 else "#f59e0b" if score > 5 else "#dc2626"
        canvas.create_rectangle(x, 250-bar_height, x+80, 250, fill=color)
        canvas.create_text(x+40, 265, text=f"#{team}", fill="white", font=("Arial",10))
        canvas.create_text(x+40, 250-bar_height-15, text=f"{score:.1f}", 
                          fill="white", font=("Arial",11,"bold"))

      {id:"sfaN1",title:"Chemical Safety in the Shop",est:"16 min",content:`## Chemical Safety for Robot Building

Robot shops use lubricants, adhesives, solvents, and coatings â€” all have hazards that are manageable with proper protocols.

### Common Chemicals and Hazards
| Chemical | Use | Hazard | Protection |
|----------|-----|--------|------------|
| WD-40 | Lubricant, loosener | Flammable, inhale hazard | Ventilation |
| Loctite | Thread locker | Skin sensitizer | Gloves |
| Acetone | Cleaning, ABS smoothing | Highly flammable, CNS depressant | Gloves + ventilation |
| Epoxy | Bonding | Skin sensitizer, eye irritant | Gloves + glasses |
| Spray paint | Finishing | Flammable, respiratory | Outdoors + mask |
| Cutting fluid | Metal machining | Low toxicity | Gloves optional |
| Electrical cleaner | PCB, connectors | Highly flammable | No flames nearby |

### SDS â€” Safety Data Sheets
Every chemical has an SDS (Safety Data Sheet):
- Find online or ask supplier
- Section 8: What PPE is required
- Section 9: Flash point (fire risk)
- Section 11: Toxicity information

**Rule:** If you don't have the SDS, don't use the chemical.

### Shop Protocols
\`\`\`
âœ… ALWAYS:
- Read SDS before first use of any chemical
- Ventilate when using solvents or sprays
- Keep flammables away from sparks and grinders
- Store in original labeled containers
- Dispose according to local regulations

âŒ NEVER:
- Mix chemicals unless the SDS says it's safe
- Use chemicals in enclosed spaces without ventilation
- Store flammables near heat sources or in direct sun
- Put chemicals in unlabeled containers
- Inhale any aerosol "just to smell it"
\`\`\`

### Spill Response
1. Don't panic â€” most spills are manageable
2. Flammable spill: eliminate ignition sources FIRST, then contain
3. Use absorbent material (paper towels, kitty litter) to contain
4. Ventilate immediately
5. Dispose per local regulations (never down the drain for solvents)

### Fire Extinguisher Knowledge
- **ABC type** covers most shop fires (wood, flammable liquid, electrical)
- **CO2** for sensitive electronics (no residue)
- PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep
- Never fight a fire that exceeds the extinguisher's capacity â€” evacuate

      {id:"jb_math",title:"Using Math in Robot Code",est:"12 min",content:`## Java's Math Class
Java has a built-in Math class with functions you'll use constantly on your robot.

## Most-Used Math Methods
\`\`\`java
// Absolute value â€” essential for motor power checks
double power = Math.abs(-0.75); // â†’ 0.75
if (Math.abs(gamepad1.left_stick_y) > 0.05) { ... } // deadzone

// Min / Max â€” clamping motor output
double rawPower = joystick + correction;
double safePower = Math.max(-1.0, Math.min(1.0, rawPower)); // clamp to [-1, 1]

// Square root
double distance = Math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy); // Pythagorean theorem

// Trig â€” heading math and vector decomposition
double angleRad = Math.toRadians(90.0);    // degrees â†’ radians
double angleDeg = Math.toDegrees(1.5708);  // radians â†’ degrees
double x = magnitude * Math.cos(angleRad);
double y = magnitude * Math.sin(angleRad);
double heading = Math.atan2(y, x); // angle from two components

// Power / rounding
double squared = Math.pow(2.0, 3.0); // 8.0 (2^3)
double rounded = Math.round(3.7);    // 4
double floor   = Math.floor(3.9);    // 3.0
double ceil    = Math.ceil(3.1);     // 4.0
\`\`\`

## Deadzone Pattern (Critical for Gamepad Input)
\`\`\`java
public double applyDeadzone(double input, double threshold) {
    if (Math.abs(input) < threshold) return 0.0;
    // Scale the remaining range to [0, 1] for smooth feel
    return (input - Math.signum(input) * threshold)
           / (1.0 - threshold);
}

double drive = applyDeadzone(-gamepad1.left_stick_y, 0.08);
\`\`\`

## Normalizing Motor Powers (Mecanum)
\`\`\`java
// After computing all four powers, normalize so no value exceeds 1.0
double[] powers = {lf, rf, lb, rb};
double max = 0;
for (double p : powers) max = Math.max(max, Math.abs(p));
if (max > 1.0) {
    for (int i = 0; i < powers.length; i++) powers[i] /= max;
}

    public static final int ARM_LOW_SCORE     =  750;
    public static final int ARM_HIGH_SCORE    = 1487;

    // â”€â”€ Servo Positions â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
    public static final double CLAW_OPEN      = 0.80;
    public static final double CLAW_CLOSED    = 0.20;
    public static final double WRIST_INTAKE   = 0.15;
    public static final double WRIST_SCORE    = 0.85;

    // â”€â”€ Autonomous Timing â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
    public static final int AUTO_SCORE_WAIT_MS   = 1200;
    public static final int AUTO_RETRACT_WAIT_MS =  800;

    // â”€â”€ PID â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
    public static final double DRIVE_KP = 0.01;
    public static final double DRIVE_KI = 0.0;
    public static final double DRIVE_KD = 0.005;
    public static final double ARM_KP   = 0.008;
}
\`\`\`

## Using Constants Anywhere
\`\`\`java
import static org.firstinspires.ftc.teamcode.Constants.*;
// Now use directly: ARM_HIGH_SCORE, CLAW_OPEN, etc.

arm.setTargetPosition(ARM_HIGH_SCORE);
claw.setPosition(CLAW_OPEN);
sleep(AUTO_SCORE_WAIT_MS);
\`\`\`

## Tuning at Competition
Constants files make competition tuning fast:
\`\`\`java
// Changed floor surface grip at regional â€” adjust once here,
// all OpModes update automatically:
public static final double AUTO_DRIVE_SPEED = 0.45; // was 0.50
\`\`\`

## Naming Convention
- ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES for constants (Java convention)
- Group by subsystem with comments
- Use units in the name: WAIT_MS, DIST_INCHES, SPEED (0-1)`,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should you use a Constants class instead of typing numbers directly in code?",opts:["Constants run faster","Named constants are self-documenting and changing a value once in Constants.java updates every OpMode â€” no hunting through files","Constants are required by FTC","Numbers work fine in code"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the Java naming convention for constants?",opts:["camelCase like motorSpeed","ALL_CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES like MOTOR_SPEED","PascalCase like MotorSpeed","lowercase like motorspeed"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is including the unit in a constant name (e.g., WAIT_MS, DIST_INCHES) a good practice?",opts:["It's required","It prevents unit errors â€” a teammate knows exactly whether WAIT_MS is in milliseconds or seconds without reading documentation","Units don't matter in robot code","It helps the compiler"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"ji_runmode",title:"Motor Run Modes â€” Deep Dive",est:"17 min",content:`## The Four Run Modes Explained Clearly

### RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER
\`\`\`java
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.5); // Raw PWM â€” you control everything
// Use for: Simple teleop drive, intake rollers, anything not needing position
\`\`\`

### RUN_USING_ENCODER
\`\`\`java
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_USING_ENCODER);
motor.setPower(0.5);
// Motor controller uses encoder to maintain CONSISTENT SPEED
// despite load changes and voltage drops
// Use for: Drive motors in auto, any motor where consistent speed matters
int pos = motor.getCurrentPosition(); // still read position
\`\`\`

### STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER
\`\`\`java
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER);
// Zeroes the encoder counter. ALWAYS call this before RUN_TO_POSITION
// Motor power is set to 0 automatically
\`\`\`

### RUN_TO_POSITION
\`\`\`java
motor.setTargetPosition(1500); // Set target BEFORE mode change
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
motor.setPower(0.8); // Power = MAX speed, not direction â€” mode handles direction
// Motor stops automatically when at target
// isBusy() returns true while moving toward target
while (motor.isBusy() && opModeIsActive()) {
    telemetry.addData("Pos", motor.getCurrentPosition());
    telemetry.update();
}
motor.setPower(0); // After isBusy() returns false, cut power
\`\`\`

## Common Mistakes
\`\`\`java
// âŒ WRONG â€” setting target AFTER changing mode
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION);
motor.setTargetPosition(1500); // TOO LATE â€” mode already active with stale target

// âœ… CORRECT
motor.setTargetPosition(1500); // Step 1
motor.setMode(DcMotor.RunMode.RUN_TO_POSITION); // Step 2
motor.setPower(0.8); // Step 3

// âŒ WRONG â€” negative power in RUN_TO_POSITION
motor.setPower(-0.8); // Negative power in RTP mode has unpredictable behavior!

// âœ… CORRECT â€” power is magnitude only
motor.setPower(0.8); // Mode figures out direction automatically
\`\`\`

## Choosing Run Modes
| Situation | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| TeleOp drive | RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER |
| Auto drive speed consistency | RUN_USING_ENCODER |
| Arm, lift, elevator presets | RUN_TO_POSITION |
| First OpMode init | STOP_AND_RESET_ENCODER â†’ then your mode |`,quiz:[
        {q:"In RUN_TO_POSITION mode, what does the setPower() value control?",opts:["Direction of movement","The maximum speed â€” the motor controller automatically determines direction based on target vs current position","Whether the encoder is active","The hold strength"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must setTargetPosition() be called BEFORE setMode(RUN_TO_POSITION)?",opts:["SDK requirement only","The mode becomes active immediately on setMode() â€” if the target isn't set yet, the motor may move to the previous stale target","It improves speed","The encoder needs to reset first"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the advantage of RUN_USING_ENCODER over RUN_WITHOUT_ENCODER for autonomous drive?",opts:["It's faster","The motor controller compensates for load and voltage changes to maintain consistent wheel speed â€” straight-line driving stays straighter","It uses less power","It allows backward movement"],ans:1},
      ]},
      {id:"ji_teleop_arch",title:"Structuring Complex TeleOp OpModes",est:"20 min",content:`## The Problem with One Giant Loop
As your robot grows to 10+ mechanisms, a single while loop becomes unmanageable. Structure it properly from the start.

## Three-Layer Architecture
\`\`\`java
@TeleOp(name = "Main TeleOp")
public class MainTeleOp extends LinearOpMode {
    // Layer 1: Hardware (through subsystem objects)
    MecanumDrive drive;
    ArmSubsystem arm;
    IntakeSubsystem intake;
    ClimberSubsystem climber;

    @Override
    public void runOpMode() {
        // â”€â”€ INIT PHASE â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
        initHardware();
        telemetry.addData("Status", "Ready");
        telemetry.update();
        waitForStart();

        // â”€â”€ RUN LOOP â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
        while (opModeIsActive()) {
            // Layer 2: Input processing
            readGamepads();

            // Layer 3: Update each subsystem
            drive.update();
            arm.update();
            intake.update();
            climber.update();

            // Telemetry last
            updateTelemetry();
        }
    }

    private void initHardware() {
        drive   = new MecanumDrive(hardwareMap);
        arm     = new ArmSubsystem(hardwareMap);
        intake  = new IntakeSubsystem(hardwareMap);
        climber = new ClimberSubsystem(hardwareMap);
    }

    private void readGamepads() {
        // Driver 1: movement
        drive.setInput(
            gamepad1.left_stick_x,
            -gamepad1.left_stick_y,
            gamepad1.right_stick_x
        );

        // Driver 2: mechanisms
        if (gamepad2.a) arm.requestPosition(ArmSubsystem.INTAKE);
        if (gamepad2.y) arm.requestPosition(ArmSubsystem.HIGH_SCORE);
        if (gamepad2.right_bumper) intake.requestToggle();
        if (gamepad2.left_bumper)  climber.requestExtend();
    }

    private void updateTelemetry() {
        telemetry.addData("Drive Mode", drive.getMode());
        telemetry.addData("Arm Pos", arm.getPosition());
        telemetry.addData("Intake", intake.getState());
        telemetry.addData("Climber", climber.getState());
        telemetry.update();
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Button Edge Detection (Press vs Hold)
\`\`\`java
// Inside IntakeSubsystem.java:
private boolean prevRB = false;
private boolean intakeRunning = false;

public void requestToggle(boolean button) {
    if (button && !prevRB) { // rising edge only
        intakeRunning = !intakeRunning;
        motor.setPower(intakeRunning ? 1.0 : 0.0);
    }
    prevRB = button;
}
\`\`\`

## Benefits of This Pattern
- **Readable:** Each method does one thing
- **Debuggable:** Add telemetry to one subsystem without touching others
- **Testable:** Can swap a subsystem mock for testing
- **Scalable:** Adding a new mechanism = new subsystem class + 3 lines in OpMode`,quiz:[
        {q:"What problem does a three-layer TeleOp architecture solve?",opts:["It speeds up code execution","It prevents a single giant loop from becoming unmanageable â€” each subsystem is self-contained, readable, and independently debuggable","It's required for advanced competitions","It reduces battery consumption"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is 'edge detection' in the context of button input?",opts:["Detecting when the robot approaches a field wall","Detecting only the moment a button is first pressed (rising edge), not while it continues to be held â€” prevents rapid toggling"],ans:1},
        {q:"In this architecture, what should the main OpMode loop ideally contain?",opts:["All motor control logic","Only high-level calls: read inputs, call subsystem update methods, output telemetry â€” actual logic lives in subsystem classes","All PID calculations","Only telemetry"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"ja_async",title:"Action Sequences & Non-Blocking Code",est:"25 min",content:`## The Problem with sleep()
\`\`\`java
// This blocks EVERYTHING â€” no teleop input, no telemetry
arm.setPosition(ARM_HIGH);
sleep(1500); // robot is frozen for 1.5 seconds
score();
sleep(500);
retract();
\`\`\`

## Non-Blocking Action Sequences with ElapsedTime
\`\`\`java
public class ActionSequencer {
    enum Step { RAISE_ARM, WAIT_FOR_ARM, SCORE, WAIT_SCORE, RETRACT, DONE }
    private Step currentStep = Step.RAISE_ARM;
    private ElapsedTime stepTimer = new ElapsedTime();

    public void update(ArmSubsystem arm, ScorerSubsystem scorer) {
        switch (currentStep) {
            case RAISE_ARM:
                arm.setPosition(ARM_HIGH_SCORE);
                stepTimer.reset();
                currentStep = Step.WAIT_FOR_ARM;
                break;
            case WAIT_FOR_ARM:
                // Non-blocking wait: check arm position OR timeout
                if (arm.atTarget() || stepTimer.seconds() > 2.0)
                    currentStep = Step.SCORE;
                break;
            case SCORE:
                scorer.eject();
                stepTimer.reset();
                currentStep = Step.WAIT_SCORE;
                break;
            case WAIT_SCORE:
                if (stepTimer.milliseconds() > 400)
                    currentStep = Step.RETRACT;
                break;
            case RETRACT:
                arm.setPosition(ARM_STOWED);
                scorer.stop();
                currentStep = Step.DONE;
                break;
            case DONE:
                break; // sequence complete
        }
    }

    public boolean isDone() { return currentStep == Step.DONE; }
    public void reset()     { currentStep = Step.RAISE_ARM; }
}
\`\`\`

## Using It in TeleOp â€” Sequence + Manual Simultaneously
\`\`\`java
ActionSequencer scoreSequence = new ActionSequencer();
boolean sequenceActive = false;

// In main loop:
if (gamepad2.y && !sequenceActive) {
    scoreSequence.reset();
    sequenceActive = true;
}

if (sequenceActive) {
    scoreSequence.update(arm, scorer);
    if (scoreSequence.isDone()) sequenceActive = false;
}

// Drive ALWAYS works â€” not blocked by the sequence!
drive.driveFieldCentric(gamepad1.left_stick_x,
                        -gamepad1.left_stick_y,
                        gamepad1.right_stick_x);
\`\`\`

## ElapsedTime Cheat Sheet
\`\`\`java
ElapsedTime timer = new ElapsedTime();
timer.reset();                   // restart timer
double ms  = timer.milliseconds(); // time in ms
double sec = timer.seconds();      // time in seconds
\`\`\`

## Why Non-Blocking Matters
A blocking \`sleep(1500)\` means your robot CANNOT respond to defense, driver corrections, or safety stops for 1.5 seconds. Non-blocking sequences keep the robot responsive while executing complex automation.`,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the fundamental problem with using sleep() for mechanism sequences in TeleOp?",opts:["It uses more battery","sleep() blocks all code execution â€” the robot cannot respond to driver input, defense, or safety stops during the wait","It's not available in TeleOp","Sleep is too imprecise"],ans:1},
        {q:"In a non-blocking state machine sequence, how do you wait for a mechanism without freezing the robot?",opts:["Use Thread.sleep()","Check a condition each loop iteration (e.g., arm.atTarget()) â€” only advance to next step when ready, but other code runs every loop","Use a longer loop delay","Only non-blocking code works in Auto"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why include a timeout (e.g., stepTimer.seconds() > 2.0) when waiting for a mechanism to reach position?",opts:["Timeouts are required by FTC rules","If the mechanism stalls or fails to reach position, the timeout prevents the sequence from freezing forever","Timeouts improve mechanism speed","It's faster than checking position"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

  // â•â• MECHANICAL â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•â•

      {id:"mb_tolerances",title:"Tolerances & Fit â€” Why Parts Stick or Wobble",est:"13 min",content:`## What is a Tolerance?
No part is perfectly the correct size. A tolerance is the allowable variation. Understanding tolerances prevents printed/machined parts that are too loose to function or too tight to assemble.

## Types of Fit
\`\`\`
Clearance Fit:   Hole is LARGER than shaft â€” parts move freely
                 â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”
                 â”‚ â—‹    â”‚  â† shaft rattles in hole
                 â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜

Interference Fit: Hole is SMALLER than shaft â€” force required to assemble
                 "Press fit" â€” parts stay together without fasteners
                 Use for: bearing seats, hubs on shafts

Transition Fit:  May be clearance or interference â€” slight snugness
                 Use for: parts that need to be removable but not wobbly
\`\`\`

## 3D Printing Tolerances (FDM)
\`\`\`
Standard FDM printers have Â±0.2 to Â±0.5mm accuracy.

If you design a 10mm hole to fit a 10mm shaft:
  It will likely be ~9.6-9.8mm â€” TOO TIGHT

Rule of thumb for FDM:
  Add 0.3-0.5mm to holes that need clearance
  10mm shaft â†’ design hole as 10.4mm

For hex shaft hubs (common in FTC):
  REV 15mm hex shaft â†’ design hex hole as 15.5mm across flats
\`\`\`

## Metal & Machined Parts
\`\`\`
For FIRST robots, typical tolerances:
  Laser cut / CNC routed:  Â±0.005" (Â±0.13mm) â€” very precise
  Bandsaw cut:             Â±0.030" (Â±0.76mm) â€” rough
  3D printed:              Â±0.020" (Â±0.51mm)
  COTS (GoBILDA, REV):     Designed to work together â€” follow their specs
\`\`\`

## Practical Tips
- **Test fit before assembly** â€” print one bearing pocket, check fit, then print the full part
- **Sandpaper** (220 grit) can open up a slightly tight 3D printed hole
- **Shims** (thin washers) fix loose fits without reprinting
- **GoBILDA and REV** hardware is designed to fit together â€” always prefer COTS fit to custom when possible`,quiz:[
        {q:"Why do 3D printed holes typically need to be designed slightly larger than the intended shaft size?",opts:["FDM printers always print too large","FDM printers tend to produce slightly undersized holes due to material shrinkage and layer adhesion â€” adding 0.3-0.5mm compensates","3D printed holes are accurate â€” no adjustment needed","Larger holes are stronger"],ans:1},
        {q:"What type of fit is used for bearing seats â€” where a bearing is pressed in and must not move?",opts:["Clearance fit","Interference (press) fit â€” the hole is slightly smaller than the bearing OD so it grips without fasteners","Transition fit","Gap fit"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the fastest fix for a 3D printed hole that is slightly too tight?",opts:["Reprint the entire part","Lightly sand the hole with 220-grit sandpaper to open it up slightly","Use a larger bolt","Add epoxy"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"mi_springs",title:"Springs, Surgical Tubing & Elastic Assistance",est:"15 min",content:`## Using Elastic Force to Help Mechanisms
Springs and surgical tubing store energy. In robot design, they can counterbalance arms, return mechanisms to resting position, and reduce motor load.

## Arm Counterbalancing
\`\`\`
Without spring:           With counterbalance spring:
Motor holds full          Spring assists on the way up,
arm weight at all         opposes on the way down.
angles. High current,     Motor does LESS WORK overall.
gets hot, stalls.

             â†— arm
    â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â—                â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â—
         |                     |~~~~ (spring)
    â–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆ (motor)           â–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆ (motor)

Benefit: Up to 40% less motor current on lifts
\`\`\`

## Types of Elastic Components Used in FIRST
| Type | Force Characteristic | Best Use |
|------|---------------------|----------|
| Extension spring | Force increases with stretch | Constant-force assist |
| Compression spring | Force increases when compressed | Return mechanism, shock absorb |
| Surgical tubing | Non-linear â€” high force when stretched far | Catapults, retraction |
| Bungee cord | Similar to surgical tubing | Large-scale retraction |
| Torsion spring | Rotational force | Hinged flaps, claw return |

## Constant Force Spring (Linear Slide Counterbalance)
\`\`\`
Constant force springs unroll like a tape measure.
Force stays CONSTANT regardless of extension.
Perfect for vertical linear slides â€” counterbalances
the mechanism weight evenly at all heights.
\`\`\`

## Surgical Tubing for Active Intake Flaps
\`\`\`
Many FTC intakes use flexible surgical tubing as "finger"
rollers. Benefits:
- Compliant â€” conforms to game piece shape
- Self-wiping â€” debris falls off spinning tubing
- Inexpensive and replaceable
- Available in different ODs for different grip levels
\`\`\`

## Key Design Consideration
\`\`\`
Spring force at max extension Ã— arm length = torque counterbalanced

Example:
  Spring force = 5 lbs
  Moment arm  = 8 inches
  Torque      = 40 in-lb

Motor torque needed WITHOUT spring: 60 in-lb
Motor torque needed WITH spring:    60 - 40 = 20 in-lb
Motor current reduced substantially!
\`\`\`
        {q:"Why is Math.abs() essential when working with gamepad joystick inputs?",opts:["It speeds up input processing","Joysticks return negative values when pushed down â€” Math.abs() lets you check magnitude regardless of direction for deadzone checks","It converts degrees to radians","It normalizes motor powers"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does 'clamping' a motor power value mean?",opts:["Physically stopping the motor","Using Math.max and Math.min to ensure the value never goes outside the allowed range of [-1.0, 1.0]","Rounding the power to the nearest integer","Applying a deadzone"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should you normalize mecanum motor powers after computing them?",opts:["It's required by FTC SDK","If any computed power exceeds 1.0, the motor will error â€” normalizing scales all four values proportionally so the largest is exactly 1.0","Normalization speeds up the motors","It reduces battery use"],ans:1},
Packaging is how you fit all subsystems into the size limits while keeping every mechanism accessible, serviceable, and safe from interference.

## Know Your Size Limits
\`\`\`
FTC:  18" Ã— 18" Ã— 18" starting configuration
      Robot may expand after match begins â€” check current game rules!

FRC:  28" wide Ã— 26" deep Ã— depends on year's rules
      Frame perimeter limit: typically 120" max
      Height limit: varies by game (often ~4.5 feet)
\`\`\`

## The Packaging Process
\`\`\`
Step 1: List ALL mechanisms with approximate dimensions
  - Drive chassis: 13" Ã— 13"
  - Vertical lift: 3" wide, 20" tall (when extended)
  - Intake: 14" wide, 6" long (stows inside frame)
  - Claw: 4" Ã— 4"

Step 2: Draw a top-down layout (CAD or paper)
  - Place drivetrain first (it determines everything else)
  - Find lowest CoG placement for heaviest parts (battery, motors)
  - Check reach: can your intake actually reach game pieces from this position?

Step 3: Check interference envelopes
  - Path of moving arm â€” does it hit the drive chassis?
  - Cable routing â€” will wires get caught in the lift?
  - Service access â€” can you swap a motor in 2 minutes at competition?
\`\`\`

## Competition Serviceability Rules
\`\`\`
âœ… Can you change a battery in under 60 seconds?
âœ… Can you reach every motor connector without disassembly?
âœ… Is the Control Hub accessible when robot is assembled?
âœ… Can you tighten a chain without removing other parts?
âœ… Can you replace a servo without tools longer than a hex key?

If any answer is NO â†’ redesign access BEFORE cutting metal.
\`\`\`

## Common Packaging Mistakes
- Battery buried under electronics â€” 3-minute battery swap = pit nightmare
- Control Hub under a plate â€” can't see status LEDs during debugging
- Arm pivot point too high â€” eats into starting height limit
- Cables routed across moving mechanisms â€” guaranteed to fail mid-competition`,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should serviceability be considered during the packaging/design phase rather than after building?",opts:["Serviceability is a competition rule","Retroactively adding access holes or redesigning mounts to reach buried components is far more costly than designing for access from the start","Serviceability only matters in teleop","Judges evaluate serviceability"],ans:1},
        {q:"What should be placed first when laying out a robot's top-down packaging diagram?",opts:["The scoring mechanism","The battery","The drive chassis â€” all other mechanisms must fit around it since it determines the robot's footprint and CoG baseline","The electronics"],ans:2},
        {q:"What is the risk of routing cables across moving mechanisms?",opts:["Minor inconvenience","Cables can be cut, pulled, or worn through by moving parts â€” causing electrical failures mid-competition that are extremely difficult to diagnose","Cable routing doesn't affect reliability","Only applies to FRC robots"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"ma_gearbox",title:"Custom Gearbox Design",est:"28 min",content:`## When to Build a Custom Gearbox
COTS gearboxes (GoBILDA, AM, VEXpro) cover 90% of FIRST needs. Build custom when:
- You need a specific ratio not available off-the-shelf
- Space constraints force a non-standard profile
- You need a specific output shaft orientation or dual-output
- You've analyzed the loads and no COTS option survives

## Gear Ratio Calculation Review
\`\`\`
Ratio = (driven gear teeth) / (driving gear teeth)
      = Output reduction

Multiple-stage gearbox:
  Stage 1: 12T â†’ 60T = 5:1
  Stage 2: 16T â†’ 48T = 3:1
  Overall:  5 Ã— 3 = 15:1 reduction

Speed:  Motor RPM / ratio = output RPM
Torque: Motor torque Ã— ratio Ã— efficiency â‰ˆ output torque
        (efficiency â‰ˆ 0.95 per stage for spur gears)
\`\`\`

## Gear Material Selection
| Material | Use | Notes |
|----------|-----|-------|
| Steel | High-torque output shaft | Heavy, strong, machines well |
| Aluminum | Mid-stage gears | Lighter, wears faster under shock loads |
| Delrin/Acetal | Low-torque, low-weight | Self-lubricating, quiet, 3D-printable |
| 3D printed PLA | Prototyping only | Will strip under real competition loads |
| Fiberglass-filled nylon | Good balance | Used by many COTS suppliers |

## Center Distance Formula
\`\`\`
For two spur gears:
  Center Distance = (Gear1 Teeth + Gear2 Teeth) / (2 Ã— Diametral Pitch)

GoBILDA uses MOD 1 gears (metric):
  Center Distance = (T1 + T2) Ã— 0.5 mm

Example: 20T driving 60T (both MOD 1):
  Center Distance = (20 + 60) Ã— 0.5 = 40 mm
\`\`\`

## Bearing Selection for Gearboxes
\`\`\`
For most FIRST gearboxes:
  Input shaft (high speed, low torque):  small radial ball bearing
  Output shaft (low speed, high torque): larger bearing, consider thrust load

Bearing press fit tolerances:
  ID should match shaft with slight interference (shaft diameter + 0.0mm/-0.001")
  OD should press into housing with interference fit
\`\`\`

## Output Shaft Power Limits
\`\`\`
Don't exceed the motor's stall torque even with reduction:
  Motor stall torque: 3.0 NÂ·m
  Gearbox ratio:      15:1
  Efficiency:         0.90 (two stages)
  Max output torque:  3.0 Ã— 15 Ã— 0.90 = 40.5 NÂ·m

Design for HALF of max to leave safety margin:
  Operating torque target: ~20 NÂ·m
\`\`\`

## Backlash Reduction
- Use anti-backlash gear pairs for precision positioning (arm, turret)
- Tension the gear mesh properly â€” a slight drag is correct
- Planet gears have less backlash than spur trains for the same ratio`,quiz:[

      {id:"eb_crimp",title:"Crimping & Connector Types",est:"14 min",content:`## Why Good Crimps Matter
A bad crimp is one of the top causes of electrical failures at competition. A wire that "looks connected" but has a high-resistance crimp will cause intermittent voltage drops, brownouts, and mystery motor stalls.

## FTC Common Connectors
| Connector | Use | Tool Needed |
|-----------|-----|-------------|
| JST-VH (2-pin) | Motor power | JST crimper or pre-made |
| XT30 | Battery main power | Soldering iron (solder, don't crimp) |
| Anderson PowerPole | High current distribution | PowerPole crimper |
| Dupont (2.54mm) | Encoder, sensor signal wires | Dupont crimper |
| Tamiya | Legacy FTC battery | Pre-made recommended |

## FRC Common Connectors
| Connector | Use |
|-----------|-----|
| Anderson SB50 | Battery to PDP |
| Wago lever nuts | PDP output terminals |
| WAGO 221 inline | Quick splice connections |
| Phoenix Contact | Motor controller signal |
| CAN/RJ45 | CANivore, roboRIO comms |

## How to Make a Good Crimp
\`\`\`
1. Strip wire: 5-6mm of insulation â€” not more
   (Too much bare wire = short risk; too little = weak crimp)

2. Insert wire fully into crimp terminal:
   All strands must enter the crimp barrel
   A strand outside the barrel = high-resistance crimp

3. Crimp properly:
   Use the correct die size for your terminal
   Crimp the WIRE portion first, then the insulation strain relief

4. Inspect:
   Tug test â€” wire should not pull out with hand force
   Look at the end â€” all wire strands should be visible and compressed
   No green/black corrosion on wire strands
\`\`\`

## The Tug Test
After EVERY crimp: grip the wire 2 inches from the terminal and pull firmly. If it pulls out, recrimp. Competition loads are rougher than your tug test â€” if it barely passes, redo it.

## Heat Shrink Protocol
\`\`\`
âœ… Apply heat shrink over every exposed crimp terminal
âœ… Cover at least 10mm of wire insulation on each side
âœ… Use a heat gun, not an open flame
âœ… Slide heat shrink onto wire BEFORE crimping (can't add after)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the main benefit of adding a counterbalance spring to a robot arm?",opts:["It makes the arm move faster","The spring assists the motor lifting the arm, reducing current draw and preventing motor overheating or stall","Springs are required for safety","It locks the arm position"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why are constant-force springs ideal for linear slide counterbalancing?",opts:["They're cheapest","They provide the same force regardless of how far the slide extends â€” perfectly offsetting the mechanism's constant weight at all heights","They are the strongest option","They don't require attachment points"],ans:1},
        {q:"What makes surgical tubing effective as intake 'finger' rollers?",opts:["It's rigid and strong","It's compliant â€” conforms to game piece shape â€” and self-clears debris while spinning","It's required by FTC rules","It has the highest grip coefficient"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the most common cause of high-resistance crimps?",opts:["Wrong wire gauge","Not all wire strands fully entering the crimp barrel â€” even one strand outside causes a poor connection","Too much heat shrink","Crimping too hard"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the 'tug test' check for after crimping?",opts:["Wire length","Whether the crimp mechanically retains the wire under force â€” if it pulls out by hand, it will fail under competition vibration","Insulation thickness","Connector polarity"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must heat shrink be placed on the wire BEFORE crimping?",opts:["It's optional","Once the crimp terminal is attached, heat shrink tubing cannot slide past it â€” it must be preloaded on the wire first","Heat shrink weakens crimps","It's only required for high-voltage wires"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"ei_ftc_power",title:"FTC Power Chain & Brownout Protection",est:"18 min",content:`## The FTC Power Chain
Every component in FTC has a maximum current draw. Understanding the chain prevents brownouts that disable your robot mid-match.

## FTC Power Chain (Complete)
\`\`\`
12V Battery (20A max)
    â†“
Main Power Switch (fused)
    â†“
REV Control Hub (main power input)
    â†“ (12V direct)         â†“ (5V regulated)
Motor ports (4Ã—)      Servo ports (6Ã—)
Expansion Hub ports   USB accessories
    â†“
Motors (each draws 0-9A stall)
\`\`\`

## Current Limits to Know
| Component | Max Continuous | Stall Current |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| REV Control Hub per motor port | 20A | â€” |
| GoBILDA 312 RPM motor | ~2A typical | ~9.2A stall |
| REV Servo (standard) | 6A total for all servos | â€” |
| REV Smart Robot Servo | 6A peak | â€” |

## What Causes a Brownout?
\`\`\`
Brownout: Battery voltage drops below ~7V under load.
Effect:   Control Hub restarts, robot goes unresponsive.

Common causes:
1. Multiple motors stalling simultaneously (arm hits hard stop + drive fighting wall)
2. Cold or old battery with high internal resistance
3. Long, thin power wires with excessive resistance
4. Running 4 drive motors + 2 arm motors + 2 servos simultaneously at full power
\`\`\`

## Preventing Brownouts
\`\`\`java
// 1. Current limiting in code â€” ramp motor power
public void setDrivePower(double target) {
    double current = motor.getPower();
    double ramp = 0.1; // max change per loop
    double next = current + Math.signum(target - current)
                          * Math.min(ramp, Math.abs(target - current));
    motor.setPower(next);
}

// 2. Limit simultaneous high-current operations
if (arm.isMoving()) {
    drive.setMaxSpeed(0.6); // reduce drive speed while arm moves
}

// 3. Check battery voltage
double voltage = hardwareMap.voltageSensor
                            .get("Control Hub").getVoltage();
if (voltage < 11.5) {
    telemetry.addData("âš ï¸ Battery Low", "%.1fV", voltage);
}
\`\`\`

## Battery Maintenance
- Charge before EVERY match â€” don't trust "it was 80% yesterday"
- Rotate between 2 batteries during competition day
- Check battery voltage: healthy 12V battery reads 12.5-13.0V at rest
- Replace batteries that sag below 11V under light load`,quiz:[
        {q:"What is a robot brownout and what causes it?",opts:["A software crash in the OpMode","The battery voltage drops below ~7V under high current draw, causing the Control Hub to restart and the robot to go unresponsive","A servo overload","A sensor timeout"],ans:1},
        {q:"What coding technique reduces brownout risk from sudden high motor loads?",opts:["Running motors at full power always","Power ramping â€” gradually increasing motor power over several loop iterations instead of jumping to full instantly","Reducing telemetry frequency","Disabling encoders"],ans:1},
        {q:"What voltage should a healthy FTC battery read at rest before a match?",opts:["9-10V","10-11V","12.5-13.0V","14-15V"],ans:2},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"sb_gamemanual",title:"How to Read the Game Manual",est:"15 min",content:`## The Game Manual Is Your Rulebook
Every FIRST season begins with a new game manual. Teams that understand it deeply find point opportunities and avoid penalties that slower-reading teams miss.

## FTC Game Manual Structure
\`\`\`
Section 1: General Rules
  - Robot size limits, weight limits
  - Allowed materials and components
  - Match structure (auto/teleop/endgame timing)

Section 2: The Game (Season-Specific)
  - Field layout and game piece descriptions
  - Scoring definitions (exactly how many points each action is worth)
  - Autonomous game-specific rules
  - Endgame rules
  - Penalty definitions
\`\`\`

## Key Reading Strategy: Point Value First
\`\`\`
Step 1: List EVERY way to score points (including bonuses)
Step 2: Calculate the MAXIMUM possible score
Step 3: Identify which high-value actions are achievable by most teams
Step 4: Identify which high-value actions are achievable only by elite teams
Step 5: Design your robot to maximize achievable points reliably
\`\`\`

## Common Penalty Traps (Check Carefully)
\`\`\`
âœ… Read what counts as a "possession" limit
âœ… Read what counts as "destroying" a game piece (auto penalty)
âœ… Read the G-code penalties (robot interaction rules)
âœ… Read what triggers a minor vs major penalty
âœ… Read the definition of "controlled" placement vs "dropping"
\`\`\`

## Qualification vs Elimination Scoring
Some actions score differently or have different rules in playoffs. Mark these clearly when reading â€” your qualification strategy may need to change in elims.

## Update Bulletins
\`\`\`
FIRST issues Q&A answers and rule updates throughout the season.
Subscribe to updates and re-read affected sections after each bulletin.
A rule clarified in Week 3 can change your entire strategy.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What should be your first analysis step after reading the game manual?",opts:["Design the drivetrain immediately","List every way to score points including bonuses and calculate the theoretical maximum â€” this tells you where the real points are","Check the field dimensions","Order parts"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must you re-read the game manual after FIRST issues update bulletins?",opts:["It's required by FIRST","Rule clarifications and updates can change how points are scored or what's legal â€” missing an update can mean penalties or missed opportunities","Bulletins only contain typo fixes","Updates only affect FRC teams"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why do many experienced teams read the 'penalties' section of the manual as carefully as the scoring section?",opts:["Penalties aren't worth reading","Avoiding penalties is free points â€” a team that gives away 30 penalty points per match loses to an equal-scoring team that doesn't","Penalties don't apply to rookies","Only referees need to read penalties"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"sa_data_elim",title:"Data-Driven Elimination Match Planning",est:"22 min",content:`## Elimination Matches Are Different
In qualifications, you play with randomly assigned partners and opponents. In eliminations, you chose your alliance and know exactly who you're facing. Use this predictability.

## Pre-Match Alliance Analysis
\`\`\`python
# Pseudocode: Before each elim match
alliance_avg  = mean([team_a_avg, team_b_avg, your_avg])
alliance_sd   = combined_variance([team_a_sd, team_b_sd, your_sd])

opponent_avg  = mean([opp_1_avg, opp_2_avg, opp_3_avg])
opponent_sd   = combined_variance([...])

# Probability of winning (rough estimate)
# If alliance_avg >> opponent_avg: play offense, don't risk anything
# If opponent_avg >> alliance_avg: consider defense on their best scorer
\`\`\`

## Strategy Card for Each Match
\`\`\`
Match: Semifinal 1-1
Our Alliance:  1234 | 5678 | 9012 (us)
Their Alliance: 2345 | 6789 | 3456

Key facts:
  Team 2345: best auto on field (avg 22 pts auto)
  Team 6789: avg 4.2 cycles/teleop â€” slowest scorer
  Team 3456: 100% climb rate â€” reliable L3

Our plan:
  - 9012 (us): play defense on 2345 in auto if legal, else run our own
  - 1234: focus on high-volume cycles
  - 5678: early climb at 1:00 remaining (confirmed with them)
  - 9012: late defense if score is close at 0:45
\`\`\`

## Live Match Adjustments
\`\`\`
Things to watch in the FIRST 30 seconds:
  â†’ Did their best auto actually work today?
  â†’ Are they running all 3 robots or is one disabled?
  â†’ Which alliance is scoring faster in teleop?

Adjustments to communicate (at next timeout or between matches):
  â†’ "Their #2345 auto failed â€” switch to full offense"
  â†’ "Their #6789 is playing defense today â€” ignore them"
  â†’ "We're 20 pts down at 1:00 â€” need faster cycles, delay climb"
\`\`\`

## The +10 Mindset
In close elimination matches, every decision should be evaluated by:
"Does this action (or avoiding this penalty) gain or prevent 10+ points?"
- Risky defense that likely triggers a major penalty: 30 pts given away â€” NOT worth it
- Securing a reliable endgame point that's worth 20: ALWAYS worth the time`,quiz:[
        {q:"How does elimination match strategy differ from qualification match strategy?",opts:["It doesn't â€” same approach","In elims you know your partners and opponents in advance, allowing specific game plans against known robot capabilities â€” qualifications are random","Elims use different scoring","Partners don't matter in qualifications"],ans:1},
        {q:"What key information should a pre-match strategy card capture?",opts:["Only the score prediction","Each team's key strengths/weaknesses, the alliance plan for autonomous and endgame, and who handles what role during teleop","Only autonomous plans","Only climb plans"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the '+10 mindset' in elimination decision-making?",opts:["Always score 10 points in auto","Evaluate every decision by whether it gains or prevents 10+ net points â€” penalizing risky actions that likely give away more than they gain","Try to score 10 points per cycle","Focus on the top 10 teams"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"tmb1",title:"Roles on a FIRST Team",est:"12 min",content:`## Why Defined Roles Matter
Every team member should know what they own. Without clear roles, important tasks fall through the cracks â€” or three people do the same thing while something critical is missed.

## Core Technical Roles
\`\`\`
Programming Lead
  â†’ Owns all code; reviews PRs; trains new programmers
  â†’ Responsible for code working on competition day

Mechanical Lead
  â†’ Owns CAD and build quality
  â†’ Final say on mechanism design decisions

Electrical Lead
  â†’ Owns all wiring; ensures documentation of pinouts
  â†’ Responsible for robot being inspection-ready electrically

Drive Team Captain
  â†’ Drives robot; leads in-match strategy calls
  â†’ Responsible for knowing every robot capability and limit
\`\`\`

## Core Non-Technical Roles
\`\`\`
Business/Outreach Lead
  â†’ Manages sponsor communications and awards submissions
  â†’ Coordinates community outreach events

Scouting Lead
  â†’ Owns scouting system design and data collection at events
  â†’ Produces pick list and match strategy reports

Safety Captain
  â†’ Enforces shop PPE rules
  â†’ Leads safety briefings; required at FRC events
  â†’ Nominated for safety pin award by FRC FIRST inspectors

Notebook Lead (FTC)
  â†’ Owns Engineering Notebook quality and completeness
  â†’ Ensures entries are dated and follow the design process
\`\`\`

## The T-Shape Skill Model
\`\`\`
Best team members have:
  Depth in ONE area (their primary role)
  Breadth across all areas (can help anywhere when needed)

   Programming â–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆâ–ˆ (deep)
   Mechanical  â–ˆâ–ˆ (familiar)
   Electrical  â–ˆâ–ˆ (familiar)
   Strategy    â–ˆâ–ˆ (familiar)
\`\`\`

## Mentors vs Students
FIRST rules (especially FRC) restrict what mentors can do:
- Mentors: guide, advise, teach â€” they should not do the work
- Students: design, build, program, drive â€” own all execution
- The robot must be student-built â€” judges and inspectors verify this`,quiz:[
        {q:"Why is it important for team members to have defined roles?",opts:["FIRST requires it","Clear ownership ensures important tasks don't fall through the cracks and prevents duplicated effort","It makes meetings shorter","Defined roles are only for large teams"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the 'T-shape' skill model in team development?",opts:["Each member learns only one skill","Having deep expertise in one primary area while being broadly familiar with all other areas â€” enabling cross-team support","Only technical skills matter","T-shape is a drive train type"],ans:1},
        {q:"In FRC, what is the primary role of a mentor according to FIRST's rules?",opts:["Build and wire the robot","Guide, advise, and teach â€” students must own the design, build, programming, and driving","Mentors run all meetings","Mentors make all technical decisions"],ans:1},
      ]},
      {id:"tmb2",title:"Build Season Planning",est:"14 min",content:`## The Build Season Clock
FRC teams get 6 weeks between Kickoff and Stop Build Day (or ship date). FTC timelines vary by region. Without a plan, the last week is always a crisis.

## The Classic FIRST Season Arc (FRC)
\`\`\`
Week 1:  Game analysis, strategy decisions, prototyping begins
Week 2:  Prototype testing, mechanism selection, CAD begins
Week 3:  CAD complete, fabrication begins, programming framework
Week 4:  First full robot integration, testing begins
Week 5:  Iteration, fixing what broke, programming matches hardware
Week 6:  Drive practice, autonomous tuning, bag/competition prep

Reality: Most teams finish the robot in Week 6 and have 0 drive practice.
Goal:    Finish by end of Week 5, dedicate Week 6 to drive practice.
\`\`\`

## The Critical Path
\`\`\`
Critical path = the sequence of tasks where any delay delays the whole robot

Example:
  CAD â†’ CNC cut chassis â†’ assemble chassis â†’ mount drive motors
      â†’ test drive code â†’ mount mechanisms â†’ test full robot

If CAD takes 2 extra days, EVERYTHING downstream is 2 days late.
\`\`\`

## Weekly Build Meeting Structure
\`\`\`
Start of meeting (10 min):
  âœ… Where are we vs. the plan?
  âœ… What did we finish since last meeting?
  âœ… What's blocking us?

During meeting:
  â†’ Work on tasks, not meetings
  â†’ Each subteam works independently
  â†’ Leads check in at midpoint

End of meeting (10 min):
  âœ… What did we complete today?
  âœ… What needs to happen before next meeting?
  âœ… Who owns each task?
\`\`\`

## The "Done" Definition
\`\`\`
NOT done:
  âŒ "The code mostly works"
  âŒ "It just needs a few more bolts"
  âŒ "It works on my test robot"

DONE:
  âœ… Tested on the actual competition robot
  âœ… Works 5/5 times in a row
  âœ… Documented in notebook/repo
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should a team aim to complete the robot by the end of Week 5 instead of Week 6?",opts:["Week 6 has no build days","Completing by Week 5 allows an entire week of drive practice â€” arguably the biggest competitive advantage a team can have","Week 5 deadline is required","Week 6 materials cost more"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the 'critical path' in a build season?",opts:["The path the robot drives during autonomous","The sequence of dependent tasks where any delay cascades to delay the entire robot completion date","The most difficult mechanism to build","The competition bracket path"],ans:1},
        {q:"By the DONE definition above, when is a feature truly complete?",opts:["When the programmer says it works","When it has been tested on the actual competition robot, works consistently (5/5 times), and is documented","When it compiles without errors","When a mentor approves it"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"tmi1",title:"Running Effective Meetings",est:"16 min",content:`## Most Team Meetings Are Too Long and Too Unfocused
The average FIRST build session wastes 40-60 minutes of productive time to socializing, unclear task ownership, and decision-making by committee. These structures prevent that.

## The Stand-Up (Daily Sync â€” 10 minutes max)
\`\`\`
Each person (or subteam lead) answers 3 questions:
1. What did I/we accomplish since the last meeting?
2. What am I/are we working on today?
3. What is blocking me/us?

RULES:
- No solutions discussed during stand-up â€” just surface blockers
- Exactly 10 minutes â€” a timer helps
- Standing up keeps it short (really works!)
\`\`\`

## Decision-Making Framework
\`\`\`
Good decisions = right scope of people involved

Type A decision (1 person, 30 seconds):
  "Which hex bolts should I use for this bracket?"
  â†’ Just the person doing the work decides

Type B decision (2-3 people, 5 minutes):
  "Should the arm pivot at frame level or 4 inches above?"
  â†’ Mechanical lead + drive team captain

Type C decision (whole technical team, 20 minutes):
  "Should we redesign the intake mechanism after Week 3 testing?"
  â†’ All leads, structured discussion, vote if needed

MISTAKE: Treating Type A decisions as Type C (whole team discusses bolt sizes)
\`\`\`

## Action Items From Every Meeting
\`\`\`
Bad ending: "Okay, let's get that done before next meeting"
Good ending:
  Task: Reprint intake roller bracket
  Owner: Marcus
  Due: Wednesday 6pm
  Dependencies: CAD export from Sara by Tuesday

If there's no named owner, it won't get done.
\`\`\`

## Conflict Resolution
\`\`\`
When two team members disagree on a design decision:
1. State both positions clearly without arguing
2. List the criteria for the decision (weight, strength, build time, cost)
3. Score each option against criteria
4. The relevant lead makes the final call

"Disagree and commit" â€” once the decision is made, everyone works toward it
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the purpose of a daily stand-up and why should it be limited to 10 minutes?",opts:["It's a design review","It surfaces blockers and aligns the team â€” brevity forces focus and prevents it from replacing actual work time","It replaces documentation","Long meetings produce better decisions"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the problem with treating 'Type A' decisions (bolt selection) as 'Type C' (whole-team discussion)?",opts:["It's against FIRST rules","It wastes the entire team's time on low-impact decisions that one person should just make and move on","Type A decisions are wrong","It reduces build quality"],ans:1},
        {q:"What makes an action item effective vs ineffective at the end of a meeting?",opts:["Effective items are longer","An effective action item has a named owner and a due date â€” 'let's get that done' with no owner assigned almost never gets done","Action items should be vague to allow flexibility","Only mentors can create action items"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"cadb1",title:"Getting Started with Onshape",est:"15 min",content:`## Why Onshape for FIRST?
Onshape is the most widely used CAD tool in FIRST robotics because:
- **Free for students and teams** (education accounts)
- **Cloud-based** â€” works on any computer, no software to install
- **Version history** â€” every change is saved automatically
- **Collaboration** â€” multiple team members edit simultaneously

## Core Concepts
\`\`\`
Document:    A container for all your robot's parts and assemblies
Part Studio: Where you create individual parts (like a single bracket)
Assembly:    Where you put parts together and check how they fit
Drawing:     2D technical drawing for manufacturing
\`\`\`

## The Modeling Workflow
\`\`\`
1. Sketch:    Draw 2D shapes on a plane (lines, circles, rectangles)
2. Constrain: Lock sketch dimensions and relationships
3. Feature:   Turn 2D sketch into 3D (Extrude, Revolve, Sweep)
4. Repeat:    Add more features to build up the part
\`\`\`

## Essential Sketch Tools
\`\`\`
Line, Rectangle, Circle    â†’ Basic shapes
Dimension (D)              â†’ Lock a size (e.g., make this 25mm)
Coincident constraint      â†’ Two points snap together
Construction Line          â†’ Reference lines that don't become geometry
Mirror                     â†’ Symmetric features
\`\`\`

## Your First Bracket in Onshape
\`\`\`
1. New Part Studio
2. Select Front plane â†’ click Sketch
3. Draw a 60mm Ã— 40mm rectangle
4. Add dimension constraints to lock it
5. Click Extrude â†’ 3mm depth
6. Add 5mm diameter holes at each corner
7. Extrude-Remove the holes through the bracket
8. Done â€” export as STL to 3D print or STEP for other CAD
\`\`\`

## FIRST Onshape Resources
- **MKCAD library:** Free library of REV, GoBILDA, VEXpro parts in Onshape
  â†’ Install from Onshape App Store â†’ search "MKCad"
  â†’ Drag and mate real COTS hardware directly into your assembly`,quiz:[
        {q:"Why is Onshape particularly useful for FIRST teams compared to other CAD software?",opts:["It has the most features","It's free for teams, cloud-based (no installs), version-controlled, and allows simultaneous collaboration â€” eliminating the 'who has the latest file' problem","It's the only legal option","It runs faster than other CAD tools"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the difference between a Part Studio and an Assembly in Onshape?",opts:["There is no difference","Part Studios are where individual parts are modeled; Assemblies are where multiple parts are mated together to check fit and interference","Assemblies are for 2D drawings","Part Studios can only contain purchased parts"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the first thing you should do after drawing a sketch shape in Onshape?",opts:["Immediately extrude it","Add dimension and geometric constraints to fully define the sketch â€” an under-constrained sketch can move unexpectedly when features are added","Delete and redraw","Export it"],ans:1},
      ]},
      {id:"cadb2",title:"Assemblies & Mates in Onshape",est:"16 min",content:`## What is an Assembly?
An Assembly places multiple parts together and defines how they connect. This is where you check if your robot's mechanisms physically fit, interfere, or move correctly.

## Types of Mates (How Parts Connect)
\`\`\`
Fastened Mate:    Parts are rigid relative to each other (bolted together)
Revolute Mate:    Parts rotate around a single axis (arm pivot, wheel axle)
Slider Mate:      Parts slide along an axis (linear slide)
Cylindrical Mate: Rotate AND slide (bolt in a slotted hole)
Planar Mate:      Parts slide in a plane (for sliding panels)
Ball Mate:        Full 3D rotation (ball joint)
\`\`\`

## Mating a Wheel to an Axle
\`\`\`
1. Import: wheel part + shaft part into assembly
2. Insert Revolute Mate:
   - Select the shaft's axis (click the cylindrical surface)
   - Select the wheel's bore axis
   - Onshape aligns them and allows rotation
3. Add a Fastened Mate for the hub to shaft:
   - Locks axial position but keeps rotation
4. Test: Click and drag the wheel â€” it should spin freely on the shaft
\`\`\`

## Interference Checking
\`\`\`
Assemblies â†’ Interference Detection
Onshape highlights parts that physically overlap.
Use this before building to catch:
  - A servo arm that hits the frame when rotated
  - A slide that hits the battery at full extension
  - Two motors mounted in the same physical space

A 10-minute interference check saves hours of rebuilding.
\`\`\`

## Assembly Tips for FIRST Teams
\`\`\`
âœ… Use MKCAD for COTS parts â€” they have correct geometry
âœ… Model mechanisms in their WORST CASE position
   (arm fully extended, slide fully up) to check interference
âœ… Name mates clearly: "Arm Pivot - Left", not "Mate 14"
âœ… Use sub-assemblies: drive chassis as one sub-assembly,
   arm as another â€” keeps the top-level assembly clean
\`\`\`

## Measuring in Assembly
\`\`\`
Tools â†’ Measure:
  Point-to-point distance: "How far is the intake from the floor?"
  Minimum clearance: "How much room between the arm and the chassis?"

Always measure at the WORST CASE pose:
  Arm fully extended â†’ measure clearance to floor
  Slide fully up â†’ measure clearance to ceiling/height limit
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What type of mate should you use for an arm that rotates around a pivot bolt?",opts:["Fastened Mate","Revolute Mate â€” it allows rotation around a single axis while holding all other degrees of freedom","Slider Mate","Ball Mate"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should you run interference detection before building physical parts?",opts:["It's required by Onshape","It reveals parts that physically overlap in the design â€” catching collisions before manufacturing saves hours of rework","It speeds up rendering","It checks for legal compliance"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why model mechanisms in their worst-case position when checking clearances?",opts:["Worst case is the average position","The mechanism will reach that position in competition â€” if it interferes there, you'll have a real failure â€” check the extreme, not just the safe middle position","CAD only shows static positions","Worst case is too pessimistic"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"cadi1",title:"Designing for Manufacturability in FIRST",est:"18 min",content:`## Designing Parts You Can Actually Build
A great-looking CAD model is worthless if your team can't make it. Design for the tools and processes you actually have.

## Matching Design to Manufacturing Process
\`\`\`
3D Printing (FDM):
  âœ… Complex shapes, custom brackets, low-torque structural parts
  âœ… Best for: sensor mounts, cable guides, game piece bumpers
  âŒ Avoid: thin walls < 2mm, unsupported overhangs > 45Â°,
           high-torque hubs (will strip), smooth circular bores (tolerance)
  Key: Add 0.3-0.5mm clearance to all mating holes

Laser Cutting / CNC Router:
  âœ… Flat plates, large structural panels, repeatable precision
  âœ… Best for: chassis plates, mounting plates, bellcranks
  âŒ Avoid: deep slots narrower than 0.1" (cutter diameter limit),
           inside corners (will have radius from cutter)
  Key: All features must be accessible from the cutting direction

Bandsaw + Drill Press:
  âœ… Simple shapes from bar stock, quick custom lengths
  âŒ Avoid: curves, complex shapes, tight tolerances
  Key: Round holes only â€” no square pockets without milling

Tube / Extrusion Cutting:
  âœ… REV/GoBILDA aluminum extrusion â€” cut to length
  âœ… Best for: frame members, structural arms
  Key: Plan hole patterns before cutting â€” adding holes later is hard
\`\`\`

## Design Rules Checklist
\`\`\`
For 3D printed parts:
â–¡ Wall thickness â‰¥ 3mm for structural parts
â–¡ Infill â‰¥ 40% for load-bearing parts (use GYROID infill)
â–¡ Bearing/shaft holes oversized by 0.3mm
â–¡ Supports required? Can you remove them? Mark in CAD.

For laser-cut parts:
â–¡ Minimum feature size â‰¥ 1/8" (3mm)
â–¡ No inside corners â€” add fillets (radius = cutter radius)
â–¡ Text and labels are "engraved" (scored), not cut through
â–¡ Kerf compensation for tight-fitting slots
\`\`\`

## Designing for Easy Assembly
\`\`\`
âœ… All fasteners accessible with a hex key (don't trap bolt heads)
âœ… Matching hole patterns align for assembly by feel
âœ… Chamfer (angle) the entrance to bearing bores â€” easier press-fit
âœ… Index features: a small nub and pocket that align parts before bolting
âœ… Mark "TOP" or a direction indicator on asymmetric parts
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should 3D-printed hubs that transmit high torque (like axle hubs) be avoided in favor of metal or COTS parts?",opts:["3D printing is not legal in FIRST","FDM printed material has limited shear strength in the hub-to-shaft interface â€” high torque will strip the interface, especially on hex shafts","3D printers can't make round shapes","Hubs don't need to transmit torque"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why do laser-cut inside corners always have a small radius instead of a sharp 90Â° corner?",opts:["It's a design preference","The circular cutting tool has a radius â€” it physically cannot produce a perfectly sharp interior corner; design must account for this radius","It makes parts stronger","Sharp corners are not legal in FIRST"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does 'kerf compensation' mean in laser cutting?",opts:["Speeding up the laser","Adjusting slot widths in the design to account for the material removed by the laser beam â€” ensures tight-fitting slots actually fit as designed","Compensating for laser misalignment","Adding extra material at corners"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ga1",title:"CI/CD for Robot Code with GitHub Actions",est:"20 min",content:`## What is CI/CD?\nContinuous Integration / Continuous Deployment. For FIRST teams, this means:\n- **CI:** Every commit is automatically compiled and tested â€” broken code is caught immediately\n- **CD:** Tagged releases automatically produce build artifacts the team can download and deploy\n\n## Basic FTC Build Check Workflow\n\\\`\\\`\\\`yaml\n# .github/workflows/build.yml\nname: FTC Build Check\n\non:\n  push:\n    branches: [ main, "feature/**" ]\n  pull_request:\n    branches: [ main ]\n\njobs:\n  build:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - name: Checkout code\n        uses: actions/checkout@v4\n\n      - name: Set up JDK 8\n        uses: actions/setup-java@v4\n        with:\n          java-version: \"8\"\n          distribution: \"temurin\"\n\n      - name: Cache Gradle\n        uses: actions/cache@v4\n        with:\n          path: ~/.gradle/caches\n          key: gradle-\\" + ({ hashFiles('**/*.gradle') }) + "\n\n      - name: Build with Gradle\n        run: ./gradlew assembleDebug\n\n      - name: Upload APK\n        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4\n        with:\n          name: ftc-debug-apk\n          path: TeamCode/build/outputs/apk/debug/*.apk\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## What This Gets You\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\nEvery push to main or any feature branch:\n  âœ… Compiles the full project\n  âœ… Fails visibly (red âœ—) if there\"s a compile error\n  âœ… Produces a downloadable APK as a build artifact\n  âœ… Takes ~2-3 minutes on GitHub\"s free runners\n\nGreen check on a PR = "at least it compiles"\nThis prevents the classic: "I merged a branch that broke main \nright before competition"\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Release Tagging Workflow\n\\\`\\\`\\\`yaml\n# .github/workflows/release.yml\nname: Competition Release\n\non:\n  push:\n    tags: [ \"comp-*\" ]  # triggers on: git tag comp-regional-2025\n\njobs:\n  release:\n    runs-on: ubuntu-latest\n    steps:\n      - uses: actions/checkout@v4\n      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4\n        with: { java-version: \"8\", distribution: \"temurin\" }\n      - run: ./gradlew assembleRelease\n      - name: Create GitHub Release\n        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2\n        with:\n          files: TeamCode/build/outputs/apk/release/*.apk\n          name: "Competition Build \\" + ({ github.ref_name }) + ""\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Team Workflow with CI\n\\\`\\\`\\\`bash\n# Normal development:\ngit checkout -b feature/auto-improvement\n# ... code ...\ngit push origin feature/auto-improvement\n# â†’ GitHub Actions runs build check on your branch\n# â†’ Green check = safe to open PR\n\n# Competition release:\ngit checkout main\ngit pull\ngit tag comp-regional-2025\ngit push origin comp-regional-2025\n# â†’ GitHub Actions builds and creates a GitHub Release\n# â†’ APK available for download from GitHub\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What does a GitHub Actions build check primarily catch in robot code?",opts:["Runtime bugs on the robot","Compile errors â€” if any code change breaks compilation, the check fails immediately and teammates are notified before merging","Electrical problems","Strategy errors in autonomous"],ans:1},
        {q:"In the release workflow above, what triggers the competition release build?",opts:["Any push to main","Pushing a Git tag matching 'comp-*' â€” this intentional action triggers a release build with a downloadable APK","Creating a pull request","A scheduled time trigger"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the key benefit of the 'cache Gradle' step in the CI workflow?",opts:["It's required","Caching Gradle dependencies means subsequent builds download fewer files, reducing build time from ~5 minutes to ~1-2 minutes","It improves code quality","It enables deployment to the robot"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"orb1",title:"What is FIRST Outreach?",est:"10 min",content:`## Outreach = Spreading the Mission
Outreach means taking FIRST's mission â€” inspiring young people to pursue STEM â€” beyond your own team. It's what separates award-winning teams from high-scoring-but-unknown teams.

## Types of Outreach Activities
\`\`\`
Direct Mentorship:
  â†’ Starting and mentoring an FLL or FTC team
  â†’ Most impactful: you create a lasting program that continues every year

School/Community Demos:
  â†’ Bringing your robot to schools, libraries, fairs
  â†’ Show what robots do, answer questions, inspire curiosity

STEM Events:
  â†’ Running a hands-on robotics activity at a school
  â†’ Game controller demos, simple Scratch coding, building contests

Peer Mentoring:
  â†’ Experienced team members mentoring rookie members
  â†’ Hosting other teams to share code, CAD, or mechanisms

Social Media & Documentation:
  â†’ Sharing your build season publicly
  â†’ Reaching students who may never see your robot in person
\`\`\`

## The Multiplier Effect
\`\`\`
Direct impact:     You demo for 50 students at one event
Multiplier impact: You start an FLL team of 12 students.
                   Each of those 12 may go on to start teams.
                   12 students Ã— their careers Ã— their future impact
                                = exponentially larger impact

Judges reward programs that MULTIPLY impact, not just events that REACH students.
\`\`\`

## Starting Your First Outreach Program
\`\`\`
Step 1: Pick ONE sustainable activity (don't do everything at once)
Step 2: Find a partner (school, library, rec center, church)
Step 3: Schedule 3-4 recurring sessions, not just one demo
Step 4: Track attendance and collect feedback
Step 5: Recruit a team member to own it going forward
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why do judges value starting new FIRST teams more than running one-time school demos?",opts:["New teams score more competition points","A new team creates a lasting program that continues every year â€” the 'multiplier effect' reaches far more students over time than a single event","Demos aren't allowed","Team starting is required for Impact Award"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the 'multiplier effect' in outreach?",opts:["A fundraising technique","Programs that inspire others who then go on to inspire more people â€” creating exponentially larger impact than direct 1:1 interactions","A way to count outreach hours","A social media strategy"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is it better to start ONE sustainable outreach program rather than many one-time events?",opts:["One program is easier to plan","Sustainable programs create lasting community impact and run every year â€” a calendar of one-time events stops when current members graduate","One program looks better on awards forms","Events cost more to run"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Intermediate: [
      {id:"ori1",title:"Measuring & Documenting Outreach Impact",est:"16 min",content:`## The Problem: Outreach That Can't Be Proved
"We inspired a lot of students this year" will not win an Impact or Inspire Award. You need systems to track, measure, and prove what your outreach actually accomplished.

## What to Track
\`\`\`
For each outreach activity, record:
  Date and duration
  Location and target audience
  Number of attendees (count, don't estimate)
  # of FIRST participants vs total
  Student age range / grade level
  Follow-up outcome (did any join a FIRST program?)

For your recurring programs:
  Attendance per session (track by individual for retention)
  Year-over-year growth
  # of students who went on to join/start teams
  Testimonials (with permission)
\`\`\`

## Simple Tracking Template
\`\`\`
Spreadsheet columns:
Date | Activity | Location | Attendees | FIRST-Age (5-18) | 
Team Members Present | Outcome Notes | Follow-Up Date

Season totals to report:
  Total unique students reached:    [number]
  Total FIRST-age students reached: [number]
  Total volunteer hours:            [number]
  New FIRST teams inspired/started: [number]
\`\`\`

## Qualitative Evidence
Numbers tell the scale; stories tell the impact:
\`\`\`
âœ… Student quote: "After your workshop, I signed up for FLL. 
   This is the first time I felt like engineering was for me."

âœ… Teacher quote: "The team returned 4 times this year. 
   Three of my students are now on a FIRST team."

âœ… Photo evidence: Before/after of a classroom that became
   an FLL team space with your team's help
\`\`\`

## Common Mistakes
\`\`\`
âŒ Counting non-FIRST-age adults (parents, teachers) as students reached
âŒ Estimating attendance: "about 200 people" â€” count or don't report
âŒ One-time activities counted as "programs"
âŒ No follow-up: did anything actually change for those students?
âŒ Forgetting to get photos/quotes in the moment (hard to get later)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why is counting exact attendees better than estimating for outreach reports?",opts:["Exact counts are required by FIRST","Judges are skeptical of round numbers like '200 students' â€” specific counts like '47 students at Lincoln Elementary on 11/14' are verifiable and credible","Estimates are always higher","Counts take too long"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why are student and teacher quotes valuable evidence alongside attendance numbers?",opts:["Quotes replace numbers","Numbers show scale; stories show real impact on individuals â€” both together are more persuasive than either alone","Quotes are required by award rules","Judges only read quotes"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is a common mistake when counting 'students reached' in outreach reports?",opts:["Counting too few students","Including non-FIRST-age adults (parents, teachers) in the student count â€” judges and award criteria focus specifically on youth (ages 5-18)","Counting students who attend multiple events","Tracking attendance by name"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },
};

  java: {
