      {id:"jb_interfaces",title:"Interfaces & Polymorphism",est:"15 min",content:`## What is an Interface?
An interface defines a contract: any class that implements it MUST have certain methods. This lets you write code that works with any subsystem, not just one specific one.

## Define an Interface
\`\`\`java
// ISubsystem.java â€” every subsystem must have these methods
public interface ISubsystem {
    void init(HardwareMap hwMap);
    void update();
    void stop();
    String getStatus();
}
\`\`\`

## Implement the Interface
\`\`\`java
public class ArmSubsystem implements ISubsystem {
    private DcMotorEx motor;

    @Override
    public void init(HardwareMap hwMap) {
        motor = hwMap.get(DcMotorEx.class, "arm");
        motor.setZeroPowerBehavior(DcMotor.ZeroPowerBehavior.BRAKE);
    }

    @Override
    public void update() {
        // PID logic runs here each loop
    }

    @Override
    public void stop() { motor.setPower(0); }

    @Override
    public String getStatus() {
        return "Arm: " + motor.getCurrentPosition() + " ticks";
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Polymorphism â€” One Loop for All Subsystems
\`\`\`java
// In your OpMode:
List<ISubsystem> subsystems = new ArrayList<>();
subsystems.add(new ArmSubsystem());
subsystems.add(new IntakeSubsystem());
subsystems.add(new ClimberSubsystem());

// Init all:
for (ISubsystem s : subsystems) s.init(hardwareMap);

// Update all â€” one line covers every mechanism:
for (ISubsystem s : subsystems) s.update();

// Emergency stop all:
for (ISubsystem s : subsystems) s.stop();

// Print all status:
for (ISubsystem s : subsystems) {
    telemetry.addLine(s.getStatus());
}
\`\`\`

## Why This Matters at Competition
If you add a new mechanism mid-season, just implement ISubsystem. It instantly plugs into the existing init/update/stop loop â€” no changes to your OpMode structure.`,quiz:[
        {q:"What does 'implements ISubsystem' mean in a class declaration?",opts:["The class extends another class","The class guarantees it will provide every method defined in the ISubsystem interface â€” the compiler enforces this","The class is optional to use","It imports the interface library"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is polymorphism in the context of a subsystem list?",opts:["Running code in parallel","Treating different subsystem types through a common interface â€” one update() loop works for Arm, Intake, and Climber without knowing their internal details","A form of inheritance","A type of sensor fusion"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the key advantage of this pattern when adding a new mechanism?",opts:["New mechanisms require no coding","The new class just implements ISubsystem â€” it automatically works with the existing init/update/stop loop in the OpMode without any structural changes","Interfaces compile faster","It reduces motor count"],ans:1},
      ]},
      {id:"jb_scope",title:"Variable Scope & Lifetime",est:"11 min",content:`## What is Scope?
A variable only exists within the block of code where it was declared. Understanding scope prevents "variable not found" errors and logic bugs.

## Local vs Instance vs Static
\`\`\`java
public class MyOpMode extends LinearOpMode {

    // INSTANCE variable â€” lives for the lifetime of this object
    DcMotor leftMotor;
    int cycleCount = 0;

    // STATIC variable â€” shared across ALL instances
    static int totalRobotRuns = 0;

    @Override
    public void runOpMode() {
        // LOCAL variable â€” only exists inside runOpMode()
        double startTime = System.currentTimeMillis();

        waitForStart();

        while (opModeIsActive()) {
            // LOCAL to while loop â€” recreated each iteration
            double power = gamepad1.left_stick_y;
            leftMotor.setPower(power);

            cycleCount++;          // âœ… can access instance variable
            totalRobotRuns++;      // âœ… can access static variable
            // startTime accessible here âœ… â€” same method scope
        }
        // power is NOT accessible here â€” out of scope
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Scope Bug Example
\`\`\`java
// âŒ COMMON BUG:
if (gamepad1.a) {
    boolean clawOpen = true; // declared inside if block
}
clawServo.setPosition(clawOpen ? 0.8 : 0.2); // ERROR: clawOpen not in scope!

// âœ… FIX:
boolean clawOpen = false; // declared at method level
if (gamepad1.a) {
    clawOpen = true;       // now accessible outside the if block
}
clawServo.setPosition(clawOpen ? 0.8 : 0.2); // âœ… works
\`\`\`

## Rule of Thumb
Declare variables at the SMALLEST scope that works:
- A loop counter only used in one for loop â†’ local in that loop
- A motor used across multiple methods â†’ instance variable
- A constant used everywhere â†’ static final in Constants class`,quiz:[
        {q:"What happens to a variable declared inside an if block after the block ends?",opts:["It retains its value","It goes out of scope â€” it no longer exists and cannot be accessed outside that block","It becomes null","It becomes an instance variable"],ans:1},
        {q:"Where should a motor object be declared so it can be used in multiple methods of an OpMode?",opts:["Inside runOpMode() as a local variable","As an instance variable at the class level â€” local variables only exist within the method they're declared in","Inside the while loop","As a static variable in Constants"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the correct principle for choosing a variable's scope?",opts:["Always use instance variables for safety","Declare at the smallest scope that still allows all required access â€” prevents unintended use elsewhere in the code","Use static for all variables","Scope doesn't affect correctness"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Intermediate: [
      {id:"ji_feedforward",title:"Feedforward Control for Arms & Elevators",est:"20 min",content:`## Why PID Alone Isn't Enough for Arms
A PID controller reacts to error after it happens. An arm fighting gravity always has error before the controller catches up â€” causing lag and oscillation.

## Feedforward: Predict Instead of React
\`\`\`
PID only:        Error â†’ Controller â†’ Output
PID + FF:        Predicted load â†’ Feedforward â†’ +
                 Error          â†’ PID         â†’ + â†’ Output
\`\`\`

## Gravity Feedforward for a Rotating Arm
\`\`\`java
// Arm rotates from 0Â° (horizontal) to 90Â° (vertical)
// Gravity torque is proportional to cos(angle)
// At 0Â° (horizontal): full gravity â†’ max feedforward needed
// At 90Â° (vertical):  no gravity component â†’ feedforward = 0

public double getGravityFF(double angleDegrees) {
    double angleRad = Math.toRadians(angleDegrees);
    return kG * Math.cos(angleRad);
    // kG is the feedforward gain â€” tune by finding the power
    // that holds the arm perfectly horizontal
}
\`\`\`

## Full PIDF Control Loop for Arm
\`\`\`java
double kP = 0.008, kI = 0.0, kD = 0.002, kG = 0.12;
double integral = 0, lastError = 0;

// In your control loop (call every 20ms):
public double calculateArmOutput(int targetTicks, int currentTicks,
                                  double currentAngleDegrees) {
    double error = targetTicks - currentTicks;

    integral  += error * 0.02;
    integral   = Math.max(-50, Math.min(50, integral)); // anti-windup
    double derivative = (error - lastError) / 0.02;
    lastError  = error;

    double pid = kP*error + kI*integral + kD*derivative;
    double ff  = getGravityFF(currentAngleDegrees);

    return Math.max(-1.0, Math.min(1.0, pid + ff));
}
\`\`\`

## Elevator Feedforward (Constant, Not Angle-Dependent)
\`\`\`java
// Elevator always lifts against constant gravity
// FF = kG (constant) â€” doesn't depend on position
double elevatorFF = kG; // tune: find power that barely holds elevator in place
double output = pidOutput + elevatorFF;
\`\`\`

## Tuning Feedforward
\`\`\`
Step 1: kI = kD = 0, kP = 0
Step 2: Slowly increase kG until arm holds position when at 0Â° (horizontal)
        That value of kG is your starting feedforward
Step 3: Now add kP for position tracking
Step 4: Add kD to reduce oscillation
Step 5: kI only if significant steady-state error remains
\`\`\`
Standard telemetry.addData() is good for competition. For tuning sessions, FTC Dashboard gives you live graphs, variable editing, and field rendering in a browser.

## FTC Dashboard Setup
\`\`\`java
// In build.gradle (TeamCode), add:
// implementation 'com.acmerobotics.dashboard:dashboard:0.4.15'

// In your OpMode:
import com.acmerobotics.dashboard.FtcDashboard;
import com.acmerobotics.dashboard.telemetry.MultipleTelemetry;

// Replace telemetry with MultipleTelemetry:
telemetry = new MultipleTelemetry(telemetry, FtcDashboard.getInstance().getTelemetry());
// Now data goes to BOTH Driver Hub AND the browser dashboard
\`\`\`

## Live Graphing â€” See Your PID in Real Time
\`\`\`java
// These show up as live graph lines in the dashboard:
telemetry.addData("Target", targetPosition);
telemetry.addData("Current", motor.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("Error", targetPosition - motor.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("Output", pidOutput);
telemetry.update();
// Tune kP/kD by watching the graph â€” no re-deploying needed for @Config vars
\`\`\`

## @Config â€” Edit Variables Live Without Re-Deploying
\`\`\`java
import com.acmerobotics.dashboard.config.Config;

@Config // makes all public static variables editable in the dashboard
public class PIDTuner {
    public static double kP = 0.008;
    public static double kD = 0.002;
    public static double kG = 0.12;
    public static int    targetPosition = 800;
}

// In your controller â€” read live values:
double output = PIDTuner.kP * error + PIDTuner.kD * derivative
              + PIDTuner.kG * Math.cos(angle);
\`\`\`

## Structured Telemetry for Multi-Subsystem Robots
\`\`\`java
// Group by subsystem â€” much easier to read
telemetry.addLine("â”€â”€ DRIVE â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€");
telemetry.addData("LF/RF/LB/RB",
    "%.2f / %.2f / %.2f / %.2f",
    lf.getPower(), rf.getPower(), lb.getPower(), rb.getPower());
telemetry.addData("Heading", "%.1fÂ°", heading);

telemetry.addLine("â”€â”€ ARM â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€");
telemetry.addData("Position", arm.getCurrentPosition());
telemetry.addData("Target",   arm.getTargetPosition());
telemetry.addData("State",    armState.name());

      {id:"ja_vision2",title:"TFOD & Custom TensorFlow Models",est:"30 min",content:`## When AprilTags Aren't Enough
AprilTags require specific field markers. TensorFlow Object Detection (TFOD) lets your robot recognize game pieces, custom objects, or anything you train it to see.

## FTC TFOD Basics
\`\`\`java
// FTC SDK includes TFObjectDetector
TFObjectDetector tfod;

private void initTFOD() {
    TFObjectDetector.Parameters tfodParameters =
        new TFObjectDetector.Parameters(/* view id */);
    tfodParameters.minResultConfidence = 0.75f;
    tfodParameters.isModelTensorFlow2  = true;
    tfodParameters.inputSize           = 300;

    tfod = ClassFactory.getInstance().createTFObjectDetector(
        tfodParameters, visionPortal);
    // Load your model asset (or use the season's default model)
    tfod.loadModelFromAsset("MyTeamModel.tflite",
                             "red_cone", "blue_cone", "yellow_cube");
    tfod.activate();
    tfod.setZoom(1.5); // digital zoom for closer view
}
\`\`\`

## Getting Detections
\`\`\`java
List<Recognition> recognitions = tfod.getRecognitions();
if (recognitions != null && !recognitions.isEmpty()) {
    for (Recognition r : recognitions) {
        double x = (r.getLeft() + r.getRight()) / 2.0;  // center X
        double y = (r.getTop()  + r.getBottom()) / 2.0; // center Y
        telemetry.addData("Label", r.getLabel());
        telemetry.addData("Confidence", "%.0f%%", r.getConfidence()*100);
        telemetry.addData("Center", "(%.0f, %.0f)", x, y);

        if (r.getLabel().equals("yellow_cube") && r.getConfidence() > 0.85) {
            targetDetected = true;
            targetX = x;
        }
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Training a Custom Model (Overview)
\`\`\`
Tools: Google Teachable Machine (easy) or Roboflow + TFOD2 (powerful)

Step 1: Collect 100-500 images of your target object
        - Various angles, lighting, distances
        - Include "negative" images (background without object)

Step 2: Label images (draw bounding boxes around each object)
        - Roboflow has a free annotation tool

Step 3: Train model (Google Colab â€” free GPU)
        - Use TF2 Object Detection API
        - Export as .tflite

Step 4: Deploy to robot
        - Place .tflite in TeamCode/src/main/assets/
        - Reference by filename in loadModelFromAsset()

Training quality checklist:
âœ… Images taken with the same camera as the robot
âœ… Images at competition-level lighting (not your garage)
âœ… At least 5 images per angle Ã— 4 angles = 20 minimum per class
âœ… Background diversity â€” different floors, field tiles, lighting
\`\`\`

## Combining TFOD + AprilTag
\`\`\`java
// Use TFOD to find the game piece, AprilTag to localize the robot
// Classic FTC "detect and approach" pattern:

if (tfodTargetVisible) {
    // Strafe toward target X center
    double strafeError = targetX - (CAMERA_WIDTH / 2.0);
    double strafePower = strafeError * 0.002; // tune gain
    drive.strafe(strafePower);
} else if (aprilTagVisible) {
    // Use AprilTag to re-orient to known field position
    drive.driveToPose(targetPose);
}
\`\`\`
Two-wheel odometry (left + right encoders) can track forward/back and turning but cannot independently measure sideways (strafe) movement. A third perpendicular wheel captures lateral movement.

## Hardware Setup
\`\`\`
         â† 90Â° horizontal wheel (measures strafe Y)
    â”Œâ”€â”€â”€â”€â”¼â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”
    â”‚   [H]            â”‚
    â”‚                  â”‚
  L â”‚   center of      â”‚ R
  [L]   robot          [R]
    â”‚                  â”‚
    â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜

L = Left encoder (parallel to robot heading)
R = Right encoder (parallel to robot heading)
H = Horizontal encoder (perpendicular â€” measures strafe)
\`\`\`

## Odometry Math
\`\`\`java
// Constants â€” measure these physically on your robot
static final double TICKS_PER_REV   = 8192;   // REV Through Bore Encoder
static final double WHEEL_DIAMETER  = 1.37795; // inches (35mm Odometry wheel)
static final double TICKS_PER_INCH  = TICKS_PER_REV / (WHEEL_DIAMETER * Math.PI);

// Track width â€” distance between left and right pods
static final double TRACK_WIDTH     = 12.5; // inches, measure precisely!
// Horizontal pod offset from robot center (+ = forward of center)
static final double H_OFFSET        = 1.5;  // inches

// Pose state
double poseX = 0, poseY = 0, poseHeading = 0; // inches, inches, radians
int prevLeft = 0, prevRight = 0, prevHoriz = 0;

public void updateOdometry() {
    int curLeft  = leftPod.getCurrentPosition();
    int curRight = rightPod.getCurrentPosition();
    int curHoriz = horizPod.getCurrentPosition();

    double dL = (curLeft  - prevLeft)  / TICKS_PER_INCH;
    double dR = (curRight - prevRight) / TICKS_PER_INCH;
    double dH = (curHoriz - prevHoriz) / TICKS_PER_INCH;

    // Change in heading (from differential drive encoders)
    double dTheta = (dR - dL) / TRACK_WIDTH;

    // Forward movement (arc midpoint)
    double dForward = (dL + dR) / 2.0;

    // Lateral movement (remove heading-induced strafe artifact)
    double dStrafe = dH - H_OFFSET * dTheta;

    // Rotate displacement into field frame
    double sinH = Math.sin(poseHeading + dTheta / 2);
    double cosH = Math.cos(poseHeading + dTheta / 2);
    poseX       += dForward * cosH - dStrafe * sinH;
    poseY       += dForward * sinH + dStrafe * cosH;
    poseHeading += dTheta;

    // Normalize heading to [-Ï€, Ï€]
    while (poseHeading >  Math.PI) poseHeading -= 2 * Math.PI;
    while (poseHeading < -Math.PI) poseHeading += 2 * Math.PI;

    prevLeft = curLeft; prevRight = curRight; prevHoriz = curHoriz;
}
\`\`\`

## Drive-to-Point Controller Using Odometry
\`\`\`java
public void driveToPose(double targetX, double targetY, double targetH) {
    while (opModeIsActive()) {
        updateOdometry();

        double dx = targetX - poseX;
        double dy = targetY - poseY;
        double distance = Math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy);

        if (distance < 1.0) break; // within 1 inch = done

        double targetAngle = Math.atan2(dy, dx);
        double angleError  = targetAngle - poseHeading;
        // Normalize angle error
        while (angleError >  Math.PI) angleError -= 2*Math.PI;
        while (angleError < -Math.PI) angleError += 2*Math.PI;

        double forward = Math.min(distance * 0.05, 0.6);
        double rotate  = angleError * 0.4;

        drive.driveRobotCentric(0, forward, rotate);
        telemetry.addData("Pose", "(%.1f, %.1f, %.1fÂ°)",
                          poseX, poseY, Math.toDegrees(poseHeading));
        telemetry.update();
    }
    drive.stop();
}

      {id:"pyb_classes2",title:"Python Dataclasses for Scouting",est:"14 min",content:`## Plain Dictionaries vs Dataclasses
When scouting data grows to 15+ fields per match, plain dictionaries become error-prone. Dataclasses give you structure, auto-complete, and type hints.

## Without Dataclass (fragile)
\`\`\`python
# Easy to mistype a key, no auto-complete
match = {
    "team": 1234,
    "auto_pts": 18,
    "cycles": 6,
    "climmb": True  # typo â€” won't be caught!
}
print(match["auto_pts"])  # works
print(match["climb"])     # KeyError â€” field was misspelled
\`\`\`

## With Dataclass (safe and readable)
\`\`\`python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List

@dataclass
class MatchResult:
    team_number: int
    auto_points: int = 0
    teleop_cycles: int = 0
    climb_level: int = 0       # 0=none, 1=L1, 2=L2, 3=L3
    notes: str = ""
    penalties_given: int = 0

    @property
    def total_contribution(self):
        return self.auto_points + self.teleop_cycles * 4 + self.climb_level * 10

# Usage:
m = MatchResult(team_number=1234, auto_points=18, teleop_cycles=6, climb_level=3)
print(m.team_number)        # 1234
print(m.total_contribution) # 18 + 24 + 30 = 72
\`\`\`

## Scouting Session Container
\`\`\`python
@dataclass
class ScoutingSession:
    event_key: str
    matches: List[MatchResult] = field(default_factory=list)

    def add_match(self, result: MatchResult):
        self.matches.append(result)

    def team_average(self, team: int) -> float:
        team_matches = [m for m in self.matches if m.team_number == team]
        if not team_matches:
            return 0.0
        return sum(m.total_contribution for m in team_matches) / len(team_matches)

# Usage:
session = ScoutingSession(event_key="2025casd")
session.add_match(MatchResult(1234, auto_points=18, teleop_cycles=7, climb_level=3))
session.add_match(MatchResult(1234, auto_points=12, teleop_cycles=5, climb_level=2))
print(session.team_average(1234))  # average contribution
\`\`\`

## Saving to JSON
\`\`\`python
import json
from dataclasses import asdict

# Save
data = [asdict(m) for m in session.matches]
with open("scouting.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(data, f, indent=2)

# Load
with open("scouting.json") as f:
    raw = json.load(f)
matches = [MatchResult(**r) for r in raw]

        {q:"What does the @property decorator on total_contribution do?",opts:["It makes the field required","It creates a calculated attribute that can be accessed like a regular field (m.total_contribution) but computes its value on-the-fly from other fields","It saves to disk automatically","It adds the field to JSON output"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why use field(default_factory=list) instead of matches: List = [] for a list field in a dataclass?",opts:["It's just a style choice","Using a mutable default like [] is shared across ALL instances â€” field(default_factory=list) creates a fresh list for each instance","default_factory is faster","Lists require special handling in Python 3"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"pi_requests",title:"HTTP Requests & The Blue Alliance API",est:"18 min",content:`## Making Web Requests in Python
The requests library lets your scouting tools pull live match data, team info, and rankings directly from The Blue Alliance API.

## Setup
\`\`\`python
pip install requests

import requests
import json

# TBA API base URL and your auth key (get free at thebluealliance.com/account)
BASE_URL = "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3"
HEADERS  = {"X-TBA-Auth-Key": "your_api_key_here"}
\`\`\`

## Basic GET Request Pattern
\`\`\`python
def tba_get(endpoint: str) -> dict | list | None:
    """Safe TBA API wrapper with error handling."""
    try:
        response = requests.get(
            f"{BASE_URL}/{endpoint}",
            headers=HEADERS,
            timeout=5  # fail fast if no internet
        )
        response.raise_for_status()  # raise on 4xx/5xx
        return response.json()
    except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
        print("TBA request timed out â€” check internet connection")
        return None
    except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as e:
        print(f"TBA API error: {e}")
        return None
\`\`\`

## Useful TBA Endpoints
\`\`\`python
# Get all matches at an event
matches = tba_get("event/2025casd/matches/simple")

# Get team list for an event
teams = tba_get("event/2025casd/teams/simple")

# Get rankings
rankings = tba_get("event/2025casd/rankings")

# Get a specific team's events this year
events = tba_get("team/frc1234/events/2025/simple")
\`\`\`

## Parsing Match Results
\`\`\`python
def get_team_scores(event_key: str, team: str) -> list[int]:
    """Return list of each match's contribution score for a team."""
    matches = tba_get(f"event/{event_key}/matches")
    if not matches:
        return []

    scores = []
    for match in matches:
        if match["comp_level"] != "qm":
            continue  # qual matches only
        alliances = match["alliances"]
        for color in ["red", "blue"]:
            if team in alliances[color]["team_keys"]:
                scores.append(alliances[color]["score"])
    return scores

scores = get_team_scores("2025casd", "frc1234")
print(f"Average: {sum(scores)/len(scores):.1f}  Max: {max(scores)}")
\`\`\`

## Caching to Avoid Repeated API Calls
\`\`\`python
import os

def tba_get_cached(endpoint: str, cache_dir="tba_cache") -> dict | list | None:
    os.makedirs(cache_dir, exist_ok=True)
    cache_file = os.path.join(cache_dir, endpoint.replace("/", "_") + ".json")

    if os.path.exists(cache_file):
        with open(cache_file) as f:
            return json.load(f)

    data = tba_get(endpoint)
    if data is not None:
        with open(cache_file, "w") as f:
            json.dump(data, f)
    return data
\`\`\`
NumPy performs math on entire arrays at once â€” 10-100x faster than Python loops for statistical calculations over hundreds of match records.

## Setup
\`\`\`python
pip install numpy
import numpy as np
\`\`\`

## Array Basics
\`\`\`python
# Create arrays from lists
auto_scores  = np.array([18, 12, 20, 15, 18, 22, 10, 18])
cycle_counts = np.array([6, 5, 8, 6, 7, 9, 4, 7])

# Stats â€” no loops needed
print(auto_scores.mean())    # 16.625
print(auto_scores.std())     # 3.64  (consistency measure!)
print(auto_scores.max())     # 22
print(auto_scores.min())     # 10
print(np.percentile(auto_scores, 75))  # 75th percentile
\`\`\`

## Filtering with Boolean Masks
\`\`\`python
teams  = np.array([1234, 5678, 1234, 9012, 5678, 1234])
scores = np.array([72,   65,   80,   55,   70,   75  ])

# Get all scores for team 1234 â€” no loop!
mask_1234 = teams == 1234
team_scores = scores[mask_1234]  # [72, 80, 75]
print(f"Team 1234 avg: {team_scores.mean():.1f}")  # 75.7

# Teams with average score above threshold
team_ids = np.unique(teams)
for t in team_ids:
    avg = scores[teams == t].mean()
    if avg > 68:
        print(f"Team {t}: {avg:.1f} â€” above threshold")
\`\`\`

## Correlation Analysis
\`\`\`python
# Do teams with higher auto scores also do more cycles?
correlation = np.corrcoef(auto_scores, cycle_counts)[0, 1]
print(f"Auto-Cycle correlation: {correlation:.2f}")
# +1.0 = perfect positive correlation
#  0.0 = no relationship
# -1.0 = perfect negative correlation

# Typical finding: strong correlation means auto success predicts overall skill
\`\`\`

## Z-Score Normalization (Comparing Across Metrics)
\`\`\`python
def zscore(arr):
    return (arr - arr.mean()) / arr.std()

# Normalize different metrics to compare fairly
auto_z   = zscore(auto_scores)
cycle_z  = zscore(cycle_counts)

# Combined score: 40% auto, 60% cycles
combined = 0.4 * auto_z + 0.6 * cycle_z
# Rank teams by combined score
ranked_indices = np.argsort(-combined)  # descending

      {id:"mi_assembly",title:"Assembly Procedures & Build Quality",est:"15 min",content:`## Why Assembly Procedure Matters
Two teams can build from identical CAD with identical parts and get robots that perform completely differently. Assembly quality â€” how parts are put together â€” determines whether a robot survives 10 matches a day.

## The Pre-Assembly Checklist
\`\`\`
Before assembling any mechanism:
â–¡ Deburr all machined edges (sharp aluminum cuts wires and hands)
â–¡ Tap all threaded holes before assembly (much harder after)
â–¡ Test-fit every part dry before adding fasteners
â–¡ Verify encoder and motor shaft direction matches code expectations
â–¡ Check bearing fits â€” should press in firmly, not rattle
\`\`\`

## Fastener Best Practices
\`\`\`
Bolt length selection:
  Thread engagement = 1.5Ã— bolt diameter minimum
  For M3 bolt: â‰¥ 4.5mm of thread in the part
  For 10-32: â‰¥ 5/16" of thread engagement

Loctite use:
  Blue (242):  Removable with hand tools â€” use for most robot fasteners
  Red (271):   Permanent â€” use only for wheel hubs, pulley set screws
  Purple (222): Light-duty â€” small fasteners that strip easily

Washer under bolt head:
  Always use when bolting into aluminum â€” distributes load, prevents pull-through
\`\`\`

## Chain/Belt Tensioning
\`\`\`
Chain:
  Correct tension: can move chain ~1/4" perpendicular to direction of travel
  Too tight: bearing load, premature wear, reduced efficiency
  Too loose: skipping, jumping off sprockets under load

Belt (HTD):
  Belts should have NO slack â€” slight tension only
  Use an idler or center-distance adjustment to tension
  Worn belts: look for missing teeth, cracking, fraying edges
  Replace before competition if in doubt
\`\`\`

## Squareness Checks
\`\`\`
A drive chassis that isn't square causes robot to drive in arcs:
  1. Measure diagonal distances: corner A to C, corner B to D
  2. If equal â†’ chassis is square âœ…
  3. If unequal â†’ adjust until both diagonals match

After assembling drive modules:
  Place robot on flat surface, push forward 10 feet
  Does it drive straight? If not â†’ check wheel alignment and axle parallelism
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should all threaded holes be tapped before assembling the robot?",opts:["Tapping is optional","It's much harder to tap holes after adjacent parts are assembled â€” tap first while all surfaces are accessible","Tapping improves strength","Taps are part of the CAD process"],ans:1},
        {q:"How do you check if a robot chassis is square before mounting mechanisms?",opts:["Use a protractor on each corner","Measure both diagonals â€” if they are equal, the chassis is square; unequal diagonals indicate racking that will cause the robot to arc when driving","Use a level","Square chassis can only be built with CNC"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does 'correct chain tension' feel like when checked by hand?",opts:["Chain is completely rigid with no movement","Chain can move approximately 1/4 inch perpendicular to the run direction â€” too tight causes bearing wear, too loose causes skipping","Chain should have 1 inch of slack","Chain tension doesn't matter for robot applications"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ma_kinematics",title:"Inverse Kinematics for Multi-Joint Arms",est:"28 min",content:`## What is Inverse Kinematics (IK)?
Forward kinematics answers: "Given joint angles, where is the end effector?"
Inverse kinematics answers: "Given where I want the end effector, what angles should each joint be?"

## Why IK Matters for FIRST Arms
Without IK, a driver must control each joint independently â€” cognitively demanding, slow, error-prone. With IK, the driver commands an (x, y) position and the math figures out the joint angles automatically.

## Two-Link Planar Arm IK
\`\`\`
       â— end effector (x, y)
      /
  L2 /
    â—  â† joint 2 (Î¸2)
   /
L1/
  â— â† joint 1 (Î¸1) â€” base pivot at origin
\`\`\`

\`\`\`java
// Two-link IK for a planar arm
// L1 = length of upper arm, L2 = length of forearm (inches)
static final double L1 = 14.0; // inches
static final double L2 = 10.0; // inches

public double[] solveIK(double targetX, double targetY) {
    double dist = Math.sqrt(targetX*targetX + targetY*targetY);

    // Check reachability
    if (dist > L1 + L2 || dist < Math.abs(L1 - L2)) {
        return null; // target unreachable
    }

    // Cosine rule for elbow angle
    double cosTheta2 = (dist*dist - L1*L1 - L2*L2) / (2 * L1 * L2);
    double theta2    = Math.acos(cosTheta2); // elbow angle (radians)

    // Shoulder angle
    double k1 = L1 + L2 * Math.cos(theta2);
    double k2 = L2 * Math.sin(theta2);
    double theta1 = Math.atan2(targetY, targetX) - Math.atan2(k2, k1);

    // Convert to degrees for motor targets
    return new double[]{ Math.toDegrees(theta1), Math.toDegrees(theta2) };
}
\`\`\`

## Mapping to Motor Encoder Ticks
\`\`\`java
// Each joint's angle â†’ encoder target
// Example: shoulder motor has 360Â° = 1440 ticks
static final double SHOULDER_TICKS_PER_DEG = 1440.0 / 360.0;
static final double ELBOW_TICKS_PER_DEG    = 1120.0 / 360.0;

double[] angles = solveIK(targetX, targetY);
if (angles != null) {
    int shoulderTarget = (int)(angles[0] * SHOULDER_TICKS_PER_DEG);
    int elbowTarget    = (int)(angles[1] * ELBOW_TICKS_PER_DEG);
    shoulderMotor.setTargetPosition(shoulderTarget);
    elbowMotor.setTargetPosition(elbowTarget);
}
\`\`\`

## Elbow-Up vs Elbow-Down Solutions
\`\`\`java
// IK typically has two solutions: elbow pointing up or down
// Use the negative of theta2 for the alternate solution
double theta2_alt = -theta2; // elbow-down configuration

// Choose based on which avoids collision with the robot body
// or which keeps the mechanism within legal height
\`\`\`

## Practical Safeguards
\`\`\`java
// Always clamp joint angles to safe physical limits
double clampedShoulder = Math.max(-30, Math.min(150, angles[0]));
double clampedElbow    = Math.max(  0, Math.min(170, angles[1]));

      {id:"ei_can",title:"CAN Bus Basics for FRC",est:"18 min",content:`## What is CAN Bus?
Controller Area Network (CAN) is a two-wire communication bus used in FRC to connect the roboRIO to motor controllers, the Power Distribution Hub, and other smart devices.

## CAN vs PWM
\`\`\`
PWM:                          CAN Bus:
- One wire per device         - All devices share 2 wires
- Only sends position/speed   - Bidirectional: send commands,
  command                       receive current, temp, voltage
- No feedback to roboRIO      - Unique device IDs (0-62)
- Works offline               - Daisy-chain topology
\`\`\`

## CAN Topology in FRC
\`\`\`
roboRIO
  â†• CAN_H / CAN_L
Power Distribution Hub (PDH)
  â†•
SPARK MAX (ID 1)
  â†•
SPARK MAX (ID 2)
  â†•
SPARK MAX (ID 3)
  â†•
120Î© terminator resistor â† REQUIRED at end of chain!
\`\`\`

## SPARK MAX on CAN â€” Java Example
\`\`\`java
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkMax;
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkMaxLowLevel.MotorType;

// Instantiate with CAN ID matching the one set via REV Hardware Client
CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
motor.restoreFactoryDefaults(); // always call on init to clear stale config

// Basic control
motor.set(0.5);            // % output: -1.0 to 1.0

// Read back data (only possible via CAN, not PWM!)
double velocity = motor.getEncoder().getVelocity();     // RPM
double current  = motor.getOutputCurrent();              // Amps
double temp     = motor.getMotorTemperature();           // Â°C
double voltage  = motor.getBusVoltage();                 // V
\`\`\`

## Setting CAN IDs
\`\`\`
Use REV Hardware Client (PC application):
1. Connect motor controller to PC via USB-C
2. Open REV Hardware Client
3. Navigate to CAN tab
4. Set unique ID (1-62) for each device
5. Each device on the bus MUST have a unique ID
   â†’ Duplicate IDs cause command collisions â€” robot behaves erratically
\`\`\`

## CAN Termination
\`\`\`
The last device in the CAN chain MUST have a 120Î© terminator.
Missing terminator â†’ signal reflections â†’ intermittent comms dropouts.
Many SPARK MAXes have a built-in terminator switch â€” enable it on the LAST unit only.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What key capability does CAN Bus provide that PWM motor control does not?",opts:["Faster motor response","Bidirectional communication â€” CAN lets you read back motor current, temperature, velocity, and voltage; PWM only sends a control signal","CAN uses fewer wires per device","PWM doesn't work with brushless motors"],ans:1},
        {q:"What happens if two devices on a CAN bus share the same ID?",opts:["The higher ID takes priority","Command collisions occur â€” both devices respond to the same address, causing erratic, unpredictable robot behavior","Only the first-configured device responds","The bus shuts down safely"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is the 120Î© terminator resistor required at the end of a CAN bus chain?",opts:["It grounds the bus","It prevents signal reflections â€” without termination, electrical reflections travel back up the bus and corrupt CAN messages, causing intermittent communication failures","It's a safety fuse","It sets the bus speed"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ea_current_limiting",title:"Smart Current Limiting & Motor Protection",est:"20 min",content:`## Why Current Limiting?
A stalled or overloaded motor draws 5-10Ã— its normal current. Without limiting:
- Motor overheats â†’ permanent magnet demagnetization
- Wiring overheats â†’ insulation damage â†’ fire risk
- Battery sags â†’ brownout disables the whole robot

## FRC Smart Current Limiting (SPARK MAX)
\`\`\`java
CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
motor.restoreFactoryDefaults();

// Smart current limit:
// setSmartCurrentLimit(stallLimit, freeLimit, limitRPM)
// Below limitRPM (stall zone): stallLimit applies
// Above limitRPM: freeLimit applies
motor.setSmartCurrentLimit(40, 60, 1000);
// Stall limit 40A is safe for Neo; free-running limit 60A

// Secondary absolute limit (hard cap regardless of RPM)
motor.setSecondaryCurrentLimit(80); // never exceed 80A
\`\`\`

## FTC Current Limiting (REV SDK)
\`\`\`java
// Set current alert â€” will trigger telemetry warning
// FTC SDK doesn't have hardware current limiting like FRC SPARK MAX
// Implement soft limiting in code:
double current = ((DcMotorEx)motor).getCurrent(CurrentUnit.AMPS);
if (current > 8.0) {
    motor.setPower(motor.getPower() * 0.7); // back off power
    telemetry.addData("âš ï¸ Motor Current High", "%.1fA", current);
}
\`\`\`

## Recommended Current Limits (FRC NEO Motor)
| Application | Stall Limit | Notes |
|-------------|------------|-------|
| Drive motors | 40A | Brief stalls in defense common |
| Arm/elevator | 30A | Slower mechanism, protect gearbox |
| Intake roller | 20A | Low inertia, fast response |
| Climber | 60A | High sustained load, short duration |

## Thermal Throttling Detection
\`\`\`java
// SPARK MAX will reduce output automatically when motor is too hot
// Monitor and alert your driver:
double temp = motor.getMotorTemperature();
if (temp > 70) { // NEO thermal limit is ~100Â°C
    telemetry.addData("âš ï¸ Motor Hot", "%.0fÂ°C", temp);
}
if (temp > 90) {
    telemetry.addData("ðŸ”´ THERMAL RISK!", "%.0fÂ°C â€” back off", temp);
}
\`\`\`

## Current Budget for a Full FRC Robot
\`\`\`
Battery max: ~120A continuous (250A peak very briefly)

Typical allocation:
  4 drive motors (40A each):     160A peak (shared, rarely simultaneous)
  2 arm motors (30A each):        60A peak
  1 intake (20A):                 20A peak
  PDP/PDH, roborio, misc:         10A
  Safety margin:                  30A headroom

Strategy: Don't run drive + arm + climb simultaneously at max current.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the difference between smart current limiting and a secondary (absolute) current limit on a SPARK MAX?",opts:["They are identical","Smart current limiting varies the limit based on RPM (stall vs free-running zones); the secondary limit is a hard absolute cap that can never be exceeded regardless of speed","Secondary limit is for servos only","Smart limiting only applies to NEO motors"],ans:1},
        {q:"What physical damage occurs to a brushless motor that repeatedly hits its thermal limit?",opts:["The motor resets its encoder","Sustained overheating causes permanent demagnetization of the rotor magnets, permanently reducing the motor's torque output","The motor controller resets","Only the wiring is damaged"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is it a problem to run drive motors + arm + climber all at full current simultaneously?",opts:["It's not a problem if wired correctly","The combined current draw can exceed the battery's output capacity, causing severe voltage sag (brownout) that disables the roboRIO and the entire robot","Motors share power automatically","Current doesn't add across different subsystems"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"sb_matchscouting",title:"Match Scouting Fundamentals",est:"13 min",content:`## What to Watch During a Match
New scouts often try to watch everything at once and end up recording nothing accurately. Focus on ONE robot. Record only what's on your sheet. Fill in gaps from video review later.

## The Scout's Priority Order
\`\`\`
1. Autonomous (most valuable â€” hardest to observe live, most repeatable)
   â†’ Did they complete their auto? What did they score?
   â†’ Did they move at all? Which zone?

2. Scoring cycle (teleop)
   â†’ Are they cycling game pieces? Rough count per match (not per minute)
   â†’ Which scoring level do they target?

3. Endgame
   â†’ Did they attempt the climb/endgame objective?
   â†’ Did it succeed? Level? Time remaining?

4. Notes (anything unusual)
   â†’ Robot broke, opponent defended heavily, driver error?
\`\`\`

## Common Scouting Mistakes
\`\`\`
âŒ Watching your own robot (not your assigned team)
âŒ Leaving the sheet blank for "I didn't see it" â€” write "N/A" or "?"
âŒ Guessing cycle counts â€” if uncertain, write the range: "4-6"
âŒ Forgetting to record the match number â€” unusable data without it
âŒ Using the same sheet for multiple matches â€” confusion during data entry
âœ… Use a fresh row/sheet per match, always record team + match number first
\`\`\`

## Paper vs Digital Scouting
\`\`\`
Paper:           Digital (phone/tablet):
+ Works offline  + Auto-timestamps
+ Never crashes  + Easier to aggregate
+ Fast to fill   + Can add video links
- Data entry lag - Battery/crash risk
- Handwriting    - Slower than paper for some
- Aggregation    - Distraction risk

Hybrid: scout on paper, enter to Google Forms at end of match
\`\`\`

## The Scout's Mindset
A scout who records "robot disabled at 1:45, returned at 0:55" is worth ten scouts who only count cycles. Context â€” why a score was low or high â€” is what transforms data into strategy.`,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should each scout focus on only ONE robot during a match?",opts:["FIRST assigns one robot per scout","Watching multiple robots simultaneously leads to inaccurate data for all of them â€” one focused scout with accurate data is worth more than scattered observations","It's easier","Teams only need one robot's data"],ans:1},
        {q:"What should a scout write when they didn't see an action clearly?",opts:["Leave it blank","Write 'N/A', '?' or a range like '4-6' â€” blank data looks like zero and skews analysis, while uncertainty markers can be filtered later","Make their best guess as a number","Estimate based on other matches"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is autonomous scouting data particularly valuable?",opts:["Auto is worth more points","Autonomous is the most repeatable phase â€” a team that scores 18 pts in auto every match is highly predictable; teleop varies more based on defense and driver focus","Autonomous is easier to observe","Scouts only observe autonomous"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"si_tiebreakers",title:"Understanding Tiebreakers & Ranking Points",est:"15 min",content:`## Why Tiebreakers Matter
At large regionals and district events, 1-2 ranking points often separate 8th place from 24th. Understanding the exact tiebreaker chain helps you decide when to go for bonus objectives vs secure a win.

## FRC Ranking System (General Structure)
\`\`\`
Primary:    Ranking Points (RP) â€” awarded for wins, ties, and bonus objectives
Tiebreaker 1: Average match points (excluding foul points)
Tiebreaker 2: Average auto points
Tiebreaker 3: Average endgame points
Tiebreaker 4: Random (for truly identical performance)
\`\`\`

## FTC Ranking System (General Structure)
\`\`\`
Primary:    Total match points across all matches
Tiebreaker 1: Highest single-match score
Tiebreaker 2: Second-highest single-match score
Tiebreaker 3: Total autonomous points
\`\`\`

## Strategic Implications
\`\`\`
When you're already winning comfortably:
  â†’ Should you go for the bonus RP objective or run safe?
  â†’ If RP threshold = 60 pts and you're at 45 with 30 sec left:
     Attempt only if you can reliably add 15 pts â€” don't risk a miss
     that causes a foul and lets opponents score

When tied on RP heading into the last match:
  â†’ Tiebreaker is average match score â†’ MAXIMIZE this match's score
  â†’ Don't play defense even if you normally would
  â†’ Every point counts

"Broken auto" scenarios:
  â†’ If autonomous fails, you drop in Tiebreaker 2 (avg auto pts)
  â†’ Running a simpler reliable auto (10 pts every time) beats
     a risky full auto (22 pts 60% of the time = 13.2 pts avg)
\`\`\`

## Reading the Live Rankings
\`\`\`
Tools:
  FRC: FRC Events app, Statbotics.io live rankings
  FTC: FTC Events app, ftcscout.org

Check before each of your last 2 qual matches:
  â†’ What's your current RP?
  â†’ What do you need to advance to top 8 (alliance captain) or top 24 (picked)?
  â†’ Does your next opponent's record affect their seeding?
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"In FRC ranking, after ranking points are equal, what is the first tiebreaker?",opts:["Auto points","Average match points (excluding fouls) â€” reward teams that consistently score regardless of alliance quality","Endgame points","Win/loss record"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why might running a simpler, more reliable autonomous be better for seeding than a high-risk high-reward auto?",opts:["Simple autos score more points","Average performance over many matches determines seeding â€” a reliable 10-pt auto scores 10 pts every match, while a 60%-reliable 22-pt auto averages only 13.2 pts","Referees prefer simple autos","Tiebreakers don't include auto"],ans:1},
        {q:"When tied on ranking points with one match left, why should you maximize your score even if you'd normally play defense?",opts:["Defense is illegal in the last match","Average match score is the tiebreaker â€” every additional point in this match directly improves your tiebreaker value against all equally-ranked teams","Defense doesn't affect score","Maximizing score violates GP"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"sfi_ergonomics",title:"Ergonomics & Repetitive Strain Prevention",est:"12 min",content:`## Build Season Bodies Break Down Too
A 6-week build season with 4-hour daily sessions puts enormous repetitive strain on students. Overuse injuries â€” especially wrist and shoulder â€” are common and preventable.

## Most Common Build Season Injuries
\`\`\`
Wrist / forearm:  Repetitive drilling, screwdriving with manual tools
Shoulder:         Overhead work, lifting heavy robot sections repeatedly
Back:             Hunching over low work surfaces for hours
Eyes:             Staring at CAD or screens without breaks
Fingers:          Cuts from metal burrs during assembly
\`\`\`

## Ergonomic Work Setup
\`\`\`
Workbench height: Elbows at ~90Â° when hands rest on surface
                  Too low â†’ hunching; too high â†’ shoulder strain

Monitor distance: 18-24 inches from eyes
                  Top of screen at or slightly below eye level

Drill/driver use:
  âœ… Keep wrist straight when driving fasteners â€” no flex
  âœ… Use power drivers for long sessions, not manual screwdrivers
  âœ… Switch hands periodically if doing repetitive tasks

Robot lifting:
  âœ… Lift with legs, not back â€” bend knees, straight back
  âœ… Ask for help with robots over 20 lbs
  âœ… Use a rolling cart for moving the robot around the shop
\`\`\`

## The 20-20-20 Rule for CAD/Coding
\`\`\`
Every 20 minutes of screen work:
  â†’ Look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds
  â†’ Blink consciously (screen work reduces blink rate â†’ dry eyes)
  â†’ Stretch neck and hands briefly

Signs of digital eye strain:
  - Headache after extended CAD work
  - Blurry vision, difficulty focusing
  - Dry, red, or tired eyes
\`\`\`

## Recognizing and Responding to Overuse
\`\`\`
Early warning signs (act immediately):
  - Tingling or numbness in fingers
  - Persistent ache in forearm/wrist during or after work
  - Shoulder pain when raising arm

Response:
  1. STOP the aggravating activity
  2. Rest the affected area â€” do different tasks
  3. Tell your mentor or safety captain
  4. Ice 20 min on / 20 min off for acute soreness
  5. Persistent pain â†’ see a doctor (don't push through)

"Robot season is 6 weeks; overuse injuries last months."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the ergonomically correct workbench height for robot assembly work?",opts:["As low as possible for stability","Height where your elbows are at approximately 90Â° when hands rest on the surface â€” prevents hunching or shoulder elevation","As high as possible to see better","Height doesn't matter for short tasks"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the 20-20-20 rule help prevent?",opts:["Electrical burns","Digital eye strain from extended screen time â€” looking at a distant target, blinking, and stretching gives eyes and neck regular recovery breaks","Wrist injuries","Back strain"],ans:1},
        {q:"What should you do at the FIRST sign of tingling or numbness in your fingers during build work?",opts:["Push through â€” it goes away","Stop the aggravating activity immediately and rest the area â€” early warning signs of overuse should be addressed promptly to prevent a serious injury","Put on gloves","Drink water"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"tmi_budget",title:"Team Budgeting & Fundraising",est:"16 min",content:`## Why a Budget Matters
Teams without budgets either run out of money mid-season or overspend and have trouble competing the next year. A simple budget prevents both.

## Creating a Season Budget
\`\`\`
INCOME SOURCES:
  School/district funding:    $___  (if applicable)
  Grants (FIRST, STEM orgs):  $___
  Sponsors:                   $___
  Fundraising:                $___
  Team dues (if applicable):  $___
  â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
  Total Income:               $___

EXPENSES:
  Registration/event fees:    $___  (FTC: ~$275/event, FRC: ~$6,000/regional)
  Robot parts (main build):   $___
  Robot parts (spare/repair):  $___  (budget 15-20% of parts budget)
  Travel + hotel:             $___
  Tools & shop consumables:   $___
  Awards/notebook materials:  $___
  Outreach activities:        $___
  T-shirts / uniforms:        $___
  â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
  Total Expenses:             $___
\`\`\`

## The Spare Parts Rule
\`\`\`
Budget 15-20% of your parts budget for spares.
Most common competition failures:
  - Motor burnout (bring 2 spares of each motor used)
  - Stripped servo gears (bring 4 spare servos)
  - Broken chain/belt (bring a full spare length of each type)
  - Bent axles (bring 3 spare shafts)
  - Burned motor controllers (1 spare per type)

"The team that arrives at competition with spares wins more than the team with the fancier robot."
\`\`\`

## Finding Sponsors
\`\`\`
Sponsor tiers (example):
  Gold ($1,000+):  Logo on robot, jersey, website; personal thank-you letter
  Silver ($500+):  Logo on website; thank-you
  Bronze ($250+):  Name in program; thank-you

Where to find sponsors:
  â†’ Parents' employers (easiest â€” start here)
  â†’ Local engineering/manufacturing companies
  â†’ Technology companies in your area
  â†’ FIRST matching programs (ask your Program Delivery Partner)
  â†’ Local community foundations

Sponsorship letter must-haves:
  â†’ What FIRST is (most sponsors don't know)
  â†’ What your team accomplishes
  â†’ Exactly what the money goes toward
  â†’ Tax-deductibility status (501c3 if applicable)
  â†’ A specific ask amount ("Would you consider a $500 sponsorship?")
\`\`\`
Every fall, a FIRST team brings in new members. Without a plan, veterans answer the same questions 20 times, new members feel lost, and 40% quit before build season ends.

## The First Two Weeks Framework
\`\`\`
Week 1: Orientation
  Day 1: Team tour, meet everyone, safety training (required before any tools!)
  Day 2: Watch last season's reveal video and match footage
          "What did we build? What worked? What didn't?"
  Day 3: Hands-on skill stations:
          - Drill, tap, and countersink a practice plate
          - Read and write a 5-line Java function (all members, not just programmers)
          - Identify every component on a wired robot

Week 2: Choose a Track
  Each new member picks a primary area: Programming, Mechanical, Electrical, Business
  Immediately assigned to a simple real task (not a "learning exercise" â€” a real task)
\`\`\`

## Mentorship Pairing
\`\`\`
Each new member â†’ paired with an experienced "buddy"
Buddy responsibilities:
  â†’ Answer questions before they go to a mentor
  â†’ Check in every build session for the first 4 weeks
  â†’ Include them in work (not just watching)
  
Buddy benefit: Teaching reinforces the buddy's own knowledge.
\`\`\`

## Retaining New Members Past Week 4
\`\`\`
Why new members quit:
  âŒ "I don't know what to do when I arrive"
  âŒ "No one talks to me / I don't know anyone"
  âŒ "I only watch â€” I don't actually do anything"
  âŒ "The veterans ignore new members"

Fixes:
  âœ… Post a task board: open tasks with skill level and estimated time
  âœ… Assign at least one REAL task per member per meeting
  âœ… Celebrate new member contributions publicly ("Marcus wrote the intake toggle today")
  âœ… Explain the WHY: "This bracket you're drilling goes on the arm that scores the game piece"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should 15-20% of your parts budget be reserved specifically for spares?",opts:["FIRST requires a spare budget","Competition failures are predictable â€” common items like motors, servos, and chain consistently break; teams with spares fix in minutes, teams without lose the event","Spare parts cost more","Spare parts only matter for FRC teams"],ans:1},
        {q:"Who are typically the easiest first sponsors to approach for a FIRST team?",opts:["Large national corporations","Parents' employers â€” they already have a personal connection to the team and the ask is warmer than a cold corporate outreach","The school administration","Professional sports teams"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the most important thing to include in a sponsorship letter that most sponsors won't know?",opts:["Your team's competition record","What FIRST is and why it matters â€” most local businesses have never heard of FIRST and need context before they'll consider donating","The robot weight","Your team's age range"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should safety training happen on Day 1 for new members, before any other hands-on work?",opts:["It's required by law","New members must understand shop safety rules before touching any tools â€” a single shop accident can injure a member and shut down the team's workspace","It's a FIRST rule","Safety training takes the least time"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is assigning a REAL task better than a 'learning exercise' for new member retention?",opts:["Real tasks are always simple","Real tasks contribute to the actual robot â€” new members feel valued and see their work matter; learning exercises feel like busy work and signal they're not trusted","Learning exercises take too long","Real tasks require more supervision"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the primary reason new members quit FIRST teams in the first four weeks?",opts:["They aren't interested in robotics","They feel inactive, invisible, or uncertain what to do when they arrive â€” belonging and purposeful tasks are the strongest retention factors","The work is too hard","Meeting times conflict with school"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"cadi_sheetmetal",title:"Sheet Metal Design in Onshape",est:"17 min",content:`## Why Sheet Metal CAD?
Flat aluminum sheet is one of the most common robot materials â€” chassis plates, bellcranks, motor mounts, and brackets. Onshape's sheet metal tools flatten and unfold parts for laser cutting automatically.

## Sheet Metal vs Regular Extrude
\`\`\`
Regular Extrude:
  â†’ Good for thick blocks, tubes, 3D shapes
  â†’ Does NOT unfold for laser cutting

Sheet Metal Feature:
  â†’ Designed for flat stock with bends
  â†’ Creates flat pattern automatically â†’ DXF for laser cutting
  â†’ Ensures consistent material thickness throughout
\`\`\`

## Creating a Sheet Metal Part in Onshape
\`\`\`
1. Sketch the base flange profile (the flat base of your bracket)
2. Sheet Metal â†’ Flange â†’ select your sketch
   Set thickness: 1/8" (3.175mm) for structural, 1/16" for lightweight brackets
3. Add bends: Sheet Metal â†’ Flange or Bend
   Set bend radius (typically 2Ã— material thickness)
4. Add holes: Sketch holes on the flat faces, then Extrude-Remove
5. Flat Pattern: Sheet Metal â†’ Flat Pattern
   â†’ Shows exact cut shape for laser cutter
   â†’ Export as DXF and send to laser cutter
\`\`\`

## Bend Allowance (Why CAD Math Matters)
\`\`\`
When you bend metal, the outer surface stretches and inner compresses.
The flat pattern length is NOT equal to folded edge lengths added together.

Flat pattern length = A + B - Bend Allowance
Bend Allowance = (Ï€/180) Ã— angle Ã— (radius + k-factor Ã— thickness)

Onshape handles this automatically in Sheet Metal mode.
If you use regular Extrude for bent parts:
  â†’ You'll measure and cut incorrectly â†’ part won't fit
  â†’ Always use Sheet Metal features for parts with bends.
\`\`\`

## DXF Export for Laser Cutting
\`\`\`
1. Right-click Flat Pattern in feature tree
2. Export as DXF
3. Check with vendor:
   â†’ Which layer is the cut line?
   â†’ Which layer is the engrave/score line?
   â†’ Scale: is 1 unit = 1 mm or 1 inch? (confirm with vendor!)
4. Nest multiple parts on one sheet to save material cost
   (many laser vendors accept multi-part DXF files or use nesting software)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should you use Onshape's Sheet Metal features instead of regular Extrude for bent aluminum brackets?",opts:["Sheet Metal is faster to use","Sheet Metal features automatically calculate the correct flat pattern including bend allowance â€” regular Extrude produces incorrect flat lengths that won't fit after bending","Sheet Metal is required for FRC","Regular Extrude can't make holes"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is 'bend allowance' and why does it matter for laser-cut parts?",opts:["The extra material at the edges","The compensation for metal stretching/compressing during bending â€” ignoring it means cut flat patterns are the wrong length and the bent part won't match the design dimensions","The minimum bend radius allowed","The safety margin between holes and edges"],ans:1},
        {q:"When exporting a DXF for laser cutting, what must you confirm with the vendor?",opts:["The file format only","Which CAD layer represents the cut line vs engrave line, and what scale units are used â€” a misunderstanding on scale means parts come back the wrong size","The number of parts","The material thickness"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"awi_deanlist",title:"Dean's List Award (FTC) Strategy",est:"16 min",content:`## What is the Dean's List Award?
The Dean's List award recognizes outstanding FTC student leaders who embody the philosophies of FIRST. Two students from each FTC World Championship qualify as Dean's List Finalists â€” a prestigious scholarship-adjacent honor.

## Who Can Be Nominated?
\`\`\`
Requirements:
  â†’ Second year or beyond FTC student (no rookies)
  â†’ Demonstrated leadership ON and OFF the robot
  â†’ Actively spreads FIRST's mission beyond their own team
  â†’ Can be a programmer, builder, strategist, business lead â€” any role
\`\`\`

## The Nomination Components
\`\`\`
1. Written essay (student-authored, 4,000 characters max):
   â†’ Why this student exemplifies FIRST's mission
   â†’ Leadership impact on their team AND community
   â†’ Specific examples â€” not general statements

2. The Interview (at regional/championship):
   â†’ 5-7 minutes with a panel of judges
   â†’ Conversational â€” judges want to know the STUDENT, not the resume
   â†’ Common questions:
      "Tell me about a challenge you overcame on your team."
      "How have you inspired someone else to join FIRST?"
      "What does Gracious Professionalism mean to YOU personally?"
\`\`\`

## What Wins: The Student's Story
\`\`\`
Strong Dean's List candidate tells a story like:
  "I joined as a shy freshman who couldn't drive a drill.
   By year 3, I was teaching 5 new members.
   I noticed our school had no FLL team â€” I started one.
   26 kids who had never touched a robot now compete every year."

This story shows:
  âœ… Personal growth
  âœ… Leadership development
  âœ… Concrete impact beyond the team
  âœ… A program that continues without them
\`\`\`

## Preparing for the Interview
\`\`\`
Practice answering:
  â†’ "What is FIRST's mission in your own words?"
  â†’ "What is your greatest contribution to your team?"
  â†’ "What are you most proud of outside of robot performance?"
  â†’ "How has FIRST changed how you approach problems?"

Tips:
  âœ… Be specific â€” "I taught 5 members to use the lathe" beats "I helped people"
  âœ… Show self-awareness â€” what did YOU personally learn?
  âœ… Don't recite your resume â€” have a conversation
  âœ… It's okay to pause and think before answering
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What type of student is the strongest Dean's List candidate?",opts:["The student with the highest GPA","A student who shows personal growth, team leadership, and concrete community impact that extends FIRST's mission â€” in any role, not necessarily the programmer or captain","Only team captains are eligible","The student who drives the robot"],ans:1},
        {q:"What do Dean's List judges most want to see during the interview?",opts:["A memorized speech","The student's authentic story â€” personal growth, real impact, genuine understanding of FIRST's mission â€” not a polished performance","The student's technical skills","A list of team achievements"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is starting a new FLL team particularly powerful in a Dean's List essay?",opts:["It's a required activity","It demonstrates the 'inspiring others to inspire others' multiplier effect â€” a core FIRST value â€” with a concrete, verifiable, lasting outcome","FLL is more prestigious than FTC","It satisfies a community service requirement"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"ori_funding",title:"Applying for STEM Grants",est:"17 min",content:`## Grants Are Free Money â€” Few Teams Apply
Most FIRST teams rely entirely on sponsors and school funding. Grants are underutilized because the application process feels intimidating. A single grant can fund an entire season.

## Where to Find FIRST-Relevant Grants
\`\`\`
FIRST-Specific:
  â†’ FIRST Scholarship and Grant programs (firstinspires.org/ways-to-help/grants)
  â†’ FIRST in Michigan, FIRST in Texas, etc. â€” regional grantmakers
  â†’ Title I school supplemental funding (if your school qualifies)

General STEM Grants:
  â†’ National Science Foundation (NSF) informal education grants
  â†’ STEM-Next Opportunity Fund
  â†’ Local community foundations (search "[your city] community foundation grants")
  â†’ Boeing, Raytheon, Lockheed STEM education programs
  â†’ Women in engineering foundations (for teams with girls)

Easiest starting points:
  â†’ Local community foundation â€” small grants ($500-$2,000), simple applications
  â†’ Parent employer STEM giving programs â€” ask parents first!
\`\`\`

## Grant Application Framework
\`\`\`
Most grant applications ask the same questions:

1. Who are you?
   â†’ Team number, school, years active, member count

2. What will you do with the money? (Be specific)
   âœ… "Purchase a REV Robotics kit ($350) and fund travel to
       3 regional events ($1,800) for our 12-student team"
   âŒ "Support our robotics team activities"

3. How does it connect to the grant's mission?
   â†’ Match YOUR language to THEIR mission statement
   â†’ Read their website carefully before writing

4. Who benefits?
   â†’ Number of students, demographics, sustainability

5. How will you measure success?
   â†’ "By June 2026, 8/12 members will complete at least one competition,
      and we'll have started one new FLL team in our district"
\`\`\`

## The Thank-You System
\`\`\`
Grant funders who receive genuine, specific thank-yous renew.
Those who don't, don't.

After receiving a grant:
  â†’ Thank-you letter within 2 weeks (student-written)
  â†’ Photo update showing the grant at work
  â†’ End-of-season report: what you achieved with the funds
  â†’ Include them in team acknowledgments at events

This 1-hour investment makes renewal 3Ã— more likely.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why do most FIRST teams underutilize grants as a funding source?",opts:["Grants aren't available for FIRST teams","The application process feels intimidating â€” but many local and FIRST-specific grants are straightforward, and few teams actually apply, reducing competition","Grants require 501c3 status","Grants take too long to process"],ans:1},
        {q:"What makes a grant application's 'use of funds' section strong?",opts:["General descriptions of team activities","Specific, itemized uses: 'REV Robotics starter kit ($350), travel to 3 events ($1,800)' â€” vague answers signal the team hasn't thought through their plan","Long explanations of FIRST's history","Mentioning as many activities as possible"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is a post-grant thank-you and progress report important?",opts:["It's legally required","Funders who receive genuine, specific updates renew grants at much higher rates â€” it closes the relationship loop and demonstrates stewardship of their investment","It's just polite","It satisfies FIRST reporting requirements"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"gi_gitignore",title:"Git Best Practices for FTC & FRC",est:"14 min",content:`## The .gitignore File â€” What NOT to Commit
Some files should never be in your repository. Generated build files, local settings, and IDE configurations bloat the repo and cause conflicts between teammates' machines.

## FTC .gitignore (put in project root)
\`\`\`gitignore
# Build output
.gradle/
build/
*/build/

# Local Android/IDE settings (different per machine)
local.properties
*.iml
.idea/
*.class

# OS files
.DS_Store        # macOS
Thumbs.db        # Windows
desktop.ini

# Sensitive data (NEVER commit API keys)
secrets.properties
api_keys.txt
\`\`\`

## FRC .gitignore
\`\`\`gitignore
# Gradle
.gradle/
build/

# IDE
.idea/
*.iml
.vscode/settings.json  # personal settings only; commit extensions.json if useful

# Python (for scouting tools in the repo)
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.venv/
venv/
*.env

# Robot-specific
networktables.json     # auto-generated, differs per robot
simgui.json
simgui-ds.json
\`\`\`

## Commit Message Best Practices
\`\`\`
Format: <type>: <short description>

Types:
  feat:     new feature added
  fix:      bug fix
  tune:     PID/constants tuning
  refactor: code restructuring (no behavior change)
  docs:     documentation/notebook
  test:     test code

Examples:
  feat: add field-centric drive mode to MecanumDrive
  fix: arm encoder no longer resets after teleop init
  tune: kP 0.007â†’0.009 for lift; reduces steady-state error to <5 ticks
  refactor: extract RobotHardware class from MainTeleOp
  docs: add intake mechanism entry to engineering notebook

Why this matters:
  git log --oneline shows a clean history:
  a3f1b2c tune: kP 0.007â†’0.009 for lift
  8d4e1a0 fix: arm encoder no longer resets after teleop init
  2c9f3b1 feat: add field-centric drive mode
  vs:
  9a2c1f0 stuff
  3b8d2a1 fix
  1f4a2b3 asdf
\`\`\`

## Secrets Management
\`\`\`
NEVER commit:
  - API keys (TBA, Discord bot tokens)
  - Passwords
  - Internal team documents

Instead, use:
  - Environment variables: os.getenv("TBA_KEY")
  - A secrets.properties file listed in .gitignore
  - GitHub Secrets for Actions workflows

If you accidentally commit a secret:
  1. Revoke/rotate the key IMMEDIATELY (assume it's compromised)
  2. Use git filter-repo to remove it from history
  3. Force push cleaned history
  Note: Simply deleting the file in a new commit is NOT sufficient â€”
        the secret still exists in git history.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should local.properties be included in .gitignore for FTC projects?",opts:["It contains robot passwords","local.properties contains machine-specific paths and SDK locations â€” committing it causes errors on teammates' different machine configurations","It's automatically generated","It contains match data"],ans:1},
        {q:"If you accidentally commit an API key to a public GitHub repo, what is the FIRST thing you must do?",opts:["Delete the commit message","Immediately revoke and rotate the key â€” it should be considered compromised the moment it touches git history, even if you delete it in the next commit","Add it to .gitignore","Make the repo private"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the benefit of using conventional commit message prefixes like 'feat:', 'fix:', 'tune:'?",opts:["GitHub requires them","They make git log readable at a glance â€” teammates can understand the history of changes without reading code, and tools can auto-generate changelogs","They compile faster","They're required for GitHub Actions"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },
};

Object.keys(LESSONS_PACK_EX3).forEach(subject => {
  if (!LESSONS[subject]) LESSONS[subject] = {};
  Object.keys(LESSONS_PACK_EX3[subject]).forEach(level => {
    if (!LESSONS[subject][level]) LESSONS[subject][level] = [];
    LESSONS[subject][level] = [...(LESSONS[subject][level]||[]), ...LESSONS_PACK_EX3[subject][level]];
  });
});
