  java: {
    Beginner: [
      {id:"jb_casting",title:"Type Casting & Number Conversion",est:"11 min",content:`## Why Casting Matters in Robot Code
Java is strongly typed â€” you can't mix ints and doubles without telling Java how to handle the conversion. Casting errors cause subtle bugs in motor math and sensor readings.

## Implicit vs Explicit Casting
\`\`\`java
// Implicit (widening) â€” safe, Java does it automatically
int ticks = 537;
double d = ticks;   // int â†’ double: 537.0 â€” no data loss, OK

// Explicit (narrowing) â€” you must cast manually
double power = 0.75;
int rounded = (int) power;  // double â†’ int: 0 (truncates, doesn't round!)

// To round instead of truncate:
int rounded2 = (int) Math.round(power);  // â†’ 1
\`\`\`

## Common Casting Bug in Encoder Math
\`\`\`java
// âŒ BUG: integer division â€” result is 0!
int ticks = 300;
int total  = 537;
double ratio = ticks / total;   // 300/537 = 0 (both ints â†’ integer division)

// âœ… FIX: cast one operand to double first
double ratio2 = (double) ticks / total;  // 300.0/537 = 0.559
// Or use double literals:
double ratio3 = ticks / 537.0;           // also works
\`\`\`

## String â†” Number Conversions
\`\`\`java
// String â†’ int (for parsing config values)
String input = "1234";
int teamNum  = Integer.parseInt(input);   // 1234

// String â†’ double
String speedStr = "0.75";
double speed    = Double.parseDouble(speedStr);

// Number â†’ String (for telemetry labels)
String label = "Team " + 1234;           // "Team 1234" â€” auto-converted
String label2 = String.valueOf(speed);   // "0.75"
String label3 = String.format("%.2f", speed); // "0.75" formatted

// Safe parsing â€” catch bad input
try {
    int val = Integer.parseInt(someString);
} catch (NumberFormatException e) {
    telemetry.addData("Parse Error", someString + " is not a number");
}
\`\`\`

## Integer Division Cheat Sheet
\`\`\`java
7 / 2    = 3      // integer division â€” truncates
7.0 / 2  = 3.5    // double division
7 / 2.0  = 3.5    // double division
(double)7 / 2 = 3.5  // explicit cast
\`\`\`
Most Java string tutorials focus on text processing. On a robot, strings show up in telemetry, hardware map names, log messages, and configuration files.

## String Formatting for Telemetry
\`\`\`java
// printf-style formatting â€” clean and readable
telemetry.addData("Power",   "%+.2f", motor.getPower());   // +0.75
telemetry.addData("Angle",   "%.1fÂ°", heading);            // 90.2Â°
telemetry.addData("Ticks",   "%6d",   encoder.getCurrentPosition()); // right-aligned
telemetry.addData("State",   "[%s]",  state.name());       // [SCORING]

// Format codes:
// %d = integer,  %f = float,  %s = string
// .2f = 2 decimal places
// +.2f = always show sign (+0.75 or -0.75)
// %6d = minimum 6 characters wide (right-aligned)
\`\`\`

## String Comparison â€” The Classic Bug
\`\`\`java
String color = "red";

// âŒ WRONG â€” compares object references, not content
if (color == "red") { /* may not work! */ }

// âœ… CORRECT â€” compares actual characters
if (color.equals("red")) { doRedAction(); }

// Case-insensitive comparison:
if (color.equalsIgnoreCase("RED")) { doRedAction(); }

// Check if string contains a word:
String name = "leftFrontMotor";
if (name.contains("Front")) { /* true */ }
if (name.startsWith("left")) { /* true */ }
\`\`\`

## Building Log Messages
\`\`\`java
// StringBuilder for building long log strings efficiently
StringBuilder log = new StringBuilder();
log.append("Auto: ");
log.append(state.name());
log.append(" | Pos=").append(arm.getCurrentPosition());
log.append(" | t=").append(String.format("%.1f", runtime.seconds()));
telemetry.addLine(log.toString());
// â†’ "Auto: SCORING | Pos=1487 | t=28.3"
\`\`\`

## Hardware Map Names â€” Naming Convention
\`\`\`java
// Hardware map names are strings â€” typos cause runtime errors
// Robot configuration on phone/DS must match exactly
DcMotor m = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, "leftFront");
// If your config says "left_front" â†’ NullPointerException!

// Best practice: store names in Constants
public static final String LEFT_FRONT  = "leftFront";
public static final String RIGHT_FRONT = "rightFront";

DcMotor m = hardwareMap.get(DcMotor.class, Constants.LEFT_FRONT);
// Now one typo fix in Constants updates all OpModes
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the result of (int)(0.9) in Java?",opts:["1","0 â€” casting a double to int truncates toward zero, it does NOT round","Error","0.9"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why does 'int result = 300 / 537' give 0 instead of 0.559?",opts:["Java has a bug","Both operands are integers so Java performs integer division, discarding the fractional part â€” cast one to double first","537 is too large","Division requires double operands"],ans:1},
        {q:"Which expression correctly produces 0.559 from two integer variables a=300 and b=537?",opts:["a / b","(int)a / b","(double)a / b","a / (int)b"],ans:2},
        {q:"Why does comparing strings with == sometimes fail in Java even when they look identical?",opts:["== is broken in Java","== compares object memory addresses, not content â€” two strings with the same characters may be different objects; always use .equals()","== only works for ints","Strings can't be compared in Java"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the format specifier '+.2f' produce when applied to the value 0.75?",opts:["0.75","0.7500","+0.75 â€” the + forces a sign character to always appear","Error"],ans:2},
        {q:"Why is storing hardware map names in a Constants class safer than typing them inline in each OpMode?",opts:["It saves memory","A single typo fix in Constants updates every OpMode â€” inline strings must be corrected in every file individually, and typos cause runtime NullPointerExceptions","String constants compile faster","The SDK requires it"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Intermediate: [
      {id:"ji_command",title:"Command Pattern for Complex Robots",est:"22 min",content:`## The Command Pattern â€” What FRC WPILib Uses
In FRC, the command-based framework separates WHAT a mechanism does (commands) from HOW it works (subsystems). FTC teams can adopt the same pattern without the full WPILib framework.

## Core Concepts
\`\`\`
Subsystem:  Owns the hardware. Only one command can use it at a time.
Command:    A task that uses one or more subsystems to achieve a goal.
Scheduler:  Runs active commands each loop; cancels conflicting ones.
\`\`\`

## Simple Command Interface
\`\`\`java
public interface Command {
    void initialize();   // called once when command starts
    void execute();      // called every loop while command runs
    boolean isFinished();// true â†’ command is done
    void end(boolean interrupted); // cleanup
}
\`\`\`

## Example: MoveArmCommand
\`\`\`java
public class MoveArmCommand implements Command {
    private final ArmSubsystem arm;
    private final int targetTicks;
    private final double timeout;
    private ElapsedTime timer;

    public MoveArmCommand(ArmSubsystem arm, int targetTicks, double timeoutSec) {
        this.arm = arm;
        this.targetTicks = targetTicks;
        this.timeout = timeoutSec;
    }

    @Override
    public void initialize() {
        arm.setPosition(targetTicks);
        timer = new ElapsedTime();
    }

    @Override
    public void execute() {
        // arm handles PID internally â€” nothing to do here
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isFinished() {
        return arm.atTarget() || timer.seconds() > timeout;
    }

    @Override
    public void end(boolean interrupted) {
        if (interrupted) arm.stop();
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Simple Scheduler (Sequential)
\`\`\`java
public class CommandScheduler {
    private Queue<Command> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    private Command current = null;

    public void schedule(Command... commands) {
        for (Command c : commands) queue.add(c);
    }

    public void run() {
        if (current == null && !queue.isEmpty()) {
            current = queue.poll();
            current.initialize();
        }
        if (current != null) {
            current.execute();
            if (current.isFinished()) {
                current.end(false);
                current = null;
            }
        }
    }

    public boolean isDone() { return current == null && queue.isEmpty(); }
}
\`\`\`

## Using It in Autonomous
\`\`\`java
CommandScheduler auto = new CommandScheduler();
auto.schedule(
    new DriveCommand(drive, 24.0, 0.5),      // drive 24 inches
    new MoveArmCommand(arm, ARM_HIGH, 2.0),  // raise arm
    new RunIntakeCommand(intake, -1.0, 0.5), // score
    new MoveArmCommand(arm, ARM_STOWED, 1.5) // retract
);

while (opModeIsActive() && !auto.isDone()) {
    auto.run();
    telemetry.update();
}
\`\`\`
Straight segments with pauses between them are slow. A robot that drives arcs and curves can complete the same route in half the time.

## Cubic BÃ©zier Curves â€” The Idea
\`\`\`
A BÃ©zier curve is defined by 4 control points:
  P0 = start point
  P1 = start tangent control (direction leaving P0)
  P2 = end tangent control (direction arriving at P3)
  P3 = end point

Point on curve at parameter t (0 to 1):
  B(t) = (1-t)Â³P0 + 3(1-t)Â²tÂ·P1 + 3(1-t)tÂ²Â·P2 + tÂ³P3
\`\`\`

## Simple BÃ©zier Parametric Evaluator
\`\`\`java
public class BezierPath {
    double[] p0, p1, p2, p3; // each is {x, y}

    public BezierPath(double[] p0, double[] p1,
                      double[] p2, double[] p3) {
        this.p0=p0; this.p1=p1; this.p2=p2; this.p3=p3;
    }

    // Get {x, y} at parameter t âˆˆ [0, 1]
    public double[] evaluate(double t) {
        double u = 1-t;
        double x = u*u*u*p0[0] + 3*u*u*t*p1[0]
                 + 3*u*t*t*p2[0] + t*t*t*p3[0];
        double y = u*u*u*p0[1] + 3*u*u*t*p1[1]
                 + 3*u*t*t*p2[1] + t*t*t*p3[1];
        return new double[]{x, y};
    }

    // Get heading (tangent direction) at t
    public double heading(double t) {
        double u = 1-t;
        double dx = 3*u*u*(p1[0]-p0[0])
                  + 6*u*t*(p2[0]-p1[0])
                  + 3*t*t*(p3[0]-p2[0]);
        double dy = 3*u*u*(p1[1]-p0[1])
                  + 6*u*t*(p2[1]-p1[1])
                  + 3*t*t*(p3[1]-p2[1]);
        return Math.atan2(dy, dx);
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Following a Path with Odometry
\`\`\`java
BezierPath path = new BezierPath(
    new double[]{0, 0},      // start: robot origin
    new double[]{12, 0},     // control 1: exit heading east
    new double[]{24, -12},   // control 2: arrive heading south
    new double[]{24, -24}    // end: target position
);

double t = 0;
while (opModeIsActive() && t <= 1.0) {
    odometry.update();
    double[] target = path.evaluate(t);
    double targetH   = path.heading(t);

    double errX = target[0] - odometry.x;
    double errY = target[1] - odometry.y;
    double dist  = Math.sqrt(errX*errX + errY*errY);

    // Advance t based on how close we are to current waypoint
    if (dist < 2.0) t += 0.05; // move to next segment

    double forward = Math.cos(targetH - odometry.heading) * 0.5;
    double strafe  = Math.sin(targetH - odometry.heading) * 0.5;
    drive.driveFieldCentric(strafe, forward, 0);
    telemetry.addData("t", "%.2f  dist=%.1f", t, dist);
    telemetry.update();
}
drive.stop();
\`\`\`

## Road Runner vs Custom Paths
\`\`\`
Road Runner (recommended for most teams):
  â†’ Full path following library with motion profiling
  â†’ Proven by hundreds of top teams
  â†’ Use it instead of custom splines unless you're sure

Custom splines (for learning / special needs):
  â†’ Full control, no dependencies
  â†’ Requires thorough testing and tuning
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the role of the 'initialize()' method in a Command?",opts:["It runs every loop","It runs exactly once when the command first starts â€” used for setup like setting a target position or resetting a timer","It checks if the command is done","It's called when the command is cancelled"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is the command pattern useful for autonomous routines?",opts:["It makes code shorter","It separates each autonomous action into a reusable, testable unit â€” complex sequences are built by scheduling commands instead of chaining sleep() calls","It runs faster than state machines","It's required for autonomous"],ans:1},
        {q:"What should the end() method do when interrupted=true?",opts:["Continue the command","Safely stop the mechanism â€” when a command is cancelled mid-execution, the hardware should be left in a safe state, not mid-motion","Do nothing","Start the next command"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the parameter t=0.5 represent on a BÃ©zier curve?",opts:["The midpoint of the straight-line distance","The point halfway along the parameterized curve â€” not necessarily the geometric midpoint, but the curve evaluated at the middle of its parameter range","The midpoint in time","The control point"],ans:1},

      {id:"ja_limelight",title:"Limelight & Vision-Assisted Targeting",est:"28 min",content:`## What is the Limelight?
The Limelight is a plug-and-play vision camera popular in FRC. It runs its own computer, detects retroreflective tape / AprilTags / TFOD targets, and streams results over NetworkTables â€” no image processing code required on the roboRIO.

## Hardware Setup
\`\`\`
Power:  12V from PDP/PDH (fused at 5A)
Data:   Ethernet cable to robot network switch (or direct to roboRIO)
Mount:  Aimed at your target â€” measure the height and angle precisely!
LEDs:   Ring LED illuminates retroreflective tape (disable for AprilTags)
\`\`\`

## Reading Limelight Data (NetworkTables)
\`\`\`java
import edu.wpi.first.networktables.NetworkTable;
import edu.wpi.first.networktables.NetworkTableInstance;

NetworkTable limelight = NetworkTableInstance.getDefault()
                             .getTable("limelight");

// Key values from Limelight:
double tv = limelight.getEntry("tv").getDouble(0); // 1=target visible, 0=none
double tx = limelight.getEntry("tx").getDouble(0); // horizontal offset (degrees)
double ty = limelight.getEntry("ty").getDouble(0); // vertical offset (degrees)
double ta = limelight.getEntry("ta").getDouble(0); // target area (% of image)

if (tv == 1.0) {
    // Target is visible â€” act on tx
    double steerAdjust = tx * 0.04; // P controller on heading
    double driveCmd    = ta < 8.0 ? 0.4 : 0.0; // drive until target fills 8%
    drive.arcadeDrive(driveCmd, steerAdjust);
}
\`\`\`

## Distance Estimation from Camera Geometry
\`\`\`java
// Estimate distance using the target's known height and ty angle
static final double CAMERA_HEIGHT_INCHES   = 24.0; // camera mount height
static final double TARGET_HEIGHT_INCHES   = 60.0; // target center height
static final double CAMERA_MOUNT_ANGLE_DEG =  30.0; // camera tilt upward

public double getDistanceToTarget() {
    double ty = limelight.getEntry("ty").getDouble(0);
    double angleToTarget = Math.toRadians(CAMERA_MOUNT_ANGLE_DEG + ty);
    return (TARGET_HEIGHT_INCHES - CAMERA_HEIGHT_INCHES)
           / Math.tan(angleToTarget);
}
\`\`\`

## Auto-Aim Command (FRC)
\`\`\`java
public class AutoAimCommand extends CommandBase {
    private final DriveSubsystem drive;
    private final double kP = 0.03;

    public AutoAimCommand(DriveSubsystem drive) {
        this.drive = drive;
        addRequirements(drive);
    }

    @Override
    public void execute() {
        double tv = limelight.getEntry("tv").getDouble(0);
        double tx = limelight.getEntry("tx").getDouble(0);
        if (tv == 1.0) {
            double rotate = -tx * kP;
            drive.arcadeDrive(0, rotate);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isFinished() {
        double tv = limelight.getEntry("tv").getDouble(0);
        double tx = limelight.getEntry("tx").getDouble(0);
        return tv == 1.0 && Math.abs(tx) < 1.5; // within 1.5Â° = aligned
    }
}
\`\`\`

Command-line scouting tools get abandoned. A real GUI form with dropdowns, buttons, and instant feedback gets filled in consistently â€” even in loud, stressful competition environments.

## Full Scouting Form
\`\`\`python
import tkinter as tk
from tkinter import ttk, messagebox
import csv
import os
from datetime import datetime

class ScoutingForm:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = tk.Tk()
        self.root.title("Match Scouting")
        self.root.configure(bg="#0f172a")
        self.root.geometry("480x620")
        self._build_form()

    def _label(self, parent, text, row, col=0):
        tk.Label(parent, text=text, bg="#0f172a", fg="#94a3b8",
                 font=("Arial", 10)).grid(row=row, column=col,
                 sticky="w", padx=8, pady=3)

    def _build_form(self):
        f = tk.Frame(self.root, bg="#0f172a")
        f.pack(fill="both", expand=True, padx=20, pady=10)

        # Match number
        self._label(f, "Match #", 0)
        self.match_var = tk.StringVar()
        tk.Entry(f, textvariable=self.match_var, width=10,
                 bg="#1e293b", fg="white").grid(row=0, column=1, sticky="w")

        # Team number
        self._label(f, "Team #", 1)
        self.team_var = tk.StringVar()
        tk.Entry(f, textvariable=self.team_var, width=10,
                 bg="#1e293b", fg="white").grid(row=1, column=1, sticky="w")

        # Auto score
        self._label(f, "Auto Points", 2)
        self.auto_var = tk.IntVar(value=0)
        tk.Spinbox(f, from_=0, to=40, textvariable=self.auto_var, width=8,
                   bg="#1e293b", fg="white").grid(row=2, column=1, sticky="w")

        # Teleop cycles
        self._label(f, "Teleop Cycles", 3)
        self.cycles_var = tk.IntVar(value=0)
        tk.Spinbox(f, from_=0, to=30, textvariable=self.cycles_var, width=8,
                   bg="#1e293b", fg="white").grid(row=3, column=1, sticky="w")

        # Climb level
        self._label(f, "Climb Level", 4)
        self.climb_var = tk.StringVar(value="None")
        ttk.Combobox(f, textvariable=self.climb_var, width=10,
                     values=["None", "L1", "L2", "L3"],
                     state="readonly").grid(row=4, column=1, sticky="w")

        # Penalties given
        self._label(f, "Penalties Given", 5)
        self.penalty_var = tk.IntVar(value=0)
        tk.Spinbox(f, from_=0, to=10, textvariable=self.penalty_var, width=8,
                   bg="#1e293b", fg="white").grid(row=5, column=1, sticky="w")

        # Notes
        self._label(f, "Notes", 6)
        self.notes_text = tk.Text(f, width=35, height=4,
                                  bg="#1e293b", fg="white")
        self.notes_text.grid(row=6, column=1, sticky="w", pady=4)

        # Submit button
        tk.Button(f, text="âœ…  Submit", command=self._submit,
                  bg="#1d4ed8", fg="white", font=("Arial", 12, "bold"),
                  padx=20, pady=8).grid(row=7, column=0, columnspan=2, pady=12)

        # Status label
        self.status_var = tk.StringVar(value="")
        tk.Label(f, textvariable=self.status_var, bg="#0f172a",
                 fg="#10b981", font=("Arial", 10)).grid(row=8, column=0, columnspan=2)

    def _submit(self):
        match  = self.match_var.get().strip()
        team   = self.team_var.get().strip()
        if not match or not team:
            messagebox.showerror("Missing Data", "Match # and Team # are required")
            return

        row = {
            "timestamp": datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S"),
            "match": match,
            "team": team,
            "auto": self.auto_var.get(),
            "cycles": self.cycles_var.get(),
            "climb": self.climb_var.get(),
            "penalties": self.penalty_var.get(),
            "notes": self.notes_text.get("1.0", tk.END).strip()
        }

        file_exists = os.path.exists("scout_data.csv")
        with open("scout_data.csv", "a", newline="") as f:
            writer = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=row.keys())
            if not file_exists:
                writer.writeheader()
            writer.writerow(row)

        self.status_var.set(f"âœ… Saved: Team {team} Match {match}")
        self._clear_form()

    def _clear_form(self):
        self.match_var.set("")
        self.team_var.set("")
        self.auto_var.set(0)
        self.cycles_var.set(0)
        self.climb_var.set("None")
        self.penalty_var.set(0)
        self.notes_text.delete("1.0", tk.END)

    def run(self):
        self.root.mainloop()

ScoutingForm().run()

At events, scouts need to know which match is next, who they're playing against, and how much time they have. A simple TBA-powered schedule parser answers all of this.

## Fetch and Parse Match Schedule
\`\`\`python
import requests
import time
from datetime import datetime, timezone

API_KEY  = "your_tba_key"
HEADERS  = {"X-TBA-Auth-Key": API_KEY}
MY_TEAM  = "frc1234"
EVENT    = "2025casd"

def get_upcoming_matches():
    url = f"https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/{MY_TEAM}/event/{EVENT}/matches"
    resp = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=5)
    if resp.status_code != 200:
        return []

    matches = resp.json()
    now = time.time()

    upcoming = [
        m for m in matches
        if m.get("predicted_time") and m["predicted_time"] > now
        and m["comp_level"] == "qm"
    ]
    upcoming.sort(key=lambda m: m["predicted_time"])
    return upcoming

def print_schedule(matches):
    print(f"\\n{'Match':<8} {'Time':>10}  {'Countdown':>12}  Alliance")
    print("â”€" * 55)
    now = time.time()
    for m in matches[:5]:   # next 5 matches
        t   = m["predicted_time"]
        num = m["match_number"]
        mins_away = int((t - now) / 60)

        # Find which alliance our team is on
        alliances = m["alliances"]
        for color in ["red", "blue"]:
            if MY_TEAM in alliances[color]["team_keys"]:
                partners  = [t for t in alliances[color]["team_keys"] if t != MY_TEAM]
                opponents = alliances["blue" if color=="red" else "red"]["team_keys"]
                dt_str = datetime.fromtimestamp(t).strftime("%I:%M %p")
                print(f"QM {num:<5} {dt_str:>10}  {mins_away:>9} min  "
                      f"{color.upper()} w/ {', '.join(partners)}")

matches = get_upcoming_matches()
print_schedule(matches)
\`\`\`

## Auto-Refreshing Schedule (Runs Every 2 Minutes)
\`\`\`python
import threading

def schedule_loop():
    while True:
        matches = get_upcoming_matches()
        print("\\033[2J\\033[H")  # clear terminal
        print_schedule(matches)
        time.sleep(120)  # refresh every 2 minutes

t = threading.Thread(target=schedule_loop, daemon=True)
t.start()
input("Press Enter to stop...\\n")

      {id:"pa_picklist",title:"Automated Pick List Generator in Python",est:"30 min",content:`## Turning Scouting Data into a Ranked Pick List
Your scouts collected 200 match records. Now what? This script turns raw CSV data into a ranked pick list with adjustable weights, consistency scores, and a printable output.

## Data Loading & Cleaning
\`\`\`python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv("scout_data.csv")

# Normalize climb level: None=0, L1=10, L2=20, L3=30
climb_map = {"None": 0, "L1": 10, "L2": 20, "L3": 30}
df["climb_pts"] = df["climb"].map(climb_map).fillna(0)

# Estimate contribution per match
df["contribution"] = (df["auto"]
                    + df["cycles"] * 4   # 4 pts per cycle (adjust per game)
                    + df["climb_pts"])

# Flag: did robot get a major penalty this match?
df["had_penalty"] = df["penalties"] > 0
\`\`\`

## Per-Team Statistics
\`\`\`python
def team_stats(df):
    stats = df.groupby("team").agg(
        matches     = ("contribution", "count"),
        avg_contrib = ("contribution", "mean"),
        std_contrib = ("contribution", "std"),
        max_contrib = ("contribution", "max"),
        avg_auto    = ("auto",         "mean"),
        avg_cycles  = ("cycles",       "mean"),
        climb_rate  = ("climb_pts",    lambda x: (x > 0).mean()),   # % of matches climbed
        penalty_rate= ("had_penalty",  "mean"),                     # % with penalties
    ).reset_index()

    # Consistency score: lower std relative to mean = more consistent
    stats["consistency"] = 1 / (1 + stats["std_contrib"] / (stats["avg_contrib"] + 1))

    return stats.round(2)

stats = team_stats(df)
\`\`\`

## Weighted Ranking
\`\`\`python
def rank_teams(stats, weights=None):
    if weights is None:
        weights = {
            "avg_contrib":  0.35,
            "consistency":  0.25,
            "avg_auto":     0.20,
            "climb_rate":   0.15,
            "penalty_rate": -0.05,  # negative: penalize teams that foul
        }

    from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler
    scaler = MinMaxScaler()

    metrics = list(weights.keys())
    scaled  = scaler.fit_transform(stats[metrics])
    scaled_df = pd.DataFrame(scaled, columns=metrics)

    stats["rank_score"] = sum(
        scaled_df[m] * w for m, w in weights.items()
    )
    return stats.sort_values("rank_score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

ranked = rank_teams(stats)
\`\`\`

    for i, row in ranked.head(top_n).iterrows():
        flag = " âš ï¸" if row["penalty_rate"] > 0.2 else ""
        print(f"{i+1:<5} {int(row['team']):<8} "

print_picklist(ranked)

      {id:"mb_hardware",title:"COTS Hardware â€” REV & GoBILDA Systems",est:"14 min",content:`## What is COTS Hardware?
COTS = Commercial Off-The-Shelf. REV Robotics and GoBILDA make modular hardware systems designed specifically for FTC. Understanding their systems saves enormous design and build time.

## REV Robotics Ecosystem
\`\`\`
Structural:
  15mm aluminum extrusion â€” the backbone of most FTC robots
  45Â° and 90Â° brackets, channel connectors
  M3 bolts throughout â€” standardized fastener size

Motion:
  HD Hex Motor (40:1, 20:1 options)
  Core Hex Motor (72:1, torquier)
  Smart Robot Servo (programmable range and speed)
  Hex shaft system (5mm hex, 8mm hex)

Electronics:
  Control Hub (Android, runs OpModes)
  Expansion Hub (adds 4 more motor ports)
  Servo Power Module (higher servo current)
\`\`\`

## GoBILDA Ecosystem
\`\`\`
Structural:
  U-channel â€” stronger than REV extrusion for load-bearing
  GoRAIL â€” linear slide system
  Pattern plate â€” grid-hole aluminum sheets

Motion:
  5202 series motors (multiple gear ratios)
  Servos (standard, speed, torque options)
  Hyper Hub â€” connects to pattern screws and hex shaft
  Aluminum and steel hex shaft

Key benefit: GoBILDA parts have consistent 8mm hex shaft across motors,
             hubs, and accessories â€” everything mates to everything

      {id:"ma_weight_reduction",title:"Weight Reduction Strategies",est:"20 min",content:`## Why Weight Matters
FTC limit is 42 lbs (~19 kg). FRC has no weight limit but heavier robots drain batteries faster, accelerate slower, and stress drivetrain components more. Weight reduction is always worth engineering time.

## Pocketing â€” Removing Interior Material
\`\`\`
Pocketing = cutting holes or recesses in structural plates
            where stress is low (not at mounting holes or load paths)

How to do it safely:
  1. Sketch the part in CAD
  2. Run FEA (or estimate by hand) to find low-stress regions
  3. Cut pockets that follow the stress flow lines (like ribs on a leaf)
  4. Leave a "web" of material between pockets (typically 3-5mm wall thickness)
  5. Never pocket within 6mm of a bolt hole or edge

Weight savings: 20-40% on aluminum plates, with minimal strength loss
\`\`\`

## Material Substitution
\`\`\`
Replace:             With:              Weight saving:
6061 Aluminum plate  Carbon fiber sheet  50% lighter
Steel bolts          Aluminum bolts      ~66% lighter (non-structural only)
Solid polycarbonate  Polycarbonate tubing  40% lighter
3D PLA bracket       3D PETG + pockets    Comparable, tougher
Solid aluminum rod   Aluminum tube (wall 1/16")  70% lighter
\`\`\`

## 3D Printing for Weight Reduction
\`\`\`python
# Infill density vs weight vs strength (FDM):
# 15% Gyroid infill:  light, good multi-directional strength (non-load-bearing)
# 40% Gyroid infill:  medium, good for most FTC brackets
# 80% infill:         heavy, use only for high-stress areas (motor mount cores)
# 100% infill:        very heavy, rarely needed â€” use metal instead

# Gyroid infill is better than rectilinear for the same density:
#   Rectilinear = strong in axis direction only
#   Gyroid      = uniform strength in all directions
\`\`\`

## The Weight Budget Process
\`\`\`
Step 1: List every component with its weight (most have specs online)
Step 2: Add up â€” are you over or under limit?
Step 3: Find the heaviest unnecessary components
Step 4: Apply pocketing, substitution, or removal

Example weight budget (FTC):
  Drive chassis + motors:   5.0 lbs
  Linear slide + arm motor: 2.5 lbs
  Battery + electronics:    3.5 lbs
  Frame + fasteners:        3.0 lbs
  Scoring mechanism:        2.0 lbs
  â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
  Total:                   16.0 lbs  â† well under 42 lb limit
  Margin for additions:    26.0 lbs  â† comfortable
\`\`\`

## What NOT to Lightweight
\`\`\`
âŒ Drive motor mounts (high vibration and torque)
âŒ Pivot points (concentrated stress)
âŒ Battery mounting (impact during matches)
âŒ Anything where failure = match-ending

        {q:"Why is Gyroid infill pattern preferred over Rectilinear for 3D-printed structural parts?",opts:["Gyroid prints faster","Gyroid provides approximately equal strength in all directions, while Rectilinear is strongest along the print axis only â€” better for parts loaded in unpredictable directions","Gyroid uses less filament","Rectilinear is only for decorative parts"],ans:1},
        {q:"Which components should NEVER be lightweighted by removing material?",opts:["All components can be pocketed if done carefully","High-stress points like drive motor mounts, pivot points, and battery mounts â€” failure in these areas during a match is catastrophic and likely match-ending","Only FRC components cannot be lightweighted","Components over 1 lb"],ans:1},

      {id:"eb_motors2",title:"Choosing the Right Motor",est:"13 min",content:`## Motor Specs You Must Understand
Picking a motor by brand name or what other teams use works until it doesn't. Know the specs to make intentional choices.

## Key Specs
\`\`\`
Free Speed (RPM):    Speed with no load. Higher = faster at zero torque.
Stall Torque (NÂ·m): Maximum torque at zero speed. Higher = more force.
Stall Current (A):  Current when shaft is held still. Very high â€” avoid prolonged stall.
Free Current (A):   Current at free speed. This is your baseline draw.
Power (W):          Free speed Ã— stall torque / 4 â‰ˆ peak mechanical power

The speed-torque tradeoff:
  Fast motors (high RPM):  Good for intakes, flywheels, drive (with reduction)
  Slow motors (high torque): Good for arms, lifts, slow precise mechanisms
\`\`\`

## FTC Motor Comparison
| Motor | Free Speed | Stall Torque | Use Case |
|-------|-----------|--------------|----------|
| GoBILDA 312 RPM | 312 RPM | 9.2 NÂ·cm | Drive, intakes |
| GoBILDA 435 RPM | 435 RPM | 6.6 NÂ·cm | Drive (fast) |
| GoBILDA 60 RPM | 60 RPM | 45 NÂ·cm | Lifts, arms |
| REV HD Hex 40:1 | 150 RPM | 25 NÂ·cm | Arms, elevators |
| REV Core Hex | 125 RPM | 34 NÂ·cm | Heavy lifts |

## FRC Motor Comparison
| Motor | Free Speed | Stall Torque | Use Case |
|-------|-----------|--------------|----------|
| NEO (REV) | 5676 RPM | 2.6 NÂ·m | Drive, most mechanisms |
| NEO 550 (REV) | 11000 RPM | 0.97 NÂ·m | Small, fast mechanisms |
| Falcon 500 (CTRE) | 6380 RPM | 4.69 NÂ·m | High-power drive |
| Kraken X60 (CTRE) | 6000 RPM | 9.37 NÂ·m | Most powerful FRC motor |

## Choosing a Motor: The Two Questions
\`\`\`
Q1: What output speed do I need?
    â†’ Calculate from gear ratio: output RPM = motor RPM / ratio

Q2: What torque do I need?
    â†’ Calculate from load: torque = force Ã— moment arm

Example: Arm needs to hold 2 lbs at 12 inches (=24 inÂ·lb = 2.7 NÂ·m)
  GoBILDA 60 RPM stall torque = 45 NÂ·cm = 0.45 NÂ·m â€” NOT enough!
  Need a gearbox: 2.7 / 0.45 = 6:1 minimum additional reduction
  Or use REV HD Hex 40:1: 25 NÂ·cm = 0.25 NÂ·m â†’ need 11:1 additional
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What does 'stall torque' mean and why is prolonged stall dangerous?",opts:["The torque needed to stop the motor","Maximum torque the motor can produce at zero speed â€” prolonged stall draws maximum current (stall current), which overheats the motor and windings","The torque at free speed","Stall is safe for most motors"],ans:1},
        {q:"If your arm needs 2.7 NÂ·m and your motor produces 0.45 NÂ·m, what minimum gear reduction is needed?",opts:["2.7 : 1","6 : 1 â€” divide the required torque by the motor torque: 2.7 / 0.45 = 6","0.45 : 1","No reduction needed"],ans:1},
        {q:"What type of motor is best suited for a high-speed intake roller in FTC?",opts:["A low-RPM high-torque motor like GoBILDA 60 RPM","A high-RPM motor like GoBILDA 312 or 435 RPM â€” intakes need speed to grab game pieces quickly, not high torque","The REV Core Hex motor","Any motor at full power"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"ei_wiring_practice",title:"Competition Wiring Standards",est:"16 min",content:`## Wiring That Survives Competition
A robot that works perfectly at practice can fail at competition from wiring issues alone â€” connectors pulling out under vibration, shorts from exposed wire, or cables caught in mechanisms. These standards prevent it.

## The Competition Wiring Checklist
\`\`\`
BEFORE leaving for competition, verify:

Mechanical security:
â–¡ Every connector fully seated and locked (push and tug each one)
â–¡ All wire runs secured with zip ties every 4-6 inches
â–¡ No wire routed across a moving mechanism (arm, slide, chain)
â–¡ Battery connector seated and retention clip locked
â–¡ Control Hub / roboRIO mounting screws tight

Wire management:
â–¡ Wires have service loops at connectors (2-3 inches of slack)
   â†’ Prevents tension on connector â€” a pulled wire is a dead robot
â–¡ All exposed wire ends covered (heat shrink or tape)
â–¡ No bare wire within 10mm of a dissimilar-polarity wire
â–¡ Wiring harness labeled at each end (use label maker or marker)

Electrical:
â–¡ All motor port connections tight at the Control Hub
â–¡ No reversed motor polarity (check before first full run, not at competition)
â–¡ Voltage sensor reads 12.5V+ at rest with fresh battery
\`\`\`

## Service Loops â€” The Most Ignored Rule
\`\`\`
A "service loop" is extra wire length at every connection point.

Without service loop:
  Connector pulls taut under chassis flex â†’ intermittent disconnection
  Robot jostled during transport â†’ wire stressed at crimp â†’ fails

With service loop:
  Wire has 2-3" of slack before connector
  Robot can flex, jostle, and vibrate without putting tension on connectors

How much slack? Enough that you can move the mating parts
through their full range of motion with the wire connected.
On a moving mechanism (arm pivot): 6-8" of slack needed.
\`\`\`

## Cable Routing for Moving Mechanisms
\`\`\`
Challenge: A cable attached to a moving arm must travel with the arm
           without getting caught, cut, or tensioned.

Options:
  Cable chain (energy chain): Best â€” contains and guides cables
  Spiral wrap: Loops of wire follow the arc of motion
  Drag chain: Flat links guide cables on linear slides

Rules:
  Route cables through the CENTER of rotation when possible
  (If cable exits at the pivot point, it doesn't move as the arm rotates)
  Never run a taut cable at max extension â€” it will fail
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is a 'service loop' in robot wiring and why is it essential?",opts:["An extra battery for backup","2-3 inches of extra wire length at every connector â€” absorbs chassis flex and transport vibration so the connector itself is never under tension","A diagnostic loop test","A backup wiring path"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the best practice for routing cables on a rotating arm mechanism?",opts:["Route cables along the outside of the arm","Route cables through or near the pivot center â€” cables exiting at the pivot point move minimally as the arm rotates, preventing tangling and stress","Use wireless signals for arm sensors","Tie cables tightly to prevent movement"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must every connector be both pushed fully seated AND tug-tested before competition?",opts:["Competition rules require it","Connectors can appear seated but be held by only the outer housing â€” a firm tug reveals whether the contact is actually engaged before a match rather than during one","Tug tests set the wire length","Seated connectors need no further checking"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"si_defense",title:"Playing and Countering Defense",est:"17 min",content:`## Defense is a Legitimate Strategy
Many teams treat defense as unsportsmanlike. It isn't â€” it's explicitly allowed and often the highest-value action an alliance can take when their offensive robot is underperforming.

## When to Play Defense
\`\`\`
Play defense when:
  âœ… Your opponent has a scorer significantly better than you
  âœ… The game penalizes hoarding or zone control â€” defense disrupts that
  âœ… Your own robot's offensive contribution < what defense prevents
  âœ… Your alliance partner is strong enough to carry offense alone

Mathematical check:
  If opponent top scorer averages 30 pts/match
  And your robot averages 20 pts/match
  And you can reduce their scorer to 15 pts:
  Defense value = 30 - 15 = 15 pts prevented
  Offense value = 20 pts scored
  â†’ Play offense! (20 > 15)
  But if opponent scores 45, you score 20, defense cuts them to 20:
  Defense value = 45 - 20 = 25 pts prevented > 20 â†’ play defense
\`\`\`

## Effective Defensive Techniques
\`\`\`
Legal defense approaches (always check the game manual):
  â†’ Shadow the opponent's scorer â€” stay between them and their scoring zone
  â†’ Deny game piece access â€” legally block pickup positions
  â†’ Slow their cycle â€” don't need to stop them, just slow them

Robot design for defense:
  âœ… Low center of gravity â€” hard to tip
  âœ… Wide wheelbase â€” stable under pushing
  âœ… Rounded bumpers â€” deflects instead of interlocking
  âœ… Mecanum or swerve â€” can match opponent heading easily
\`\`\`

## Countering Defense Against You
\`\`\`
When being defended:
  â†’ Change direction quickly â€” mecanums are harder to follow than tank drive
  â†’ Score lower-value targets that defenders ignore (small pts are free)
  â†’ Communicate to your driver: "Defender is on your left"
  â†’ Use your alliance partner to draw the defender away

Robot design to be defense-resistant:
  âœ… Low bumper profile â€” hard to get under
  âœ… Protected game piece storage â€” pieces can't be knocked out
  âœ… Wide grip intake â€” picks up pieces quickly under pressure
  âœ… Fast drive acceleration â€” create separation quickly
\`\`\`

## Defense Foul Awareness
\`\`\`
Before playing defense, read the relevant G-codes carefully:
  G205 (FRC): Initiating contact with an opponent in their protected zone
  G206 (FRC): Pinning an opponent for more than 5 seconds
  G207 (FRC): Tripping or tipping an opponent

A major foul during defense often costs MORE than your defense prevented.
Rule: If uncertain whether an action is legal â†’ don't do it.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Using the mathematical framework, when is playing defense more valuable than playing offense?",opts:["Defense is always better","When the points your defense prevents (opponent's current average minus defended average) exceed the points your robot would score offensively","Whenever your robot is losing","Only in elimination matches"],ans:1},
        {q:"What design feature makes a robot most resistant to being defended?",opts:["Tall frame for visibility","Fast acceleration combined with mecanum/swerve mobility â€” allows the robot to create separation and change direction quickly before a defender can match heading","Heavy robot for stability","Large bumpers"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must you read the G-code penalties before playing defense at a specific event?",opts:["G-codes are optional","Foul rules vary by game year â€” certain defensive actions that were legal last season may trigger major penalties this season, costing more than the defense prevented","Defense never causes fouls","G-codes only apply to offensive robots"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"sa_auto_strategy",title:"Autonomous Strategy & Reliability Engineering",est:"22 min",content:`## The Most Undervalued Phase
Teams spend 80% of their time on TeleOp and 20% on Auto. In competition, a reliable autonomous can swing 20-30 points per match and determines seeding rankings. Flip the time investment.

## Reliability is More Valuable Than Max Points
\`\`\`
Scenario: Your auto can score 22 points but works 60% of the time.
          A simpler auto scores 10 points and works 95% of the time.

Expected value:
  Complex: 22 Ã— 0.60 = 13.2 expected points
  Simple:  10 Ã— 0.95 = 9.5 expected points
  â†’ Complex is better here (13.2 > 9.5)

But change failure to 40%:
  Complex: 22 Ã— 0.60 = 13.2 pts  (but also: 0 pts 40% of the time!)
  And add consistency to tiebreakers â†’ high variance hurts you more.

Rule of thumb: Don't run a complex auto until it succeeds 9/10 times in testing.
\`\`\`

## The Autonomous Reliability Stack
\`\`\`
Level 1 â€” Encoder-only auto (simplest):
  Hardcoded distances, no sensor feedback
  Fails when: battery low, field surface different, wheel slip
  Reliability: 70-80% on consistent fields

Level 2 â€” Encoder + IMU heading correction:
  Drive uses heading PID to go straight
  Fails when: encoder slip is lateral (mecanum)
  Reliability: 85-90%

Level 3 â€” Encoder + IMU + distance sensor checkpoints:
  Verify position at key waypoints, correct if off
  Fails when: sensor interference, objects in path
  Reliability: 90-95%

Level 4 â€” Full odometry + vision resets:
  Continuous position tracking + AprilTag correction
  Fails rarely â€” most robust autonomous architecture
  Reliability: 95%+
\`\`\`

## Autonomous Test Protocol
\`\`\`
Before calling an auto "done":
  â–¡ 10 consecutive successful runs on practice field
  â–¡ 10 runs with battery at 50% charge (tests voltage sag behavior)
  â–¡ 10 runs from each valid starting position
  â–¡ 5 runs with a distraction (someone walking nearby, noise)
  â–¡ Test on a different field tile material if possible

At competition:
  â–¡ Run auto on actual competition field during practice match
  â–¡ Check for field surface differences vs practice
  â–¡ Run backup (simpler) auto first in qual 1 if unsure
\`\`\`

## Alliance Auto Conflict Resolution
\`\`\`
Two robots targeting the same game pieces = collision.
Before each elimination match:
  1. Each robot describes their auto starting zone and first 3 actions
  2. Identify conflicts (same zone, same game piece)
  3. Designate one robot as "primary scorer", other as "secondary scorer"
  4. Secondary robot either starts 0.5 sec delayed OR uses a different path
  5. Practice the joint auto at least once if possible
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"According to the reliability framework, when is a complex autonomous ready to compete?",opts:["As soon as it works once","When it succeeds in 9 out of 10 consecutive test runs â€” lower reliability means your expected points may not justify the risk of frequent failures","When the programmer says it's done","After passing robot inspection"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the most important upgrade from Level 1 to Level 2 in the autonomous reliability stack?",opts:["Adding more game piece scoring","Adding IMU heading correction â€” a gyroscope-guided straight-line drive prevents the gradual heading drift that causes encoder-only autos to miss targets","Faster drive speed","Adding a camera"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should you run autonomous on battery at 50% charge during testing?",opts:["It simulates the last match of the day","Motor speed varies with voltage â€” an auto tuned on a full battery may undershoot distances on a depleted battery; testing at reduced voltage reveals this before competition","50% is the competition battery level","To save battery life"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"sfa_inspection",title:"FRC/FTC Robot Inspection â€” Safety Perspective",est:"15 min",content:`## Inspection Is Safety Enforcement
Robot inspection at FIRST events isn't bureaucratic â€” inspectors are verifying that your robot won't injure other robots, the field, or people. Failing inspection means you don't compete until it's fixed.

## FTC Inspection Checklist (Key Safety Items)
\`\`\`
Size & Weight:
â–¡ Starting configuration fits 18"Ã—18"Ã—18" cube
â–¡ Weight â‰¤ 42 lbs (19 kg)

Electrical:
â–¡ Main power switch accessible and labeled
â–¡ All wiring covered or protected (no exposed live conductors)
â–¡ Battery secured (won't fall during match)
â–¡ REV Control Hub or Expansion Hub (no unapproved electronics)

Mechanical:
â–¡ No sharp protrusions that could puncture field perimeter
â–¡ All moving parts contained within robot's footprint when starting
â–¡ Bumper material (if required) per game specs

Software:
â–¡ Robot operates only from Driver Hub (no autonomous during teleop unless allowed)
â–¡ No external networking devices
\`\`\`

## FRC Inspection Checklist (Key Safety Items)
\`\`\`
Frame & Bumpers:
â–¡ Frame perimeter â‰¤ 120" (typical)
â–¡ Bumpers correct height (7.5"â€“10.5" from floor in most years)
â–¡ Bumper pool noodle intact and pool noodle core solid
â–¡ Team number on all bumper panels (all 4 sides)

Electrical:
â–¡ Main breaker accessible and labeled
â–¡ All wiring meets AWG minimums for current-carrying capacity
â–¡ No exposed connectors or uninsulated wire runs
â–¡ RSL (Robot Signal Light) functional and unobstructed

Pneumatics (if used):
â–¡ Working pressure â‰¤ 60 PSI (downstream of regulator)
â–¡ Storage pressure â‰¤ 120 PSI
â–¡ All fittings leak-tested (use soap bubble test)
â–¡ Relief valve functional
\`\`\`

## Common Inspection Failures & How to Prevent Them
\`\`\`
Failure: Robot slightly over 18" in a dimension
Fix: Measure before every event â€” components shift after transport

Failure: Bumpers wrong height
Fix: Measure bumper bottom from actual ground with robot assembled, not from CAD

Failure: Wiring has exposed conductors
Fix: Heat shrink ALL crimp terminals before you leave the shop

Failure: Battery falls out during tip test
Fix: Add a retention strap or second mounting point

Failure: Sharp aluminum edges on frame
Fix: Deburr all cut edges before the event â€” file + sandpaper
\`\`\`

## Re-Inspection After Modifications
\`\`\`
Any significant change between matches requires re-inspection:
  â†’ Adding a mechanism that changes starting size
  â†’ Replacing a structural component
  â†’ Significant wiring changes

Ask an inspector if you're unsure â€” they would rather advise you
than discover a violation that pulls you from a match.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the purpose of the tip test during FRC/FTC robot inspection?",opts:["To test driver skill","To verify the battery is securely mounted â€” an unsecured battery that falls during a match can short, start a fire, or cause electrical failure","To check bumper height","To test the main power switch"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should you re-inspect with an inspector after making significant changes between matches?",opts:["It's required for all changes","Changes that affect size, weight, or safety-critical systems may bring the robot out of compliance â€” proactive re-inspection prevents disqualification during a match","Re-inspection is optional","Inspectors only check robots once per event"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the easiest way to prevent 'exposed conductor' inspection failures?",opts:["Use thicker wire","Apply heat shrink tubing to ALL crimp terminals before leaving the shop â€” if it becomes a standard practice, you'll never fail this inspection item","Only inspect power wires","Use electrical tape instead"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"tma_leadership",title:"Leading a FIRST Team â€” Student Leadership",est:"18 min",content:`## The Difference Between a Title and Leadership
Many teams have a "team captain" who issues orders. High-performing FIRST teams have student leaders who create the conditions for everyone to do their best work. These are different skills.

## The Leader's Primary Responsibilities
\`\`\`
1. Clarity: Does everyone know what to do when they arrive?
   â†’ Post task boards, assign roles, communicate priorities

2. Momentum: Is the team making progress or spinning wheels?
   â†’ Identify blockers fast, make decisions when the team is stuck,
     know when to escalate to a mentor and when to handle it yourself

3. Culture: Do people feel respected, included, and valued?
   â†’ Set the tone â€” how you treat the quietest member determines the culture
   â†’ Correct problems privately; celebrate wins publicly

4. Communication: Are the right people informed?
   â†’ Mentors know status without having to ask
   â†’ Parents know when events are happening
   â†’ Team members know the plan for next meeting
\`\`\`

## Giving Effective Feedback
\`\`\`
SBI Model: Situation â†’ Behavior â†’ Impact

Situation: "During last Tuesday's build session..."
Behavior:  "...you left the drill press without deburring the work piece."
Impact:    "...the next person to pick it up got cut on the edge."

NOT: "You're careless with tools." (vague, personal attack)
NOT: "Try to be more careful." (vague, no action)

Good feedback:
  â†’ Is specific (situation and behavior)
  â†’ Focuses on the behavior, not the person
  â†’ Describes the actual impact
  â†’ Suggests the corrected behavior: "Next time, deburr before leaving the press"
\`\`\`

## Handling Conflict Between Members
\`\`\`
Step 1: Hear both sides separately (don't mediate a group argument)
Step 2: Find the legitimate concern on each side (there almost always is one)
Step 3: Separate the people from the problem
   "We disagree about which mechanism to build"
   vs. "Marcus and Sara hate each other"
   The first is solvable. Address the first.
Step 4: Propose a decision process, not a solution
   "Let's prototype both and decide by Friday's results"
Step 5: Follow through â€” check in after the decision is made
\`\`\`

## Student Leader Limits
\`\`\`
Know when to involve a mentor:
  â†’ Safety concerns (always immediate)
  â†’ Personal conflicts that you can't resolve in two attempts
  â†’ Budget decisions over a threshold your mentor set
  â†’ A member in distress (mental health, family crisis)

Students lead; mentors support and backstop.
The goal is a team that can function well even if the mentor is absent.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Using the SBI model, what is wrong with feedback like 'You're careless with tools'?",opts:["It's too long","It attacks the person's character rather than describing a specific behavior and its impact â€” it provides no actionable correction and damages the relationship","It should be given in public","It doesn't mention the mentor"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the first step when two team members are in conflict?",opts:["Call a full team meeting","Hear each person separately â€” group mediations escalate emotions; understanding each side's legitimate concern is easier in private","Ask the mentor to decide","Ignore it and focus on the robot"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the key principle of 'separating people from the problem' in conflict resolution?",opts:["Removing conflicting members from the team","Framing the conflict as a solvable technical or process disagreement rather than a personality clash â€” 'which design is better' is solvable; 'who is right' is not","Having only one person solve the problem","Assigning blame to resolve conflict"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"cada_fea",title:"Intro to FEA in Onshape & Fusion 360",est:"22 min",content:`## What is FEA?
Finite Element Analysis (FEA) splits a part into thousands of tiny elements and simulates how stress, deformation, and failure propagate through it under load. It's how engineers predict whether parts will break before building them.

## When to Use FEA on a Robot Part
\`\`\`
FEA is worth the effort when:
  âœ… You're designing a custom gearbox housing
  âœ… A mechanism failed in testing and you want to know why
  âœ… You're lightweighting a structural part and need confidence
  âœ… A load path is unclear from geometry alone

Skip FEA when:
  âŒ Using COTS parts (already validated by manufacturer)
  âŒ Clearly over-designed brackets (obvious overkill)
  âŒ Quick prototypes meant to be iterated
\`\`\`

## Running a Simple FEA in Onshape (SimScale Integration)
\`\`\`
1. Design part in Onshape Part Studio
2. Open the SimScale app from the Onshape App Store (free tier available)
3. Set material: 6061 Aluminum (E=69 GPa, yield strength=270 MPa)
4. Apply fixtures: select bolt hole faces â†’ Fixed Support
5. Apply loads: select load face â†’ Force â†’ enter value in N
   (Convert lbs to N: 1 lb = 4.45 N)
6. Mesh: use Automatic fine mesh
7. Run simulation â†’ view stress map

Interpret results:
  Red zones  â†’ highest stress (check against yield strength)
  Blue zones â†’ low stress (pocketing candidates)
  If max stress < 0.6 Ã— yield strength: part is safe with 1.67Ã— safety factor
\`\`\`

## Hand Calculation vs FEA
\`\`\`
You don't always need FEA. For simple beams, use these:

Cantilever beam (arm protruding from pivot):
  Max stress = M Ã— c / I
  M = moment = Force Ã— arm length
  c = distance from neutral axis to outer fiber
  I = moment of inertia (depends on cross section)

For a 1" Ã— 0.25" aluminum bar, 8" long, 2 lb force at tip:
  M = 2 lbs Ã— 8" = 16 lbÂ·in
  c = 0.125" (half of 0.25" height)
  I = (1 Ã— 0.25Â³) / 12 = 0.00130 inâ´
  Ïƒ = 16 Ã— 0.125 / 0.00130 = 1538 psi

6061-T6 yield strength = 40,000 psi â†’ Safety factor = 26Ã— â€” over-designed!
Could reduce to 0.125" thick â†’ safety factor still 13Ã— â†’ save weight
\`\`\`

## Reading an FEA Stress Map
\`\`\`
Von Mises stress is the common output:
  Green / blue: stress well below yield â†’ safe
  Yellow / orange: approaching yield â†’ add material or redesign
  Red: exceeding yield â†’ WILL FAIL under this load

Safety factor targets for robots:
  Static loads (arm holding position): 2Ã— minimum
  Dynamic loads (arm moving fast):     3-4Ã— minimum  
  Impact loads (game piece catch):     5Ã— minimum
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What does a red zone in an FEA stress map indicate?",opts:["The part is well-designed there","Stress is exceeding or approaching the material's yield strength â€” the part will permanently deform or fail under this load in that region","Red indicates maximum stiffness","Temperature distribution"],ans:1},
        {q:"What are blue zones in an FEA stress map useful for?",opts:["They indicate failure points","Low-stress regions â€” candidates for pocketing or material removal during weight reduction without compromising structural integrity","They show where bolts should go","They indicate the center of mass"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is a higher safety factor required for impact loads compared to static loads?",opts:["Static loads don't need safety factors","Impact loads are brief but generate forces 3-5Ã— the average load â€” a part safe under steady force can still fail instantly under a spike load if the safety margin is too low","Impact is always less than static","The game manual requires it"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

  awards: {
    Advanced: [
      {id:"awa_sustainability",title:"Building Sustainable Award-Winning Programs",est:"20 min",content:`## The Graduation Problem
Most FIRST teams rebuild their outreach and awards programs every year because the graduating seniors take all the institutional knowledge with them. Top award-winning teams don't â€” they build systems that outlast any individual.

## The Succession Planning Mindset
\`\`\`
Every program, role, and responsibility needs:
  1. A current lead (does the work now)
  2. A shadow (learning the role)
  3. Written documentation (survives both of them leaving)

Example â€” Impact Award submission:
  Year 1: Senior writes it with mentor guidance
  Year 2: Junior co-writes it with senior â†’ becomes the expert
  Year 3: Former junior (now senior) writes it â†’ trains new junior
  
Result: Submission quality improves every year because knowledge compounds.
\`\`\`

## Documentation That Survives Turnover
\`\`\`
What to document (team Google Drive, always updated):
  â†’ Contact list for every sponsor (name, email, giving amount, renewal month)
  â†’ Outreach partner contact list (school principal, librarian, event coordinator)
  â†’ Grant application history (what was applied to, result, renewal date)
  â†’ "How we do X" guides for every repeating process

What NOT to do:
  âŒ Storing contacts only in a graduating member's phone
  âŒ "I'll send you the sponsor list before I leave"
  âŒ Undocumented relationships: "Call Jamie â€” she knows"
\`\`\`

## Compounding Impact Over Multiple Years
\`\`\`
Year 1: Start 1 FLL team (12 students)
Year 2: Those students inspire 2 new teams (24 students) + your 1 ongoing
Year 3: 3 teams active, some students move to FTC â†’ 2 new FTC teams
Year 5: Your original outreach ecosystem involves 150+ students annually

This is the "long game" judges at World Championship see in winning Impact Award teams.
No single event creates this â€” sustained investment over years does.
\`\`\`

## Program Health Metrics (Review Annually)
\`\`\`
  â†’ # of programs that ran without graduating seniors driving them
  â†’ # of new programs started by current members (not alumni)
  â†’ Sponsor renewal rate (>80% = healthy)
  â†’ # of students in FIRST teams you started (cumulative)
  â†’ Outreach attendance trend (growing, stable, or shrinking?)

If any metric is declining â†’ diagnose before it becomes a crisis.
\`\`\`

## The Letter to Future Members
One high-impact tradition: each graduating senior writes a letter to their future successor â€” what they learned, what they wish they'd known earlier, what they're most proud of, what still needs to be improved.
Collected over years, these letters become the team's living institutional memory.`,quiz:[

        {q:"What makes compounding outreach impact (starting 1 FLL team that spawns more teams) so valuable for awards?",opts:["It's easier to manage","It demonstrates the FIRST mission multiplier effect â€” exponential reach over time is exactly what World Championship judges look for in the most prestigious awards","FLL teams count more for awards","It reduces team workload"],ans:1},

      ]},

      {id:"ora_social",title:"Social Media & Digital Outreach Strategy",est:"16 min",content:`## Why Digital Outreach Counts
Judges for Inspire and Impact Awards look for reach beyond your immediate community. A team that documents its journey publicly â€” and does it well â€” reaches students who will never attend one of your events.

## Platform Strategy for FIRST Teams
\`\`\`
Instagram / TikTok: Best for visual content â€” mechanism reveals, match highlights
  â†’ Best content: 30-60 sec build clips, side-by-side mechanism tests, match day
  â†’ Post frequency: 3-5x per week during build season
  â†’ Audience: Students, parents, potential sponsors, other FIRST teams

YouTube: Best for long-form documentation
  â†’ Best content: Full robot reveal, full match recordings, tutorial series
  â†’ Post frequency: Weekly during season, monthly off-season
  â†’ Audience: Recruits, sponsors needing proof of impact, judges

Twitter/X: Best for community and industry connection
  â†’ Use for: Engaging with FIRST HQ, FRC teams, engineering professionals
  â†’ Tag: @FIRSTRobotics, @REVRobotics, @GoBILDA, sponsors

LinkedIn: Best for sponsor and professional community
  â†’ Post your season recap, award wins, outreach
  â†’ Useful for connecting with local engineering professionals
\`\`\`

## Content That Performs Well
\`\`\`
High engagement content:
  âœ… "Before vs After" mechanism improvement clips
  âœ… "First run of the season" robot demo
  âœ… Behind-the-scenes: "How we built X in 4 days"
  âœ… Team member spotlights: "Meet [Name], our lead programmer"
  âœ… Competition day content: "We just won our first match!"
  âœ… Outreach impact: "12 kids who had never seen a robot â€” watch their reactions"

Low engagement content:
  âŒ Stock-photo style posed photos
  âŒ "We're excited for the season!" text posts
  âŒ Long text posts on visual platforms
  âŒ Posting only final results, never the journey
\`\`\`

## Measuring Digital Reach for Awards
\`\`\`
Track these for your awards essay:
  â†’ Total followers across platforms
  â†’ Post reach (impressions) for top 5 posts of the season
  â†’ # of students who reached out after seeing content
  â†’ # of teams that followed/messaged asking for advice

Report them specifically:
  "Our season documentary (YouTube) reached 1,240 views from 
   12 countries â€” we received 4 messages from students in areas
   with no FIRST teams asking how to start one."
\`\`\`

## Privacy & Safety Rules
\`\`\`
Always required:
  â†’ Parental permission before posting photos of minors
  â†’ Never post last names or school names of non-team students
  â†’ Get explicit permission before sharing a student's story

FIRST-specific:
  â†’ Check your school's social media policy
  â†’ Some districts require all content to be posted from a team account,
     not personal accounts of members

      {id:"gi_monorepo",title:"Organizing a FIRST Team Monorepo",est:"15 min",content:`## What is a Monorepo?
A monorepo stores all team code â€” robot OpModes, scouting tools, dashboard, and documentation â€” in a single repository. This simplifies onboarding, ensures everyone has everything, and avoids the "where's the scouting script?" problem.

## Recommended FTC Monorepo Structure
\`\`\`
team-1234/
â”œâ”€â”€ robot/                  â† FTC SDK project (your main robot code)
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ FtcRobotController/ â† Official SDK (don't modify)
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ TeamCode/
â”‚   â”‚   â””â”€â”€ src/main/java/.../teamcode/
â”‚   â”‚       â”œâ”€â”€ hardware/   â† RobotHardware, ArmSubsystem, etc.
â”‚   â”‚       â”œâ”€â”€ teleop/     â† TeleOp OpModes
â”‚   â”‚       â”œâ”€â”€ autonomous/ â† Autonomous OpModes
â”‚   â”‚       â””â”€â”€ utils/      â† Constants, PIDController, MathUtils
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ build.gradle
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ scouting/               â† Python scouting tools
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ scout_form.py       â† Tkinter input form
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ analyze.py          â† Pandas analysis + pick list
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ dashboard.py        â† Live match dashboard
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ requirements.txt    â† pip dependencies
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ data/               â† CSV files (add to .gitignore if sensitive)
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ docs/                   â† Team documentation
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ notebook/           â† Engineering notebook entries (Markdown)
â”‚   â”œâ”€â”€ wiring/             â† Pinout diagrams, wiring maps
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ onboarding/         â† New member guide
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ .github/
â”‚   â””â”€â”€ workflows/
â”‚       â””â”€â”€ build.yml       â† CI/CD build check
â”‚
â”œâ”€â”€ .gitignore              â† Combined FTC + Python gitignore
â””â”€â”€ README.md               â† Team info, setup instructions
\`\`\`

      {id:"jb_collections",title:"HashMaps & Sets for Robot Data",est:"13 min",content:`## Beyond Arrays and ArrayLists
Arrays and ArrayLists store ordered lists. HashMaps store keyâ†’value pairs. Sets store unique values. Both appear constantly in scouting tools, configuration, and telemetry systems.

## HashMap â€” Key to Value Lookups
\`\`\`java
import java.util.HashMap;

// Map hardware names to their calibrated zero offsets
HashMap<String, Double> servoOffsets = new HashMap<>();
servoOffsets.put("claw",    0.02);
servoOffsets.put("wrist",  -0.05);
servoOffsets.put("rotate",  0.00);

// Get a value:
double offset = servoOffsets.get("claw");          // 0.02
double safe   = servoOffsets.getOrDefault("elbow", 0.0); // returns 0.0 if missing

// Check if key exists:
if (servoOffsets.containsKey("claw")) {
    clawServo.setPosition(basePos + servoOffsets.get("claw"));
}

// Iterate all entries:
for (Map.Entry<String, Double> entry : servoOffsets.entrySet()) {
    telemetry.addData(entry.getKey(), "offset=%.3f", entry.getValue());
}
\`\`\`

## HashMap for State Machine Targets
\`\`\`java
// Map arm states to encoder tick targets â€” clean and extendable
HashMap<String, Integer> armTargets = new HashMap<>();
armTargets.put("STOWED",     0);
armTargets.put("INTAKE",   220);
armTargets.put("LOW_SCORE",750);
armTargets.put("HIGH_SCORE",1487);

// Set arm from current state string:
String currentState = "HIGH_SCORE";
if (armTargets.containsKey(currentState)) {
    arm.setTargetPosition(armTargets.get(currentState));
}
\`\`\`

## HashSet â€” Unique Values Only
\`\`\`java
import java.util.HashSet;

// Track which AprilTag IDs have been seen this auto
HashSet<Integer> seenTags = new HashSet<>();
seenTags.add(1);
seenTags.add(3);
seenTags.add(1); // duplicate â€” silently ignored

boolean sawTag3 = seenTags.contains(3); // true
int uniqueCount = seenTags.size();       // 2

// Use: avoid processing the same detection twice
for (AprilTagDetection det : detections) {
    if (!seenTags.contains(det.id)) {
        seenTags.add(det.id);
        processNewTag(det);
    }
}
\`\`\`

## When to Use Each Collection
| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Ordered list, index access | Array or ArrayList |
| Key â†’ value lookup | HashMap |
| Fast membership check | HashSet |
| Insertion order matters | LinkedHashMap |
| Sorted order | TreeMap / TreeSet |`,quiz:[
        {q:"What does getOrDefault(key, fallback) do on a HashMap?",opts:["Throws an exception if key is missing","Returns the value for key if it exists, or returns the fallback value if the key is not in the map â€” prevents NullPointerException on missing keys","Sets the default for all missing keys","Removes the key after getting it"],ans:1},
        {q:"If you add the same value to a HashSet twice, what happens?",opts:["An exception is thrown","The value is stored twice","The duplicate is silently ignored â€” Sets only store unique values by definition","The first value is replaced"],ans:2},
        {q:"Why is a HashMap better than a long if/else chain for mapping arm states to encoder targets?",opts:["HashMaps run faster","HashMap is data-driven â€” adding a new state means one .put() call with no code logic changes; an if/else chain requires editing conditional branches every time","if/else can't store ints","HashMap requires less memory"],ans:1},
      ]},
      {id:"jb_lambda",title:"Lambda Expressions & Functional Patterns",est:"13 min",content:`## What is a Lambda?
A lambda is a compact way to write a single-method function inline. In Java 8+, they make sorting, filtering, and callbacks much cleaner.

## Sorting with Lambda
\`\`\`java
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;

ArrayList<Double> powers = new ArrayList<>();
powers.add(0.8); powers.add(-0.5); powers.add(0.3);

// Old way (anonymous class):
Collections.sort(powers, new Comparator<Double>() {
    public int compare(Double a, Double b) { return Double.compare(Math.abs(b), Math.abs(a)); }
});

// Lambda way (same result, much shorter):
powers.sort((a, b) -> Double.compare(Math.abs(b), Math.abs(a)));
// Now sorted by absolute value descending: [0.8, -0.5, 0.3]
\`\`\`

## Runnable Lambda for Background Tasks
\`\`\`java
// Old way:
Thread t = new Thread(new Runnable() {
    public void run() { monitorBattery(); }
});

// Lambda way:
Thread t = new Thread(() -> monitorBattery());
t.setDaemon(true);
t.start();
\`\`\`

## Filtering a List
\`\`\`java
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.List;

List<Double> rawPowers = List.of(0.9, 0.04, -0.8, 0.01, 0.6);

// Keep only values above deadzone threshold:
List<Double> active = rawPowers.stream()
    .filter(p -> Math.abs(p) > 0.05)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
// active = [0.9, -0.8, 0.6]

// Transform all powers (scale by 0.7):
List<Double> scaled = rawPowers.stream()
    .map(p -> p * 0.7)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());
\`\`\`

## Practical: Find Max Sensor Reading
\`\`\`java
List<Double> distances = List.of(23.4, 15.1, 45.6, 8.9);

double min = distances.stream()
    .mapToDouble(Double::doubleValue)
    .min()
    .orElse(Double.MAX_VALUE);
// min = 8.9
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the main advantage of a lambda expression over an anonymous class?",opts:["Lambdas run faster","Lambdas express single-method implementations compactly inline â€” the same logic with far less boilerplate code","Lambdas require Java 11","Anonymous classes can't be used for sorting"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the .filter() stream operation do?",opts:["Modifies each element","Returns a new stream containing only the elements that satisfy the given predicate â€” elements that return false are excluded","Sorts the elements","Converts the stream to an array"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does .map() do in a stream pipeline?",opts:["Creates a HashMap","Transforms each element by applying a function to it, producing a new stream with the transformed values","Filters elements","Maps index to value like an array"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
