      {id:"ji_sparkmax",title:"Configuring SPARK MAX Motors (FRC)",est:"18 min",content:`## SPARK MAX â€” The Standard FRC Brushless Controller
The REV SPARK MAX controls NEO and NEO 550 brushless motors. Compared to older PWM controllers, it offers CAN feedback, integrated encoders, and onboard PID.

## Initial Setup
\`\`\`java
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkMax;
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkBase.IdleMode;
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkMaxLowLevel.MotorType;
import com.revrobotics.RelativeEncoder;
import com.revrobotics.SparkPIDController;

CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
motor.restoreFactoryDefaults(); // always do first â€” clears stale config

// Set idle mode:
motor.setIdleMode(IdleMode.kBrake);  // holds position when stopped
// motor.setIdleMode(IdleMode.kCoast); // freewheels â€” use for flywheels

// Current limits (protect motor):
motor.setSmartCurrentLimit(40); // 40A stall limit for NEO drive motors

// Invert direction if needed:
motor.setInverted(true);

// Burn to flash â€” config survives power cycle!
motor.burnFlash();
\`\`\`

## Reading the Built-In Encoder
\`\`\`java
RelativeEncoder encoder = motor.getEncoder();

double position = encoder.getPosition();    // rotations (default unit)
double velocity = encoder.getVelocity();    // RPM

// Convert to useful units:
// For a 4" wheel with 8.46:1 gearbox:
double wheelRotations = encoder.getPosition() / 8.46;
double distanceInches = wheelRotations * Math.PI * 4.0;

// Reset encoder:
encoder.setPosition(0);
\`\`\`

## Onboard PID Controller
\`\`\`java
SparkPIDController pid = motor.getPIDController();

// Set PIDF gains:
pid.setP(0.1);
pid.setI(0.0);
pid.setD(0.005);
pid.setFF(0.0);

// Output range (safety):
pid.setOutputRange(-0.8, 0.8); // limit to Â±80% power

// Run to position:
pid.setReference(100.0, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kPosition);
// Motor will PID to 100 rotations on its own!

// Velocity control:
pid.setReference(2000, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kVelocity); // 2000 RPM
\`\`\`

## Follower Motor (Two Motors, One Command)
\`\`\`java
CANSparkMax leader   = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
CANSparkMax follower = new CANSparkMax(2, MotorType.kBrushless);
follower.restoreFactoryDefaults();
follower.follow(leader, true); // true = inverted relative to leader
// Now only command leader â€” follower mirrors it automatically
\`\`\`
WPILib's command-based framework is the standard for FRC programming. Every subsystem is a class; every action is a command; the scheduler runs them.

## Creating a Subsystem
\`\`\`java
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.SubsystemBase;
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkMax;

public class ArmSubsystem extends SubsystemBase {
    private final CANSparkMax motor;
    private final SparkPIDController pid;
    private int targetTicks = 0;

    // Arm positions as constants
    public static final int STOWED     =    0;
    public static final int INTAKE     =  200;
    public static final int HIGH_SCORE = 1500;

    public ArmSubsystem() {
        motor = new CANSparkMax(3, MotorType.kBrushless);
        motor.restoreFactoryDefaults();
        motor.setIdleMode(IdleMode.kBrake);
        pid = motor.getPIDController();
        pid.setP(0.1);
        pid.setOutputRange(-0.6, 0.6);
        motor.burnFlash();
    }

    // Called every scheduler loop (~20ms):
    @Override
    public void periodic() {
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Arm Position",
            motor.getEncoder().getPosition());
    }

    public void setPosition(int position) {
        targetTicks = position;
        pid.setReference(position, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kPosition);
    }

    public boolean atTarget() {
        return Math.abs(motor.getEncoder().getPosition() - targetTicks) < 10;
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Creating a Command
\`\`\`java
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Command;

public class MoveArmCommand extends Command {
    private final ArmSubsystem arm;
    private final int target;

    public MoveArmCommand(ArmSubsystem arm, int target) {
        this.arm    = arm;
        this.target = target;
        addRequirements(arm); // locks the subsystem while running
    }

    @Override
    public void initialize() { arm.setPosition(target); }

    @Override
    public void execute() {} // PID runs onboard â€” nothing to do here

    @Override
    public boolean isFinished() { return arm.atTarget(); }

    @Override
    public void end(boolean interrupted) {
        if (interrupted) arm.setPosition(arm.getEncoder().getPosition()); // hold current
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Binding Commands to Buttons (RobotContainer)
\`\`\`java
// In RobotContainer.java:
ArmSubsystem arm = new ArmSubsystem();
CommandXboxController controller = new CommandXboxController(0);

// Button bindings:
controller.a().onTrue(new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.INTAKE));
controller.y().onTrue(new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.HIGH_SCORE));
controller.b().onTrue(new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.STOWED));

// Sequential command group â€” for autonomous:
Command scoreSequence = new SequentialCommandGroup(
    new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.HIGH_SCORE),
    new WaitUntilCommand(arm::atTarget),
    new RunIntakeCommand(intake, -1.0).withTimeout(0.5),
    new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.STOWED)
);
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should restoreFactoryDefaults() always be called on a SPARK MAX at initialization?",opts:["It's required by WPILib","It clears any stale configuration from previous code that may have been burned to flash â€” prevents unexpected behavior from leftover settings","It resets the encoder","It enables CAN communication"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does motor.burnFlash() do and why does it matter?",opts:["It sets the motor on fire (LED effect)","It saves the current configuration to the controller's non-volatile flash memory â€” without it, settings like current limits revert to defaults after a power cycle","It uploads the robot program","It's required for brushless motors"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the advantage of using the SPARK MAX's onboard PID controller over running PID in robot code?",opts:["It's more accurate","The onboard PID runs at ~1kHz on the controller itself â€” much faster than the robot code's 50Hz loop, giving tighter control especially for velocity and position","It uses less battery","It only works with CAN"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does addRequirements(arm) do in a WPILib command?",opts:["It imports the subsystem","It declares that the command needs exclusive use of the arm subsystem â€” the scheduler will cancel any other command using the arm when this one starts","It starts the arm motor","It's optional documentation"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the purpose of the periodic() method in a WPILib subsystem?",opts:["It runs once at startup","It runs every ~20ms scheduler loop â€” used for continuous tasks like reading sensors, updating SmartDashboard, or running safety checks that must happen regardless of which command is active","It's called when a command finishes","It runs only during teleop"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does SequentialCommandGroup do?",opts:["Runs all commands simultaneously","Runs commands one after another in order â€” each command starts only after the previous one finishes, creating a clean sequential autonomous routine without sleep() calls","It groups subsystems","It's for parallel actions only"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Advanced: [
      {id:"ja_motionprofile",title:"Motion Profiling â€” Trapezoidal Profiles",est:"26 min",content:`## Why Motion Profiling?
If you command a mechanism to jump instantly from 0 to full speed, motors demand huge current spikes, cause mechanical shock, and lose position accuracy. A motion profile smooths the velocity over time.

## The Trapezoidal Velocity Profile
\`\`\`
Velocity
   ^
   |    ___________
   |   /           \\
   |  /             \\
   | /               \\
   |/                 \\________
   +----+----------+---+------â†’ Time
       t1          t2  t3

Phase 1 (t0â†’t1): Accelerate at max acceleration
Phase 2 (t1â†’t2): Cruise at max velocity
Phase 3 (t2â†’t3): Decelerate at max deceleration
\`\`\`

## Implementing a Trapezoidal Profile Generator
\`\`\`java
public class TrapezoidProfile {
    private final double maxVel;   // ticks/sec
    private final double maxAccel; // ticks/secÂ²
    private double startPos, endPos, startVel;
    private double t1, t2, t3;     // phase transition times

    public TrapezoidProfile(double maxVel, double maxAccel) {
        this.maxVel   = maxVel;
        this.maxAccel = maxAccel;
    }

    public void plan(double startPos, double endPos, double startVel) {
        this.startPos = startPos;
        this.endPos   = endPos;
        this.startVel = startVel;
        double dist   = Math.abs(endPos - startPos);

        // Time to accelerate to max velocity:
        t1 = (maxVel - startVel) / maxAccel;
        // Distance covered during acceleration:
        double d_accel = startVel*t1 + 0.5*maxAccel*t1*t1;
        // Distance for deceleration (symmetric):
        double d_decel = 0.5*maxVel*maxVel / maxAccel;

        if (d_accel + d_decel > dist) {
            // Triangle profile â€” too short to reach maxVel
            t1 = Math.sqrt(dist / maxAccel);
            t2 = t1;
            t3 = 2 * t1;
        } else {
            // Cruise phase exists
            double d_cruise = dist - d_accel - d_decel;
            t2 = t1 + d_cruise / maxVel;
            t3 = t2 + maxVel / maxAccel;
        }
    }

    // Get target velocity at time t since profile start:
    public double getVelocity(double t) {
        int dir = endPos > startPos ? 1 : -1;
        double v;
        if      (t <= t1) v = startVel + maxAccel * t;
        else if (t <= t2) v = maxVel;
        else if (t <= t3) v = maxVel - maxAccel * (t - t2);
        else              v = 0;
        return dir * v;
    }

    public boolean isDone(double t) { return t >= t3; }
}
\`\`\`

## Using the Profile in an Arm Controller
\`\`\`java
TrapezoidProfile profile = new TrapezoidProfile(
    2000,  // max 2000 ticks/sec
    4000   // accelerate at 4000 ticks/secÂ²
);
ElapsedTime profileTimer = new ElapsedTime();

// When new target commanded:
profile.plan(arm.getCurrentPosition(), ARM_HIGH_SCORE, 0);
profileTimer.reset();

// In control loop (called every 20ms):
double targetVel = profile.getVelocity(profileTimer.seconds());
// Feed target velocity to motor velocity PID:
sparkMaxPid.setReference(targetVel, ControlType.kVelocity);
\`\`\`

## WPILib TrapezoidProfile (FRC â€” Use This Instead)
\`\`\`java
// WPILib has a built-in class â€” prefer this for FRC:
import edu.wpi.first.math.trajectory.TrapezoidProfile;

var constraints = new TrapezoidProfile.Constraints(2000, 4000);
var profile = new TrapezoidProfile(constraints);
var state = profile.calculate(
    0.02, // dt = 20ms
    new TrapezoidProfile.State(currentPos, currentVel),
    new TrapezoidProfile.State(targetPos, 0)
);
// state.position and state.velocity are the profile targets for this timestep

      {id:"pyb_json",title:"JSON for Robot Config & Scouting Data",est:"13 min",content:`## What is JSON?
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format for storing and exchanging structured data. Python reads and writes it natively. Perfect for robot configuration files and scouting exports.

## Reading a JSON Config File
\`\`\`python
import json

# config.json:
# {
#   "team": 1234,
#   "auto_drive_speed": 0.45,
#   "arm_positions": {"stowed": 0, "intake": 220, "high": 1487},
#   "climb_enabled": true
# }

with open("config.json") as f:
    config = json.load(f)

print(config["team"])                          # 1234
print(config["auto_drive_speed"])              # 0.45
print(config["arm_positions"]["high"])         # 1487
print(config["climb_enabled"])                 # True (Python bool)
\`\`\`

## Writing JSON
\`\`\`python
match_data = {
    "match": 12,
    "team": 1234,
    "auto_pts": 18,
    "cycles": 7,
    "climb": "L3",
    "notes": "Dropped one game piece near scoring zone"
}

with open("match_12.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(match_data, f, indent=2)  # indent=2 makes it human-readable

# Result in match_12.json:
# {
#   "match": 12,
#   "team": 1234,
#   ...
# }
\`\`\`

## JSON List of Matches (Append Pattern)
\`\`\`python
import os

def save_match(match_data: dict, filepath="scouting.json"):
    # Load existing data or start fresh
    if os.path.exists(filepath):
        with open(filepath) as f:
            all_data = json.load(f)
    else:
        all_data = []

    all_data.append(match_data)

    with open(filepath, "w") as f:
        json.dump(all_data, f, indent=2)

# Load all matches back:
def load_matches(filepath="scouting.json") -> list:
    if not os.path.exists(filepath):
        return []
    with open(filepath) as f:
        return json.load(f)

      {id:"pi_pandas2",title:"Advanced Pandas â€” Pivots, Groupby & Merge",est:"20 min",content:`## Taking Scouting Analysis Further
Basic Pandas covers reading CSVs and computing averages. These intermediate operations let you answer deeper questions: which alliances win, how scores correlate with seeding, and what auto strategy correlates with final rank.

## GroupBy + Aggregation
\`\`\`python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("scouting.csv")
# Columns: match, team, auto, cycles, climb_pts, alliance_color

# Per-team summary stats:
summary = df.groupby("team").agg(
    matches    = ("auto", "count"),
    avg_auto   = ("auto", "mean"),
    avg_cycles = ("cycles", "mean"),
    max_cycles = ("cycles", "max"),
    climb_rate = ("climb_pts", lambda x: (x > 0).mean())
).round(2)

# Add derived column:
summary["avg_total"] = summary["avg_auto"] + summary["avg_cycles"] * 4
summary = summary.sort_values("avg_total", ascending=False)
print(summary.head(10))
\`\`\`

## Pivot Table â€” Match Scores by Alliance
\`\`\`python
# Create a match-level view: one row per match showing red/blue totals
pivot = df.pivot_table(
    values="cycles",
    index="match",
    columns="alliance_color",
    aggfunc="sum"
)
pivot.columns = ["blue_cycles", "red_cycles"]
pivot["blue_wins"] = pivot["blue_cycles"] > pivot["red_cycles"]
win_rate = pivot["blue_wins"].mean()
print(f"Blue alliance win rate: {win_rate:.1%}")
\`\`\`

## Merging Datasets â€” Combine Scouting with TBA Rankings
\`\`\`python
import requests

# Pull rankings from TBA
resp = requests.get("https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/event/2025casd/rankings",
                    headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": "YOUR_KEY"})
rankings_raw = resp.json()["rankings"]

rankings = pd.DataFrame([{
    "team": int(r["team_key"].replace("frc", "")),
    "rank": r["rank"],
    "wins": r["record"]["wins"]
} for r in rankings_raw])

# Merge scouting averages with official rankings:
merged = summary.reset_index().merge(rankings, on="team", how="left")
merged = merged.sort_values("rank")

# Correlation: does higher avg_auto predict better ranking?
corr = merged["avg_auto"].corr(merged["rank"])
print(f"Auto score vs rank correlation: {corr:.2f}")
# Negative correlation means higher auto â†’ lower (better) rank
\`\`\`

## Filtering Outlier Matches
\`\`\`python
# Remove matches where team was clearly defended or disabled
# Heuristic: drop bottom 10% of each team's cycle counts
def drop_low_outliers(group):
    threshold = group["cycles"].quantile(0.10)
    return group[group["cycles"] >= threshold]

df_clean = df.groupby("team", group_keys=False).apply(drop_low_outliers)

Most FIRST teams use Discord. A bot can auto-post match results, battery voltage alerts, scouting summaries, and competition schedule â€” information that used to require someone manually sharing it.

## Setup
\`\`\`bash
pip install discord.py requests
\`\`\`

\`\`\`python
import discord
from discord.ext import commands, tasks
import requests
import os

TOKEN   = os.getenv("DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN")  # never hardcode tokens!
TBA_KEY = os.getenv("TBA_KEY")
CHANNEL_ID = 1234567890  # your #match-alerts channel ID

intents = discord.Intents.default()
bot = commands.Bot(command_prefix="!", intents=intents)
\`\`\`

## Auto-Post Match Results Every 5 Minutes
\`\`\`python
MY_TEAM  = "frc1234"
EVENT    = "2025casd"
last_seen_matches = set()

@tasks.loop(minutes=5)
async def check_new_matches():
    channel = bot.get_channel(CHANNEL_ID)
    if not channel:
        return

    url = f"https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/{MY_TEAM}/event/{EVENT}/matches"
    resp = requests.get(url, headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": TBA_KEY}, timeout=5)
    if resp.status_code != 200:
        return

    for match in resp.json():
        key = match["key"]
        if key in last_seen_matches or match["actual_time"] is None:
            continue
        if match.get("alliances") is None:
            continue

        last_seen_matches.add(key)
        alliances = match["alliances"]
        for color in ["red", "blue"]:
            if MY_TEAM in alliances[color]["team_keys"]:
                score_us   = alliances[color]["score"]
                opp        = "blue" if color == "red" else "red"
                score_them = alliances[opp]["score"]
                won = score_us > score_them
                emoji = "ðŸ†" if won else "ðŸ“‰"
                msg = (f"{emoji} **QM{match['match_number']}** â€” "
                       f"{color.upper()} {score_us} vs {score_them}  "
                       f"{'WIN' if won else 'LOSS'}")
                await channel.send(msg)

@bot.event
async def on_ready():
    print(f"Bot ready: {bot.user}")
    check_new_matches.start()

bot.run(TOKEN)
\`\`\`

@bot.tree.command(name="stats", description="Show scouting stats for a team")
async def stats_command(interaction: discord.Interaction, team: int):
    # Load from your scouting CSV

      {id:"mi_bumpers",title:"FRC Bumper Design & Construction",est:"16 min",content:`## Bumpers Are Safety-Critical
FRC bumpers protect other robots and the field from your robot. They're also heavily inspected â€” incorrect bumpers mean you don't play until they're fixed.

## Bumper Rules (Typical â€” Always Verify Current Manual)
\`\`\`
Material:
  Pool noodle (2.5" diameter) â€” 1 layer
  â‰¥ 5/8" plywood backing
  â‰¥ 4" tall Cordura fabric covering

Height: Bottom 7.5" to 10.5" from floor (most years)
Mandatory coverage: Must cover protected corners + sides per game spec
Team number: Clearly visible on all four sides, â‰¥ 4" tall digits
\`\`\`

## Bumper Construction Process
\`\`\`
Step 1: Cut Â¾" plywood to bumper segment lengths
        Length = frame side length + corner overlaps
        Keep segments short enough to be removable

Step 2: Attach pool noodle
        Hot glue or staple to plywood face
        Noodle must be continuous â€” no gaps at corners
        Cut 45Â° angles where segments meet at corners

Step 3: Cover with Cordura fabric
        Pull tight, staple to back of plywood every 2-3 inches
        No wrinkles on the front face â€” inspectors check this
        Double-fold fabric at corners for clean appearance

Step 4: Apply team number
        4"+ tall digits cut from fabric or painted
        Must be visible when robot is on the field

Step 5: Install mounting brackets
        Â¼-20 bolts through frame into bumper backing
        Must be removable by hand or with simple tools
        Verify bumper height FROM THE FLOOR with robot assembled
\`\`\`

## The Bumper Height Trap
\`\`\`
Measure bumper height with:
  âœ… Robot fully assembled and on the competition floor
  âœ… Battery installed (battery weight affects ride height)
  âœ… All mechanisms in starting configuration

NOT:
  âŒ Robot on a workbench
  âŒ Measuring from chassis bottom (wheel compression changes floor height)
  âŒ CAD measurement (build tolerances shift the real height)

Many teams fail inspection for Â½" height violations from measuring wrong.
\`\`\`

## Quick-Release Bumper Mount
\`\`\`
Design for pit speed: bumpers removed/installed in < 60 seconds.
Good mount: Â¼-20 bolts in T-nuts on frame, wing nuts or Â¼-turn fasteners
Avoid: Buried bolt heads requiring robot disassembly to access
\`\`\`
Most FIRST robots use either spur gearboxes (gears in a flat line) or planetary gearboxes (gears arranged in a circle). Each has trade-offs worth understanding.

## Spur Gearbox
\`\`\`
Layout: Input gear â†’ intermediate gears â†’ output gear (in a plane)
       [Motor] â†’ [12T] â†’ [60T] â†’ [16T] â†’ [48T] â†’ [Output]

Pros:
  âœ… Simple to design and manufacture
  âœ… Easy to inspect and repair â€” gears are visible
  âœ… Efficient at low ratios
  âœ… Can use standard COTS gears (MOD 1, DP32, etc.)

Cons:
  âŒ Gets physically large at high ratios
  âŒ Single gear contact point â€” high stress per tooth
  âŒ Longer axial length for multi-stage designs
\`\`\`

## Planetary Gearbox
\`\`\`
Layout: Sun gear at center, planet gears orbit it, ring gear surrounds all
       [Motor shaft = sun] â†’ [3 planet gears] â†’ [carrier output]
       All planets share the load simultaneously

Pros:
  âœ… Very high torque density (compact for the ratio)
  âœ… Load shared across multiple planets â€” stronger
  âœ… Coaxial (input and output on same axis) â€” clean packaging
  âœ… Standard in most FIRST gearbox products (UltraPlanetary, VersaPlanetary)

Cons:
  âŒ Harder to service (internal planet gears)
  âŒ More expensive to manufacture custom
  âŒ Ring gear wear is hard to inspect without disassembly
\`\`\`

## FIRST COTS Planetary Gearboxes
| Product | Compatible Motors | Notes |
|---------|-----------------|-------|
| REV UltraPlanetary | NEO, NEO 550, Core Hex | Modular cartridges (3:1, 4:1, 5:1) â€” stack for custom ratios |
| VEXpro VersaPlanetary | CIM, MiniCIM, 775pro | Popular in FRC |
| GoBILDA 5202 Series | Built-in gearbox | Motor + gearbox as one unit |

## Choosing Between Them
\`\`\`
Use spur when:
  â†’ You need a specific non-standard ratio
  â†’ You're integrating with custom hardware
  â†’ Low ratio (< 5:1) and space isn't critical

Use planetary (COTS) when:
  â†’ You need a compact high-ratio gearbox (15:1â€“100:1)
  â†’ Reliability matters more than custom optimization
  â†’ Time matters â€” COTS planetaries install in minutes
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why must bumper height be measured with the robot fully assembled, battery installed, and on the competition floor?",opts:["Rules require this process","Battery weight and wheel compression change the actual floor-to-bumper measurement from CAD estimates â€” many teams fail inspection measuring off the chassis bottom or on a bench","It's the fastest method","Floor material affects the rule"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should bumper segments be kept short enough to be individually removable?",opts:["Shorter bumpers are lighter","Easy removal allows quick bumper replacement if one section is damaged in a match â€” a single damaged segment shouldn't force you to remove the entire assembly","Short segments are required","They are easier to construct"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the purpose of cutting pool noodle corners at 45Â° angles?",opts:["It reduces weight","Mitered corners allow noodle coverage to wrap continuously around robot corners without gaps or bunching â€” gaps are an inspection failure and also reduce protection","It's the only way to attach noodle","45Â° is required by the game manual"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the main structural advantage of a planetary gearbox over a spur gearbox at the same ratio?",opts:["Planetary gearboxes are cheaper","Load is distributed across multiple planet gears simultaneously â€” each tooth carries a fraction of the total load, allowing much higher torque in a smaller package","Spur gearboxes are lighter","Planetary gearboxes have less backlash"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why do planetary gearboxes use coaxial geometry (input and output on the same axis)?",opts:["It's a manufacturing limitation","The ring gear forces the output carrier to be concentric with the input sun gear â€” this clean inline layout simplifies installation in tight spaces and motor integration","It's required by FIRST rules","Coaxial is stronger than offset"],ans:1},
        {q:"When is using a COTS planetary gearbox (like UltraPlanetary) preferred over a custom spur design?",opts:["COTS is never preferred","When you need a high ratio quickly and reliably â€” COTS gearboxes are pre-validated, install in minutes, and support common motors directly without custom adapters","COTS is only for FTC","Spur gearboxes are always more reliable"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ma_intake_design",title:"Intake System Design Principles",est:"24 min",content:`## The Intake Is Often the Hardest Mechanism to Get Right
Drives and lifts are well-understood. Intakes deal with the chaotic, unpredictable real world â€” game pieces at random orientations, bouncing on carpet, being contested by opponents. This is engineering design at its messiest.

## Design Requirements Gathering
\`\`\`
Before sketching anything, answer:
  1. Game piece geometry: What shape? Size range? Weight?
  2. Contact: Where can you legally touch it?
  3. Acquisition zone: Where on the field? Floor? Mid-air? Station?
  4. Throughput: How many pieces per match? Cycle time target?
  5. Storage: How many pieces does the robot hold simultaneously?
  6. Error tolerance: Does it need to work when piece is tilted 30Â°?

These answers constrain your design space before you draw anything.
\`\`\`

## Intake Mechanism Types
\`\`\`
Roller intake (most common in FTC/FRC):
  Compliant wheels or surgical tubing spin to grab and pull in
  Works on: balls, discs, cubes with a face
  Advantages: fast, forgiving of off-axis pieces
  Tune: roller gap = 70-80% of piece width for good compression

Over-the-bumper intake (FRC):
  Folded arm swings over bumper to floor level
  Required when: pieces must be picked up off the floor
                 and robot frame clearance is insufficient
  Design challenge: must fold to start configuration

Funnel intake:
  Angled walls guide pieces into a narrow throat
  Works best: cylindrical pieces (rings, balls)
  Advantage: self-centering, wide acceptance angle
\`\`\`

## Compression & Gap Tuning
\`\`\`
Too much compression (rollers too close):
  â†’ Game piece stalls â€” high current, possible jam
  â†’ Excess friction damages or deforms game piece

Too little compression (rollers too far):
  â†’ Piece slips through â€” no acquisition
  â†’ Works 3/5 times in testing â†’ fails at competition

Starting point: gap = piece width Ã— 0.75
Fine-tune: increase gap 2mm at a time until slip appears,
           then back off 1-2mm

Test on actual game pieces â€” foam balls, FTC game pieces are inconsistent
\`\`\`

## The Jam Recovery Problem
\`\`\`
Every intake will jam eventually. Design for recovery:

Reversible intake:
  Run motors backward to eject jammed piece
  Add a "reverse" button to driver gamepad
  Test jam recovery â€” should take < 2 seconds

Detection option:
  Current spike detection = likely jam
  if (motorCurrent > jamThreshold) {
      runReverse(1.0, 300ms);
      runForward again;
  }
\`\`\`

## Field-Testing Protocol
\`\`\`
Week 2 (prototype):   5/5 consistent pickups from ideal position
Week 3 (refined):     5/5 pickups at 30Â° piece tilt
                      5/5 pickups at 12" off-center from centerline
Week 5 (final):       50 consecutive picks with no jam
                      5 successful jam recoveries from intentional jams
                      Tested by a driver who didn't build the intake
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What does the compression ratio (gap = piece width Ã— 0.75) achieve in a roller intake?",opts:["It sets the motor speed","The rollers compress the game piece by ~25%, creating enough friction to pull it in reliably â€” too much compression stalls the motor, too little allows the piece to slip","It sets the roller diameter","It's required by game rules"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should the final intake test be performed by a driver who didn't build it?",opts:["Builders are not allowed to test","The builder knows the mechanism's quirks and avoids actions that cause jams â€” a fresh driver operates it as it will be used in competition, revealing real usability issues","It's faster","It satisfies safety requirements"],ans:1},
        {q:"What design feature ensures fast recovery when an intake jams during a match?",opts:["More powerful motors","A reversible intake with a dedicated driver control â€” the driver runs the intake backward to eject the jam and resumes within seconds","Adding more rollers","Reducing compression"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"ei_network",title:"FRC Robot Networking & Radio Setup",est:"16 min",content:`## The FRC Network Architecture
FRC robots communicate over a dedicated Wi-Fi network. Understanding the architecture prevents the most frustrating competition problem: losing communication mid-match.

## Network Topology
\`\`\`
Driver Station (laptop)
       â†• Wi-Fi (2.4 or 5 GHz)
Robot Radio (OpenMesh OM5P or similar)
       â†• Ethernet
roboRIO
       â†• Ethernet (switch optional)
Limelight / co-processor (if used)
       â†• CAN bus
Motor controllers, PDH
\`\`\`

## Radio Configuration
\`\`\`
At home (pre-event):
  1. Download FRC Radio Configuration Utility
  2. Connect radio to PC via Ethernet (NOT Wi-Fi)
  3. Set team number â€” this sets the SSID to "1234" (your team number)
  4. Mode: "2.4 GHz" or "5 GHz" â€” check event preference (ask FTA)

At competition (FTA flashes radio):
  The Field Technical Advisor re-configures your radio for the competition
  network. This is REQUIRED and happens at radio check-in.
  Your home config is overwritten â€” don't skip this step.

Event network:
  â†’ Competition uses its own Wi-Fi infrastructure (OpenMesh AP on field)
  â†’ 2.4 GHz is more reliable through crowds; 5 GHz is faster but shorter range
\`\`\`

## roboRIO Network Settings
\`\`\`
Default roboRIO IP: 10.TE.AM.2 (e.g., team 1234 â†’ 10.12.34.2)
Driver Station IP:  10.TE.AM.X (auto-assigned via DHCP)
Radio IP:           10.TE.AM.1

If comms aren't working, check:
  1. roboRIO booted fully (RSL blinking + DS shows green)
  2. Radio power light is on
  3. DS shows correct team number in configuration
  4. Ethernet cable seated at both ends
  5. roboRIO IP hasn't been changed (use Imaging Tool to reset)
\`\`\`

## Latency & Bandwidth Management
\`\`\`java
// Camera streams consume significant bandwidth
// Disable vision streams during competition if not used for auto-aim:
// In RobotContainer or robotInit():
UsbCamera camera = CameraServer.startAutomaticCapture();
camera.setResolution(320, 240);  // lower resolution = less bandwidth
camera.setFPS(15);               // lower FPS = less bandwidth

// Only stream during teleop if needed:
// NetworkTableInstance.getDefault().getTable("CameraPublisher")...
\`\`\`

## Diagnosing Communication Dropouts
\`\`\`
Symptoms â†’ likely causes:
  Instant disconnect and reconnect â†’ Radio power issue (check connector)
  Gradual degradation â†’ Bandwidth overload (reduce camera streams)
  Only at certain robot positions â†’ Radio line-of-sight blocked
  During defense/pushing â†’ Loose Ethernet at roboRIO
  Never connects â†’ wrong team number in DS or radio not FTA-flashed
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why must the FRC radio be re-flashed by the FTA at competition even if it worked perfectly at home?",opts:["Home configuration is incorrect","The competition uses its own managed Wi-Fi infrastructure â€” the FTA flashes the radio with event-specific settings so it communicates with the competition field's access points instead of your home network","Radio firmware expires","It's a safety requirement"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the default roboRIO IP address format for FRC team 1234?",opts:["192.168.1.2","10.12.34.2 â€” FIRST uses the 10.TE.AM.2 convention where TE and AM are split from the team number","172.16.0.2","10.0.0.2"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should camera stream resolution and FPS be reduced during competition matches?",opts:["Cameras are illegal during competition","Camera streams consume network bandwidth â€” high resolution/FPS streams can cause latency and communication dropouts if they saturate the limited bandwidth available on the competition network","Reduced quality improves targeting","FTC rules require low resolution"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ea_custom_pcb2",title:"Sensor Breakout Boards for FIRST",est:"22 min",content:`## Why a Custom Breakout Board?
Commercial sensors (IMUs, time-of-flight sensors, color sensors) come in tiny packages with fragile 1.27mm pin headers. A custom PCB converts them to robust JST connectors, adds filtering, and mounts cleanly on the robot.

## Common Sensor Interface Circuits

### I2C Pull-Up Resistors
\`\`\`
I2C requires pull-up resistors on SDA and SCL lines.
The REV Control Hub has internal pull-ups, but long cable runs
or multiple devices need external resistors.

Standard values:
  4.7kÎ© for short runs (< 30cm)
  2.2kÎ© for longer runs or multiple sensors on one bus

Schematic:
  3.3V â”€â”€â”€ 4.7kÎ© â”€â”€â”€ SDA line â”€â”€â”€ (to sensor)
  3.3V â”€â”€â”€ 4.7kÎ© â”€â”€â”€ SCL line â”€â”€â”€ (to sensor)
\`\`\`

### Decoupling Capacitor (Every Sensor Circuit)
\`\`\`
Place 100nF (0.1ÂµF) ceramic capacitor between VCC and GND
as close to each sensor's power pins as possible.
Filters high-frequency noise from motor switching.

Without decoupling: sensor reads erratic values during motor bursts
With decoupling:    clean reads even at full drive power
\`\`\`

### Time-of-Flight Sensor (VL53L1X) Breakout
\`\`\`
Connections (I2C):
  VCC â†’ 3.3V (NOT 5V â€” this sensor is 3.3V only)
  GND â†’ GND
  SDA â†’ I2C SDA + 4.7kÎ© pullup to 3.3V
  SCL â†’ I2C SCL + 4.7kÎ© pullup to 3.3V
  XSHUT â†’ GPIO (allows software reset and address change for multi-sensor)
  INT â†’ GPIO (interrupt-driven reading instead of polling)

FTC code:
  Rev2mDistanceSensor dist = hardwareMap.get(Rev2mDistanceSensor.class, "tof");
  double mm = dist.getDistance(DistanceUnit.MM);
\`\`\`

## PCB Layout Rules for Robots
\`\`\`
1. Route power traces wide: 0.5mm minimum for signal, 1mm+ for power
2. Separate analog sensor ground from digital/motor ground (star ground)
3. Keep I2C and SPI traces short â€” route directly, no long detours
4. Add mounting holes: M3 or M2.5, in known positions matching robot frame
5. Include test points: small pads on each signal line for probing
6. Silkscreen labels: mark every connector pin, voltage, and signal name
\`\`\`

## Manufacturing Options for FIRST Teams
\`\`\`
JLCPCB / PCBWay:
  $5-10 for 5 boards (2-layer, 100mmÃ—100mm)
  7-14 day lead time for economy shipping
  Minimum trace width: 0.1mm (use 0.2mm for safety)
  Students design in KiCad (free, open-source)

Fabrication timeline:
  Week 1: Schematic â†’ layout
  Week 2: Design review â†’ submit to fab
  Week 3-4: Boards arrive
  Week 4-5: Assemble and test
  Not for last-minute changes!
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What does a 100nF decoupling capacitor placed near a sensor's power pins accomplish?",opts:["It amplifies the sensor signal","It filters high-frequency voltage spikes from motor switching â€” without it, the power supply noise corrupts sensor readings during heavy motor use","It reduces power consumption","It sets the sensor's I2C address"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must the VL53L1X time-of-flight sensor be connected to 3.3V and not 5V?",opts:["3.3V sensors are faster","The VL53L1X is a 3.3V-only device â€” applying 5V will damage it immediately and irreversibly","5V is only for motors","3.3V is required by I2C protocol"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the purpose of the XSHUT pin on a time-of-flight sensor when using multiple sensors?",opts:["It shuts down the robot","It allows software control of each sensor's power â€” useful to temporarily disable sensors during I2C address assignment so multiple VL53L1X sensors can coexist on the same bus with different addresses","It resets the distance reading","It's only used during calibration"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"sb_alliance_coord",title:"Alliance Coordination Before the Match",est:"13 min",content:`## The Pre-Match Meeting â€” Use Every Second
FRC gives alliances 6 minutes before elimination matches to talk. Most teams waste it. Top alliances use it to build a specific game plan.

## What to Accomplish in the Pre-Match Meeting
\`\`\`
1. Autonomous paths (5 min, highest priority)
   â†’ Each robot describes: where they start, what they do,
     where they end up after auto
   â†’ Identify conflicts: two robots going for the same game piece
   â†’ Resolve conflicts: one robot takes left, one takes right
   â†’ Agree on any delayed starts (robot B waits 1 sec)

2. Teleop roles (2 min)
   â†’ Who focuses on high scoring? Who handles low?
   â†’ Who plays defense if needed?
   â†’ Who climbs first? (climb timing â€” both can't be in the same zone)

3. Endgame plan (1 min)
   â†’ At what time does each robot begin endgame sequence?
   â†’ If one robot can't climb â€” does another assist?
   â†’ Who communicates "I'm starting now"?

4. Communication during match (30 sec)
   â†’ What signals does your alliance use?
   â†’ Who is the "in-match voice" â€” one person calls adjustments
\`\`\`

## Common Pre-Match Mistakes
\`\`\`
âŒ "We'll just figure it out during the match"
   â†’ Teleop chaos, duplicate actions, missed points

âŒ Spending all 6 minutes on autonomous, ignoring endgame
   â†’ Run out of time discussing endgame timing, then both robots
     try to climb the same structure simultaneously

âŒ Drive team talks; alliance partners nod but didn't understand
   â†’ Check comprehension: "Can you repeat back what we agreed on?"

âŒ No conflict resolution for autonomous
   â†’ Two robots collide at 0:03 â†’ both disabled
\`\`\`

## Communicating During the Match
\`\`\`
Before the match, agree on simple signals:
  Thumbs up     = "I completed my task, moving on"
  Wave toward   = "Come to my side / I need your help here"
  Point at clock = "Check the timer â€” time-sensitive action now"
  Thumbs down    = "I'm having a problem â€” cover for me"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why is resolving autonomous path conflicts the highest priority in the pre-match alliance meeting?",opts:["Autonomous is worth the most points","Two robots colliding in the first seconds of autonomous can disable both â€” a 3-second collision costs more points than a missed game piece ever could","FRC requires a written autonomous plan","Autonomous conflicts are the hardest to fix"],ans:1},
        {q:"How should you verify that alliance partners actually understood the pre-match plan?",opts:["Assume they understood if they nodded","Ask them to repeat back what you agreed on â€” nodding during a stressful pre-match meeting doesn't mean the plan was understood clearly","Send them a text","Review video of previous matches"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should exactly ONE person be designated as the 'in-match voice' for an alliance?",opts:["FRC rules allow only one communicator","Multiple voices calling adjustments simultaneously confuse drivers and operators â€” one calm, focused communicator reduces chaos and allows drivers to stay focused on their robot","It's faster","One person has better vision"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
    Intermediate: [
      {id:"si_qual_strategy",title:"Qualification Match Strategy",est:"16 min",content:`## Qualification Matches Are Different From Elims
In qualifications, you can't pick your partners â€” random assignment. Your strategy must be flexible enough to work with both strong and weak random allies.

## The Three Qualification Goals
\`\`\`
Primary:   Win the match (contributes 2 RP)
Secondary: Earn bonus RP objectives (adds 1-2 RP per match)
Tertiary:  Maximize average score (tiebreaker metric)

You don't always need all three â€” sometimes 1 goal requires
sacrificing another.
\`\`\`

## Adapting to Your Alliance Partner
\`\`\`
Partner is weak (low cycle count, unreliable auto):
  â†’ YOU carry the offense
  â†’ Prioritize safety over bonus RP â€” a win is better than a loss chasing bonus
  â†’ Communicate clearly: "Our plan is to score high, you support"

Partner is strong (high cycle count, reliable auto):
  â†’ Focus on complementary actions (different scoring zones)
  â†’ Both trying to do the same thing is wasteful
  â†’ Discuss before match: "You take left side, I take right"

Partner is broken/partially functional:
  â†’ Treat them as a bystander â€” plan for 2-robot alliance
  â†’ Adjust score expectations; don't panic, just adapt
\`\`\`

## When to Chase Bonus RP vs When to Secure the Win
\`\`\`
Bonus RP threshold = 60 pts (example â€” varies by game)
Your alliance is at 48 pts with 30 seconds left.
Needed: 12 more pts.

Decision tree:
  Can you score 12 pts in 30 sec reliably?
    Yes â†’ GO for it (RP is more valuable than margin-of-win)
    No  â†’ Protect what you have, don't risk a costly foul
          trying to reach a threshold you'll probably miss

Remember: A loss that earns 0 RP is always worse than a win
          that misses the bonus RP (2 RP > 1 RP bonus only).
\`\`\`

## Scouting Your Next Opponents (10-Min Pre-Match)
\`\`\`
Before each qualification match, check:
  1. Their alliance's 3 robots â€” what does each do?
  2. Have you seen them play? Any obvious weaknesses?
  3. Do they have a fast scorer you should focus away from?

Even 2 minutes of opponent research beats zero.
Use FRC Events app â†’ match predictions and previous scores.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why is a win worth more than a bonus RP threshold miss even if you came close?",opts:["Wins always give more RP","A win earns 2 RP; a loss with a missed bonus earns 0 RP â€” consistently winning while not chasing unreachable bonuses produces better seeding than chasing bonuses and losing","Bonus RP is worth 3","Wins only count in elimination"],ans:1},
        {q:"If your random alliance partner's robot is broken, what is the best adjustment?",opts:["Forfeit the match","Treat your alliance as a 2-robot alliance â€” adjust score expectations, focus on what two robots can reliably achieve, and don't panic-play trying to compensate for a missing robot","Try to carry 3 robots worth of scoring","Request a partner swap from the referee"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the main reason to scout your next qualification match opponents in the 10 minutes before the match?",opts:["It's required by FIRST","Even brief opponent research reveals fast scorers to avoid defending against, unreliable auto paths, and weaknesses to exploit â€” better than walking in with zero knowledge","Scouting gives bonus RP","To fill out the scouting sheet"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"sfb_firstaid",title:"First Aid Basics for the Robot Shop",est:"12 min",content:`## Every Shop Needs a First Aid Responder
FIRST events require a Safety Captain. Your shop should have at least one person trained in basic first aid and a stocked first aid kit accessible to everyone.

## The Shop First Aid Kit â€” Minimum Contents
\`\`\`
Cuts and abrasions (most common shop injuries):
  âœ… Adhesive bandages (multiple sizes â€” fingertips are most common)
  âœ… Sterile gauze pads (2"Ã—2" and 4"Ã—4")
  âœ… Medical tape
  âœ… Antiseptic wipes or solution
  âœ… Nitrile gloves (non-latex â€” for the helper, not the patient)
  âœ… Tweezers (metal slivers in hands)

Eye injuries:
  âœ… Eyewash station OR sterile saline eyewash (8 oz minimum)
  âœ… Eye cup for flushing

Burns:
  âœ… Burn gel or cool running water (don't use ice)
  âœ… Non-stick burn dressing

Other:
  âœ… Instant cold pack
  âœ… First aid manual or QR code to reference
  âœ… Emergency contact list (mentor phone numbers, school nurse)
\`\`\`

## Responding to Common Shop Injuries
\`\`\`
Cut from metal edge:
  1. Put on gloves (protect yourself)
  2. Apply direct pressure with clean gauze for 3-5 minutes
  3. If bleeding stops â†’ clean, apply antiseptic, bandage
  4. If bleeding doesn't slow or cut is deep â†’ seek medical attention
  5. Never remove embedded metal â€” leave for medical professional

Metal splinter:
  1. Clean the area with antiseptic
  2. Use clean tweezers to remove if surface-level and visible
  3. Clean again after removal, apply antiseptic
  4. If deep or under a nail â†’ seek medical attention

Eye splash (chemical or metal chip):
  1. Go to eyewash station IMMEDIATELY â€” do not rub
  2. Flush for at least 15 minutes
  3. Seek medical evaluation after flushing, even if it feels better
  4. For serious chemical exposure â€” call 911

Burn (heat from soldering/motor):
  1. Cool with cool running water for 10-20 minutes
  2. Do NOT apply ice, butter, or toothpaste
  3. Cover loosely with sterile non-stick dressing
  4. Seek medical attention for burns larger than 1" or on hands/face
\`\`\`

## When to Call 911 Immediately
\`\`\`
â†’ Uncontrolled bleeding (soaks through multiple dressings in 5 min)
â†’ Eye injury from chemicals or penetrating object
â†’ Electric shock â€” even if the person "feels fine"
â†’ Loss of consciousness
â†’ Suspected broken bone
â†’ Any injury to the head, neck, or spine
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why must you put on nitrile gloves before helping someone with a bleeding cut?",opts:["It looks professional","Gloves protect the helper from bloodborne pathogens â€” hand protection is as important for the first responder as wound care is for the patient","Gloves prevent infection in the wound","FIRST requires it"],ans:1},
        {q:"What should you NOT do when someone gets a chemical splash in their eye?",opts:["Flush with water","Rub the eye â€” rubbing drives the chemical or particle deeper; immediately flush at the eyewash station for at least 15 minutes without rubbing","Remove contact lenses first","Seek medical evaluation"],ans:1},
        {q:"For a minor burn from a soldering iron, what is the correct first treatment?",opts:["Apply ice immediately","Cool with running water for 10-20 minutes â€” ice constricts blood vessels and can worsen tissue damage; running water is the correct treatment","Apply butter or lotion","Pop any blisters immediately"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"tmb_timeline",title:"The FIRST Season Timeline",est:"11 min",content:`## Knowing What Comes When
Both FTC and FRC follow predictable seasonal timelines. Understanding the full calendar helps teams plan sponsor deadlines, parts orders, and practice time so nothing is a surprise.

## FRC Season Timeline (Approximate)
\`\`\`
Late Aug / Sep:   Pre-season â€” team recruitment, new member training
                  Sponsor outreach, budget planning

Early Jan:        Kickoff â€” game revealed on national stream
                  Teams have 6 weeks to design, build, and program

Mid-February:     Stop Build Day (bag day eliminated in 2019)
                  Robots can still be worked on between events
                  Transition to drive practice focus

Late Feb / Mar:   District and Regional events begin
                  Typical: 2-3 qualification events per team

Apr:              District Championships (for district model teams)
Aprâ€“May:          State / Regional Championships

May:              FRC World Championship (Houston / Detroit)
                  Only top teams from each regional championship

Summer:           Awards submissions, off-season events, team debrief
\`\`\`

## FTC Season Timeline (Approximate)
\`\`\`
Sep:              Kickoff â€” game and challenge revealed
Sepâ€“Nov:          Build season (most teams have more time than FRC)

Novâ€“Jan:          Qualifier tournaments begin (varies by region)
                  Engineering Notebook judging begins at qualifiers

Janâ€“Feb:          League / Regional championships

Mar:              FTC World Championship (Houston)
                  Invite + Inspire Award advancement
\`\`\`

## Critical Deadlines Most Teams Miss
\`\`\`
â†’ Impact/Inspire Award executive summary:
  Submitted BEFORE the event â€” often 1-2 weeks ahead
  Missing the deadline = no award consideration

â†’ Dean's List nominations:
  Must be submitted through the team portal by a deadline
  Check firstinspires.org â€” date varies by region

â†’ Robot registration for events:
  FRC: robots added to the event roster by registration deadline
  FTC: team must register in the FTC scoring system

â†’ Parts orders:
  Order BEFORE build season starts (motors, sensors, gearboxes)
  "2-week shipping + 6-week build = missed your window"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should FIRST teams order key parts BEFORE kickoff instead of after?",opts:["Parts are cheaper before kickoff","Build season is only 6 weeks â€” a 2-week shipping delay means you can't install parts until Week 3, leaving only 3 weeks for integration and testing","Pre-season orders get discounts","Kickoff reveals exact part requirements"],ans:1},
        {q:"What happens if a team misses the Impact Award executive summary submission deadline?",opts:["They can submit late with a penalty","They are ineligible for the award at that event â€” the submission is reviewed before judging begins and cannot be accepted after the deadline","Judges accept late submissions","They present anyway without submission"],ans:1},
        {q:"What major change occurred in FRC in 2019 regarding the build season?",opts:["FRC added a fourth build week","The Stop Build Day 'bag' rule was eliminated â€” teams can continue working on robots between events, but the 6-week initial build season leading to first competition remains","FRC reduced to 4 weeks","Kickoff moved to February"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"cadi_motion",title:"Simulating Mechanism Motion in Onshape",est:"16 min",content:`## Why Simulate Motion Before Building?
A mechanism that looks fine in a static CAD model can collide with itself, the frame, or a wiring harness when it moves. Motion simulation catches these before any aluminum is cut.

## Setting Up a Moving Assembly
\`\`\`
1. In Onshape Assembly, create your mechanism with all parts
2. Add Revolute Mate at the pivot point (arm to frame)
3. Add Slider Mates for any linear motion (slides)
4. Add Fastened Mates for all rigid connections

Key: Only ONE DOF per mechanism at a time for clean simulation
\`\`\`

## Using the "Move with Triad" Tool
\`\`\`
1. Select a moving part (e.g., arm)
2. Use Move with Triad (keyboard shortcut: T)
3. Click the rotation arc â†’ drag to sweep the arm through its range
4. Watch for:
   â†’ Interference with the frame (highlighted in red automatically)
   â†’ Wire routing clearance (model critical cables as cylinders)
   â†’ Game piece clearance (model game piece at intake position)
\`\`\`

## Linear Motion Check (Slides)
\`\`\`
For a telescoping slide:
1. Mate the inner tube to outer tube with a Slider Mate
2. Add limit mates at full extension and full retraction:
   Assembly â†’ Mate Limits â†’ set min/max distance
3. Drag to extend â€” visually verify no interference at max extension
4. Measure: does it actually reach the scoring height you need?
   Use Measure tool at full extension
\`\`\`

## Checking Field Legal Starting Config
\`\`\`
After modeling the robot, import field elements (if available) or model
an 18"Ã—18"Ã—18" cube:
  1. Create a new Part Studio
  2. Extrude a transparent cube 18"Ã—18"Ã—18"
  3. Add it to the assembly as a reference
  4. Position around the robot at starting config
  5. Run Interference Detection â€” the robot must fit entirely inside

This is faster than measuring every dimension and prevents
the "we're 0.5" over" surprise at inspection.
\`\`\`

## Animation Export for the Notebook
\`\`\`
Onshape doesn't export video natively, but you can:
  1. Use screen recording while dragging the mechanism through motion
  2. Export multiple screenshots at key positions
     (fully retracted, mid-travel, fully extended)
  3. Include in engineering notebook as a "motion study"
     â†’ Judges appreciate seeing that you analyzed motion before building
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the purpose of adding Mate Limits to a Slider Mate on a telescoping slide?",opts:["They speed up the simulation","They constrain the slide to its physical minimum and maximum extension, so dragging in the simulation shows exactly what the real mechanism can do â€” including whether it hits anything at max extension","Limits are required for Onshape to work","They add weight to the part"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should critical wiring harnesses be modeled as simple cylinders in the assembly before running a motion simulation?",opts:["Cables can be any size","Cables routed through a mechanism's sweep path will be pinched, cut, or torn in the real robot â€” modeling them as cylinders lets the interference check catch routing problems before building","CAD cables reduce file size","Modeling cables is required by FIRST"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does Onshape's Interference Detection tool do in an assembly?",opts:["It checks the BOM for missing parts","It identifies parts that physically overlap in the current configuration, shown in red â€” essential for catching designs where two parts occupy the same space that would be physically impossible to build","It checks for mate errors","It simulates dynamic forces"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

  awards: {
    Beginner: [
      {id:"awb_rookieaward",title:"Rookie Awards & First-Year Teams",est:"11 min",content:`## First-Year Teams Have Their Own Path
Being a rookie team is harder in some ways and easier in others. There are awards specifically for first-year teams, and judges calibrate expectations differently. Understanding this helps you compete effectively from day one.

## FRC Rookie-Specific Awards
\`\`\`
Rookie All-Star Award:
  â†’ Most prestigious rookie-only award
  â†’ Recognizes overall excellence in a team's first year
  â†’ Strong robot + strong team program + community involvement
  â†’ Winning = strong recommendation for Engineering Inspiration (next year)

Rookie Inspiration Award:
  â†’ Recognizes exceptional progress and community impact for a first-year team
  â†’ Focuses more on spirit, effort, and inspiration potential than robot score

FRC Rookie Seed:
  â†’ Based purely on performance â€” highest-ranked rookie team
  â†’ May receive an automatic invitation to Championship
\`\`\`

## FTC Rookie Award Strategy
\`\`\`
Judges know you're a first-year team.
What they evaluate:
  â†’ Did you complete the engineering design process (even if rough)?
  â†’ Does your notebook show genuine learning and iteration?
  â†’ Did your team start any outreach, even small?
  â†’ Is there a plan to grow?

What they don't expect from rookies:
  â†’ Polished outreach programs (you have no track record)
  â†’ Perfect robot (everyone starts somewhere)
  â†’ Expert-level technical documentation
\`\`\`

## The Best Rookie Investment: The Notebook
\`\`\`
For a first-year FTC team, a strong engineering notebook
returns more award value per hour than any robot improvement.

Document EVERYTHING from week 1:
  â†’ Brainstorming sessions (even bad ideas)
  â†’ Why you chose your drivetrain
  â†’ What broke in testing and what you learned
  â†’ Who joined and why

A first-year team with a thorough notebook beats a 5-year team
with a sparse one in Think Award judging.
\`\`\`

## Realistic First Season Goals
\`\`\`
Technical:     Get a driving robot to every match you're registered for
               (Reliable > scoring)
Judged:        Submit awards materials, show up to judging interviews
               (Participation builds skills for future years)
Community:     Run ONE outreach event before your first tournament
               (Shows judges you're already engaging the mission)
Long-term:     Learn what you'd do differently â€” document it in the notebook
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the most valuable investment a first-year FTC team can make for awards?",opts:["Buying the most expensive parts","Maintaining a thorough engineering notebook from week one â€” documenting the learning process, decisions, and failures returns more award value than robot performance improvements","Hiring a professional coach","Attending every event possible"],ans:1},
        {q:"What do judges specifically NOT expect from first-year teams?",opts:["Any robot at all","Polished multi-year outreach programs, perfect documentation, or an expert-level robot â€” judges calibrate for rookie status and value genuine learning over polished output","Attending qualification matches","A drive team"],ans:1},
        {q:"What realistic technical goal should a first-year team prioritize above all others?",opts:["Winning the first regional","Having a robot that drives reliably to every match â€” a consistent, moving robot shows execution and earns drive practice; a spectacular broken robot earns neither","Achieving maximum autonomous score","Building a custom swerve drive"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

  outreach: {
    Beginner: [
      {id:"orb_stem_events",title:"Running a STEM Demo Event",est:"13 min",content:`## Your Robot Is Your Best Recruiting Tool
Bringing your robot to a school, library, or community event is the fastest way to spark interest in FIRST. Kids who see a real robot working up close are far more likely to join than kids who read a flyer.

## Planning a Successful Demo Event
\`\`\`
6 weeks before:
  â†’ Confirm venue, date, and expected attendance
  â†’ Get a formal contact (teacher, librarian, event coordinator)
  â†’ Confirm power availability and floor space (at least 10Ã—10 ft)
  â†’ Ask about age range â€” tailor activities accordingly

2 weeks before:
  â†’ Verify robot is in drivable condition
  â†’ Prepare a short (3-5 min) presentation if requested
  â†’ Create a simple hands-on activity (see below)
  â†’ Bring permission forms if collecting photos

Day of:
  â†’ Arrive 30 min early to set up
  â†’ Assign one driver, one explainer, one crowd manager
  â†’ Don't just drive â€” engage: ask kids "What do you think it does?"
\`\`\`

## Engagement Activities That Work
\`\`\`
For ages 6-10 (elementary):
  â†’ Gamepad driving: Let kids try driving (with supervision)
  â†’ "Robot Hands" activity: Have students use their hands to pick up a ball,
    then your robot shows how it does the same task
  â†’ Paper robot: Fold a simple paper robot while explaining "this is how
    we design on paper before building in metal"

For ages 11-14 (middle school):
  â†’ Programming demo: Show how changing a number changes robot behavior
  â†’ Challenge them: "Can you tell me what the robot should do to score?"
  â†’ Obstacle course: Set up simple cones and let kids try driving through

For ages 15-18 (high school):
  â†’ Show the code: Brief overview of the programming
  â†’ Career path: "Here's where FIRST members go â€” MIT, SpaceX, NASA"
  â†’ Invite to shadow a build session
\`\`\`

## What to Bring
\`\`\`
Essential:
  âœ… Fully charged robot battery (two if possible)
  âœ… Spare battery charger
  âœ… Team banner or tablecloth (makes the setup look official)
  âœ… Gamepads Ã— 2 (let kids drive)
  âœ… Sign-up sheet for interested students

Nice to have:
  âœ… CAD model on laptop showing robot design
  âœ… Old robot parts to handle (gears, motors, servos)
  âœ… Team stickers to give out
  âœ… QR code to your team's social media

      {id:"gb_github",title:"Using GitHub for Your FIRST Team",est:"12 min",content:`## GitHub vs Git
Git is the version control system (runs locally). GitHub is a hosting platform that stores your repository online, enabling collaboration, backups, and sharing.

## Creating a Team Repository
\`\`\`bash
# Option 1: Start from scratch
git init my-robot-2025
cd my-robot-2025
# Add files, then:
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git remote add origin https://github.com/team1234/robot2025.git
git push -u origin main

# Option 2: Clone the FTC template (recommended for FTC)
# 1. Go to github.com/FIRST-Tech-Challenge/FtcRobotController
# 2. Click "Use this template" â†’ "Create a new repository"
# 3. Name it "robot2025" under your team's GitHub organization
# 4. Clone locally:
git clone https://github.com/team1234/robot2025.git
\`\`\`

## GitHub Organization vs Personal Account
\`\`\`
Personal account (github.com/yourname/robot):
  â†’ Fine for a solo project
  â†’ Team loses access if that person graduates

GitHub Organization (github.com/team1234/robot):
  â†’ Repository belongs to the TEAM, not one person
  â†’ New members added as collaborators; graduating members removed
  â†’ All team repos in one place â€” scouting, robot, docs
  â†’ FREE for public repos, very cheap for private

Strongly recommend: Set up a GitHub Org for your team
  â†’ Go to github.com â†’ + â†’ New Organization â†’ Free plan
\`\`\`

## Essential GitHub Features for FIRST Teams
\`\`\`
Issues:
  â†’ Bug tracker â€” "Arm encoder resets during auto (Issue #42)"
  â†’ Assign to a team member, label by priority
  â†’ Close with a commit message: "Fixes #42"

Pull Requests:
  â†’ Code review before merging to main
  â†’ Required for branches â†’ keeps main stable

GitHub Releases:
  â†’ Tag competition builds: "comp-regional-2025"
  â†’ Download APK artifacts without needing Android Studio

GitHub Actions (CI):
  â†’ Auto-build on every push â€” catch broken code immediately
  â†’ See previous lesson on CI/CD setup
\`\`\`

## Protecting the Main Branch
\`\`\`
Settings â†’ Branches â†’ Branch protection rules:
  âœ… Require pull request before merging (prevents direct commits)
  âœ… Require 1 approval before merging
  âœ… Require status checks (CI build must pass)
  
This one-time setup prevents the "someone pushed broken code
to main the night before competition" crisis.

        {q:"What does branch protection ('require pull request before merging') prevent?",opts:["It prevents deleting branches","Direct commits to the main branch â€” ensuring all changes go through code review before reaching the competition-ready codebase","It prevents force pushes","It slows down development"],ans:1},

      ]},

      {id:"jb_threads2",title:"Basic Threading for FTC Sensors",est:"14 min",content:`## Why Thread a Sensor Read?
Some sensors are slow â€” a color sensor or distance sensor blocking your main loop for 20ms can cause noticeable lag. Threading lets slow sensors run in the background while your robot stays responsive.

## The Problem Without Threading
\`\`\`java
// âŒ This blocks your entire loop for however long the read takes
while (opModeIsActive()) {
    double dist = slowSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM); // might take 20-50ms
    leftMotor.setPower(gamepad1.left_stick_y); // delayed!
    telemetry.update();
}
\`\`\`

## Simple Background Sensor Thread
\`\`\`java
// Shared volatile variable â€” safe to read from main thread
volatile double latestDistance = 0;
volatile boolean threadRunning = true;

Thread sensorThread = new Thread(() -> {
    while (threadRunning && !isStopRequested()) {
        latestDistance = distanceSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM);
        // Small sleep to avoid hammering the sensor
        try { Thread.sleep(25); } catch (InterruptedException e) { break; }
    }
});

@Override
public void runOpMode() {
    // Start sensor thread before waitForStart
    sensorThread.setDaemon(true);
    sensorThread.start();
    waitForStart();

    while (opModeIsActive()) {
        // Main loop reads the cached value â€” no blocking!
        if (latestDistance < 15.0) robot.stop();
        leftMotor.setPower(gamepad1.left_stick_y);
        telemetry.addData("Dist", latestDistance);
        telemetry.update();
    }

    threadRunning = false; // signal thread to exit
}
\`\`\`

## volatile Keyword â€” Why It Matters
\`\`\`java
// Without volatile:
double latestDistance = 0; // CPU may cache this in a register
// Thread A writes 23.5, but Thread B still reads cached 0.0!

// With volatile:
volatile double latestDistance = 0;
// Forces every read/write to go to main memory â€” always current value
\`\`\`

## Thread Safety Rules for FTC
\`\`\`
âœ… Read/write a single primitive (int, double, boolean) with volatile
âœ… Use daemon threads â€” they die when the OpMode ends
âœ… Only read sensor hardware from ONE thread (the sensor thread)
âœ… Only write to motors/servos from the MAIN thread

âŒ Never call telemetry.update() from a background thread
âŒ Never set motor power from two threads simultaneously
âŒ Avoid shared mutable objects without synchronization
\`\`\`
Generics let you write one class or method that works with any type. Instead of writing a separate list for Doubles, Integers, and Strings, you write one list that works for all of them.

## The Problem Generics Solve
\`\`\`java
// Without generics â€” need a separate class for each type:
class DoubleRingBuffer { double[] data; ... }
class IntRingBuffer    { int[]    data; ... }
class StringRingBuffer { String[] data; ... }

// With generics â€” one class works for all:
class RingBuffer<T> { T[] data; ... }
\`\`\`

## A Generic Ring Buffer for Sensor Smoothing
\`\`\`java
public class RingBuffer<T extends Number> {
    private final Object[] buffer;
    private int head = 0;
    private int size = 0;
    private final int capacity;

    public RingBuffer(int capacity) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.buffer   = new Object[capacity];
    }

    public void add(T value) {
        buffer[head] = value;
        head = (head + 1) % capacity;
        if (size < capacity) size++;
    }

    public double average() {
        if (size == 0) return 0;
        double sum = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            sum += ((Number) buffer[i]).doubleValue();
        }
        return sum / size;
    }

    public int size() { return size; }
}

// Usage â€” works for any Number type:
RingBuffer<Double> distFilter = new RingBuffer<>(5);
distFilter.add(distanceSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM));
distFilter.add(distanceSensor.getDistance(DistanceUnit.CM));
double smoothed = distFilter.average(); // average of last 5 readings
\`\`\`

## Generic Pair â€” Store Two Related Values
\`\`\`java
public class Pair<A, B> {
    public final A first;
    public final B second;
    public Pair(A first, B second) {
        this.first  = first;
        this.second = second;
    }
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + first + ", " + second + ")";
    }
}

// Usage:
Pair<String, Double> sensorReading = new Pair<>("distance", 23.5);
Pair<Integer, Boolean> encoderState = new Pair<>(1487, true);
telemetry.addData(sensorReading.first, sensorReading.second);
\`\`\`

## When to Use Generics
- When your class or method logic doesn't depend on the specific type
- When you'd otherwise copy-paste the same class for different types
- Standard Java collections (ArrayList, HashMap) all use generics`,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the main benefit of a generic RingBuffer<T> over separate DoubleRingBuffer and IntRingBuffer classes?",opts:["Generics are faster","One generic class handles all numeric types â€” eliminates code duplication and ensures bug fixes apply everywhere simultaneously","Generics use less memory","Java requires generics for collections"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does <T extends Number> in the class declaration enforce?",opts:["T must be exactly Number","T must be Number or a subclass of it (Double, Integer, Float) â€” prevents using the buffer with non-numeric types like String that can't be averaged","T can be any type","It makes the class abstract"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why is a ring buffer useful for smoothing noisy sensor readings?",opts:["It stores infinite values","It maintains a fixed-size window of the most recent readings â€” averaging them filters momentary spikes while still tracking real changes in sensor value","Ring buffers are required for sensors","It compresses sensor data"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ji_auto_chooser",title:"Autonomous Mode Selector at Init",est:"15 min",content:`## The Problem: One Auto for All Situations
Different matches call for different autonomous strategies â€” left vs right start, park only vs full auto, red vs blue alliance. Hard-coding one auto wastes opportunities.

## Telemetry-Based Chooser (No Dashboard)
\`\`\`java
enum AutoMode {
    FULL_AUTO_LEFT,
    FULL_AUTO_RIGHT,
    PARK_ONLY,
    DO_NOTHING
}

AutoMode selectedMode = AutoMode.FULL_AUTO_LEFT;

@Override
public void runOpMode() {
    telemetry.addLine("=== AUTO SELECTOR ===");
    telemetry.addLine("DPAD UP/DOWN to change mode");
    telemetry.addLine("Press START to lock in");

    // Selection loop â€” runs until Start pressed
    while (!isStarted() && !isStopRequested()) {
        if (gamepad1.dpad_up   && !prevUp)   selectedMode = nextMode(selectedMode, 1);
        if (gamepad1.dpad_down && !prevDown)  selectedMode = nextMode(selectedMode, -1);
        prevUp   = gamepad1.dpad_up;
        prevDown = gamepad1.dpad_down;

        telemetry.addData("Selected", selectedMode.name());
        telemetry.addData("Modes",
            "LEFT | RIGHT | PARK | NOTHING");
        telemetry.update();
    }

    waitForStart();

    // Run the chosen auto
    switch (selectedMode) {
        case FULL_AUTO_LEFT:  runFullAutoLeft();  break;
        case FULL_AUTO_RIGHT: runFullAutoRight(); break;
        case PARK_ONLY:       runParkOnly();      break;
        case DO_NOTHING:      break;
    }
}

AutoMode nextMode(AutoMode current, int direction) {
    AutoMode[] values = AutoMode.values();
    int next = (current.ordinal() + direction + values.length) % values.length;
    return values[next];
}
\`\`\`

## FTC Dashboard Chooser (if Dashboard is installed)

}

SmartDashboard.putData("Auto Mode", autoChooser);

// In autonomousInit():

if (selectedAuto != null) selectedAuto.schedule();

        {q:"What does the volatile keyword guarantee when sharing a variable between two threads?",opts:["It makes the variable constant","Every read and write goes directly to main memory â€” prevents threads from seeing stale cached values of the variable","It locks the variable to one thread","It doubles the variable's size"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should motor power only be set from the main thread, not the sensor thread?",opts:["Motors can't read from other threads","Calling setPower from two threads simultaneously causes race conditions â€” the motor controller receives conflicting commands and behavior becomes unpredictable","It's required by FTC SDK","The sensor thread is too slow"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does setDaemon(true) do to a thread, and why is it important for FTC?",opts:["It makes the thread run faster","A daemon thread automatically terminates when the main program exits â€” without it, the sensor thread keeps running after the OpMode ends, potentially causing issues with the next run","It gives the thread higher priority","It prevents the thread from sleeping"],ans:1},
Many teams tune PID by randomly changing values until it "feels right." Systematic tuning converges to good values in 15 minutes instead of hours.

## The Four-Step Tuning Process
\`\`\`
Step 1: Start with all gains at zero
  kP = 0, kI = 0, kD = 0

Step 2: Increase kP until oscillation
  Slowly increase kP by small increments (e.g., 0.001 for arm position)
  Target: mechanism moves toward setpoint but oscillates (overshoots back and forth)
  Note the oscillating kP value = kP_crit

Step 3: Add kD to damp oscillation
  Start kD at approximately kP / 10
  Increase until oscillation stops and response is critically damped
  (Reaches setpoint without overshoot, or with one small overshoot)

Step 4: Add kI only if steady-state error persists
  If mechanism stops 5-10 encoder ticks short of target under load:
  Add small kI (e.g., 0.00001) and monitor for wind-up
  Add integral clamping: integral = Math.max(-MAX, Math.min(MAX, integral))
\`\`\`

## Gain Values by Mechanism Type
\`\`\`
These are starting ranges â€” your robot will differ:

Drive heading correction (degrees):
  kP â‰ˆ 0.010â€“0.025
  kD â‰ˆ 0.001â€“0.005
  kI â‰ˆ 0 (rarely needed)

Arm position (encoder ticks):
  kP â‰ˆ 0.005â€“0.015
  kD â‰ˆ 0.0005â€“0.002
  kI â‰ˆ 0.0001 (only if sag under load)

Velocity control (RPM):
  kP â‰ˆ 0.0001â€“0.001 (very small â€” RPM errors are large numbers)
  kI â‰ˆ 0.00001
  kD â‰ˆ 0 (derivative of velocity = jerk, usually unhelpful)
\`\`\`

## Diagnosing Common PID Problems
\`\`\`
Symptom â†’ Cause â†’ Fix
â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
Oscillates (constant back-and-forth)
  â†’ kP too high OR kD too low
  â†’ Reduce kP 20% OR increase kD 50%

Overshoots once, then settles
  â†’ kD slightly too low â†’ increase kD 10-20%
  â†’ Usually acceptable behavior

Crawls to target very slowly
  â†’ kP too low â†’ increase kP 50%

Stops short of target (steady-state error)
  â†’ Load opposing the motor â†’ add kG feedforward
  â†’ Or add small kI with anti-windup

Violent initial jump then normal behavior
  â†’ kP way too high â†’ halve kP immediately
  â†’ Or derivative kick from sudden setpoint change â†’ use setpoint ramping
\`\`\`

## Using FTC Dashboard for Live Tuning
\`\`\`java
@Config
public class ArmPID {
    public static double kP = 0.008;
    public static double kI = 0.0;
    public static double kD = 0.002;
    public static double kG = 0.12;
    public static int    TARGET = 800;
}
// Change values in browser while robot runs â€” see response immediately
// No redeploying needed. This cuts tuning sessions from 2 hours to 20 min.

        {q:"Why run the selection loop with 'while (!isStarted())' rather than just checking once?",opts:["isStarted() is unreliable","The loop allows the driver to scroll through options repeatedly and confirm their choice before pressing Start â€” a single check would lock in the default before any selection","It's required by FTC SDK","Loop gives more processing time"],ans:1},

        {q:"In the four-step tuning process, why is kD added before kI?",opts:["kD is always more important","kD reduces the oscillation caused by high kP, bringing the system to stability â€” adding kI before damping the oscillation causes the integral term to wind up wildly and make control worse","The order doesn't matter","kI requires kD to function"],ans:1},

        {q:"Why is integral anti-windup (clamping the integral variable) important when using kI?",opts:["It speeds up response","If the error persists for a long time (e.g., mechanism blocked), the integral accumulates to enormous values â€” when the block clears, the accumulated integral causes violent overshoot that takes seconds to recover from","Anti-windup is optional","It prevents the integral from being negative"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"ja_pathplanner",title:"PathPlanner Integration (FRC)",est:"28 min",content:`## What is PathPlanner?
PathPlanner is a GUI path-planning tool for FRC that lets you draw autonomous paths visually and generates WPILib-compatible trajectory code. It handles all the spline math and generates both the path and the follower commands.

## Installing PathPlanner
\`\`\`groovy
// build.gradle (inside dependencies block):
implementation "com.pathplanner.lib:pathplannerlib:2024.2.8"
// Check github.com/mjansen4857/pathplanner for latest version
\`\`\`

## Creating a Path in the GUI
\`\`\`
1. Download PathPlanner from pathplanner.me
2. Open your robot project folder
3. Create new path:
   â†’ Set field image to current year's field
   â†’ Click to place waypoints
   â†’ Drag control handles to shape curves
   â†’ Set max velocity (m/s) and max acceleration (m/sÂ²) per path
   â†’ Name the path: "Score1_Pickup"
4. Paths save to deploy/pathplanner/paths/ in your project
   â†’ They're deployed to the robot with your code automatically
\`\`\`

## Running a PathPlanner Path (WPILib Java)
\`\`\`java
import com.pathplanner.lib.auto.AutoBuilder;
import com.pathplanner.lib.path.PathPlannerPath;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj2.command.Command;

// In DriveSubsystem constructor â€” configure AutoBuilder once:
AutoBuilder.configureHolonomic(
    this::getPose,           // method to get current robot pose
    this::resetPose,         // method to reset odometry to a pose
    this::getRobotRelativeSpeeds, // ChassisSpeeds getter
    this::driveRobotRelative,     // ChassisSpeeds consumer
    new HolonomicPathFollowerConfig(
        new PIDConstants(5.0, 0.0, 0.0), // translation PID
        new PIDConstants(5.0, 0.0, 0.0), // rotation PID
        4.5, // max module speed (m/s)
        0.4, // drive base radius (m) â€” center to wheel
        new ReplanningConfig()
    ),
    () -> {
        // Mirror path for red alliance
        var alliance = DriverStation.getAlliance();
        return alliance.isPresent() && alliance.get() == Alliance.Red;
    },
    this // the drive subsystem (requirement)
);
\`\`\`

## Building a Full Auto Routine
\`\`\`java
// In RobotContainer:
public Command getAutonomousCommand() {
    // Load paths from deploy folder:
    PathPlannerPath path1 = PathPlannerPath.fromPathFile("Score1_Pickup");
    PathPlannerPath path2 = PathPlannerPath.fromPathFile("Pickup_Score2");

    return new SequentialCommandGroup(
        AutoBuilder.followPath(path1),
        new ScoreCommand(arm, scorer),  // score at first position
        AutoBuilder.followPath(path2),
        new ScoreCommand(arm, scorer)   // score at second position
    );
}
\`\`\`

## Named Commands â€” GUI-Triggered Events
\`\`\`java
// Register commands by name â€” trigger from PathPlanner GUI at any path point:
NamedCommands.registerCommand("RaiseArm",
    new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.HIGH_SCORE));
NamedCommands.registerCommand("Score",
    new RunIntakeCommand(intake, -1.0).withTimeout(0.4));
NamedCommands.registerCommand("LowerArm",
    new MoveArmCommand(arm, ArmSubsystem.STOWED));

// In the GUI: right-click on path point â†’ "Add event marker" â†’ type "RaiseArm"
// PathPlanner triggers the command at that point automatically

        {q:"What do 'Named Commands' in PathPlanner allow you to do?",opts:["Name your robot","Trigger subsystem commands at specific points along a path directly from the GUI â€” e.g., raise the arm exactly when the robot arrives at the scoring position","Rename path files","Set maximum velocity"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why does the alliance-flip lambda (checking for Red alliance) matter in AutoBuilder setup?",opts:["Red alliance scores differently","FRC fields are symmetric â€” a path designed for Blue alliance must be mirrored for Red alliance to follow the same game-relative route; this lambda tells PathPlanner when to flip automatically","Red alliance starts on the left","Alliance flipping is optional"],ans:1},
      ]},
