      {id:"eb_solder2",title:"Advanced Soldering â€” Connectors & Heat Shrink",est:"14 min",content:`## Beyond the Basics
Once you can solder two wires together, the next skill is soldering connectors cleanly â€” XT30, Anderson PP15, JST, and servo connectors that survive a competition season.

## XT30 Connectors (FTC Battery)
\`\`\`
XT30 = standard FTC battery connector (30A rating)
Male side (with pins) = typically on the battery side
Female side (sockets) = on the robot wiring harness

Soldering process:
  1. Tin the connector pin: touch iron to pin, touch solder to pin (not iron)
     until solder flows smoothly â€” takes ~2 sec at 380Â°C
  2. Tin the wire: strip 4mm, tin the strands together
  3. Pre-heat the pin, insert tinned wire, touch solder â€” should flow immediately
  4. Hold still for 3 seconds until solder solidifies
  5. Do NOT blow on it â€” thermal shock causes cold joints
  6. Inspect: shiny, smooth joint = good; dull/grainy = cold joint (redo it)

Heat shrink sequence:
  1. Slide heat shrink onto wire BEFORE soldering
  2. Solder connector
  3. Slide heat shrink over joint
  4. Apply heat gun 1-2 seconds â€” shrinks to seal
  5. Never use a lighter â€” uneven heat melts the wire insulation
\`\`\`

## Anderson PP15 (FRC Power)
\`\`\`
PP15 powerpole connectors carry main FRC drive current.
These are crimped, not soldered â€” requires a proper crimping tool.

Crimp process:
  1. Strip 8mm of insulation from 12 AWG wire
  2. Insert into PP15 contact, verify wire fills the barrel
  3. Crimp with Anderson/IWISS PP15 crimper â€” one firm squeeze
  4. Tug test: wire should NOT pull out with hand force
  5. Insert contact into housing until it clicks
  6. Check: pull the contact back out with a pick tool â€” it should resist

Common mistake: using pliers instead of proper crimper
  â†’ Pliers crush unevenly â†’ contact fails under vibration
\`\`\`

## JST Connectors (Sensor Wiring)
\`\`\`
JST connectors are small (1.25mm or 2.54mm pitch) â€” used for sensors,
encoders, and small servo/signal wiring.

For JST-PH (2mm pitch, standard FTC sensor connector):
  â†’ Use a dedicated JST crimp tool (PA-09 or similar)
  â†’ Never solder into the tiny JST contacts â€” heat damage is likely
  â†’ Pre-made JST pigtails with tinned wire ends are available and save time

For robot wiring: buy pre-wired JST harnesses and solder the OTHER
                  end to your PCB or connector â€” avoid crimping JST if possible
\`\`\`

## Heat Shrink Sizing Guide
\`\`\`
Wire gauge â†’ heat shrink diameter (expanded â†’ shrunk):
  28-24 AWG: 1/16" (1.6mm)
  22-18 AWG: 3/32" (2.4mm)
  16-14 AWG: 1/8"  (3.2mm)
  12-10 AWG: 3/16" (4.8mm)

Buy 3:1 ratio heat shrink for connectors (shrinks to 1/3 diameter)
Use 2:1 ratio for straight wire (cheaper, enough for insulation)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should heat shrink tubing be slid onto the wire before soldering, not after?",opts:["It protects the wire during soldering","The connector body is larger than the heat shrink bore â€” it cannot slide past the soldered connector after the joint is made; it must be pre-positioned on the wire first","Heat shrink melts during soldering","Post-solder application is standard practice"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is wrong with using standard pliers to crimp Anderson PP15 contacts?",opts:["Pliers aren't strong enough","Pliers apply uneven pressure, crushing the contact asymmetrically â€” a proper crimping tool deforms the barrel uniformly around the wire for reliable contact that won't fail under vibration","Pliers are fine for large contacts","Anderson contacts don't require crimping"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does a dull or grainy solder joint indicate and how is it fixed?",opts:["It indicates a strong joint","A cold solder joint â€” the joint cooled while disturbed or the connection wasn't hot enough when solder was applied; reheat the joint until solder flows liquid and allow it to cool undisturbed","Grainy appearance is normal for thick wire","It means too much solder was used"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ea_pid_hardware",title:"Hardware PID on SPARK MAX & TalonFX",est:"20 min",content:`## Why Hardware PID?
Software PID runs at the roboRIO's 50Hz loop. Hardware PID runs on the motor controller at 1kHz â€” 20Ã— faster. For precise position and velocity control, hardware PID wins every time.

## SPARK MAX Closed-Loop Control
\`\`\`java
import com.revrobotics.CANSparkMax;
import com.revrobotics.SparkPIDController;
import com.revrobotics.RelativeEncoder;

CANSparkMax motor = new CANSparkMax(1, MotorType.kBrushless);
motor.restoreFactoryDefaults();

RelativeEncoder encoder = motor.getEncoder();
SparkPIDController pid   = motor.getPIDController();

// Slot 0 â€” position control gains:
pid.setP(0.1,    0); // slot 0
pid.setI(0.0,    0);
pid.setD(0.005,  0);
pid.setFF(0.0,   0);
pid.setIZone(0,  0);             // integral only acts within Â±IZone ticks
pid.setOutputRange(-0.8, 0.8, 0);

// Slot 1 â€” velocity control gains:
pid.setP(0.0001, 1);
pid.setI(0.0,    1);
pid.setD(0.0,    1);
pid.setFF(0.000156, 1); // FF = 1/maxRPM (typical)
pid.setOutputRange(-1.0, 1.0, 1);

motor.burnFlash(); // persist to flash

// Position control (slot 0):
pid.setReference(200.0, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kPosition, 0);

// Velocity control (slot 1):
pid.setReference(3000.0, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kVelocity, 1);

// Smart motion (trapezoidal profile built-in!):
pid.setSmartMotionMaxVelocity(4000, 0);  // RPM
pid.setSmartMotionMaxAccel(2000, 0);      // RPM/sec
pid.setSmartMotionAllowedClosedLoopError(5, 0); // ticks
pid.setReference(500.0, CANSparkMax.ControlType.kSmartMotion, 0);
// Robot handles the profile â€” smoother than step command
\`\`\`

## TalonFX / Kraken (CTRE Phoenix 6)
\`\`\`java
import com.ctre.phoenix6.hardware.TalonFX;
import com.ctre.phoenix6.controls.PositionVoltage;
import com.ctre.phoenix6.controls.VelocityVoltage;
import com.ctre.phoenix6.configs.TalonFXConfiguration;

TalonFX motor = new TalonFX(1); // CAN ID 1
TalonFXConfiguration cfg = new TalonFXConfiguration();

// Position PID slot 0:
cfg.Slot0.kP = 24.0;   // Volts per rotation of error
cfg.Slot0.kI = 0.0;
cfg.Slot0.kD = 0.5;
cfg.Slot0.kV = 0.12;   // Volts per RPS (feedforward)
cfg.Slot0.kS = 0.25;   // Static friction compensation (Volts)

// Motion Magic (TalonFX trapezoidal profile):
cfg.MotionMagic.MotionMagicCruiseVelocity = 80; // RPS
cfg.MotionMagic.MotionMagicAcceleration   = 160; // RPS/sec
cfg.MotionMagic.MotionMagicJerk           = 1600; // RPS/secÂ² (smooth start/end)

motor.getConfigurator().apply(cfg);

// Request position (rotations):
PositionVoltage posReq = new PositionVoltage(0).withSlot(0);
motor.setControl(posReq.withPosition(5.0)); // go to 5 rotations

// Request velocity (RPS):
VelocityVoltage velReq = new VelocityVoltage(0).withSlot(0);
motor.setControl(velReq.withVelocity(30.0)); // 30 rotations/sec
\`\`\`

## Tuning Hardware PID â€” Key Difference from Software
\`\`\`
SPARK MAX position (rotations):
  kP ~ 0.05â€“0.2 (Volts output per rotation of error)
  kD ~ 0.001â€“0.01

TalonFX (Phoenix 6):
  kP ~ 10â€“30 (Volts per rotation of error â€” much larger because units differ)
  kS = measure: minimum voltage to move at all (overcome static friction)
  kV = 1 / (free speed in RPS) â€” theoretical, then fine-tune

Always verify units: SPARK MAX uses RPM, TalonFX uses RPS in Phoenix 6.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the key performance advantage of hardware PID on a SPARK MAX or TalonFX over software PID on the roboRIO?",opts:["Hardware PID is more accurate","Hardware PID runs at ~1kHz on the motor controller vs ~50Hz on the roboRIO â€” 20Ã— faster feedback allows much tighter position and velocity control, especially for fast mechanisms","Hardware PID uses less power","Software PID can't control position"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does Smart Motion (SPARK MAX) or Motion Magic (TalonFX) do beyond basic position PID?",opts:["It selects the best PID gains automatically","It applies a built-in trapezoidal velocity profile â€” the controller ramps velocity smoothly to the target instead of commanding full power immediately, reducing current spikes and mechanical shock","It's the same as regular position control","It requires no tuning"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the kS (static friction) gain in TalonFX Phoenix 6 compensate for?",opts:["The motor's inductance","The minimum voltage needed to overcome static friction and start moving â€” without kS, the PID output near zero error isn't enough to move the mechanism and it stalls short of the target","kS adjusts the velocity feed-forward","It's the same as kI"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"sb_endgame",title:"Endgame Strategy & Timing",est:"12 min",content:`## Endgame Points Are Often Decisive
In many FRC and FTC games, the endgame phase (last 30 seconds) awards the most points per action. A team that efficiently executes a consistent endgame climb outperforms a team that scores 3 more cycles but misses the climb.

## Calculating the Endgame Break-Even
\`\`\`
Example: Climb worth 15 pts. Takes 20 seconds.
         Teleop cycle = 4 pts. Takes 10 seconds.

In 20 seconds you could score: 2 cycles Ã— 4 = 8 pts
Climb scores: 15 pts
â†’ Climb is worth 7 more pts â€” start climbing at T-20!

If cycle takes 8 seconds (fast cycler):
  20 sec / 8 sec = 2.5 cycles = 10 pts
  Climb = 15 pts â†’ still worth climbing at T-20

If cycle takes 5 seconds (very fast):
  20 sec / 5 sec = 4 cycles = 16 pts > 15 â†’ keep cycling until T-15!
  Then climb for the remaining 15 seconds

Your endgame start time = climb time + safety buffer
Calculate this before every event, not during a match.
\`\`\`

## Consistent Endgame vs Optimized Endgame
\`\`\`
Optimized approach (risky):
  â†’ Try L3 climb every match for 30 pts
  â†’ Succeed 50% of matches â†’ 15 pts average
  â†’ L2 is 20 pts, 90% success â†’ 18 pts average
  â†’ L2 is MORE VALUABLE for seeding despite lower peak

Consistency rule: choose the highest climb level you can achieve
                  9 out of 10 practice attempts.
\`\`\`

## Alliance Endgame Coordination
\`\`\`
Two robots climbing the same structure can collide.
Before elimination match:
  â†’ Robot A starts climb at T-25 (faster climber)
  â†’ Robot B starts at T-20 (slightly slower)
  â†’ Robot A signals done by flashing LEDs or radio call
  â†’ If A fails at T-10: B makes decision to assist or not

Simple rule: if you have a communication system, use it.
             If not, agree on fixed start times and stick to them.
\`\`\`

## Endgame Reliability Testing Protocol
\`\`\`
The climb should be tested 10 times in a row from:
  â†’ Battery at 100% charge
  â†’ Battery at 50% charge (lower voltage = slower motors)
  â†’ With alliance partner robot parked nearby (space constraints)
  â†’ With driver who hasn't climbed recently (muscle memory check)

If success rate drops below 9/10 â†’ fix the mechanism before competition.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"How do you calculate when to start your endgame routine during a match?",opts:["Always start at T-30","Add your climb time plus a safety buffer â€” e.g., a 20-second climb needs to start at T-25 or earlier to complete reliably before time expires","Start when you feel ready","Start only after your alliance partner finishes"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why might a consistent L2 climb (90% success rate) be strategically better than an attempted L3 climb (50% success)?",opts:["L2 is always worth more","Expected value: L2 at 90% = 18 expected pts; L3 at 50% of its 30pt value = 15 expected pts â€” consistent lower scores beat unreliable higher scores in seeding math","L3 is always attempted in elims","L2 is worth 30 points"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the purpose of testing the endgame climb with the battery at 50% charge?",opts:["To see if the battery needs replacing","Motor speed decreases with voltage â€” a climb that works perfectly on a fresh battery may fail or time out on a depleted end-of-day battery; testing at 50% reveals this before competition","50% is the required test level","Battery level doesn't affect motors"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"sa_meta_analysis",title:"Cross-Event Meta Analysis",est:"20 min",content:`## What the Whole Season Tells You
Regional scouting data is local â€” it only tells you about the teams at that event. Championship scouting requires understanding the global meta: which robots and strategies consistently win across all events.

## Building a Cross-Event Dataset
\`\`\`python
import requests
import pandas as pd

API_KEY = "your_tba_key"
YEAR    = 2025

def get_all_event_teams(year):
    """Get all events and their teams for the year."""
    events = requests.get(
        f"https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/events/{year}/simple",
        headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": API_KEY}
    ).json()
    return [e["key"] for e in events if e["event_type"] in [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]]
    # Types 0-4: regionals, districts, district champs

def get_team_event_awards(team, year):
    awards = requests.get(
        f"https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/frc{team}/awards/{year}",
        headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": API_KEY}
    ).json()
    return [a["award_type"] for a in awards]
\`\`\`

## Identifying Championship-Level Teams
\`\`\`python
def team_season_record(team, year):
    matches = requests.get(
        f"https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/team/frc{team}/matches/{year}",
        headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": API_KEY}
    ).json()
    wins = losses = ties = 0
    for m in matches:
        if m["comp_level"] != "qm" or m["alliances"] is None:
            continue
        for color in ["red", "blue"]:
            if f"frc{team}" in m["alliances"][color]["team_keys"]:
                opp = "blue" if color == "red" else "red"
                us   = m["alliances"][color]["score"]
                them = m["alliances"][opp]["score"]
                if us > them:   wins   += 1
                elif us < them: losses += 1
                else:           ties   += 1
    total = wins + losses + ties
    return {"team": team, "wins": wins, "losses": losses,
            "win_rate": wins/total if total > 0 else 0,
            "matches": total}

# Build season records for all championship-qualifying teams:
records = pd.DataFrame([team_season_record(t, YEAR) for t in champ_teams])
records = records.sort_values("win_rate", ascending=False)
\`\`\`

      {id:"sfi_pneumatics",title:"Pneumatic Safety in FRC",est:"14 min",content:`## Pneumatics Are High-Risk if Mishandled
A pneumatic system stores compressed air at 120 PSI working pressure. A failed fitting at that pressure is a serious safety event. FIRST's pneumatic rules exist because these risks are real.

## FRC Pneumatic System Overview
\`\`\`
Storage: tanks at up to 120 PSI (FIRST legal max)
Working: downstream regulator set to â‰¤ 60 PSI
Safety:  relief valve set to open at 125 PSI maximum

Components:
  Compressor â†’ check valve â†’ storage tank â†’ pressure switch
    â†’ manual shutoff valve â†’ regulator â†’ solenoids â†’ cylinders
  Relief valve at storage tank (mandatory safety device)
\`\`\`

## Safe Handling Practices
\`\`\`
When pressurizing for the first time:
  âœ… Stand to the side of the system (not in line with fittings)
  âœ… Pressurize slowly â€” don't let compressor run to full immediately
  âœ… Listen for leaks (hissing) before reaching working pressure
  âœ… Check every fitting with soapy water â€” bubbles = leak

Leak detection:
  Spray or brush soapy water on every push-connect and threaded fitting
  Tiny leaks cause: inconsistent mechanism, compressor running constantly,
                   pressure loss mid-match at critical moment

NEVER:
  âŒ Point a pressurized fitting at anyone
  âŒ Use damaged or kinked tubing
  âŒ Exceed 60 PSI downstream of regulator
  âŒ Defeat the pressure relief valve
  âŒ Work on a pressurized system â€” depressurize completely first
\`\`\`

## Depressurization Procedure
\`\`\`
Before ANY maintenance on pneumatic components:
  1. Turn off compressor (software or main breaker)
  2. Actuate all cylinders to release downstream pressure
  3. Open the manual bleed valve on the storage tank
  4. Wait until gauge reads 0 PSI
  5. Verify with a second person: "System is depressurized"
  6. Only THEN remove any fitting, tubing, or component

Never assume low pressure just because the compressor is off â€”
stored tanks can hold pressure for hours after the robot is disabled.
\`\`\`

## Inspection Points (FRC Inspection)
\`\`\`
â–¡ Relief valve present and accessible
â–¡ Pressure switch set to cut off at â‰¤ 120 PSI
â–¡ Regulator set to â‰¤ 60 PSI downstream
â–¡ All tubing secured (not loose and unsupported)
â–¡ No damaged or kinked tubing
â–¡ Manual shutoff valve accessible from outside the robot
â–¡ All fittings leak-tested (soap test at inspection counts)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why must you stand to the side of a pneumatic fitting (not directly in front) when first pressurizing?",opts:["It's a FIRST rule","A fitting failure under pressure ejects in the direction it was facing â€” standing to the side removes you from the projectile path if a fitting fails during initial pressurization","Side access is easier","Pressure equalizes faster from the side"],ans:1},
        {q:"What is the correct depressurization procedure before working on any pneumatic component?",opts:["Turn off the compressor and wait 5 minutes","Turn off compressor, actuate cylinders to release pressure, open the manual bleed valve, wait for 0 PSI on the gauge, and verify with a second person â€” stored tanks hold pressure for hours after shutdown","Disconnect the battery only","Remove the component quickly before pressure builds"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why does a small air leak that seems minor actually cause serious competition problems?",opts:["Small leaks are never a problem","The compressor runs constantly to maintain pressure, draining battery capacity; the system may not maintain working pressure during a critical match action when the cylinder can't fully actuate","Leaks only matter if large","FIRST penalizes all leaks"],ans:1},
      ]},

      {id:"tmi_conflict2",title:"Technical Disagreements & Design Decisions",est:"15 min",content:`## The Hardest Disagreements Are Technical
Personal conflicts are uncomfortable. Technical disagreements feel worse because both sides think they're objectively right. A structured decision process resolves them faster and with less damage to the team.

## Why Technical Arguments Stall Teams
\`\`\`
Common patterns:
  â†’ "My design is better" (opinion presented as fact)
  â†’ "We've always done it this way" (tradition as argument)
  â†’ "I read it online" (unverified authority)
  â†’ "The veterans should decide" (authority substitutes for analysis)
  â†’ Argument continues until someone gives up (unhappy team)

None of these resolve the actual question: which design is better for THIS robot?
\`\`\`

## The Decision Framework
\`\`\`
Step 1: State the question as a requirement, not a preference
  âŒ "Should we use chain or belt drive?"
  âœ… "Which transmission is more reliable at 80W continuous load,
      given 4 sprocket/pulley changes and a 3-week build window?"

Step 2: List measurable criteria
  â†’ Reliability (failure rate over 100 matches)
  â†’ Build time (hours to complete)
  â†’ Adjustability (can we change tension at competition?)
  â†’ Cost
  â†’ Team experience with this system

Step 3: Rate each option on each criterion (1-5)
  Chain: Reliability 4, Build time 3, Adjustability 5, Cost 4, Experience 4
  Belt:  Reliability 4, Build time 4, Adjustability 2, Cost 3, Experience 2

Step 4: Weight criteria by what matters most for THIS robot
  (Reliability Ã— 3) + (Adjustability Ã— 2) + (Build time Ã— 1) + ...

Step 5: Make the decision â€” commit, don't revisit without new information
\`\`\`

## When to Prototype Instead of Argue
\`\`\`
If the disagreement is about real-world performance:
  â†’ Build BOTH options to minimum viable standard
  â†’ Test for the one metric that matters most
  â†’ Data decides

Example: "Will the intake work with 1" or 1.5" wheels?"
  â†’ Don't argue â€” build both in 1 hour and test on actual game pieces
  â†’ 10 pickup attempts each â†’ results resolve the argument in 2 hours
  â†’ Much faster than a meeting that could last 3 hours
\`\`\`

## After the Decision: No Second-Guessing
\`\`\`
After a decision is made by vote or data:
  âœ… Everyone supports the chosen path, even those who disagreed
  âœ… Concerns are logged: "If X happens by Week 3, we reconsider"
  âŒ Continued lobbying for the rejected option
  âŒ "I told you so" when problems arise (problems arise regardless of design)

Teams that relitigate every decision lose build time to meetings.
Teams that commit and iterate build better robots than teams that debate.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why does reframing a design argument as a specific requirement improve decision quality?",opts:["It's more polite","A requirement like 'must survive 100 matches at 80W' is measurable and testable â€” it removes opinion from the discussion and focuses both sides on verifiable criteria rather than preferences","Requirements take less time","It's required for engineering notebooks"],ans:1},
        {q:"When should a team prototype both options instead of continuing to argue about which is better?",opts:["Always â€” never argue","When the disagreement is about real-world performance that can be tested â€” a 2-hour prototype test often resolves arguments that a 3-hour meeting cannot because data replaces opinion","Only if the lead programmer agrees","Prototyping is always slower than deciding"],ans:1},
        {q:"What behavior should team members who disagreed with a decision avoid after the decision is made?",opts:["Continuing to support the robot","Continued lobbying for the rejected option or 'I told you so' when problems occur â€” both undermine team cohesion and don't help solve the actual problem that arises","Documenting their concerns","Testing the chosen design"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"cadi_bom",title:"Bill of Materials & Procurement Tracking",est:"14 min",content:`## The CAD-to-Parts Pipeline
A robot design is only as good as the parts you actually receive. Managing a BOM (Bill of Materials) from CAD to procurement to inventory prevents the "we designed it but can't build it" problem.

## Generating a BOM from Onshape
\`\`\`
Onshape has a built-in BOM tool:
  1. In Assembly, click the BOM icon (table icon in left toolbar)
  2. Onshape automatically lists all unique parts with quantities
  3. Add custom properties to each Part Studio:
     Part Properties â†’ Add Property â†’ "Vendor", "Part Number", "Unit Cost"
  4. Export BOM as CSV for procurement tracking

Organize part properties:
  Name:        Left Drive Motor
  Vendor:      GoBILDA
  Part #:      3213-3606-0014
  Unit cost:   $39.99
  Qty needed:  2
\`\`\`

## Procurement Tracking Spreadsheet
\`\`\`
Columns:
  Part Name | Vendor | Part # | Qty Needed | Qty On Hand | To Order | Unit Cost | Total Cost | Order Status | Notes

Status values:
  NOT ORDERED â†’ IN CART â†’ ORDERED â†’ SHIPPED â†’ RECEIVED â†’ INSTALLED

Formulas (Google Sheets):
  To Order = MAX(0, Qty Needed - Qty On Hand)
  Total Cost = To Order Ã— Unit Cost
  Budget remaining = Budget - SUM(Total Cost column)
\`\`\`

## Lead Time Planning
\`\`\`
Most common FIRST vendors' typical lead times (days):
  REV Robotics:     3-5 business days
  GoBILDA:          3-5 business days
  Amazon Prime:     1-2 days (limited selection)
  WCP/Andymark:     5-7 days
  McMaster-Carr:    1-3 days (vast hardware selection)
  Custom PCB fab:   10-14 days (JLCPCB economy)
  3D printed parts: 0 days (in-house) or 7-14 (service)

Order critical-path parts FIRST â€” parts that block other work.
Critical path example: motor must arrive before gearbox can be assembled
                       before arm can be built and tested.
\`\`\`

## Inventory Management During Build Season
\`\`\`
Running inventory system:
  â†’ One person owns inventory (not everyone digs through the parts bins)
  â†’ Parts checked out: sign the bin label with date and who took it
  â†’ End of each build session: verify critical spares are in the pit kit

Pit kit essentials (keep separate from main inventory):
  â†’ 2Ã— each motor type used
  â†’ 4Ã— servos
  â†’ Spare chain/belt (1 full length of each)
  â†’ 2Ã— each motor controller type
  â†’ Common fasteners (M3, 10-32, #6-32) Ã— 50 each
  â†’ Extra wire and connectors
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why should custom properties like Vendor and Part Number be added to Onshape parts rather than tracked separately?",opts:["Onshape requires them","When the BOM is exported, vendor and part number appear automatically with each part â€” no manual cross-referencing between the CAD model and a separate spreadsheet, reducing errors","Custom properties improve rendering","It speeds up the export"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does the 'To Order' formula MAX(0, Qty Needed - Qty On Hand) prevent?",opts:["Over-ordering by any amount","Negative order quantities â€” if you have 3 on hand and only need 2, the formula returns 0 rather than -1, preventing orders for parts you already have","It calculates cost automatically","It checks vendor stock"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should critical-path parts be ordered before non-critical parts when the budget allows ordering all of them?",opts:["Critical parts cost more","Critical-path parts block other work from starting â€” a motor that arrives late delays gearbox assembly, arm integration, and testing; non-critical parts can arrive later without affecting the schedule","Vendors ship critical parts faster","Order timing doesn't matter if budget is sufficient"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"awb_engineering_notebook",title:"Engineering Notebook â€” FTC Fundamentals",est:"14 min",content:`## The Notebook Is a Year-Long Project
Most teams start their engineering notebook in January. Top teams start on Day 1 of the season in September. The notebook is not a summary of the season â€” it's a live record of the engineering process as it happens.

## What to Record in Every Entry
\`\`\`
Each build session entry should include:
  Date:       Always â€” judges check for consistency
  Members:    Who was present (shows team breadth)
  Goal:       What were you trying to accomplish today?
  Work done:  What was actually built, tested, or programmed?
  Results:    Quantitative if possible (cycle time, success rate)
  Problems:   What failed or surprised you?
  Next steps: What will you do next based on today's results?
\`\`\`

## The Engineering Design Process in the Notebook
\`\`\`
Judges specifically look for evidence of:
  1. Problem identification (what does the game require?)
  2. Research (what solutions exist? what did other teams do?)
  3. Brainstorming (multiple possible approaches â€” show alternatives)
  4. Selection and justification (why did you choose this approach?)
  5. Build and test (iterative â€” show failures, not just successes)
  6. Evaluation (did it meet your original requirements?)

A notebook showing only the final successful design is weak.
A notebook showing 3 failed prototypes and why you changed direction is strong.
\`\`\`

## Format Rules (FTC)
\`\`\`
Required:
  â†’ Bound notebook (not loose-leaf â€” entries can't be added or removed)
  â†’ Hand-written or typed entries (both are acceptable)
  â†’ Dated entries in chronological order
  â†’ Engineering drawings or sketches with dimensions
  â†’ Photos of physical work with captions

Best practices:
  â†’ One person writes while others work (rotation responsibility)
  â†’ Add photos the same day â€” memory of context fades fast
  â†’ Use engineering sketch paper for drawings (grid or isometric)
  â†’ Cross-reference: "See Page 14 for the arm prototype failure"
\`\`\`

## Common Notebook Mistakes
\`\`\`
âŒ Writing it all at the end of the season from memory
âŒ Only showing successes â€” no failures, no iterations
âŒ Loose-leaf pages (can be judged as potentially out of order)
âŒ Undated entries
âŒ Photos without captions explaining what's being shown
âŒ One student's handwriting throughout (suggests one person wrote it all)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"Why is a notebook that shows three failed prototypes stronger than one showing only the final successful design?",opts:["Failures take more pages","Judges evaluate the engineering design process, not the final product â€” documented failures, analysis of why they failed, and design changes in response demonstrate genuine engineering thinking","Successful designs are harder to document","Three designs show more work"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why must FTC engineering notebooks be bound (not loose-leaf)?",opts:["Bound notebooks look more professional","A bound notebook prevents adding or removing pages â€” it ensures entries are genuinely in chronological order, giving judges confidence that the documentation wasn't rearranged or backdated","Loose-leaf is harder to carry","FIRST requires bound notebooks by law"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should rotating who writes the notebook entries strengthen your submission?",opts:["Multiple handwriting styles are prettier","Different handwriting and writing styles demonstrate that multiple team members are engaged â€” a notebook written entirely in one style suggests it was compiled by one person, not the whole team","Rotation is required","Each writer knows more about different topics"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },

      {id:"ori_metrics",title:"Tracking & Reporting Outreach Impact",est:"15 min",content:`## Numbers Tell the Story Judges Can't Ignore
"We do a lot of outreach" doesn't win awards. "We reached 847 students across 14 events in 6 schools, resulting in 3 new FLL teams representing 36 kids who had never competed before" wins awards.

## The Five Outreach Metrics to Track
\`\`\`
1. Reach (how many students?)
   â†’ Total unique students who participated in your activities
   â†’ Tip: count sign-in sheets, not rough crowd estimates

2. Events (how many?)
   â†’ Total outreach events run or participated in
   â†’ Separate: events you organized vs events you attended

3. Programs sustained (how many ongoing?)
   â†’ FLL/FTC teams you mentor
   â†’ Clubs or programs that now run independently

4. Depth (how intensive was engagement?)
   â†’ One-hour demo: low depth
   â†’ Weekly mentoring all season: high depth
   â†’ Report both â€” they tell different stories

5. Impact downstream
   â†’ Students who joined FIRST teams after your outreach
   â†’ Teachers you trained who now run programs
   â†’ Programs you started that continued without you
\`\`\`

      {id:"gi_rebase",title:"Git Rebase vs Merge â€” Keeping History Clean",est:"16 min",content:`## Two Ways to Integrate Changes
When your feature branch diverges from main, you need to bring in the latest changes. Merge and rebase both accomplish this â€” but leave very different histories.

## Merge â€” Preserves Branch History
\`\`\`bash
# You're on feature/arm-pid, main has new commits
git checkout feature/arm-pid
git merge main
# Creates a merge commit â€” history shows the branch and merge point

# History looks like:
# o---o---o  main
#      \\     \\
#       o--o--M  feature/arm-pid (M = merge commit)
\`\`\`

## Rebase â€” Linear History
\`\`\`bash
# Rebase your commits on top of main's latest
git checkout feature/arm-pid
git rebase main
# Re-applies your commits one by one on top of current main

# History looks like:
# o---o---o  main
#             \\
#              o'--o'  feature/arm-pid (commits replayed as o')
# Clean, linear â€” looks like you branched from the latest main
\`\`\`

## Interactive Rebase â€” Clean Up Before Pull Request
\`\`\`bash
# Squash 5 messy commits into 1 clean commit before merging:
git rebase -i HEAD~5
# Opens editor showing last 5 commits:
# pick a1b2c3 add arm PID
# pick d4e5f6 fix typo
# pick g7h8i9 fix another typo
# pick j0k1l2 add feedforward
# pick m3n4o5 tune kP

# Change to:
# pick a1b2c3 add arm PID
# squash d4e5f6 fix typo
# squash g7h8i9 fix another typo
# squash j0k1l2 add feedforward
# squash m3n4o5 tune kP

# Result: one clean commit "feat: arm PID with feedforward (tuned kP=0.009)"
\`\`\`

## When to Use Each
\`\`\`
Use MERGE when:
  â†’ The branch history is meaningful (shows a development arc)
  â†’ Working with external contributors (don't rebase their work)
  â†’ Merging completed feature into main (preserves PR history)

Use REBASE when:
  â†’ Updating your local feature branch with main's latest changes
  â†’ Cleaning up messy commit history before a PR (interactive rebase)
  â†’ You want a linear history for easier git bisect and log reading

NEVER rebase:
  â†’ Commits that have been pushed to a shared branch
  â†’ After other people have based work on your commits
  â†’ "Rebase rewrites history â€” only on your local/private work"
\`\`\`

## Resolving Rebase Conflicts
\`\`\`bash
git rebase main
# Conflict in src/ArmSubsystem.java
# Fix the conflict in the file, then:
git add src/ArmSubsystem.java
git rebase --continue
# If you want to abort and return to pre-rebase state:
git rebase --abort
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the main visual difference between git merge and git rebase in the repository history?",opts:["Merge is faster","Merge creates a branch structure with explicit merge commits showing where branches joined; rebase creates a linear history as if all commits happened sequentially on one branch","Rebase creates more commits","They produce identical histories"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why should you never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch?",opts:["It slows down git","Rebase rewrites commit hashes â€” if teammates have based work on the original commits, their history diverges from the rewritten history and the repository becomes difficult to reconcile","Push prevents rebasing","It deletes remote commits"],ans:1},
        {q:"What does interactive rebase (git rebase -i HEAD~5) allow you to do before submitting a pull request?",opts:["It rebases 5 branches at once","It lets you squash, reorder, edit, or drop the last 5 commits â€” useful for combining 'fix typo' and 'actually fix typo' into one clean commit before the PR history becomes permanent","It compares 5 branches","It cherry-picks 5 commits"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],
  },
};

      {id:"jb_arrays2",title:"Multidimensional Arrays & Lookup Tables",est:"12 min",content:`## Beyond 1D Arrays
A single array is a list. A 2D array is a table â€” rows and columns. In robotics, 2D arrays are perfect for lookup tables, field grids, and trajectory waypoints.

## Declaring and Accessing 2D Arrays
\`\`\`java
// Declare a 3Ã—4 grid (3 rows, 4 columns):
int[][] grid = new int[3][4];
grid[0][0] = 10;  // row 0, col 0

\`\`\`

## Autonomous Speed Lookup Table
\`\`\`java
// Map distance (inches) â†’ motor power for smooth deceleration
// Row 0 = distance thresholds, Row 1 = corresponding power
double[][] speedTable = {
    {72.0, 48.0, 24.0, 12.0, 6.0},   // distance from target
    { 0.8,  0.6,  0.4,  0.25, 0.15}  // drive power at that distance
};

public double getPowerForDistance(double distToTarget) {
    // Find the right power level for current distance:
    for (int i = 0; i < speedTable[0].length; i++) {
        if (distToTarget >= speedTable[0][i]) {
            return speedTable[1][i];
        }
    }
    return 0.1; // minimum power close to target
}
\`\`\`

## Field Zone Scoring Grid
\`\`\`java
// Represent the field as a scoring-value grid
// Value = points for placing a game piece in that zone
int[][] fieldValue = {
    {2, 3, 3, 2},   // row 0 (near alliance wall)
    {3, 5, 5, 3},   // row 1
    {4, 6, 6, 4},   // row 2 (center, high value)
};

// Find highest-value reachable zone:
int bestRow = 0, bestCol = 0, bestVal = 0;
for (int r = 0; r < fieldValue.length; r++) {
    for (int c = 0; c < fieldValue[r].length; c++) {
        if (fieldValue[r][c] > bestVal && isReachable(r, c)) {
            bestVal = fieldValue[r][c];
            bestRow = r; bestCol = c;
        }
    }
}
telemetry.addData("Target zone", bestRow + "," + bestCol + " (" + bestVal + " pts)");

      {id:"ji_fsm2",title:"Hierarchical State Machines",est:"18 min",content:`## Flat vs Hierarchical State Machines
A flat state machine works well up to ~8-10 states. More states create a web of transitions that's hard to follow and debug. Hierarchical state machines group related states into "super-states" with shared behavior.

## The Problem: Too Many States
\`\`\`java
// Flat â€” gets unwieldy fast:
enum RobotState {
    IDLE,
    DRIVING_TO_PICKUP, APPROACHING_PIECE, INTAKING, RETRYING_INTAKE,
    DRIVING_TO_SCORE, RAISING_ARM, AIMING, SCORING, RETRACTING_ARM,
    CLIMBING_STAGE1, CLIMBING_STAGE2, CLIMBING_STAGE3, CLIMB_COMPLETE
}
// 14 states, each needing transitions to/from many others
\`\`\`

## Hierarchical Approach â€” Super-States
\`\`\`java
// Two levels: SuperState â†’ SubState
enum SuperState { PICKUP, SCORING, CLIMBING, IDLE }
enum SubState   { DRIVING, APPROACHING, ACTING, RETRACTING, WAITING }

SuperState superState = SuperState.IDLE;
SubState   subState   = SubState.WAITING;

// Shared behavior lives in the super-state handler:
void update() {
    // Super-state: common behavior for all sub-states
    switch (superState) {
        case PICKUP:
            runIntakePreload(0.3);  // always spin intake slightly in pickup mode
            break;
        case SCORING:
            holdArmPosition();      // always hold arm when scoring
            break;
        case CLIMBING:
            disableDrive();         // always lock drive during climb
            break;
    }

    // Sub-state: specific phase within the super-state
    switch (superState) {
        case PICKUP:  updatePickup();  break;
        case SCORING: updateScoring(); break;
        case CLIMBING: updateClimb(); break;
    }
}

void updatePickup() {
    switch (subState) {
        case DRIVING:
            if (nearPickupZone()) transitionTo(SuperState.PICKUP, SubState.APPROACHING);
            break;
        case APPROACHING:
            if (pieceDetected()) transitionTo(SuperState.PICKUP, SubState.ACTING);
            break;
        case ACTING: // intaking
            if (hasPiece())      transitionTo(SuperState.SCORING, SubState.DRIVING);
            if (intakeTimeout())  transitionTo(SuperState.PICKUP,  SubState.DRIVING);
            break;
    }
}

void transitionTo(SuperState sup, SubState sub) {
    superState = sup; subState = sub;
    transitionTimer.reset();
}
\`\`\`

## Benefits
\`\`\`
Flat (14 states): 14Ã—13 = 182 possible transitions to consider
Hierarchical (4 super Ã— 5 sub): transitions mostly local to sub-states
                                 super-state handles global concerns

Debugging: "Robot stuck in SCORING / RAISING_ARM" is immediately clear
Shared behavior: changing arm hold behavior for ALL scoring states = 1 line change
\`\`\``,quiz:[
        {q:"What is the main advantage of hierarchical state machines over flat state machines for complex robot behavior?",opts:["Hierarchical machines run faster","Grouping related states into super-states reduces the number of transitions to reason about and allows shared behavior to be defined once at the super-state level rather than repeated in every sub-state","Flat machines have more bugs","Hierarchical machines require fewer enums"],ans:1},
        {q:"In a hierarchical state machine, where does behavior that should apply to ALL sub-states of a super-state belong?",opts:["In every sub-state individually","In the super-state handler â€” code there runs regardless of which sub-state is active, making it the right place for things like 'always hold arm position during any scoring sub-state'","In a separate utility method","In the transition function"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why does transitionTimer.reset() belong in the transitionTo() method rather than scattered in each case block?",opts:["It's optional","Resetting the timer at every transition in one place guarantees it's always reset when state changes â€” scattered resets can be forgotten in individual cases, causing incorrect timeout behavior","Timers must be reset externally","transitionTo doesn't support timers"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"ja_photon",title:"PhotonVision Pipeline Integration (FRC)",est:"24 min",content:`## PhotonVision â€” Full Vision on a Coprocessor
PhotonVision runs on a Raspberry Pi or similar coprocessor, processing camera frames for AprilTags or reflective targets at full rate without burdening the roboRIO. Results arrive via NetworkTables.

## Hardware Setup
\`\`\`
Coprocessor options (PhotonVision supported):
  Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB+) â€” most common, good performance
  Raspberry Pi 5 â€” best performance
  Orange Pi 5 â€” high performance, cost-effective

Camera options:
  Arducam OV9281 â€” global shutter, excellent for AprilTags
  Limelight 2+ â€” integrated hardware (alternate software option)
  USB webcams â€” supported but rolling shutter causes blur on movement

Flash PhotonVision to SD card â†’ insert â†’ connect via USB or Ethernet to robot network
Access UI at photonvision.local:5800 to configure pipelines
\`\`\`

## Adding PhotonLib to Your Robot Project
\`\`\`groovy
// build.gradle:
repositories {
    maven { url = uri("https://maven.photonvision.org/repository/internal") }
}
dependencies {
    implementation "org.photonvision:photonlib-java:v2024.3.1"
}
\`\`\`

## Basic AprilTag Detection
\`\`\`java
import org.photonvision.PhotonCamera;
import org.photonvision.targeting.PhotonTrackedTarget;

PhotonCamera camera = new PhotonCamera("OV9281"); // matches name in PhotonVision UI

@Override
public void periodic() {
    var result = camera.getLatestResult();

    if (result.hasTargets()) {
        PhotonTrackedTarget best = result.getBestTarget();

        int tagId      = best.getFiducialId();       // which AprilTag
        double yaw     = best.getYaw();              // degrees left/right
        double pitch   = best.getPitch();            // degrees up/down
        double area    = best.getArea();             // % of frame
        Transform3d pose = best.getBestCameraToTarget(); // 3D pose if configured

        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Tag ID",  tagId);
        SmartDashboard.putNumber("Tag Yaw", yaw);
    }
}
\`\`\`

## Multi-Tag Pose Estimation (Field Localization)
\`\`\`java
import org.photonvision.PhotonPoseEstimator;
import org.photonvision.PhotonPoseEstimator.PoseStrategy;
import edu.wpi.first.apriltag.AprilTagFieldLayout;
import edu.wpi.first.apriltag.AprilTagFields;
import edu.wpi.first.math.geometry.Transform3d;

AprilTagFieldLayout fieldLayout =
    AprilTagFieldLayout.loadFromResource(AprilTagFields.k2024Crescendo.m_resourceFile);

// Camera position relative to robot center (measure carefully!):
Transform3d camToRobot = new Transform3d(
    new Translation3d(0.3, 0.0, 0.6),   // 30cm forward, 60cm up
    new Rotation3d(0, Math.toRadians(-15), 0) // 15Â° down tilt
);

PhotonPoseEstimator estimator = new PhotonPoseEstimator(
    fieldLayout,
    PoseStrategy.MULTI_TAG_PNP_ON_COPROCESSOR, // runs on Pi, less roboRIO load
    camera,
    camToRobot
);

@Override
public void periodic() {
    var result = estimator.update();
    result.ifPresent(pose -> {
        // Feed into SwerveDrivePoseEstimator for sensor fusion:
        swervePoseEstimator.addVisionMeasurement(
            pose.estimatedPose.toPose2d(),
            pose.timestampSeconds,
            VecBuilder.fill(0.5, 0.5, Math.toRadians(10)) // std devs
        );
    });
}

        {q:"What does PoseStrategy.MULTI_TAG_PNP_ON_COPROCESSOR do differently from single-tag estimation?",opts:["It uses multiple cameras","It uses all visible AprilTags simultaneously to compute a more accurate 3D pose estimate â€” multiple tags constrain the solution better than one, and running the computation on the Pi keeps roboRIO load low","It runs faster on the roboRIO","Multi-tag only works outdoors"],ans:1},
        {q:"Why are standard deviations passed to addVisionMeasurement() when fusing vision with odometry?",opts:["They set the vision update rate","They tell the Kalman filter how much to trust the vision measurement â€” larger values reduce vision influence (useful when far from tags or moving fast); smaller values weight vision more heavily in the pose estimate","They are required by WPILib","Standard deviations set the camera resolution"],ans:1},
      ]},
    ],

      {id:"pyb_dataclass",title:"Python Enums for Scouting Categories",est:"11 min",content:`## Stop Using Magic Strings for Categories
\`climb = "L2"\` works until someone types \`"l2"\` or \`"Level 2"\`. Python Enums replace stringly-typed categories with constants that are impossible to mistype and carry useful behavior.

## Basic Enum
\`\`\`python
from enum import Enum, IntEnum

class ClimbLevel(Enum):
    NONE = "None"
    L1   = "L1"
    L2   = "L2"
    L3   = "L3"
    L4   = "L4"

class Alliance(Enum):
    RED  = "red"
    BLUE = "blue"

class MatchResult(Enum):
    WIN  = "win"
    LOSS = "loss"
    TIE  = "tie"

# Usage:
rec_climb = ClimbLevel.L2
print(rec_climb)        # ClimbLevel.L2
print(rec_climb.value)  # "L2"
print(rec_climb.name)   # "L2"

# Safe comparison â€” no typo risk:
if rec_climb == ClimbLevel.L2:
    pts = 6
\`\`\`

## IntEnum for Point Values
\`\`\`python
class ClimbPoints(IntEnum):
    NONE = 0
    L1   = 3
    L2   = 6
    L3   = 10
    L4   = 15

# IntEnum values behave like integers:
pts = ClimbPoints.L2
print(pts + 12)  # 18 â€” works directly in arithmetic

# Map ClimbLevel string â†’ ClimbPoints:
CLIMB_PTS = {
    ClimbLevel.NONE: ClimbPoints.NONE,
    ClimbLevel.L1:   ClimbPoints.L1,
    ClimbLevel.L2:   ClimbPoints.L2,
    ClimbLevel.L3:   ClimbPoints.L3,
    ClimbLevel.L4:   ClimbPoints.L4,
}
\`\`\`

## Parsing CSV Data Into Enums
\`\`\`python
# When loading scouting CSV, convert strings to Enums safely:
def parse_climb(raw: str) -> ClimbLevel:
    try:
        return ClimbLevel(raw.strip())  # "L2" â†’ ClimbLevel.L2
    except ValueError:
        return ClimbLevel.NONE          # unknown string â†’ safe default

# In CSV loading loop:
climb = parse_climb(row.get("climb", ""))
pts   = CLIMB_PTS[climb]

# Validate at import time â€” find bad data before analysis:
df = pd.read_csv("scouting.csv")
valid = set(c.value for c in ClimbLevel)
bad   = df[~df["climb"].isin(valid)]
if len(bad):
    print(f"âš ï¸ {len(bad)} rows with invalid climb values:")
    print(bad[["team","match","climb"]])
\`\`\`

## Enum Iteration â€” Building Dropdowns
\`\`\`python
# List all valid climb options for a UI dropdown:
options = [c.value for c in ClimbLevel]
# ["None", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4"]

# Iterate to print a scoring reference:
for level in ClimbLevel:
    print(f"{level.value}: {CLIMB_PTS[level]} pts")

        {q:"What makes IntEnum values more convenient than regular Enum values for point calculations?",opts:["IntEnum is always faster","IntEnum values behave as integers in arithmetic â€” ClimbPoints.L2 + 12 = 18 directly, without needing to call .value first","Regular Enum can't store integers","IntEnum values are larger"],ans:1},

      {id:"pi_config",title:"Config Files & Environment Management",est:"16 min",content:`## No More Hardcoded Constants
A scouting tool with \`API_KEY = "abc123"\` in the source code gets accidentally committed to GitHub. A tool with database paths hardcoded breaks when someone else runs it on their laptop. Config files solve both.

## .env Files with python-dotenv
\`\`\`bash
pip install python-dotenv
\`\`\`
\`\`\`

TBA_API_KEY=your_actual_key_here
DB_PATH=/home/scout/scouting.db
EVENT_KEY=2025casd
DEBUG=false
\`\`\`

DB_PATH   = os.getenv("DB_PATH", "scouting.db")  # default if not set

    raise ValueError("TBA_API_KEY not set â€” check your .env file")

      {id:"pa_dashboard",title:"Full-Stack Scouting Dashboard with Flask & React",est:"32 min",content:`## Building a Real Scouting App
A terminal script works for one person. A web dashboard works for your whole alliance selection team simultaneously â€” coaches, strategists, and scouts all see the same live data.

## Architecture
\`\`\`
Flask backend  â†’ REST API + WebSocket
SQLite         â†’ persistent storage
React frontend â†’ live dashboard (served from Flask)

All runs on a laptop at competition connected to a hotspot
Scouts submit via phone browser â†’ coaches see live updates
\`\`\`

## Flask Backend (app.py)
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, jsonify, request, send_from_directory
from flask_socketio import SocketIO, emit
import sqlite3, os

app = Flask(__name__, static_folder="frontend/build")
socketio = SocketIO(app, cors_allowed_origins="*", async_mode="eventlet")
DB = "scouting.db"

# Serve React build:
@app.route("/", defaults={"path": ""})
@app.route("/<path:path>")
def serve(path):
    if path and os.path.exists(app.static_folder + "/" + path):
        return send_from_directory(app.static_folder, path)
    return send_from_directory(app.static_folder, "index.html")

# API: get top teams
@app.route("/api/top_teams")
def top_teams():
    event = request.args.get("event", "")
    with sqlite3.connect(DB) as conn:
        rows = conn.execute("""
            SELECT team,
                   COUNT(*) matches,
                   AVG(auto_pts + cycles*4) avg,
                   AVG(CASE climb WHEN 'L3' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) climb_rate
            FROM matches WHERE event_key=?
            GROUP BY team HAVING matches>=2
            ORDER BY avg DESC LIMIT 30
        """, (event,)).fetchall()
    return jsonify([{"team":r[0],"matches":r[1],"avg":round(r[2],1),"climb":round(r[3],2)} for r in rows])

# API: submit match
@app.route("/api/submit", methods=["POST"])
def submit():
    d = request.json
    with sqlite3.connect(DB) as conn:
        conn.execute(
            "INSERT INTO matches(event_key,match_num,team,auto_pts,cycles,climb,notes)"
            " VALUES(?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
            (d["event"],d["match"],d["team"],d["auto"],d["cycles"],d["climb"],d.get("notes","")))
    socketio.emit("new_match", d, broadcast=True)
    return jsonify({"ok": True})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    socketio.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
\`\`\`

async function moduleStoreSet(k, v, s=false) {
