              <div><label style={TC.lbl}>Tool Name*</label><input style={TC.inp} value={toolForm.name} onChange={e=>setToolForm(p=>({...p,name:e.target.value}))} /></div>
              <div style={{display:"grid",gridTemplateColumns:"1fr 1fr",gap:10}}>
                <div><label style={TC.lbl}>Category</label>
                  <select style={TC.sel} value={toolForm.category} onChange={e=>setToolForm(p=>({...p,category:e.target.value}))}>
                    {CATEGORIES.map(c=><option key={c} value={c}>{c}</option>)}
                  </select>
                </div>
                <div><label style={TC.lbl}>Quantity</label><input style={TC.inp} type="number" min="1" value={toolForm.quantity} onChange={e=>setToolForm(p=>({...p,quantity:e.target.value}))} /></div>
              </div>
              <div><label style={TC.lbl}>Serial Number</label><input style={TC.inp} value={toolForm.serialNum} onChange={e=>setToolForm(p=>({...p,serialNum:e.target.value}))} /></div>
              <div><label style={TC.lbl}>Notes</label><input style={TC.inp} value={toolForm.notes} onChange={e=>setToolForm(p=>({...p,notes:e.target.value}))} /></div>
              <button style={TC.btnS()} onClick={saveTool}>ðŸ’¾ {editId?"Update":"Add"} Tool</button>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      )}

      {/* Checkout Modal */}
      {modal==="checkout"&&checkoutTool&&(
        <div style={{position:"fixed",inset:0,background:"rgba(0,0,0,0.5)",display:"flex",alignItems:"center",justifyContent:"center",zIndex:999}} onClick={()=>setModal(null)}>
          <div style={{background:"#fff",borderRadius:16,width:"100%",maxWidth:380,padding:24}} onClick={e=>e.stopPropagation()}>
            <div style={{fontWeight:800,fontSize:17,marginBottom:4}}>ðŸ“¤ Check Out Tool</div>
            <div style={{fontWeight:700,fontSize:16,color:"#ea580c",marginBottom:16}}>{checkoutTool.name}</div>
            <label style={TC.lbl}>Return Due Date (optional)</label>
            <input style={{...TC.inp,marginBottom:16}} type="date" value={dueDate} onChange={e=>setDueDate(e.target.value)} />
            <button style={{...TC.btnS(),width:"100%"}} onClick={checkout}>ðŸ“¤ Check Out to {user.name}</button>
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}


// â”€â”€â”€ HANDBOOKMODULE â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
const HB = {
  card:  {background:"#fff",border:"1px solid #e2e8f0",borderRadius:14,padding:"18px 20px",boxShadow:"0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.06)"},
  btn:   (c="#1e3a8a",b="#eff6ff")=>({background:b,color:c,border:"1.5px solid "+c+"30",borderRadius:8,padding:"8px 18px",fontWeight:700,fontSize:13,cursor:"pointer"}),
  btnS:  (bg="#1e3a8a")=>({background:bg,color:"#fff",border:"none",borderRadius:8,padding:"9px 20px",fontWeight:700,fontSize:13,cursor:"pointer"}),
  inp:   {border:"1.5px solid #e2e8f0",borderRadius:8,padding:"9px 14px",fontSize:14,width:"100%",boxSizing:"border-box",outline:"none"},
  ta:    {border:"1.5px solid #e2e8f0",borderRadius:8,padding:"9px 14px",fontSize:14,width:"100%",boxSizing:"border-box",outline:"none",fontFamily:"Georgia,serif",resize:"vertical",lineHeight:1.9},
  lbl:   {fontWeight:600,fontSize:13,color:"#374151",marginBottom:4,display:"block"},
};

const DEFAULT_HANDBOOK_SECTIONS = [
  { id:"welcome",    title:"Welcome",              icon:"ðŸ‘‹", body:"Welcome to the team! We\'re excited to have you." },
  { id:"mission",    title:"Team Mission",          icon:"ðŸŽ¯", body:"Our mission is to inspire young people through FIRST robotics." },
  { id:"expectations",title:"Member Expectations", icon:"ðŸ“‹", body:"Attend meetings, treat teammates with respect, complete tasks on time." },

function HandbookModule({ user, isAdmin }) {
  const [sections, setSections] = useState([]);
  const [acks, setAcks] = useState([]);
  const [myAck, setMyAck] = useState(false);
  const [view, setView] = useState("read");
  const [selSec, setSelSec] = useState(null);
  const [editSec, setEditSec] = useState(null);
  const [newSec, setNewSec] = useState({title:"",icon:"ðŸ“„",body:""});
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);

  useEffect(()=>{
    (async()=>{
      const saved = await moduleStoreGet("handbook-sections",true);
      setSections(saved||DEFAULT_HANDBOOK_SECTIONS);
      const a=(await moduleStoreGet("handbook-acks",true))||[];
      setAcks(a);
      setMyAck(a.some(x=>x.name===user.name));
      setLoading(false);
    })();
  },[user.name]);

  const saveSection = async (sec) => {
    const u=sections.map(s=>s.id===sec.id?sec:s);
    await moduleStoreSet("handbook-sections",u,true); setSections(u); setEditSec(null);
  };
  const addSection = async () => {
    if (!newSec.title.trim()) return alert("Title required.");
    const u=[...sections,{...newSec,id:Date.now().toString()}];
    await moduleStoreSet("handbook-sections",u,true); setSections(u); setNewSec({title:"",icon:"ðŸ“„",body:""}); setView("read");
  };
  const deleteSection = async id => {
    if (!window.confirm("Delete this section?")) return;
    const u=sections.filter(s=>s.id!==id); await moduleStoreSet("handbook-sections",u,true); setSections(u);
    if (selSec===id) setSelSec(null);
  };
  const acknowledge = async () => {
    const u=[...acks,{name:user.name,at:new Date().toISOString()}];
    await moduleStoreSet("handbook-acks",u,true); setAcks(u); setMyAck(true);
  };

  if (loading) return <div style={{textAlign:"center",padding:60,color:"#9ca3af"}}>Loading handbookâ€¦</div>;

  if (selSec) {
    const sec = sections.find(s=>s.id===selSec);
    if (!sec) { setSelSec(null); return null; }
    return (
      <div>
        <button style={{...HB.btn(),marginBottom:16}} onClick={()=>setSelSec(null)}>â† Handbook</button>
        {editSec?.id===sec.id ? (
          <div style={HB.card}>
            <div style={{display:"flex",gap:10,marginBottom:12}}>
              <div style={{flex:"0 0 60px"}}><label style={HB.lbl}>Icon</label><input style={HB.inp} value={editSec.icon} onChange={e=>setEditSec(p=>({...p,icon:e.target.value}))} /></div>
              <div style={{flex:1}}><label style={HB.lbl}>Title</label><input style={HB.inp} value={editSec.title} onChange={e=>setEditSec(p=>({...p,title:e.target.value}))} /></div>
            </div>
            <textarea style={{...HB.ta,minHeight:300}} value={editSec.body} onChange={e=>setEditSec(p=>({...p,body:e.target.value}))} />
            <div style={{display:"flex",gap:10,marginTop:12}}>
              <button style={HB.btnS()} onClick={()=>saveSection(editSec)}>ðŸ’¾ Save</button>
              <button style={HB.btn()} onClick={()=>setEditSec(null)}>Cancel</button>
            </div>
          </div>
        ) : (
          <div style={HB.card}>
            <div style={{display:"flex",justifyContent:"space-between",alignItems:"flex-start",marginBottom:16}}>
              <div style={{fontWeight:900,fontSize:22}}>{sec.icon} {sec.title}</div>
              {isAdmin&&<div style={{display:"flex",gap:6}}>
                <button style={HB.btn()} onClick={()=>setEditSec({...sec})}>âœï¸ Edit</button>
                <button style={HB.btn("#dc2626","#fef2f2")} onClick={()=>deleteSection(sec.id)}>ðŸ—‘ï¸</button>
              </div>}
            </div>
            <div style={{fontSize:15,lineHeight:1.9,color:"#1e293b",whiteSpace:"pre-wrap"}}>{sec.body}</div>
          </div>
        )}
      </div>
    );
  }

  return (
    <div>
      <div style={{display:"flex",justifyContent:"space-between",alignItems:"center",marginBottom:20}}>
        <div style={{fontWeight:900,fontSize:24}}>ðŸ“– Team Handbook</div>
        {isAdmin&&<button style={HB.btn()} onClick={()=>setView(view==="edit"?"read":"edit")}>{view==="edit"?"Done Editing":"âœï¸ Edit"}</button>}
      </div>
      {!myAck&&(
        <div style={{background:"#fffbeb",border:"2px solid #d97706",borderRadius:12,padding:"14px 18px",marginBottom:18,display:"flex",justifyContent:"space-between",alignItems:"center"}}>
          <div>
            <div style={{fontWeight:700,color:"#d97706",marginBottom:2}}>ðŸ“‹ Please read and acknowledge the handbook</div>
            <div style={{fontSize:13,color:"#6b7280"}}>Read all sections then click Acknowledge.</div>
          </div>
          <button style={HB.btnS("#d97706")} onClick={acknowledge}>âœ… I\'ve Read It</button>
        </div>
      )}
      {myAck&&(
        <div style={{background:"#f0fdf4",border:"1px solid #16a34a",borderRadius:10,padding:"10px 16px",marginBottom:16,fontSize:13,color:"#16a34a",fontWeight:700}}>
          âœ… You\'ve acknowledged the handbook.
        </div>
      )}
      <div style={{display:"grid",gridTemplateColumns:"repeat(auto-fill,minmax(260px,1fr))",gap:12,marginBottom:20}}>
        {sections.map(sec=>(
          <div key={sec.id} style={{...HB.card,cursor:"pointer"}} onClick={()=>setSelSec(sec.id)}>
            <div style={{fontSize:32,marginBottom:8}}>{sec.icon}</div>
            <div style={{fontWeight:800,fontSize:15,marginBottom:4}}>{sec.title}</div>
            <div style={{fontSize:12,color:"#9ca3af"}}>{sec.body.slice(0,80)}â€¦</div>
          </div>
        ))}
        {view==="edit"&&(
          <div style={{...HB.card,border:"2px dashed #e2e8f0",background:"#f8fafc"}}>
            <div style={{fontWeight:700,fontSize:14,marginBottom:10,color:"#9ca3af"}}>+ New Section</div>
            <div style={{display:"flex",gap:8,marginBottom:8}}>
              <input style={{...HB.inp,width:50}} placeholder="ðŸ”§" value={newSec.icon} onChange={e=>setNewSec(p=>({...p,icon:e.target.value}))} />
              <input style={{...HB.inp,flex:1}} placeholder="Section title" value={newSec.title} onChange={e=>setNewSec(p=>({...p,title:e.target.value}))} />
            </div>
            <textarea style={{...HB.ta,minHeight:60,fontSize:13}} placeholder="Contentâ€¦" value={newSec.body} onChange={e=>setNewSec(p=>({...p,body:e.target.value}))} />
            <button style={{...HB.btnS(),marginTop:8,width:"100%",padding:"7px"}} onClick={addSection}>Add Section</button>
          </div>
        )}
      </div>
      {isAdmin&&(
        <div style={HB.card}>
          <div style={{fontWeight:700,fontSize:14,marginBottom:10}}>âœ… Acknowledgments ({acks.length})</div>
          {acks.length===0&&<div style={{color:"#9ca3af",fontSize:13}}>No one has acknowledged yet.</div>}
          <div style={{display:"flex",gap:8,flexWrap:"wrap"}}>
            {acks.map(a=>(
              <div key={a.name} style={{background:"#f0fdf4",border:"1px solid #16a34a",borderRadius:8,padding:"6px 12px",fontSize:12}}>
                <span style={{fontWeight:700,color:"#16a34a"}}>âœ… {a.name}</span>
              </div>
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

      {id:"jb_comparable",title:"Comparable & Sorting Custom Objects",est:"12 min",content:`## Sorting Beyond Primitives
Arrays.sort works on ints and Strings. For sorting your own objects â€” say, alliance picks by average score â€” you need Comparable or a Comparator.

## Implementing Comparable
\`\`\`java
// Make a class sortable by implementing Comparable<T>:
public class TeamStats implements Comparable<TeamStats> {
    public final int    team;
    public final double avgScore;
    public final int    matchCount;

    public TeamStats(int team, double avgScore, int matchCount) {
        this.team       = team;
        this.avgScore   = avgScore;
        this.matchCount = matchCount;
    }

    @Override
    public int compareTo(TeamStats other) {
        // Negative = this comes first, Positive = other comes first, 0 = equal
        // Sort by avgScore descending (highest first):
        return Double.compare(other.avgScore, this.avgScore);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return String.format("Team %d: %.1f avg (%d matches)", team, avgScore, matchCount);
    }
}

// Now sort a list:
List<TeamStats> picks = new ArrayList<>();
picks.add(new TeamStats(1234, 42.3, 8));
picks.add(new TeamStats(5678, 38.1, 7));
picks.add(new TeamStats(9012, 51.0, 9));

Collections.sort(picks); // uses compareTo
// or: picks.sort(null);

for (TeamStats t : picks) telemetry.addLine(t.toString());
// Output: Team 9012: 51.0, Team 1234: 42.3, Team 5678: 38.1
\`\`\`

## Comparator â€” Sort Multiple Ways Without Changing the Class
\`\`\`java
// Sort by match count (most-scouted first):
picks.sort(Comparator.comparingInt((TeamStats t) -> t.matchCount).reversed());

// Sort by two criteria â€” avgScore first, then team number as tiebreaker:
picks.sort(Comparator.comparingDouble((TeamStats t) -> t.avgScore)
    .reversed()
    .thenComparingInt(t -> t.team));
\`\`\`

## Practical Use: Auto-Sorting Pick List
\`\`\`java
// Load scouting data into TeamStats list, then sort automatically:
List<TeamStats> pickList = loadScoutingData(csvPath);
Collections.sort(pickList); // sorted by avgScore descending
for (int i = 0; i < Math.min(20, pickList.size()); i++) {
    telemetry.addData("Pick " + (i+1), pickList.get(i).toString());
}
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What must compareTo return to indicate that 'this' object should come BEFORE the 'other' object when sorting?",opts:["true","A negative integer â€” negative means 'this' is less than 'other' in sort order, placing it earlier in an ascending sort","Zero","Any non-zero value"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why use a Comparator instead of implementing Comparable when you need multiple sort orders for the same class?",opts:["Comparator is faster","Comparable defines one fixed sort order baked into the class â€” Comparator is a separate object defining a specific sort, so you can have as many as you need (by score, by match count, by team number) without modifying the class","Comparable requires an interface","Comparator works on arrays only"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does Comparator.comparingDouble(...).reversed() do?",opts:["It sorts by absolute value","It creates a comparator that sorts doubles in descending order â€” reversed() flips the natural ascending order so the highest value appears first","It sorts in random order","reversed() is only for Integers"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.java.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ji_slew",title:"Slew Rate Limiting for Smooth Drive Control",est:"14 min",content:`## The Problem: Instant Velocity Changes
A joystick command that jumps from 0 to 100% instantly draws maximum current, spins wheels, and jerks the robot. A slew rate limiter restricts how fast the output can change â€” smoothing acceleration without the driver noticing.

## Manual Slew Rate Limiter
\`\`\`java
double prevLeft  = 0;
double prevRight = 0;
static final double SLEW_RATE = 0.05; // max change per loop (50Hz loop = 2.5/sec)

// In teleop loop:
double targetLeft  = -gamepad1.left_stick_y;
double targetRight = -gamepad1.right_stick_y;

// Limit how fast output can change:
double newLeft  = slew(prevLeft,  targetLeft,  SLEW_RATE);
double newRight = slew(prevRight, targetRight, SLEW_RATE);

leftMotor.setPower(newLeft);
rightMotor.setPower(newRight);
prevLeft  = newLeft;
prevRight = newRight;

double slew(double current, double target, double maxDelta) {
    double delta = target - current;
    if (Math.abs(delta) <= maxDelta) return target;
    return current + Math.signum(delta) * maxDelta;
}
\`\`\`

## WPILib SlewRateLimiter (FRC)
\`\`\`java
import edu.wpi.first.math.filter.SlewRateLimiter;

// 3.0 = max 3 units per second (e.g., 0 to full in 0.33 sec)
SlewRateLimiter xLimiter = new SlewRateLimiter(3.0);
SlewRateLimiter yLimiter = new SlewRateLimiter(3.0);
SlewRateLimiter rotLimiter = new SlewRateLimiter(3.0);

// In teleopPeriodic():
double xSpeed   = xLimiter.calculate(-driver.getLeftY());
double ySpeed   = yLimiter.calculate(-driver.getLeftX());
double rotation = rotLimiter.calculate(-driver.getRightX());

drive.drive(xSpeed, ySpeed, rotation, fieldRelative);
\`\`\`

## Separate Rates for Acceleration vs Deceleration
\`\`\`java
// Robots can decelerate faster than they accelerate safely:
// Use a higher slew rate for deceleration (toward zero):
double slew(double current, double target, double accelRate, double decelRate) {
    double delta = target - current;
    boolean decelerating = Math.signum(target) == 0 ||
                           Math.signum(target) != Math.signum(current);
    double rate = decelerating ? decelRate : accelRate;
    if (Math.abs(delta) <= rate) return target;
    return current + Math.signum(delta) * rate;
}

// Example: accelerate slowly (smooth), decelerate fast (responsive stops)
double output = slew(prevOutput, joystick, 0.04, 0.1);
\`\`\`

## Tuning the Slew Rate
\`\`\`
Too low (< 0.02 per loop at 50Hz):
  â†’ Robot feels sluggish, driver can't make quick corrections
  â†’ Auto routines might not track tight curves

Too high (> 0.15 per loop):
  â†’ Wheels slip on acceleration, current spikes, not much smoother than no limiter

Good starting values:
  FTC tank/mecanum drive: 0.05 per loop (50Hz) = 0 to full in 0.4 sec
  FRC swerve (50Hz):      2.5-4.0 units/sec with SlewRateLimiter
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does a slew rate limiter do to motor commands and what physical problem does it solve?",opts:["It reduces maximum motor speed","It limits how fast the commanded output can change per loop â€” prevents sudden full-power commands that cause wheel spin, excessive current draw, and jerky motion that makes precise driver control difficult","It smooths encoder readings","It prevents motor overheating"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why use a higher slew rate for deceleration than acceleration?",opts:["Deceleration uses more power","Robots can physically stop faster than they can safely accelerate without wheel slip â€” a high decel rate makes stops feel crisp and responsive while keeping acceleration smooth; matching rates forces a compromise that sacrifices both qualities","Deceleration limits are always faster","FRC rules require different rates"],ans:1},
      {q:"What symptom indicates the slew rate is set too low?",opts:["Wheels spin on acceleration","The robot feels sluggish and unresponsive â€” the driver turns the joystick to full but the robot takes so long to reach full speed that quick directional corrections are impossible","Current spikes","The robot vibrates"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.java.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ja_traj_math",title:"Manual Trajectory Interpolation",est:"22 min",content:`## When PathPlanner Is Overkill
PathPlanner is great for swerve. For simple tank drive point-to-point moves or quick autonomous corrections, a hand-written trajectory interpolator is faster to implement and easier to debug.

## Linear Interpolation (LERP)
\`\`\`java
// LERP: smoothly blend from start to end based on parameter t (0.0 to 1.0)
public static double lerp(double start, double end, double t) {
    return start + t * (end - start);
}

// Example: interpolate heading from 0Â° to 90Â° over 1 second
ElapsedTime timer = new ElapsedTime();
double duration = 1.0; // seconds

while (timer.seconds() < duration && opModeIsActive()) {
    double t       = timer.seconds() / duration; // 0.0 â†’ 1.0
    double heading = lerp(0, 90, t);
    turnToHeading(heading);
}
\`\`\`

## Trapezoidal Velocity Profile (Manual)
\`\`\`java
// Ramp up â†’ cruise â†’ ramp down
// Gives smooth motion without overshoot

public double trapezoidVelocity(double elapsed, double totalDist,
                                 double maxVel, double accelTime) {
    double decelStart = totalDist / maxVel - accelTime;
    double t = elapsed;

    if (t < accelTime) {
        // Ramp up: linearly increase from 0 to maxVel
        return maxVel * (t / accelTime);
    } else if (t < decelStart) {
        // Cruise at max velocity
        return maxVel;
    } else {
        // Ramp down: linearly decrease to 0
        double timeLeft = (totalDist / maxVel) - t;
        return maxVel * (timeLeft / accelTime);
    }
}

// Usage in a drive-to-distance routine:
double totalIn = 48.0;
double maxPow  = 0.7;
double accelSec = 0.4;
ElapsedTime moveTimer = new ElapsedTime();

while (getDistanceTraveled() < totalIn && opModeIsActive()) {
    double power = trapezoidVelocity(
        moveTimer.seconds(), totalIn / INCHES_PER_SEC, maxPow, accelSec);
    setDrivePower(power);
}
\`\`\`

## Hermite Spline â€” Smooth Direction Changes
\`\`\`java
// Cubic Hermite interpolates between two points with specified tangents
// Useful for pre-planned autonomous paths without PathPlanner

public double hermite(double p0, double p1, double m0, double m1, double t) {
    double t2 = t * t;
    double t3 = t2 * t;
    return (2*t3 - 3*t2 + 1) * p0
         + (t3  - 2*t2 + t)  * m0
         + (-2*t3 + 3*t2)    * p1
         + (t3  - t2)        * m1;
}

// Interpolate an X path from x=0 (tangent=1) to x=4 (tangent=1):
for (double t = 0; t <= 1.0; t += 0.01) {
    double x = hermite(0, 4, 1, 1, t);
    double y = hermite(0, 2, 0, 0, t); // straight vertical
    // Command robot to (x, y) using odometry feedback
}
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does LERP(start, end, t=0.5) return?",opts:["start","The midpoint between start and end â€” t=0.5 means 50% of the way from start to end, so lerp(0, 90, 0.5) = 45","end","Zero"],ans:1},
      {q:"In a trapezoidal velocity profile, what is the purpose of the 'accelTime' parameter?",opts:["It sets the cruise speed","It defines how long the robot spends ramping from zero to maximum velocity â€” longer accel time means smoother start but requires more total travel distance to reach full speed","It limits total move time","It controls deceleration only"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes a Hermite spline more useful than linear interpolation for robot paths that change direction?",opts:["Hermite is computationally cheaper","Hermite splines control both position AND tangent (direction) at each endpoint â€” the path arrives at waypoints traveling in the specified direction, preventing the sharp corners that linear interpolation creates at waypoint junctions","Linear interpolation doesn't support multiple waypoints","Hermite requires no tuning"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.python.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"pi_unittest2",title:"Unit Testing Scouting Logic with unittest",est:"17 min",content:`## Test Your Data Pipeline Before Competition Day
A scouting app with silent bugs produces wrong pick lists at the worst possible time. Python's built-in unittest module lets you verify every calculation and transformation before you ever bring the laptop to an event.

## Writing Your First Test
\`\`\`python
import unittest
from analysis import compute_contribution, normalize_climb, top_teams

class TestContribution(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_basic_contribution(self):
        """Contribution = auto + (cycles * 4) + climb_pts"""
        result = compute_contribution(auto=12, cycles=6, climb="L2")
        self.assertEqual(result, 12 + 24 + 6)  # 42

    def test_zero_cycles(self):
        result = compute_contribution(auto=0, cycles=0, climb="None")
        self.assertEqual(result, 0)

    def test_highest_climb(self):
        result = compute_contribution(auto=0, cycles=0, climb="L4")
        self.assertEqual(result, 15)

    def test_unknown_climb_defaults_to_zero(self):
        result = compute_contribution(auto=5, cycles=2, climb="UNKNOWN")
        self.assertEqual(result, 5 + 8 + 0)  # unknown â†’ 0 climb pts

class TestNormalize(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_normalizes_lowercase(self):
        self.assertEqual(normalize_climb("l2"), "L2")

    def test_normalizes_spaces(self):
        self.assertEqual(normalize_climb("  L3  "), "L3")

    def test_invalid_returns_none(self):
        self.assertEqual(normalize_climb("garbage"), "None")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
\`\`\`

## Running Tests
\`\`\`bash
python -m unittest test_analysis.py     # run one file
python -m unittest discover             # run all test*.py in current folder
python -m unittest -v test_analysis     # verbose output
\`\`\`

## Testing Data Loading
\`\`\`python
import tempfile, os

class TestCSVLoading(unittest.TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        # Create a temporary CSV for each test:
        self.tmpfile = tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(
            mode="w", suffix=".csv", delete=False, newline="")
        self.tmpfile.write("team,match,auto,cycles,climb\\n")
        self.tmpfile.write("1234,1,12,6,L2\\n")
        self.tmpfile.write("5678,1,8,4,None\\n")
        self.tmpfile.close()

    def tearDown(self):
        os.unlink(self.tmpfile.name)  # delete temp file after each test

    def test_loads_correct_row_count(self):
        from loader import load_scouting_csv
        df = load_scouting_csv(self.tmpfile.name)
        self.assertEqual(len(df), 2)

    def test_team_column_is_int(self):
        from loader import load_scouting_csv
        df = load_scouting_csv(self.tmpfile.name)
        self.assertEqual(df["team"].dtype, int)
\`\`\`

## What to Test for Scouting Apps
\`\`\`
Test these before every event:
  â†’ Contribution calculation with various climb levels
  â†’ Normalization of messy climb strings (l2, Level 2, L2, etc.)
  â†’ CSV loading handles missing fields gracefully
  â†’ Average computation excludes zero-match teams
  â†’ ELO or ranking update is symmetric (if A beats B, A goes up, B goes down)
  â†’ Output CSV has correct column names and types
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the main benefit of writing unit tests for scouting analysis functions before a competition?",opts:["Tests speed up the code","Silent bugs in contribution calculations or data normalization produce wrong pick lists â€” tests verify each function behaves correctly on known inputs before real data is processed under time pressure","Tests are required for Python","They document the code automatically"],ans:1},
      {q:"What do setUp() and tearDown() methods do in a unittest.TestCase?",opts:["They start and stop the test runner","setUp runs before each individual test method and tearDown runs after â€” creating fresh state (like a temporary file) for each test ensures tests don't interfere with each other","They're aliases for each other","They only run once for the whole class"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why test that normalize_climb('garbage') returns 'None' rather than raising an exception?",opts:["Exceptions are slow","Scouting data is entered by humans and will contain typos â€” a function that crashes on unexpected input would break the entire data pipeline; returning a safe default keeps processing running and the bad row is handled conservatively","Python unittest requires this","'None' is the only valid return"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.mechanical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"mb_chain2",title:"Chain Drive â€” Sizing, Tensioning & Maintenance",est:"14 min",content:`## Chain Drive Fundamentals
Roller chain is reliable, strong, and field-repairable. It's a staple of FRC drivetrains and mechanisms. Knowing how to size, install, and maintain chain prevents the most common chain-related match failure.

## Chain Sizes Used in FIRST
\`\`\`
Chain is specified by pitch (distance between roller centers):
  #25 (1/4" pitch): light-duty â€” intake rollers, small mechanisms
  #35 (3/8" pitch): medium â€” standard FRC drivetrain, most mechanisms
  #25H (heavy):     like #25 but stronger plates â€” upgrade over #25 for higher loads

Sprockets are matched to chain by pitch number:
  #25 chain â†’ #25 sprockets
  #35 chain â†’ #35 sprockets (do NOT mix)

Max load comparisons (approximate, single strand):
  #25:    5,500 N breaking (~1,200 lbf)
  #35:   11,000 N breaking (~2,500 lbf)
  Most FRC mechanisms work well within 1/10 of breaking strength.
\`\`\`

## Calculating Chain Length
\`\`\`
Inputs: N1 = teeth on small sprocket, N2 = teeth on large sprocket, C = center distance
Length in links: L = 2C/p + (N1+N2)/2 + ((N2-N1)/2Ï€)Â²/(C/p)
  where p = chain pitch (0.25" for #25, 0.375" for #35)

Practical shortcut for FTC/FRC:
  1. Use REV or AndyMark's online chain calculator
  2. Add 1 master link slack for adjustability
  3. Round to even number of links (master link requires even count)

Master link vs press-fit link:
  Master link (clip-and-pin): easily added/removed â€” use for adjustable runs
  Press-fit:                  stronger but requires chain tool to remove
\`\`\`

## Tensioning â€” Getting It Right
\`\`\`
Correct tension:
  Slack side should have ~1/4 inch of up/down play at midspan
  Too tight: increased bearing load, wear, noise
  Too loose: chain jumps sprocket teeth under load (catastrophic failure)

Tensioning methods:
  1. Adjustable motor mount: slot the motor mounting holes â†’ slide motor
  2. Eccentric spacer/nut:   rotate an eccentric to change center distance
  3. Chain tensioner:        spring-loaded idler sprocket (most forgiving)

Anti-vibration tip: for long chain runs (> 8"), add a chain guide or center support
to prevent the slack side from flapping and causing intermittent jumping.
\`\`\`

## Competition Maintenance Schedule
\`\`\`
Between matches:
  â†’ Inspect for chain stretch: grab any link and push perpendicular to run
    If it deflects > 1/2 inch easily: replace the chain

After every event:
  â†’ Wipe chain clean with a dry rag
  â†’ Apply dry lubricant (NOT WD-40 â€” it attracts dirt)
  â†’ Inspect sprocket teeth: hook-shaped wear â†’ replace sprocket immediately
  â†’ Re-check tension: chain stretches ~1-2% over a season
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What happens to a drive chain that is tensioned too loosely?",opts:["The chain wears faster","The chain can jump sprocket teeth under load â€” the shock load from sudden re-engagement can break the chain or damage the sprocket instantly, ending a match","Loose chain vibrates more","It's better than tight"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should WD-40 not be used to lubricate drive chain?",opts:["WD-40 is too thick","WD-40 is primarily a solvent and water displacer â€” it attracts and holds dirt that forms an abrasive paste between chain rollers and pins, accelerating wear faster than running dry","WD-40 is flammable","It dissolves chain links"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'even number of links' mean for chain, and why is it required?",opts:["Even links are lighter","A master link (the removable connecting link) connects two outer link plates, which requires both ends of the chain to be the same type (both inner or both outer plates) â€” an even link count ensures this alignment","Odd link counts are illegal","Chain must be symmetric"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.mechanical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"mi_cam",title:"Cam Mechanisms for Repeatable Positioning",est:"15 min",content:`## What a Cam Does
A cam converts continuous rotation into a specific, repeatable motion profile. In FIRST robots, simple cam mechanisms provide rock-solid position repeatability that encoder-based control sometimes can't match â€” because the cam physically stops the mechanism in exactly the right place.

## Disc Cam â€” Simplest Form
\`\`\`
A disc cam is an off-center circle (eccentric):
  Rotation of disc â†’ follower riding on edge â†’ linear or rocking motion

Simple eccentric (for deployment latches):
  Bolt offset from center â†’ rotating 180Â° extends a latch by 2Ã— offset distance
  The follower can only be in two positions (0Â° and 180Â°)
  â†’ Zero encoder calibration needed â€” position is physically defined
\`\`\`

## Applications in FTC & FRC
\`\`\`
Intake deployment:
  Servo rotates cam 90Â° â†’ cam pushes intake arm from stowed to deployed position
  Hard surface contact defines both endpoints â€” no PID needed

Wrist orientation locks:
  Cam engages a slot when wrist reaches horizontal â€” holds position under
  vertical load without motor torque (cam is self-locking in slot)

Trigger/latch mechanisms:
  Cam pin rides along a slot path â†’ at one position, pin drops into detent
  â†’ Mechanism latches without any powered hold

Ball indexer:
  Rotating cam pushes game pieces one at a time from a hopper
  Each rotation = one piece indexed â€” inherently periodic
\`\`\`

## Designing a Simple Deployment Cam in Onshape
\`\`\`
Step 1: Define follower path
  â†’ Where should the follower (arm end) be at 0Â°, 90Â°, 180Â°?
  â†’ Draw these positions in a sketch

Step 2: Create cam profile
  â†’ In the sketch, draw tangent arcs connecting the follower positions
  â†’ The cam edge is the envelope your follower rides on
  â†’ Add dwell (flat section) where you want the follower to hold still

Step 3: Determine follower type
  â†’ Flat follower: simple, wears, not recommended
  â†’ Roller follower: bearing on the follower tip â€” preferred
  â†’ Choose bearing size to match cam profile radius

Step 4: Check for undercut
  â†’ Zoom into the inner cam radius
  â†’ If cam profile curves inward faster than the follower circle:
    undercut occurs â†’ follower loses contact â†’ replace with smaller follower
\`\`\`

## Cam vs PID â€” When to Choose Which
\`\`\`
Choose cam when:
  â†’ Two or three fixed positions are sufficient
  â†’ Position must be exact despite encoder drift or power cycles
  â†’ Load at end position is high (cam is passive, motor holds nothing)
  â†’ Simplicity is more important than flexibility

Choose PID when:
  â†’ Multiple configurable positions needed
  â†’ Position changes during season
  â†’ Continuous range of motion required
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a cam mechanism provide better position repeatability than encoder-based PID in some cases?",opts:["Cam mechanisms are always more accurate","The cam physically constrains the mechanism to a defined position â€” it cannot be at any other position when the cam is at that angle, regardless of encoder calibration, battery voltage, or software bugs","PID is less accurate","Cams use less power"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is 'dwell' on a cam profile and what does it do to the follower?",opts:["Dwell is a type of follower","A dwell is a constant-radius arc section on the cam â€” while the cam rotates through the dwell angle, the follower doesn't move, holding the mechanism in the same position for that rotation range","Dwell changes follower speed","It's the cam's center hole"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is a 'roller follower' and why is it preferred over a flat follower?",opts:["It spins faster","A roller follower uses a bearing on the follower tip to contact the cam â€” the bearing rolls on the cam surface instead of sliding, dramatically reducing friction and wear compared to a flat surface dragging on the cam","Roller followers are lighter","It's required for round cams"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.mechanical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ma_frame2",title:"Space Frame vs Monocoque â€” Chassis Architecture",est:"20 min",content:`## The Robot's Skeleton Defines Everything
The frame determines where every mechanism mounts, how loads distribute, and how the robot survives defense. Most FIRST teams build one type without understanding the tradeoffs. Choosing deliberately improves weight and rigidity.

## Space Frame (Tube Construction)
\`\`\`
Definition: structural members (tubes, extrusions) carry loads along their length
            Members connect at nodes â€” loads transfer at joints

Example: welded steel box frame, bolted 1"Ã—1" aluminum square tube

Characteristics:
  Weight: depends on tube wall thickness and total length
  Rigidity: high for load paths along tubes; low for torsion unless braced
  Repairability: high â€” individual tubes can be replaced
  Manufacturability: accessible to most teams (hand tools, drill press)
  FTC relevance: REV/GoBILDA extrusion systems are space frames

FTC space frame with REV extrusion:
  Pros: bolt-together, no welding, slots everywhere for mounting
  Cons: aluminum extrusion heavier per length than tube; less torsionally stiff
        than welded box
\`\`\`

## Monocoque / Semi-Monocoque (Sheet Construction)
\`\`\`
Definition: skin (sheet material) carries loads in shear â€” no discrete columns

Example: laser-cut 1/8" aluminum belly pan + thin side walls
          Sheet wraps around the robot perimeter

Characteristics:
  Weight: very light if well-designed â€” sheet distributes load without extra mass
  Rigidity: excellent torsional stiffness from closed-section geometry
  Repairability: lower â€” bent sheet is hard to replace mid-event
  Manufacturability: requires laser cutter or CNC (or careful waterjet)
  FRC prevalence: high â€” most competitive FRC robots use some monocoque elements

Semi-monocoque (hybrid â€” most common in competitive FRC):
  Structural tube rails + laser-cut aluminum belly pan + side electronics plate
  Tubes handle bending; sheet handles torsion and mechanism mounting
\`\`\`

## Load Path Analysis for Frame Design
\`\`\`
Load path = the route that force travels from application point to ground.

Example: elevator force path
  Elevator carriage â†’ drive shaft â†’ top stage tube â†’
  connecting plates â†’ main frame rails â†’ drivetrain â†’ floor

Every joint in this path must be stronger than the expected load.
Identify the weakest link: usually bolted connections, not tubes themselves.

FRC gusset best practice:
  At tube corners: gusset plates distribute load over both tube walls
  Without gusset: bolts pull through tube wall (tube wall failure)
  With gusset:    load spreads â†’ bolts in shear (much stronger)
\`\`\`

## Weight Comparison Example
\`\`\`
Drive base for 18"Ã—28" robot:

Space frame (1" REV extrusion, 4 rails + crossmembers, ~15 ft total):
  15 ft Ã— 0.28 lbs/ft = 4.2 lbs extrusion + 0.5 lbs hardware = 4.7 lbs

Space frame (1"Ã—1"Ã—0.065" 6061-T6 tube, same layout):
  15 ft Ã— 0.17 lbs/ft = 2.5 lbs + 0.5 lbs hardware = 3.0 lbs

Semi-monocoque (welded 1.5" tube rails + 0.050" 5052 belly pan):
  Rails:      8 ft Ã— 0.26 lbs/ft = 2.1 lbs
  Belly pan:  18"Ã—28" Ã— 0.050" = 1.4 lbs
  Total:      3.5 lbs â€” similar weight, MUCH stiffer torsionally
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What structural property does a monocoque (skin-covered) frame provide that open space frame lacks?",opts:["Higher bending stiffness along tubes","Torsional stiffness â€” a closed box cross-section resists twisting along the robot's length, preventing the frame from racking (parallelogram deformation) when forces don't act symmetrically","Lighter weight in all cases","Better heat dissipation"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is a gusset plate and what failure mode does it prevent at tube frame corners?",opts:["A weight reduction feature","A gusset distributes the connection load over both tube walls instead of concentrating it at bolt holes â€” without a gusset, bolt loads pull through thin tube walls (wall shear-out failure); with a gusset, bolts act in shear which is 2-3Ã— stronger","A spacer between tubes","It's decorative"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do most competitive FRC robots use a semi-monocoque (hybrid) design rather than pure space frame or pure monocoque?",opts:["It's the only legal option","Tubes efficiently handle bending along the frame rails while the sheet belly pan adds torsional stiffness and mechanism mounting surface â€” together they achieve better stiffness-to-weight than either pure approach","Hybrid designs are easier to build","Monocoque is too expensive"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.electrical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"eb_wire",title:"Wire Gauge Selection & Current Capacity",est:"12 min",content:`## Wrong Wire Gauge Causes Fires
A wire that's too thin for its current load gets hot. Hot enough, and the insulation melts â€” causing a short circuit or fire. Wire gauge selection is safety-critical, not just electrical performance.

## AWG â€” The Gauge System
\`\`\`
AWG (American Wire Gauge): LOWER number = THICKER wire = more current capacity
  28 AWG: signal wires, sensor data (< 1A)
  22 AWG: servo signal + power (< 3A)
  18 AWG: motor control signal, low-current motors
  16 AWG: medium current runs (< 15A)
  14 AWG: higher-current motor leads (< 25A)
  12 AWG: main power distribution runs (< 40A)
  10 AWG: battery leads, main breaker (< 60A)

FTC wire guide:
  Sensor/servo signal: 22-24 AWG
  Motor power:         18 AWG minimum
  Battery connection:  18 AWG minimum (FTC battery XT30)
\`\`\`

## Current Capacity vs Temperature Rise
\`\`\`
Wire is rated for a temperature rise above ambient:
  A 14 AWG wire is "rated" for 15A â€” but that means 60Â°C above ambient
  At 70Â°F ambient, wire reaches 130Â°F (uncomfortable to touch but OK)
  In a robot's enclosed frame at 90Â°F ambient, same current = 160Â°F â€” concerning

Conservative rule: use wire rated for 2Ã— the expected continuous current
  Motor drawing 5A continuous â†’ use 14 AWG (rated 15A)
  Adds cost/weight but prevents heat damage in worst-case conditions
\`\`\`

## Voltage Drop â€” Why Wire Resistance Matters
\`\`\`
Every wire has resistance. Current through resistance = voltage drop.
  V_drop = I Ã— R  (I in amps, R in ohms per foot Ã— length)

14 AWG copper resistance: â‰ˆ 0.0025 Î©/ft
10 ft of 14 AWG at 10A: V_drop = 10 Ã— 10 Ã— 0.0025 = 0.25V
  At 12V supply, motor receives: 12 - 0.25 = 11.75V â€” acceptable

1 ft of 28 AWG sensor wire at 0.5A: V_drop â‰ˆ negligible â€” fine for sensors

Long runs to motors: use thicker wire to keep drop under 0.5V
  FRC belly runs from PDB to motors across 4 feet: 12 AWG is appropriate
\`\`\`

## FRC & FTC Wire Color Standards
\`\`\`
Always follow color conventions â€” they prevent life-safety mistakes:
  Red:     positive / power
  Black:   negative / ground
  White or yellow: signal wires
  Green:   CAN Low (FRC)
  Yellow:  CAN High (FRC)

Do NOT use red for ground or black for positive â€” ever.
When a field inspector or electrical engineer looks at your robot in an emergency,
correct color coding tells them instantly which wires to disconnect.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"If an AWG number decreases (e.g., from 18 to 14), what happens to wire thickness and current capacity?",opts:["Thinner wire, more current","Thicker wire, higher current capacity â€” AWG is an inverse scale where lower numbers indicate larger cross-sectional area, which allows more current with less resistance and less heat generation","AWG only affects length","Thinner wire, same current"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should wire current ratings be derated (not used at the full rated value) inside a robot's enclosed frame?",opts:["Derating is required by FIRST","Wire temperature ratings assume ambient temperature â€” inside an enclosed robot frame, ambient temperature is higher than room temperature, so the wire generates more heat for the same current; running at full rated current risks reaching unsafe temperatures","Robot vibration affects current","Wire insulation dissolves at rated current"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the practical consequence of voltage drop in a long motor power wire run?",opts:["The motor spins faster","The motor receives less than supply voltage â€” a 0.5V drop on a 12V system means the motor operates at 95.8% of its capability; on a depleted 10V battery, the same drop represents 5% loss at a critical moment","Voltage drop only affects sensors","Long wires cause current spikes"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.electrical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ea_brushless2",title:"Brushless Motor Physics & FOC Control",est:"20 min",content:`## Why Brushless Motors Are Different
Brushed motors have physical commutator brushes that wear out. Brushless motors commutate electronically â€” the controller must know rotor position to fire the correct windings. This is why NEO, Falcon, and Kraken motors require specific smart motor controllers.

## BLDC vs PMSM â€” Two Brushless Types
\`\`\`
BLDC (Brushless DC):
  Trapezoidal back-EMF waveform
  Simple commutation: 6 discrete switching states per revolution
  Most FTC motors use BLDC
  Controller: REV Expansion Hub drives these directly

PMSM (Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor):
  Sinusoidal back-EMF waveform
  FRC NEO, Falcon 500, Kraken X60 are PMSM
  Requires Field-Oriented Control (FOC) for best performance
  Controller: SPARK MAX, TalonFX, Vortex (all have on-board FOC)
\`\`\`

## How Field-Oriented Control Works
\`\`\`
Traditional voltage control (6-step):
  Apply voltage in 6 discrete steps per rotation
  Torque ripple: varies by up to 30% per rotation â†’ non-smooth output

FOC (Field-Oriented Control):
  Continuously measures rotor electrical angle
  Decomposes motor current into:
    Id: magnetizing current (creates rotor flux â€” should be near 0 for max torque)
    Iq: torque-producing current (perpendicular to flux â€” maximize this)
  Controls these vectors continuously with sinusoidal drive
  Result: smooth torque, efficient, lower heat, faster response

Benefits you notice on the robot:
  â†’ Smoother drive at low speeds (less cogging)
  â†’ Better efficiency under load â†’ less heat â†’ longer battery life
  â†’ Better velocity control (TalonFX TorqueCurrentFOC mode)
\`\`\`

## Enabling FOC on TalonFX (Phoenix 6)
\`\`\`java
// Phoenix 6 enables FOC by default for position/velocity requests:
import com.ctre.phoenix6.controls.VelocityTorqueCurrentFOC;

VelocityTorqueCurrentFOC velReq = new VelocityTorqueCurrentFOC(0);
// Set velocity to 30 RPS with FOC enabled:
motor.setControl(velReq.withVelocity(30.0));

// For position with FOC:
import com.ctre.phoenix6.controls.PositionTorqueCurrentFOC;
PositionTorqueCurrentFOC posReq = new PositionTorqueCurrentFOC(0);
motor.setControl(posReq.withPosition(5.0));
\`\`\`

## Back-EMF and Speed Limiting
\`\`\`
As a brushless motor speeds up, it generates back-EMF (counter-voltage):
  V_back = kE Ã— Ï‰   (kE = motor constant, Ï‰ = angular velocity)
  Net voltage available for torque = V_supply - V_back

At free speed: V_back â‰ˆ V_supply â†’ almost no torque available
This is why motors have a theoretical maximum speed at any given voltage.

Kraken X60 at 12V: free speed â‰ˆ 6,000 RPM
At 5,000 RPM: significant back-EMF â†’ torque is reduced
At stall: full torque available, but current is V/R â‰ˆ very high

Implication: current limiting is essential â€” without it, a stalled brushless motor
             draws enough current to damage the controller and heat the windings in seconds.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What physical property of brushless motors requires the controller to know rotor position?",opts:["Brushless motors have no magnets","Without brushes for mechanical commutation, the controller must electronically switch which windings receive current â€” doing this correctly requires knowing where the rotor magnets are at every moment","Back-EMF requires position sensing","Brushless motors spin in only one direction"],ans:1},
      {q:"What are the two current components that Field-Oriented Control manages, and which one produces torque?",opts:["Voltage and current","Id (flux-producing, ideally near zero for max efficiency) and Iq (torque-producing, perpendicular to rotor flux) â€” FOC maximizes Iq while minimizing Id, providing smooth torque with less heat","AC and DC components","Phase A and Phase B current"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do motors produce less torque as they approach their free-speed maximum?",opts:["Magnets weaken at high RPM","Back-EMF increases with speed, opposing the supply voltage â€” the net voltage driving current through the windings decreases, so the torque-producing current decreases; at free speed, back-EMF nearly equals supply voltage and torque approaches zero","Bearings create more friction at speed","The controller reduces power at high RPM"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.strategy.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sb_kickoff2",title:"Game Analysis at Kickoff",est:"15 min",content:`## The First 4 Hours After Reveal Define Your Season
Teams that analyze the game carefully at kickoff choose better strategies and build more focused robots. Teams that rush to the shop after a 30-minute game review often rebuild in Week 5.

## The Kickoff Analysis Process
\`\`\`
Watch the game reveal video 2Ã— before doing anything else:
  First watch: understand the game. Don't take notes â€” just absorb it.
  Second watch: take notes. Write down every scoring action and its value.

Then: read the game manual, not just the reveal.
  The reveal is marketing. The manual is truth.
  Reveal omits: nuances, penalties, autonomous specifics, endgame rules.
\`\`\`

## Scoring Decomposition
\`\`\`
For each game action, record:
  Action:         Score amp note (example)
  Points:         2 pts teleop / 5 pts if amp activated
  Time to perform: ~8 seconds per cycle
  Points/second:  0.25 pts/sec (or 0.625 if amp is activated)
  Robot requirement: intake + shooter + driving

Repeat for every game action.
Then rank by points/second Ã— achievability:
  High points/second AND achievable â†’ high priority
  High points/second BUT complex    â†’ prototype first, decide Week 2
  Low points/second, simple         â†’ fill remaining time
\`\`\`

## Autonomous Value Analysis
\`\`\`
For the first 2-3 years studying a game, students undervalue auto.
Common mistake: "Auto is only 15 seconds â€” we'll focus on teleop."

The math:
  A reliable 2-piece auto (typical upper bound for most teams):
  At 2pts/piece = 4 pts.
  But: autonomous ranking points (RP) often require specific actions in auto.
  An RP is worth ~4-6 additional wins worth of seeding value.
  Missing an RP every match because of weak auto costs you seeding
  more than 10 extra teleop cycles could recover.

Auto analysis questions:
  â†’ What is the maximum RP-qualifying auto? How many teams will achieve it?
  â†’ What is the minimum auto to avoid hurting your alliance? (don't go nowhere)
  â†’ Which autonomous elements amplify your teleop strategy?
\`\`\`

## Robot Concept Brainstorm Structure
\`\`\`
After scoring decomposition, brainstorm robot concepts:

For each scoring action in the top 3 priority list:
  Mechanism A: [type, rough size, motor count, known challenges]
  Mechanism B: [alternative approach]
  Mechanism C: [simplest possible approach]

Then: identify which combination of mechanisms fits in:
  â†’ The game's robot size limit
  â†’ Your budget
  â†’ Your team's build capabilities

Trim the robot concept to the minimum that scores reliably â€”
then add complexity only if you have capacity and time.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should teams read the full game manual rather than relying on the reveal video for game analysis?",opts:["The manual is shorter","The reveal is marketing and omits important details â€” penalty rules, autonomous scoring specifics, endgame constraints, and edge cases that significantly affect strategy only appear in the manual","Videos are inaccurate","The manual has different rules"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does analyzing scoring actions by 'points per second' reveal?",opts:["Which action is easiest","Which game actions produce the most scoring rate for the time invested â€” this identifies where robot capability should be prioritized and which actions are time-efficient vs point-poor","How many motors are needed","Which game pieces are lightest"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do teams often undervalue autonomous during initial game analysis?",opts:["Auto is too hard","Autonomous looks short at 15 seconds, but autonomous ranking points (RP) affect seeding disproportionately â€” missing a qualification RP every match has a much larger impact on final standing than the raw point value suggests","Auto doesn't count in playoffs","Autonomous is easier than teleop"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.strategy.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"si_alliance_meeting2",title:"Running the Pre-Match Alliance Meeting",est:"13 min",content:`## Five Minutes That Define the Match
The pre-match alliance meeting happens in the queue â€” usually 5-7 minutes before you're on the field. Teams that use it well coordinate effectively. Teams that skip it collide in autonomous and score half their potential.

## Meeting Structure
\`\`\`
Minute 1: Introductions + role assignment
  â†’ "We're Team 1234. We'll be scoring [high/low]. What are you doing?"
  â†’ Establish: who scores where, who plays defense if any

Minute 2: Autonomous coordination
  â†’ Each team states their starting position and auto path
  â†’ Identify any collision risk: "We go across the center â€” does your auto too?"
  â†’ Assign: who runs full auto, who runs park-only to avoid collisions
  â†’ Agree on: if auto fails, what's the fallback behavior?

Minute 3: Teleop strategy
  â†’ Agree on game piece distribution if limited
  â†’ Confirm who goes for climb first (space conflicts)
  â†’ Agree on any game-specific coordination (e.g., who activates the amplifier)

Minute 4: Endgame timing
  â†’ Who climbs first? At what time?
  â†’ Signal if a partner fails a climb: "If we can't climb by T-10, park"
  â†’ Who parks vs climbs if the highest level isn't achievable?

Minute 5: Questions + field position confirmation
  â†’ "Any questions?" â€” pause and actually wait
  â†’ Walk to starting positions together if possible
\`\`\`

## Communication Shortcuts That Actually Work
\`\`\`
Establish at the start of the meeting:
  Thumbs up from your operator  = "we're holding a game piece â€” pass"
  Flashing LEDs or pre-agreed motion = "I need help, I'm defended"
  Driver station radio (if legal): use sparingly, only critical info

What NOT to say over driver station radio during a match:
  "What should I do?" â€” you should have decided this already
  Anything that takes > 3 seconds to convey â€” it's too long
  Anything that requires the other driver to stop driving to understand
\`\`\`

## When Your Alliance Partner Disagrees With Your Plan
\`\`\`
In a qualification match: defer to the alliance captain's robot (seeded highest)
  â†’ They likely know the game better
  â†’ Even a suboptimal plan executed coherently beats a conflict

In an elimination match: if you're the captain, you have final say
  â†’ Still listen â€” your partner may know something you don't
  â†’ Make a decision, commit, communicate it clearly
  â†’ "We'll do it your way â€” I'll adjust my position to match"

Never: leave a meeting with two robots planning the same path
       or without knowing who climbs when.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is autonomous coordination the highest-priority item in the pre-match alliance meeting?",opts:["Autonomous is worth the most points","Autonomous paths are pre-programmed and can't be changed during the match â€” two robots with conflicting auto paths collide regardless of driver skill; identifying and resolving conflicts in the queue is the only opportunity to prevent it","Meeting time is shortest for autonomous","Autonomous errors are easiest to correct"],ans:1},
      {q:"What should a team do when their alliance partner proposes a strategy they disagree with in a qualification match?",opts:["Ignore their plan and run your own","Generally defer to the higher-seeded robot's plan â€” even an imperfect plan executed by both robots coherently outperforms two robots executing conflicting strategies that interfere with each other","Demand a different partner","Switch strategies mid-match"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should driver station radio communication during a match be limited to very brief, pre-agreed messages?",opts:["Radio communication is illegal","Processing incoming voice communication requires cognitive attention that the driver needs for robot control â€” long or unexpected messages cause the driver to hesitate or stop driving at a critical moment","Radio delay makes it useless","The other team can hear your radio"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.safety.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sfb_ppe",title:"PPE Guide â€” What to Wear and When",est:"11 min",content:`## PPE Is the Last Line of Defense
Engineering controls (guards, enclosures) and safe work practices are better than PPE â€” they prevent the hazard from reaching you. But when those fail, PPE is the difference between an incident and an injury.

## Eye Protection
\`\`\`
When: ANY time you are near:
  â†’ Power tools (drill press, grinder, saw, rotary tool)
  â†’ Any cutting or grinding operation, even by someone else nearby
  â†’ Chemical handling (solvent cleaning, battery work)
  â†’ Soldering (flux splatter is rare but permanent eye damage)

Type to use:
  Safety glasses: ANSI Z87.1 marked â€” not regular glasses, not sunglasses
  Side shields required if debris could approach from the side
  Face shield (over safety glasses): grinding, large chips, chemical splash

Never:
  âŒ Regular prescription glasses alone (no impact rating)
  âŒ Sunglasses (no impact rating)
  âŒ "It's just a quick cut" â€” that's when accidents happen
\`\`\`

## Hearing Protection
\`\`\`
When: noise above 85 dB â€” use the following guide:
  Drill press:      ~85 dB â†’ borderline, short duration OK
  Angle grinder:   ~100 dB â†’ earplugs required
  Shop vacuum:      ~85 dB â†’ short use OK
  Metal cutting:    ~90-105 dB â†’ earplugs required

Types:
  Foam earplugs (NRR 29-33): insert correctly â€” roll, insert, hold
  Earmuffs (NRR 24-30): good for shorter sessions, easier to use

Long-term exposure at 85 dB causes permanent hearing loss over time.
Damage is cumulative and irreversible.
\`\`\`

## Gloves â€” Use and Don't Use
\`\`\`
USE gloves for:
  â†’ Handling chemicals (nitrile gloves)
  â†’ Hot parts after machining (leather gloves)
  â†’ Battery handling (nitrile for acid protection)
  â†’ Sheet metal (cut-resistant gloves)

DO NOT USE gloves for:
  â†’ Rotating machinery (drill press, lathe, grinder)
  â†’ Reason: a glove caught in a rotating tool pulls your hand in
    with no ability to pull back â€” bare hand can sometimes be released

The rule: gloves OFF near rotating equipment, ON for chemicals and sharp edges
\`\`\`

## Foot Protection
\`\`\`
Closed-toe shoes are mandatory in any robot shop, no exceptions.
  â†’ Dropped tools, falling robot batteries, rolling heavy frames
  â†’ Steel-toed boots: not required but recommended for battery handling
  â†’ No sandals, flip flops, or bare feet â€” ever

Additional: don't reach under the robot with your feet
            (common if you're kneeling and need to push something)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why are regular prescription glasses insufficient as eye protection in a shop environment?",opts:["They're less comfortable","Standard prescription lenses are not impact-rated â€” they can shatter from tool debris, sending fragments into the eye; ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses are specifically tested to resist impact and fragmentation","Prescription glasses don't fit under goggles","They block peripheral vision"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why must gloves NOT be worn near rotating power tools like drill presses?",opts:["Gloves reduce dexterity","A glove caught in a rotating chuck or bit wraps around instantly with enough force to pull the hand in before the wearer can react â€” bare hands can sometimes slip free; the glove removes that option","FIRST requires bare hands near tools","Gloves prevent feeling the tool"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is cumulative noise-induced hearing loss and why is it a serious concern for shop safety?",opts:["It recovers between sessions","Repeated exposure above 85 dB permanently damages hair cells in the cochlea â€” the damage accumulates over time and is irreversible; there is no medical treatment to restore hearing lost this way","It only affects people over 40","It only occurs above 120 dB"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.safety.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"sfi_machine",title:"Lathe & Milling Machine Safety",est:"15 min",content:`## Machine Tools Are the Most Dangerous Equipment in Your Shop
A lathe can pull in loose clothing or hair at 800 RPM and amputate fingers before the operator can react. A mill cutter spinning at 3,000 RPM ejects broken tooling across the shop. These are not hypothetical â€” they are documented injuries in FIRST team shops.

## Lathe Safety
\`\`\`
Before operating a lathe:
  â–¡ Remove all jewelry (rings, bracelets, watches â€” always)
  â–¡ Roll up sleeves above elbow, tuck in shirt
  â–¡ Tie back hair completely â€” shoulder-length or longer is the risk zone
  â–¡ Safety glasses with side shields â€” chips fly at face level
  â–¡ Know the emergency stop location BEFORE touching the power switch

During operation:
  âœ… Stand to the SIDE, not directly in front of the chuck
  âœ… Remove chuck key BEFORE turning on the lathe (zero exceptions)
  âœ… Keep hands away from rotating workpiece and chuck at all times
  âœ… Use a chip hook â€” never reach into chips with bare hands
  âœ… Start at low RPM for setup, increase after confirming workpiece is secure

NEVER:
  âŒ Measure a rotating workpiece
  âŒ Use a file on a rotating workpiece without a handle (the tang punctures hands)
  âŒ Leave the lathe running unattended
  âŒ Reverse direction while workpiece is still spinning
\`\`\`

## Milling Machine Safety
\`\`\`
Before operating a mill:
  â–¡ Inspect cutting tool â€” broken or chipped tools shatter; replace them
  â–¡ Ensure workpiece is clamped securely â€” unsecured stock becomes a projectile
  â–¡ Verify collet or arbor is fully tightened
  â–¡ Clear all wrenches and setup tools from the table before spindle power

During operation:
  âœ… Stand to the side, not directly behind the spindle direction
  âœ… Use flood coolant or cutting fluid to manage chip heat
  âœ… Take conservative cuts â€” deeper than recommended causes chatter and tool breakage
  âœ… Let the spindle come to full stop before changing tools or measuring

NEVER:
  âŒ Blow chips with compressed air while spindle runs (airborne chips)
  âŒ Reach around a moving cutter to clear chips
  âŒ Run a tool that vibrates (chatter) â€” it will break
  âŒ Climb mill with a manual mill (feeds in the wrong direction â€” machine grabs)
\`\`\`

## First Operation Checklist (Beginner Protocol)
\`\`\`
For any new student operating a machine tool for the first time:
  1. Watch an experienced operator complete one full setup and operation
  2. Verbally explain the setup back to the observer before touching the machine
  3. First operation is supervised â€” observer stands within arm's reach
  4. First solo operation requires pre-approval checklist (signed by mentor)
  5. No unsupervised machine operation until 5 supervised sessions completed

This protocol is not optional â€” it reflects how machine tool injuries actually occur:
most happen in the first 5 uses, when operators are still building muscle memory
for checking guards and removing chuck keys.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must the chuck key be removed from a lathe chuck before turning on the power, with zero exceptions?",opts:["Chuck keys are expensive","A chuck key left in the chuck becomes a high-speed projectile when the lathe starts â€” at typical lathe speeds, it strikes with enough force to cause fatal injury; this is why the rule has no exceptions","It damages the chuck","Chuck keys interfere with cutting"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is 'climb milling' and why is it dangerous on a manual mill?",opts:["Milling on an incline","Climb milling means the cutter rotates in the same direction as workpiece feed â€” on a manual mill, this causes the machine to grab and pull the workpiece violently; conventional milling (cutter rotating against feed) is required","Any high-speed milling","Milling without coolant"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a student watch a complete setup and operation before attempting a machine tool themselves, rather than just reading safety instructions?",opts:["Reading instructions is insufficient","Machine tool safety requires physical muscle memory for reflexive actions like removing chuck keys and checking guards â€” watching and verbalizing the procedure activates procedural learning that text alone cannot establish","Watching is faster","Mentors are required by insurance"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.teammanagement.Beginner.push(
  {id:"tmb_kickoff2",title:"Kickoff Day â€” Planning Your Strategy Session",est:"12 min",content:`## The Day That Sets Your Season Trajectory
Kickoff day is chaotic â€” excitement, reveal videos, game manual downloads, and everyone with opinions. Teams that structure kickoff day with a deliberate agenda walk out with a focused strategy. Teams that don't often spend Week 3 backtracking.

## Kickoff Day Agenda Template
\`\`\`
Morning (9amâ€“12pm): Understanding
  9:00  Watch reveal video together (all members)
  9:30  Read game manual: each subteam reads their relevant sections
        Programming: autonomous rules, sensor restrictions
        Mechanical: robot size/weight limits, mechanism rules
        Strategy: scoring, ranking point rules, endgame rules
  11:00 Whole team: clarifying questions â€” "what did we find?"
        No opinions yet â€” just facts from the manual

Afternoon (12pmâ€“3pm): Analysis
  12:00 Lunch break â€” informal conversation OK
  1:00  Scoring decomposition: fill in the points/time table together
  2:00  Robot concept brainstorm: each subteam proposes 3 mechanism ideas
        for their section (no criticism during brainstorm â€” quantity first)
  3:00  Quick dot vote: each member places 3 dots on the best concept ideas
        Top-dotted concepts go to the "prototype short list"

Evening (3pmâ€“5pm): Planning
  3:30  Set Week 1 prototyping goals (one goal per subteam)
  4:00  Assign research tasks: who looks into which mechanism by Wednesday?
  4:30  Establish: "Here is what we WILL build" vs "here is what we MIGHT add"
        Core robot = must work. Additional = only if core is complete.
  5:00  Kickoff dinner / celebration
\`\`\`

## The "Dot Vote" Decision Method
\`\`\`
Prevents: 20-person argument about which mechanism to prototype
Method:
  1. List all proposed mechanisms on a whiteboard
  2. Give everyone 3 sticky dots (or votes on a shared document)
  3. Members vote silently and simultaneously
  4. Count dots â€” top 2-3 go to prototype list
  5. Discuss only the top ideas, not the rejected ones

Benefits:
  â†’ Quieter members' votes count equally
  â†’ Reduces social pressure to agree with loud voices
  â†’ Fast: 5 minutes instead of 30
\`\`\`

## What to Avoid on Kickoff Day
\`\`\`
âŒ Starting to build anything on Kickoff day
   â†’ You don't understand the game well enough yet
   â†’ Parts cut today are almost always wrong by Week 2

âŒ Letting one person (mentor or captain) decide the whole strategy
   â†’ Buy-in from the team is required for good execution
   â†’ The quietest person may have the best idea

âŒ Committing to a "robot like [top team] did last year"
   â†’ The game changed â€” their solution was for a different game
   â†’ Your resources and skills are also different

âŒ Ending Kickoff without written-down decisions
   â†’ What was decided verbally at 4pm will be misremembered by Wednesday
   â†’ Assign someone to take notes and send them out before everyone leaves
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should teams avoid cutting or building any robot parts on Kickoff day?",opts:["It's against FIRST rules","Game understanding is too shallow on Day 1 â€” parts built before the scoring system and robot constraints are fully understood are almost always wrong and become waste","Kickoff day is too short","Building requires full team presence"],ans:1},
      {q:"What problem does the dot vote method solve during mechanism selection?",opts:["It speeds up the build process","It equalizes quieter members' input against louder voices and prevents a 20-person argument â€” simultaneous silent voting removes social pressure and produces a prioritized list in 5 minutes","Dot votes are required by FIRST","It reduces the number of options"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why must decisions from Kickoff day be written down before everyone leaves?",opts:["FIRST requires documentation","Verbal decisions from a long, exciting day are misremembered by Wednesday â€” without a written record, teams spend the first build session re-arguing what was already decided instead of executing it","Decisions change overnight","Writing forces clarity"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.cad.Beginner.push(
  {id:"cadb_drawing",title:"Creating 2D Manufacturing Drawings from CAD",est:"13 min",content:`## Why You Need Drawings Even With 3D CAD
A 3D model is the design. A 2D drawing is the manufacturing instruction. When you hand a part to a machinist, waterjet service, or teammate who doesn't know the design history, the drawing tells them every measurement, material, and tolerance they need â€” without needing to open the CAD file.

## When to Create a Drawing
\`\`\`
Create a drawing for:
  â†’ Parts sent to external fabrication (waterjet, lathe shop, print service)
  â†’ Any part where dimensions are critical for assembly fit
  â†’ Parts a new team member will build without supervision
  â†’ Parts you'll rebuild next season from scratch

Skip the drawing for:
  â†’ 3D-printed decorative parts (just send the STL)
  â†’ Parts machined by the same person who designed them (they use the model)
  â†’ Simple bent sheet where the bend lines are obvious
\`\`\`

## Onshape Drawing Workflow
\`\`\`
1. Open Part Studio â†’ Drawing button (or File â†’ New Drawing)
2. Set paper size: A-size (8.5Ã—11) for small parts, B-size (11Ã—17) for large
3. Insert view â†’ Front orthographic (shows the most features)
4. Add Right and Top views for full 3D understanding
5. Add Isometric view for context (no dimensions here)
6. Add dimensions by clicking edges:
   â†’ Overall width and height always first
   â†’ Then hole diameters and positions
   â†’ Then any critical internal dimensions
7. Add title block info: part name, material, revision, date, drawn by
8. Export â†’ PDF â†’ ready for fabrication
\`\`\`

## What Goes in a Title Block
\`\`\`
Minimum title block contents:
  Part name:      Left Motor Bracket
  Part number:    1234-MEC-0014
  Material:       6061-T6 Aluminum 0.125"
  Scale:          1:1 (or 1:2 if large)
  Drawn by:       [your name]
  Date:           [today]
  Revision:       A
  Sheet:          1 of 1

Why revision letters matter:
  When you update a part, increment from Rev A â†’ Rev B
  The shop knows to make the latest revision
  "Make me 3 of part 1234-MEC-0014 Rev B" is unambiguous
\`\`\`

## Reading Drawings as a Maker
\`\`\`
Before making a cut or drilling a hole, answer:
  â†’ What is the overall size? (Outer dimensions always visible)
  â†’ Are any dimensions "reference only" (marked REF)? â†’ Don't cut to these
  â†’ Is there a note like "BREAK ALL SHARP EDGES"? â†’ File all edges after cutting
  â†’ Any holes marked with depth? â†’ Blind holes don't go all the way through
  â†’ Dimensions with tolerance boxes? â†’ These are the critical ones â€” measure twice
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"When is creating a 2D manufacturing drawing necessary even if the 3D CAD model exists?",opts:["Always â€” 3D models aren't sufficient","When the part is sent to external fabrication or built by someone who doesn't have access to or experience with the CAD software â€” the drawing communicates all needed information without requiring CAD knowledge","Drawings are optional","Only for metal parts"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do parts have revision letters (Rev A, Rev B) in their title block?",opts:["Revisions indicate quality grade","Revision letters track design iterations â€” when a part is updated, incrementing the revision ensures the fabricator knows to make the latest version and allows tracking which version of a part is installed on the robot","Rev A is always the best version","Letters replace part numbers"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a dimension marked 'REF' (reference) mean on an engineering drawing?",opts:["It's the most important dimension","It is informational only â€” it shows a dimension that's defined elsewhere or derived from other dimensions; fabricators should not try to meet this as a specification because it may conflict with directly toleranced dimensions","REF means the measurement is approximate","It indicates a reference edge for measuring"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.awards.Beginner.push(
  {id:"awb_safety_award",title:"Safety Captain Award Strategy",est:"13 min",content:`## The Safety Award is Winnable
The Safety Award (FTC) and Safety Captain Award (FRC) are undercompeted relative to Impact and Inspire. Many events have fewer than 5 teams seriously pursuing them. A prepared safety captain with documented programs wins more often than they expect.

## What the Award Actually Evaluates
\`\`\`
FRC Safety Captain Award judges look for:
  1. Team safety culture (is safety proactive, not reactive?)
  2. Safety captain's knowledge (can they answer unexpected questions?)
  3. Safety documentation (procedures, training records, inspection logs)
  4. Pit safety (is the pit organized, LOTO practiced, PPE visible?)
  5. Community safety awareness (did you share safety with other teams?)

FTC Safety Award is evaluated by pit inspectors and judges who visit the pits.
  They observe: PPE availability, safe power-up procedures, battery handling,
                whether tools are safely stored when not in use.
\`\`\`

## Safety Captain Interview Preparation
\`\`\`
Likely questions â€” prepare answers:
  "What is your team's process for handling a robot malfunction?"
    â†’ Describe your LOTO procedure step by step

  "What PPE does your team use and when is each required?"
    â†’ List: safety glasses, gloves, ear protection, closed-toe shoes
      + specific situations for each

  "Has your team had any near-misses this season? What did you learn?"
    â†’ Honest answer with 5-Why analysis wins respect
    â†’ "No incidents" sounds rehearsed if you haven't documented

  "How do you onboard new members to safety procedures?"
    â†’ Describe your specific onboarding session

  "What makes your team's safety culture different from other teams?"
    â†’ Specific programs, specific stories â€” not "we care about safety"
\`\`\`

## Documentation That Wins Safety Awards
\`\`\`
Bring to the interview (physical or digital):
  â†’ Safety training log: date, topic, attendees (signed)
  â†’ Near-miss log: dates, incidents, corrective actions
  â†’ SOPs: 1-page procedures for battery handling, robot enable, power-up
  â†’ PPE inventory sheet: what you have, last inspection date
  â†’ Safety walkthrough checklist you use before each build session

One-page summary card:
  Teams that hand judges a well-designed one-pager with their key stats
  ("0 recordable incidents, 12 safety training sessions, 3 SOPs written")
  make a stronger impression than verbal-only presentations.
\`\`\`

## Pit Safety That Judges Notice
\`\`\`
During the event â€” judges walk through pits:
  âœ… Robot on stands when being worked on (not on the floor)
  âœ… Safety glasses available and worn by pit crew
  âœ… Battery charging area clearly designated, away from traffic
  âœ… Tools stored when not in use (not scattered on the floor)
  âœ… Clear path to exit (not blocked by tool boxes or robot carts)
  âœ… Main breaker accessible without removing panels

Red flags judges document:
  âŒ Robot operated in pit with students' hands near mechanisms
  âŒ PPE not available or not worn
  âŒ Charging batteries in an unsafe location
  âŒ Disorganized pit with tripping hazards
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does an honest answer about a near-miss â€” with 5-Why analysis â€” impress Safety Award judges more than claiming no incidents?",opts:["Near-misses score points","A team that never admits near-misses likely hasn't analyzed them â€” judges know incidents occur in active robot shops; a team that documented, analyzed, and fixed a near-miss demonstrates a mature safety culture rather than a performative one","Judges require near-miss reports","Near-misses are positive events"],ans:1},
      {q:"What physical documentation most strengthens a Safety Award submission compared to verbal answers alone?",opts:["Robot inspection reports","Training logs with dates and signatures, near-miss logs with corrective actions, and written SOPs â€” these prove the safety culture exists year-round rather than only on competition day","Business cards","Awards from previous years"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'LOTO' stand for and why do Safety Award judges ask about it?",opts:["Lockout Total Operation","Lockout/Tagout â€” a procedure for safely disabling energy sources before maintenance; judges ask because LOTO is the most important safeguard against a robot being unexpectedly energized while someone is working on it","Level One Team Operation","Limit Output Transfer Order"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_actions",title:"GitHub Actions for Robot Code CI",est:"15 min",content:`## Automated Checks Every Time You Push
A robot code repository with no automation silently accumulates broken code until someone deploys it. GitHub Actions runs checks automatically on every push and pull request â€” catching issues before they reach the robot.

## What CI Does for a FIRST Team
\`\`\`
On every push to any branch:
  â†’ Build the robot code (catches compile errors immediately)
  â†’ Run unit tests (catches logic regressions)
  â†’ Check code style (optional â€” enforces team standards)

On every pull request to main:
  â†’ All of the above PLUS
  â†’ Require the build to pass before merging is allowed
  â†’ Require at least one review (optional, but recommended)

Result: main branch always compiles; deploy from main is always safe.
\`\`\`

## FRC Java Workflow (WPILib Gradle)
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: Build Robot Code

on:
  push:
    branches: [ "**" ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up JDK 17
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '17'
          distribution: 'temurin'

      - name: Grant execute permission for gradlew
        run: chmod +x gradlew

      - name: Build robot code
        run: ./gradlew build

      - name: Run tests
        run: ./gradlew test
\`\`\`

## FTC Java Workflow
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: FTC Build

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up JDK 11
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          java-version: '11'
          distribution: 'temurin'

      - name: Build TeamCode
        run: ./gradlew :TeamCode:assemble

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: ./gradlew :TeamCode:test
\`\`\`

## Python Scouting Tool CI
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/test.yml
name: Scouting Tests

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: python -m unittest discover -v

      - name: Check types (optional)
        run: pip install mypy && mypy analysis.py loader.py
\`\`\`

## Enabling Branch Protection
\`\`\`
GitHub Settings â†’ Branches â†’ Add rule:
  Branch name pattern: main
  âœ… Require status checks to pass before merging
  âœ… Select "build" check (your workflow job name)
  âœ… Require branches to be up to date before merging
  Optional: Require pull request reviews (1 reviewer)

Now: pushing broken code to main is physically impossible.
     The merge button stays grayed out until CI passes.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What problem does requiring CI to pass before merging to main solve for a FIRST team?",opts:["It speeds up development","It prevents broken code from ever reaching the main branch â€” without protection, one push of code that doesn't compile could block the whole team from deploying until the error is found and fixed","CI is required by FIRST","It reduces the number of branches"],ans:1},
