      {q:"What happens in GitHub Actions when the 'build' step fails?",opts:["The code is automatically fixed","The workflow is marked as failed â€” a red X appears on the commit and on any open pull request, and if branch protection is enabled, merging is blocked until the build passes","The push is rejected","The file is deleted"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is automated building especially valuable for a student team compared to manual testing?",opts:["Automated builds are faster","Students forget to test before pushing â€” automation runs the same checks consistently on every push without relying on anyone remembering to run them, catching the errors that get pushed in late-night sessions","Manual testing is inaccurate","Automation requires less knowledge"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.git.Beginner.push(
  {id:"gb_hooks",title:"Pre-Commit Hooks for Code Quality",est:"10 min",content:`## Catch Problems Before They Reach the Repo
A pre-commit hook is a script that runs automatically before git commit finalizes. If it fails, the commit is rejected. This catches formatting issues, syntax errors, and common mistakes before they're ever recorded in history.

## Setting Up a Basic Hook (All Platforms)
\`\`\`bash
# Git hooks live in .git/hooks/ â€” this file runs before every commit:
# Create/edit .git/hooks/pre-commit (no extension)

#!/bin/bash
echo "Running pre-commit checks..."

# Check for Java syntax errors in TeamCode (FTC):
find TeamCode/src -name "*.java" -newer .last_check | while read file; do
  javac -classpath "$(find . -name '*.jar' | tr '\\n' ':' )" \
        -proc:none "$file" 2>&1 | grep "error:" && exit 1
done

echo "Pre-commit checks passed!"
exit 0
\`\`\`
\`\`\`bash
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit  # make it executable
\`\`\`

## Python Scouting Repo Hook
\`\`\`bash
#!/bin/bash
# .git/hooks/pre-commit

# Run Python syntax check on all staged .py files:
staged_py=$(git diff --cached --name-only --diff-filter=ACM | grep '.py$')

if [ -n "$staged_py" ]; then
  echo "Checking Python syntax..."
  for file in $staged_py; do
    python -m py_compile "$file" || {
      echo "Syntax error in $file â€” commit rejected"
      exit 1
    }
  done

  # Run tests if any exist:
  if [ -f "test_analysis.py" ]; then
    python -m unittest test_analysis -v || {
      echo "Tests failed â€” commit rejected"
      exit 1
    }
  fi
fi

echo "All checks passed."
exit 0
\`\`\`

## pre-commit Framework (Easier to Maintain)
\`\`\`bash
pip install pre-commit
\`\`\`
\`\`\`yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml (committed to repo â€” shared with all contributors)
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v4.5.0
    hooks:
      - id: check-yaml        # valid YAML files
      - id: check-json        # valid JSON files
      - id: end-of-file-fixer # files end with newline
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: check-merge-conflict  # catches forgotten merge markers

  - repo: https://github.com/psf/black
    rev: 24.1.0
    hooks:
      - id: black  # auto-formats Python code on commit
\`\`\`
\`\`\`bash
pre-commit install  # one-time setup per clone
\`\`\`

## What to Enforce for FIRST Teams
\`\`\`
For robot code repos:
  â†’ No obvious syntax errors (build step catches this in CI too â€” defense in depth)
  â†’ No TODO comments accidentally committed to main
  â†’ No debug prints: System.out.println("HERE") or print("DEBUGGING")

For scouting repos:
  â†’ Python syntax check
  â†’ Unit tests pass
  â†’ No .env or credential files accidentally staged
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"At what point in the git workflow does a pre-commit hook run?",opts:["Before git push","After git add but before the commit is finalized â€” if the hook exits with a non-zero code, git cancels the commit and the developer must fix the issue before the commit is recorded","After git commit","During git merge"],ans:1},
      {q:"What advantage does the pre-commit framework (.pre-commit-config.yaml) have over a manually written hook script?",opts:["It runs faster","The config file is committed to the repo â€” every contributor who clones and runs 'pre-commit install' automatically gets the same hooks; a manually written .git/hooks script isn't tracked by git and disappears on fresh clones","It catches more errors","The framework is required for Python"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should preventing accidentally committed debug print statements be a hook check for robot code?",opts:["Print statements break compilation","Debug prints slow down telemetry loops and produce noise that hides real diagnostic output â€” finding and removing them before they reach main keeps the codebase clean and prevents confusion during competition debugging","Print statements are illegal","Hooks can only check syntax"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.outreach.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ora_alumni",title:"Building an Alumni Network",est:"16 min",content:`## Your Graduates Are Your Greatest Asset
The student who built your intake in 2021 is now an engineering sophomore. The student who wrote your autonomous in 2019 is a software engineer at a robotics company. Alumni are mentors, donors, sponsors, and recruiters â€” if you maintain the connection after graduation.

## Why Alumni Networks Fade Without Effort
\`\`\`
Natural drift:
  â†’ Students graduate â†’ go to college â†’ lose contact naturally
  â†’ Team communication moves to new platforms
  â†’ New members don't know who the alumni are
  â†’ Alumni don't know they're still wanted

The team that graduates 10 students per year and maintains connections
has 60 alumni after 6 years â€” a substantial resource pool.
The team that loses contact with graduates has zero.
\`\`\`

## Building the Foundation (While Students Are Still Members)
\`\`\`
Senior year tasks before graduation:
  â†’ Collect: email address (not school email â€” personal only), graduation year,
             area of study, what they're most proud of from their time on the team
  â†’ Store in: a shared document (Google Sheet), not in someone's phone contacts
  â†’ Ask: "Would you like to be contacted for mentoring opportunities?"
  â†’ Give: a "team alumni" email address to reach back out

The goodbye tradition:
  â†’ Final meeting of senior year: each graduating member shares
    one lesson and one piece of advice to the team
  â†’ This creates a ritual that makes them WANT to stay connected
\`\`\`

## The Annual Alumni Touch Point
\`\`\`
Once per year (summer is best): send an alumni update email.
  â†’ 3 paragraphs max
  â†’ Season recap: results, new programs, team milestones
  â†’ Member update: "We now have 32 members including 8 freshmen"
  â†’ Ask: "Are you open to a virtual Q&A session with our team?"
  â†’ One ask only: don't request mentoring AND donations AND connections in one email

Subject line: "Team 1234 â€” 2025 Season Recap & What's Next"
Sender: a current student who knew the recipient, not a generic address
\`\`\`

## Alumni Engagement Programs
\`\`\`
Career panel (virtual, 1 hour):
  â†’ 4-6 alumni from different fields join a video call
  â†’ Current students ask questions about college, careers, what FIRST prepared them for
  â†’ Requires almost no coordination â€” high value for students

Mentor matching:
  â†’ Alumni who are in engineering/CS offer 1-hour virtual sessions with students
  â†’ Match by interest area: programming alum â†’ programming students
  â†’ One session per semester is sustainable for most busy alumni

Donation program (for teams with 501c3 status):
  â†’ Alumni who are employed can often donate small amounts
  â†’ Even $50/year from 20 alumni = $1,000 â€” meaningful for a FIRST team
  â†’ NEVER ask for money in the first re-contact after a gap
    Rebuild the relationship first

Sponsor referrals:
  â†’ Alumni at companies may be able to introduce you to their corporate giving programs
  â†’ This is the highest-leverage alumni benefit â€” one introduction can yield thousands
  â†’ Ask: "Is there someone at your company we should speak with about sponsorship?"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should alumni contact information be stored in a shared team document rather than in individual students' phones?",opts:["Phones are insecure","Contact in a phone belongs to that student â€” when they graduate, the connection is lost; a shared team document transfers with leadership and keeps alumni accessible to future teams indefinitely","Documents are more private","FIRST requires records of alumni"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should the annual alumni email come from a student who knew the recipient, rather than a generic team address?",opts:["Generic addresses get spam-filtered","Personal sender context triggers a human connection â€” the recipient knows who's writing, which increases open rates and response rates dramatically compared to an impersonal institutional email","Students have better writing","Generic addresses require approval"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a team never request money in the first re-contact with an alumni after a significant gap?",opts:["It's against FIRST rules","The relationship needs to be re-established before a request is appropriate â€” a cold donation ask to someone who feels forgotten comes across as transactional and damages the relationship; rebuilding connection first makes any subsequent ask far more likely to succeed","Alumni never donate","First contact should be a survey"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€â”€ PACK 11 â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€

LESSONS.java.Beginner.push(
  {id:"jb_immutable",title:"Immutability & Final Fields in Robot Code",est:"11 min",content:`## Why Mutable State Causes Bugs
When any part of your code can change a variable, bugs are hard to trace. Marking things final tells both the compiler and your teammates: this value doesn't change, and it shouldn't.

## final Variables
\`\`\`java
// Constant that never changes:
static final double WHEEL_DIAMETER_IN = 4.0;  // cannot be reassigned
static final int    TICKS_PER_REV     = 28;

// final local variable â€” set once, then read-only:
public void moveToTarget(double targetIn) {
    final double targetTicks = targetIn * (TICKS_PER_REV / (Math.PI * WHEEL_DIAMETER_IN));
    // targetTicks can't be accidentally overwritten below this line
    motor.setTargetPosition((int) targetTicks);
}

// Constructor-set final field â€” set at construction, never changed:
public class ArmConfig {
    public final double maxAngleDeg;
    public final double ticksPerDeg;

    public ArmConfig(double maxAngle, double ticksPerDeg) {
        this.maxAngleDeg = maxAngle;
        this.ticksPerDeg = ticksPerDeg;
    }
}
// Passed around safely â€” no code can accidentally modify these
ArmConfig cfg = new ArmConfig(160.0, 5.3);
\`\`\`

## Immutable Data Transfer Objects
\`\`\`java
// A snapshot of robot state â€” immutable so it's safe to share between threads
public final class RobotSnapshot {
    public final double heading;
    public final double velocityInPerSec;
    public final int    leftTicks, rightTicks;
    public final long   timestampMs;

    public RobotSnapshot(double heading, double vel, int left, int right) {
        this.heading          = heading;
        this.velocityInPerSec = vel;
        this.leftTicks        = left;
        this.rightTicks       = right;
        this.timestampMs      = System.currentTimeMillis();
    }
}

// Thread-safe â€” once created, no field can change:
RobotSnapshot snap = new RobotSnapshot(imu.getYaw(), velocity, leftEnc, rightEnc);
// Pass snap to autonomous planner, logger, telemetry â€” all read the same values
\`\`\`

## When NOT to Use final
\`\`\`
Avoid making everything final â€” it has a cost:
  â†’ Loop variables (must change each iteration â€” can't be final)
  â†’ Accumulated totals (totalDistance += delta â€” must be mutable)
  â†’ PID state (prevError, integral â€” must update each loop)

Use final for:
  â†’ Configuration constants (gear ratios, distances, PID gains)
  â†’ Objects that represent a fixed snapshot of data
  â†’ Parameters inside a method that should not be modified
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does declaring a field 'static final' guarantee?",opts:["The field is private","The value is set once (usually at declaration) and can never be reassigned anywhere in the program â€” the compiler enforces this, catching accidental overwrites that would otherwise be silent bugs","static final means the value is zero","It makes the field faster to read"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is an immutable RobotSnapshot object safer to pass between threads than a mutable state object?",opts:["Snapshots use less memory","Once created, no thread can modify a snapshot's fields â€” threads reading the snapshot always see consistent data with no risk of reading a partially-updated state that another thread is in the middle of changing","Threads can't access mutable objects","Snapshots are automatically synchronized"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should PID state variables (prevError, integral) not be marked final?",opts:["PID variables are always static","They must be updated on every control loop iteration â€” prevError must store the current error for the next loop, and integral accumulates over time; making them final would prevent these essential updates","PID doesn't use variables","Final fields are slower for PID"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.java.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ji_observer",title:"Observer Pattern for Sensor Events",est:"16 min",content:`## Event-Driven vs Polling
Polling: every loop, check if the sensor changed â€” wastes CPU when nothing changed.
Observer pattern: subsystem notifies listeners when something happens â€” clean, decoupled, no wasted checks.

## Building a Simple Observer
\`\`\`java
// 1. Define the event interface (what listeners receive):
public interface PieceDetectedListener {
    void onPieceDetected(boolean hasGamePiece);
}

// 2. The subsystem that publishes events:
public class IntakeSubsystem {
    private final List<PieceDetectedListener> listeners = new ArrayList<>();
    private boolean lastState = false;

    public void addListener(PieceDetectedListener listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
    }

    // Call this in periodic() â€” only fires when state changes:
    public void periodic() {
        boolean current = pieceColorSensor.getProximity() > PIECE_THRESHOLD;
        if (current != lastState) {
            lastState = current;
            for (PieceDetectedListener l : listeners) {
                l.onPieceDetected(current);   // notify all listeners
            }
        }
    }
}

// 3. Subscribers react to events:
intake.addListener(hasPiece -> {
    if (hasPiece) {
        LEDs.setColor(Color.GREEN);
        rumbleController(0.3, 0.5); // 0.3s rumble
    } else {
        LEDs.setColor(Color.RED);
    }
});

intake.addListener(hasPiece -> {
    if (hasPiece) elevatorSubsystem.prepareForScore(); // start pre-positioning
});
\`\`\`

## Limit Switch Events
\`\`\`java
public interface LimitSwitchListener {
    void onTriggered(String switchName);
}

public class ArmSubsystem {
    private List<LimitSwitchListener> limitListeners = new ArrayList<>();

    public void periodic() {
        if (topLimitSwitch.isPressed() && !topWasPressed) {
            for (LimitSwitchListener l : limitListeners) {
                l.onTriggered("ARM_TOP");
            }
            motor.setPower(0); // immediate stop
        }
        topWasPressed = topLimitSwitch.isPressed();
    }
}

// Listener: log every limit trigger for debugging
arm.addLimitListener(name -> {
    telemetry.addData("Limit triggered", name + " at " + System.currentTimeMillis());
});
\`\`\`

## Advantages Over Polling
\`\`\`
Polling version â€” couples everything together:
  if (intake.hasPiece()) { LEDs.setGreen(); }
  if (intake.hasPiece()) { elevator.prepareForScore(); }
  // Both checks in the main loop â€” add more reactions = modify main loop

Observer version â€” decoupled:
  intake.addListener(hasPiece -> LEDs.setGreen());
  intake.addListener(hasPiece -> elevator.prepareForScore());
  // Add more reactions without touching IntakeSubsystem code at all
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the core difference between polling a sensor and using the observer pattern?",opts:["Polling is more accurate","Polling checks the sensor every loop regardless of change; the observer pattern notifies listeners only when the value actually changes â€” eliminating wasted checks and decoupling the subsystem from its reactions","Observer pattern uses interrupts","They produce identical results"],ans:1},
      {q:"In the observer pattern, why can you add multiple listeners to the same event?",opts:["Java limits listeners to 10","Each listener is an independent subscriber â€” when the event fires, all listeners in the list are notified sequentially; this lets LED control, elevator prep, and telemetry all react to the same piece detection event without knowing about each other","Listeners share state","Multiple listeners cause ordering issues"],ans:1},
      {q:"What must be tracked alongside the current sensor reading to detect a state change and avoid firing the event every loop?",opts:["The sensor's raw voltage","The previous loop's reading â€” comparing current != lastState triggers the event only on the transition (falseâ†’true or trueâ†’false) rather than continuously while the state holds steady","The sensor's calibration offset","The time since last read"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.python.Beginner.push(
  {id:"pyb_pathlib",title:"File Paths with pathlib",est:"10 min",content:`## Forget String Concatenation for Paths
\`"data/" + event + "/matches.csv"\` breaks on Windows (backslash vs forward slash) and becomes unreadable fast. Python's pathlib.Path handles paths correctly on every OS and makes file operations readable.

## Basic pathlib
\`\`\`python
from pathlib import Path

# Create paths by dividing with /  (works on Windows AND Mac/Linux):
data_dir  = Path("data")
event_dir = data_dir / "2025casd"
csv_file  = event_dir / "matches.csv"

print(csv_file)             # data/2025casd/matches.csv
print(csv_file.name)        # matches.csv
print(csv_file.stem)        # matches  (no extension)
print(csv_file.suffix)      # .csv
print(csv_file.parent)      # data/2025casd
print(csv_file.exists())    # True or False
\`\`\`

## Creating Directories and Files
\`\`\`python
# Create directory (and parents) if it doesn't exist:
output_dir = Path("exports") / "2025casd"
output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # no error if already exists

# Write a file:
report = output_dir / "picklist.txt"
report.write_text("Team 1234: 51.2 avg\\nTeam 5678: 48.7 avg\\n")

# Append to a file:
report.open("a").write("Team 9012: 45.1 avg\\n")

# Read a file:
content = report.read_text()
\`\`\`

## Finding Files by Pattern
\`\`\`python
data = Path("data")

# All CSV files anywhere under data/:
all_csvs = list(data.rglob("*.csv"))  # recursive

# All JSON files in one specific directory:
configs = list((data / "2025casd").glob("*.json"))

# Process every CSV found:
for csv_path in sorted(data.rglob("matches_*.csv")):
    event = csv_path.parent.name       # folder name = event key
    df = pd.read_csv(csv_path)
    print(f"{event}: {len(df)} matches")
\`\`\`

## The HOME and Script Directories
\`\`\`python
# Always find files relative to the script's own location (not where you run it from):
SCRIPT_DIR = Path(__file__).parent
data_dir   = SCRIPT_DIR / "data"
config     = SCRIPT_DIR / "config.toml"
# Works correctly whether you run: python analysis.py
#                                  python tools/analysis.py
#                                  ./scripts/analysis.py

# Home directory (for storing team-wide settings):
home_config = Path.home() / ".first_scout" / "settings.json"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does pathlib.Path handle cross-platform file paths better than string concatenation?",opts:["pathlib is faster","Path uses the correct separator for the current OS automatically â€” / on Mac/Linux, \\ on Windows; string concatenation with '/' breaks on Windows paths and becomes unreadable when paths nest several levels deep","String concatenation is deprecated","pathlib works offline"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does Path('data').rglob('*.csv') do differently from Path('data').glob('*.csv')?",opts:["rglob is recursive","rglob searches recursively through all subdirectories â€” it finds matches.csv inside data/2025casd/matches.csv; plain glob only matches files directly inside data/ without descending into subdirectories","They are identical","rglob requires a full path"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why use Path(__file__).parent instead of Path('.') to locate files relative to a script?",opts:["__file__ is more accurate","Path('.') resolves to the current working directory â€” which changes depending on where you run the script from; __file__.parent always points to the directory containing the script itself, regardless of where it was invoked","Path('.') doesn't work on Python 3","__file__ is faster to compute"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.python.Advanced.push(
  {id:"pa_type_hints",title:"Type Hints & Static Analysis for Large Scouting Codebases",est:"22 min",content:`## Why Type Hints Pay Off at 2000+ Lines
A 200-line scouting script is readable without type hints. A 2000-line codebase with 30 functions is not â€” you forget what every function returns and what it expects. Type hints make the code self-documenting and let tools catch errors before runtime.

## Basic Type Hints
\`\`\`python
from typing import Optional, Union
from pathlib import Path

# Function signature with types:
def compute_contribution(auto: int, cycles: int, climb: str) -> int:
    pts = {"None":0, "L1":3, "L2":6, "L3":10, "L4":15}
    return auto + cycles * 4 + pts.get(climb, 0)

# Return type can be None:
def find_team(teams: list[int], target: int) -> Optional[int]:
    for i, t in enumerate(teams):
        if t == target:
            return i
    return None  # caller must handle this

# Multiple possible types:
def load_config(source: Union[str, Path]) -> dict:
    return {}

# Complex types:
def top_n_teams(
    data: list[dict[str, int | float | str]],
    n: int = 20
) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    ...
\`\`\`

## Running mypy for Static Analysis
\`\`\`bash
pip install mypy
mypy analysis.py          # check one file
mypy .                    # check entire project
mypy --strict analysis.py # strictest mode (requires all types)
\`\`\`
\`\`\`python
# mypy catches mistakes before runtime:
def get_avg_cycles(data: list[dict]) -> float:
    return sum(d["cycles"] for d in data) / len(data)

get_avg_cycles("not a list")  # mypy: error: Argument 1 has incompatible type "str"
\`\`\`

## TypedDict for Scouting Records
\`\`\`python
from typing import TypedDict, Literal

class MatchRecord(TypedDict):
    team:      int
    match_num: int
    event_key: str
    auto_pts:  int
    cycles:    int
    climb:     Literal["None", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4"]  # only valid strings
    notes:     str

def process_record(rec: MatchRecord) -> int:
    # mypy knows rec["climb"] is one of the 5 valid strings
    pts = {"None":0,"L1":3,"L2":6,"L3":10,"L4":15}
    return rec["auto_pts"] + rec["cycles"]*4 + pts[rec["climb"]]

# Invalid climb value caught at analysis time:
bad: MatchRecord = {"team": 1234, "match_num": 1, "event_key": "2025casd",
                    "auto_pts": 12, "cycles": 6,
                    "climb": "L5",  # mypy: error: "L5" not assignable to Literal
                    "notes": ""}
\`\`\`

## Protocol â€” Duck Typing with Types
\`\`\`python
from typing import Protocol

class Scoreable(Protocol):
    def contribution(self) -> int: ...

def rank_entries(entries: list[Scoreable]) -> list[Scoreable]:
    return sorted(entries, key=lambda e: e.contribution(), reverse=True)

# Any class with a .contribution() -> int method satisfies Scoreable
# No inheritance needed â€” purely structural
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does mypy do that Python's runtime type checking does not?",opts:["mypy runs the code faster","mypy analyzes type hints without executing the code, catching type mismatches at analysis time â€” passing a string where a list is expected is flagged before the program runs, preventing runtime errors during competition","mypy generates type hints automatically","Runtime checking is more thorough"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does Literal['None', 'L1', 'L2', 'L3', 'L4'] as a type annotation accomplish?",opts:["It limits string length","It restricts the field to exactly those five string values â€” mypy reports an error if any code assigns any other string to that field, catching typos like 'L5' or 'l2' at analysis time rather than when the calculation produces a wrong result","It creates an enum automatically","Literal types only work in TypedDict"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the difference between a Protocol and a base class for defining a shared interface?",opts:["They are identical in Python","Protocol uses structural subtyping â€” any class with the required methods satisfies the Protocol without explicitly inheriting from it; a base class requires explicit inheritance, coupling the class hierarchy to the interface","Protocols are faster","Base classes support more methods"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.mechanical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"mi_bearings",title:"Bearing Selection & Installation",est:"15 min",content:`## Bearings Are Not Interchangeable
Using the wrong bearing â€” or installing a correct one poorly â€” causes premature failure, binding, and mechanism noise. Every rotating shaft in your robot deserves a deliberate bearing choice.

## Bearing Types in FIRST Robots
\`\`\`
Ball bearing (deep groove):
  Most common in FIRST â€” REV, WCP, AndyMark all use these
  Handles: radial load (perpendicular to shaft), small thrust load
  Sizes: ID Ã— OD Ã— width, e.g. 8Ã—16Ã—5mm (common FTC), 1/2"Ã—1-1/8"Ã—5/16" (FRC)

Flanged bearing:
  Same as ball bearing + a flange on the outer race
  The flange lets you press it into a bore from one side with no separate retainer
  Preferred for tube walls and 3D-printed housings
  FTC: very common in GoBILDA and REV systems

Needle bearing:
  Very thin â€” fits in tight radial spaces
  High radial load capacity, but ZERO thrust load capacity
  Use: pivot points where axial is constrained by other features

Thrust bearing:
  Designed ONLY for axial (along-shaft) loads
  Use: where a mechanism pushes along the shaft (worm gear output, screw jacks)
  NEVER use a ball bearing as a thrust-only bearing â€” it will fail fast
\`\`\`

## Installation â€” How to Press Bearings Correctly
\`\`\`
Bearings must be pressed in, not hammered in unevenly:

Into a bore:
  âœ… Use a press (arbor press, bench vise with flat plates)
  âœ… Press on the OUTER race only â€” never the inner race
  âœ… Apply even force across the full circumference
  âŒ Don't hammer one side â€” brinelling (denting the raceways) occurs
  âŒ Don't heat aluminum bores with a torch â€” 200Â°C is enough, not 400Â°C

Onto a shaft:
  âœ… Press on the INNER race only
  âœ… Shaft should be a light interference fit (see tolerance lesson for values)
  âŒ Don't drive through the bearing by pressing the inner â†’ outer (damages balls)

FTC DIY press method:
  1. Thread a long 10-32 bolt through the bearing center
  2. Two washers on each side (one inside bore, one outside)
  3. Tighten the nut â€” draws bearing squarely into bore
  4. Check that it's fully seated (flush or below surface)
\`\`\`

## Preload, Clearance & Lubrication
\`\`\`
Preload: slight axial force on the bearing (spring or shimming)
  â†’ Eliminates slop in the axial direction
  â†’ Use when mechanism must not rock on its shaft
  â†’ Too much preload â†’ increased friction, heat, premature failure

Clearance fit (shaft slightly smaller than inner race):
  â†’ Bearing can spin on shaft â€” wrong for most applications
  â†’ Correct only when the OUTER race rotates (like a wheel bearing hub)

Lubrication for FIRST robots:
  Factory grease on new bearings: adequate for most uses â€” don't wash out
  Dry lube (PTFE spray): after a season of heavy use
  Never: WD-40 on bearings (washes out real grease, attracts debris)
  Never: Over-grease (excess grease churns, generates heat, attracts debris)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must a ball bearing never be used as a thrust-only bearing?",opts:["Ball bearings can't handle thrust","A ball bearing's internal geometry allows balls to carry both radial and small axial loads â€” pure axial load pushes balls against the side of the raceway rather than the designed contact zone, causing rapid fatigue failure","Thrust bearings are illegal","Ball bearings are too small for thrust loads"],ans:1},
      {q:"When pressing a bearing onto a shaft, why must force be applied only to the inner race?",opts:["The outer race is softer","Force applied to the outer race to push a bearing onto a shaft transmits through the balls â€” this damages the raceways and balls with brinelling (small dents); applying force to the inner race presses it directly without stressing the internal components","Inner race is always stronger","Outer race installation is acceptable"],ans:1},
      {q:"What installation problem does the bolt-and-washer method solve for FTC teams without an arbor press?",opts:["It provides more force than a press","It applies even, controlled force across the full bearing circumference by drawing it squarely into the bore as the bolt is tightened â€” unlike a hammer blow which applies force unevenly and can tilt the bearing","It's faster than a press","The bolt prevents corrosion"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.electrical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ei_servo2",title:"Servo Control Deep Dive â€” Feedback & Custom Ranges",est:"16 min",content:`## Beyond setPower(1.0)
Standard servo control sets position by pulse width. Understanding the actual PWM protocol lets you control servos from any microcontroller, recover from miscalibrated ranges, and use continuous rotation servos with precise control.

## How Servo PWM Actually Works
\`\`\`
Servo control signal: PWM at 50 Hz (20ms period)
  Pulse width determines position:
  1000 Î¼s (1.0 ms) = full counter-clockwise (-1.0 in FTC/FRC)
  1500 Î¼s (1.5 ms) = center (0.0)
  2000 Î¼s (2.0 ms) = full clockwise (+1.0)

In FTC/FRC frameworks, setPosition(0.0 to 1.0) maps:
  0.0 â†’ 1000 Î¼s â†’ CCW
  0.5 â†’ 1500 Î¼s â†’ center
  1.0 â†’ 2000 Î¼s â†’ CW

Some servos use narrower ranges (600-2400 Î¼s) for larger angles.
Calling setPosition(1.0) with a narrow-range servo may not reach full travel.
\`\`\`

## Calibrating a Servo's Range in FTC
\`\`\`java
// REV Smart Robot Servo (SRS) â€” programmable range:
// Connect SRS to a servo programmer or Control Hub, use REV Hardware Client
// Set min/max pulse widths to match your mechanism's actual travel

// In code â€” map 0.0-1.0 to a custom pulse range:
// If servo full travel is 600-2400 Î¼s but you only want 600-1800:
public double scalePosition(double pos, double minUs, double maxUs) {
    // Standard 1000-2000 Î¼s range: normalize target to 0-1
    double normalizedMin = (minUs - 1000) / 1000.0;
    double normalizedMax = (maxUs - 1000) / 1000.0;
    return normalizedMin + pos * (normalizedMax - normalizedMin);
}

// Use: servo.setPosition(scalePosition(0.0, 600, 1800)); // CCW end of custom range
\`\`\`

## Continuous Rotation Servos
\`\`\`java
// Continuous rotation servo: pulse width â†’ speed, not position
// 1500 Î¼s = stop; < 1500 = CCW; > 1500 = CW
// In FTC: setPosition(0.5) = stop, 0.0 = full CCW, 1.0 = full CW

CRServo intakeServo = hardwareMap.get(CRServo.class, "intake");
intakeServo.setDirection(CRServo.Direction.FORWARD);
intakeServo.setPower(0.8);  // 80% CW speed
intakeServo.setPower(0);    // stop
intakeServo.setPower(-0.6); // 60% CCW speed

// Dead band: servos near 0 may still creep â€” find the actual dead band:
// Set power to 0.05, 0.03, 0.01 until creep stops â†’ that's your dead band
\`\`\`

## Servo Feedback â€” Position Sensors
\`\`\`java
// Standard servos have no position feedback â€” you command, not confirm.
// For position verification, add an external sensor:

// Option 1: Analog potentiometer on the mechanism (not on the servo shaft)
double rawAnalog = analogInput.getVoltage(); // 0-3.3V
double angleDeg  = rawAnalog / 3.3 * 270.0; // if pot has 270Â° range

// Option 2: REV Through Bore Encoder (absolute, 0-3.3V analog output):
double encoderVoltage = analogInput.getVoltage();
double positionDeg    = encoderVoltage / 3.3 * 360.0;

// Verify servo reached position:
servo.setPosition(targetPosition);
sleep(500); // wait for movement
if (Math.abs(positionDeg - expectedDeg) > 5.0) {
    telemetry.addLine("âš ï¸ Servo position mismatch!");
}
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does a 1500 microsecond PWM pulse command to a standard servo vs a continuous rotation servo?",opts:["Both commands full clockwise","A standard servo moves to its center position; a continuous rotation servo stops â€” the pulse width means 'position' to a standard servo and 'speed' to a continuous rotation servo","Both command counterclockwise","1500 Î¼s is the shutdown signal"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why might calling setPosition(1.0) on a servo not reach the mechanism's intended full-travel position?",opts:["setPosition(1.0) is always correct","setPosition(1.0) sends 2000 Î¼s, which is the standard maximum â€” but some servos have a wider travel range (600-2400 Î¼s); the last portion of mechanical travel is unreachable without custom pulse width configuration or a servo programmer","The servo is broken","setPosition requires a different range"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the dead band of a continuous rotation servo and why does it matter?",opts:["The angle where the servo can't rotate","The range of power values near 0 where the servo receives a command but doesn't actually move â€” commands within the dead band produce no rotation; finding the boundary prevents setting a power that looks like 'stop' in code but actually causes slow creep","Dead band is the servo's maximum speed","It defines the servo's minimum angle"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.strategy.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sa_auto_design",title:"Autonomous Route Optimization",est:"20 min",content:`## Auto Points Are Multiplied by Alliance Partners
A good autonomous routine doesn't just score â€” it sets up a better starting position, avoids alliance partner collisions, and maximizes ranking points efficiently. Optimizing means thinking about all three simultaneously.

## The Autonomous Value Equation
\`\`\`
Autonomous value = raw points scored
                 + RP contribution (binary: qualifies or not)
                 + teleop position advantage (where you end up)
                 - collision risk cost (expected point loss from partner collision)

Most teams optimize only for raw points and ignore the other three.
Top teams know: avoiding a 10-pt auto collision > scoring 8 pts in auto.
\`\`\`

## Mapping All Legal Starting Positions
\`\`\`
For each legal starting position:
  â†’ Sketch the auto path (2-3 waypoints)
  â†’ Calculate: max pts achievable, time remaining, ending position
  â†’ Note: what game elements are accessible from this start?
  â†’ Check: does this path conflict with any common partner paths?

Build a starting position Ã— auto mode matrix:
           | Far start    | Center start | Near start
-----------+--------------+--------------+-------------
2-piece    | 14 pts, ends center | 18 pts, ends near | 12 pts, ends far
1-piece+park | 9 pts, ends far | 11 pts, ends far | 8 pts, ends center
Park only  | 4 pts        | 4 pts        | 4 pts

This becomes your pre-match selection tool â€” pick row + column based
on what your alliance partners are doing.
\`\`\`

## Collision Avoidance Protocol
\`\`\`
Two common collision scenarios:
  1. Both robots start center â†’ both try to cross the midfield simultaneously
  2. Alliance partner's auto piece collection path crosses your scoring path

Avoidance strategy in autonomous:
  â†’ Assign robot A: fast/direct path
  â†’ Assign robot B: slower or slightly offset path
  â†’ Add a brief initial delay to robot B (150-300ms) if paths are close
  â†’ Use a field-relative coordinate system so paths are unambiguous

In match: if auto collision occurs and both teams use the same code,
  which robot delays? Agree in pre-match meeting EVERY time.
\`\`\`

## Measuring and Improving Auto Reliability
\`\`\`
Practice tracking (per drive practice session):
  Track each auto attempt:
  Attempt | Start Position | Mode | Result | Failure point if failed
  --------+---------------+------+--------+------------------------
  1       | Near          | 2-pc | 18 pts | â€”
  2       | Near          | 2-pc | 8 pts  | Missed 2nd pickup (piece too far right)
  3       | Center        | 2-pc | 18 pts | â€”

From 30 tracked attempts per mode:
  â†’ Calculate mode success rate (not just "it mostly works")
  â†’ Identify the most common failure step
  â†’ Fix the failure step before adding complexity

If 2-piece auto succeeds 7/10 (70%): expected value = 18 Ã— 0.7 = 12.6 pts
If 1-piece auto succeeds 10/10 (100%): expected value = 11 Ã— 1.0 = 11 pts
â†’ 2-piece is slightly better EV â€” but adds failure risk. Is the 1.6 pt gain worth it?
  At a district event (seeding matters): probably yes.
  At championship (reliability matters): depends on competition level.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does avoiding a 10-point auto collision take priority over scoring 8 additional auto points?",opts:["Collisions are illegal","The collision eliminates 10 pts while the scoring adds 8 â€” net result is -2 pts vs taking the lower-scoring but collision-free route; collision avoidance is worth more than equivalent scoring","Auto points matter more","Collisions don't affect final score"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does tracking 'failure point if failed' for each practice auto attempt reveal?",opts:["Whether the route is too long","The specific step in the auto sequence that fails most often â€” knowing that '2nd piece pickup fails when piece spawns right-of-center' leads to a targeted fix rather than general debugging","It proves the auto is reliable","Failure points are random"],ans:1},
      {q:"When does a lower expected-value auto mode become strategically preferable to a higher expected-value mode?",opts:["Never â€” always maximize EV","When reliability matters more than peak performance â€” at championship where seeding margins are small and every match counts, a consistent 11-pt auto may be better than a 12.6-pt expected value with a 30% failure risk that produces 0 pts 3 matches in 10","Lower EV autos are always defensive","Expected value doesn't apply to robots"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.teammanagement.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"tmi_documentation",title:"Technical Documentation Standards",est:"14 min",content:`## Code Without Docs Is a Liability
A mechanism documented only in one programmer's head becomes a crisis the moment that programmer is sick on competition day. Good technical documentation transfers knowledge before you need it, not after.

## The Four Things That Must Be Documented
\`\`\`
1. WHAT it does (not obvious from the name)
   â†’ "This subsystem controls the telescoping arm AND manages the wrist pivot"
   â†’ Not: "This is ArmSubsystem" (the class name already says that)

2. WHY this approach (not the obvious one)
   â†’ "We use a CAN bus position loop instead of software PID because the
      arm oscillates at 50Hz loop frequency â€” hardware PID at 1kHz is stable"

3. HOW to tune it (if configurable)
   â†’ "kP: increase until oscillation, then halve it. Start at 0.05."
   â†’ "Acceptable error: Â±5 encoder ticks at any target position"

4. HOW to recover from failure (field repair instructions)
   â†’ "If arm misses home on startup: manually lower arm to bottom hard stop,
      reset encoder in Driver Hub â†’ restart OpMode"
\`\`\`

## Java/FTC Documentation Standard
\`\`\`java
/**
 * Telescoping arm subsystem â€” 3-stage linear slides driven by a single
 * motor through a cascade chain system. Encoder measures motor shaft
 * rotation; multiply by TICKS_PER_INCH to get slide extension.
 *
 * <p>Tuning: Set kP = 0.005 initially. Increase until oscillation at full
 * extension, then reduce by 30%. Acceptable position error: Â±10 ticks.
 *
 * <p>Field recovery: If arm stalls mid-extension, manually push to full
 * retraction. Zero the encoder by holding BACK + A on Gamepad 2 for 2 sec.
 */
public class ArmSubsystem {

    /** Target position in encoder ticks. Set via {@link #setTargetInches}. */
    private int targetTicks = 0;

    /** Minimum safe power to hold arm against gravity (feed-forward). */
    static final double GRAVITY_FF = 0.07;

    /**
     * Commands arm to a target height.
     * @param inches extension from fully retracted (0.0 to MAX_EXTENSION_IN)
     * @throws IllegalArgumentException if inches is negative or above maximum
     */
    public void setTargetInches(double inches) { ... }
}
\`\`\`

## The README Every Robot Repository Needs
\`\`\`markdown
# Team 1234 â€” 2025 Robot Code

## Quick Start
1. Clone this repo
2. Open in Android Studio (FTC) or VS Code with WPILib (FRC)
3. Deploy via USB to Control Hub / roboRIO

## Hardware Map
| Config Name    | Physical Device            | Port  |
|----------------|----------------------------|-------|
| leftFront      | GoBILDA 5202 Motor         | Motor 0 |
| rightFront     | GoBILDA 5202 Motor         | Motor 1 |
| armMotor       | REV HD Hex Motor           | Motor 2 |
| intakeServo    | REV Smart Robot Servo      | Servo 0 |
| imu            | Built-in BNO055            | I2C 0  |

## Tunable Constants
All in: TeamCode/src/.../Constants.java
  ARM_KP: 0.009 (last tuned 2025-02-14)
  INTAKE_SPEED: 0.85 (adjust for game piece grip)

## Known Issues
- Arm oscillates slightly at max extension under heavy game piece load
  â†’ Workaround: reduce ARM_KP to 0.007 if this occurs at competition
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should technical documentation explain WHY an approach was chosen, not just WHAT it does?",opts:["WHY is required by FIRST","A future member or ally reading the code sees what it does from the code itself â€” they can't know WHY without documentation; understanding the reason prevents well-intentioned changes that break the system for the same reason the original approach was chosen","WHAT is obvious from comments","WHY is only relevant for awards"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'field recovery instructions' the most operationally critical part of subsystem documentation?",opts:["Recovery instructions are longest","Recovery procedures are needed when something goes wrong under time pressure â€” a programmer who documented how to reset the arm encoder saves the team from a 20-minute match queue debugging session","Recovery is the most complex code","It's required by inspection"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a hardware map table be included in the README rather than embedded only in code comments?",opts:["Tables format better","The hardware map is needed during physical robot setup, inspection, and field repair â€” situations where the code may not be open; a README accessible from any device provides the port assignments without requiring Android Studio to be running","Code comments aren't visible","README files are searched by judges"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.cad.Advanced.push(
  {id:"cada_generative",title:"Topology Optimization & Weight Reduction",est:"18 min",content:`## Algorithmic Weight Reduction
Traditional weight reduction means adding pockets manually. Topology optimization uses algorithms (FEA-based) to find the material distribution that meets load requirements with minimum mass â€” automatically finding shapes a human wouldn't design.

## What Topology Optimization Produces
\`\`\`
Input:
  â†’ Part volume (the design space)
  â†’ Applied loads (forces and their directions)
  â†’ Constraints (fixed faces, required keep-out zones)
  â†’ Target: retain X% of original mass

Output:
  â†’ Optimized material distribution â€” organic, web-like structure
  â†’ Shows where material is critical and where it's wasted
  â†’ Typically 30-50% mass reduction while meeting stiffness requirements

Result looks like: irregular web of ribs rather than a solid block.
Best manufactured with: 3D printing (SLS, SLA) or 5-axis CNC
Most useful for: mounting brackets, arm links, non-standard shaped supports
\`\`\`

## Topology Optimization in Fusion 360
\`\`\`
Design â†’ Generative Design â†’ New Study

1. Define preserved geometry (mounting holes, interface surfaces):
   Add Preserved Geometry â†’ select faces that must remain unchanged

2. Define obstacle geometry (things the part cannot intersect):
   Add Obstacle Geometry â†’ select nearby components

3. Add structural loads:
   Add Load â†’ select face, enter force magnitude and direction
   Tip: use worst-case loads â€” the peak force at stall, not typical

4. Add constraints (fixed points):
   Add Constraint â†’ select mounting face (zero displacement here)

5. Set goal:
   Minimize mass, meet stiffness target
   OR minimize deflection under fixed mass reduction

6. Run â†’ wait (5-20 min) â†’ review outcomes
   Fusion generates multiple outcomes at different mass targets
   Pick the one that meets your rigidity requirement at lowest weight
\`\`\`

## Manual Weight Reduction for Bracket Parts (When No Generative Design)
\`\`\`
Guided by topology optimization intuition:
  1. Identify load path: where does force enter and exit the part?
  2. Material along the load path â†’ keep it
  3. Material far from the load path â†’ remove it (add pockets)

Pocket shapes:
  Circular: cleanest stress flow around the hole
  Elongated oval: where load is directional
  Lightening triangle: inside corners where stress concentrates at corners anyway

Minimum wall thickness after pocketing:
  6061-T6 aluminum: 0.060" (1.5mm) for non-structural pockets
                    0.100" (2.5mm) for load-bearing walls
  Carbon fiber:     0.040" (1.0mm) for CFRP plates

Reality check: weigh the part before and after â†’ confirm actual savings
  Expected: 15-30% reduction from pocketing a bracket
  If < 10%: you're not removing enough material
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does topology optimization produce that manual CAD pocketing typically does not?",opts:["Lighter parts by default","An algorithmically optimal material distribution for the given load case â€” the result often has organic shapes (curved ribs, unexpected cutouts) that a human wouldn't design but that efficiently use material where stress actually flows","Topology optimization is always faster","It generates assembly drawings"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should worst-case (stall) forces be used as inputs to topology optimization rather than typical operating forces?",opts:["FEA requires maximum input","Topology optimization removes material everywhere the stress is low â€” if designed for typical forces, the part will be too light to survive peak loads; designing for worst-case ensures the optimized geometry holds up in every operating condition including robot defense and mechanism jams","Stall forces are easier to measure","Typical forces produce better shapes"],ans:1},
      {q:"Along what geometric feature should material be retained when manually pocketing a bracket without simulation tools?",opts:["The outermost edges","The load path â€” the route force travels from where it's applied to where the part is constrained; material along this route carries the stress and must remain; material far from the load path is candidates for pockets","The thickest section","The heaviest regions"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.awards.Advanced.push(
  {id:"awa_presentation",title:"Impact & Inspire Presentation Strategy",est:"16 min",content:`## The Presentation Is Harder Than the Essay
You spent months on the work and hours on the essay. Then you have 5 minutes in front of judges to make them feel why it matters. Teams that practice presentations win awards that better-documented teams lose.

## What Judges Are Trying to Decide in 5 Minutes
\`\`\`
Three questions judges are mentally answering:
  1. Is this impact real and verifiable? (Not just claims â€” evidence)
  2. Does this team truly embody FIRST's mission, or are they performing it?
  3. Would FIRST be meaningfully diminished without this team?

Every sentence in your presentation should serve one of these three questions.
Cut anything that doesn't.
\`\`\`

## Presentation Structure That Works
\`\`\`
0:00 â€” Hook (30 seconds)
  Not "Hi, we're Team 1234 and we're passionate about FIRST's mission."
  Instead, open with a specific story:
  "Two years ago, Maria was a 4th grader at Lincoln Elementary with no idea
   what a robot was. Last month, she won a design award at the FLL state
   tournament â€” on a team that didn't exist before we showed up."

0:30 â€” Who you are (20 seconds)
  Team number, years active, number of members. That's it.

0:50 â€” Three impact pillars (3 minutes)
  ONE slide or visual per pillar. Each pillar:
  â†’ Name the program ("Our FLL mentorship program")
  â†’ One number ("47 students across 4 schools")
  â†’ One outcome ("3 of those teams now operate independently")
  â†’ 30-45 seconds max per pillar

3:50 â€” Sustainability + looking forward (30 seconds)
  "Our programs now run without us â€” and our alumni are returning as mentors."
  "Next season, we're expanding to two more Title I schools."

4:20 â€” Close (10 seconds)
  One sentence. Your team's defining impact in 15 words or fewer.
\`\`\`

## Answering Unexpected Questions
\`\`\`
Judges WILL ask off-script questions. Common ones:

"If your team disappeared, what would be lost?"
  â†’ Be specific: "These four FLL teams would lose their mentors.
    Two of them might fold without our support."

"How do you measure whether your outreach is actually effective?"
  â†’ Describe your tracking system. Mention numbers.
  â†’ "We follow up with schools 6 months after events â€” 3 of 14 created
    new programs directly."

"What's a program that didn't work and why?"
  â†’ Have a real answer prepared. Judges trust teams that acknowledge failure.
  â†’ "Our summer camp in 2023 had 40% attendance â€” we learned that parents
    need shorter commitments. We changed to 2-hour workshops and now average
    85% attendance."

"What makes your team unique?"
  â†’ Answer with a story, not a list. One specific thing, not five vague things.
\`\`\`

## Presentation Mechanics
\`\`\`
Speakers: 2-3 max. More speakers = more transitions = lost time.
  Assign sections to each: hook + intro, two pillars, third pillar + close.

Practice: must run-through the full presentation 8+ times before the event.
  Time each run. Stay under 4:30 to leave buffer for questions.
  Practice answering the unexpected questions cold.

Physical presence:
  â†’ Don't read from notes during the presentation â€” memorize or internalize
  â†’ Make eye contact with each judge, not just the one who asked the question
  â†’ If you have a visual, point to specific elements while speaking

What NOT to bring:
  â†’ Long slide decks (more than 4-5 slides in 5 minutes is too many)
  â†’ Props that take time to set up
  â†’ Video that takes > 45 seconds (time is your scarcest resource)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does opening a presentation with a specific student's story work better than stating your team name and mission?",opts:["Stories are more emotional","A specific, verifiable story immediately establishes that your impact is real and human â€” judges have heard hundreds of teams say they're passionate about FIRST; a named student and a specific outcome they can verify is evidence, not a claim","Stories are shorter","Judges prefer informal openings"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should an Impact presentation include a program that didn't work, with an honest explanation?",opts:["FIRST requires failure disclosure","Acknowledging a failure and what you learned demonstrates genuine reflection and credibility â€” judges who have reviewed many submissions are skeptical of teams that report only successes; a real failure story signals that the successes are also real","Failures improve the score","Judges expect at least one failure"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is 2-3 speakers the recommended maximum for a 5-minute presentation?",opts:["More speakers confuse judges","Every speaker transition costs time and risks losing momentum â€” with 5 minutes total, 3 transitions between 4 speakers consume 30+ seconds just in handoffs, leaving less time for substantive content than 2 speakers would have","FIRST limits speakers","Fewer speakers know more content"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_curriculum",title:"Building a Robotics Curriculum for Younger Students",est:"15 min",content:`## Teaching Robot Concepts Without Jargon
A 4th grader doesn't know what a PID controller is â€” and doesn't need to. But they can absolutely understand feedback loops, gears, and programming decisions. The skill is translating what you know into concepts appropriate for the audience.

## Grade-Level Appropriate Content
\`\`\`
Grades K-2 (ages 5-8):
  Core concept: robots follow instructions
  Activity: Unplugged â€” program a friend to walk an obstacle course
             using only directional commands (like code)
  Key idea: computer == instruction follower, not a thinking machine
  Duration: 30-45 minutes, high energy, hands-on

Grades 3-5 (ages 8-11):
  Core concept: sensors + decisions = smart robots
  Activity: Simple block-based programming (Scratch/Code.org) + a real robot demo
  Key idea: if/then decisions, what happens when sensor detects something?
  Duration: 45-60 minutes, guided exploration

Grades 6-8 (ages 11-14):
  Core concept: design process + iteration
  Activity: Build a simple robot from a kit (LEGO Education, VEX IQ)
            with a specific challenge (push a ball across a line)
  Key idea: prototype â†’ test â†’ improve â†’ repeat
  Duration: 60-90 minutes, full design cycle possible
\`\`\`

## The Lesson Plan Template
\`\`\`
Title: [specific and activity-focused, not "Robotics Introduction"]
Age group: [grade range]
Duration: [minutes]
Materials: [specific list â€” everything needed, no surprises day-of]

Learning objectives: (3 max â€” "Students will be able to...")
  1. Explain that a robot follows instructions step by step
  2. Write a 4-step sequence that moves a robot through an obstacle
  3. Identify what happens when one instruction is wrong

Warm-up (5 min): [hook question or quick game]
Main activity (25 min): [step-by-step instructions]
  Step 1: Demonstrate once
  Step 2: Students try with partner support
  Step 3: Increase challenge (add a constraint)
Debrief (5 min): [3 questions to ask the class]
Wrap-up (5 min): [connection to real FIRST teams + how to join]

Facilitator notes: [what went wrong last time + how you fixed it]
\`\`\`

## Managing a Classroom of 30 Students
\`\`\`
The biggest failure mode in school visits: poor classroom management.
A lesson that works with 8 scouts doesn't scale to 30 without planning.

Group the students: 4-5 per table/station before you arrive
                   Pre-assign roles: "driver, programmer, builder, recorder, presenter"
Timing: set a visible timer â€” students respond to visible countdowns
        "You have 3 minutes to complete Step 2 â€” go!"

Volume control: establish a signal (raise hand, countdown from 5)
                practice it BEFORE starting the activity
                "When I count down from 5, everyone freeze and look at me"

Transitions: pre-tell the next step before ending the current one
             "In 2 minutes, we're going to share what you built.
              Start thinking about one thing that surprised you."

When something goes wrong: name it and move on
  "Our robot's battery just died â€” that happens in real competitions too!
   Let's use this time to look at how the code would work."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must the same robotics lesson be redesigned for K-2 vs 6-8 rather than simplified for younger students?",opts:["Younger students learn less","The core concept, activity format, and key vocabulary must all match the developmental stage â€” K-2 students grasp 'robots follow instructions' through physical movement activities; 6-8 students can run a full design cycle; simplifying a 6-8 lesson for K-2 isn't the same as designing for K-2","Simplified lessons are always worse","FIRST requires grade-specific lessons"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the most common classroom management failure when FIRST students run school visits?",opts:["Students don't participate","Not planning for 30 students at once â€” activities designed for 8 scouts in a small group break down when 30 students in a classroom need simultaneous engagement, clear transitions, and structured group roles","Teachers interfere too much","The lesson content is wrong"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should facilitator notes include 'what went wrong last time and how you fixed it'?",opts:["Notes must be comprehensive","Each time the lesson runs, the team learns what actually happens vs what was planned â€” documenting failures and fixes transfers that knowledge to the next facilitator, preventing the same surprises from disrupting a lesson at a different school","Notes are required for outreach credit","Wrong things improve scores"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€â”€ PACK 12 â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€

// â”€â”€ OUTREACH (add 9 â†’ ~20) â”€â”€
LESSONS.outreach.Beginner.push(
  {id:"orb_email",title:"Writing Outreach Emails That Get Replies",est:"11 min",content:`## Most Cold Emails Are Ignored for One Reason
They ask the recipient to do work without giving them a reason to care. A great outreach email is short, specific about the ask, and makes it easy to say yes.

## The Three-Sentence Formula
\`\`\`
Sentence 1: Who you are and why it's relevant to them
  "We're a FIRST Robotics team of 25 high school students
   from Lincoln High School in your city."

Sentence 2: What you're asking for (specific, bounded)
  "We're looking for a 30-minute virtual tour of your engineering
   department for 8 students on any weekday in March."

Sentence 3: Why you chose them + easy yes
  "We saw your team's work on autonomous vehicle safety systems â€”
   several of our members want to pursue that field.
   Would a 30-minute call on a day that works for you be possible?"
\`\`\`

## What Kills Reply Rates
\`\`\`
âŒ "We would love to partner with you in any way you see fit"
   â†’ You've made them do all the work figuring out what you want.

âŒ Five-paragraph email describing your whole season
   â†’ They stopped reading after paragraph one.

âŒ "We need a $5,000 sponsorship by Friday"
   â†’ First contact should never lead with money.
   â†’ Build the relationship first.

âŒ Generic "Dear Sir or Madam"
   â†’ Always find a specific name (LinkedIn, company website, Google).
   â†’ "Dear Ms. Chen" gets a higher open rate than any greeting else.
\`\`\`

## Following Up
\`\`\`
No reply after 5 business days: one follow-up only.
  "Hi [Name], just following up on my note from [date].
   Completely understand if timing isn't right.
   Happy to connect whenever works for your team."

Never: send more than two emails without a reply.
       Call before a third unanswered email, not after.

Track everything: keep a contact log with date of first email,
                  date of follow-up, outcome, and who you spoke to.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should the first contact with a potential partner never lead with a sponsorship request?",opts:["Sponsorship is illegal in outreach","Relationships require established trust before financial requests are appropriate â€” a cold sponsorship ask is likely to be declined; a relationship built through a smaller first interaction (tour, mentorship hour) makes a later sponsorship ask far more likely to succeed","First emails should always be short","Money requests must go through mentors"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'We would love to partner with you in any way you see fit' an ineffective ask?",opts:["It's too casual","It transfers all decision-making work to the recipient â€” an open-ended ask requires them to invent the partnership, which most busy professionals won't do; a specific, bounded ask (30-minute tour, one mentorship session) is easy to say yes or no to","It uses too many words","It doesn't mention FIRST"],ans:1},
      {q:"How many follow-up emails should you send without a reply?",opts:["As many as it takes","One â€” a second unanswered email signals the person isn't interested or doesn't have capacity; a third email damages the relationship and may get your address marked as spam","Three, then call","No follow-ups are appropriate"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"orb_tabling",title:"Running a Tabling Booth",est:"10 min",content:`## A Table at an Event Is Only Valuable If People Stop
Walk past any career fair and notice: tables with people facing their laptop get zero traffic. Tables with something happening, something to touch, or someone making eye contact get a crowd.

## The Two-Minute Tabling Pitch
\`\`\`
The moment someone slows near your table:
  Step 1 (5 sec): Eye contact + open question
    "Have you ever seen a robot up close?"
    "What do you think this thing does?"
    NOT: "Hi do you want to hear about our robotics team?"
         (that's a yes/no question with an obvious polite "no")

  Step 2 (30 sec): Let them interact first
    â†’ Hand them a game piece. Let them drive the robot if you have one.
    â†’ Speaking while they're touching something: 4Ã— more memorable.

  Step 3 (60 sec): One hook story
    â†’ "A kid on our team didn't know what code was. Two years later he
       got an internship at [local company]."
    â†’ NOT a list of accomplishments. ONE story.

  Step 4 (15 sec): The ask
    â†’ "We have a team for your grade. Want to take a flyer?"
    â†’ Hand it to them â€” don't leave it on the table for them to pick up.
\`\`\`

## Table Setup That Attracts People
\`\`\`
Front of table (visible from 10 feet):
  â†’ Robot or mechanism (real hardware beats posters every time)
  â†’ One bold sign: "DRIVE THE ROBOT" or "BUILD THINGS. WRITE CODE. WIN."
  â†’ Nothing else on the front surface â€” clutter repels

Back of table (support materials):
  â†’ Flyers with QR code to sign up page
  â†’ Signup sheet (name, grade, school, email, interest)
  â†’ Photos/poster board: 6-8 photos max, large, captioned with 1 line each

What NOT to have:
  â†’ Laptop open and facing the booth staff (you look busy/unapproachable)
  â†’ Candy bowls (people take candy and leave â€” no contact info)
  â†’ Five different signs competing for attention
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'Have you ever seen a robot up close?' a better opening than 'Do you want to hear about our team?'",opts:["It's shorter","It's an open-ended question that invites curiosity rather than a closed yes/no that makes it easy to politely decline â€” curiosity-based openers create engagement; direct pitches create an exit","It mentions robots","It avoids the word 'team'"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does putting physical hardware (a robot or mechanism) at the front of a tabling booth outperform posters and flyers?",opts:["Hardware is always available","Real hardware creates a reason for people to slow down and approach â€” something tangible and unfamiliar triggers curiosity that flat visual materials rarely achieve, especially at crowded events where every table competes for the same attention","Posters are less durable","Hardware is required at fairs"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_school_visit",title:"Planning an Effective School Visit",est:"13 min",content:`## The Logistics Determine the Impact
A perfectly designed lesson fails if the projector doesn't work, the class period is 35 minutes instead of 45, or the teacher doesn't know you're coming. Pre-visit logistics are as important as the content.

## The Four-Week Lead Time Checklist
\`\`\`
4 weeks before:
  â–¡ Confirm date, time, location, and grade level with teacher
  â–¡ Get headcount (# of students) and room layout (rows vs tables)
  â–¡ Confirm AV availability: projector? HDMI? Screen?
  â–¡ Ask: any students with disabilities needing accommodations?
  â–¡ Confirm parking or access badge needs

2 weeks before:
  â–¡ Send teacher a one-paragraph description of the activity
  â–¡ Confirm number of team members coming (and their roles)
  â–¡ Prepare and print all materials: handouts, worksheets, sign-up sheets
  â–¡ Test robot battery and all demo equipment

2 days before:
  â–¡ Confirm with teacher again (reply to the original chain)
  â–¡ Pack: robot + charger, game pieces, handouts, signup sheet, flyers,
          extension cord, backup laptop with offline slides

Day of:
  â–¡ Arrive 15 minutes early to set up
  â–¡ Have a 10-minute shortened version of the activity ready if class runs short
  â–¡ Assign roles before entering the building: facilitator, assistant, demo operator
\`\`\`

## Managing the Teacher Relationship
\`\`\`
Teachers receive dozens of volunteer requests. The ones they invite back:
  â†’ Always do exactly what they said they'd do (no scope creep)
  â†’ Leave the room cleaner than they found it
  â†’ Send a thank-you email within 24 hours
  â†’ Include a 3-sentence summary of what students learned
    (helps teacher document the activity for their own records)

What to say in the thank-you:
  "Thank you for having us. The students were engaged and asked great questions.
   We covered [specific concept] using [specific activity] â€”
   about 24 of 28 students participated actively.
   We'd love to come back next year if helpful."

Ask at the end of the visit (not the email):
  "Do you know any other teachers at this school who might want this?"
  â†’ The best referrals come from satisfied teachers to their colleagues.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a team always prepare a 10-minute shortened version of their school visit activity?",opts:["Short activities are better","Class periods are often interrupted or run short without warning â€” a team with no fallback either rushes the full activity poorly or runs out of time without completing; a pre-planned short version ensures the key learning moment always happens","Short versions require less prep","Teachers prefer short visits"],ans:1},
      {q:"What single question asked at the end of a successful school visit has the highest yield for expanding outreach?",opts:["Can we come back next year?","'Do you know any other teachers at this school who might want this?' â€” a referred introduction from one satisfied teacher to a colleague converts far better than a cold email, and costs nothing beyond asking","Can we get a photo for social media?","How many students are interested in FIRST?"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ori_social2",title:"Social Media Strategy for FIRST Teams",est:"12 min",content:`## Your Feed Is a Recruiting and Sponsor Tool
A team Instagram with 47 followers and photos of a robot in a gym is a missed opportunity. A consistent, story-driven feed builds the team's reputation in ways that directly affect sponsor retention and student recruitment.

## Content That Performs for FIRST Teams
\`\`\`
High engagement (post these):
  â†’ Behind-the-scenes: "midnight before bag day" energy
  â†’ Member spotlights: 3-5 sentences about one person and what they do
  â†’ Mechanism reveals: short video showing a mechanism working for the first time
  â†’ Competition day: match clips, pit photos, alliance selection moment
  â†’ Outreach: photos of students reacting to seeing the robot (with permission)

Low engagement (skip or minimize):
  â†’ Award certificate photos (boring to non-team audiences)
  â†’ Group photos in matching shirts with no caption
  â†’ Long wall-of-text captions
  â†’ "Happy [holiday]!" posts with no robotics content

Optimal caption length: 2-4 lines for Instagram/TikTok
                        1-2 sentences for X/Twitter
\`\`\`

## The Weekly Post Cadence
\`\`\`
Build season (Jan-Mar): 3-4 posts/week â€” content is abundant
Off-season (Apr-Dec):   1 post/week â€” team news, member updates, outreach

The mistake: going silent for 3 months then spamming 10 posts in one week.
Followers (especially sponsors and parents) lose track of the team.
Consistent 1x/week keeps the audience engaged year-round.

Content calendar: assign one person as social media lead each season.
                  Plan 2 weeks of content at a time â€” don't post reactively.
\`\`\`

## Permissions and Safety
\`\`\`
Required before posting any photo of a student:
  â†’ Signed media release (usually part of team registration)
  â†’ Verify the release covers social media specifically (not just event use)
  â†’ Never post last names, school names, or home towns
  â†’ Extra caution with students under 13 (COPPA â€” don't tag or name them)

Before posting about another team:
  â†’ Tag them â€” teams appreciate the acknowledgment
  â†’ Don't post another team's CAD, code, or unrevealed mechanisms
    without explicit permission
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do member spotlight posts typically outperform award certificate photos on social media?",opts:["Spotlights have more text","Stories about individual people are relatable and shareable â€” a parent, teacher, or potential member can see themselves in a student's story; a certificate photo has no narrative and gives a non-team follower no reason to engage","Awards violate social media rules","Photos of people get more likes algorithmically"],ans:1},
      {q:"What posting consistency mistake do many FIRST teams make with their social media?",opts:["Posting too many videos","Going silent for months then posting a large batch â€” this causes followers to lose track of the team during the gap, and algorithms deprioritize accounts with inconsistent posting patterns","Posting too frequently during build season","Using too many hashtags"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ora_corp_day",title:"Hosting a Corporate Volunteer Day",est:"15 min",content:`## Flip the Relationship â€” Bring Them to You
Instead of your team always visiting companies, invite engineers to spend 2-4 hours at your build space. They mentor, troubleshoot, and leave with a visceral understanding of what your team does. The conversion rate from corporate volunteer day to multi-year sponsor is dramatically higher than cold asks.

## Planning the Event
\`\`\`
Timeline: 6 weeks out
  Week 6: Identify your target company contact (HR/community affairs OR an alumni)
  Week 5: Send formal invitation (see template below)
  Week 4: Confirm headcount and specific skills needed (mechanical, software, etc.)
  Week 3: Plan the day's agenda; assign student hosts for each visitor
  Week 2: Prepare challenge stations and any materials for them to work on
  Week 1: Confirm logistics; send reminder with parking/access info
  Day of: Brief the team on the visitors' backgrounds before they arrive

Target group size: 4-8 engineers. More than 8 is hard to integrate into robot work.
Best timing: Weekday 4-7pm or Saturday 10am-2pm (matches team meeting times)
\`\`\`

## The Day's Agenda
\`\`\`
0:00 - 0:20: Arrival + robot demo
  â†’ One student per visitor â€” assigned before they arrive
  â†’ Student: "I'm [name], I'm in [grade], I work on [subsystem]"
  â†’ Show the current season game; have the robot move

0:20 - 2:30: Working session
  â†’ Visitors join ongoing build/code work â€” not observation, participation
  â†’ Pre-identify 2-3 problems students genuinely need help with:
    "We can't figure out why this gearbox is binding"
    "Our autonomous path isn't following the curve correctly"
  â†’ Engineers who solve real problems feel useful; ones who just watch don't

2:30 - 3:00: Q&A + tour
  â†’ Students ask questions about careers (visitors expect this)
  â†’ Show the competition field setup if you have one

3:00 - 3:20: Wrap-up
  â†’ Thank-you cards (handwritten, from a student, specific to what they helped with)
  â†’ Photo with the group
  â†’ Mention the sponsorship program â€” do NOT ask for money today
\`\`\`

## The Follow-Up That Converts to Sponsorship
\`\`\`
48 hours after: student email + mentor email to HR/community affairs
  "Thank you for sending [name] and [name]. They helped us solve [specific problem].
   Our team would love to build a formal relationship with [company] â€”
   could we schedule a 20-minute call to discuss what partnership might look like?"

Success rate: teams that run corporate volunteer days report 60-70% of
              participating companies entering some form of formal partnership
              within the next 12 months, vs < 10% for cold sponsorship asks.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the corporate volunteer day format convert to sponsorship more effectively than a cold sponsorship ask?",opts:["It costs less money","The engineer experiences the team directly rather than reading a sponsor packet â€” the personal connection, problem they solved, and student relationship make the program feel real; when they return to HR and advocate for a partnership, the ask comes with personal endorsement","Corporate days are required","It avoids discussing money"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should students be pre-assigned to specific visitors before the corporate volunteer day begins?",opts:["It's more organized","Pre-assignment ensures every visitor has a dedicated student host who can give personal context â€” improvised assignments create awkward moments where visitors stand around waiting while students figure out who's responsible for them","Pre-assignment is a FIRST requirement","Students should choose their own partners"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ FUNDRAISING (add 10 â†’ ~20) â”€â”€
LESSONS.fundraising.Beginner.push(
  {id:"fb_grant2",title:"Finding FIRST-Eligible Grants",est:"12 min",content:`## Grants Exist Specifically for FIRST Teams
Several foundations and government programs fund STEM education initiatives â€” including FIRST teams directly. Teams that don't apply leave money on the table that was budgeted for exactly their situation.

## Where to Find Grants
\`\`\`
FIRST-specific:
  â†’ FIRST Robotics official grants database (firstinspires.org/ways-to-help/grants)
  â†’ FIRST Dean's List Scholarship (for students)
  â†’ FIRST Tech Challenge Youth Grant (FTC Beginner teams)

STEM education foundations:
  â†’ STEM Funders Network
  â†’ IEEE Foundation
  â†’ Society of Women Engineers scholarships + team grants
  â†’ National Science Foundation (NSF) informal science education grants

Corporate foundations (all have grant programs):
  â†’ Google.org STEM grants
  â†’ Boeing Community Investment
  â†’ Lockheed Martin STEM grants
  â†’ Local utilities often have community education funds

State/local:
  â†’ Community foundations (your city or county usually has one)
  â†’ State STEM education offices
  â†’ Local school district innovation grants
\`\`\`

## Evaluating If a Grant Is Worth Applying For
\`\`\`
Quick filter before spending time on an application:
  â–¡ Does the grant explicitly include FIRST or robotics programs?
  â–¡ Is your team a registered nonprofit (501c3) or fiscally sponsored?
     (Most grants require this â€” some accept school-based programs)
  â–¡ Is the award amount > 4Ã— the time you'll spend applying?
     ($500 grant, 20-hour application = $25/hour â€” usually not worth it
      $5,000 grant, 20-hour application = $250/hour â€” worth it)
  â–¡ Is the deadline > 4 weeks away? (Less: skip unless it's a template reuse)
  â–¡ Does the grant require reporting? Can you fulfill the reporting requirements?
\`\`\`

## The One-Page Grant Summary Template
\`\`\`
Keep a pre-written one-page summary of your program ready:
  â†’ Team history (1 sentence)
  â†’ Student demographics (numbers, grade levels, school districts served)
  â†’ Season outcomes (competitions, awards, members this year)
  â†’ Outreach reach (students touched by your programs, events run)
  â†’ Budget and how this grant would be used (specific items/costs)

Most grant applications ask for a subset of this â€” copy and adapt
rather than writing fresh for every application.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What quick filter helps determine if a grant is worth the application time investment?",opts:["Always apply for every grant","Comparing the award amount to 4Ã— the estimated application hours â€” a $500 grant requiring 20 hours is effectively $25/hour; a $5,000 grant for the same effort is $250/hour; the ratio helps prioritize high-yield applications","Only apply for grants over $1,000","Submit if the deadline is soon"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should teams maintain a pre-written one-page program summary regardless of active grant applications?",opts:["It satisfies FIRST requirements","Most grant applications ask for the same core information â€” a ready summary lets you copy and adapt rather than rewriting from scratch each time, turning a 4-hour application into a 1-hour application","It replaces the full application","Summaries must be updated quarterly"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fb_events",title:"Fundraising Events That Actually Work",est:"13 min",content:`## Not All Fundraising Events Are Worth Running
A car wash that requires 20 students for a Saturday to net $400 is $20/student-day. A well-run robot demo at a local business that leads to a $2,000 sponsorship is $2,000/student-day. Evaluate fundraising events by return on student time, not just gross revenue.

## High-Yield Formats
\`\`\`
Restaurant nights (% of sales go to team):
  â†’ Effort: 3-4 hours flyer distribution + evening at restaurant
  â†’ Typical yield: $150-400
  â†’ Best for: community visibility, easy to execute repeatedly
  â†’ Key: choose a restaurant already popular with school families

Silent auction:
  â†’ Effort: 2-3 weeks soliciting item donations + event setup
  â†’ Typical yield: $800-2,500 depending on items and attendance
  â†’ Best for: teams with active parent network or business contacts
  â†’ Key: items with perceived scarcity (local experiences, signed items)
           outperform generic gift cards

Skills demonstrations for fee:
  â†’ Invite local professionals (engineers, doctors) to learn CAD or coding
  â†’ Students teach; attendees pay $30-50 for a 2-hour session
  â†’ Effort: moderate prep, high execution quality required
  â†’ Typical yield: $300-600 per session
  â†’ Best for: teams with strong technical skills and presentation ability

FIRST season ticket drives:
  â†’ Sell "pit crew passes" to parents for $50-100
  â†’ Perks: team t-shirt, access to pit area at one competition,
            name on the robot's sponsor panel
  â†’ Effort: low; yield: depends on parent engagement
\`\`\`

## What to Avoid
\`\`\`
âŒ Candy bar / product sales: low margin, student effort is high
   Exception: if you have a captive audience (school store, office building)

âŒ GoFundMe without a story: generic campaigns raise almost nothing
   Exception: a specific, compelling story tied to a competition need
   ("Our robot earned a spot at Worlds â€” we need $3,000 to get there")

âŒ Events requiring renting a venue: overhead often exceeds revenue
   Always negotiate the venue free or borrowed before committing to the event

âŒ Events that compete with other school fundraisers: coordinate with
   the school calendar â€” a candy sale the same week as the school's candy
   sale splits the same buyer pool
\`\`\``,quiz:[
