      {q:"What is the most useful metric for comparing different fundraising event options?",opts:["Total gross revenue","Return on student time (dollars raised per student-day invested) â€” a $400 car wash using 20 students is less efficient than a $2,000 sponsor conversation using 2 students, even though both take roughly the same calendar day","Number of participants","Which event is most fun"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does a specific fundraising story ('We earned a Worlds spot and need $3,000') outperform generic online campaigns?",opts:["Specific stories are more honest","A concrete, time-bound need creates urgency and emotional connection â€” donors understand exactly what their contribution enables; 'help our robotics team' without context gives donors no reason to choose you over other general causes","Generic campaigns get blocked","Specific campaigns are shorter"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fb_budget",title:"Team Budget Planning & Tracking",est:"11 min",content:`## A Budget Prevents End-of-Season Crises
Every team that runs out of money at Worlds, misses a part order because they didn't know the balance, or surprises their school with an overrun â€” did so because they didn't track spending against a plan.

## Building the Season Budget
\`\`\`
Budget categories for a typical FRC team:
  Category              Estimate    Actual    Notes
  Registration/entry    $6,000
  Parts (build season)  $3,000
  Travel (local events) $1,500
  Travel (district/reg) $2,500
  Travel (championship) $5,000      (if qualified)
  Tools & consumables   $500
  Outreach materials    $300
  T-shirts & uniform    $800
  Misc./contingency     $400
  TOTAL                 $20,000

FTC teams: scale by ~3-5Ã— smaller across most categories

Build the budget in a shared Google Sheet.
Update actual spend within 48 hours of any purchase.
\`\`\`

## Tracking Purchases
\`\`\`
Every purchase needs:
  â†’ Date
  â†’ Who bought it (and who needs to be reimbursed)
  â†’ Amount
  â†’ Category (from budget)
  â†’ Receipt (photo in shared Drive folder)
  â†’ Status: pending / approved / reimbursed

A purchase that isn't tracked within 48 hours will be forgotten.
A forgotten purchase creates a phantom balance â€” you think you have
$800 but you've actually spent $300 of it already.
\`\`\`

## When Budget Is Running Short
\`\`\`
Priority order for cuts:
  1. Cut contingency (it exists for this â€” use it last)
  2. Delay non-essential tool purchases
  3. Find donated substitutes (mentor's personal tools, borrowed equipment)
  4. Run an emergency fundraiser (but these raise less than planned ones)
  5. Reduce travel: attend regional instead of two events

What you should NEVER cut:
  â†’ Registration (already sunk cost if paid)
  â†’ Safety equipment (PPE, robot stands)
  â†’ Parts critical to robot function
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should actual spending be updated within 48 hours of any purchase?",opts:["Accounting requires it","Delayed tracking creates a phantom balance â€” the team thinks they have more money than they do, leading to over-spending; within 48 hours purchases are still fresh and receipts are easy to find","Monthly updates are sufficient","FIRST requires real-time tracking"],ans:1},
      {q:"In what order should budget cuts be made when funds run short?",opts:["Cut travel first","Start with contingency (budgeted for this purpose), then defer non-essential tools, then seek donations, then run emergency fundraising â€” cutting safety equipment or critical parts should never happen","Cut outreach first","Cut registration last"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"fi_sponsorship2",title:"Building a Multi-Year Sponsor Relationship",est:"14 min",content:`## One-Year Sponsors Are Acquired; Multi-Year Sponsors Are Built
A company that sponsored you once can be gone next year when a new budget cycle arrives and you've provided no ongoing value. A company that has seen students grow, hired your alumni, and been thanked publicly for four years renews without being asked.

## The Annual Sponsor Touch Point Calendar
\`\`\`
Month       Action
September:  Season preview email â€” "Here's what we're planning this year"
            Include: season goals, student numbers, returning members
January:    Kickoff announcement â€” "Build season starts tomorrow!"
            Include: game reveal link, photo of excited students
March/April: Competition results + thank-you
            Include: results, specific mention of what their support enabled
            ("your contribution funded our swerve drive modules")
June:       End-of-season report
            Include: full year stats, notable student outcomes, photo
            Ask: "Are you open to renewing for next season?"
October:    Alumni mention â€” "One of your past sponsored students just [X]"
            This is pure goodwill, no ask â€” keeps the relationship warm

Total touches: 5-6 per year. Never more than one ask in the set.
\`\`\`

## What to Put in the End-of-Season Report
\`\`\`
One page, designed, with photos:
  â†’ Events attended + results
  â†’ Member count + demographics
  â†’ Outreach numbers (students reached, events run, programs started)
  â†’ Named student outcome: "[Student] is now studying engineering at [university]"
  â†’ How the sponsor's specific contribution was used
  â†’ Sponsorship renewal tiers + amounts for next season

The named student outcome is the most powerful element.
Engineers at sponsor companies went into engineering for a reason.
Showing them they helped create the next generation of engineers
creates emotional investment that survives budget cuts.
\`\`\`

## Escalating the Relationship
\`\`\`
Year 1: Financial sponsor (they give money)
Year 2: Invite them to a competition + demo day
Year 3: Named sponsor on robot; their engineers mentor one session
Year 4: Formal partnership â€” internship pipeline, annual event partnership

Each year, offer them one more touchpoint that deepens the relationship.
Don't jump to Year 4 asks in Year 1.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is the named student outcome ('Student X is now studying engineering at Y') the most powerful element of an end-of-season sponsor report?",opts:["Names are required by sponsors","Engineers at sponsoring companies chose their careers for a reason â€” connecting their financial support to a specific student who is now pursuing engineering creates personal emotional investment that survives budget pressures and leadership changes","Named outcomes are required by FIRST","It's the easiest content to write"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the purpose of October's 'alumni mention' touch point that contains no ask?",opts:["It satisfies reporting requirements","Pure goodwill touchpoints maintain a warm relationship during the off-season without asking for anything â€” sponsors who only hear from you when you want money feel transactional; sponsors who receive unexpected positive updates feel like partners","Alumni mentions generate donations","It replaces the end-of-season report"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fi_in_kind",title:"In-Kind Donations â€” Getting What You Need Without Cash",est:"12 min",content:`## In-Kind Donations Often Exceed Cash Value
A $500 check is useful. A $3,000 machining order donated by a local shop is more useful AND the shop benefits from the relationship differently than a cash transaction. In-kind donations are often easier to get because they don't touch a company's direct budget.

## What to Ask For (With Specific Framing)
\`\`\`
Machining shops / fabrication:
  "Could your team spare 4-6 hours of CNC time to cut our drive rails?
   We'll provide the CAD files and material â€” we just need the machine time."
  â†’ They use spare capacity that would otherwise sit idle
  â†’ They get portfolio work (robot part) and relationship with your team

Electrical / electronics companies:
  "Could you donate 20 XT30 connectors, 10 feet of 12AWG wire,
   and two JST harnesses? Here's our specific part list."
  â†’ Specific ask â†’ yes/no answer â†’ no negotiation needed
  â†’ Parts they may have as surplus inventory

Print shops:
  "Could you print our team banner (48"Ã—24") and 100 flyers as a donation?
   We'll credit you on our sponsors panel and social media."
  â†’ Low cost to them ($30-50 material), high value to you ($150+ retail)

Food / catering (for events):
  "Could [restaurant] donate food for 25 students for our build-season dinner?
   We'll post about it on our social media and include you in our event recap."
  â†’ Restaurants often have community donation budgets separate from cash budgets
\`\`\`

## Documenting and Acknowledging In-Kind Gifts
\`\`\`
For 501c3 purposes: in-kind donations need:
  â†’ Written acknowledgment from your team with the date and description
  â†’ Fair market value estimate (donor provides this for tax purposes)
  â†’ No cash value stated by you â€” only description

Acknowledgment template:
  "Thank you for your in-kind donation to Team 1234 on [date].
   Your donation of [description] enables [specific use].
   No goods or services were provided in exchange for this gift.
   Please consult your tax advisor regarding deductibility."

Public acknowledgment:
  â†’ Sponsor panel (same tier as cash donors at equivalent value)
  â†’ Social media tag
  â†’ Verbal mention at your event if applicable
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why are in-kind donations sometimes easier to secure than cash donations from the same company?",opts:["In-kind donations are smaller","In-kind gifts often come from spare capacity, surplus inventory, or discretionary community budgets that don't affect the main operating budget â€” a machining shop can donate 4 hours of idle CNC time without a budget approval that a $500 cash donation might require","Cash is more useful","In-kind donations have no tax benefit"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes a specific in-kind ask ('20 XT30 connectors, 10 feet of 12AWG wire') more effective than a general ask?",opts:["Specific asks are shorter","A specific ask requires only a yes or no answer â€” the potential donor doesn't have to figure out what to give; they either have those exact items or they don't, making the decision immediate and low-friction","General asks get larger donations","Specific asks show team knowledge"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fi_alumni_fund",title:"Starting a Team Alumni Fund",est:"11 min",content:`## Your Graduates Can Fund Your Future
Alumni who graduated three years ago are starting careers. In five years, some will have discretionary income. A formal alumni fund creates a reliable, diversified funding stream that doesn't depend on any single corporate sponsor.

## Legal Foundation First
\`\`\`
To accept donations and issue receipts, your team needs one of:
  Option A: 501(c)(3) status in your own name
    â†’ Takes 6-12 months and $600 IRS fee
    â†’ Full control over funds
    â†’ Best for large, stable teams

  Option B: Fiscal sponsorship through an existing nonprofit
    â†’ Partner with a STEM education nonprofit or community foundation
    â†’ They receive donations on your behalf, take 5-10% admin fee
    â†’ You control spending within their guidelines
    â†’ Best for smaller teams or new programs

  Option C: School-administered account
    â†’ School district receives funds, administers purchases
    â†’ No tax-receipt complexity
    â†’ Less flexible (school procurement rules apply)

Talk to your mentor or school before collecting any money â€”
using personal accounts for team funds creates serious legal problems.
\`\`\`

## Launching the Fund
\`\`\`
Year 1: Set it up quietly
  â†’ Open the fund structure
  â†’ Send one email to graduating seniors: "We've created an alumni fund.
     Any amount, whenever you're able. Here's how."
  â†’ No dollar goal, no pressure. First year is planting seeds.

Year 2: First public ask
  â†’ End-of-season report to all alumni includes fund mention
  â†’ One specific need tied to the ask: "We need $1,200 for a new battery kit.
     If 12 alumni give $100 each, we're covered for the season."
  â†’ Matching incentive if a mentor or company will match alumni gifts

Year 3+: Annual drive
  â†’ One email per year with update + ask
  â†’ Recognize cumulative donors: "Since 2023, our 34 alumni donors have
     contributed $8,400 â€” thank you."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should teams use fiscal sponsorship or school administration rather than personal accounts for team donations?",opts:["Personal accounts have fees","Collecting donations through personal accounts creates legal and tax liability for the individual account holder â€” the money belongs to no clear entity, donors can't get tax receipts, and disputes over spending have no formal resolution process","Schools are always more efficient","Fiscal sponsors give more money"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is Year 1 of an alumni fund 'planting seeds' rather than running a full campaign?",opts:["Year 1 alumni don't have money","Recent graduates have limited disposable income and haven't yet experienced the value of the alumni network â€” introducing the fund without pressure builds awareness that leads to donations when they're ready, rather than burning goodwill with an aggressive ask to people who can't yet give","Year 1 is setup only","FIRST requires a waiting period"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Advanced.push(
  {id:"fa_roi",title:"Measuring & Communicating Fundraising ROI",est:"13 min",content:`## Sponsors and Grants Want to Know Their Money Worked\nThe teams that secure the largest, most consistent funding are the ones that demonstrate impact in terms funders care about â€” not just robot performance, but student outcomes and community reach. Learning to quantify and present this data is the difference between a team that replaces sponsors every year and one that grows them.\n\n## Metrics That Matter to Different Funder Types\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\nCorporate sponsors care about:\n  â†’ Employees engaged / volunteered (hours Ã— headcount)\n  â†’ Brand visibility (event attendance, social media reach, media mentions)\n  â†’ Student pipeline: "2 of our alumni interned at sponsor companies last summer"\n  â†’ Community perception (FIRST programs in their service area)\n\nFoundations / grants care about:\n  â†’ Students directly served (headcount, demographics)\n  â†’ Programs created or sustained\n  â†’ Evidence of lasting change (programs that continued independently)\n  â†’ Cost per student served (lower is better for grant makers)\n\nAlumni donors care about:\n  â†’ What the team is accomplishing that they remember wanting to accomplish\n  â†’ That the culture they valued is still present\n  â†’ That their small gift actually matters (micro-impact stories)\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Building Your Impact Dashboard\n\\\`\\\`\\\`python\n# Track these numbers throughout the year â€” report at year end:\nmetrics = {\n    "students_on_team":     28,\n    "new_members":          9,\n    "competitions_attended": 3,\n    "awards_won":           2,\n    "outreach_events":      14,\n    "students_reached":     847,\n    "new_teams_started":    1,\n    "alumni_in_stem":       12,   # of last 3 graduating classes\n    "volunteer_hours":      340,\n    "budget_total":         18400,\n    "cost_per_student":     18400 / 847,  # ~$21.72/student reached\n}\n\n# Cost per student served is a powerful grant metric:\n# $21 to bring one student a meaningful STEM experience is very competitive\nprint(f"Cost per student reached: \\" + (metrics['cost_per_student']:.2f) + "")\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## The One-Page Impact Report\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\nLayout: two columns, visual-heavy, one page only\n\nLeft column:\n  Large number: "847 students reached in 2025"\n  Large number: "28 team members"\n  Large number: "3 new FLL teams mentored"\n  Photo: students at outreach event\n\nRight column:\n  One student story (5-6 sentences, named with permission)\n  Budget breakdown (simple pie chart: competitions 45%, parts 25%, travel 20%, outreach 10%)\n  Sponsor recognition (logos in tier order)\n\nBottom bar:\n  "Your investment: [sponsorship amount] â†’ [what it funded specifically]"\n\nDesign rule: a reader should understand your team\"s full year impact in < 30 seconds.\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'cost per student served' a particularly useful metric for grant applications?",opts:["It's required by all foundations","Grant makers evaluate programs on efficiency â€” a program that reaches hundreds of students for $21 each demonstrates high leverage and justifies investment; the same money spent on a program reaching 10 students for $1,840 each is much harder to justify","Cost metrics are always the most important","Foundations don't care about cost"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do corporate sponsors care about employee volunteer hours as a metric?",opts:["They need it for tax purposes","Employee engagement and volunteer activity are tracked as corporate social responsibility (CSR) metrics that affect company reporting, culture surveys, and recruitment brand â€” a team that provides employee volunteering opportunities delivers a measurable CSR benefit beyond the tax deduction","Volunteer hours determine sponsorship tier","They use it to evaluate students"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ GIT (add 4 â†’ ~17) â”€â”€
LESSONS.git.Beginner.push(
  {id:"gb_branches",title:"Branching â€” Working in Parallel Without Breaking Main",est:"12 min",content:`## One Branch Per Feature
When three subteam members commit to the same branch simultaneously, someone's changes will overwrite someone else's. Branches solve this by giving each person (or feature) an isolated workspace.

## Creating and Switching Branches
\`\`\`bash
# See all branches:
git branch               # local branches
git branch -a            # local + remote

# Create a new branch and switch to it:
git checkout -b feature/intake-pid
# or (modern Git):
git switch -c feature/intake-pid

# Switch between branches:
git checkout main
git switch main

# Naming conventions for FIRST teams:
feature/intake-redesign   # new mechanism or code feature
fix/encoder-calibration   # bug fix
auto/red-alliance-2piece  # autonomous routine variant
tune/arm-pid-gains        # constants tuning
\`\`\`

## The Basic Branch Workflow
\`\`\`bash
# 1. Always start from an up-to-date main:
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. Create your branch:
git switch -c feature/vision-targeting

# 3. Make changes, commit regularly:
git add VisionSubsystem.java
git commit -m "Add AprilTag detection to VisionSubsystem"

# 4. Push branch to GitHub:
git push origin feature/vision-targeting

# 5. When done, open a Pull Request on GitHub
#    â†’ teammate reviews â†’ merge to main â†’ delete branch

# 6. Delete local branch after merge:
git branch -d feature/vision-targeting
\`\`\`

## Keeping Your Branch Up to Date
\`\`\`bash
# If main has advanced while you were working on your branch:
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch feature/vision-targeting
git merge main    # bring main's changes into your branch

# Resolve any conflicts, then:
git add .
git commit -m "Merge main into feature/vision-targeting"
\`\`\`

## FIRST Team Branch Rules
\`\`\`
main branch:  always deployable â€” only merge tested code here
              protected: require PR + passing CI before merge

dev branch:   optional â€” integration branch for testing before main
              merge features here first, test robot, then merge to main

Rules:
  â†’ Never commit directly to main
  â†’ One branch per feature/fix â€” don't mix unrelated changes
  â†’ Delete branches after merging â€” a repo with 40 stale branches
    is confusing and slows everyone down
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What problem does working on separate branches solve for a FIRST team with multiple programmers?",opts:["It speeds up compilation","Each programmer works in isolation â€” their changes don't interfere with others until they're deliberately merged; without branches, concurrent commits to the same file create conflicts or silently overwrite each other's work","Branches reduce file size","It prevents compilation errors"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a FIRST team's main branch be protected from direct commits?",opts:["It saves storage","Main should always contain deployable code â€” direct commits bypass code review and CI checks, risking broken code being deployed to the robot; requiring a PR and passing CI before merge keeps main reliable","Protection is a git default","Direct commits are slower"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_pr",title:"Pull Requests â€” Code Review for Robot Teams",est:"13 min",content:`## Code Review Catches Bugs Before the Robot Does
A second pair of eyes on new code catches obvious mistakes, style inconsistencies, and logic errors that the author is too close to notice. For FIRST teams, a PR review process means broken code gets caught in GitHub, not during a match.

## What a Good PR Description Contains
\`\`\`markdown
## What this changes
Adds vision-assisted targeting to the shooter subsystem using PhotonVision.
The new VisionSubsystem tracks AprilTag 7 and calculates aim correction.

## Why
Auto-aim reduces cycle time by ~1.5 seconds per shot by removing
the need for driver manual aim correction.

## How to test
1. Deploy to robot with PhotonVision running on coprocessor
2. Position robot 3m from AprilTag 7
3. Hold right bumper â€” robot should auto-aim within 2Â°
4. Verify on SmartDashboard: "Vision/Aim Error" should show < 2.0

## Related issues
Closes #42 (vision targeting feature request)

## Checklist
- [x] Tested on robot
- [x] No new compiler warnings
- [x] Constants added to Constants.java (not hardcoded)
- [ ] Unit test added (not feasible for hardware-dependent code)
\`\`\`

## Reviewing a PR â€” What to Look For
\`\`\`
Correctness:
  â†’ Does the logic match what the description says it does?
  â†’ Are there off-by-one errors in array access or loop bounds?
  â†’ Are all edge cases handled (null checks, division by zero, empty lists)?

Constants:
  â†’ Are magic numbers in Constants.java, not hardcoded?
  â†’ Are motor IDs consistent with the hardware map?

Safety:
  â†’ Does the code have a safe default when a sensor fails?
  â†’ Are motor power values clamped to [-1, 1]?

Style:
  â†’ Can you understand what each method does from its name?
  â†’ Are there TODO comments that should be resolved?
\`\`\`

## Giving Constructive Review Comments
\`\`\`
âŒ "This is wrong"
âœ… "This will throw a NullPointerException if camera.getLatestResult()
    returns null when no targets are visible. Add a null check or
    use result.hasTargets() before accessing result.getBestTarget()."

âŒ "Why did you do it this way?"
âœ… "I notice you're using a while loop here instead of the command scheduler.
    Is there a reason? I'd suggest SubsystemCommand to keep this consistent
    with the rest of the codebase."

Comment levels:
  "Nit:" â€” minor style thing, fine to ignore
  "Suggestion:" â€” better approach, not blocking
  "Issue:" â€” real bug, must fix before merge
  "Question:" â€” I don't understand this, explain or clarify
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the purpose of a 'How to test' section in a pull request description?",opts:["It proves the code works","It tells the reviewer exactly how to verify the change works â€” without this, reviewers either skip testing (missing bugs) or spend 20 minutes figuring out how to test something the author could describe in 4 lines","Testing sections are required","It documents the test framework used"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'This will throw NullPointerException if...' a better PR comment than 'This is wrong'?",opts:["It's more polite","Specific comments explain the exact failure mode and what's needed to fix it â€” the author can act immediately; vague comments require a follow-up conversation to understand what 'wrong' means before any fix can happen","Specific comments are shorter","It references Java"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"gi_conflict",title:"Resolving Merge Conflicts",est:"12 min",content:`## Conflicts Are Normal â€” Panic Is Optional
A merge conflict means two people changed the same lines differently and Git can't decide which is right. It marks both versions and waits for a human to choose. Once you've resolved five conflicts, they stop being stressful.

## What a Conflict Looks Like
\`\`\`java
// Git marks conflicts like this in the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
    static final double ARM_KP = 0.009;  // your branch
=======
    static final double ARM_KP = 0.007;  // incoming change (main)
>>>>>>> main

// You must:
// 1. Delete the conflict markers (<<<, ===, >>>)
// 2. Keep the correct version â€” or combine them:
    static final double ARM_KP = 0.008;  // tuned value: compromise
\`\`\`

## Step-by-Step Conflict Resolution
\`\`\`bash
# Conflict appears during merge:
git merge main
# Auto-merging Constants.java
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in Constants.java

# 1. See which files have conflicts:
git status
# both modified: Constants.java

# 2. Open the file, find all <<<< markers, resolve each one
#    (VS Code and IntelliJ have built-in conflict resolution UI)

# 3. After resolving all conflicts, stage the file:
git add Constants.java

# 4. Complete the merge:
git commit -m "Merge main: resolve ARM_KP conflict (tuned to 0.008)"

# 5. Verify â€” no remaining markers:
grep -r "<<<<<<" src/  # should return nothing
\`\`\`

## Preventing Conflicts Before They Happen
\`\`\`
Most conflicts occur in:
  â†’ Constants.java / RobotConstants.java (everyone touches it)
  â†’ Main OpMode / RobotContainer (central coordination file)
  â†’ Config files

Prevention:
  â†’ Merge main into your branch frequently â€” don't let branches diverge for weeks
  â†’ Coordinate before editing Constants.java â€” "I'm adding arm constants today"
  â†’ Split Constants.java by subsystem: ArmConstants.java, DriveConstants.java
    â†’ fewer people touching each file â†’ fewer conflicts

If the conflict is complex (both changes are needed):
  â†’ Don't resolve alone â€” get both authors together
  â†’ The best merge is often a combination, not choosing one side
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What do the <<<<<, =====, and >>>>> markers in a conflict mean?",opts:["Git syntax errors","They mark the two conflicting versions â€” everything between <<<< and ==== is your branch's version, everything between ==== and >>>> is the incoming version; you delete all three markers and keep whichever content (or combination) is correct","They show file corruption","They indicate deleted lines"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does splitting Constants.java into per-subsystem files (ArmConstants.java, DriveConstants.java) reduce merge conflicts?",opts:["Smaller files are faster","Fewer people need to touch each file â€” the arm programmer only edits ArmConstants.java and the drive programmer only edits DriveConstants.java, so simultaneous edits rarely target the same file","Per-subsystem files are a git requirement","Constants files can't conflict"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT (add 5 â†’ ~18) â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"tmi_meeting2",title:"Running Efficient Build Season Meetings",est:"13 min",content:`## 90 Minutes Can Feel Like 20 Minutes or 4 Hours
The difference is structure. A meeting with an agenda, clear goals, and defined end time moves. A meeting without these meanders until someone checks the clock and everyone realizes nothing got done.

## The 90-Minute Build Session Template
\`\`\`
0:00 - 0:10: Standup (whole team, standing up)
  Each subteam: 30 seconds
    â†’ What did we complete since last session?
    â†’ What is our goal for today?
    â†’ What's blocking us?
  Rule: no problem-solving during standup â€” blockers are noted, solved after

0:10 - 1:10: Work blocks (subteams split to their areas)
  Check-in at 0:40: leads briefly confirm teams are on track
  At 1:05: "5-minute warning" â€” begin cleanup and task close-out

1:10 - 1:20: End-of-session debrief (whole team)
  â†’ What did we complete today?
  â†’ What is each subteam's goal for next session?
  â†’ Any decisions that need full-team input before next meeting?
  â†’ Recognition: call out one person for good work today
\`\`\`

## The Blocker Rule
\`\`\`
A blocker is anything that prevents someone from doing their work:
  "I can't continue the arm until the frame mounting holes are drilled"
  "I don't know the CAN IDs for the new motors yet"
  "I'm waiting for the motors to arrive"

How to handle blockers immediately after standup:
  â†’ Blockers within your subteam: solve in your subteam work block
  â†’ Blockers between subteams: assign a 5-minute conversation before work starts
  â†’ Blockers outside the team (shipping, parts): assign to mentor to track

Never: let a blocker sit unstated for two sessions.
A blocker that isn't surfaced is invisible to everyone who could fix it.
\`\`\`

## Reducing Decision Latency
\`\`\`
The most common meeting time waste: a decision that should take 2 minutes
takes 20 because the right people aren't in the conversation.

Prevention:
  â†’ Define decision authorities before build season:
    "Mechanism design decisions: mechanical lead makes final call"
    "Constants and tuning: programming lead makes final call"
    "Build/competition schedule: leadership team decides by majority"
  â†’ Log every decision in a shared doc with date and who made it
  â†’ When someone challenges a past decision: review the log,
    understand why it was made, then decide if conditions have changed
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the purpose of the standup rule 'no problem-solving during standup'?",opts:["Problems are solved elsewhere","Standup is for surfacing information â€” problem-solving during standup keeps the whole team standing for 30 minutes while two people debug a sensor issue; blockers are noted and solved in targeted conversations immediately after, respecting everyone's time","Problems can't be solved in standup","Standup is only for mentors"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should decision-making authority be defined before build season begins?",opts:["FIRST requires authority charts","Unclear authority creates the most common meeting time waste â€” when it's unclear who decides, decisions get re-discussed at every meeting until someone with unclear authority makes a call that others challenge; pre-defined authority means one person decides and everyone moves on","Authority prevents mistakes","Pre-defined authority limits creativity"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmi_retention",title:"Reducing Mid-Season Member Dropout",est:"12 min",content:`## Half of Dropouts Are Preventable
Students leave mid-season for predictable, addressable reasons. Teams that track why people leave and act on the patterns retain more members and don't spend build season re-onboarding replacements.

## The Four Dropout Patterns and Solutions
\`\`\`
Pattern 1: "I don't feel useful"
  Signal: member shows up but stands around during work sessions
  Cause: unclear role, no tasks at their skill level
  Fix: every member leaves each meeting with 1 concrete task
       due by next session. Leads check in on it.

Pattern 2: "I can't keep up with school"
  Signal: attendance drops starting Week 3 (exam pressure)
  Cause: build season conflicts with test/project schedules
  Fix: know the school calendar. Reduce meeting frequency around
       major test weeks. Allow async contributions (CAD at home).

Pattern 3: "I don't fit in"
  Signal: member is quiet, doesn't interact with others, leaves early
  Cause: social friction â€” no friend on the team, different background
  Fix: pair them with a mentor student (1:1 check-in monthly).
       Social belonging predicts retention better than task engagement.

Pattern 4: "I don't know what's happening"
  Signal: member asks "wait, when is the competition?" or
          "I didn't know we had a meeting today"
  Cause: communication gaps â€” not in the right channels,
         information shared verbally only
  Fix: all schedule/decision info in one written place.
       Require confirmation from every member of key announcements.
\`\`\`

## The Monthly 1:1 Check-In
\`\`\`
5-minute conversation, student lead â†’ each member, once per month:
  "What's going well for you on the team?"
  "Anything that's frustrating or confusing?"
  "Is there anything you wish you could do that you're not doing?"

Rules:
  â†’ Leads do this, not mentors â€” peer conversations surface
    different things than adult-student conversations
  â†’ Information stays confidential unless it's a safety concern
  â†’ Every piece of feedback gets acknowledged even if not acted on:
    "Thanks for telling me that â€” I'm going to look into it"

Teams that run monthly check-ins retain ~30% more members than those
that rely on members to self-report problems.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Which dropout pattern is most reliably predicted by a member being quiet and leaving early?",opts:["They don't understand the material","Social isolation â€” members who haven't formed friendships on the team lose the social motivation to keep attending; social belonging predicts retention better than task engagement or skill level","They have too many tasks","They're unhappy with leadership"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do peer-to-peer monthly check-ins surface different information than mentor-student conversations?",opts:["Peers have more time","Students often won't tell a mentor about social friction, feeling underutilized, or frustration with how decisions are made â€” a peer student lead can receive this feedback without triggering the filtering that authority relationships create","Peers are always more available","Mentors aren't allowed to do check-ins"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmi_handoff",title:"Leadership Transitions â€” Passing the Baton",est:"14 min",content:`## The Most Common FIRST Team Failure Mode
A team runs beautifully for four years under a strong student captain. They graduate. Within two years the team is struggling â€” not because the program changed, but because the knowledge, relationships, and culture lived in one person rather than in the institution.

## What Needs to Be Transferred
\`\`\`
Explicit knowledge (easy to document):
  â†’ Contact list: sponsors, mentors, school admin, parts suppliers
  â†’ Budget history: what things actually cost over 3 years
  â†’ Process docs: how you register for events, how you order parts,
                  how you communicate with judges
  â†’ Hardware map, robot constants, build procedure docs

Tacit knowledge (hard to document, must be experienced):
  â†’ How your mentor prefers to be communicated with
  â†’ Which sponsors care about what
  â†’ When the principal needs to be consulted vs when you can act
  â†’ How to run an alliance selection meeting under pressure
  â†’ How to handle a team conflict without it becoming a public split
\`\`\`

## The Shadow Year Model
\`\`\`
12 months before a leadership handoff:
  Every action taken by the current captain is shadowed by the successor.
  Successor attends every sponsor meeting, every judge interaction,
  every alliance selection â€” as an observer first, then as co-lead.

6 months before:
  Successor takes primary lead on 1-2 sponsor relationships
  and one cross-team coordination event.

3 months before:
  Successor runs the day-to-day; current captain is available for advice.

At handoff:
  Current captain writes a "State of the Team" document:
    â†’ Current relationships and their history
    â†’ Unresolved issues to watch
    â†’ What worked this year vs prior years
    â†’ Advice for their first month

Never: announce the new captain without the outgoing one having
       personally introduced them to key external contacts.
\`\`\`

## Institutional Memory Systems
\`\`\`
Build these so knowledge doesn't walk out the door:
  â†’ Annual "year in review" doc written before summer (not after)
  â†’ Sponsor CRM: company, contact, relationship history, last contact date
  â†’ Decision log: major decisions and their reasoning
  â†’ Lessons learned: what went wrong and why, for each competition

Rule: if the only place a piece of knowledge exists is in one person's head,
      it will be lost. Write it down before graduation season.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the difference between 'explicit' and 'tacit' knowledge in a leadership handoff?",opts:["Explicit is more important","Explicit knowledge can be documented (contact lists, budget history, processes); tacit knowledge is experiential â€” how to read a mentor's communication style, when to escalate vs decide independently â€” and can only be transferred through direct experience, not documentation alone","Tacit knowledge is always lost","They are the same thing in FIRST context"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why must the outgoing captain personally introduce the successor to key sponsors rather than just forwarding their contact information?",opts:["Email introductions are inefficient","Sponsor relationships are personal â€” the new captain inheriting contact information has no context or relationship; a personal introduction from someone the sponsor trusts transfers credibility and signals continuity, dramatically improving the chance the sponsor renews","Sponsors prefer in-person contact","FIRST requires personal introductions"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ CAD (add 6 â†’ ~18) â”€â”€
LESSONS.cad.Beginner.push(
  {id:"cadb_version",title:"Version Control for CAD Files",est:"11 min",content:`## CAD Files Change Constantly â€” Without a System, You Lose Work
"RobotArm_v3_FINAL_USE_THIS_ONE.f3d" is not version control. It's panic. Onshape has native version history; Fusion 360 files on Google Drive need a different approach. Either way, you need a system before you need it.

## Onshape â€” Built-In Version History
\`\`\`
Onshape saves every change automatically â€” you never lose work.

Creating named versions (milestones):
  â†’ In the document, click the clock icon (Versions and History)
  â†’ "Create Version" â†’ name it with date + description:
    "2025-01-15 â€” Arm pivot bracket before hole pattern change"
  â†’ Create versions at major decision points, not every save

Branching in Onshape:
  â†’ "Branch" creates a copy of the document at the current state
  â†’ Use for: "I want to try a completely different approach"
    without overwriting the working version
  â†’ Name branches: "intake-compliant-wheel-concept" vs "intake-belt-concept"
  â†’ Merge the chosen branch back to main when decided

Reverting:
  â†’ Click any version in history â†’ "Restore workspace to this version"
  â†’ Previous state is restored; your history is preserved
\`\`\`

## Fusion 360 â€” Milestone Management
\`\`\`
Fusion has version history within a project, but it's less reliable.
Recommended practice:

  1. Store all Fusion files in a shared Google Drive folder
  2. At each major milestone, export a copy:
     File â†’ Export â†’ Fusion 360 Archive (.f3d)
     Name: ArmBracket_2025-01-15_pre-modification.f3d
     Store in: /Archives/2025/ subfolder

  3. The "working" file is always in the main folder
     Archives are never edited â€” they're snapshots only

For shared team CAD (multiple people touching same assembly):
  â†’ Onshape is better â€” cloud-based, true multi-user
  â†’ Fusion's multi-user requires a paid Team plan
\`\`\`

## Naming Conventions
\`\`\`
File names should answer: what is it + what state is it in?

Format: [subsystem]-[part]-[date]-[status].extension
  Good: arm-pivot-bracket-2025-01-20-reviewed.step
  Bad:  bracket_final.step

Status suffixes:
  -wip     : work in progress, not reviewed
  -reviewed: checked by a second person
  -released: sent to fabrication / printed

Never delete old files â€” archive them to an /old/ or /archive/ subfolder.
Storage is cheap; recreating a lost design is expensive.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"When should a named version (milestone) be created in Onshape's version history?",opts:["After every change","At major decision points â€” before making significant modifications, after a design is reviewed, or before sending to fabrication; creating a version at every change is unnecessary since Onshape auto-saves everything and named versions are for meaningful rollback points","Weekly on Fridays","Only when a design is complete"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should old CAD files be archived in a subfolder rather than deleted when no longer current?",opts:["Storage is unlimited","Old files preserve design history â€” a mechanism that was discarded in Week 2 might have a geometry that solves a problem in Week 5; recreating lost design work takes hours that archived files make unnecessary in seconds","FIRST requires file retention","Old files improve new designs automatically"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cadb_assembly2",title:"Assembly Best Practices â€” Mates & Constraints",est:"13 min",content:`## Assemblies Break When Mates Are Wrong
A CAD assembly that behaves correctly during design tells you early if parts collide, if motion is constrained correctly, and if the mechanism fits. An assembly built with wrong mates gives you false confidence â€” it looks fine until you build the physical version.

## Degrees of Freedom â€” The Foundation
\`\`\`
Every rigid body has 6 degrees of freedom (DOF):
  Translation: X, Y, Z
  Rotation:    Rx, Ry, Rz

Fully constrained = 0 DOF remaining (no motion, correct for fixed parts)
Under-constrained = some DOF free (usually wrong, unless intentional)
Over-constrained = redundant constraints (causes solver errors)

In Onshape, each mate removes specific DOFs:
  Fastened mate:    removes all 6 DOF â€” part is fixed to another
  Revolute mate:    removes 5 DOF â€” allows rotation about one axis only
  Slider mate:      removes 5 DOF â€” allows translation along one axis only
  Planar mate:      removes 3 DOF â€” allows sliding on a plane
  Ball mate:        removes 3 DOF â€” allows rotation in all directions
\`\`\`

## Choosing the Right Mate Type
\`\`\`
Arm pivot bearing â†’ Revolute mate
  â†’ Allows only the rotation the arm actually has

Linear slide carriage â†’ Slider mate
  â†’ Allows only the translation the slide actually has

Motor bolted to bracket â†’ Fastened mate
  â†’ Zero motion; motor doesn't move relative to bracket

Chain-driven sprocket â†’ Revolute mate (on shaft)
  + gear relation to drive sprocket (for motion simulation)

Common mistake: using Fastened mates for everything
  â†’ Assembly looks right but you can't simulate motion
  â†’ Collisions during mechanism travel aren't detected
\`\`\`

## Clash Detection
\`\`\`
In Onshape: right-click any revolute/slider mate â†’ "Drive"
  â†’ Animate the mechanism through its full travel range
  â†’ Watch for any parts that intersect (shown in red)
  â†’ Check at both extremes AND in between â€” worst case often isn't at the endpoint

What to check on every mechanism:
  â†’ Arm at full extension: does it hit the frame?
  â†’ Arm at full retraction: does it hit itself or another mechanism?
  â†’ Intake at full deploy: does it stay within the robot's max extension?
  â†’ Drive at full width: does the bumper stay within the frame perimeter?

Detecting a collision in CAD: 30 seconds to fix
Detecting a collision at 11pm during build: 2-3 hours to fix
Detecting at competition: match loss and an emergency pit session
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a Revolute mate be used for an arm pivot rather than a Fastened mate, even if you don't need to simulate motion?",opts:["Revolute mates are more accurate","The mate type communicates the actual physical constraint â€” a Revolute mate correctly models that the arm can only rotate about one axis; if you later use clash detection or motion simulation, only the correct mate type will reveal real collisions","Fastened mates cause errors","Revolute mates use less memory"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is the worst-case collision often not visible at the mechanism's endpoint positions?",opts:["Endpoints are always safe","Mechanisms can pass through interference zones in the middle of their travel range that the start and end positions avoid â€” full travel animation reveals collisions at intermediate positions that endpoint-only checking misses","Endpoints are not modeled","Onshape only checks endpoints"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"cadi_configs",title:"Onshape Configurations for Variants",est:"14 min",content:`## One Part, Many Versions â€” Without Duplicating Files
If you need a bracket in three hole spacing variants, you could duplicate the file three times. Or you could use Configurations â€” a single Onshape part that switches between variants without creating separate files.

## Creating a Configuration
\`\`\`
In the Part Studio:
  1. Right-click the feature tree background â†’ "Add configuration"
  2. Name it: "Hole Spacing"
  3. Add input type: List (for discrete variants) or Variable (for numeric)

List configuration example â€” three robot sizes:
  Small  | Medium | Large
  4-inch | 6-inch | 8-inch mount width

In the sketch or feature:
  Right-click any dimension â†’ "Configure..."
  Set the value for each configuration:
    Small: 4 in
    Medium: 6 in
    Large: 8 in

Now: switching the configuration in the dropdown changes the part geometry.
\`\`\`

## Configurations in Assemblies
\`\`\`
When you insert a configured part into an assembly:
  Insert Part Studio â†’ select the configuration from the dropdown
  Both versions can exist in the same assembly:
    ArmBracket (config: Short) â€” for 14" reach
    ArmBracket (config: Tall)  â€” for 18" reach

Useful for:
  â†’ Testing multiple mechanism lengths in the same assembly
  â†’ Showing a sponsor/judge "here are our two design options"
  â†’ Creating a single part that serves multiple build years
\`\`\`

## Variable Studio for Team-Wide Parameters
\`\`\`
Onshape Variable Studio: define shared variables once, use everywhere.

Create a Variable Studio in your document:
  robotWidth  = 18 in
  robotLength = 28 in
  armLength   = 20 in

Reference in any Part Studio:
  #robotWidth, #armLength

Change robotWidth from 18 to 16:
  Every part and assembly that references #robotWidth updates automatically.

Best practice for FIRST teams:
  All game-constraint dimensions in Variable Studio:
    framePerimeterMax = 120 in (from game manual)
    startingHeightMax = 48 in
    extensionLimit    = 16 in
  â†’ If the Q&A changes a limit, update one variable â†’ everything updates
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What problem does an Onshape Configuration solve compared to duplicating a part file for each variant?",opts:["Configurations are smaller files","A single configured part stays in sync â€” if you change the base geometry, all variants update; three duplicate files require the same fix to be applied three times and risk diverging as each gets independently modified","Configurations use less storage","Part duplication creates conflicts"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the key advantage of storing game-constraint dimensions in a Variable Studio rather than hardcoded in individual sketches?",opts:["Variable Studio is required by Onshape","Changing one Variable Studio entry propagates to every part and assembly that references it â€” if a Q&A ruling changes the extension limit, one update instead of finding and changing 15 individual sketch dimensions prevents missed updates","Variables compute faster","It satisfies judges for the design award"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cadi_export",title:"Exporting from CAD for Fabrication",est:"12 min",content:`## Wrong Export Format = Wrong Parts
Sending an Onshape STEP file to a waterjet service that wants a DXF gets your email ignored. Sending a DXF of a 3D part to a sheet metal shop that needs the flat profile misaligns the holes. Each fabrication method needs a specific output.

## Format Guide by Fabrication Method
\`\`\`
Waterjet / Laser cutting:
  Format: DXF (2D, flat profile only)
  Process: Flatten the 3D part to 2D â†’ export face as DXF
  In Onshape: right-click a flat face â†’ Export as DXF/DWG
  Check: the DXF opens in the shop's software correctly (correct units: inches)
  Include: sheet thickness and material on the drawing or in the email

3D Printing (FDM/SLA):
  Format: STL or 3MF (3MF preferred â€” preserves color and scale)
  In Onshape: Part Studio â†’ right-click part â†’ Export â†’ STL
  Check: units (mm usually required), scale = 1:1, no inverted normals
  Resolution: 0.01mm chord tolerance for detailed parts; 0.1mm for structural

CNC Milling:
  Format: STEP (for CAM software like Fusion 360 CAM or Mastercam)
  or: the shop's preferred format (ask first â€” some use native Onshape link)
  Include: drawing PDF with critical tolerances, material spec, quantity

Off-the-shelf ordering (GoBILDA, REV, WCP):
  Format: not applicable â€” use their exact part numbers
  Confirm: part numbers from current catalog (GoBILDA changes numbers often)
  Check: check stock before placing the order (same-day vs backordered)
\`\`\`

## Pre-Export Checklist
\`\`\`
Before sending any file to fabrication:
  â–¡ Correct units (inches vs mm â€” confirm with the shop)
  â–¡ Correct scale (1:1 is not always the default)
  â–¡ All intended geometry is present (spot-check after opening exported file)
  â–¡ Hole positions match your drawing dimensions (measure 2-3 holes)
  â–¡ Material and thickness noted (in the file or in the email)
  â–¡ Quantity noted
  â–¡ Delivery/pickup date requested
  â–¡ Contact info included (who to call if questions)

Bonus: attach the engineering drawing PDF alongside any DXF or STEP â€”
       it gives the shop a visual reference for what the finished part should look like.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is DXF the correct format for waterjet cutting rather than a STEP file?",opts:["Waterjet machines don't support STEP","Waterjet cuts flat sheet material using a 2D path â€” a DXF file describes the 2D cut profile that the machine follows; a STEP file is a 3D format that waterjet software can't directly use for cutting path generation","DXF files are smaller","STEP files have incorrect units for waterjet"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a 3MF file be preferred over STL for 3D printing when both are available?",opts:["3MF is always smaller","3MF preserves scale, units, and color in a standardized format â€” STL only stores geometry with no scale information, making it possible to print at the wrong size if the slicer defaults to millimeters when you designed in inches","Printers can't read STL","3MF has better resolution"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS (add 5 â†’ ~19) â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_judges",title:"Understanding How Award Judging Works",est:"13 min",content:`## Demystifying the Process
Judges aren't mysterious. They're engineers, educators, and FIRST alumni following a rubric. Understanding their process â€” how they're briefed, what they document, how they discuss â€” helps you give them what they need to advocate for your team.

## How Judges Are Organized at an Event
\`\`\`
Typical FRC event judging:
  â†’ 8-12 judges, organized into panels of 2-3
  â†’ Each panel interviews multiple teams in assigned time slots (usually 5 minutes)
  â†’ Judges rotate pit observation throughout the event independently
  â†’ Award deliberations happen 30-60 minutes before the ceremony
    in a private room with all judges together

FTC events:
  â†’ 2-4 judges; smaller scale
  â†’ More informal pit visits, often longer team interviews
  â†’ Same deliberation structure before ceremony

What judges receive before the event:
  â†’ Your submitted essays and executive summaries (Impact, Dean's List, etc.)
  â†’ Previous award history (optional â€” varies by competition)
  â†’ The award rubrics for each category
  â†’ They do NOT receive your robot specs, ranking, or performance data
    (unless they observe competition themselves)
\`\`\`

## What Happens in Deliberations
\`\`\`
Judges discuss each nominated team for each award.
The conversation looks like:
  "Team 1234 â€” Impact submission was strong. What did we observe in pits?"
  "I saw them helping Team 5678 debug their intake. Very GP."
  "Their sustainability story was specific â€” three FLL teams running independently."
  "Did anyone get a chance to verify the student reach numbers?"
  "I asked the captain directly â€” they had program rosters for each school."

What wins deliberations:
  â†’ Judges who observed you and can speak positively (not just read the essay)
  â†’ Numbers that were verified when asked, not waved off
  â†’ A story that stuck with at least one judge from the interview

What loses deliberations:
  â†’ "I don't remember anything distinctive about this team"
  â†’ Claims in the essay that judges couldn't verify during pit visits
  â†’ A team that only shone in the formal interview and not observed elsewhere
\`\`\`

## Making Yourself Memorable to Judges
\`\`\`
Before the event: submit your essay on time, clean, well-organized
  â†’ Judges read dozens of submissions; formatting and clarity matter

During the event:
  â†’ Be available when a judge walks by your pit â€” don't have the whole team
    scattered when judges are on the floor (usually marked as "judging period")
  â†’ Any team member should be able to give a 2-minute overview of the team's
    mission and key programs â€” not just the captain
  â†’ When a judge asks a question to a non-captain student, that student
    giving a confident, specific answer is a very positive signal

After your formal interview:
  â†’ Thank the judges by first name if you know them (you have the schedule)
  â†’ Don't loiter â€” but a genuine "thank you for your time" as you leave counts
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is it important that non-captain team members can also answer judge questions about the team's mission?",opts:["Judges only interview non-captains","A student other than the captain giving a specific, confident answer signals that the culture and values are genuinely shared across the team â€” if only the captain knows the program details, judges may infer that one person built the program rather than the team","Captains are too busy","Judges prefer non-captain answers"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes a judge able to 'advocate for your team' in deliberations?",opts:["A well-formatted essay","Personal observation of your team during the event â€” a judge who watched your members help other teams, verified your outreach numbers, and had a memorable pit conversation can speak with firsthand experience, which carries more weight than reading the same essay all judges received","The highest score in their rubric","Friendship with the team captain"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awi_deanslist",title:"Dean's List Award â€” Student Submission Strategy",est:"14 min",content:`## The Dean's List Is Different From Team Awards
Impact and Inspire recognize the team. Dean's List recognizes individual students â€” specifically 10th and 11th grade students who exemplify the FIRST ideal: strong academic performance, leadership, technical achievement, and community contribution. The submission strategy is completely different from team awards.

## Eligibility and Process
\`\`\`
FRC Dean's List:
  â†’ Must be in 10th or 11th grade at time of submission
  â†’ Each team may submit up to two nominees
  â†’ Submission: online essay questions (varies by year)
  â†’ Event finalist selected at each qualifying event (2 finalists per event)
  â†’ Finalists advance to Championship; winner announced at Championship

Key insight: the first selection happens at your qualifying event.
The judges at YOUR event make the finalist selection â€” not a national panel.
This means the local interview matters as much as the written submission.
\`\`\`

## What the Submission Must Show
\`\`\`
Four pillars, all required:
  1. Academic excellence
     â†’ GPA or academic standing
     â†’ Specific courses relevant to STEM (AP CS, Calculus, Physics)
     â†’ Academic honors or recognitions

  2. Demonstrated leadership
     â†’ Named role on the team (lead, captain, mentor)
     â†’ Specific decisions or programs they drove
     â†’ How did they grow in leadership over their FIRST career?

  3. Technical accomplishment
     â†’ Specific mechanism they designed, code they wrote
     â†’ Not "contributed to the robot" â€” what EXACTLY did they do?
     â†’ Measurable result: "The arm design they led enabled 95% pickup success"

  4. Community advocacy for FIRST
     â†’ Did they recruit new students?
     â†’ Did they mentor younger students (FLL, FTC)?
     â†’ Did they represent FIRST outside the team (school presentations, media)?
\`\`\`

## Writing the Submission â€” Avoiding Common Mistakes
\`\`\`
Common weak submission:
  "Jane has been on the team for 3 years and has contributed significantly
   to both the mechanical and programming aspects of the robot."

Strong submission:
  "In Year 2, Jane identified that our team had no systematic approach to
   mechanism reliability testing. She designed and implemented a 100-cycle
   durability test protocol that caught 3 critical failures before our first
   event â€” contributing directly to a season with zero in-competition
   mechanism failures."

Rule: every claim needs a specific example.
      "Contributed significantly" is invisible.
      "Designed the test protocol that caught 3 failures" is visible.

Have the student write a first draft â€” then a mentor edits for specificity.
Students undersell themselves; mentors can identify the most compelling stories
that the student takes for granted.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the qualifying event interview matter as much as the written Dean's List submission?",opts:["Written submissions aren't read","The finalist selection happens at the qualifying event â€” local judges select the two finalists who advance; the written submission informs their reading, but the in-person interview and observed behavior at that specific event is the deciding factor, not a national panel","The interview replaces the submission","Interviews are optional"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should students write the first draft of their own Dean's List submission before mentor editing?",opts:["Mentors can't write the submission","Students own their story â€” a mentor-written submission often sounds polished but generic; a student's draft reveals the genuine experiences and growth that mentors can then help articulate more specifically and compellingly","Student drafts are always better","Rules require student authorship"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Advanced.push(
  {id:"awa_multi",title:"Managing Multiple Award Submissions in One Season",est:"16 min",content:`## More Submissions = More Chances â€” But Also More Risk
A team that submits for 6 awards and does them all poorly wins nothing. A team that submits for 3 awards, does each well, and integrates the stories strategically wins more than any of those 6. Knowing which awards to prioritize and how to share work across submissions is the skill.

## Award Selection Matrix
\`\`\`
Before committing to any award, score it on three dimensions:
  1. Fit: how well does your team's work match this award's criteria? (1-5)
  2. Effort: how much work does the submission require? (1=low, 5=high)
  3. Competition: how many strong teams typically compete for this award?

Award           Fit  Effort  Competition  Priority
Impact/Inspire   4     5         high       Yes (if fit â‰¥ 3)
Safety Captain   5     2          low        Yes â€” always try
Dean's List      4     3        medium       Yes if strong candidate
Engineering      3     4         medium      Only if design is distinctive
Excellence       3     3         medium      Good for FTC strong teams
Rookie All-Star  N/A   2          low        Yes if first/second year
\`\`\`

## Sharing Work Across Submissions
\`\`\`
Core content that feeds multiple awards:
  â†’ Team outreach numbers â†’ Impact AND Inspire AND Dean's List
  â†’ Student success stories â†’ Impact, Dean's List, Excellence Award
  â†’ Technical accomplishments â†’ Engineering Inspiration, Dean's List
  â†’ Safety programs â†’ Safety Captain AND Engineering Inspiration

Build one "master story bank" document with:
  â†’ 10-15 specific stories, each 50-100 words
  â†’ Key statistics (students reached, programs started, awards won)
  â†’ Student quotes (with permission)
  â†’ Photos organized by topic

Each award submission draws from the same story bank.
You're not writing new content for each â€” you're selecting and adapting.
\`\`\`

## Award-Specific Differentiation
\`\`\`
The danger of a master story bank: every submission sounds the same.
Each award needs a distinct emphasis:

Impact/Inspire:
  Lead with community multiplication â€” teams started, teachers trained
  Minimize robot accomplishments (judges have already seen your performance)

Engineering Inspiration:
  Lead with design innovation and technical reasoning
  Show the decision-making process, not just the result

Dean's List:
  Focus entirely on ONE student's specific journey
  The team's accomplishments are context, not the story

Safety Captain:
  Focus on documented programs and near-miss culture
  Quantify: training sessions conducted, SOPs written, incidents prevented

Rule: if you can swap the first paragraph of one submission into another
      without noticing, they're too similar.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does submitting for 3 awards carefully often outperform submitting for 6 awards broadly?",opts:["Fewer submissions take less time","Award judges evaluate quality; a well-crafted targeted submission for 3 awards demonstrates genuine alignment with each criteria, while 6 surface-level submissions reveal that the team is collecting attempts rather than making a case â€” quality focus wins","You can only win 3 awards","Rules limit to 3 submissions"],ans:1},
      {q:"What risk does a master story bank create, and how is it mitigated?",opts:["It takes too long to build","If every submission draws from the same stories without differentiation, they sound identical and judges notice â€” the mitigation is emphasizing different angles for each award: multiplication for Impact, individual journey for Dean's List, technical reasoning for Engineering Inspiration","Story banks create copyright issues","The bank must be rebuilt each season"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ WEB (add 5 â†’ ~18) â”€â”€
LESSONS.webdev.Beginner.push(
  {id:"wb_forms",title:"HTML Forms & User Input",est:"13 min",content:`## Forms Are How Users Give You Data
Every scouting input page, every signup form, every settings panel starts with an HTML form. Understanding how forms collect data is foundational to building interactive web tools for your team.

## Basic Form Structure
\`\`\`html
<form id="scoutForm">
  <!-- Text input -->
  <label for="teamNum">Team Number:</label>
  <input type="number" id="teamNum" name="team" min="1" max="99999" required>

  <!-- Dropdown -->
  <label for="climbLevel">Climb Level:</label>
  <select id="climbLevel" name="climb">
    <option value="None">None</option>
    <option value="L1">L1 (3 pts)</option>
    <option value="L2">L2 (6 pts)</option>
    <option value="L3">L3 (10 pts)</option>
    <option value="L4">L4 (15 pts)</option>
  </select>

  <!-- Number with range validation -->
  <label for="cycles">Teleop Cycles:</label>
  <input type="number" id="cycles" name="cycles" min="0" max="30" value="0">

  <!-- Checkboxes -->
  <label>Auto Actions:</label>
  <input type="checkbox" name="autoLeave" value="true"> Left starting zone<br>
  <input type="checkbox" name="autoScore" value="true"> Scored in auto<br>

  <!-- Text area for notes -->
  <label for="notes">Notes:</label>
  <textarea id="notes" name="notes" rows="3" cols="40"></textarea>

  <button type="submit">Submit Match</button>
</form>
\`\`\`

## Handling Form Submission in JavaScript
\`\`\`javascript
document.getElementById('scoutForm').addEventListener('submit', function(e) {
  e.preventDefault(); // stop page reload

  // Read all form values:
  const data = {
    team:      parseInt(document.getElementById('teamNum').value),
    climb:     document.getElementById('climbLevel').value,
    cycles:    parseInt(document.getElementById('cycles').value),
    autoLeave: document.querySelector('[name=autoLeave]').checked,
    autoScore: document.querySelector('[name=autoScore]').checked,
    notes:     document.getElementById('notes').value.trim(),
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
  };

  console.log('Submitting:', data);

  // Store in localStorage for offline use:
  const existing = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('matchData') || '[]');
  existing.push(data);
  localStorage.setItem('matchData', JSON.stringify(existing));

  // Reset form for next match:
  this.reset();
  alert('Match saved!');
});
\`\`\`

## Input Validation
\`\`\`javascript
function validateForm(data) {
  const errors = [];
  if (!data.team || data.team < 1) errors.push("Team number is required");
  if (data.cycles < 0 || data.cycles > 30) errors.push("Cycles must be 0-30");
  return errors;
}

// In submit handler:
const errors = validateForm(data);
if (errors.length > 0) {
  alert(errors.join('\\n'));
  return; // stop submission
}
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does e.preventDefault() do in a form submit event handler?",opts:["It prevents the form from being created","It stops the browser's default behavior of reloading the page on form submit â€” without it, the page refreshes and all JavaScript state is lost before the handler can process the form data","It validates the form fields","It sends the form data automatically"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is localStorage used for form data in an offline scouting tool rather than sending to a server?",opts:["Servers are slow","localStorage stores data in the browser without needing any network connection â€” at a competition venue with poor Wi-Fi, a form that saves to localStorage works reliably even when the network is down","localStorage is faster than all servers","Servers require Python"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wb_css",title:"CSS Layout for Scouting Dashboards",est:"12 min",content:`## Layout Makes Data Readable\nA scouting dashboard with all the right data but poor layout forces users to hunt for what they need under pressure. CSS Flexbox and Grid turn cluttered data into scannable dashboards in 30 lines of code.\n\n## Flexbox â€” One-Dimensional Layout\n\\\`\\\`\\\`css\n/* Make the nav bar a horizontal row: */\n.nav-bar {\n  display: flex;\n  flex-direction: row;      /* default: horizontal */\n  justify-content: space-between; /* spread items to edges */\n  align-items: center;      /* vertically centered */\n  padding: 8px 16px;\n  background: #1a1a2e;\n  color: white;\n}\n\n/* Card row â€” wrap when screen is narrow: */\n.team-cards {\n  display: flex;\n  flex-wrap: wrap;\n  gap: 12px;\n  padding: 16px;\n}\n\n.team-card {\n  flex: 0 0 200px;  /* don"t grow, don"t shrink, 200px base */\n  border: 1px solid #ccc;\n  border-radius: 8px;\n  padding: 12px;\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## CSS Grid â€” Two-Dimensional Layout\n\\\`\\\`\\\`css\n/* Three-column dashboard: sidebar | main | detail panel */\n.dashboard {\n  display: grid;\n  grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr 300px;\n  grid-template-rows: 60px 1fr;  /* header row + content row */\n  height: 100vh;\n  gap: 0;\n}\n\n.header  { grid-column: 1 / -1; }  /* span all columns */\n.sidebar { grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; background: #f4f4f4; }\n.main    { grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; overflow-y: auto; }\n.detail  { grid-column: 3; grid-row: 2; border-left: 1px solid #ddd; }\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Color Coding for Quick Scanning\n\\\`\\\`\\\`css\n/* Team performance tiers â€” scouts can see rank instantly: */\n.score-high   { background: #d4edda; color: #155724; } /* green */\n.score-medium { background: #fff3cd; color: #856404; } /* yellow */\n.score-low    { background: #f8d7da; color: #721c24; } /* red */\n\n/* Apply in JS based on score: */\nfunction scoreClass(avg) {\n  if (avg >= 40) return "score-high";\n  if (avg >= 25) return "score-medium";\n  return "score-low";\n}\n// element.className = \\\`team-card \\" + (scoreClass(team.avg)) + "\\\`;\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the key difference between Flexbox and CSS Grid for layout purposes?",opts:["Grid is newer","Flexbox is one-dimensional â€” it arranges items in a row OR a column; Grid is two-dimensional â€” it arranges items in both rows AND columns simultaneously, making it better suited for full-page dashboard layouts with header, sidebar, and content areas","Flexbox requires less CSS","Grid only works in Chrome"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is color-coding team scores (green/yellow/red) useful specifically during alliance selection?",opts:["Colors are more attractive","Alliance selection happens under time pressure with 30+ teams to evaluate â€” color coding allows scouts to instantly identify tier groups by visual scan rather than reading individual numbers, which takes significantly longer","Colors reduce data entry errors","Color coding is required for web apps"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"wi_charts",title:"Chart.js for Scouting Data Visualization",est:"15 min",content:`## A Chart Communicates in 3 Seconds What a Table Takes 30\nAt alliance selection, your strategy team has 30 seconds per team. A bar chart of average contribution by team is faster to process than a sorted table of numbers. Chart.js adds interactive charts to any HTML page in under 30 lines.\n\n## Basic Bar Chart\n\\\`\\\`\\\`html\n<canvas id="teamChart" width="600" height="300"></canvas>\n<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js"></script>\n<script>\nconst teams = [\"1234\",\"5678\",\"9012\",\"3456\",\"7890\"];\nconst avgScores = [51.2, 48.7, 45.1, 42.3, 38.6];\n\nnew Chart(document.getElementById(\"teamChart\"), {\n  type: \"bar\",\n  data: {\n    labels: teams,\n    datasets: [{\n      label: \"Avg Contribution\",\n      data: avgScores,\n      backgroundColor: avgScores.map(s =>\n        s >= 48 ? \"rgba(40,167,69,0.8)\" :   // green for top\n        s >= 42 ? \"rgba(255,193,7,0.8)\"  :   // yellow for mid\n                  \"rgba(220,53,69,0.8)\"        // red for low\n      ),\n      borderWidth: 1,\n    }]\n  },\n  options: {\n    responsive: true,\n    plugins: { legend: { display: false } },\n    scales: { y: { beginAtZero: true, max: 60 } }\n  }\n});\n</script>\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Stacked Bar Chart â€” Score Breakdown\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\nnew Chart(ctx, {\n  type: \"bar\",\n  data: {\n    labels: teams,\n    datasets: [\n      { label: \"Auto\", data: [12, 10, 8, 6, 4],\n        backgroundColor: \"rgba(54,162,235,0.8)\" },\n      { label: \"Teleop\", data: [24, 26, 28, 24, 24],\n        backgroundColor: \"rgba(255,159,64,0.8)\" },\n      { label: \"Climb\", data: [15.2, 12.7, 9.1, 12.3, 10.6],\n        backgroundColor: \"rgba(40,167,69,0.8)\" },\n    ]\n  },\n  options: {\n    scales: {\n      x: { stacked: true },\n      y: { stacked: true, beginAtZero: true }\n    }\n  }\n});\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Scatter Plot â€” Reliability vs Avg Score\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// X = average score, Y = success rate (0-1)\nconst scatterData = teams.map((t, i) => ({\n  x: avgScores[i],\n  y: successRates[i],\n  label: t\n}));\n\nnew Chart(ctx, {\n  type: \"scatter\",\n  data: { datasets: [{ label: \"Teams\", data: scatterData,\n                       pointRadius: 8, pointHoverRadius: 10 }] },\n  options: {\n    scales: {\n      x: { title: { display: true, text: \"Avg Score\" } },\n      y: { title: { display: true, text: \"Reliability (0-1)\" }, min: 0, max: 1 }\n    },\n    plugins: {\n      tooltip: {\n        callbacks: {\n          label: ctx => \\\`Team \\" + (ctx.raw.label) + ": \\" + (ctx.raw.x) + " pts, \\" + ((ctx.raw.y*100).toFixed(0)) + "% reliable\\\`\n        }\n      }\n    }\n  }\n});\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a bar chart preferable to a sorted table during alliance selection?",opts:["Bar charts are more accurate","Visual pre-attentive processing allows the brain to perceive relative magnitudes in a bar chart in under 1 second, without reading â€” tables require sequential reading of numbers, which takes significantly longer under time pressure with 30+ teams to evaluate","Bar charts use less data","Tables require more code"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does backgroundColor: avgScores.map(s => ...) achieve in the bar chart code?",opts:["It sets one color for all bars","It assigns a different color to each bar based on the score value â€” bars above 48 are green, 42-48 yellow, below 42 red; this color tiers teams visually without requiring the reader to read the exact numbers","It requires a color library","It maps CSS class names"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wi_offline",title:"Making Scouting Apps Work Offline",est:"14 min",content:`## Competition Wi-Fi Is Unreliable â€” Plan for It\nEvery veteran scouting team has a horror story about the venue Wi-Fi dying during alliance selection. A scouting app that can"t function offline is a liability. Making a web app work offline is a solved problem â€” it just requires planning.\n\n## localStorage for Offline Data Storage\n\\"\\"\\"javascript\n// Save a match record offline:\nfunction saveMatch(matchData) {\n  const key = \"matches\";\n  const existing = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(key) || \"[]\");\n  existing.push({ ...matchData, savedAt: Date.now(), synced: false });\n  localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(existing));\n}\n\n// Load all matches:\nfunction loadMatches() {\n  return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(\"matches\") || \"[]\");\n}\n\n// Mark matches as synced after server upload:\nfunction markSynced(indices) {\n  const matches = loadMatches();\n  indices.forEach(i => matches[i].synced = true);\n  localStorage.setItem(\"matches\", JSON.stringify(matches));\n}\n\n// Get only unsynced matches:\nfunction getUnsynced() {\n  return loadMatches().filter(m => !m.synced);\n}\n\\"\\"\\"\n\n## Sync When Connected\n\\"\\"\\"javascript\nasync function syncToServer() {\n  if (!navigator.onLine) {\n    console.log(\"Offline â€” skipping sync\");\n    return;\n  }\n\n  const unsynced = getUnsynced();\n  if (unsynced.length === 0) return;\n\n  try {\n    const res = await fetch(\"/api/sync\", {\n      method: \"POST\",\n      headers: { \"Content-Type\": \"application/json\" },\n      body: JSON.stringify(unsynced)\n    });\n    if (res.ok) {\n      const matches = loadMatches();\n      matches.forEach((m, i) => { if (!m.synced) m.synced = true; });\n      localStorage.setItem(\"matches\", JSON.stringify(matches));\n      console.log(\\"Synced \\" + (unsynced.length) + " matches\\");\n    }\n  } catch (err) {\n    console.log(\\"Sync failed â€” will retry:\\", err.message);\n  }\n}\n\n// Auto-sync when connection returns:\nwindow.addEventListener(\\"online\\", syncToServer);\n// Also sync on page load:\nsyncToServer();\n\\"\\"\\"\n\n## Offline Status Indicator\n\\"\\"\\"html\n<div id=\"statusBar\">\n  <span id=\"onlineStatus\">â—</span>\n  <span id=\"pendingCount\"></span>\n</div>\n<script>\nfunction updateStatus() {\n  const dot = document.getElementById(\\"onlineStatus\\");\n  const count = document.getElementById(\\"pendingCount\\");\n  const unsynced = getUnsynced().length;\n\n  dot.style.color = navigator.onLine ? \\"green\\" : \\"orange\\";\n  dot.title = navigator.onLine ? \\"Connected\\" : \\"Offline\\";\n  count.textContent = unsynced > 0 ? \\"\\" + (unsynced) + " pending\\" : \"\";\n}\n\nwindow.addEventListener(\"online\", updateStatus);\nwindow.addEventListener(\"offline\", updateStatus);\nsetInterval(updateStatus, 5000); // refresh every 5 seconds\nupdateStatus();\n</script>\n\\"\\"\\"`,quiz:[
      {q:"What does the 'synced: false' flag on saved match records enable?",opts:["It prevents editing the record","It allows the app to identify which records haven't been sent to the server yet â€” when connection is restored, only unsynced records need to be uploaded rather than re-sending all data or manually tracking what was sent","Synced records are deleted","It triggers automatic backup"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is window.addEventListener('online', syncToServer) needed in addition to calling syncToServer() on page load?",opts:["Page load sync is unreliable","The page might load while offline â€” the page load sync silently fails; the 'online' event fires whenever the browser detects network connectivity is restored, triggering a sync automatically without the user needing to reload the page","Events are faster than direct calls","syncToServer() only works in event handlers"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€â”€ PACK 13 â€” balance pass (no java) â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€

// â”€â”€ SAFETY +10 (21â†’31) â”€â”€
LESSONS.safety.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sfb_lockout",title:"Lockout / Tagout (LOTO) for Robots",est:"11 min",content:`## LOTO Is the Most Important Safety Procedure You'll Learn
Lockout/Tagout prevents a robot from being energized while someone is working on it. A robot that powers on unexpectedly while a hand is near a mechanism can cause serious injury in under a second.

## The LOTO Sequence
\`\`\`
Before working on any energized robot, in this exact order:

1. Notify: tell everyone in the pit "I'm locking out the robot"
2. Power down: turn off the main breaker (FRC) or power button (FTC)
3. Disconnect: physically unplug the main battery
4. Verify: press the enable button â€” confirm robot does NOT respond
5. Lockout: place a physical lock or tag on the battery connector
   (even a zip tie through the connector prevents accidental reconnection)

6. Work: now it is safe to reach into the robot

After work is done:
7. Clear: announce "hands clear, reconnecting power"
8. Reconnect: reinstall battery
9. Restore: restore main breaker / power
\`\`\`

## Why Disconnecting Isn't Enough Without Verification
\`\`\`
Teams sometimes skip step 4 (verify).
Scenario: battery was disconnected, but a capacitor in a motor controller
held charge. The arm twitches when the enable button is pressed.
Result: person working on the intake is startled â€” or injured.

The verify step costs 3 seconds and catches this.
Never skip it.
\`\`\`

## Tags and Who Uses Them
\`\`\`
A LOTO tag is a physical label that says "DO NOT ENERGIZE"
attached to the battery connector or main breaker.

In a shop: each person working on the robot attaches their own tag.
           The robot cannot be re-energized until ALL tags are removed.
           This prevents one person re-energizing while another is still inside.

Minimum acceptable FRC pit version:
  â†’ Unplug battery
  â†’ Put battery under the pit table (not next to robot)
  â†’ Announce to pit crew: robot is de-energized
  â†’ Never reconnect without announcing first
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is the 'verify' step (pressing enable after disconnecting battery) important in the LOTO sequence?",opts:["It tests the enable button","Capacitors in motor controllers can hold charge after battery disconnection â€” the verify step confirms the robot truly cannot move before anyone reaches inside, catching stored-energy failures that disconnecting alone misses","Verification is required by FIRST","It resets the robot controller"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should each person working on a robot attach their own LOTO tag rather than one shared tag?",opts:["Multiple tags are more visible","If one person re-energizes the robot thinking work is complete but another person is still inside, a single tag system has no protection â€” individual tags mean the robot cannot be powered until every person who attached a tag has removed their own","Tags are cheap","It documents who did the work"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfb_electrical_safety",title:"Electrical Safety Basics for Robot Builders",est:"10 min",content:`## Robot Electrical Systems Can Hurt You
