FRC runs at 12V nominal â€” low enough that most skin contact is not dangerous. But the battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a short circuit, causing burns, fires, and battery explosion. Understanding the hazards prevents accidents.

## The Short Circuit Hazard
\`\`\`
A short circuit occurs when positive and negative conductors touch.
  FRC battery: 12V, 18Ah, can deliver 100-200A into a short
  Energy in 1 second: 12V Ã— 150A = 1,800 watts
  Result: wires melt, insulation ignites, battery vents or explodes

Prevention:
  â†’ Main breaker is always the FIRST thing connected when wiring
  â†’ Never run bare wire ends near any other conductors
  â†’ Tape or cap unused wire ends immediately after cutting
  â†’ Main power runs (battery cables, PDP/PDH output) are fused appropriately
  â†’ Never bridge the main breaker terminals with any conductive object
\`\`\`

## Battery Handling Safety
\`\`\`
FRC batteries are lead-acid (sealed, AGM):
  â†’ Never puncture, crush, or expose to fire
  â†’ Never invert a damaged battery (electrolyte leak)
  â†’ Store upright, in a battery tray, away from metal objects
  â†’ Charge only with a FIRST-legal charger at the correct rate
  â†’ Never charge an unattended battery overnight without a fire-safe bag

FTC batteries (LiFePO4 or NiMH):
  â†’ LiFePO4 is safer than LiPo but still requires care
  â†’ Never use a damaged or swollen pack
  â†’ Use only the matching charger â€” wrong charger = fire risk

Signs a battery needs retirement:
  â†’ Swelling or deformation of the casing
  â†’ Unusual heat during charging (normal = slightly warm, not hot)
  â†’ Internal resistance test shows > 30mÎ© (FRC battery tester)
  â†’ Voltage drops rapidly under load
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a 12V battery pose a fire hazard despite its low voltage?",opts:["12V is actually high voltage","Voltage determines shock risk; current capacity determines fire risk â€” a 12V battery capable of 150A delivers 1,800 watts into a short circuit in one second, which is enough to instantly melt wire insulation and ignite surrounding material","Lead-acid batteries are always dangerous","12V systems are completely safe"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should the main breaker be the first component connected when wiring a robot's electrical system?",opts:["Main breakers are most expensive","The main breaker provides the only means to quickly de-energize the system â€” connecting the battery before the breaker means the system is live with no shutoff point during the entire wiring process, creating maximum short circuit risk at the most vulnerable time","Breakers must be grounded first","FIRST rules require it"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"sfi_inspection2",title:"Technical Inspection â€” Passing First Time",est:"13 min",content:`## Inspection Is Not the Enemy
Robot inspection ensures every robot at a competition is safe and legal. Teams that treat it as a surprise fail more often. Teams that self-inspect against the same checklist inspectors use pass on the first walk-through.

## The Pre-Event Self-Inspection
\`\`\`
Run this the week before your first competition:

Size and weight:
  â–¡ Measure frame perimeter with bumpers on (FRC: use official gauge if possible)
  â–¡ Weigh robot with battery â€” on a calibrated scale, not a bathroom scale
  â–¡ Measure starting height with all mechanisms stowed
  â–¡ Confirm all extension mechanisms retract within starting limits

Electrical:
  â–¡ All wires are secured â€” no loose wires that could contact moving parts
  â–¡ All connectors are fully seated (tug test each one)
  â–¡ Main breaker accessible without tools
  â–¡ No exposed wire between crimp and connector (inspect each terminal)
  â–¡ All motors are legal for this year (check approved list)

Bumpers:
  â–¡ Pool noodles contact frame â€” no gap > 1/4" between noodle and hard structure
  â–¡ Bumper fabric is taut and securely fastened
  â–¡ Bumpers cover the required portion of frame perimeter
  â–¡ Team number is displayed in 4"+ numbers in high-contrast colors
  â–¡ Bumpers sit in the correct height zone above floor

Pneumatics (if used):
  â–¡ System pressure does not exceed 60 PSI working / 120 PSI storage
  â–¡ Relief valve is present and operational
  â–¡ All tubing and fittings are rated for the pressure used
  â–¡ System passes a leak-down test (pressurize, wait 30 seconds, check gauge)
\`\`\`

## Common First-Inspection Failures
\`\`\`
1. Bumper height â€” most common FRC failure
   Check: bumper must sit entirely within 4.5"-7.5" from floor
   Fix: adjust bumper mount height; shim if needed

2. Robot weight â€” often surprises teams who didn't track adds
   Check: weigh without anything students might forget to remove
   Fix: identify heaviest removable items; have a removal plan ready

3. Main breaker access â€” inspector must be able to reach it
   Fix: ensure no wires, panels, or mechanisms block the breaker path

4. Bumper number size â€” 4" minimum, high contrast
   Fix: reprint and reattach numbers day before inspection

After each fix: re-check that item before moving on.
One fix sometimes exposes a second problem.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should teams run a self-inspection against the official checklist before the competition rather than waiting for the inspector?",opts:["Inspectors are unreliable","Official inspectors use the same checklist â€” self-inspection finds the same issues before competition day, giving time to fix them without time pressure, while passing inspection at the event requires no queue wait or emergency repair","Self-inspection replaces official inspection","Inspectors use different criteria"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is bumper height the most common first-inspection failure?",opts:["Bumpers are hard to build","The legal height zone is specific (4.5\"-7.5\" from floor) and bumpers shift after being mounted and bolted; without measuring with the actual bumpers attached in their final configuration, the height is often wrong by 1/4\"-1\" which fails inspection","Bumpers are usually too heavy","Bumper rules change every year"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfi_fire",title:"Fire Prevention & Response in the Robot Shop",est:"12 min",content:`## Robotics Shops Have Real Fire Hazards
Soldering, battery charging, LiPo cells, flammable adhesives, sawdust, and overloaded circuits all create fire risk. A shop that has never had a fire incident almost certainly has prevented fires through good practices â€” not luck.

## The Four Fire Sources in a Robot Shop
\`\`\`
1. Electrical â€” the most common
   â†’ Short circuit in battery or wiring
   â†’ Overloaded extension cord or power strip
   â†’ Motor stall (draws 10Ã— rated current â†’ extreme heat)
   â†’ Prevention: fusing, wire gauge selection, stall detection in code

2. Soldering
   â†’ Iron left powered on and unattended
   â†’ Flux fumes igniting near ignition source
   â†’ Iron contacting flammable materials
   â†’ Prevention: iron holder always in use, turn off when leaving bench,
                 clear workspace of all paper and plastic before soldering

3. Battery charging
   â†’ LiPo cells (if used) failing during charge â†’ thermal runaway
   â†’ Wrong charger for battery chemistry
   â†’ Prevention: charge in LiPo-safe bag, never leave unattended,
                 use correct charger for each battery type

4. Cutting and grinding sparks
   â†’ Sparks from angle grinder travel 10+ feet
   â†’ Sparks ignite sawdust, shavings, cardboard
   â†’ Prevention: clear area of combustibles before grinding,
                 use fire-resistant blanket if sparks are unavoidable
\`\`\`

## Fire Response Protocol
\`\`\`
Small fire (just started, containable):
  1. Alert everyone in the room immediately
  2. Cut power to the area if safe (electrical fires)
  3. Use correct extinguisher type:
     â†’ Class C (electrical): CO2 or dry chemical â€” NEVER water
     â†’ Class A (paper/wood): water or dry chemical
     â†’ LiPo battery: CO2 or dry sand â€” contain the area, don't fight it
  4. If extinguisher fails to knock it down in 10 seconds: evacuate

Larger fire / LiPo thermal runaway:
  1. EVACUATE immediately â€” announce loudly
  2. Close the door (slows fire spread)
  3. Pull fire alarm
  4. Call 911 â€” don't assume someone else did
  5. Never re-enter to retrieve robot or equipment

Fire extinguisher location: every team member should know before Build Day 1.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should water never be used on an electrical fire?",opts:["Water damages the robot","Water conducts electricity â€” using water on a live electrical fire risks electrocution and can spread the fire by connecting the current to additional surfaces; CO2 or dry chemical extinguishers work on electrical fires without this risk","Water causes short circuits","Only CO2 is FIRST-approved"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the appropriate response when a LiPo battery enters thermal runaway in the shop?",opts:["Submerge it in water immediately","Evacuate the area immediately â€” thermal runaway releases flammable gases and can accelerate to fire or explosion within seconds; the priority is people out of the room, not fighting the fire with a small extinguisher","Cover it with a wet cloth","Turn off all lights and wait"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfi_power_tools",title:"Power Tool Safety â€” Drills, Sanders & Rotary Tools",est:"11 min",content:`## The Most Common Workshop Injuries Are from Portable Tools
Angle grinders, rotary tools, and drills cause more workshop injuries than stationary machines â€” because people treat them casually. A drill at 2,000 RPM can catch a sleeve, spin a loose workpiece, or drive a bit through a hand faster than the brain can react.

## Cordless Drill and Drill Press â€” Safety Rules
\`\`\`
Cordless drill (handheld):
  âœ… Secure the workpiece â€” clamp it or hold firmly with both hands
  âœ… Keep the wrist straight â€” rotation force from a bind can sprain or break
  âœ… Reduce speed when the bit is about to break through
  âœ… Remove bit from chuck when not actively drilling
  âŒ Never use a drill as a screwdriver at high speed on soft materials
  âŒ Never reach around a spinning bit to clear chips

Drill press (stationary):
  âœ… Clamp workpiece to the table â€” never hold by hand
  âœ… Set depth stop before drilling to avoid plunge-through
  âœ… Remove chuck key before any power on â€” zero exceptions
  âœ… Lower quill slowly through plastic (it melts and grabs)
  âŒ Never wear gloves near the drill press chuck
  âŒ Never use a twist drill on sheet metal without a center punch and backing
\`\`\`

## Rotary Tool (Dremel) and Angle Grinder
\`\`\`
Rotary tool (Dremel):
  â†’ Use the correct bit for the material â€” wrong bit shatters
  â†’ Cutting discs are fragile: no side pressure, no flexing
  â†’ Face shield over safety glasses â€” discs fragment without warning
  â†’ Max speed for each accessory is on the packaging â€” don't exceed it

Angle grinder:
  â†’ This is the most dangerous portable tool in the shop
  â†’ Always use the side handle â€” two hands, always
  â†’ Guard must be in place â€” it deflects disc fragments toward floor
  â†’ Sparks travel 10+ feet â€” clear the area
  â†’ Never use a cutting disc for grinding or vice versa
  â†’ Disc swap: UNPLUG before changing â€” no exceptions

Both tools: if the disc or bit snags and stalls â†’ LET GO of the workpiece,
            keep hold of the tool. Workpiece spinning is safer than tool spinning.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must a workpiece be clamped to the drill press table rather than held by hand?",opts:["Clamping is faster","A drill bit that catches or breaks through can rotate the workpiece instantly with enough torque to break fingers or cause the workpiece to strike the operator â€” a clamp transfers that force to the table instead of the operator's hands","Clamping improves accuracy","FIRST requires clamped workpieces"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the correct response when a rotary tool cutting disc snags and stalls on the workpiece?",opts:["Release the tool","Keep hold of the tool and let go of the workpiece â€” a free workpiece spinning is far less dangerous than a spinning disc on a free tool; the operator's priority is maintaining control of the powered device","Push through the snag","Increase speed to break through"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sfa_culture",title:"Building a Team Safety Culture",est:"14 min",content:`## Rules Without Culture Don't Work
A team can write 10 safety procedures and have every member ignore them. A team with genuine safety culture has members who correct each other, report near-misses without embarrassment, and who genuinely believe safety improves rather than slows down their work.

## Why Safety Cultures Fail
\`\`\`
The most common failure modes:
  1. Safety as compliance theater
     â†’ PPE worn only when a mentor is watching
     â†’ Near-miss reporting feels like getting in trouble
     â†’ Safety captain's role = "reads rules at the start of the year"
     â†’ Fix: separate safety reporting from punishment

  2. "We've never had an accident" = "we're safe"
     â†’ Past luck is not future protection
     â†’ Near-misses that weren't reported = same hazards still present
     â†’ Fix: track leading indicators (near-misses, close calls)
             not just lagging indicators (injuries)

  3. Speed pressure overrides safety
     â†’ "We need this done tonight" + "the guard takes 2 minutes to install"
     â†’ The guard goes on the floor; nobody says anything
     â†’ Fix: leadership explicitly reinforces that slowing down for safety
             is always the right call â€” faster is not better if it's riskier
\`\`\`

## The Near-Miss Reporting System That Works
\`\`\`
Barriers to reporting:
  â†’ Fear of blame or embarrassment
  â†’ Belief that "it wasn't a real incident so why report it"
  â†’ No easy way to report (no form, no process)

Create a no-blame system:
  â†’ Anonymous reporting option (paper form + drop box is fine)
  â†’ Near-miss reports are celebrated, not investigated for fault
  â†’ At the next meeting: "We had a near-miss this week.
     Here's what happened and here's what we changed."
  â†’ Frame it explicitly: "Reporting a near-miss makes us safer â€”
     the person who reported this helped protect everyone"

Monthly safety review meeting (15 minutes):
  â†’ What near-misses were reported?
  â†’ What was the root cause?
  â†’ What changed?
  â†’ What's the one safety improvement this month?
\`\`\`

## Leading Indicators to Track
\`\`\`
Lagging indicators (things that already went wrong):
  â†’ Injuries, incidents, near-misses (record these but act on leading)

Leading indicators (predict future safety performance):
  â†’ % of sessions that started with a safety check
  â†’ % of PPE compliance (spot-checked, not self-reported)
  â†’ Number of near-misses reported (more = better culture, not worse)
  â†’ % of power tools with working guards in place
  â†’ Number of safety improvements implemented this month

A team with rising near-miss reports is becoming safer â€”
they're reporting things that were always happening but not recorded.
A team with zero near-misses is probably not reporting.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a rising near-miss report count indicate improving safety culture rather than deteriorating safety?",opts:["More near-misses means more accidents","Near-misses that previously went unreported were still occurring â€” a rising count means people now feel safe to report them, which allows root causes to be found and fixed; zero near-miss reports most likely means underreporting, not a genuinely hazard-free environment","Teams should aim for zero reports","Near-miss tracking is not useful"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes separating safety reporting from punishment critical to a functional near-miss reporting system?",opts:["Punishment improves safety","Fear of blame causes people to stay silent after incidents â€” a no-blame reporting system removes the personal risk of disclosure, which means hazards get surfaced and fixed before they cause injury rather than hidden until they repeat","Punishment and reporting are unrelated","Only mentors should report incidents"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfa_risk",title:"Risk Assessment for Mechanism Design",est:"13 min",content:`## Engineering Out the Hazard Before It's Built
The cheapest time to fix a safety problem is during design. A mechanism that traps hands, throws debris, or creates pinch points costs nothing to redesign in CAD â€” and significant time and pain to fix after it's built and someone is hurt.

## The Risk Assessment Process
\`\`\`
For each new mechanism, before building, ask:
  1. What can go wrong? (List every failure mode)
  2. What is the severity if it does? (1=minor, 5=severe injury)
  3. What is the likelihood? (1=rare, 5=frequent during normal use)
  4. Risk score = Severity Ã— Likelihood
  5. For scores â‰¥ 9: must redesign or add a control before building

Example â€” pneumatic claw:
  Failure mode:         Unexpected actuation while hand is inside
  Severity:            5 (finger crush)
  Likelihood:          2 (requires solenoid fault or code bug)
  Risk score:          10 â€” must address

  Controls added:
  â†’ Physical hard stop prevents full closure (can't crush to bone)
  â†’ Manual override requires two simultaneous inputs (prevents single fault)
  â†’ New score after controls: Severity 3 Ã— Likelihood 1 = 3 â€” acceptable
\`\`\`

## Design-Level Hazard Elimination
\`\`\`
In priority order (most effective to least):

1. Eliminate the hazard: redesign so the hazard doesn't exist
   â†’ Spinning intake: can a linear intake work? (no spinning hazard)
   â†’ Sharp edges: specify "break all sharp edges" â€” costs nothing

2. Substitute: use a less hazardous approach
   â†’ High-speed flywheel: use slower, softer wheels with same result
   â†’ Pneumatics: can a servo achieve the same motion? (lower stored energy)

3. Guard: physically prevent contact with the hazard
   â†’ Spinning mechanism: add a guard that blocks hand access
   â†’ Linear slide: add end stops preventing carriage from ejecting

4. Warning: alert people to the hazard (last resort for design)
   â†’ Labels on robot
   â†’ Startup beep before moving

5. PPE (last line of defense, not a design solution)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is the 'eliminate the hazard' approach listed as highest priority over guarding?",opts:["Guards are more expensive","A guard can fail, be removed, or be bypassed â€” an eliminated hazard cannot reoccur; if the mechanism can be redesigned so the dangerous feature doesn't exist, no amount of guard failure can produce the injury","Elimination is easier","Guards require maintenance"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a Risk Score of Severity Ã— Likelihood â‰¥ 9 indicate should happen before building?",opts:["The mechanism should be abandoned","The risk is high enough that it must be redesigned or have controls added â€” the goal is to either reduce severity (redesign so the worst case is less severe) or reduce likelihood (add safeguards) until the score falls below the threshold","Score 9 requires FIRST approval","Only mentors can evaluate score 9"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS +10 (17â†’27) â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Beginner.push(
  {id:"awb_spirit",title:"Spirit Award â€” What It Is and How to Win It",est:"10 min",content:`## Spirit Is the Most Visible Award
You can't perform GP behind closed doors and expect a Spirit Award. The Spirit Award at FRC/FTC events goes to the team that makes the event more fun, welcoming, and alive for everyone â€” and does it genuinely, all day.

## What Spirit Award Judges Look For
\`\`\`
Observable behaviors (judges watch all day):
  â†’ Team cheer: is it original? enthusiastic? inclusive?
  â†’ Pit energy: do they greet visitors? help strangers without being asked?
  â†’ Stands: do they cheer for other teams, not just themselves?
  â†’ Loss response: same energy and warmth after a tough match loss?
  â†’ Match queuing: are they fun and friendly to all three alliance partners?
\`\`\`

## Building Genuine Spirit (Not Performed Spirit)
\`\`\`
Genuine spirit is the team's actual culture visible from the outside.
You can't manufacture it the week before competition.

Build it during the season:
  â†’ Team traditions: a ritual before every match (chant, stack, song)
  â†’ Inside jokes that become outward energy
  â†’ Members who know each other well enough to be genuinely excited together

The performance trap:
  Many teams create a choreographed cheer for competitions â€”
  judges can feel the difference between a team actually having fun
  and a team performing fun. The former wins.

Practical things that help:
  â†’ A team mascot or costume element (consistent, not over the top)
  â†’ A simple, repeatable cheer that even new members can join instantly
  â†’ Cheering by name for opposing alliance members who do something great
  â†’ Random acts of encouragement: write a note to a team that had a rough day
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do judges distinguish between genuine team spirit and a performed cheer?",opts:["Judges have seen all cheers","Genuine enthusiasm emerges from real team culture and shows consistent warmth throughout the entire event â€” a performed routine is typically visible only in scheduled moments and drops when the team thinks nobody is watching; judges observe all day","Cheers must be original","Performed cheers are not allowed"],ans:1},
      {q:"What behavior specifically demonstrates Spirit Award-worthy conduct after a difficult match loss?",opts:["Leaving the field quickly","Maintaining the same warmth and enthusiasm â€” congratulating opponents, supporting alliance partners, and engaging positively with the event despite disappointment; the Spirit Award specifically recognizes teams whose attitude doesn't change based on results","Analyzing what went wrong immediately","Staying in the pits"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awb_volunteer",title:"Volunteering & Giving Back to FIRST",est:"9 min",content:`## The Awards You Win Are Built on Volunteer Work
Every event you attend was organized by hundreds of volunteers â€” field reset crews, referees, judges, pit administrators, AV technicians. Teams that volunteer at events outside their own competition give back to the ecosystem that makes their season possible.

## How to Get Involved as Volunteers
\`\`\`
Student volunteering at events:
  â†’ Field reset crew: physically the most needed role at any event
  â†’ Alliance field crew: assists during matches, field reset between
  â†’ Robot transport: moves robots between pit and field
  â†’ Minimum age: varies by role (most 14+, field reset 16+ at some events)

Mentor/adult volunteering:
  â†’ Referee: requires training and certification (FIRST provides this)
  â†’ Judge: requires application and approval
  â†’ Pit admin: registration and hardware questions
  â†’ Safety advisor: evaluates pit safety and assists teams

How to sign up:
  FRC: firstinspires.org â†’ Volunteer â†’ Event Volunteer Sign-Up
  FTC: same portal, different event types
  Sign up 6+ weeks out â€” popular events fill specific roles quickly
\`\`\`

## How Volunteering Affects Awards
\`\`\`
Directly:
  â†’ Impact and Inspire judges ask about your team's contribution to FIRST
  â†’ Volunteering at non-team events is strong evidence of genuine commitment
  â†’ "Our team provided 8 volunteers for two off-season events this year"
    is a verifiable, concrete Impact claim

Indirectly:
  â†’ Teams that volunteer understand the event structure better
  â†’ Volunteer experience improves your team's behavior at competitions
    (you know what referees are watching because you've been one)
  â†’ Judges who see your members volunteering in other roles form positive impressions
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does volunteering at events outside your own competition specifically strengthen Impact Award submissions?",opts:["Volunteering adds team hours","It demonstrates genuine commitment to FIRST's mission rather than participation for personal benefit â€” helping events where your own team isn't competing shows the team values the community, not just its own competitive outcomes","Volunteer hours count as outreach","Event staff are always Impact judges"],ans:1},
      {q:"What practical insight do team members gain from serving as field reset crew that helps their own performance at competitions?",opts:["They learn field dimensions","Seeing exactly what referees observe, how fouls are triggered, and what field reset involves gives team members operational knowledge that improves driver behavior and reduces unintentional rule violations","Reset crew learns match timing","They get early robot access"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_engineering",title:"Engineering Inspiration Award Strategy",est:"15 min",content:`## Engineering Inspiration Recognizes Design Thinking
Unlike Impact (community reach), Engineering Inspiration focuses on the robot design process â€” how your team approaches engineering challenges, documents decisions, and inspires others through the quality of your technical work.

## What the Engineering Inspiration Award Evaluates
\`\`\`
Judges look for evidence of:
  1. Design process (not just the result)
     â†’ Did you prototype before committing to a design?
     â†’ Can you articulate why you chose this approach over alternatives?
     â†’ Does your engineering notebook show iteration?

  2. Technical excellence
     â†’ Is the robot well-built and does it work reliably?
     â†’ Is your code clean, tested, and documented?
     â†’ Did you solve a genuinely difficult technical problem?

  3. Inspiration of others
     â†’ Have you shared your technical work (open-source code, design files)?
     â†’ Do you mentor other teams on specific technical topics?
     â†’ Did you demonstrate at a non-FIRST technical event?
\`\`\`

## The Engineering Notebook as Evidence
\`\`\`
The notebook is not a journal â€” it's an evidence repository.
Judges use it to verify your verbal claims during the interview.

What must be in the notebook:
  â†’ Decision matrices: "We evaluated 3 intake designs â€” here's why we chose this one"
  â†’ Prototype data: "Roller design A: 6/10 pickups. Roller design B: 9/10. We chose B."
  â†’ Failure analysis: "The gearbox stripped on Day 14. Root cause: insufficient module reduction.
                        Fix: redesigned with 5:1 additional stage."
  â†’ CAD screenshots with dates
  â†’ Photo documentation of build stages

What doesn't belong:
  â†’ "Today we worked on the robot" without specifics
  â†’ Meeting attendance sheets without engineering content
  â†’ Essays about how great FIRST is (save this for Impact)
\`\`\`

## The Interview â€” Showing Design Thinking Live
\`\`\`
Engineering Inspiration judges will ask questions like:
  "Walk me through one design decision you're most proud of"
  â†’ Don't describe the final product â€” describe the DECISION
  â†’ "We had three options. Here's what we measured. Here's why we chose this."

  "What would you do differently next season?"
  â†’ Have a specific, honest answer â€” shows reflective engineering practice
  â†’ "Our arm pivot bearing selection created more backlash than we wanted â€”
     next year we'd use a crossed-roller bearing for that application."

  "How do you verify your code works before deploying to the robot?"
  â†’ Describe your actual testing process (simulation, unit tests, HIL)
  â†’ Judges can tell when teams have genuine processes vs ad hoc approaches
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the key difference between an Engineering Inspiration interview answer about the arm and an Impact interview answer about the arm?",opts:["Engineering answers are longer","Engineering Inspiration focuses on the decision-making process â€” the alternatives considered, the data collected, the reasoning for the choice; Impact focuses on community reach, so the arm is context for how it inspired others, not the centerpiece","Engineering answers mention motors","Impact answers are more emotional"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'Today we worked on the robot' an inadequate engineering notebook entry?",opts:["It's too short","It contains no engineering content â€” judges need to see what was decided, what was tested, what data was collected, and what changed; a record of attendance without engineering reasoning isn't evidence of a design process","Notebook entries must be longer","It doesn't mention team members"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awi_rookie",title:"Rookie Award vs Rookie All-Star â€” Know the Difference",est:"10 min",content:`## Two Awards, Very Different Criteria
FRC has two rookie-specific awards. Submitting for the wrong one â€” or pursuing both with a strategy designed for only one â€” is a common first-year mistake.

## Rookie Inspiration Award
\`\`\`
Criteria: the rookie team that best represents the FIRST experience
Focus: community impact, team culture, inspiration of others
Evidence needed:
  â†’ Outreach programs run during your first season
  â†’ How you engaged your school and community
  â†’ Gracious Professionalism at competition
  â†’ How FIRST changed your members this year

Judging: same process as Impact â€” submission + interview + observed behavior
Best for: teams with strong outreach and community programs
\`\`\`

## Rookie All-Star Award
\`\`\`
Criteria: the rookie team with the most competitive and well-rounded robot
Focus: robot performance, reliability, and completeness
Evidence needed:
  â†’ Ranking in qualification matches
  â†’ Specific match performance highlights
  â†’ Robot design quality (inspectors and judges observe the robot)
  â†’ Design process â€” how did you build a competitive robot in year 1?

Judging: more weight on performance metrics than Rookie Inspiration
Best for: teams whose robot was genuinely competitive in qualifications
\`\`\`

## Pursuing Both
\`\`\`
You can submit for both â€” but your preparation differs:

Rookie Inspiration prep:
  â†’ Same as Impact: outreach numbers, community stories, GP behavior
  â†’ Interview focuses on people and community

Rookie All-Star prep:
  â†’ Have a student ready to walk a judge through robot design decisions
  â†’ Know your match stats (OPR, ranking, best match highlights)
  â†’ Clean, accessible robot in pit â€” judges may want to examine closely

Rookie All-Star winner often advances to Entrepreneurship or engineering
awards at championship. Rookie Inspiration winner often leads to Impact-type
recognition at championship. Know which path fits your team's strengths.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Which rookie award is most appropriate for a team that built a competitive robot but ran few outreach events in their first year?",opts:["Rookie Inspiration","Rookie All-Star â€” it specifically evaluates robot performance, reliability, and design process; Rookie Inspiration emphasizes community impact and outreach which this team didn't develop in year 1","Both awards equally","Neither award fits"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the primary distinguishing factor between Rookie Inspiration and Rookie All-Star judging?",opts:["Rookie Inspiration requires more documentation","Rookie Inspiration emphasizes community impact, outreach, and culture (same criteria family as Impact Award); Rookie All-Star emphasizes robot performance, competitive results, and technical design process â€” the two recognize different dimensions of a successful rookie season","All-Star requires a presentation","Inspiration is judged by different people"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Advanced.push(
  {id:"awa_champs",title:"Championship Award Preparation",est:"15 min",content:`## Championship Is a Different Competition
At a regional or district event, you compete against 30-50 teams for awards. At Championship, you compete against 600+ teams â€” and the award finalists all qualified by winning at the event level. Your regional-winning submission needs to be significantly stronger.

## What Changes at Championship
\`\`\`
The bar rises in four ways:
  1. Competition depth: every team there has already won something
  2. Judge expertise: championship judges are often multi-year veterans
  3. Presentation length: some awards have longer interview slots
  4. Essay scrutiny: judges have more time to cross-reference your claims

What stays the same:
  â†’ The award criteria don't change
  â†’ GP behavior still matters all day
  â†’ Observed behavior during the event still counts
  â†’ A great story still beats a long list of accomplishments
\`\`\`

## Elevating Your Submission
\`\`\`
Regional submission â†’ Championship submission upgrades:

"We reached 500 students through outreach events"
â†’ "We reached 847 students in 14 events across 6 school districts,
    verified by attendance sheets from each event coordinator.
    3 of those schools have since started their own programs."

"We built a competitive robot"
â†’ "Our intake redesign in Week 5 improved pickup reliability from 68%
    to 94% across 50 measured trials. This directly enabled our climb
    to the 6th seed at the regional."

"We help other teams"
â†’ "We provided technical assistance to 4 teams at our regional â€”
    Team 9876's battery issue we diagnosed in 12 minutes;
    they won the event. We don't consider them competitors."

The pattern: quantify + verify + be specific enough that it's checkable.
\`\`\`

## Championship Interview Strategy
\`\`\`
At championship, assume judges have read your essay thoroughly.
Don't repeat what's in the essay â€” deepen it.

If the essay says: "We mentored 3 FLL teams"
The interview should add: which teams, what specifically you taught,
what outcomes they achieved, and what the experience taught YOUR students.

Practice questions your judges will ask:
  "How is what you're doing unique among the 600 teams here?"
  â†’ Have a genuine, specific answer â€” not "we care more"

  "Which program had the most impact and why?"
  â†’ Pick one, go deep â€” don't list everything again

  "What's the next evolution of your program?"
  â†’ Shows thinking beyond the current season
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a championship interview presentation not repeat what's in the submitted essay?",opts:["Repetition wastes time","Championship judges have read the essay â€” repeating it wastes the limited interview time on information they already have; the interview should go deeper, add context, and answer the questions the essay raises, demonstrating that the team's knowledge goes beyond what fit in the word limit","Essays are not read at championship","Interview and essay have different audiences"],ans:1},
      {q:"What pattern transforms a regional-level outreach claim into a championship-level one?",opts:["Making it longer","Adding quantification + verification + enough specificity that the claim is checkable â€” a claim that names specific schools, has verified attendance numbers, and describes measurable outcomes gives judges confidence that the work was real","Using more impressive words","Including photos"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ FUNDRAISING +8 (17â†’25) â”€â”€
LESSONS.fundraising.Beginner.push(
  {id:"fb_crowdfund",title:"Crowdfunding for FIRST Teams",est:"11 min",content:`## Crowdfunding Works When There's a Story
A generic GoFundMe for "our robotics team" raises almost nothing. A campaign tied to a specific, emotionally resonant goal with a clear deadline and visible progress raises meaningful amounts â€” because donors understand exactly what their contribution enables.

## The Campaign Formula
\`\`\`
Story headline (one sentence):
  "Team 1234 earned a spot at the FIRST World Championship â€”
   help us get there."

The need (specific and bounded):
  "We need $3,400 by April 14th to cover travel and hotel for 12 students.
   Without this, we can't attend the event we qualified for."

What makes it real:
  "This will be the first World Championship appearance in our team's
   12-year history. Seven of our 12 members are first-generation college students."

How they can help:
  $25 = one meal for one student
  $100 = one night of hotel for one person
  $400 = one student's full travel cost
  â†’ Tiered giving with specific items makes any amount feel meaningful

Progress bar + deadline:
  â†’ Visible progress drives contributions (nobody wants to fund a failing campaign)
  â†’ A deadline creates urgency ("4 days left!")
\`\`\`

## Platforms
\`\`\`
GoFundMe: simplest, no nonprofit needed, takes 2.9% + $0.30/transaction
Patronicity: STEM-focused, some have matching programs
Experiment.com: science and education projects (requires pitch review)
Donor Drive: designed for nonprofit fundraising
Your team website: requires payment processor setup but 0% platform fee

For amounts < $5,000: GoFundMe is fastest to launch
For amounts > $5,000 or recurring: use your fiscal sponsor's platform
\`\`\`

## Promoting the Campaign
\`\`\`
Day 1 push is critical â€” campaigns that reach 30% in the first 48 hours
have much higher total completion rates.

Step 1: Every team member shares to personal social media simultaneously
Step 2: School shares to parent email list (get permission first)
Step 3: Mentor network shares to professional contacts
Step 4: Local press â€” "local students qualified for World Championship"
        is newsworthy; one article can drive 50+ contributions

Never: buy followers or fake engagement â€” platforms flag and remove campaigns
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do campaigns that reach 30% funding in the first 48 hours have higher completion rates?",opts:["30% unlocks platform features","Early momentum signals to potential donors that others believe in the cause â€” a campaign visibly progressing creates social proof and urgency; stalled campaigns at 5% make donors hesitant to be one of the few contributors to a failing effort","Platforms promote fast-starting campaigns","The deadline is shorter"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why do tiered giving amounts with specific items ($25 = one meal, $100 = one night hotel) increase donation rates?",opts:["Tiers are required by platforms","Specific amounts give donors a concrete mental image of their contribution's impact â€” 'fund one student's meal' is more emotionally satisfying than '$25 toward travel costs'; the specificity converts hesitation into action","Tiered giving reduces platform fees","It prevents large donations"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fb_merchandise",title:"Team Merchandise as Fundraising",est:"9 min",content:`## Merch Can Fund Equipment â€” If Margins Are Managed
A team hoodie that costs $28 to produce and sells for $30 raises $2 per unit. The same hoodie sold for $45 raises $17. Merch is viable fundraising only when margins are planned deliberately â€” not as an afterthought.

## What Sells and What Doesn't
\`\`\`
High demand (sell reliably at competition and to families):
  â†’ Team hoodie / crewneck (most popular â€” people wear them)
  â†’ T-shirts with current season design
  â†’ Stickers (low cost, easy to give as thank-yous)
  â†’ Phone stands / accessories with team branding

Low demand (requires extra marketing):
  â†’ Keychains, pins â€” low perceived value unless distinctive
  â†’ Coffee mugs â€” heavy to ship, low margin
  â†’ "Generic" designs with just team number â€” buy for the story, not the item

Seasonal timing:
  â†’ Kickoff: sell early-season merch (people excited about new season)
  â†’ First competition: parents and family want something to wear
  â†’ Championship: limited-edition championship merch sells at premium
\`\`\`

## Production Options
\`\`\`
Print-on-demand (no inventory risk):
  â†’ Printful, Printify, Bonfire â€” upload design, sell, they ship
  â†’ Margin: $10-15 per shirt after production + platform fee
  â†’ Best for: teams without upfront capital or storage space

Bulk order (higher margin, requires capital):
  â†’ Local screen printer: 50+ shirts at $8-12 each, sell at $25-30
  â†’ Margin: $13-18 per unit â†’ higher, but you hold inventory risk
  â†’ Best for: teams with an established buyer base (enough members + families)

Hybrid:
  â†’ Bulk 50 hoodies for members at cost (builds team identity)
  â†’ Print-on-demand for public/family sales (no inventory risk)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the fundamental margin calculation that determines whether merchandise is viable as fundraising?",opts:["Gross sales divided by team size","Selling price minus production cost per unit â€” a $30 item costing $28 to produce raises $2 and is not viable; the same item at $45 raises $17; planning the margin before ordering is the difference between fundraising and breaking even","Production cost only","The number of units sold"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is print-on-demand recommended for teams without an established buyer base?",opts:["Print-on-demand has better quality","It eliminates inventory risk â€” the team never pays for items that don't sell; with bulk orders, buying 100 hoodies and selling 40 means paying for 60 items that generate no revenue","Print-on-demand is always cheaper","Bulk orders are illegal for school teams"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fb_sponsorship3",title:"Creating a Sponsor Packet",est:"12 min",content:`## The Sponsor Packet Is Your Leave-Behind
When you ask a company for sponsorship, they'll ask "do you have anything in writing?" A great sponsor packet answers every question they'll ask, removes friction from saying yes, and presents your team professionally.

## What Goes in the Packet
\`\`\`
Page 1: Who You Are (half page)
  â†’ Team name, number, location, founding year
  â†’ Current member count, school affiliation
  â†’ One compelling stat: "We've started 4 FLL teams in the past 3 years"
  â†’ One sentence on your mission

Page 2: What Sponsors Get (the most important page)
  Tiered benefits table:
  Level     | Amount  | Logo on robot | Logo on shirts | Social posts | Event invite
  Bronze    | $500    |               | âœ“              | 2/year       |
  Silver    | $1,500  | âœ“             | âœ“              | 4/year       |
  Gold      | $3,000  | âœ“ prominent   | âœ“ prominent    | 8/year       | âœ“
  Platinum  | $5,000+ | âœ“ title       | âœ“ title        | 12/year      | âœ“ VIP

Page 3: Our Impact
  â†’ Season results (events attended, awards)
  â†’ Outreach reach (students, events, programs)
  â†’ One student success story (named, with permission)

Page 4: How to Give
  â†’ Check payable to: [legal entity name]
  â†’ Online: [donation link]
  â†’ Contact: [mentor name, email, phone]
  â†’ Tax deductibility: [EIN or fiscal sponsor info]
\`\`\`

## Design Standards
\`\`\`
Non-negotiables:
  â†’ Professional design (Canva free tier is sufficient)
  â†’ Team colors and logo consistent throughout
  â†’ No spelling or grammar errors (have 3 people proofread)
  â†’ PDF format for email, print-ready for in-person meetings

Length: 4 pages maximum. A company executive has 3 minutes.
        Longer is not more persuasive â€” it's more likely to be unread.

Include an editable section for the specific company:
  "Prepared for: [Company Name]" on page 1
  Shows it's not a mass mailing; took effort to customize.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is Page 2 (What Sponsors Get) described as the most important page in the packet?",opts:["It's the prettiest page","Sponsors need to know what their investment returns â€” a clear tiered benefits table lets them immediately evaluate which level makes sense for their budget and what visibility they receive; without this, every conversation requires manual negotiation","Page 2 contains legal terms","Companies read in order"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should the sponsor packet be 4 pages maximum?",opts:["Printing costs money","A company executive evaluating a sponsorship request has limited time â€” a longer packet is less likely to be read fully; 4 focused pages that answer every key question are more persuasive than 12 pages of context that dilutes the core ask","FIRST has packet length rules","4 pages is easier to email"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"fi_tax",title:"Tax Basics for FIRST Team Finances",est:"11 min",content:`## Financial Compliance Protects the Team and Its Supporters
Teams that accept money without proper documentation put their donors, school, and mentors at legal risk. Understanding the basics of 501(c)(3) status, fiscal sponsorship, and required records keeps everything above board.

## 501(c)(3) â€” What It Means
\`\`\`
501(c)(3) is an IRS designation for tax-exempt nonprofit organizations.
Benefits:
  â†’ Donations are tax-deductible for the donor
  â†’ Organization doesn't pay federal income tax on received donations
  â†’ Eligible for many foundation grants (required by many grant applications)

Requirements to maintain it:
  â†’ Annual tax return (Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-N depending on revenue)
  â†’ No private benefit to individuals (team members can't personally profit)
  â†’ No political campaign activity
  â†’ Records of all donations and expenses kept for 7 years

Most teams don't have their own 501(c)(3) â€” they use one of these instead:
  â†’ School-administered funds (school's nonprofit status)
  â†’ Fiscal sponsorship through FIRST or a local organization
\`\`\`

## Required Records (Keep These)
\`\`\`
For every donation received:
  â†’ Amount, date, donor name and address
  â†’ Acknowledgment letter sent to donor (required for donations â‰¥ $250)
  â†’ Description of what was given (for in-kind)

Acknowledgment letter must include:
  â†’ Organization name and EIN (tax ID)
  â†’ Date and amount of donation
  â†’ Statement: "No goods or services were provided in exchange for this contribution"
    (if true â€” if you gave them sponsor benefits, you must note the fair market value)

For every expense:
  â†’ Receipt
  â†’ Who authorized the expense
  â†’ What it was for and how it relates to the team's mission

Storage: at minimum 7 years. Digital backups in Google Drive are acceptable.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must acknowledgment letters be sent for donations of $250 or more?",opts:["It's good practice","IRS regulations require donors to have written acknowledgment from the organization to claim a deduction of $250 or more on their tax return â€” without the letter, the donor cannot legally deduct the donation, which may affect their willingness to give","FIRST requires acknowledgment letters","Letters allow the team to keep records"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the statement 'No goods or services were provided in exchange for this contribution' accomplish on an acknowledgment letter?",opts:["It thanks the donor","It confirms the donation is fully deductible â€” if the team provides sponsor benefits (logo placement, event access) in exchange for the donation, the fair market value of those benefits must be subtracted from the deductible amount; the statement certifies this isn't the case","It's required by the post office","It establishes the donation date"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fi_annual_plan",title:"Building an Annual Fundraising Plan",est:"12 min",content:`## Random Fundraising Raises Random Money
Teams that run whatever fundraiser someone suggests raise inconsistently. Teams with an annual plan know their goal, their sources, their timeline, and how they'll fill gaps if a source underperforms.

## The Annual Fundraising Plan Template
\`\`\`
Total budget need: $18,000 (example)
Reserve target:    $2,000 (maintain for equipment failures / unexpected travel)
Total to raise:    $20,000

Source            Target    Timeline      Owner        Status
Returning sponsors $8,000   Sept-Nov      Lead mentor  In progress
New sponsors       $3,000   Oct-Jan       Student lead Outreach started
Grants             $2,500   Sept (apps)   Mentor       2 apps submitted
Restaurant nights  $600     3Ã— in season  Parent org   Scheduled
Team merchandise   $800     Nov + March   Social lead  Design pending
Crowdfunding       $3,000   If needed     Full team    Contingency plan
Alumni fund        $1,100   June appeal   Captain      Prior year raised $900

Total planned:    $19,000
Gap to close:     $1,000   â†’ second crowdfunding round if sponsor goal misses
\`\`\`

## Monthly Fundraising Calendar
\`\`\`
September:  Renew top 3 sponsors from prior year (highest priority)
October:    Submit all grant applications (deadlines cluster here)
November:   Launch merchandise pre-order + pitch new sponsors
December:   Year-end giving appeal to all prior donors (tax deadline drives Dec)
January:    Kickoff announcement to sponsors (build season starts = excitement)
February:   Restaurant night #1
March:      Championship crowdfunding if needed (specific goal)
April:      Competition thank-you notes to all sponsors
June:       Alumni fund annual appeal
August:     Review what worked, what didn't â†’ update plan for next year
\`\`\`

## When a Source Underperforms
\`\`\`
If a sponsor doesn't renew and you lose $2,000 in planned income:
  1. Don't panic for 2 weeks â€” pursue the replacement plan
  2. Activate the first contingency source (usually crowdfunding)
  3. If gap remains at 6 weeks before the event: reduce costs first,
     not raise more â€” travel is often the most cuttable category
  4. Tell the team the situation honestly: "We're $1,500 short â€”
     here's what we're doing about it and what it might mean"
     (surprises at competition are worse than early honest planning)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does December specifically represent an opportunity for a year-end donation appeal?",opts:["December has the most events","Tax-deductible donations must be made by December 31st for that tax year â€” donors who want a deduction have a natural deadline-driven motivation to give before year end, making December appeals more effective than other months","Donors are in a holiday mood","Grant applications are due in December"],ans:1},
      {q:"What should a team do immediately when a planned funding source underperforms?",opts:["Cut the robotics program","Activate the contingency plan for that source â€” not by panicking, but by systematically pursuing the replacement option prepared in advance; having a contingency pre-identified means the team responds in days rather than weeks","Cancel competition travel","Ask mentors for personal contributions"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ GIT +8 (16â†’24) â”€â”€
LESSONS.git.Beginner.push(
  {id:"gb_ignore",title:".gitignore â€” What Not to Track",est:"9 min",content:`## Not Every File Belongs in Version Control
Build artifacts, IDE settings, credential files, and compiled outputs change constantly and belong to one machine. Tracking them creates noise in your git history, merge conflicts, and security risks.

## FRC Robot Code .gitignore
\`\`\`gitignore
# .gitignore for FRC WPILib Gradle project

# Build outputs:
build/
.gradle/
out/

# IDE files (VS Code, IntelliJ, Eclipse):
.vscode/
.idea/
*.iml
.classpath
.project
.settings/

# macOS system files:
.DS_Store

# Windows system files:
Thumbs.db

# Deployment artifacts (regenerated by WPILib):
*.halsim

# Never commit credentials:
*.env
secrets.properties
\`\`\`

## FTC Robot Code .gitignore
\`\`\`gitignore
# Android build outputs:
.gradle/
build/
local.properties          # machine-specific Android SDK path
*.apk
*.aab

# IDE:
.idea/
*.iml

# System:
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db

# Key files â€” NEVER commit:
keystore.properties
release.keystore
\`\`\`

## Python Scouting Repo .gitignore
\`\`\`gitignore
# Python:
__pycache__/
*.py[cod]
*.egg-info/
.eggs/
dist/
build/

# Virtual environment:
venv/
.venv/
env/

# Credentials and secrets â€” NEVER commit:
.env
secrets.py
config_local.py

# Data files (often too large for git, contain private info):
data/
*.csv
*.sqlite
*.db

# IDE:
.vscode/
.idea/
\`\`\`

## Adding a File That's Already Being Tracked
\`\`\`bash
# If you forgot to ignore something before first commit:
echo "secrets.py" >> .gitignore
git rm --cached secrets.py   # remove from tracking without deleting the file
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Stop tracking secrets.py, add to .gitignore"

# IMPORTANT: if secrets were already pushed, rotate/regenerate them.
# Deleting from history is possible but complex â€” prevent rather than fix.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should .env and secrets files always be in .gitignore regardless of whether the repository is private?",opts:["Private repos are safe","Private repos can be made public accidentally, forked, or have access revoked â€” credentials committed to git history are extremely difficult to fully remove and remain a security risk indefinitely; never committing them is the only reliable protection","Secrets don't work in git","FIRST prohibits credential files"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'git rm --cached secrets.py' do without deleting the file from disk?",opts:["It hides the file from git","It removes the file from git's index (staging area) so it is no longer tracked â€” the file remains on disk; combined with adding it to .gitignore, git will no longer track changes to it in future commits","It permanently deletes the file","It marks the file as read-only"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"gb_commit_msg",title:"Writing Useful Commit Messages",est:"9 min",content:`## Your Future Self Reads Commit Messages
"fixed stuff" and "wip" tell you nothing six weeks later at 2am trying to find when a bug was introduced. A useful commit message explains what changed AND why, in one line you can scan in 'git log'.

## The Commit Message Format
\`\`\`
type(scope): short summary (â‰¤ 72 chars)

Optional longer body explaining WHY (not what â€” the diff shows what):
The arm encoder was occasionally returning stale data on the second
loop after restart. Root cause: bulk cache wasn't being cleared before
the first read. This was masking a 50ms position error on startup.

Optional footer:
Fixes #47
\`\`\`

## Types for FIRST Robot Repos
\`\`\`
feat:  new capability added
fix:   bug fix
tune:  constants adjustment (PID gains, speeds, etc.)
refac: restructuring without behavior change
docs:  comments or documentation only
test:  adding or fixing tests
chore: build, CI, dependency updates

Examples:
  feat(intake): add beam break sensor for piece detection
  fix(auto): correct heading offset after crossing field center
  tune(arm): increase kP from 0.007 to 0.009, reduce oscillation
  refac(drive): extract velocity calculation to DriveHelper class
  docs(elevator): document tuning procedure in class header
\`\`\`

## What Not to Write
\`\`\`
âŒ "fixed"     â€” fixed what? for whom? how?
âŒ "update"    â€” every commit updates something
âŒ "wip"       â€” never commit unfinished work to main
âŒ "asdfasdf"  â€” common at 11pm but completely unhelpful
âŒ "per code review" â€” what changed? the message should say

Reading git log --oneline with good messages:
  feat(vision): add AprilTag 7 targeting for shooter auto-aim
  fix(auto): robot drives into wall when encoder resets mid-match
  tune(drive): reduce slew rate for smoother low-speed control
  fix(intake): beam break fires false positive near field lights

vs bad messages:
  update
  fix
  changes
  fixed the thing
  more stuff
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a commit message body explain WHY rather than WHAT the code changed?",opts:["The why is more important","The 'what' is already visible in the diff â€” a reviewer can see exactly which lines changed; the 'why' is not visible anywhere else, and without it, future readers can't distinguish an intentional design decision from an apparent bug and may accidentally revert it","Bodies must always explain both","The what is harder to write"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'tune(arm): increase kP from 0.007 to 0.009' communicate that 'update constants' does not?",opts:["It's shorter","The specific change (which constant, from what value, to what value) plus the scope (arm subsystem) â€” a reader can immediately understand what happened and why without opening the file; 'update constants' tells you nothing actionable","tune is a standard type","It references the subsystem"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_cherry",title:"Cherry-Pick â€” Applying Specific Commits",est:"10 min",content:`## Sometimes You Need One Commit, Not the Whole Branch
Cherry-pick applies a single commit from any branch to your current branch. For FIRST teams, the most common use: a bug fix was developed on a feature branch that isn't ready to merge, but the fix is needed on main right now.

## Basic Cherry-Pick
\`\`\`bash
# Scenario: you fixed a motor direction bug on feature/elevator branch
# but feature/elevator isn't ready to merge to main yet.
# You need the bug fix on main for tomorrow's practice.

# 1. Find the commit hash on the feature branch:
git log feature/elevator --oneline
# a3f92b1 fix(drive): reverse left motor direction â€” was inverted
# 7c44d02 feat(elevator): add position control loop (WIP)
# ...

# 2. Switch to main:
git switch main

# 3. Cherry-pick just the bug fix commit:
git cherry-pick a3f92b1

# 4. Push:
git push origin main

# Result: the bug fix is now on main.
# The WIP elevator code is still only on feature/elevator.
\`\`\`

## Cherry-Pick Conflicts
\`\`\`bash
# If the same code was edited differently on both branches:
git cherry-pick a3f92b1
# error: CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in DriveSubsystem.java

# Resolve the conflict (same as merge conflict):
# Edit the file, remove conflict markers, choose the right code.

git add DriveSubsystem.java
git cherry-pick --continue   # complete the cherry-pick
# or:
git cherry-pick --abort      # undo and go back to before
\`\`\`

## When NOT to Cherry-Pick
\`\`\`
Cherry-pick creates a copy of the commit â€” the same change exists in two branches
with different commit hashes. When feature/elevator later merges to main,
git may see the "same" change applied twice â†’ potential conflict.

Alternatives:
  â†’ If the fix is small and needed everywhere: fix on main first,
    then merge main into the feature branch
  â†’ If feature/elevator is almost ready: rush it to review and merge everything
  â†’ Cherry-pick is best for: critical bug fixes, isolated changes,
    emergency patches to a release branch
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What problem does cherry-pick solve that a full branch merge cannot?",opts:["Cherry-pick is faster","Cherry-pick applies a single specific commit without bringing all other commits from the source branch â€” useful when a branch contains a needed fix alongside unfinished work that shouldn't merge yet","Cherry-pick resolves conflicts automatically","Merging always requires review"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why can cherry-pick create issues when the source branch is eventually merged?",opts:["It corrupts the commit graph","Cherry-pick creates a copy of the commit with a different hash â€” when the original branch merges, git may see what appears to be the same change applied twice, potentially causing conflicts in the files that were cherry-picked","Cherry-picks expire","The original commit is deleted"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"gi_tag",title:"Tags â€” Marking Competition Releases",est:"9 min",content:`## A Tag Is a Named Snapshot in History
When you deploy robot code to a competition, you want to know exactly which code ran â€” even months later when debugging. Git tags give a permanent, human-readable name to the exact commit deployed at any event.

## Creating Tags
\`\`\`bash
# Annotated tag (recommended â€” includes message, author, date):
git tag -a competition-2025-02-22 -m "Week 3 Regional, Ventura CA"
git push origin competition-2025-02-22

# Lightweight tag (just a pointer, no metadata):
git tag v2.3-auto-redesign
git push origin v2.3-auto-redesign

# Tag naming conventions for FIRST teams:
competition-YYYY-MM-DD     # matches competition date
v[major].[minor]-[feature] # semantic versioning style
district-week2-2025        # descriptive event name
\`\`\`

## Viewing and Using Tags
\`\`\`bash
# List all tags:
git tag

# Show tag info + the commit it points to:
git show competition-2025-02-22

# Check out the code at a tag (detached HEAD â€” read-only view):
git checkout competition-2025-02-22
# to return to normal:
git switch main

# Compare current code to competition code:
git diff competition-2025-02-22 main -- src/main/java/frc/robot/
\`\`\`

## Tag-Based Debugging Workflow
\`\`\`bash
# At a competition, robot drives fine. One week later, something broke.
# When did it break? Binary search with tags:

git checkout competition-2025-02-22   # works fine
git checkout main                      # broken

# Find the commit that broke it:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                         # current main is broken
git bisect good competition-2025-02-22 # this commit is known good
# git bisect checks out middle commits
# you test, mark git bisect good or git bisect bad
# git bisect finds the exact breaking commit in logâ‚‚(n) steps
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should an annotated tag (git tag -a) be used instead of a lightweight tag for competition releases?",opts:["Annotated tags are faster","An annotated tag stores a message, the tagger's name, email, and the date â€” making it a proper record of when and why the tag was created; a lightweight tag is just a pointer with no metadata, providing less context months later when debugging","Annotated tags use less space","Lightweight tags can be deleted"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'git bisect' do and why are competition tags useful for starting a bisect search?",opts:["Bisect splits the repository","Bisect performs a binary search through commit history to find which commit introduced a bug â€” competition tags mark a known-good state, giving bisect a reliable starting point that eliminates all commits before that tag from consideration","Bisect compares two branches","Tags are required for bisect"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ga_monorepo2",title:"Monorepo Workflow for Multi-Subteam Code",est:"12 min",content:`## One Repo, Multiple Concerns â€” Managing the Complexity
A FIRST monorepo containing robot code, scouting app, dashboard, and documentation is powerful but creates coordination challenges. Paths, CI jobs, and branch policies all need to account for the repo's multi-project structure.

## Directory Structure
\`\`\`
team-1234/
  robot/          # FRC/FTC robot code (Gradle/Android)
  scouting/       # Python scouting app
  dashboard/      # Web dashboard (HTML/JS)
  docs/           # Markdown documentation
  tools/          # Shared utilities and scripts
  .github/
    workflows/
      robot.yml       # CI only for robot/ changes
      scouting.yml    # CI only for scouting/ changes
      dashboard.yml   # CI only for dashboard/ changes
\`\`\`

## Path-Filtered CI (Only Run What Changed)
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/robot.yml
name: Robot Build

on:
  push:
    paths:
      - 'robot/**'       # only trigger on robot/ changes
      - '.github/workflows/robot.yml'

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build robot code
        working-directory: robot
        run: ./gradlew build
\`\`\`
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/scouting.yml
on:
  push:
    paths: ['scouting/**', '.github/workflows/scouting.yml']
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: scouting
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.11' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python -m unittest discover -v
\`\`\`

## Codeowner Rules for Review Requirements
\`\`\`
# .github/CODEOWNERS
# Lines: [path pattern] [GitHub username(s) who must approve PRs]

robot/          @team1234-prog-lead
scouting/       @team1234-scout-lead
dashboard/      @team1234-scout-lead
docs/           @team1234-captain
\`\`\`

## Branch Naming for Monorepos
\`\`\`
Include the subproject prefix so it's clear where the work lives:
  robot/feature/vision-targeting
  scouting/fix/csv-encoding-bug
  dashboard/feat/pick-list-chart
  docs/update/build-season-recap
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does path-filtered CI (paths: ['robot/**']) accomplish in a monorepo?",opts:["It limits repository size","It prevents robot CI from running when only the scouting app changes â€” without path filtering, every push to any file would trigger all CI jobs, wasting build minutes and making the CI history noisy for reviewers","It restricts who can edit robot files","Path filtering is required for Gradle"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a CODEOWNERS file specify?",opts:["Who can clone the repository","Which GitHub users must approve pull requests for specific paths â€” changes to robot/ require the programming lead's review; changes to docs/ require the captain's review; this enforces domain expertise in code review without a global policy","File ownership for billing purposes","It sets read permissions"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT +8 (16â†’24) â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Beginner.push(
  {id:"tmb_roles",title:"Defining Subteam Roles Before Build Season",est:"11 min",content:`## Undefined Roles Create Chaos at the Worst Time
Build season is Week 1: 15 students stand around a whiteboard. Nobody knows who's making decisions. Everyone has opinions. Nothing gets done. Teams that define roles before Day 1 spend that whiteboard time building.

## The Minimum Role Set
\`\`\`
Every team needs these roles filled before kickoff:

Student roles:
  Captain:            final decision authority on strategy and cross-team conflicts
  Mechanical Lead:    owns design decisions, build planning, part orders
  Programming Lead:   owns code architecture, autonomous, control loops
  Electrical Lead:    owns wiring, sensor placement, power budget
  Drive Team:         driver + operator + human player (competition roles)

Mentor roles:
  Lead Mentor:        accountability, safety, major purchases
  Technical Mentors:  subject-matter support (not decision-making)

Optional but helpful:
  Scout Lead:         owns scouting system and alliance strategy
  Safety Captain:     owns safety procedures, inspection prep
  Awards Lead:        owns essay submissions and judge preparation
\`\`\`

## The RACI Matrix â€” Who Owns What
\`\`\`
RACI: Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed

Decision                | Captain | Mech Lead | Prog Lead | Lead Mentor
Mechanism approach      |    C    |     A/R   |    C      |     I
Motor selection         |    I    |     A     |    R      |     C
Code architecture       |    I    |     C     |    A/R    |     I
Major purchase > $200   |    C    |     C     |    C      |     A
Competition strategy    |    A    |     C     |    C      |     I
Team conflict resolution|    A/R  |     C     |    C      |     C

A = Accountable (one person only â€” the decision owner)
R = Responsible (does the work)
C = Consulted (input before decision)
I = Informed (notified after decision)
\`\`\`

## Role Handoff When Someone's Out
\`\`\`
Plan before it's needed:
  â†’ Each lead designates a backup: "If I can't make it, [name] runs the session"
  â†’ Backup has read-access to all the lead's ongoing work
  â†’ No single-person knowledge bottlenecks: "only Jamie knows how to order parts"
    is a crisis waiting to happen

Competition day roles are most critical:
  â†’ Driver backup: tested at least 3 drive practices
  â†’ Operator backup: same
  â†’ Head of queuing: someone who knows the match schedule process
    cold, even if they've never done it under real pressure
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"In a RACI matrix, why can only one person be 'Accountable' for a decision?",opts:["It's an organizational rule","Multiple accountable parties means no one is clearly responsible for the outcome â€” when a decision goes wrong, shared accountability creates blame diffusion and finger-pointing; one accountable owner ensures the decision is made and owned by a specific person","RACI requires single ownership","Accountability requires a vote"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should backup roles be designated and practiced before competition, not assigned during the competition?",opts:["Practice is required by FIRST","Someone filling a role for the first time under competition pressure will perform worse than the primary â€” backup roles practiced at drive team sessions or test events are semi-reliable; someone stepping in cold during a match queue is not","Backups are cheaper","Competition day roles are easier"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmb_communication",title:"Team Communication Systems",est:"10 min",content:`## Information That Isn't Shared Is Useless
A mentor who knows the competition schedule, a student who knows what parts were ordered, and a lead who knows what's broken are all holding information other people need. A communication system ensures information flows without depending on memory.

## The Communication Stack
\`\`\`
Real-time (fast, ephemeral): Slack, Discord, or GroupMe
  â†’ Match updates during competition
  â†’ Quick questions ("which port is the arm motor?")
  â†’ Announcements to the full team
  â†’ Rule: check this at least once per build session

Async coordination: Google Drive + Docs
  â†’ Meeting notes (searchable, permanent)
  â†’ Part order lists (who needs what)
  â†’ Schedule and event logistics
  â†’ Rule: if it needs to persist, it goes in Drive

External communication: Email
  â†’ Sponsors, school admin, event coordinators
  â†’ Never use Discord/Slack for external contacts
  â†’ Rule: mentors should CC on all external emails from students

Do NOT have: information that exists only in someone's head,
             competing "official" channels (two Slacks, two Drives),
             group texts used for anything that needs to be searchable
\`\`\`

## The Weekly Update
\`\`\`
Once per week during build season: one page summary to the whole team.
  â†’ What each subteam accomplished this week
  â†’ What each subteam is working on next week
  â†’ Decisions made (and who made them)
  â†’ Blockers that need full-team attention
  â†’ Upcoming dates (competitions, ordering deadlines, meetings)

Format: Google Doc posted in Slack + emailed to mentor list
Length: 1 page maximum
Responsibility: rotates through subteam leads weekly

Teams that send weekly updates have fewer "I didn't know that" moments
and fewer repeated conversations about already-made decisions.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should external contacts (sponsors, school admin) always be communicated with by email rather than Discord or Slack?",opts:["Discord is not secure","External contacts don't have access to your team's internal platforms and expect professional, searchable communication â€” email creates a formal record, is universally accessible, and signals professionalism; an ad-hoc Discord DM to a sponsor looks casual and can easily be missed","Email is required by FIRST","Discord requires accounts"],ans:1},
      {q:"What problem does a weekly written update solve that verbal updates in meetings cannot?",opts:["Written updates are faster","Verbal updates are forgotten, misremembered, or missed by anyone absent â€” a written update is searchable, persistent, and consistent for everyone on the team; it eliminates 'I didn't know that was decided' conversations that repeat work","Meetings don't allow updates","Written updates satisfy sponsors"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmb_calendar",title:"Season Planning with a Gantt-Style Calendar",est:"11 min",content:`## The Season Has a Shape â€” Know It Before It Starts
FIRST seasons run roughly 6-8 weeks from kickoff to first competition. Teams that visualize the full timeline in Week 1 make better decisions about when to cut scope, when parts must be ordered, and when autonomous needs to be done.

## The Season Milestone Calendar
\`\`\`
Week 1 (Kickoff):
  â†’ Game analysis complete by Day 3
  â†’ Robot concept selected by Day 5
  â†’ Prototype goals assigned for Week 2

Week 2:
  â†’ Prototypes running by midweek
  â†’ Design decisions locked by Friday
  â†’ CAD started for primary mechanisms

Week 3:
  â†’ First parts ordered (long lead items: motors, extrusions, electronics)
  â†’ Frame design in CAD, ready for cutting

Week 4:
  â†’ Frame complete and assembled
  â†’ Primary mechanisms on robot for first time
  â†’ Basic teleop driving possible

Week 5:
  â†’ All mechanisms on robot
  â†’ Autonomous first prototype working
  â†’ Bumpers ordered / built

Week 6:
  â†’ Robot at competition weight
  â†’ Drive practice begins (minimum: 2 hours before first event)
  â†’ Autonomous reliable on multiple starting positions

First competition weekend

Post-competition:
  â†’ Day 1: fix everything that broke
  â†’ Day 2-3: tune based on competition data
  â†’ Day 4-5: add features missed in initial build
\`\`\`

## Using a Shared Calendar
\`\`\`
Google Calendar for the team:
  â†’ Share with all members + parents + mentors
  â†’ Color-code: build sessions, competitions, outreach, deadlines
  â†’ Add calendar invites for everything â€” don't rely on Slack reminders

Critical deadlines that must be on the calendar Day 1:
  â†’ Part ordering deadline (week before first comp)
  â†’ Bumper completion deadline (2 days before first comp)
  â†’ Robot weigh-in date (if your team does pre-comp check)
  â†’ First drive practice session
  â†’ Outreach events committed during build season

Rule: if it's not on the calendar, it probably won't happen.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should long-lead-time parts (motors, extrusions) be ordered in Week 3 rather than Week 5?",opts:["Week 3 prices are better","Parts can take 5-10 business days to arrive and suppliers sometimes backorder items â€” ordering in Week 3 means parts arrive by Week 4 when construction begins; ordering in Week 5 risks waiting for parts during the critical final build push","Week 3 has the most budget","Orders in Week 5 don't ship"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the minimum drive practice time recommended before a team's first competition, and why?",opts:["None â€” competition is the practice","At least 2 hours of actual driving practice â€” drivers need time with the physical robot on a simulated field to build reflexes, learn the robot's feel, and develop match strategies; first competition with no drive practice dramatically increases driver errors and missed cycles","10 hours minimum","Practice time doesn't affect performance"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Advanced.push(
  {id:"tma_mentor",title:"Working Effectively With Mentors",est:"13 min",content:`## Mentors Are Partners, Not Parents
A great mentor relationship is a collaboration. Mentors bring experience and resources. Students bring fresh eyes, energy, and ownership. Teams where mentors design the robot and students assemble it aren't learning. Teams where students design and mentors support are building engineers.

## What Good Mentorship Looks Like
\`\`\`
Good mentor behaviors:
  â†’ Asks "what have you tried?" before giving the answer
  â†’ Provides resources and connections students can't access alone
  â†’ Reviews decisions but doesn't override them without explanation
  â†’ Sets up failure in a safe environment: "let's test that assumption"
  â†’ Takes on administrative work so students can focus on technical work

Not-good mentor behaviors:
  â†’ Solving the problem while the student watches
  â†’ Making design decisions without student input
  â†’ Overriding student decisions because "I know better"
  â†’ Being unavailable at critical moments (inspection week, competition morning)
  â†’ Undermining student authority in front of other team members
\`\`\`

## When You Disagree With a Mentor
\`\`\`
The right way:
  1. Understand their position first: "Can you help me understand why you think X?"
  2. Present your reasoning with evidence: "We tested option B 20 times and..."
  3. Ask for their criteria: "What would change your mind?"
  4. Accept the final decision, even if you disagree:
     "I understand â€” I'll implement it your way.
      Can we revisit after we see how it performs?"

The wrong way:
  â†’ Going around the mentor to another adult
  â†’ Agreeing in the meeting and implementing your own way anyway
  â†’ Making the disagreement public or involving the rest of the team

When to escalate:
  â†’ Safety disagreement: always escalate immediately
  â†’ Ethical issue: escalate through the appropriate channel
  â†’ Persistent technical disagreement: request a structured decision review
\`\`\`

## Getting More From Your Mentors
\`\`\`
Mentors give more when they're engaged effectively:
  â†’ Brief them before sessions: "Today we're working on X, I'd love your input on Y"
  â†’ Ask specific questions: "What failure mode would you worry about here?"
     not "Is this design good?"
  â†’ Respect their time: mentors volunteer; they can't attend every session
  â†’ Follow up: "The change you suggested last week â€” it worked. Here's the data."
  â†’ Involve them in wins, not just problems
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a mentor solving a problem while the student watches fail to develop the student?",opts:["It's faster for the mentor","Watching someone else solve a problem doesn't build the neural pathways that doing it yourself creates â€” the student may understand the solution intellectually but won't be able to apply the reasoning independently next time a similar problem arises","Students can't solve problems","Mentors always know the best answer"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the appropriate way to handle a persistent technical disagreement with a mentor?",opts:["Override the mentor's decision","Request a structured decision review where both positions are documented, criteria for the decision are made explicit, and both parties evaluate the options against those criteria â€” this is more productive than repeated arguing and models the decision-making engineers use professionally","Accept the mentor's position always","Involve other students as tiebreakers"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ CAD +8 (16â†’24) â”€â”€
LESSONS.cad.Beginner.push(
  {id:"cadb_measurements",title:"Taking Physical Measurements for CAD",est:"10 min",content:`## Your CAD Is Only as Good as Your Measurements
A bracket designed around a 48mm bore that's actually 47.5mm either jams or rattles. Precise measurement before CAD prevents expensive reprints and remachining. The right tools used correctly take 2 minutes; using them wrong takes hours to discover.

## Tools and Their Uses
\`\`\`
Ruler (steel, 12"):
  â†’ Overall dimensions, reference measurements
  â†’ Accuracy: Â±0.5mm
  â†’ Use for: rough sketches, layout, checking a part is approximately right

Calipers (digital or vernier):
  â†’ Precision: Â±0.02mm (digital), Â±0.05mm (vernier)
  â†’ Three measurement types:
    Outside jaws (top):   measure outer diameter or width
    Inside jaws (bottom): measure inner diameter or slot width
    Depth rod (back tip): measure hole depth or step height
  â†’ Always close gently â€” forcing the jaws distorts them
  â†’ Zero before each use: close fully, press zero button

Tape measure:
  â†’ Long distances (field elements, robot travel)
  â†’ Accuracy: Â±1mm over 1m when pulled taut
  â†’ Never use for anything going into a CAD drawing â€” use calipers

Angle gauge / digital protractor:
  â†’ Measure existing angles on mechanisms or field elements
  â†’ Useful for: intake approach angles, arm pivot alignment
\`\`\`

## Measuring For CAD â€” Best Practices
\`\`\`
Before starting any CAD from a physical part:
  1. Measure 3Ã— for each critical dimension â€” record all three
     If they differ by > 0.1mm: re-measure. If consistent: use that value.
  2. Sketch the part on paper first with all dimensions labeled
  3. Identify the datum (reference corner / edge) â€” this is X=0, Y=0
  4. All other dimensions referenced from the datum
  5. Note material and thickness on your sketch
