When measuring a hole position:
  Wrong: measure hole-to-hole (errors accumulate)
  Right: measure hole-to-datum edge for every hole
         â†’ If datum is the left edge: left edge â†’ hole 1 = 12mm,
           left edge â†’ hole 2 = 36mm, etc.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should all hole positions be measured from the datum edge rather than from hole to hole?",opts:["It's faster","Hole-to-hole measurements accumulate error â€” if hole 1 is 0.2mm off, hole 2 measured from hole 1 adds another 0.2mm, hole 3 adds another, and by hole 5 the position error is 1mm; measuring each hole from the same datum edge keeps error independent","Datum measurements are more precise","Hole-to-hole measurements aren't possible with calipers"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the depth rod on digital calipers measure that the outer jaws cannot?",opts:["Large diameters","The depth of a hole, slot, or step below a reference surface â€” the depth rod extends from the end of the caliper body into the feature, measuring how deep it is; outer jaws can only measure the width of features that can be spanned from outside","Curved surfaces","Small diameters"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cadb_onshape_basics",title:"Onshape Fundamentals â€” First Part",est:"13 min",content:`## Your First Part Studio Part
Onshape's Part Studio is where you create 3D parts from 2D sketches. Every part follows the same flow: create a sketch â†’ constrain it â†’ extrude or revolve â†’ add features. This workflow becomes muscle memory within your first 10 parts.

## The Three-Step Part Flow
\`\`\`
Step 1: Sketch (2D)
  â†’ Select a face or plane to sketch on
  â†’ Draw the profile using: Rectangle, Circle, Line, Arc tools
  â†’ Add constraints and dimensions until the sketch turns black
    (black = fully constrained â€” no degrees of freedom remain)
  â†’ Blue = under-constrained (something can still move)
    Red = over-constrained (conflicting constraints â€” resolve these)

Step 2: Feature (3D from 2D)
  â†’ Extrude: push the sketch profile into 3D along a direction
     Enter depth as a number (12 mm, 0.5 in)
  â†’ Revolve: spin the sketch profile around an axis
     Enter angle (360Â° for full cylinder)

Step 3: Additional features on the 3D solid
  â†’ Fillet: rounds a sharp edge (select edge, enter radius)
  â†’ Chamfer: bevels a sharp edge (select edge, enter distance)
  â†’ Hole: parametric holes with thread options
  â†’ Shell: hollows a solid (select faces to remove)
\`\`\`

## Sketch Constraints
\`\`\`
Constraints are geometric relationships between sketch elements:
  Horizontal/Vertical: forces a line to be exactly horizontal or vertical
  Coincident:          forces two points to be at the same location
  Tangent:             forces a line to meet a curve smoothly
  Parallel:            forces two lines to be exactly parallel
  Perpendicular:       forces two lines to be exactly 90Â°
  Equal:               forces two lengths or radii to be identical
  Symmetric:           forces elements to mirror about a centerline

Why constraints matter:
  A circle without constraints can be anywhere at any size.
  Add: Coincident to origin (locks position) + diameter dimension (locks size).
  Result: fully constrained â€” moving won't change it.

Shortcut: fully constrain using only dimensions if geometry is simple.
          Use geometric constraints for relationships that must always hold
          regardless of dimension changes.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does a sketch element turning black in Onshape indicate?",opts:["The element has an error","The element is fully constrained â€” all degrees of freedom are removed by constraints and dimensions; nothing can move or resize unintentionally, which is the goal before extruding","Black means it's been exported","The element is selected"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why use a 'Perpendicular' geometric constraint rather than just dimensioning two lines to 90 degrees apart?",opts:["Dimensions can't be 90 degrees","A geometric constraint maintains the relationship regardless of other dimension changes â€” if you make the part narrower, the perpendicular constraint keeps the sides exactly 90Â°; a dimension of '90Â°' might conflict or require manual updates as the design changes","Perpendicular constraints are automatic","Dimensions are less precise"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"cadi_standard_content",title:"Onshape Standard Content & MKCAD Library",est:"12 min",content:`## Don't Model What Already Exists
REV extrusion, GoBILDA channel, AndyMark sprockets, standard fasteners â€” modeling these from scratch wastes hours and introduces dimensional errors. MKCAD and Onshape's standard content library provide accurate, manufacturer-provided models ready to drop in.

## MKCAD â€” The FIRST Robotics Parts Library
\`\`\`
MKCAD is a free Onshape library of common FTC and FRC parts:
  â†’ REV Robotics: extrusion, motors, hubs, sensors
  â†’ GoBILDA: channel, motors, servos, linear slides
  â†’ AndyMark: drivetrain components, wheels, gears
  â†’ WCP: swerve modules, gearboxes, belts

Adding MKCAD to your account:
  1. onshape.com â†’ sign in
  2. Search "MKCAD" in Public Documents
  3. Open the MKCAD document
  4. Click "Copy to My Documents" (or just use the public link each time)

Using in your assembly:
  Insert â†’ Browse Documents â†’ MKCAD â†’ find part â†’ Insert
  Mate it into position like any other part
\`\`\`

## Standard Content for Fasteners
\`\`\`
Onshape has a built-in library of standard screws, bolts, and nuts.
Use it instead of modeling fasteners yourself.

In Assembly:
  Insert â†’ Standard Content â†’ search "M4 socket head cap screw"
  Enter length (M4 Ã— 12mm)
  Place at each mounting hole

Advantages:
  â†’ Correct dimensions and thread representation
  â†’ Collision checking works (see if bolt head clears the mechanism)
  â†’ BOM auto-populates with correct part numbers
  â†’ Looks professional in assembly drawings

Fastener sizing for FIRST robots:
  FTC: M4 Ã— [8-30mm] for most mechanism mounts
       M3 Ã— [6-12mm] for sensor brackets and light-duty parts
  FRC: 1/4-20 Ã— [1/2"-2"] for mechanism mounts
       10-32 Ã— [3/8"-1.5"] for electronics and light structure
\`\`\`

## Building Your Team Parts Library
\`\`\`
After a season, you've modeled parts specific to your robot.
Make them reusable:
  1. Create a "Team Library" Onshape document
  2. Move or copy custom parts there (motor mounts, brackets, etc.)
  3. Share with all team members (Edit access for leads, View for all)
  4. Next season: insert from Team Library instead of re-modeling

Track which revision each part is on (use description field):
  "Arm Pivot Bracket Rev B â€” wider flange, 4 bolt holes instead of 2"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is using MKCAD library parts preferable to modeling GoBILDA or REV parts from scratch?",opts:["MKCAD parts are prettier","Library parts are dimensionally verified by manufacturers or experienced users â€” self-modeled parts often have subtle errors (wrong hole spacing, incorrect bore diameter) that only manifest during physical assembly; library parts also insert in seconds vs hours","Library parts are required by FIRST","Self-modeled parts won't export correctly"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific benefit does inserting standard content fasteners provide beyond appearance?",opts:["Standard fasteners are cheaper","The assembly's collision detection checks whether bolt heads clear surrounding parts, the BOM auto-populates with correct part numbers and quantities, and the fastener thread representation allows checking whether tapped holes are accessible â€” none of which works with a placeholder cylinder","Standard content is faster to insert","Fasteners require standard content for strength calculations"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ OUTREACH +8 (16â†’24) â”€â”€
LESSONS.outreach.Beginner.push(
  {id:"orb_photography",title:"Documenting Outreach for Awards",est:"9 min",content:`## Photos and Numbers Are Your Evidence
"We reached 500 students" without any documentation is a claim. The same statement with attendance sheets and photos is evidence. Award judges verify â€” and teams that document well win more than teams with better programs but worse records.

## What to Capture at Every Outreach Event
\`\`\`
Photos (take these systematically, not just when you remember):
  â†’ Students actively interacting with the robot or activity (not posed)
  â†’ Wide shot showing the number of people in the space
  â†’ Any signage or banners showing event name and date
  â†’ Your team members working alongside students (shows engagement)
  â†’ Before/after shots: setup vs packed room

Numbers (record same day, not from memory weeks later):
  â†’ Headcount of students reached (actual count, not "about 30")
  â†’ Grade levels or age range
  â†’ School name or organization
  â†’ Date and duration
  â†’ Team members present (for volunteer hour tracking)

Quotes (if the teacher or organizer says something great):
  â†’ Ask: "Can I quote you on that?" â†’ write it down immediately
  â†’ Quotes with attribution are compelling in award submissions
\`\`\`

## The Post-Event Log Entry
\`\`\`
Within 24 hours of each event, one team member enters:

Date:             2025-03-08
Event:            Lincoln Elementary Career Day
Location:         Lincoln Elementary, Ventura CA
Team members:     5 (names or just count)
Students reached: 87 (actual count from sign-in sheet)
Grade levels:     3rd-5th
Duration:         3 hours
Activity:         Robot demo + drive-it-yourself station
Outcome notes:    3 teachers asked for return visit next year
                  One student's parent is an engineer at Northrop â€” gave contact
Photos:           Uploaded to Drive/Outreach/2025/Lincoln-Elementary/
Follow-up needed: Email thank-you to Ms. Garcia

This entry takes 5 minutes and is irreplaceable at award time.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should outreach event headcounts be recorded the same day rather than from memory later?",opts:["Memory always improves with time","Memory consistently underestimates or misremembers specific numbers â€” the actual count of 87 students becomes 'about 80' or 'maybe 100' a week later; award judges ask for specific, verifiable numbers, and 'about 80' is less credible than the actual 87 from a signed attendance sheet","Same-day entries are required","It satisfies FIRST record requirements"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a wide shot showing the number of people in the room provide that a close-up photo of students cannot?",opts:["Better image quality","Visual evidence of scale â€” a judge reading '87 students reached' and seeing a wide photo of 87 students in a packed room has visual confirmation of the claim; a close-up of three engaged students doesn't validate the 87","Wide shots are required","Close-ups violate privacy rules"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"orb_press",title:"Getting Local Press Coverage",est:"11 min",content:`## A Newspaper Story Reaches More People Than 10 Events
A single article in a local paper or community news site can put your team in front of 50,000 readers who'd never see your robot at a school visit. Local press coverage is also compelling evidence in Impact Award submissions.

## What Makes a FIRST Story Newsworthy
\`\`\`
Local press covers stories that are:
  â†’ New or unusual: "Local students build robot that qualified for Worlds"
  â†’ Human: "15-year-old's first year on robotics team led to [outcome]"
  â†’ Relatable: "Students learning code and engineering at [local school]"
  â†’ Timely: kickoff week, before first competition, after a major award

What doesn't work:
  â†’ "Our robotics team had another great season" â€” not a story
  â†’ Anything requiring significant background knowledge to understand
  â†’ Stories without a specific human being at the center

Your pitch in 3 sentences:
  "A team of 25 students from [School] in [City] just qualified for the
   FIRST Robotics Championship in Houston â€” one of 600 teams from 60 countries.
   Would you be interested in covering their story? I'm [name], and I can connect
   you with our student captain and arrange access to see the robot."
\`\`\`

## Who to Contact and How
\`\`\`
Priority order:
  1. Local newspaper reporter who covers school/education beat
  2. Local TV news station community interest segment
  3. School district communications office (they often syndicate stories)
  4. Community news sites / NextDoor neighborhood blogs

Finding the right contact:
  â†’ Look for bylines on recent school district or youth stories
  â†’ Email the reporter directly (not the general tip line)
  â†’ One paragraph pitch + your contact info + one compelling detail

Best timing:
  â†’ 2 weeks before first competition: "Here's what they've built,
    here's where they're competing"
  â†’ Day after winning an award: "[Local students] won [award] at Worlds"
  â†’ Kickoff: "Students have 6 weeks to build a robot from scratch"

Follow up if no reply after 5 business days â€” once only.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a local newspaper story reach more potential FIRST supporters than running 10 school outreach events?",opts:["Newspapers are more credible","A newspaper article reaches the entire readership at once â€” a local paper with 50,000 readers exposes the team to that audience in a single publication; 10 school events reaching 100 students each reaches 1,000 people over weeks of effort","Stories require no budget","Events are less effective with older audiences"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should press pitches be sent directly to a specific reporter rather than to the general tip line?",opts:["General tip lines are slow","A specific reporter who covers education or community stories is more likely to find FIRST relevant to their beat â€” a personal email shows you've researched who might care; general tip lines are high-volume and most pitches are ignored","Reporters require direct contact","The tip line blocks FIRST stories"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_mentoring",title:"Mentoring Younger FIRST Teams",est:"13 min",content:`## Teaching Others Is the Highest-Leverage Outreach
Starting or mentoring an FLL or FTC team multiplies your team's impact by 10-15 students per team â€” who then go on to be FIRST alumni themselves. It also generates the most compelling Impact Award evidence.

## What "Mentoring a Younger Team" Actually Means
\`\`\`
Not effective:
  â†’ Showing up once and demonstrating your robot
  â†’ "We're available if they have questions"
  â†’ Giving them spare parts without teaching them to use them

Effective:
  â†’ Regular (at least monthly) structured sessions with a specific agenda
  â†’ Teaching a skill they'll apply to their robot that same week
  â†’ Following up to see how it went and adjusting the next session
  â†’ Being consistent â€” the best mentor teams have a specific person
    assigned to each mentored team who attends every session

What younger teams need most by season stage:
  Sept-Oct: brainstorming and game analysis (how to think about the game)
  Nov-Dec:  design process (how to choose between options systematically)
  Jan-Feb:  build quality and testing methodology
  March:    competition preparation and award submissions
\`\`\`

## Running a Technical Mentoring Session
\`\`\`
Template for a 90-minute session:
  0:00 - 0:10: Standup â€” what did they try since last session?
                         what's working? what's stuck?
  0:10 - 0:50: Main topic (one topic per session â€” don't try to cover everything)
    Example: "Today we're talking about how to tune intake compression"
    â†’ Explain concept (5 min)
    â†’ Show on their robot (10 min)
    â†’ Them try with your guidance (25 min)
  0:50 - 1:15: Work time â€” they work on their actual problem, you assist
  1:15 - 1:30: Debrief â€” what did they learn? what do they do before next session?

One concept per session, practiced on their actual robot:
more effective than five concepts in a lecture.
\`\`\`

## Documenting the Mentoring Relationship for Awards
\`\`\`
Keep a log for each team you mentor:
  Team name/number:  FLL Team "Robotic Rangers"
  School:            Jefferson Elementary
  Session dates:     Oct 5, Nov 2, Nov 30, Jan 11, Feb 8
  Topics covered:    Brainstorm, design matrix, build quality, competition prep
  Student count:     12
  Outcomes:          Placed 2nd at state qualifier; team running independently

This log + photos is your evidence for:
  â†’ Impact Award: "We mentored 2 FLL teams across 10 sessions this season"
  â†’ Sustainability: "Both teams are now running with local coaches we trained"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a 'we're available if they have questions' mentoring model ineffective for younger FIRST teams?",opts:["Younger teams don't have questions","Beginning teams don't know what they don't know â€” they lack the experience to identify the gaps in their own understanding and formulate questions; proactive structured sessions with a specific topic bring knowledge to them rather than waiting for them to seek it","Availability isn't enough time","Questions take too long to answer"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the pedagogical reason for limiting each mentoring session to one main concept?",opts:["Sessions are too short for more","One concept practiced on their actual robot builds genuine skill â€” multiple concepts in one session create cognitive overload and surface-level understanding of all of them; a student who truly understands intake compression after one session can apply it next season","One concept is a rules requirement","Multiple concepts confuse younger students"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ori_impact_programs",title:"Programs That Count as High-Impact Outreach",est:"14 min",content:`## Not All Outreach Is Equal in Judges' Eyes
Bringing a robot to a festival and 300 kids walk by is outreach. Starting an FLL team at a Title I school that runs for three years is impact. Judges evaluating Impact and Inspire awards explicitly weight programs that create lasting change over one-time events.

## The Impact Hierarchy
\`\`\`
Highest impact (what judges remember and vote for):
  â†’ Starting new FIRST teams: multiplies your reach by years Ã— team members
  â†’ Training teachers to run robotics independently
  â†’ Programs that run without you after the first year

High impact:
  â†’ Regular school partnerships (monthly, full year)
  â†’ Mentoring an existing FIRST team through a full season
  â†’ STEM camps with curriculum (not just robot show-and-tell)

Moderate impact:
  â†’ School visits with structured curriculum
  â†’ Community events where students actively participate in activities

Lower impact:
  â†’ Passive demonstrations (robot runs, people watch)
  â†’ One-time events with no follow-up
  â†’ Social media posts (awareness, not change)
\`\`\`

## Starting an FLL Team â€” The Highest-Leverage Action
\`\`\`
FLL (FIRST LEGO League) for grades 4-8:
  â†’ 10-student teams, season runs September-January
  â†’ Local qualifier in November/December
  â†’ Your team's involvement: initial recruitment, coach training,
    and ongoing technical mentoring through the season

What it takes to start one:
  1. Find a school or community organization willing to host
  2. Identify a teacher or parent willing to be the registered coach
  3. Train them: 3-4 sessions on FLL rules, robot building, mission strategy
  4. Help with first robot building session
  5. Be available for questions through the season (2-3 more visits)

What you get:
  â†’ 10 students who experience FIRST directly
  â†’ A program that continues each year without you
  â†’ The most compelling Impact evidence you can create
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does starting a new FLL team rank higher in impact than running 10 one-time events?",opts:["FLL events are larger","A started FLL team runs every year with new students â€” the impact compounds over time as the same program reaches new cohorts; one-time events have no continuity and their reach ends the day the event does","FLL counts for more points","One-time events are harder to plan"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'training a teacher to run robotics independently' categorized as highest-impact outreach?",opts:["Teachers have more authority","A teacher who can run robotics independently without your team's continued involvement becomes a self-sustaining force multiplier â€” every year they run the program, they reach new students without requiring your team's time","Teachers are required for outreach","Training is faster than visiting"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ WEB +8 (17â†’25) â”€â”€
LESSONS.webdev.Beginner.push(
  {id:"wb_js_basics",title:"JavaScript Fundamentals for Scouting Tools",est:"12 min",content:`## JavaScript Makes Web Pages Interactive\nHTML structures the page. CSS styles it. JavaScript makes it respond to the user â€” updating the display when data changes, fetching new information, validating form input. Every interactive scouting tool runs on JavaScript.\n\n## Variables, Arrays, and Objects\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Variables:\nlet teamNumber = 1234;          // can change later\nconst eventKey = "2025casd";   // cannot change (constant)\n\n// Array â€” ordered list:\nconst picks = [1234, 5678, 9012, 3456];\npicks.push(7890);               // add to end\npicks[0];                       // 1234 (first element)\npicks.length;                   // 5\n\n// Object â€” named properties:\nconst team = {\n  number:   1234,\n  name:     "Team Example",\n  avgScore: 51.2,\n  wins:     6,\n  losses:   2\n};\nteam.avgScore;    // 51.2\nteam["name"];     // "Team Example" (bracket notation)\nteam.losses = 3;  // update a property\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Functions and Array Methods\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Function:\nfunction computeContribution(auto, cycles, climbPts) {\n  return auto + (cycles * 4) + climbPts;\n}\ncomputeContribution(12, 6, 6); // 42\n\n// Arrow function (shorter):\nconst contrib = (auto, cycles, climbPts) => auto + cycles * 4 + climbPts;\n\n// Array methods â€” the most useful three:\nconst teams = [\n  { number: 1234, avg: 51.2 },\n  { number: 5678, avg: 38.6 },\n  { number: 9012, avg: 45.1 }\n];\n\n// filter: keep only teams where avg > 40\nconst strong = teams.filter(t => t.avg > 40);\n// strong = [{1234, 51.2}, {9012, 45.1}]\n\n// map: transform each element\nconst numbers = teams.map(t => t.number);\n// numbers = [1234, 5678, 9012]\n\n// sort: sort by avg descending\nconst ranked = [...teams].sort((a, b) => b.avg - a.avg);\n// ranked = [{1234, 51.2}, {9012, 45.1}, {5678, 38.6}]\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Updating the Page\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Get an element, change its content:\ndocument.getElementById("topTeam").textContent = "Team " + teams[0].number;\n\n// Create elements dynamically:\nconst list = document.getElementById("pickList");\nranked.forEach((team, index) => {\n  const li = document.createElement("li");\n  li.textContent = \\\`#\\" + (index+1) + ": Team \\" + (team.number) + " (\\" + (team.avg) + " avg)\\\`;\n  list.appendChild(li);\n});\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the difference between 'let' and 'const' variable declarations in JavaScript?",opts:["let is faster","let declares a variable that can be reassigned later; const declares a variable that cannot be reassigned â€” const is preferred for values that should never change (event keys, team numbers) as it prevents accidental reassignment","const only works for strings","let variables are local to functions"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does Array.filter() return?",opts:["The number of matching elements","A new array containing only the elements that satisfy the test function â€” the original array is not modified; filter is used to extract subsets (teams above average, matches in a specific event) without mutating the source data","The first matching element","It modifies the original array"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wb_api",title:"Using The Blue Alliance API in a Web App",est:"13 min",content:`## Live Event Data Without a Backend\nThe Blue Alliance (TBA) provides a free REST API that returns FRC match schedules, team data, event results, and rankings. Your web app can call it directly from the browser â€” no server needed for read-only data.\n\n## Getting an API Key\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n1. Create account at thebluealliance.com\n2. Account â†’ Account Overview â†’ Read API Keys\n3. Create a new key with a description: "Team 1234 scouting app"\n4. Copy the key â€” store it in a .env or config file\n   (NEVER hardcode in JS that\"s committed to a public repo)\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Basic Fetch Request\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\nconst TBA_KEY = "your_key_here"; // move to config in production\n\nasync function getEventTeams(eventKey) {\n  const response = await fetch(\n    \\\`https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/event/\\" + (eventKey) + "/teams/simple\\\`,\n    { headers: { "X-TBA-Auth-Key": TBA_KEY } }\n  );\n\n  if (!response.ok) {\n    throw new Error(\\\`TBA API error: \\" + (response.status) + "\\\`);\n  }\n\n  const teams = await response.json();\n  // teams = array of {team_number, nickname, city, state_prov, ...}\n  return teams.sort((a, b) => a.team_number - b.team_number);\n}\n\n// Usage:\ntry {\n  const teams = await getEventTeams("2025casd");\n  console.log(\\\`\\" + (teams.length) + " teams at this event\\\`);\n} catch (err) {\n  console.error("Failed to load teams:", err.message);\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Getting Rankings\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\nasync function getEventRankings(eventKey) {\n  const res = await fetch(\n    \\\`https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3/event/\\" + (eventKey) + "/rankings\\\`,\n    { headers: { "X-TBA-Auth-Key": TBA_KEY } }\n  );\n  const data = await res.json();\n\n  // data.rankings = array sorted by rank\n  return data.rankings.map(r => ({\n    rank:   r.rank,\n    team:   r.team_key.replace("frc", ""),  // "frc1234" â†’ "1234"\n    wins:   r.record.wins,\n    losses: r.record.losses,\n    rp:     r.extra_stats[0]  // ranking points (index varies by year)\n  }));\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Caching TBA Responses\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// TBA data doesn\"t change mid-match â€” cache aggressively\nconst cache = {};\n\nasync function cachedFetch(url) {\n  if (cache[url]) return cache[url];\n  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { "X-TBA-Auth-Key": TBA_KEY } });\n  const data = await res.json();\n  cache[url] = data;\n  return data;\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a TBA API key never be hardcoded in JavaScript committed to a public repository?",opts:["API keys must be rotated","JavaScript files in a public repo are visible to anyone â€” a hardcoded API key can be scraped by automated tools and used to make requests on your behalf, potentially hitting rate limits or violating TBA's terms of use","Public repos don't serve JavaScript","API keys slow down the fetch request"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does caching TBA API responses in a JavaScript object accomplish?",opts:["It reduces API key exposure","Subsequent calls for the same URL return stored data instantly rather than making another network request â€” TBA data is stable during a match, so fetching team rankings 20 times is wasteful; a cache returns the same data from memory after the first request","Caching is required by TBA","It updates data automatically"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"wi_websocket",title:"Real-Time Updates with WebSockets",est:"14 min",content:`## HTTP vs WebSocket â€” When Polling Isn't Enough
HTTP: client asks â†’ server responds â†’ connection closes. Repeat.
WebSocket: connection stays open â†’ either side can send data at any time.
For a live scouting dashboard where new match data appears instantly without refreshing, WebSocket is the right tool.

## Client-Side WebSocket
\`\`\`javascript
// Connect to WebSocket server:
const ws = new WebSocket("ws://192.168.1.100:8765"); // laptop IP

ws.onopen = () => {
  console.log("Connected to scouting server");
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "subscribe", event: "2025casd" }));
};

ws.onmessage = (event) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(event.data);

  if (data.type === "match_result") {
    updateTeamStats(data.team, data.result);
    refreshPickList();
  } else if (data.type === "alert") {
    showAlert(data.message);
  }
};

ws.onclose = () => {
  console.log("Disconnected â€” attempting reconnect in 3s...");
  setTimeout(connectWebSocket, 3000);
};

ws.onerror = (err) => {
  console.error("WebSocket error:", err);
};
\`\`\`

## Python WebSocket Server (on the pit laptop)
\`\`\`python
import asyncio
import websockets
import json

connected_clients = set()

async def handler(websocket):
    connected_clients.add(websocket)
    try:
        async for message in websocket:
            data = json.loads(message)
            # Echo to all other connected clients:
            if data.get("type") == "match_result":
                for client in connected_clients:
                    if client != websocket:
                        await client.send(json.dumps(data))
    finally:
        connected_clients.discard(websocket)

async def main():
    async with websockets.serve(handler, "0.0.0.0", 8765):
        await asyncio.Future()  # run forever

asyncio.run(main())
\`\`\`

## Use Case: Scout Tablets â†’ Pit Dashboard
\`\`\`
Architecture:
  Scout tablet (browser) â†’ POST match data â†’ Python server
  Python server â†’ WebSocket broadcast â†’ Pit dashboard browser

Each scout submits a match, server broadcasts to the pit dashboard.
The strategy team sees new data appear in real time
without anyone refreshing the page.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What fundamental difference between HTTP and WebSocket makes WebSocket better for a real-time scouting dashboard?",opts:["WebSocket is faster for large files","HTTP closes the connection after each response, requiring the client to repeatedly poll for updates; WebSocket maintains a persistent open connection allowing the server to push new match data to all connected dashboards instantly when it arrives, without any polling","WebSocket is simpler to code","HTTP can't handle JSON"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the ws.onclose handler with setTimeout accomplish in the client code?",opts:["It cleans up memory","It automatically attempts to reconnect after 3 seconds if the server closes the connection â€” competition venue networks are unreliable and the server may restart; automatic reconnection means the dashboard recovers without manual intervention","It prevents multiple connections","setTimeout is required for WebSocket"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wi_mobile",title:"Making Scouting Apps Mobile-Friendly",est:"12 min",content:`## Scouts Use Phones and Tablets, Not Laptops
A scouting input form designed on a laptop looks fine on a 1920px monitor. On a 375px phone screen at field-side, buttons are too small to tap accurately, text overflows, and scrolling feels broken. Mobile-first design is not optional for field-use tools.

## The Viewport Meta Tag
\`\`\`html
<!-- This is required in every mobile-capable HTML page: -->
<head>
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
</head>
<!-- Without this: the browser renders at laptop width and scales down.
     With this: the browser uses the actual screen width. -->
\`\`\`

## Mobile-Friendly Input Design
\`\`\`css
/* Large touch targets â€” minimum 44px height for buttons */
button, select, input[type="number"] {
  min-height: 48px;
  font-size: 16px;      /* prevents iOS from zooming on focus */
  padding: 8px 16px;
  border-radius: 6px;
}

/* Full-width inputs on small screens */
input, select, textarea {
  width: 100%;
  box-sizing: border-box;
}

/* Bigger spacing between form elements for fat fingers */
.form-group {
  margin-bottom: 20px;
}
\`\`\`

## Responsive Layout with CSS Grid
\`\`\`css
/* One column on mobile, two on tablets, three on desktop */
.team-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr;
  gap: 12px;
}

@media (min-width: 600px) {
  .team-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}

@media (min-width: 900px) {
  .team-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; }
}
\`\`\`

## Testing on Real Devices
\`\`\`
Browser DevTools:
  Chrome â†’ F12 â†’ Toggle Device Toolbar (Ctrl+Shift+M)
  Set device: iPhone SE (375px), iPad (768px), Galaxy S20 (360px)
  Test interactions: clicking, scrolling, form submission

Common mobile bugs to check:
  â†’ Horizontal scroll (content overflows screen width)
  â†’ Text too small to read without zooming
  â†’ Buttons too small to tap on first try (aim for 48px minimum)
  â†’ Form field zooms the page on focus (fix: font-size: 16px minimum)
  â†’ Select dropdowns look styled on desktop but use native on iOS
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does font-size: 16px minimum on input elements specifically prevent a common iOS behavior?",opts:["16px is the accessible minimum","iOS Safari automatically zooms the page when a text input is focused if the font size is below 16px â€” this zoom disrupts the layout and requires the user to pinch-zoom back out; 16px inputs prevent the automatic zoom behavior","16px is required by Apple","iOS requires 16px for form validation"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the viewport meta tag 'width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0' change about mobile rendering?",opts:["It sets the screen resolution","It tells the browser to render at the actual device screen width rather than a default desktop width (typically 980px) that gets scaled down â€” without it, a 375px phone renders a 980px layout and everything appears tiny","It enables JavaScript","It prevents pinch-zooming"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
