LESSONS.cad.Beginner.push(
  {id:"cadb_3dprint",title:"Designing Parts for 3D Printing",est:"12 min",content:`## 3D Printing Has Design Rules
A bracket that's perfect for aluminum machining will fail in PLA if it's oriented wrong or has overhangs that the printer can't bridge. Designing for 3D printing means understanding how the printer builds layers and aligning your design with those constraints.

## Layer Orientation Is Everything
\`\`\`
FDM (filament) printers build layer by layer from bottom to top.
Strength runs ACROSS layers (within a layer) much more than BETWEEN layers.
A part loaded between layers will delaminate at a fraction of its rated strength.

Rule: orient the part so the primary load runs WITHIN layers, not between them.

Example â€” mounting bracket:
  Wrong:  print with arm pointing up â†’ bolt holes are between layers
          â†’ pulling force separates layers â†’ part fails at ~20% of material strength
  Right:  print with arm flat â†’ bolt holes are within layers
          â†’ pulling force loads within the layer direction â†’ full strength

Before designing: decide how this part will be printed.
Sketch the print orientation. Check where loads go relative to layer lines.
\`\`\`

## Overhangs, Bridges & Support
\`\`\`
Overhang: any surface angled > 45Â° from vertical needs support material
Bridge: horizontal span between two supported points
  â†’ Bridging works up to ~50mm without support (depends on printer/material)
  â†’ Beyond 50mm: add support or redesign the geometry

Design strategies to avoid support:
  â†’ Split the part and assemble (two simple prints instead of one complex one)
  â†’ Use chamfers (45Â°) instead of horizontal overhangs
  â†’ Hollow bottom â†’ print upside down (flip orientation to avoid overhangs)
  â†’ Add teardrop holes instead of round holes for horizontal hole printing:
    Round hole printed horizontally â†’ top needs support
    Teardrop (round + upward point) â†’ no support needed

Adding support in slicer: support material is wasted filament + post-processing time
Designing out support: better, cleaner, stronger parts
\`\`\`

## Wall Thickness & Infill
\`\`\`
Wall thickness (perimeters):
  Minimum functional:   2mm (2 perimeters at 0.4mm nozzle)
  Structural bracket:   3-4mm (3-4 perimeters)
  High stress:          4-6mm + increased infill

Infill patterns for robot parts:
  Gyroid or Cubic: strong in all directions, good for general brackets
  Grid: fast, strong in 2 directions, weaker diagonally
  0% (hollow):   only for aesthetic/non-load parts

Infill percentage guidelines:
  Display parts, covers:   15-20% infill
  Light structural:        30-40% infill
  Load-bearing brackets:   60-80% infill or solid
  Hinges, snap fits:       80-100% infill at hinge point
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must a bracket's bolt holes be oriented within layers rather than between layers when designing for FDM printing?",opts:["Holes print better within layers","FDM parts are significantly weaker between layers than within them â€” a bolt hole loaded in the between-layers direction can delaminate the part at a fraction of the material's rated strength; within-layer loading engages the full material strength of each printed line","Layer orientation only affects appearance","Bolt holes can't be between layers"],ans:1},
      {q:"What design modification converts a round horizontal hole (which needs support) into a self-supporting feature?",opts:["Making it smaller","A teardrop shape â€” the circular bottom plus an upward-pointing triangular extension â€” the peak angle is printable without support because it's steeper than 45Â°; a pure circle printed horizontally has a flat top that requires support material","Adding a chamfer to the hole edge","Increasing infill percentage"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cadb_gears",title:"Gear Geometry in CAD â€” Designing Gear Interfaces",est:"13 min",content:`## Gears Only Mesh Correctly at the Right Center Distance
Two gears that are 0.5mm too close bind. Too far apart: excessive backlash, noise, and wear. Understanding the relationship between tooth count, module/pitch, and center distance lets you design correct gear arrangements in CAD before cutting metal.

## Gear Terminology
\`\`\`
Module (metric): m = pitch diameter / tooth count
  â†’ Module 1: 1mm per tooth on the pitch circle
  â†’ Module 2: 2mm per tooth (larger, stronger teeth)
  â†’ FTC: GoBILDA uses Mod 1.5 and Mod 0.8 throughout their system
  â†’ FRC: many vendors use Mod 1 or Mod 1.5; AndyMark often uses DP (imperial)

Diametral Pitch (DP, imperial): DP = tooth count / pitch diameter (inches)
  â†’ DP 32: 32 teeth per inch of pitch diameter (fine, common in FRC)
  â†’ DP 20: 20 teeth per inch (coarser, stronger)
  â†’ Cannot mesh gears of different modules or different DPs

Pitch diameter: the theoretical circle where gears contact
  Metric: PD = module Ã— tooth count  (mm)
  Imperial: PD = tooth count / DP    (inches)

Center distance (correct mesh):
  C = (PDâ‚ + PDâ‚‚) / 2
  Example: Mod 1, 20T + 40T:
    PDâ‚ = 1 Ã— 20 = 20mm
    PDâ‚‚ = 1 Ã— 40 = 40mm
    C = (20 + 40) / 2 = 30mm
\`\`\`

## CAD Layout for Gear Pairs
\`\`\`
In Onshape or Fusion:
  1. Sketch the gear centers as points at the calculated center distance
  2. Draw pitch circles (construction circles) at each center:
     diameter = module Ã— tooth count
  3. Verify pitch circles are tangent to each other
     (they should touch at exactly one point)
  4. Place or model gears at those center positions
  5. Use revolute mates at each center point

Gear train layout (3+ gears):
  â†’ Chain gear centers connected by calculated center distances
  â†’ Idler gear: changes rotation direction, does not change ratio
    Ratio = output teeth / input teeth (idler teeth cancel out)
  â†’ Compound gear: two gears on one shaft â†’ multiply ratios

Quick ratio check:
  Ratio = driven / driver = output RPM / input RPM (inverted)
  20T â†’ 40T: ratio 2:1 (output half the speed, double the torque)
  20T â†’ 60T â†’ 40T compound: 60/20 Ã— 40/60 = 2:1 (same result)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What happens mechanically when two meshing gears are placed 0.5mm closer than their calculated center distance?",opts:["They mesh more smoothly","The gear teeth interfere â€” they cannot pass each other without binding or skipping; the tight mesh creates high contact stress, rapid wear, and potentially strips teeth or stalls the motor under load","Backlash increases","The gear ratio changes"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why can a Module 1 gear and a Diametral Pitch 32 gear not mesh with each other?",opts:["They are different sizes","Module and Diametral Pitch define different tooth proportions and pitch angles â€” even if two gears appear similar in size, the tooth profiles are geometrically incompatible; mixing systems creates incorrect contact and rapid tooth failure","Different materials are required","Module gears are metric only"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"cadi_simulation",title:"Motion Simulation & Interference Detection",est:"14 min",content:`## Find the Collision Before It Happens
A mechanism that works in CAD but binds on the physical robot costs hours of debugging and machining. Motion simulation detects interference during the mechanism's full travel range â€” in 30 seconds of virtual animation rather than 3 hours of physical debugging.

## Driving a Revolute or Slider Mate in Onshape
\`\`\`
Setup:
  1. All moving joints must be the correct mate type:
     â†’ Arm pivot: Revolute mate
     â†’ Linear slide: Slider mate
     â†’ Wrist: Revolute mate (separate from arm)
  2. Set limits on the mate (optional but recommended):
     â†’ Right-click the mate â†’ Edit â†’ check "Set limits"
     â†’ Set minimum and maximum angle/distance (your physical hard stops)

Animating:
  1. Right-click the primary joint mate â†’ "Drive"
  2. Set start and end values (e.g., -30Â° to 130Â° for an arm)
  3. Set number of steps (30-50 for smooth animation)
  4. Click Play â€” watch for any red/highlighted interference

What to look for during animation:
  â†’ Any part turning red (Onshape highlights interference)
  â†’ Unexpected collisions mid-travel (not at the endpoints)
  â†’ Mechanism requiring clearance from bumpers or frame
  â†’ Whether intake deploys within legal extension limit
\`\`\`

## Multi-DOF Mechanism Simulation
\`\`\`
For a robot with arm + wrist:
  â†’ Drive the arm through full range first
  â†’ Then with arm at each extreme, drive the wrist through its range
  â†’ Identify combinations where the two mechanisms conflict

Document results:
  Arm angle | Wrist angle | Interference?
  ----------+-------------+--------------
  0Â°        | -30Â° to 90Â° | No
  45Â°        | -30Â° to 90Â° | No
  90Â°        | -30Â° to 60Â° | Yes at 65Â°+ (hits frame)

This table defines the allowed operating envelope â€” and feeds directly
into software limits you set in code (arm at 90Â° â†’ max wrist = 60Â°).
\`\`\`

## Mass Properties for Weight Budget
\`\`\`
In Onshape Part Studio:
  Right-click a part â†’ "Mass properties" â†’ enter material density

Common densities:
  6061-T6 Aluminum:  2.70 g/cmÂ³  (set in Material Library)
  1018 Steel:        7.87 g/cmÂ³
  PLA (3D print):    1.24 g/cmÂ³
  PETG:              1.27 g/cmÂ³
  Carbon fiber tube: ~1.60 g/cmÂ³ (varies)

Workflow:
  1. Set material on every part in the assembly
  2. Assembly â†’ right-click top level â†’ "Mass properties"
  3. Total mass = current robot weight estimate
  4. Compare to your weight budget (125 lb max for FRC)
  5. Sort by heaviest parts â†’ identify candidates for lightening
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should mechanism interference be checked at intermediate positions during animation, not just at the travel endpoints?",opts:["Endpoints are always safe","Mechanisms can pass through a collision zone in the middle of their travel range that both the start and end positions avoid â€” a door that opens and closes fine but collides at 45Â° mid-swing is only caught by watching the full animation, not checking the open and closed states","Intermediate positions are less important","Animation only checks endpoints by default"],ans:1},
      {q:"How does a simulated operating envelope table (arm angle vs wrist angle vs interference) directly improve robot code?",opts:["It replaces the need for code","The table defines the physical limits of safe combined positions â€” software joint limits can be set to match this envelope, preventing the robot from commanding a combination that physically causes interference without relying solely on hard stops","Tables are used in documentation only","Code limits come from datasheets"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cadi_weldment",title:"Tube Frame Design â€” Joints & Gussets",est:"13 min",content:`## Tubes Are Strong; Joints Are Weak
A 1"Ã—1" aluminum tube handles enormous bending loads along its length. The same tube joint, without proper gusseting, fails at a fraction of that load because the joint is a stress concentration point. Almost all robot frame failures happen at joints, not in the tube spans.

## Joint Types and Their Strengths
\`\`\`
Butt joint (tube end against tube face):
  Strength: very low â€” held only by fasteners in shear
  Use: only for low-load connections with gusset reinforcement

Mitered joint (both tubes cut at angle to meet at center):
  Strength: medium â€” more surface area than butt joint
  Fabrication: harder (requires angled cuts)
  Use: cosmetic frames, low-stress corners

Gusseted butt joint (butt joint + triangular bracket across the corner):
  Strength: high â€” gusset transfers load from one tube to the other
  Use: most FRC frame corners, mechanism mounting points
  Best gusset material: 1/8" 6061 aluminum plate, riveted or bolted

Tube-inside-tube (inner tube slides into outer, fastened through):
  Strength: very high â€” load carried by tube-to-tube contact, not fasteners alone
  Use: drive rail extension joints, critical structural connections
\`\`\`

## Designing a Gusset in CAD
\`\`\`
Gusset geometry for a 90Â° corner joint:
  â†’ Triangle with legs equal to 2Ã— the tube width
    For 1" tube: gusset legs = 2" minimum
  â†’ Fastener holes at: 0.5" from each corner (in the tube face area)
  â†’ Use 3-4 fasteners per leg (not 1 or 2 â€” spreads the load)
  â†’ Through-bolted (bolt all the way through both walls) is stronger than riveted
    but riveted is faster and often adequate for secondary structure

In Onshape: sketch the gusset outline â†’ extrude at 0.125" â†’ add holes â†’ fillet corners

Lightening holes in gussets:
  â†’ A circular cutout in the center of the gusset reduces weight
    without significantly reducing strength (stress flows around holes)
  â†’ Rule: hole diameter â‰¤ 1/3 of gusset width
  â†’ Don't put lightening holes near the edges or fastener areas
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do robot frame failures almost always occur at joints rather than in the middle of tube spans?",opts:["Joints use weaker material","Joints are stress concentration points where loads transfer between members â€” a butt joint held only by fasteners concentrates the full load on a small number of fastener holes in shear; a continuous tube span distributes the load evenly along its length with no concentration points","Tubes are specifically reinforced","Joints are always drilled incorrectly"],ans:1},
      {q:"What load path does a gusset create that makes a gusseted butt joint much stronger than an ungusseted one?",opts:["Gussets add more fasteners","The gusset creates a direct material path from one tube face to the other â€” load flows through the gusset plate rather than through fasteners in shear alone; the triangular geometry distributes bending moment across the full gusset area","Gussets increase tube wall thickness","Gussets prevent corrosion at joints"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Advanced.push(
  {id:"cada_surfacing",title:"Surface Modeling for Ergonomic Handles",est:"12 min",content:`## When You Need a Shape, Not Just a Feature
Most robot parts are prismatic â€” boxes, tubes, brackets. But a driver station controller grip, an ergonomic intake chute guide, or a custom bumper mounting rail sometimes needs a curved shape that extruding a sketch can't produce. Surface modeling creates those shapes.

## Loft â€” Transitioning Between Two Profiles
\`\`\`
Loft creates a solid by smoothly transitioning between two or more sketches on parallel planes.

Use case: intake funnel that transitions from a 6" wide opening to a 2" exit slot
  Sketch 1 (Plane 1):  6" Ã— 1" rectangle (wide intake mouth)
  Sketch 2 (Plane 2):  2" Ã— 0.5" rectangle (narrow exit, 4" above)
  Loft â†’ select Sketch 1, then Sketch 2 â†’ creates smooth funnel shape

Guide curves (optional):
  Draw a 3D curve connecting corresponding points on each sketch
  Loft follows the curve â†’ controls the profile at each height
  Use for: asymmetric shapes, curved paths, handles that taper along a curve

In Onshape: Features â†’ Loft â†’ select profiles â†’ add guides â†’ adjust end conditions
End conditions:
  Normal to sketch plane: smooth, flat end faces
  Tangent:               smooth tangent transition to adjacent faces
\`\`\`

## Sweep â€” Extruding Along a Curved Path
\`\`\`
Sweep takes a profile sketch and moves it along a path curve.

Use case: a curved cable channel that routes around a corner
  Profile sketch: 8mm Ã— 5mm rectangle (the channel cross-section)
  Path: a spline curve following the desired cable route
  Sweep â†’ creates a 3D tube following the exact path

Use case: ergonomic grip contour
  Profile: hand cross-section oval (~40mm Ã— 30mm)
  Path: curved line matching hand position when gripping
  Sweep + shell â†’ hollow ergonomic grip shell

Key constraint: the profile sketch must be perpendicular to the path start point
\`\`\`

## When to Use Surface Modeling vs Solid Modeling
\`\`\`
Solid modeling (default):
  â†’ Brackets, gearbox housings, most robot parts
  â†’ Defined by sketch + feature operations
  â†’ Always watertight (manufacturable)

Surface modeling (when needed):
  â†’ Complex curved shapes where loft/sweep would distort a solid
  â†’ Wrapping a shape around another curved surface
  â†’ Creating a complex mold shape
  â†’ Post-process: Thicken the surface â†’ solid part

Hybrid approach: model the basic solid, then use surface tools
for just the complex curved faces and merge them.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What fundamental difference between Loft and Extrude makes Loft necessary for an intake funnel design?",opts:["Loft is faster","Extrude moves a single unchanging profile in a straight direction â€” it can only create prisms; Loft transitions between two different profiles (wide opening and narrow exit) creating the changing cross-section geometry that a funnel requires","Loft supports curved paths","Extrude can't create holes"],ans:1},
      {q:"What constraint must the profile sketch satisfy relative to the path in a Sweep operation?",opts:["The profile must be circular","The profile sketch plane must be perpendicular to the path at its starting point â€” a non-perpendicular profile creates a twisted or incorrectly oriented sweep that doesn't match the intended cross-section at each point along the path","The path must be straight","Profile and path must be on the same plane"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT +8 (20â†’28) â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Beginner.push(
  {id:"tmb_onboarding",title:"Onboarding New Members â€” The First 30 Days",est:"11 min",content:`## The First Month Determines Retention
A new member who feels useful and connected after 30 days stays. One who feels like an observer for a month leaves â€” and tells their friends the team wasn't welcoming. Intentional onboarding is the highest-return investment a team leader makes.

## Day 1: Make It Count
\`\`\`
Before they arrive:
  â†’ Have a workspace and a task ready (not "go watch for now")
  â†’ Assign a buddy: one existing member responsible for this person this session
  â†’ Put their name on a team roster or whiteboard â€” visible belonging

Day 1 session:
  â†’ Personal intro: name, grade, what brought them here
  â†’ Team tour: each area, who works there, what they're building
  â†’ First real task within 20 minutes:
    Even if simple ("help me count these rivets" / "hold this while I drill"),
    physical participation beats observation every time
  â†’ End of session: "What did you think? What sounds most interesting?"

Do NOT on Day 1:
  â†’ Give them a 1-hour lecture about the team's history
  â†’ Make them watch experienced members work without participating
  â†’ Forget to learn their name before they leave
\`\`\`

## The 30-Day Checklist
\`\`\`
Week 1:
  â–¡ Buddy assigned (same person for at least 2 weeks)
  â–¡ Added to team communication channel
  â–¡ First real task completed
  â–¡ Introduced to their subteam by name

Week 2:
  â–¡ One skill taught (even small: crimping a wire, sketching in Onshape)
  â–¡ Name known by at least 3 other team members
  â–¡ Knows where to find team resources (Drive, parts, tools)

Week 3-4:
  â–¡ Has an ongoing responsibility (something that's "theirs")
  â–¡ Attended a meeting where they spoke at least once
  â–¡ 5-minute check-in: "How's it going? Anything confusing?"

30-day outcome: new member should be able to describe what they're
working on and who they work with. If they can't â€” the onboarding failed.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is physical participation in a task within the first 20 minutes of Day 1 important for retention?",opts:["Tasks take 20 minutes","Immediate participation creates a sense of contribution and belonging that passive observation cannot â€” a new member who does something with their hands on Day 1 has a concrete memory of being useful; one who watched for an hour has a memory of being a bystander","Tasks must start on time","FIRST requires immediate participation"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific outcome should a member be able to demonstrate at the 30-day mark that indicates successful onboarding?",opts:["They can build a robot independently","They can describe what they're working on and who they work with â€” demonstrating they have both a functional role and social connections; a member without both is at high dropout risk regardless of their enthusiasm on Day 1","They've attended all meetings","They've completed the safety test"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmb_conflict",title:"Resolving Team Conflicts Early",est:"12 min",content:`## Conflict Is Normal â€” Escalation Is Optional
Build season stress, high stakes, and strong opinions create friction. Teams that address conflict early keep it from poisoning the working environment. Teams that avoid it until it explodes spend more energy on drama than on the robot.

## The Three Types of Team Conflict
\`\`\`
Type 1: Task conflict â€” disagreement about how to do something
  "I think we should use a 4-bar linkage, you think a linear slide is better"
  â†’ Usually healthy â€” leads to better decisions if handled well
  â†’ Resolution: evaluate both options against shared criteria, decide, move on

Type 2: Process conflict â€” disagreement about how decisions are made
  "Why did they decide that without consulting us?"
  â†’ Signals unclear decision authority or communication gaps
  â†’ Resolution: clarify the RACI, improve communication

Type 3: Relationship conflict â€” interpersonal friction
  "I don't want to work with that person"
  â†’ Most damaging â€” if unaddressed, poisons team culture
  â†’ Resolution: direct conversation, mediated if needed, root cause addressed
\`\`\`

## The Early Intervention Conversation
\`\`\`
Signs to act (don't wait for an explosion):
  â†’ Two members avoid each other or speak curtly
  â†’ Someone becomes quiet and withdrawn in sessions
  â†’ Side conversations replacing direct communication
  â†’ "Fine" as the answer to "how's it going?"

The conversation (private, lead to affected person):
  "I noticed things seem tense between you and [name].
   I'm not asking for details â€” I just want to check in.
   Is there something we can address to make things better?"

Give them room to respond. Don't take sides in the first conversation.
Goals of first conversation:
  â†’ Person feels heard, not interrogated
  â†’ You understand if it's task/process/relationship conflict
  â†’ You and the person agree on a next step

When to escalate to a mentor:
  â†’ Any safety concern
  â†’ Harassment or bullying
  â†’ Conflict that involves you (can't be neutral)
  â†’ Repeated conflict with same parties after attempted resolution
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is task conflict (disagreement about the best solution) described as 'usually healthy'?",opts:["Conflict is never healthy","Task conflict forces teams to articulate their reasoning, consider alternatives, and make more explicit decisions â€” teams that avoid all disagreement often pick the first idea rather than the best one; structured task conflict improves outcomes when it's managed well","All conflict must be prevented","Task conflict is easier to manage"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific observable signs indicate that early intervention is needed before a conflict escalates?",opts:["Raised voices in meetings","Members avoiding each other, someone becoming withdrawn, side conversations replacing direct communication, and curt responses to check-in questions â€” these are low-intensity signals that precede escalation; acting at this stage is far less disruptive than acting after an explosion","Missing meetings","Disagreement in meetings"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"tmi_goals",title:"Setting Season Goals That Actually Get Used",est:"11 min",content:`## Goals Written in September Should Drive February Decisions
Most teams set season goals during kickoff energy and forget about them by Week 3. Useful goals are specific enough to create tradeoffs â€” when a decision has to be made, the goals tell you which option to choose.

## Why Most Goals Fail
\`\`\`
Useless goal: "Do our best and work as a team"
  â†’ Cannot make any decision from this

Weak goal: "Compete well and have fun"
  â†’ Still no decision guidance

Useful goal: "Qualify for Championship in at least one of our two district events,
              while mentoring the two new FLL teams we started this fall"

The test: if two options appear and you can't use the goals to choose between them,
           the goals are too vague to be useful.
\`\`\`

## The Goal-Setting Session at Kickoff
\`\`\`
40-minute session, whole team, before robot design begins:

Step 1 (10 min): Brainstorm â€” what do we want this season?
  â†’ Everyone writes on sticky notes, no filtering
  â†’ Categories: competition, growth, outreach, culture

Step 2 (10 min): Theme â€” what pattern do we see?
  â†’ Group stickies into 3-5 themes
  â†’ Name each theme in one sentence

Step 3 (15 min): Specific goals from themes
  â†’ For each theme, write one SMART goal:
    Specific â€” "qualify for championships"
    Measurable â€” "seed in top 8 at districts"
    Achievable â€” given your team's current level
    Relevant â€” connects to why people joined the team
    Time-bound â€” "by end of district play"

Step 4 (5 min): Priority order
  â†’ If you can't do everything, which goal matters most?
  â†’ Write the priority order explicitly â€” it will be needed in Week 5
\`\`\`

## Using Goals to Make Decisions
\`\`\`
Week 5: You can add one more mechanism OR spend the week on autonomous.
Goal: "seed in top 8" â†’ auto matters more for ranking points â†’ choose auto.

Goal: "mentor our FLL teams through their qualifier" â†’
Do you skip a team meeting night to attend their event?
Yes â€” this goal explicitly matters.

Review goals at midpoint (Week 3) and post-competition:
  â†’ Which goals are on track?
  â†’ Which need to be adjusted based on what you've learned?
  â†’ Did any goals become irrelevant? (Remove them â€” zombie goals waste energy)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the practical test for whether a season goal is specific enough to be useful?",opts:["It must be written down","Can it help choose between two real options? â€” a goal that can't resolve any actual decision is too vague to guide behavior; 'do our best' can't help you decide between adding a mechanism or polishing autonomous, but 'seed top 8' can","It must be SMART","Goals must be reviewed weekly"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should goals be prioritized explicitly in order at the goal-setting session?",opts:["Priority order is required","Build season creates moments where pursuing one goal means sacrificing another â€” without a pre-established priority, every such tradeoff becomes a debate; an explicit ranking converts those debates into quick reference lookups","Priority determines resources","Lower-priority goals are abandoned"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmi_offseason2",title:"Off-Season Projects â€” Building Skills Without Competition Pressure",est:"13 min",content:`## Off-Season Is Where Growth Happens
During build season, every decision is driven by competition deadlines. New members can't experiment; experienced members can't try unfamiliar approaches. The off-season â€” May through December â€” is where teams build the skills and systems that make next build season better.

## What Off-Season Projects Should Accomplish
\`\`\`
Valuable off-season goals:
  â†’ Teach new members skills they'll use in January
  â†’ Try approaches that were too risky during season (new code architecture,
    new mechanism type, unfamiliar materials)
  â†’ Build tools that make the team faster (jigs, fixtures, test rigs)
  â†’ Document the current robot before the design knowledge walks out the door
  â†’ Compete in off-season events (practice under real competition conditions)

Not valuable:
  â†’ Rebuilding the same robot from scratch with no new goal
  â†’ Off-season that only senior members participate in
  â†’ Projects that nobody continues because interest fades after summer
\`\`\`

## The Off-Season Project Template
\`\`\`
Before starting any off-season project, answer:
  What skill does this teach that we need in January?
  Who will own this project start to finish?
  What is the concrete deliverable? (not "learn programming" â€” "working PID loop")
  What is the end date?
  Who is the intended audience? (the whole team? just new members? leads?)

Example:
  Project:       Vision targeting proof-of-concept
  Skill built:   AprilTag detection and targeting
  Owner:         Two junior programmers + senior mentor
  Deliverable:   Robot reliably auto-aims at AprilTag at 3m distance
  End date:      October 31
  Audience:      Programming subteam â€” demonstrated to all at November meeting

Without an owner and a concrete deliverable, projects die by July.
\`\`\`

## Off-Season Events
\`\`\`
Off-season FRC events (e.g., Chezy Champs, Fall Classic, CMP off-season):
  â†’ Drive practice under match conditions
  â†’ New drive team members can practice without qualification pressure
  â†’ Alliance selection practice for strategy leads
  â†’ Great for testing new autonomous routines in a real field setting

What to learn at off-season events that you can't learn in practice:
  â†’ How your robot breaks under repeated match cycles
  â†’ Whether your queue/pit coordination is actually working
  â†’ How your scouting system performs under real time pressure
  â†’ Whether new team members can operate independently
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'rebuilding the same robot from scratch' identified as a low-value off-season project?",opts:["Rebuilding takes too long","It produces a known outcome with a known process â€” the team learns nothing new and builds no skills they didn't already have; valuable off-season projects specifically target skills the team needs but doesn't yet have, or test approaches that were too risky during competition season","Robot rebuilds violate FIRST rules","Off-season budgets are too small for rebuilds"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific capability can off-season events develop that regular practice cannot replicate?",opts:["Better robot performance","Real match conditions â€” repeated match cycles that reveal mechanical failure points, queue and pit coordination under actual time pressure, and new member operation without qualification stakes; these conditions cannot be simulated in a practice space","Off-season events have no value","Events only test driving"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Advanced.push(
  {id:"tma_strategy_team",title:"Building a Dedicated Strategy Team",est:"14 min",content:`## Strategy Is a Skill, Not a Role Anyone Fills
Teams that treat strategy as "the captain decides" leave points on the field. A dedicated strategy team with clear roles, prepared data systems, and practiced decision-making wins alliances they shouldn't win â€” because they chose better partners and made better match decisions.

## Strategy Team Roles
\`\`\`
Scout Lead: owns data collection system, manages scout assignments,
            ensures data quality during competition
            Needs: organized, detail-oriented, comfortable with spreadsheets/apps

Data Analyst: aggregates scout data into rankings and team profiles
              Needs: comfortable with data tools (Sheets, Python, SQL)

Alliance Strategist: uses data to identify ideal alliance partners,
                     prepares pick list and backup picks
                     Needs: deep game knowledge, can think 3 picks ahead

Match Strategist: develops match-specific strategy (auto paths, teleop roles),
                  communicates plan in the pre-match meeting
                  Needs: understands robot capabilities of all alliance members

Team Captain: final call in alliance selection, manages relationships with other captains
              Needs: calm under pressure, clear communicator
\`\`\`

## The Alliance Selection Preparation
\`\`\`
Start this before the event â€” not during:
  Pre-event (using TBA data + your knowledge):
    â†’ Identify 20-30 teams you'd consider partnering with
    â†’ Note each team's strengths, weaknesses, recent performance

At the event (update continuously):
    â†’ Scout every team on the pick list (min 2 matches)
    â†’ Flag any teams that broke down or showed unexpected issues
    â†’ Add pit observations (robot quality, spare parts, team composure)

Day-of-selection (during last qual matches):
    â†’ Rank 1-8: who would you pick at each position?
    â†’ Identify which 1-seeds will decline to captain
    â†’ Plan your offer: "If we're seed 4, who do we call first?"
    â†’ Identify your second pick for each possible first pick

Never enter alliance selection without a pre-ranked list.
Selection happens in seconds; decisions made cold cost you the event.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must the alliance selection pick list be prepared before selection begins rather than during it?",opts:["Selection is too short","Alliance selection decisions happen in 30-45 seconds per pick â€” thinking through the implications of each choice from scratch under that time pressure and public attention leads to reactive rather than strategic decisions; a pre-built ranked list converts selection into execution rather than analysis","Lists are required by FIRST","Pre-built lists prevent changes"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific information from pit scouting during the event can override a team's positive pre-event profile?",opts:["Pit visits are for sponsors","Observations of robot breakdown patterns, missing spare parts, team panic behavior under pressure, and discovered mechanical issues that TBA data can't capture â€” a team that performed well at prior events but has a clearly damaged mechanism at this event is a higher pick risk than their historical data suggests","Pit scouting is less reliable","Only match data matters"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ OUTREACH +8 (20â†’28) â”€â”€
LESSONS.outreach.Beginner.push(
  {id:"orb_ambassador",title:"Being a FIRST Ambassador at School",est:"10 min",content:`## Every Member Is a Recruiter
The easiest recruitment happens when team members talk naturally about what they're building. A student who casually says "we figured out how to make our arm hold a game piece without dropping it" to a curious friend does more recruiting than a formal presentation.

## How to Talk About the Team Naturally
\`\`\`
The one-sentence version (for anyone asking "what do you do?"):
  "I'm on the school robotics team â€” we build a competition robot every year
   and compete against teams from across the state."

The curious follow-up version (when they want more):
  â†’ Pick ONE thing you're personally working on
  â†’ Explain what the challenge was and how you solved it
  â†’ End with: "It's harder than it sounds â€” want to come see it sometime?"

What doesn't work:
  â†’ Starting with FIRST acronyms ("We're in FRC, which is the FTC equivalent...")
  â†’ Listing accomplishments ("We won the design award at the regional...")
  â†’ Explaining the game before they care what the game is
\`\`\`

## Recruiting at School Events
\`\`\`
Opportunities most teams overlook:
  â†’ Science class: ask your teacher for 5 minutes to show a robot clip
  â†’ School fair or club day: the robot needs to be there, not just a poster
  â†’ After school clubs: robotics adjacent (coding club, engineering club, art) â€”
    these students already self-identify as interested
  â†’ Lunch: bring a small mechanism or game piece to show one person
    â†’ they show their friends â†’ chain reaction

Follow up within 48 hours of any expressed interest:
  "Hey, you mentioned robotics sounds interesting â€” we meet Thursday at 3pm.
   Want to come and see what we're working on?"
  One specific invitation > "you should come sometime"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is explaining FIRST acronyms (FRC, FTC) a poor opening when recruiting at school?",opts:["Acronyms are confusing","Acronyms require prior context to be meaningful â€” to someone who's never heard of FIRST, FRC and FTC are just letters; starting with what the team actually does (builds competition robots, solves engineering challenges) creates immediate mental images without requiring any background knowledge","FIRST discourages acronyms","Acronyms take too long to explain"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes a specific same-week invitation ('we meet Thursday at 3pm') more effective than a general 'you should come sometime'?",opts:["Specific invitations are required","A specific time requires a specific decision â€” the person either can or can't come Thursday; 'sometime' is easy to agree to and easy to defer indefinitely; specificity converts vague interest into a first visit","Specific invitations are shorter","People only respond to specific times"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"orb_community",title:"Community Visibility Events",est:"10 min",content:`## Being Seen Makes Recruiting and Sponsorship Easier
A team that only appears at FIRST competitions is invisible to the community that funds and joins it. Local parades, community fairs, library events, and civic events give your team visibility with parents, local businesses, and potential members who'd never seek you out.

## Event Types Worth Attending
\`\`\`
High visibility, low effort:
  â†’ City parades: most welcome community groups and organizations
    â†’ Robot in a wagon, team members walking, sign with team name/number
    â†’ Seen by hundreds to thousands; easy to coordinate

  â†’ Library STEM days: libraries actively seek presenters
    â†’ Often already have an audience assembled (no recruiting needed)
    â†’ Contact: children's librarian or programs coordinator

  â†’ School district science nights: principals already want this
    â†’ Direct access to students and parents who came specifically for STEM
    â†’ Often leads to standing annual invitations

Lower visibility, higher engagement:
  â†’ State/county fair: multi-day commitment but sustained exposure
  â†’ Civic club presentations (Rotary, Lions Club): sponsors in the room
  â†’ Community college STEM events: college students as potential team mentors
\`\`\`

## What to Bring to a Community Event
\`\`\`
Essential:
  â†’ The robot (or a substantial mechanism if the robot isn't mobile)
  â†’ Game pieces for people to handle
  â†’ Signup sheet: name, email, grade/age, interest (drive? build? code?)
  â†’ Team flyers with QR code to website/signup form

Optional but high-value:
  â†’ A driving challenge: cone on the floor, robot must push it to a zone
    â†’ People wait in line to try â†’ creates a crowd â†’ crowd attracts more crowd
  â†’ Branded canopy or banner: visible from 50 feet
  â†’ Business cards with team contact info for parents and potential sponsors

After the event:
  â†’ Send a personalized follow-up to everyone on the signup sheet within 48 hours
  â†’ One community visibility event per month (even small) maintains momentum
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does creating a driving challenge at community events (rather than just a static display) increase crowd size?",opts:["Challenges are more educational","A line of people waiting creates social proof â€” passersby see other people engaged and assume it's worth stopping for; a crowd attracts more crowd; a static robot with no interaction gets a 5-second glance while an active challenge creates sustained engagement and a visible queue","Challenges require consent","Static displays are equally effective"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_stem_camp",title:"Running a Multi-Day STEM Camp",est:"15 min",content:`## A Multi-Day Camp Creates Deeper Learning Than Single Events
A student who attends a 4-hour robotics camp and builds something that moves goes home with a memory that lasts years. A student who sees a robot demo at a fair goes home and forgets it by dinner. Camps are more work â€” and produce far more lasting impact per student.

## Camp Structure (3-Day Format)
\`\`\`
Day 1: Introduction and design
  Morning (2h): Team FIRST introductions, game challenge reveal,
                students form teams of 3-4
  Afternoon (2h): Design process â€” brainstorm â†’ sketch â†’ decide
                  Build shopping list from available materials

Day 2: Build and code
  Morning (3h): Physical build using kit materials (LEGO, cardboard, basic hardware)
  Afternoon (2h): Introduction to coding (Scratch or block-based)
                  Program one simple autonomous behavior

Day 3: Compete and reflect
  Morning (2h): Iteration â€” fix what broke, improve what worked
  Afternoon (2h): Mini-competition, celebration, debrief
                  Student presentations: "what we built and what we'd do differently"
\`\`\`

## Materials and Budget Planning
\`\`\`
Per-student cost estimates (basic camp):
  LEGO Education kit share (1 per 4 students): $0 if borrowed from school
  OR Cardboard/PVC pipe construction:          $8-12 per team
  Game pieces (foam balls, cups):              $15-25 for the full camp
  Printed worksheets and challenge cards:      $2 per student
  Snacks (if included):                        $5-8 per student per day
  Name badges and certificates:                $1 per student

Total: $15-45 per student depending on materials
Charge: $30-75 per student (or free if grant/sponsor funded)

Registration: collect via Google Forms
  â†’ Medical information (allergies, medications)
  â†’ Photo release (explicit opt-in)
  â†’ T-shirt size if providing
  â†’ Emergency contact
\`\`\`

## The Curriculum Design Rule
\`\`\`
Each day should produce something visible and physical.
Students who can point to something they built stay engaged.
Students who sat through two hours of instruction disengage.

Ratio target: â‰¤ 20% instruction, â‰¥ 80% building and doing
Schedule buffer: add 20% extra time to every activity estimate
  â†’ 30-minute activity â†’ plan 36 minutes
  â†’ Children consistently need more time than adults estimate

Facilitator training: run through every activity yourself before camp.
If something confuses YOU during prep, it will confuse students.
Revise the activity until it's clear to a first-time facilitator.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a 3-day camp produce more lasting impact per student than three separate 1-hour visits?",opts:["Camps cover more material","Sustained engagement allows iteration â€” students build something, test it, discover why it doesn't work, fix it, and experience the engineering design cycle as a process rather than a single event; this experiential loop is what creates lasting memory and genuine understanding","Camps have better equipment","Visits are harder to schedule"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the instruction-to-activity ratio that keeps students engaged, and why?",opts:["50% instruction is ideal","At most 20% instruction with 80% building and doing â€” children learn by doing far more than by listening; more than 20 minutes of continuous instruction without a hands-on activity consistently produces visible disengagement, side conversations, and wandering attention","Equal ratios are best","Instruction should dominate to cover all content"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ori_parent",title:"Engaging Parents as Team Supporters",est:"11 min",content:`## Parents Are Your Most Reliable Volunteers
A parent who understands what their child is building will drive them to every meeting, donate when asked, volunteer at competitions, and recruit other parents. A parent who doesn't understand what's happening will pull their child for any schedule conflict.

## The Parent Communication Strategy
\`\`\`
Monthly parent email (not more, not less):
  â†’ What the team accomplished this month (robot milestone, outreach event)
  â†’ What's coming next month (competitions, deadlines, opportunities)
  â†’ One ask (never more): volunteer opportunity OR donation request, never both at once

Competition day packet (sent one week before):
  â†’ Schedule: when is the robot competing? when can parents come to the pit?
  â†’ Location: venue address, parking, entrance
  â†’ How to watch: livestream link + what to look for ("red alliance, match 12")
  â†’ How to help: "We need 2 parents to handle team lunches"

Never assume parents know:
  â†’ What FIRST is (explain briefly every time)
  â†’ What position their child plays on the team
  â†’ How alliance selection works
  â†’ Why the robot costs this much
\`\`\`

## Parent Volunteer Roles
\`\`\`
Roles that need no technical knowledge:
  â†’ Pit lunch coordinator: brings food to the pit on competition day
  â†’ Transportation coordinator: organizes carpools to meetings and competitions
  â†’ Hospitality: coordinates end-of-season celebration, team events
  â†’ Photography: documents team events (especially useful at competitions)

Roles requiring moderate knowledge (teach them):
  â†’ Pit organization: manages the pit setup, restocking, tool tracking
  â†’ Spirit section lead: coordinates cheering sections, team merchandise sales

Rules for parent volunteers:
  â†’ Parents help; they don't direct students in technical work
  â†’ Direct questions about robot design to student leads, not adult volunteers
  â†’ Clear communication about the boundary: "In the pit, students lead"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should parent emails contain only one ask per message rather than combining volunteer requests and donation requests?",opts:["Multiple asks are confusing","Multiple asks reduce response rate â€” a reader who sees two requests often decides on neither or picks the easier one; a single, specific ask with a clear call to action ('we need 2 parents for Saturday pit lunch â€” reply here') produces far higher compliance than a menu of options","Parents prefer simple emails","Email clients limit content"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should parents in the pit be explicitly told that students lead technical work, with parents helping?",opts:["Parents can't do technical work","Without clear role definition, well-intentioned parents often direct students or take over tasks, which undermines student ownership and creates confusion about authority â€” students who feel supervised by parents disengage; explicit role clarity preserves student leadership","FIRST rules prohibit parent work","Parents must be supervised by mentors"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ora_year_plan",title:"Building a Year-Round Outreach Calendar",est:"13 min",content:`## Outreach Shouldn't Stop at Championship
Teams that do outreach only during build season report 6-8 events. Teams with a year-round calendar report 15-25. The difference isn't more effort â€” it's planning events into seasons when the robot exists and students have more time.

## The Annual Outreach Calendar Template
\`\`\`
Month       Event type                          Lead
-----------+-----------------------------------+------------------
September   School club fair, recruitment        Outreach lead
October     FLL kickoff support                  Scout/outreach
November    STEM night at one partner school      Whole team
December    Light workload (finals, holidays)    â€”
January     Community event (library, parade)    2-3 members
February    School visits during build season    Off-day schedule
March       Competition + outreach at venue      All
April       STEM fair demo                       Outreach lead
May         End-of-year school visits            Seniors
June        Summer camp planning                 Camp lead
July        STEM camp execution                  Camp team
August      Off-season prep, new team recruit    Leads

Total events: 14-20 per year at this cadence
Impact report total: 400-900 students reached per year
\`\`\`

## Making Outreach Sustainable
\`\`\`
The burnout pattern: a small group does everything â†’ exhausted by March â†’
  outreach stops when people who care most check out

Prevention:
  â†’ Rotate event ownership: each event has a different lead
  â†’ Minimum viable events: commit to 1 per month â€” more is bonus
  â†’ Match event type to season energy:
    Build season: simple events (1 person demoing at a library)
    Off-season: complex events (multi-day camp)
  â†’ Allow saying no: if a committed event conflicts with competition week, skip it

The sustainability metric: can the team run its outreach plan without the outreach lead?
If the answer is no, the lead is a single point of failure.
\`\`\`

## Tracking Cumulative Impact for Awards
\`\`\`
Maintain a running impact log (Google Sheet):
  Date | Event | Location | Students | Duration | Team members | Notes
  ---  | ---   | ---      | ---      | ---      | ---          | ---

Year-end totals (auto-calculated with SUM):
  â†’ Total students reached: 847
  â†’ Total events: 18
  â†’ Total volunteer hours: 240
  â†’ New programs started: 3

This log is the evidence base for every Impact Award submission.
With a maintained log, writing the Impact essay takes 2 hours.
Without it, you spend those 2 hours trying to remember what you did.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the specific sustainability test for an outreach program?",opts:["The program runs every month","Whether the outreach lead could be absent and the events would still happen â€” if all outreach depends on one person's knowledge and motivation, a single person's burnout or graduation eliminates the program; a sustainable program has multiple owners and documented processes","Impact awards verify sustainability","The program has 15+ events"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does matching event complexity to season energy prevent outreach burnout?",opts:["Complex events are harder","Students have dramatically less capacity during build season â€” requiring complex outreach (multi-day camps, large-scale events) at the same time as robot build causes both to suffer; simple events (one person at a library) during busy periods maintain continuity without overloading anyone","Season energy is predictable","Simple events always produce more impact"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
