LESSONS.webdev.Beginner.push(
  {id:"wb_localStorage",title:"Storing Data in the Browser with localStorage",est:"11 min",content:`## Make Your App Remember Things Between Sessions
Every time a page reloads, JavaScript variables reset to zero. localStorage persists data in the browser even after closing the tab â€” perfect for scouting apps that need to survive a phone restart mid-competition.

## Basic localStorage Operations
\`\`\`javascript
// Store a value (everything must be a string):
localStorage.setItem("scoutName", "Alex");
localStorage.setItem("eventKey", "2025casd");

// Retrieve a value:
const name = localStorage.getItem("scoutName"); // "Alex"
const missing = localStorage.getItem("nope");   // null (not an error)

// Delete a specific key:
localStorage.removeItem("scoutName");

// Delete ALL stored data (nuclear option â€” use carefully):
localStorage.clear();

// Check all stored keys:
for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++) {
  const key = localStorage.key(i);
  console.log(key, localStorage.getItem(key));
}
\`\`\`

## Storing Arrays and Objects (JSON)
\`\`\`javascript
// Arrays and objects MUST be serialized with JSON.stringify:
const matches = [
  { team: 1234, auto: 12, cycles: 6, climb: "L3" },
  { team: 5678, auto: 8,  cycles: 4, climb: "None" }
];

// Save:
localStorage.setItem("matchData", JSON.stringify(matches));

// Load (parse back from string):
const stored = localStorage.getItem("matchData");
const loaded = stored ? JSON.parse(stored) : []; // handle null case

// Add a new match and save:
function addMatch(matchObj) {
  const data = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("matchData") || "[]");
  data.push(matchObj);
  localStorage.setItem("matchData", JSON.stringify(data));
}

// Get all matches:
function getAllMatches() {
  return JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("matchData") || "[]");
}
\`\`\`

## Limitations to Know
\`\`\`
Capacity: ~5MB per origin (more than enough for scouting data)
Scope: data is per-browser, per-device â€” not shared between phones
Security: visible to any JavaScript on the same page â€” don't store passwords
Availability: always synchronous (no async/await needed)
Persistence: survives page reload, tab close, browser restart
             Cleared by: user clearing browser data, incognito mode (session only)

Competition use: each scout's phone stores its own data
                 sync to a central server when on Wi-Fi
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must objects and arrays be passed through JSON.stringify before storing in localStorage?",opts:["localStorage requires JSON format","localStorage only stores strings â€” passing an object directly stores '[object Object]' which is useless; JSON.stringify converts the object to a JSON string that can be stored, then JSON.parse converts it back to a JavaScript object when retrieved","JSON is more compressed","Arrays require special handling"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('matchData') || '[]') accomplish compared to just JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('matchData'))?",opts:["It prevents errors","If the key doesn't exist, getItem returns null, and JSON.parse(null) throws an error; the || '[]' fallback ensures that when no data is stored yet, the function returns an empty array rather than crashing","It improves performance","It validates the stored data"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wb_components",title:"Building Reusable UI Components",est:"12 min",content:`## Don\"t Write the Same HTML Twice\nA scouting dashboard might show 40 team cards, each with the same structure but different data. Writing 40 copies of the same HTML is maintenance hell â€” change the card layout and you change it 40 places. A component function generates the HTML from data, once.\n\n## The Component Pattern in Vanilla JS\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Component: generates HTML for one team card\nfunction TeamCard(team) {\n  const tierClass = team.avg >= 45 ? \"tier-high\" : team.avg >= 30 ? \"tier-mid\" : \"tier-low\";\n  return \\\`\n    <div class="team-card \\" + (tierClass) + "" data-team="\\" + (team.number) + "">\n      <h3>Team \\" + (team.number) + "</h3>\n      <p class="nickname">\\" + (team.nickname) + "</p>\n      <div class="stats">\n        <span class="stat">Auto: \\" + (team.avgAuto.toFixed(1)) + "</span>\n        <span class="stat">Cycles: \\" + (team.avgCycles.toFixed(1)) + "</span>\n        <span class="stat">Climb: \\" + (team.climbRate) + "%</span>\n      </div>\n      <div class="total">Avg: \\" + (team.avg.toFixed(1)) + " pts</div>\n    </div>\n  \\\`;\n}\n\n// Render all teams:\nfunction renderTeamList(teams) {\n  const container = document.getElementById("teamGrid");\n  container.innerHTML = teams.map(TeamCard).join("");\n}\n\n// Update is simple â€” re-render:\nrenderTeamList(sortedTeams);\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Adding Interactivity to Components\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Event delegation: one listener on the parent handles all cards\ndocument.getElementById("teamGrid").addEventListener("click", (e) => {\n  const card = e.target.closest(".team-card");\n  if (!card) return;\n  const teamNumber = card.dataset.team;\n  showTeamDetail(teamNumber);\n});\n\n// Avoid: adding event listeners inside the component function\n// (creates hundreds of listeners, causes memory leaks)\n\n// Team detail panel:\nfunction showTeamDetail(teamNumber) {\n  const team = teams.find(t => t.number == teamNumber);\n  document.getElementById("detailPanel").innerHTML = \\\`\n    <h2>Team \\" + (team.number) + " â€” \\" + (team.nickname) + "</h2>\n    <p>Matches scouted: \\" + (team.matchCount) + "</p>\n    <p>Best match: \\" + (team.bestMatch) + " pts</p>\n    <p>Notes: \\" + (team.notes || "None") + "</p>\n  \\\`;\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is event delegation (one listener on the parent) preferred over adding individual event listeners inside each component?",opts:["Delegation is more accurate","One parent listener handles all child elements â€” adding a listener inside a component function that renders 40 cards creates 40 separate listeners, wasting memory; delegation creates one listener that handles events from any card regardless of how many cards exist","Delegation is required for data-* attributes","Child listeners don't work in JavaScript"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the primary maintenance advantage of a component function over writing repeated HTML?",opts:["Functions are shorter","Changing the layout requires one edit in one function â€” all rendered components update on next render; manually repeated HTML requires the same change to be made at every occurrence, with risk of missing one","Components load faster","HTML repetition causes errors"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"wi_search",title:"Search & Filter for Scouting Dashboards",est:"12 min",content:`## Alliance Selection Needs Instant Filtering
At alliance selection, your captain needs to filter 60 teams by 'best climber who can also score in auto' in 10 seconds. A search and filter system turns your scouting dashboard from a data dump into a decision tool.

## Live Search by Team Number or Name
\`\`\`javascript
let allTeams = []; // populated from your data source

function filterTeams(query) {
  const q = query.toLowerCase().trim();
  if (!q) return allTeams;
  return allTeams.filter(t =>
    t.number.toString().includes(q) ||
    t.nickname.toLowerCase().includes(q)
  );
}

// Wire to input:
document.getElementById("searchBox").addEventListener("input", (e) => {
  const results = filterTeams(e.target.value);
  renderTeamList(results);
});
\`\`\`

## Multi-Criteria Filter Panel
\`\`\`javascript
// Read filter state from UI:
function getFilters() {
  return {
    minAvg:   parseFloat(document.getElementById("minAvg").value)   || 0,
    minAuto:  parseFloat(document.getElementById("minAuto").value)   || 0,
    climbMin: document.getElementById("climbFilter").value,  // "L2", "L3", etc.
    maxBreakdowns: parseInt(document.getElementById("maxBreakdowns").value) || 99,
  };
}

// Apply all filters:
function applyFilters(teams, filters) {
  return teams.filter(t => {
    if (t.avg < filters.minAvg) return false;
    if (t.avgAuto < filters.minAuto) return false;
    if (filters.climbMin !== "any") {
      const climbOrder = ["None","L1","L2","L3","L4"];
      if (climbOrder.indexOf(t.bestClimb) < climbOrder.indexOf(filters.climbMin)) return false;
    }
    if (t.breakdowns > filters.maxBreakdowns) return false;
    return true;
  });
}

// Re-render when any filter changes:
document.querySelectorAll(".filter-input").forEach(el => {
  el.addEventListener("change", () => {
    const filtered = applyFilters(allTeams, getFilters());
    renderTeamList(filtered);
  });
});
\`\`\`

## Sortable Columns
\`\`\`javascript
let sortKey = "avg";
let sortDir = -1; // -1 = descending, 1 = ascending

function sortTeams(teams) {
  return [...teams].sort((a, b) => (b[sortKey] - a[sortKey]) * sortDir);
}

// Column header click:
document.querySelectorAll("th[data-sort]").forEach(th => {
  th.addEventListener("click", () => {
    const key = th.dataset.sort;
    if (sortKey === key) sortDir *= -1; // toggle direction
    else { sortKey = key; sortDir = -1; }
    th.parentElement.querySelectorAll("th").forEach(h => h.classList.remove("sort-active"));
    th.classList.add("sort-active");
    renderTeamList(sortTeams(applyFilters(allTeams, getFilters())));
  });
});
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the climb filter comparison use an ordered array (climbOrder) rather than a direct string comparison?",opts:["Strings can't be compared","Climb levels are ordinal â€” L3 is higher than L2 even though string comparison would say L2 > L3 alphabetically; the ordered array converts each level to a numeric index that allows correct minimum-level filtering","Arrays are more efficient","Direct comparison doesn't work for strings"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does [...teams].sort() (spread into new array) accomplish that teams.sort() does not?",opts:["Spread creates a faster array","Array.sort() mutates the original array in place â€” spreading creates a copy so allTeams remains in its original order; the sort affects only the copy used for rendering, allowing re-sort and re-filter without corrupting the source data","Spread enables async sort","teams.sort() requires a comparator"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wi_export",title:"Exporting Scouting Data to CSV & PDF",est:"11 min",content:`## Your Data Needs to Leave the Browser\nThe alliance selection meeting happens on a laptop â€” not in a browser. The backup strategy for when the scouting app crashes is a printed CSV. Exporting in multiple formats makes your scouting system resilient.\n\n## CSV Export\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\nfunction exportCSV(teams, filename = "picklist.csv") {\n  // Define column order:\n  const headers = ["Team","Nickname","AvgTotal","AvgAuto","AvgCycles","BestClimb","Breakdowns"];\n\n  // Build rows:\n  const rows = teams.map(t => [\n    t.number,\n    \\\`"\\" + (t.nickname.replace(/"/g, '""')) + ""\\",  // escape quotes in names\n    t.avg.toFixed(1),\n    t.avgAuto.toFixed(1),\n    t.avgCycles.toFixed(1),\n    t.bestClimb,\n    t.breakdowns\n  ]);\n\n  const csv = [headers.join(\",\"), ...rows.map(r => r.join(\",\"))].join(\"\\\\n\");\n\n  // Trigger download:\n  const blob = new Blob([csv], { type: \"text/csv\" });\n  const url  = URL.createObjectURL(blob);\n  const a    = document.createElement(\"a\");\n  a.href     = url;\n  a.download = filename;\n  a.click();\n  URL.revokeObjectURL(url);\n}\n\n// Wire to button:\ndocument.getElementById(\"exportBtn\").addEventListener(\"click\", () => {\n  exportCSV(sortedTeams, \\"picklist_\\" + (eventKey) + "_\\" + (Date.now()) + ".csv\\");\n});\n\\"\\"\\"\n\n## Print-Optimized View\n\\"\\"\\"css\n@media print {\n  /* Hide interactive UI when printing: */\n  .filter-panel, .search-box, .export-btn, nav { display: none; }\n\n  /* Show print-specific layout: */\n  .team-card {\n    break-inside: avoid;    /* don\\"t split cards across pages */\n    border: 1px solid #000; /* borders visible when printed */\n    margin-bottom: 4px;\n  }\n\n  /* Print in black and white safely: */\n  .tier-high { background: #eee; }\n  .tier-mid  { background: #fff; }\n  .tier-low  { background: #ddd; }\n}\n\\"\\"\\"\n\n## Triggering Print\n\\"\\"\\"javascript\n// Print button:\ndocument.getElementById(\"printBtn\").addEventListener(\"click\", () => {\n  window.print();  // uses @media print CSS\n});\n\n// Print to PDF: user selects \"Save as PDF\" in the print dialog\n// â†’ gives you a fully formatted PDF without any library\n\\"\\"\\"`,quiz:[
      {q:"What does URL.revokeObjectURL(url) accomplish after triggering the CSV download?",opts:["It cancels the download","It releases the memory held by the object URL â€” createObjectURL allocates browser memory for the file; revoking after the download is triggered frees that memory; without this, each export would leak memory in a long-running session","It encrypts the file","It confirms the download succeeded"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does the @media print CSS use gray backgrounds instead of the color tier classes?",opts:["Color printing is slow","Color backgrounds often don't print unless 'Print background graphics' is enabled â€” gray shades reliably distinguish high/mid/low tiers in black-and-white print without requiring any user setting changes","Printers can't use CSS classes","Color is too expensive"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wi_pwa",title:"Progressive Web Apps â€” Add to Home Screen",est:"13 min",content:`## A Web App Scouts Can Install Like a Native App
A Progressive Web App (PWA) can be added to a phone's home screen, opens without a browser bar, caches assets for offline use, and feels like a real app. For a scouting tool, this means one-tap access during matches.

## The Two Required Files
\`\`\`
To become a PWA, you need:
  1. A Web App Manifest (manifest.json)
  2. A Service Worker (sw.js)
\`\`\`
\`\`\`json
// manifest.json â€” tells the browser about your app:
{
  "name": "Team 1234 Scout",
  "short_name": "Scout",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#1a1a2e",
  "theme_color": "#e63946",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "/icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "/icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
  ]
}
\`\`\`
\`\`\`html
<!-- Link in your HTML <head>: -->
<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.json">
<meta name="theme-color" content="#e63946">
\`\`\`

## Service Worker â€” Cache for Offline
\`\`\`javascript
// sw.js â€” runs in a background thread
const CACHE = "scout-v1";
const ASSETS = ["/", "/index.html", "/app.js", "/style.css", "/icon-192.png"];

// Install: cache all assets:
self.addEventListener("install", e => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then(c => c.addAll(ASSETS)));
});

// Fetch: serve from cache, fall back to network:
self.addEventListener("fetch", e => {
  e.respondWith(
    caches.match(e.request).then(cached => cached || fetch(e.request))
  );
});

// Register the service worker in your main JS:
if ("serviceWorker" in navigator) {
  navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js");
}
\`\`\`

## Testing PWA Install
\`\`\`
Chrome DevTools â†’ Application tab â†’ Manifest (check for errors)
                               â†’ Service Workers (check registered)

Install prompt on mobile:
  â†’ Android Chrome: "Add to Home Screen" appears automatically after 30 seconds
  â†’ iOS Safari: Share â†’ "Add to Home Screen" (manual)

For competition use: have scouts install before the event.
Once installed, the app works fully offline from the cached assets.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the purpose of the Service Worker's 'fetch' event handler in a PWA?",opts:["It handles form submissions","It intercepts all network requests and serves cached assets when available â€” this allows the app to function offline by returning cached HTML, JS, and CSS without any network connection; if the asset isn't cached, it falls back to the real network request","Service workers replace fetch()","It caches responses automatically"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should scouts install the PWA before the competition event rather than at the venue?",opts:["Installation requires internet","The initial installation and asset caching requires a network connection â€” once cached, the app works offline; installing at a venue with unreliable Wi-Fi risks incomplete caching; a pre-installed app has all assets ready before Wi-Fi becomes critical","Apps must be installed at home","Installation takes too long"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ SAFETY +6 (28â†’34) â”€â”€
LESSONS.safety.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sfb_shop_rules",title:"The 10 Non-Negotiable Shop Rules",est:"9 min",content:`## Rules Exist Because Someone Got Hurt
Every safety rule in a workshop traces back to an injury that didn't have to happen. These 10 rules aren't suggestions â€” they're the minimum standard for anyone entering a build space.

## The 10 Rules
\`\`\`
1. Safety glasses on before entering, on until you leave.
   â†’ Flying chips are unpredictable. "I was just watching" is not protection.

2. Closed-toe shoes. Always.
   â†’ Dropped tools and heavy parts fall on feet. Sandals are not allowed.

3. Tie back long hair and remove loose jewelry before any machine.
   â†’ Rotating equipment catches hair and bracelets in milliseconds.

4. No food or drink near electronics or power tools.
   â†’ Liquid + circuit = short. Spilled drink near the robot = expensive.

5. Never use a tool you haven't been trained on.
   â†’ One 5-minute demonstration before first use. Then you can use it.

6. Announce before starting loud equipment.
   â†’ "Starting the drill press!" gives everyone a chance to step clear.

7. Secure the workpiece before cutting or drilling.
   â†’ Clamp it or use a vise. Never hold with your hand against a spinning tool.

8. Clean up your workspace at the end of every session.
   â†’ Metal chips on the floor cause falls and tire punctures.
     Loose tools are tripping hazards and get lost.

9. Report every injury, no matter how minor.
   â†’ A small cut today tells us where the hazard is.
     An unreported hazard causes a worse cut next week.

10. When in doubt, stop and ask.
    â†’ No robot part is worth an injury. Ask a mentor.
\`\`\`

## Enforcement and Culture
\`\`\`
Rules only work with consistent enforcement:
  â†’ First violation: private reminder ("Hey, glasses?")
  â†’ Second violation: public reminder
  â†’ Third violation: leave the work area for the session

The person who enforces rules consistently
is more valuable to the team than the best builder.
A team where safety is everyone's responsibility
is safer than one where only the safety captain watches.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must safety glasses be worn throughout the entire shop session rather than only while actively using a tool?",opts:["Glasses fog up from heat","Flying chips, sparks, and debris travel unpredictably â€” someone cutting metal 10 feet away can send a chip to an unprotected eye of a nearby observer; the risk exists anywhere in the work area, not only at the tool being used","Safety glasses are required by FIRST","Constant wear is more convenient"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should minor injuries be reported even when they seem insignificant?",opts:["FIRST tracks injury statistics","A minor injury reveals an existing hazard â€” a small cut from a sharp edge means the edge is present and will cut the next person harder; reporting creates an opportunity to fix the hazard before it causes a serious injury","Reports protect mentors from liability","Minor injuries heal quickly"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfb_battery_care",title:"Battery Safety & Maintenance",est:"10 min",content:`## Your Battery Powers Everything â€” Including Failures
A failing battery doesn't just slow the robot. It causes brownouts that corrupt sensor data, behaves unpredictably during matches, and in severe cases poses fire and acid hazards. Proper maintenance is safety and performance.

## FRC Battery Maintenance
\`\`\`
Storage:
  â†’ Store upright in a dedicated battery tray â€” never on their side
  â†’ Keep at 50-80% charge for long-term storage (not fully charged, not dead)
  â†’ Storage temperature: 50-70Â°F (10-21Â°C) â€” not in a hot car trunk
  â†’ Never store multiple batteries stacked without trays (contact = short risk)

Charging:
  â†’ Use only FIRST-legal chargers at the correct rate (6A maximum)
  â†’ Never charge a battery above 13.8V on a lead-acid charger
  â†’ Never leave batteries charging overnight unattended
  â†’ Charge in an area with ventilation (sealed lead-acid vents hydrogen gas when overcharged)

Before each use â€” check:
  â†’ Open circuit voltage: 12.6-12.8V = fully charged, healthy
                          12.0-12.5V = partially charged
                          Below 12.0V = heavily discharged, may be damaged
  â†’ Internal resistance test (battery analyzer): < 20mÎ© = good
                                                 20-30mÎ© = aging, monitor
                                                 > 30mÎ© = replace

Signs a battery needs immediate retirement:
  â†’ Physical swelling or deformation of the case
  â†’ Voltage drops below 10V under match load (watch SmartDashboard during test)
  â†’ Internal resistance > 35mÎ© on analyzer
  â†’ Battery is > 4 years old (regardless of test results)
\`\`\`

## FTC Battery Safety (NiMH & LiFePO4)
\`\`\`
NiMH (Matrix/Tetrix):
  â†’ Never fully discharge (stops below 1.0V per cell)
  â†’ Use a matched charger only
  â†’ Storage at 60-70% charge

LiFePO4 (REV Slim, etc.):
  â†’ Safest lithium chemistry but still requires care
  â†’ Never puncture or compress
  â†’ Store at 3.2-3.3V per cell for long term
  â†’ If swelling occurs: isolate immediately, dispose properly (lithium battery recycling)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should FRC batteries not be stored at 100% charge for the off-season?",opts:["Full charge damages chargers","Lead-acid batteries stored fully charged for months undergo sulfation â€” lead sulfate crystals form on the plates, permanently reducing capacity; the 50-80% storage range minimizes this effect and extends battery life","100% storage causes fires","Full charge takes too long"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does an internal resistance reading above 30mÎ© on a battery analyzer indicate about a battery's fitness for competition?",opts:["The battery needs more charging","High internal resistance means the battery cannot deliver current efficiently â€” under match load, voltage drops faster and further than a healthy battery, causing brownouts that reset sensors and motor controllers mid-match; a > 30mÎ© battery should be removed from competition rotation","Internal resistance is a charger setting","30mÎ© is within the normal range"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sfa_competition",title:"Competition Safety â€” Pit & Field Protocols",est:"12 min",content:`## Competition Is the Highest-Risk Environment
More people, more robots, more time pressure. Injured people at competitions damage the team, affect other teams, and reflect on FIRST. Teams with deliberate competition safety protocols have far fewer incidents than teams who apply shop rules informally.

## Pit Safety Rules (Different from Shop)
\`\`\`
The pit is different from your shop:
  â†’ Smaller space, more people (team + visitors + volunteers)
  â†’ Robot on a stand at unusual angles
  â†’ Tools deployed in a small area with foot traffic

Specific pit rules:
  1. Robot stand always deployed when robot is above floor height
     â†’ Never hold the robot by hand while working underneath
  2. Power disconnected (battery removed) before reaching into the robot
  3. Bystanders behind the pit tape when robot is powered
  4. Announce "power on" before enabling the robot in the pit
  5. No running in the pit â€” ever
  6. Keep tools in your pit, not on the floor between pits
  7. Visitors: behind the front table unless invited in

Crowd control in the pit:
  â†’ Excited parents + curious visitors + 15-person team in a 10'Ã—10' space
     = someone gets hurt
  â†’ Designate one person per pit session as "pit traffic control"
     Their only job: manage who's in the pit and what they're doing
\`\`\`

## Field Safety During Matches
\`\`\`
Before queuing:
  â†’ Battery fully secured (check retention twice)
  â†’ All panels closed and latched
  â†’ Nothing loose in or on the robot that could fall during match

On the field:
  â†’ Drive team: stay behind the driver station barrier at all times
  â†’ Human player: follow field staff instructions exactly
  â†’ If the robot behaves unexpectedly: stop it immediately
    "I'd rather lose the match than have the robot hit someone"

After match loss (mechanical failure visible):
  â†’ Don't run onto the field until field staff signals it's safe
  â†’ Don't attempt to free a stuck robot by hand while field is active
  â†’ Report any field damage to the FTA (Field Technical Advisor) immediately

When the robot is being transported:
  â†’ Robot stand + carpet transport, not carried by hand
  â†’ Battery disconnected or bumper switch disabled during transit
  â†’ One person at each corner if carrying by hand is unavoidable
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a dedicated 'pit traffic control' person the most effective approach to pit crowd management at competitions?",opts:["Crowd control is required","Pit safety requires constant monitoring â€” everyone else in the pit is focused on the robot; a designated person with no other responsibility can consistently enforce the pit boundary, direct visitors, and prevent the gradual accumulation of people that creates unsafe conditions","Traffic control requires training","Visitors cause most injuries"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a drive team stop a malfunctioning robot and accept a match loss rather than continuing to operate it?",opts:["Match losses are acceptable","An unpredictable robot creates hazards for field staff, opposing teams, and game pieces â€” a stopped robot is a known state; a malfunctioning robot still being driven is an unpredictable hazard whose next behavior cannot be controlled; safety overrides match outcome","Matches can be replayed","Field staff will stop the match"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS +6 (22â†’28) â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_notebook2",title:"Engineering Notebook â€” Daily Habits",est:"12 min",content:`## The Notebook Nobody Keeps Is Useless at Award Time
Engineering notebooks submitted for awards are often filled in the week before submission from memory â€” and judges can tell. An authentic notebook built through daily habits over the season is richer, more specific, and far more credible.

## The 10-Minute Daily Log Habit
\`\`\`
At the end of every build session (10 minutes, one person per subteam):
  Date: January 18, 2025
  Present: 8 members (list names or count)
  Completed: Prototype intake roller #2 â€” 12mm compliant wheel, 200rpm
  Data collected: Tested 3 game pieces. Pickup rate: 8/10 from carpet, 6/10 from tile
  Decision: Switched from 12mm to 16mm wheel â†’ more compliance, better grip on tile
  Next session goal: Repeat test with 16mm wheel, target 9/10 on tile

This takes 10 minutes. After 6 weeks, you have 30 entries â€”
more evidence than most teams produce in a full season.
\`\`\`

## What Makes an Entry "Engineering Evidence"
\`\`\`
Not evidence (narrative):
  "Today we worked on the intake. We tried a few things and figured out
   what worked better."

Evidence:
  "We tested 3 configurations of our ball intake. Configuration A (12mm wheel,
   single stage) scored 4/10 on carpet in 30 seconds. Configuration B (16mm
   wheel, single stage) scored 7/10. Configuration C (16mm, dual stage)
   scored 9/10. Selected Configuration C for prototype build."

The difference: testable claim vs outcome vs decision.
An evaluator can repeat the test to verify the claim.
\`\`\`

## Digital vs Physical Notebooks
\`\`\`
Physical:
  âœ“ Handwritten = authentic dates (hard to retroactively fill in)
  âœ“ Easy to sketch and annotate photos
  âœ— Not searchable, harder to back up

Digital (Google Docs / Notion):
  âœ“ Searchable, shareable, easy to paste screenshots and data
  âœ“ Automatic date stamps (Google Docs revision history)
  âœ— Easier to fill in retroactively (judges may be skeptical)

Hybrid (best for most teams):
  Physical daily logs during session â†’ digital compilation for submission
  Physical dates are authentic; digital format is submission-ready
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What three elements transform a narrative notebook entry into engineering evidence?",opts:["Date, time, and team members","A testable claim (the setup and what was measured), a quantified outcome (the data collected), and a decision (what was chosen based on that data) â€” entries with all three allow an evaluator to verify the work was real and understand the reasoning","Sketches, photos, and text","Test number, team name, and result"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is a physical daily log considered more authentic than a digital equivalent for engineering notebook submissions?",opts:["Judges prefer paper","Handwritten entries with physical dates are difficult to retroactively fabricate â€” the ink and date sequence demonstrates real-time documentation; digital entries can be back-dated or filled in later without evidence, making their authenticity harder to verify","Physical notebooks are required","Digital logs are not accepted"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awi_interview2",title:"Handling Unexpected Judge Questions",est:"11 min",content:`## You Will Be Asked Something You Didn't Prepare For
The best award interviews feel like conversations. That means judges will go off-script. Teams that have only memorized their prepared presentation freeze when the judge takes a different direction. Teams that understand their programs deeply handle anything.

## The Four Hardest Questions (and How to Answer Them)
\`\`\`
"What would you do differently?"
  Wrong: "Nothing â€” we're proud of everything we did"
  Wrong: "We'd have more time" (not actionable)
  Right: be specific about one real limitation:
    "Our mentoring sessions were inconsistent in the first half of the year â€”
     we didn't have a standard structure. We created a template in January
     and the sessions improved significantly. Next year we'd implement
     that structure from September."

"How do you know your outreach is working?"
  Wrong: "We can feel the impact"
  Right: describe a concrete measurement:
    "We follow up with schools 6 months after our first visit.
     3 of 8 schools we visited in 2024 have since started new robotics clubs.
     We track this in a spreadsheet and report it annually."

"What's unique about your team?"
  Wrong: "We're passionate about STEM"
  Right: one specific, verifiable thing:
    "We're the only team in our district that has a bilingual scouting app â€”
     our scouts can enter data in English or Spanish. 30% of our students
     speak Spanish at home; this made scouting accessible to all of them."

"Why does FIRST need your team?"
  Wrong: "We help spread FIRST's mission"
  Right: name the specific gap you fill:
    "Without us, the three FLL teams we mentor would have no technical support.
     The nearest other team is 45 miles away."
\`\`\`

## When You Don't Know the Answer
\`\`\`
The honest answer is better than a wrong confident one:
  "I don't have that number with me, but I can tell you approximately..."
  "That's a great question â€” I'd have to check our records for the exact figure"
  "I'm not the person who runs that program â€” [name] leads it.
   I can answer for what I personally know."

Never: make up a number and state it confidently.
Judges often know the right answer. Being caught inventing data
destroys credibility for everything else you said.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'We'd have more time' a poor answer to 'what would you do differently?'",opts:["Time is always scarce","It's not actionable â€” every team wants more time; a useful answer identifies a specific decision, process, or approach that could be changed, demonstrating genuine reflection on what went wrong and what the team learned","Time management isn't relevant","The question asks about budget"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the correct approach when a judge asks about a specific number or fact you don't have memorized?",opts:["Give a confident estimate","Acknowledge you don't have the exact figure, provide what you do know approximately, and offer to follow up if appropriate â€” making up a number that's later discovered to be wrong destroys your credibility for the entire presentation","Redirect to a different topic","Only captains should answer factual questions"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Advanced.push(
  {id:"awa_essay",title:"Impact Award Essay â€” Structure & Common Mistakes",est:"14 min",content:`## The Essay Is Read Before You Enter the Room
Judges read Impact submissions the night before or morning of the event. Your essay shapes their expectations, questions, and first impressions. A well-structured essay makes the interview easier â€” the judge already knows what's impressive and wants to hear more.

## The Essay Structure That Works
\`\`\`
Section 1: Mission statement (2-3 sentences)
  â†’ What problem does your team address?
  â†’ Don't start with "Team 1234 was founded in..."
  â†’ Start with the impact: "In a county where only 12% of students have
    access to STEM enrichment programs, Team 1234 has reached 847 students
    across 14 Title I schools in the past three years."

Section 2: Three flagship programs (one paragraph each)
  â†’ Program name + specific numbers + outcome
  â†’ "Our FLL Mentorship Program supports 4 teams at elementary schools..."
  â†’ Each paragraph: what it is, who it serves, what changed because of it

Section 3: Sustainability (1 paragraph)
  â†’ What happens if your team disappears next year?
  â†’ "Three of the programs we started operate independently â€”
    teachers we trained now run the programs without us."

Section 4: Looking forward (1 paragraph)
  â†’ Next season's specific plan
  â†’ Shows the judges this isn't the end of the story

Total: 1,200-1,500 words for FRC Impact (check current year limit)
\`\`\`

## The Five Most Common Essay Mistakes
\`\`\`
1. Starting with team history instead of impact
   Fix: put the most impressive thing first

2. Vague numbers: "hundreds of students" / "many events"
   Fix: always use the specific number ("847 students, 18 events")

3. Describing activities instead of outcomes:
   "We visited 6 schools and showed students our robot"
   Fix: "We visited 6 schools; 2 of those schools now have robotics clubs"

4. Passive voice that hides student action:
   "Programs were created and events were organized"
   Fix: "Our students designed, ran, and evaluated each program"

5. Saying everything is amazing with no specificity:
   "Our incredible team achieved tremendous impact across many dimensions"
   Fix: one concrete story with a specific person or place is more
        convincing than five superlatives
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should an Impact essay start with the team's impact rather than its founding history?",opts:["History is less interesting","Judges read many submissions; the first sentence determines whether they continue reading with interest or duty â€” an immediate impressive impact claim hooks attention; founding history context can come later after the reader is already engaged","History violates essay rules","Impact statements are required first"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the difference between describing an activity and describing an outcome in an Impact essay?",opts:["Outcomes are always numbers","An activity describes what was done ('we visited 6 schools'); an outcome describes what changed because of it ('2 of those schools now have robotics clubs'); judges evaluate impact, not effort â€” what you did is only evidence if it produced a measurable change","Activities should be removed","Outcomes require judge verification"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ GIT +6 (21â†’27) â”€â”€
LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_submodule",title:"Git Submodules for Shared Libraries",est:"11 min",content:`## When Multiple Robot Projects Share Code
If your team maintains a shared scouting library, utility functions, or game-year code that multiple projects use, a Git submodule embeds one repository inside another â€” keeping the shared code in sync across projects without copying it.

## Adding a Submodule
\`\`\`bash
# Add a shared library repo as a submodule in the scouting project:
git submodule add https://github.com/team1234/scout-utils lib/scout-utils
# Creates: .gitmodules file + lib/scout-utils directory tracked as a pointer

# Commit the addition:
git commit -m "chore: add scout-utils as submodule"

# When cloning a repo WITH submodules:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/team1234/scouting-app
# OR if already cloned:
git submodule update --init --recursive
\`\`\`

## Updating a Submodule to Latest
\`\`\`bash
# Go into the submodule:
cd lib/scout-utils
git pull origin main

# Return to parent repo, stage the updated pointer:
cd ../..
git add lib/scout-utils
git commit -m "chore: update scout-utils to latest"
git push

# All team members: after pulling, update submodules:
git pull
git submodule update --recursive
\`\`\`

## When to Use Submodules vs Copying Files
\`\`\`
Use submodules when:
  â†’ The shared code is maintained independently with its own git history
  â†’ Multiple projects NEED the same version of the shared code
  â†’ You want updates in the library to be deliberately opted into

Just copy files when:
  â†’ The shared code is small and rarely changes
  â†’ You don't need version synchronization across projects
  â†’ The overhead of submodule management exceeds the benefit

Submodule gotchas:
  â†’ Forgetting --recurse-submodules on clone â†’ empty submodule directory
  â†’ Submodule update not run after pull â†’ stale submodule code
  â†’ Both are common sources of "why does this work on your machine but not mine?"
\"\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does 'git submodule update --init --recursive' do for a freshly cloned repository?",opts:["It updates git itself","It initializes and fetches the content of all submodules â€” cloning a parent repo doesn't automatically download submodule contents; without this command, submodule directories are empty and code referencing them fails to compile","It creates new submodules","It pushes submodule changes"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the key risk of using submodules for frequently updated shared code?",opts:["Submodules can't be updated","Team members who pull the parent repo but don't run submodule update will have stale submodule code that doesn't match the current pointer â€” this causes 'works on my machine' failures that can be hard to diagnose without knowing submodules are involved","Submodules reduce performance","Submodule history is deleted"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"gi_log",title:"Git Log â€” Reading History Like a Detective",est:"10 min",content:`## The Commit History Tells You What Changed and When
When something breaks and you need to find when it was introduced, or when you need to understand why a decision was made, git log is your time machine. Knowing how to query it turns a vague bug into a specific commit in minutes.

## Essential Log Commands
\`\`\`bash
# Standard one-line log:
git log --oneline
# a3f92b1 feat(vision): add AprilTag targeting
# 7c44d02 tune(arm): kP 0.007 â†’ 0.009
# 1a8b3d4 fix(auto): correct heading after crossing midfield

# With diff stats (what files changed):
git log --oneline --stat

# Filter by author:
git log --oneline --author="Alex"

# Filter by date:
git log --oneline --since="2025-01-15" --until="2025-02-01"

# Filter by file:
git log --oneline -- src/main/java/frc/robot/Constants.java

# Search commit messages:
git log --oneline --grep="arm"      # all commits mentioning "arm"
git log --oneline --grep="kP"       # all tuning commits

# Show what actually changed in a commit:
git show a3f92b1                    # full diff
git show a3f92b1 --stat             # just file names
\`\`\`

## The Bug Hunt Workflow
\`\`\`bash
# "The arm oscillates now but it didn't at competition"
# Competition was tagged: competition-2025-02-22

# 1. What changed between then and now?
git log --oneline competition-2025-02-22..HEAD -- src/main/java/

# Output:
# 9b2a1c3 tune(arm): increase kP 0.008 â†’ 0.011
# 4f7d8e1 feat(arm): add gravity feedforward
# d2a9b3c fix(arm): clamp output to [-0.8, 0.8]

# 2. Which change most likely caused oscillation? Probably kP increase.
# 3. See exactly what changed:
git show 9b2a1c3

# 4. Either revert to competition constants:
git checkout competition-2025-02-22 -- src/main/java/frc/robot/Constants.java
# Or use bisect to confirm which commit broke it.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does 'git log --oneline -- src/main/java/frc/robot/Constants.java' show?",opts:["The full contents of Constants.java","Only the commits that touched the Constants.java file â€” useful for finding when a specific constant was changed without searching through commits that affected other files","The current value of constants","All changes to the java directory"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is a competition tag the ideal starting point for a bug hunt using git log?",opts:["Tags are always bug-free","A competition tag marks a known-good state â€” filtering commits between the tag and HEAD shows exactly what changed since the robot last worked correctly, narrowing the search from all commits in history to only the relevant candidates","Tags contain test results","All bugs occur after competitions"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ga_hooks",title:"Git Hooks for Automated Quality Checks",est:"12 min",content:`## Run Checks Before Bad Code Reaches the Repo
Git hooks are scripts that run automatically at specific points in the git workflow â€” before a commit, before a push, after checkout. A pre-commit hook that runs the build and fails if it doesn't compile prevents broken code from ever being committed.

## Pre-Commit Hook (FRC Gradle)
\`\`\`bash
# .git/hooks/pre-commit (make this file executable: chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit)
#!/bin/bash
echo "Running pre-commit checks..."

# Build the robot code:
cd robot/ && ./gradlew build --quiet
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "âŒ Build failed â€” commit blocked. Fix errors before committing."
  exit 1
fi

# Check for TODO/FIXME left in robot code (optional):
if grep -r "FIXME" src/main/java/ --quiet; then
  echo "âš ï¸  FIXME comments found. Resolve or remove before committing."
  exit 1
fi

echo "âœ… Pre-commit checks passed."
exit 0
\`\`\`

## Pre-Push Hook (Python Scouting)
\`\`\`bash
# .git/hooks/pre-push
#!/bin/bash
echo "Running tests before push..."

cd scouting/ && python -m unittest discover -q
if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "âŒ Tests failed â€” push blocked."
  exit 1
fi

echo "âœ… All tests passed. Pushing..."
exit 0
\`\`\`

## Sharing Hooks With the Team
\`\`\`bash
# .git/hooks/ is NOT tracked by git (each clone gets fresh empty hooks/).
# Solution: store hooks in a tracked directory, then install them.

# Store hooks in:
repo/
  hooks/
    pre-commit   â† tracked in git, shareable
    pre-push     â† tracked in git, shareable

# Install script (run once after cloning):
#!/bin/bash
# install-hooks.sh
cp hooks/pre-commit .git/hooks/pre-commit
cp hooks/pre-push   .git/hooks/pre-push
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit .git/hooks/pre-push
echo "Hooks installed."

# Add to README: "Run ./install-hooks.sh after cloning"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why are git hooks stored in the hooks/ directory of the repository rather than directly in .git/hooks/?",opts:[".git/hooks is easier to find","The .git directory is not tracked by git â€” hooks placed there exist only on one machine and aren't shared when others clone the repository; a tracked hooks/ directory lets the team maintain consistent hooks in version control, with an install script to copy them to .git/hooks/ on each machine","Hooks must be in a tracked directory","The .git directory has permission restrictions"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does returning exit code 1 from a pre-commit hook script accomplish?",opts:["It creates an error log","It causes git to abort the commit â€” any non-zero exit code signals failure to git, which blocks the commit from proceeding; exit code 0 signals success and allows the commit to continue","It sends an email notification","It deletes the staged changes"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ FUNDRAISING +6 (22â†’28) â”€â”€
LESSONS.fundraising.Beginner.push(
  {id:"fb_pitch",title:"The 60-Second Sponsorship Pitch",est:"10 min",content:`## You'll Have One Minute â€” Make It Count
A team member runs into a local business owner at a community event. They have 60 seconds before the person needs to leave. A student who can deliver a crisp, compelling 60-second pitch converts that random encounter into a follow-up conversation. A student who rambles about FIRST's mission for three minutes does not.

## The Pitch Formula
\`\`\`
[Who we are] (10 seconds)
  "We're Team 1234, a student robotics team from Lincoln High School."

[What we do that's impressive] (15 seconds)
  "We compete in FIRST Robotics â€” 600 teams nationally. This year we
   qualified for the World Championship."

[The community connection] (15 seconds)
  "Beyond competing, we run robotics programs at 4 elementary schools â€”
   we reached 300 kids last year who'd never touched a robot before."

[The ask] (10 seconds)
  "We're looking for local companies to sponsor us â€” as little as $500
   gets your logo on the robot."

[The leave-behind] (10 seconds)
  "Can I email you our sponsor packet? Here's my card."
\`\`\`

## Practicing the Pitch
\`\`\`
Practice it aloud â€” not in your head.
The first 5 times will feel awkward. By the 10th, it flows naturally.

Practice scenarios:
  â†’ Parent of a student you don't know: how do you explain the team?
  â†’ A business owner at a community fair
  â†’ A relative at a family gathering ("so what's this robot thing?")
  â†’ A teacher from another school

What to practice adjusting:
  â†’ The "impressive thing" changes: competition result, outreach number,
    an award won â€” always lead with the best current news
  â†’ The ask adjusts to the audience: a small business owner hears "$500";
    a large company contact hears "we have sponsorship levels starting at $1,500"

Red flags in your pitch:
  â†’ Explaining FIRST acronyms (FRC/FTC) to someone who doesn't know them
  â†’ More than 3 sentences before the "impressive thing"
  â†’ Forgetting to ask for anything at the end
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should the 'impressive thing' come within the first 25 seconds of a sponsorship pitch?",opts:["Pitches must be short","Listeners decide in the first 15-30 seconds whether to stay engaged or politely disengage â€” leading with an impressive, concrete fact (World Championship qualification, 300 students reached) earns the listener's continued attention; building up to it at the end means most listeners have already checked out","The ask must always come first","FIRST recommends this order"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does the pitch end with 'Can I email you our sponsor packet?' rather than immediately asking for a commitment?",opts:["Email is more formal","Most people won't commit money in a 60-second encounter â€” the email packet continues the conversation in writing where the person can review details on their own time; asking for an email address is a low-friction yes that keeps the relationship open","Packets are required by FIRST","Commitments can't be made verbally"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fb_auction",title:"Running a Silent Auction Fundraiser",est:"12 min",content:`## Silent Auctions Raise More Per Item Than Retail
A dinner for two at a local restaurant costs the restaurant $80. At your auction, it sells for $120 â€” because bidders compete and the social context increases perceived value. The restaurant gets exposure; you get more than the item's cost.

## Item Sourcing (6 Weeks Before)
\`\`\`
Best items (high perceived value, easy to get):
  â†’ Local restaurant gift cards or dining experiences
  â†’ Sports team tickets (contact front office â€” many have community donation programs)
  â†’ Hotel one-night stay (front desk manager can often approve)
  â†’ Local experiences: winery tour, cooking class, kayak rental
  â†’ Services: professional photo session, home cleaning, oil change
  â†’ Student-created: robot art, custom framed team photo, painted robot part

How to ask for donations:
  In person > phone > email (in person converts ~3Ã— better)
  Specific request: "Could you donate a $50 gift card?"
  What they get: tax deduction receipt, name in program, social media mention

Documentation for each item:
  â†’ Item description, donor name, fair market value
  â†’ Restrictions (expiration date, blackout dates, geographic limits)
  â†’ Starting bid = 40-50% of fair market value
  â†’ Buy-It-Now price = 110-120% of fair market value (optional but drives urgency)
\`\`\`

## Running the Auction at the Event
\`\`\`
Setup (1 hour before opening):
  â†’ Number each item (1-N, large visible number)
  â†’ Bid sheet under each item: Item name, value, min bid, increments, BID HERE lines
  â†’ Bid increment: $5 for items under $50; $10 for $50-$200; $25 for $200+
  â†’ Rope or table setup so bidders can walk past without crowding

During bidding (90-120 minutes):
  â†’ Announce "30 minutes left" and "10 minutes left" loudly
  â†’ Final 5 minutes: have a volunteer stand at the highest-value items
    â†’ Creates excitement and prevents last-second disputes

Closing:
  â†’ Announce "bidding is now closed" clearly
  â†’ Pull bid sheets immediately after closing
  â†’ Enter winners into a simple spreadsheet while they pay
  â†’ Cash/check/Venmo â€” set up before the event, not during
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do auction items often sell for above retail price when the same item could be bought elsewhere for less?",opts:["Auctions have higher prices by default","The competitive bidding context and social setting increase perceived value â€” bidders compete emotionally, value the unique access (you can't just walk in and get restaurant tickets), and the event atmosphere makes spending feel different than a normal purchase","Donors overprice their items","Bidders don't know retail prices"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the purpose of setting a starting bid at 40-50% of fair market value?",opts:["To make items look cheaper","A starting bid that's too high discourages initial bids â€” no first bid means no bidding war; starting low creates easy first bids, which triggers the commitment and competition that drives the price up; the auction mechanism handles price discovery","Starting bids are tax-deductible","Low starting bids prevent disputes"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ ELECTRICAL +6 (58â†’64) â”€â”€
LESSONS.electrical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"eb_pwm",title:"PWM Signals â€” How Robot Control Works",est:"11 min",content:`## Every Servo and Most Motor Controllers Speak PWM
Pulse Width Modulation is how the robot brain communicates with motors and servos. Understanding what a PWM signal actually is â€” not just calling setPower() â€” helps you debug signal problems and understand why certain wiring practices matter.

## What PWM Is
\`\`\`
PWM = Pulse Width Modulation
A digital signal that switches rapidly between HIGH and LOW.
The ratio of HIGH time to total period encodes the value.

              â”Œâ”€â”€â”           â”Œâ”€â”€â”
              â”‚  â”‚           â”‚  â”‚
â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜  â””â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”˜  â””â”€â”€
              â”‚â—„â”€â–ºâ”‚
         pulse width

Period (T): time for one complete cycle
  â†’ Most servo/ESC PWM: T = 20ms (50Hz)

Duty cycle: pulse width / period Ã— 100%
  Duty cycle controls output:
    25%  = LOW output (motor reverse or servo CCW)
    50%  = neutral / stop
    75%  = HIGH output (motor forward or servo CW)

In practice, servo/ESC uses pulse width in microseconds:
  1000 Î¼s = min (motor reverse / servo CCW)
  1500 Î¼s = neutral
  2000 Î¼s = max (motor forward / servo CW)
\`\`\`

## Why PWM Wire Length and Quality Matters
\`\`\`
PWM signal wires are low-current signal lines (not power wires).
They carry a 3.3V or 5V digital pulse that must arrive clean.

Problems caused by poor PWM wiring:
  â†’ Noise pickup from motor power cables nearby â†’ servo jitter or ESC fault
  â†’ Wire too long â†’ signal degrades, motor controller may see invalid pulse
  â†’ Poor connector â†’ intermittent connection â†’ random motor shutoff

Best practices:
  â†’ Keep PWM signal wires away from motor power wires
  â†’ Use shielded cable for long PWM runs (> 30cm)
  â†’ Route PWM cables along the frame, not floating loose
  â†’ Keep PWM connectors seated and locked at both ends

Diagnosing a PWM problem:
  â†’ Servo jitters without command â†’ noise injection from nearby motor wires
    Fix: reroute, add ferrite bead on signal wire
  â†’ Motor randomly stops â†’ intermittent PWM connection
    Fix: reseat connectors, inspect for bent pins
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does a 1500 microsecond pulse width command to a standard PWM servo or ESC?",opts:["Full forward speed","The neutral or center position â€” for a servo, this is typically the mechanical center; for an ESC controlling a brushed motor, this is stopped; the 1000-2000Î¼s range represents the full command range with 1500Î¼s as the midpoint","Full reverse speed","The minimum position"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should PWM signal wires be routed away from motor power wires?",opts:["They carry different voltages","Motor power wires carry high currents that rapidly change direction, creating electromagnetic fields â€” these fields induce noise on nearby signal wires; the noise looks like a legitimate PWM pulse variation, causing servos to jitter or motor controllers to receive invalid commands","PWM wires are fragile","Signal and power wires use incompatible connectors"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"eb_can2",title:"CAN Bus Basics for FTC",est:"10 min",content:`## FTC's Growing CAN Ecosystem
FTC teams using REV hardware have access to CAN bus through the REV Control Hub and Expansion Hub. CAN-enabled devices (like the REV Smart Robot Servo and certain sensors) offer faster communication and better feedback than standard PWM or analog connections.

## How CAN Bus Works
\`\`\`
CAN (Controller Area Network): a two-wire differential bus
  CAN-High and CAN-Low carry the signal differentially
  â†’ Noise on one wire appears on both â†’ difference remains clean
  â†’ Allows much longer wire runs than single-ended signals
  â†’ Multiple devices share the same two wires (bus topology)

Each device has a CAN ID (address, 0-127):
  â†’ No two devices on the same bus can share an ID
  â†’ REV Control Hub auto-assigns IDs in some configurations
  â†’ Conflicts: two devices with the same ID = bus errors for both

CAN bus in FTC:
  â†’ REV Control Hub â†” Expansion Hub: uses CAN internally (RS485)
  â†’ REV Smart Robot Servo (SRS): can communicate over CAN for position feedback
  â†’ External CAN devices: some sensors and motor controllers support CAN
\`\`\`

## Practical CAN Wiring for FTC
\`\`\`
Standard REV RS485/CAN connector:
  â†’ Uses a 4-wire JST-PH connector: GND, VCC, CAN-H, CAN-L
  â†’ Daisy-chain topology: Hub â†’ Device 1 â†’ Device 2 (not star topology)
  â†’ Termination resistors: REV hubs have built-in termination
    â†’ Don't add external 120Î© resistors unless explicitly required

Wire length:
  â†’ Maximum practical length per segment: ~1 meter in an FTC robot
  â†’ Use the shortest path â€” don't route wire in large loops

Diagnosing CAN issues:
  â†’ Error in Driver Hub: "COMM Error" on CAN device â†’ loose connector or ID conflict
  â†’ Device not showing in hardware config â†’ CAN connection not established
  â†’ Intermittent errors â†’ connector not fully seated, check clip engagement
  â†’ All devices offline â†’ check RS485 cable from Control Hub to Expansion Hub
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does CAN bus (differential signaling) reject electrical noise better than a single-ended signal wire?",opts:["CAN uses thicker wire","Noise appears equally on both CAN-H and CAN-L wires â€” the receiver subtracts one from the other, so common-mode noise cancels out; only the intended difference signal remains; single-ended signals have no such noise rejection and read any induced noise as part of the signal","CAN uses shielded cable only","Differential signals travel faster"],ans:1},
      {q:"What happens when two CAN devices on the same bus are accidentally assigned the same ID?",opts:["The newer device overwrites the older","Both devices respond simultaneously when the shared ID is addressed, causing their signals to collide on the bus â€” this creates bus errors for both devices and may corrupt communication for other devices on the same bus","One device automatically changes its ID","The bus stops all communication"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.electrical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ei_power_dist",title:"Power Distribution & Fusing Strategy",est:"14 min",content:`## Every Circuit Needs the Right Fuse
A fuse protects the wire, not the device. The fuse must blow before the wire can overheat â€” which means fuse rating must be appropriate for the wire gauge being protected, not just the device's normal current draw.

## Wire Gauge vs Maximum Fuse Size
\`\`\`
AWG â†’ safe fuse maximum (in a robot environment):
  6 AWG  â†’ 50-60A  (main power from battery)
  10 AWG â†’ 30A     (large motor circuits)
  12 AWG â†’ 20A     (medium motor circuits)
  14 AWG â†’ 15A     (smaller mechanisms, sensors)
  18 AWG â†’ 10A     (servos, sensors, logic)
  22 AWG â†’ 3-5A    (signal wires, low-current sensors)

Rule: if the fuse blows repeatedly at rated current,
      don't increase the fuse â€” increase the wire gauge.
      The fuse is telling you the circuit is undersized.
\`\`\`

## FRC Power Distribution Panel (PDP/PDH) Layout
\`\`\`
Channels and their typical assignments:
  40A (large) channels: drive motors (these draw 40A+ at stall)
  30A channels:         arm/elevator motors
  20A channels:         intake, shooter, climber motors
  20A regulated:        robot controller, VRM (5V/12V regulated)
  10A:                  sensors, cameras, co-processors

Layout best practices:
  â†’ Drive motors near the battery terminals (shortest high-current path)
  â†’ Route positive and negative wires for each circuit together
    (reduces magnetic loop area â†’ less noise)
  â†’ Label every channel on the PDP with a label maker
    â†’ "RF Drive", "LF Drive", "Arm", etc.
    â†’ During competition pit work, unlabeled channels cost time

Voltage sag calculation:
  Total current draw = sum of all active consumers
  V_sag = I_total Ã— R_battery_internal
  A healthy 18Ah battery: ~15mÎ© internal resistance
  At 100A total draw: V_sag = 100 Ã— 0.015 = 1.5V â†’ robot sees ~10.5V
  â†’ Plan: limit total simultaneous peak current
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a repeatedly-blown fuse be replaced with larger wire rather than a larger fuse?",opts:["Larger fuses are expensive","A fuse blowing repeatedly means the wire is carrying more current than it's rated for â€” the fuse is correctly protecting the wire; installing a larger fuse removes the protection and allows the wire to overheat, melt insulation, and potentially start a fire","Fuses are designed to be replaced","Wire upgrades require rewiring"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should positive and negative wires for the same circuit be routed together rather than separately?",opts:["It's neater","Running the supply and return wires together minimizes the area of the magnetic loop they form â€” a large loop acts as an antenna that both radiates electromagnetic interference and picks up noise from other circuits; tight wire pairs minimize this loop and reduce both emission and susceptibility","Separate routing causes shorts","Together routing satisfies inspection"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.strategy.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sb_cycles",title:"Understanding Cycle Time & Its Impact on Scoring",est:"11 min",content:`## Cycle Time Is the Core Performance Metric
Every game comes down to: how quickly can your robot complete the fundamental scoring action? A robot that scores once every 20 seconds vs once every 12 seconds doesn't just score faster â€” it scores 67% more in the same period. Small cycle time differences compound across a 2:15 match.

## Measuring Cycle Time
\`\`\`
Cycle = intake â†’ travel â†’ score â†’ return â†’ repeat

Measure from: moment the robot contacts a game piece at the intake
Measure to:   moment the robot contacts the next game piece

FRC example timing (typical 2-piece auto):
  Pickup:     1.5 seconds
  Travel:     2.0 seconds (across field)
  Score:      1.5 seconds (aim + release)
  Return:     2.0 seconds
  Total:      7.0 seconds / cycle = ~8 cycles in 60s teleop

At 4 pts/cycle: 32 pts
Same robot at 5.5-second cycle: ~10 cycles â†’ 40 pts (+25%)

The 1.5-second improvement comes from:
  â†’ Faster drivetrain: 0.5s savings on travel
  â†’ Faster intake: 0.5s savings on pickup
  â†’ Auto-aim: 0.5s savings on scoring
\`\`\`

## Cycle Time vs Mechanism Complexity
\`\`\`
A simpler robot often has a faster cycle time:
  â†’ Less state transitions to manage
  â†’ Fewer ways for the operator to make mistakes
  â†’ More reliable (fewer things to break)

A complex robot can have a faster cycle time IF:
  â†’ Automation removes operator delays
  â†’ Multi-function mechanisms eliminate travel steps
  â†’ All mechanisms work reliably in matches (not just in the shop)

Scout observation: measure cycle time for each team you scout.
Count cycles visible in match video, divide by teleop time.
This is more predictive of their alliance value than peak scores.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a 1.5-second cycle time improvement produce a disproportionately large increase in match score?",opts:["Faster cycles earn bonus points","Cycle time is multiplicative â€” a 1.5-second improvement on a 7-second cycle is a 21% reduction, which enables roughly 21% more cycles in the same time window; each additional cycle earns full game piece points, so the improvement compounds across the entire 2:15 match","Faster cycles are worth more points","Time improvements only affect auto"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is average cycle time a better predictor of alliance value than a team's peak match score?",opts:["Peak scores are inaccurate","Cycle time reflects a repeatable, systematic capability â€” peak scores can result from unusual field conditions or opponent behavior; a team that consistently completes 8 cycles per match at 4 pts each is more predictable and reliable than a team that occasionally scores 50 pts but averages 28","Alliance picks require cycle time","Peak scores require more matches to evaluate"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sb_autonomous",title:"Autonomous Strategy â€” More Than Just Points",est:"12 min",content:`## Auto Sets the Match Tone
A successful autonomous doesn't just score â€” it positions your robot advantageously for teleop, avoids collisions with alliance partners, and ideally contributes to ranking point triggers. Teams that think about auto holistically score more in both periods.

## The Auto Value Framework
\`\`\`
Evaluate every autonomous routine on four dimensions:

1. Raw points scored
   â†’ How many game piece / location points?
   â†’ Every auto point is worth 1.5Ã— in ranking because auto is shorter

2. Ranking Point contribution
   â†’ Does this auto help trigger the auto RP?
   â†’ Coordinate with alliance partners on who covers which RP threshold

3. Ending position for teleop
   â†’ Where does the robot end the auto period?
   â†’ Does that position give a fast first-cycle advantage?
   â†’ Or does it require traveling far before first teleop score?

4. Alliance partner compatibility
   â†’ Do your auto paths conflict?
   â†’ Which alliance member runs first? (heading toward same source)
   â†’ Can both partners run their best auto simultaneously?
\`\`\`

## Pre-Match Auto Coordination
\`\`\`
30-second pre-match alliance conversation:
  Captain to partners: "We run red-side 2-piece. We start near the speaker.
                        We end near the amp. Does either of you need that area?"

  If conflict: "We can run 1-piece instead to give you the center path"
  â†’ A clean 2+2 piece auto from both partners > one 3-piece and one collision

  After the conversation:
    â†’ Driver/operator confirm which auto routine is selected before enabling
    â†’ Say it out loud: "Center 2-piece loaded." â†’ partner confirms: "Got it."
    â†’ This takes 15 seconds and prevents the most common auto mistake
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is an autonomous point multiplied as '1.5Ã— in ranking' compared to teleop?",opts:["Auto points are worth more","The auto period is approximately 15 seconds vs 135 seconds for teleop â€” points scored in 1/9th of the match time have dramatically higher points-per-second value; every auto point that could alternatively be a teleop point takes ~6Ã— longer to earn in teleop on a per-second basis","Auto has a scoring multiplier","Ranking systems value auto differently"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does a '2+2 piece auto from both partners' outperform 'one partner running 3-piece'?",opts:["More pieces are always better","Two consistent 2-piece autos eliminate the risk of inter-robot collision while reliably scoring 4 game pieces total; one robot attempting 3-piece often sacrifices consistency and occupies space that prevents the second partner from running any auto at all","3-piece auto is illegal","Two autos score bonus points"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.strategy.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"si_pit_scouting",title:"Pit Scouting â€” Reading Robots Before They Play",est:"13 min",content:`## Pit Information Predicts Match Performance
Match scouting shows you what a robot did. Pit scouting shows you what a robot can do â€” and, importantly, what it can't. A robot that looks great in matches but has a cracked frame, no spare gearboxes, and an overwhelmed team is a riskier pick than its scores suggest.

## What to Observe in the Pit
\`\`\`
Robot physical condition:
  â†’ Does the robot look carefully built or hastily assembled?
  â†’ Are there obvious repairs or structural cracks visible?
  â†’ How is the wiring organized â€” clean and bundled, or loose and exposed?
  â†’ Are bumpers properly attached and compliant?

Team condition:
  â†’ How does the team respond when their robot breaks? (calm vs panic)
  â†’ Are there spare parts visible (spare motors, gearboxes, PCBs)?
  â†’ Is the pit organized (tools easy to find) or chaotic?
  â†’ How many people are actively working vs standing around?

Questions to ask (be brief, they're busy):
  "What does your robot do best?"
  "Any mechanisms you're still working through?"
  "What's your autonomous strategy?"
  "What starting position do you typically run?"
\`\`\`

## Interpreting What You See
\`\`\`
Green flags (good pick indicators):
  â†’ Well-organized pit, spare parts visible
  â†’ Team discusses robot failures calmly and has a plan
  â†’ Clear answer to "what do you do best" without hesitation
  â†’ Robot looks the same as in match video (no emergency mods)

Yellow flags (investigate further):
  â†’ Major modifications mid-event (could be improvements or desperate fixes)
  â†’ Robot not yet repaired from a previous match breakdown
  â†’ Team seems uncertain about their robot's capabilities

Red flags (reconsider picking):
  â†’ No spare parts, team is scrambling for help from other teams
  â†’ Evasive answers about what the robot can do
  â†’ Structural damage with no clear repair plan
  â†’ "We're still figuring out the controls" at an elimination event
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the presence of visible spare parts in a pit suggest a team is a safer alliance pick?",opts:["Spare parts mean more budget","A team with organized spare parts anticipated failure modes and prepared â€” this reflects systematic thinking about reliability; when their robot inevitably breaks during eliminations, they can repair it quickly; a team with no spares hopes nothing breaks and may be unable to continue if something does","Spare parts indicate experience only","Teams with spare parts don't break down"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a calm, organized team response to a robot breakdown during competition indicate about their reliability as an alliance partner?",opts:["They break down more often","A calm response demonstrates practiced procedures and experience with failures â€” teams that stay organized under breakdown pressure fix robots faster and are less likely to forfeit an elimination match due to panic or disorganization; breakdown composure is a leading indicator of elimination reliability","Calm teams perform worse","Breakdowns disqualify teams from selection"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.mechanical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"mb_tolerances2",title:"Fit Types â€” Press, Clearance & Running Fits",est:"12 min",content:`## Two Parts That Need to Fit Have Different Requirements
A bearing pressed into a bore shouldn't fall out, but it also shouldn't require a sledgehammer. A shaft through a hole that needs to spin freely shouldn't bind. Fit type determines exactly how much bigger or smaller each part should be â€” by tenths of a millimeter.

## The Three Fit Categories
\`\`\`
Clearance fit (shaft smaller than hole):
  â†’ Shaft can slide or rotate freely through the hole
  â†’ Used for: bearing outer race in a housing that must be removable,
              pivot pin in a hole, shaft through a non-rotating spacer
  â†’ Typical clearance for aluminum: 0.1-0.3mm (bore = 10.1-10.3mm for 10mm shaft)

Transition fit (shaft nominally same size as hole):
  â†’ Might be slightly loose or slightly tight depending on tolerance
  â†’ Used for: locating features that need to align precisely but be disassembled
  â†’ Typical: Â±0.05mm (could slide in or require gentle press)

Interference fit / press fit (shaft larger than hole):
  â†’ Shaft must be forced in â€” creates holding force through elastic deformation
  â†’ Used for: bearing inner race on a shaft, permanent sub-assembly connections
  â†’ Typical interference for aluminum: 0.05-0.15mm (shaft = 10.05-10.15mm for 10mm bore)
  â†’ Too much interference: part splits or cracks; too little: slips under load
\`\`\`

## Practical Examples for FIRST Robots
\`\`\`
REV hex shaft (5/16" hex) in a REV hex hub:
  â†’ Hex geometry provides torque transmission; fit is clearance
  â†’ Shaft slides in and out easily â†’ intentional, retained by collar

Bearing (8mm ID) pressed onto a 8mm shaft:
  â†’ Light interference (~0.05mm) â†’ requires arbor press to install
  â†’ Should not slip under motor torque; should require press to remove

Wheel hub bolted to sprocket:
  â†’ Clearance fit on bolt holes â†’ bolts provide clamping, not fit
  â†’ Tight enough to align; loose enough to assemble by hand

3D-printed bore fit recommendations:
  â†’ FDM printing tends to make bores smaller than designed (shrinkage)
  â†’ Add 0.2mm to bore diameter for clearance-fit shafts
  â†’ Add 0.1mm for press-fit shafts (part will shrink onto them)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a bearing outer race need a light interference fit in its housing rather than a clearance fit?",opts:["Interference makes assembly easier","A clearance fit would allow the bearing to rotate in the housing rather than only rotating internally â€” if the outer race spins in the bore, it wears both the bearing seat and the housing quickly; an interference fit locks the outer race so all rotation happens at the balls and inner race where it's designed to occur","Clearance fits cause corrosion","Interference fits are required by bearing manufacturers"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should FDM 3D-printed bore diameters be designed 0.2mm larger than the target shaft for a clearance fit?",opts:["FDM materials expand when heated","FDM bores consistently print slightly smaller than designed due to material shrinkage and the finite resolution of layer-by-layer deposition â€” designing to nominal results in a fit that's tighter than intended; the 0.2mm addition compensates for this systematic error","0.2mm is the standard tolerance","FDM parts must always be oversized"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.mechanical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"mi_pneumatics2",title:"Pneumatic Systems â€” Design & Sizing",est:"15 min",content:`## Pneumatics Give You Fast, High-Force Linear Motion
An air cylinder extends in 50-100 milliseconds with hundreds of pounds of force â€” faster than any motor-driven mechanism can match. For game pieces requiring a sudden high-force action (punching, clamping, latching), pneumatics are often the right choice.

## System Components and Layout
\`\`\`
FRC pneumatics (CTRE/REV legal):
  Compressor â†’ Storage tank â†’ Pressure regulator â†’ Solenoid valve â†’ Cylinder

  Compressor: fills system when pressure below threshold (~115 PSI)
  Storage tank: legal to run one (holds reserve for multiple actuations)
  Pressure regulator: reduces 115 PSI stored â†’ 60 PSI working pressure
  Solenoid valve: electrically controlled valve (single or double acting)
    Single: spring returns to default when unpowered
    Double: stays in last position when unpowered (power required to extend AND retract)
  Cylinder: converts air pressure to linear force

Pressure relief valve: REQUIRED at storage tank â†’ vents at 125 PSI
\`\`\`

## Cylinder Sizing â€” Force Calculation
\`\`\`
Force (lbs) = Pressure (PSI) Ã— Area (inÂ²)
Area = Ï€ Ã— (bore diameter / 2)Â²

At 60 PSI working pressure:
  1.5" bore cylinder: F = 60 Ã— Ï€ Ã— (0.75)Â² = 60 Ã— 1.77 = 106 lbs
  2.0" bore cylinder: F = 60 Ã— Ï€ Ã— 1.0Â²   = 60 Ã— 3.14 = 188 lbs
  2.5" bore cylinder: F = 60 Ã— Ï€ Ã— 1.5625Â² = 60 Ã— 4.91 = 295 lbs

Note: retraction force is less (rod area reduces piston area)
  1.5" bore, 5/8" rod: retract area = Ï€Ã—(0.75Â² - 0.3125Â²) = 1.46 inÂ²
  Retract force = 60 Ã— 1.46 = 88 lbs

Size the cylinder for worst-case load + 30% safety margin.
\`\`\`

## Speed and Flow Control
\`\`\`
Too fast: cylinder slams into hard stop â†’ impacts damage cylinder and frame
Too slow: mechanism misses timing window during match

Flow control (needle valve on exhaust side of solenoid):
  â†’ Restricts how fast air escapes â†’ controls cylinder speed
  â†’ Always restrict the exhaust, not the supply
    Restricting supply = reduced force AND reduced speed (wrong)
    Restricting exhaust = full force, controlled speed (right)

Target extension time: 100-300ms for most robot applications
Set flow control: start fully open â†’ tighten gradually until target speed
Check at full system pressure (not low pressure during bench testing)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a double-acting solenoid valve hold its position when unpowered, while a single-acting solenoid does not?",opts:["Double-acting uses more power","A single-acting solenoid uses a spring to return to default position â€” the spring force retracts the cylinder when power is removed; a double-acting solenoid has no spring, relying on a second air port for retraction â€” it holds wherever the last power state left it until powered again in either direction","Double-acting solenoids are newer","Spring return is more reliable"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should flow control (speed limiting) restrict the exhaust side rather than the supply side of a cylinder?",opts:["Exhaust valves are cheaper","Restricting the supply reduces both force and speed â€” the cylinder has lower pressure available throughout its stroke; restricting the exhaust maintains full supply pressure (full force) and only slows the cylinder by limiting how fast air escapes the opposite chamber, preserving force while controlling speed","Exhaust restriction is more precise","Supply restriction causes valve damage"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"mi_wheels",title:"Wheel Selection â€” Grip, Omni & Mecanum",est:"13 min",content:`## The Wrong Wheels Ruin an Otherwise Good Drivetrain
High-traction wheels on a 4-wheel skid steer make turning nearly impossible. Omni wheels on a 2-wheel drive provide zero lateral force. Understanding the geometry of force transmission determines which wheel type belongs where.

## Wheel Type Comparison
\`\`\`
Standard (colson, rubber, traction):
  â†’ Grip in all directions â€” can't slide laterally
  â†’ High static friction â†’ robot doesn't get pushed around easily
  â†’ Turning: requires wheels to scrub sideways (resistance)
  â†’ Best for: 4-wheel drive with turning via differential (speed difference)
              West Coast Drive center modules (where lateral force is needed)

Omni wheel (rollers around circumference):
  â†’ Drives forward/backward with full traction
  â†’ Slides laterally freely (low resistance)
  â†’ Turning: very easy â€” no scrubbing
  â†’ Best for: corners of a 6-wheel drive (with traction center wheels)
              swerve drive (allows rotation without resisting translation)

Mecanum wheel (angled rollers):
  â†’ Drives in any direction including diagonal without rotation
  â†’ Each wheel generates force at 45Â° from drive direction
  â†’ Requires all 4 wheels powered and independently controlled
  â†’ Best for: tanks that need lateral movement without rotating
  â†’ Limitation: diagonal force vectors make defense/pushing poor

Anti-tip wheels (omnis in the rear, traction in front):
  â†’ Allows rotation around front wheels without rear dig
\`\`\`

## The 6-Wheel Drive Layout
\`\`\`
Most common FRC configuration:
  â† Front omni â†’
  â† Center traction â†’ (dropped 1/8" below others)
  â† Rear omni â†’

Why this works:
  â†’ Center traction wheels: provide forward grip and resistance to being pushed
  â†’ Front and rear omni: freely scrub sideways during turning
  â†’ 1/8" center drop: robot pivots on center wheels â†’ even less turning resistance

Center drop amount: 1/8" for most robots
  Too little: still scrubs too much
  Too much: only center wheels contact the floor â†’ unstable

For carpet: 1/8" nominal
For polished floors (off-season events): may need 3/16"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do omni wheels placed at the corners of a 6-wheel drive reduce turning resistance?",opts:["Omni wheels have less rolling resistance","During a turn, the front and rear wheels must scrub laterally while the robot rotates about its center â€” traction wheels resist this lateral motion with high friction; omni wheels have free-rolling side rollers that eliminate the lateral scrub, allowing the robot to turn with much less motor effort","Corner wheels don't contribute to turning","Omni wheels generate more grip"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does mecanum drive perform poorly when another robot pushes it sideways?",opts:["Mecanum robots are lighter","Mecanum's angled rollers, which enable lateral movement, also allow lateral forces from opposing robots to freely translate the robot sideways â€” the same roller geometry that generates lateral motion when driven also accepts lateral force without resistance; traction wheels lock in all directions except forward/back","Mecanum robots are slower","Pusher robots target mecanum specifically"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
