LESSONS.python.Beginner.push(
  {id:"pyb_tuples",title:"Tuples â€” Immutable Data You Can Trust",est:"9 min",content:`## When Your Data Shouldn't Change
A Python list can be accidentally modified anywhere in your code. A tuple cannot â€” once created, its contents are fixed. For robot constants, scouting field definitions, and coordinate pairs, tuples communicate intent: this data is permanent.

## Tuples vs Lists
\`\`\`python
# List (mutable):
speeds = [0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0]
speeds[0] = 0.4  # allowed

# Tuple (immutable):
AUTO_WAYPOINTS = (0.0, 3.0, 6.5, 9.2)
AUTO_WAYPOINTS[0] = 1.0  # TypeError: tuple object does not support item assignment

# Tuple syntax: parentheses (often optional) with commas
point = (3.5, 7.2)     # (x, y)
color = 255, 128, 0    # also a tuple â€” parens optional
single = (42,)         # single-element: trailing comma required

# Tuples support all read operations:
x, y = point           # tuple unpacking
first = AUTO_WAYPOINTS[0]
last  = AUTO_WAYPOINTS[-1]
subset = AUTO_WAYPOINTS[1:3]  # returns a tuple
length = len(AUTO_WAYPOINTS)
\`\`\`

## Named Tuples for Readable Structured Data
\`\`\`python
from collections import namedtuple

# Without namedtuple: hard to remember what index 2 means
match = (1234, 15, 6, 3)
print(match[2])  # is this cycles? climb? nobody knows

# With namedtuple: fields have names
MatchResult = namedtuple("MatchResult", ["team", "auto_pts", "cycles", "climb_pts"])

m = MatchResult(team=1234, auto_pts=15, cycles=6, climb_pts=3)
print(m.cycles)     # 6 â€” readable
print(m.auto_pts)   # 15
print(m.team)       # 1234

# Named tuples are immutable like regular tuples
# They also print nicely: MatchResult(team=1234, auto_pts=15, cycles=6, climb_pts=3)

# List of match results:
results = [
    MatchResult(1234, 15, 6, 3),
    MatchResult(5678, 8,  4, 0),
]
best_auto = max(results, key=lambda r: r.auto_pts)
print(best_auto.team)  # 1234
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why are tuples preferable to lists for robot constants like waypoint coordinates?",opts:["Tuples use less memory","Tuples are immutable â€” they cannot be accidentally modified anywhere in the codebase; using a list for constants allows any function to accidentally append, overwrite, or delete values, while a tuple communicates that this data is fixed and makes such modification impossible","Tuples are faster to iterate","Lists don't support coordinates"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does tuple unpacking (x, y = point) accomplish in one line?",opts:["It converts a tuple to a list","It assigns each element of the tuple to a separate variable simultaneously â€” x receives the first element and y receives the second; this is cleaner than x = point[0]; y = point[1] and communicates that the variables are related as a pair","It creates a copy of the tuple","Unpacking only works with two-element tuples"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"pyb_sets",title:"Sets â€” Fast Membership Testing and Deduplication",est:"9 min",content:`## When You Need Unique Items or Fast Lookups
A Python set is an unordered collection with no duplicates. Looking up whether a team number is in a set of 200 teams takes the same time as looking it up in a set of 2 â€” unlike a list, which searches every element. Sets are the right tool for team rosters, seen-team tracking, and event overlap analysis.

## Set Basics
\`\`\`python
# Create a set:
registered_teams = {1234, 5678, 9012, 3456}

# Add and remove:
registered_teams.add(7890)
registered_teams.discard(9012)  # remove if present (no error if missing)
registered_teams.remove(5678)   # remove â€” raises KeyError if missing

# Membership test (O(1) â€” same speed regardless of size):
if 1234 in registered_teams:
    print("Team 1234 is registered")

# Deduplication (remove duplicates from a list):
raw_scout_data = [1234, 5678, 1234, 9012, 5678, 1234]
unique_teams = list(set(raw_scout_data))
# [1234, 5678, 9012] â€” order not guaranteed

# Size:
len(registered_teams)
\`\`\`

## Set Operations for Event Analysis
\`\`\`python
event_a_teams = {1234, 5678, 9012, 3456, 7890}
event_b_teams = {9012, 3456, 1111, 2222, 7890}

# Teams at both events (intersection):
both = event_a_teams & event_b_teams
# {9012, 3456, 7890}

# Teams at either event (union):
either = event_a_teams | event_b_teams
# {1234, 5678, 9012, 3456, 7890, 1111, 2222}

# Teams only at event A (difference):
only_a = event_a_teams - event_b_teams
# {1234, 5678}

# Teams at exactly one event (symmetric difference):
exclusive = event_a_teams ^ event_b_teams
# {1234, 5678, 1111, 2222}

# Practical use: which of our scouted teams appear at the next event?
scouted = {1234, 5678, 9012, 4321}
next_event = {9012, 4321, 7777, 8888, 5555}
already_know = scouted & next_event   # {9012, 4321}
need_to_scout = next_event - scouted  # {7777, 8888, 5555}
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'if team in my_set' faster than 'if team in my_list' when the collection has 500 elements?",opts:["Sets are stored in RAM","Sets use hash tables that compute a location directly from the value â€” checking membership is O(1) regardless of set size; lists must check each element sequentially making membership O(n); for 500 items, the set approach is approximately 500Ã— faster in the worst case","Sets have a faster syntax","Lists require sorting before lookup"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the set difference operation (event_a_teams - event_b_teams) return?",opts:["The larger set minus the smaller","Only the elements in the first set that are NOT in the second set â€” teams exclusive to event A; elements present in both sets are excluded from the result","All elements from both sets","Elements in the second set only"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

  {id:"pi_dataclass2",title:"Dataclasses â€” Clean Data Models for Scouting",est:"12 min",content:`## Replace Dictionaries With Structured Classes
A dictionary of scouting data works until you misspell a key, forget a field, or try to sort a list of them. Dataclasses give you the structure of a class â€” type hints, default values, comparison methods â€” with almost no boilerplate.

## Basic Dataclass
\`\`\`python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class ScoutEntry:
    team_number:  int
    match_number: int
    auto_pts:     float
    teleop_cycles: int
    climb_level:  str            # "None", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4"
    notes:        str = ""       # default value
    breakdown:    bool = False   # default value

# Creating entries:
e1 = ScoutEntry(1234, 15, 12.0, 6, "L3")
e2 = ScoutEntry(team_number=5678, match_number=15,
                auto_pts=8.0, teleop_cycles=4,
                climb_level="None", breakdown=True)

# Accessing fields (no ['key'] syntax â€” uses attribute access):
print(e1.team_number)   # 1234
print(e1.auto_pts)      # 12.0
e1.notes = "Very fast intake"  # mutable by default
\`\`\`

## Advanced: Computed Properties and Validation
\`\`\`python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from functools import cached_property

CLIMB_PTS = {"None": 0, "L1": 2, "L2": 4, "L3": 6, "L4": 10}

@dataclass
class ScoutEntry:
    team_number:   int
    match_number:  int
    auto_pts:      float
    teleop_cycles: int
    climb_level:   str = "None"
    cycle_pts:     int = 4       # pts per cycle (may vary by game)

    def __post_init__(self):
        # Validation runs after __init__:
        if self.climb_level not in CLIMB_PTS:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid climb level: {self.climb_level}")

    @property
    def total_pts(self) -> float:
        return self.auto_pts + (self.teleop_cycles * self.cycle_pts) + CLIMB_PTS[self.climb_level]

# Use:
e = ScoutEntry(1234, 15, 12.0, 6, "L3")
print(e.total_pts)  # 12.0 + 24 + 6 = 42.0

# Sort a list of entries:
entries = [ScoutEntry(1234, 15, 12.0, 6, "L3"),
           ScoutEntry(5678, 15, 8.0, 4, "None")]
sorted_entries = sorted(entries, key=lambda e: e.total_pts, reverse=True)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does the __post_init__ method accomplish in a dataclass that a regular class __init__ cannot do more simply?",opts:["It runs after the file loads","It adds validation and computed setup after the auto-generated __init__ sets all fields â€” without __post_init__, validation would require writing the entire __init__ manually; __post_init__ lets the dataclass handle field assignment while you add only the extra logic you need","It creates read-only fields","It converts field types automatically"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is e1.auto_pts preferable to e1['auto_pts'] for accessing scouting data?",opts:["Attribute access is faster","Attribute access on a dataclass field generates a clear AttributeError if the field doesn't exist; a dictionary silently returns None for a misspelled key like e1['auto_pst'], which propagates a wrong value through the entire calculation without any immediate error signal","Dictionaries require string keys","Dataclasses don't support bracket syntax"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"pi_tba2",title:"TBA API in Python â€” Bulk Data Processing",est:"13 min",content:`## Python Unlocks Full Event Analysis
The Blue Alliance API returns data for entire seasons â€” every match, every team, every event. Python's requests library and data tools let you pull a full season's worth of match data and compute statistics that no scouting app could produce in real time.

## Setup and Auth
\`\`\`python
import requests
import os

TBA_BASE = "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3"
TBA_KEY  = os.environ.get("TBA_KEY")  # export TBA_KEY=yourkey

def tba_get(endpoint: str) -> dict | list:
    url = f"{TBA_BASE}{endpoint}"
    resp = requests.get(url, headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": TBA_KEY}, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()
\`\`\`

## Getting All Matches for an Event
\`\`\`python
def get_event_matches(event_key: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Returns all qualification matches for an event, sorted by match number."""
    matches = tba_get(f"/event/{event_key}/matches")
    qual = [m for m in matches if m["comp_level"] == "qm"]
    return sorted(qual, key=lambda m: m["match_number"])

def compute_team_stats(event_key: str) -> dict:
    """Compute per-team stats from match score breakdowns."""
    matches = get_event_matches(event_key)
    stats = {}

    for match in matches:
        breakdown = match.get("score_breakdown") or {}
        for alliance in ["red", "blue"]:
            teams = match["alliances"][alliance]["team_keys"]
            score = match["alliances"][alliance]["score"]

            for team_key in teams:
                t = team_key.replace("frc", "")
                if t not in stats:
                    stats[t] = {"scores": [], "wins": 0, "matches": 0}
                stats[t]["scores"].append(score)
                stats[t]["matches"] += 1

    # Compute averages:
    for t, s in stats.items():
        s["avg"] = sum(s["scores"]) / len(s["scores"]) if s["scores"] else 0
        s["max"] = max(s["scores"]) if s["scores"] else 0

    return dict(sorted(stats.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]["avg"], reverse=True))

# Usage:
stats = compute_team_stats("2025casd")
for team, data in list(stats.items())[:10]:
    print(f"Team {team:5s}: avg={data['avg']:.1f}  max={data['max']}")
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is os.environ.get('TBA_KEY') used instead of hardcoding the API key in the Python file?",opts:["Environment variables are faster","An API key in source code is readable by anyone with access to the file â€” including in git history even after deletion; environment variables are set on the machine running the script and are not stored in the codebase, preventing accidental exposure in version control","The key changes frequently","Python can't process string keys"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does resp.raise_for_status() accomplish in the TBA API wrapper function?",opts:["It prints the response status","It raises an HTTPError exception if the response code indicates failure (4xx or 5xx) â€” without it, a failed request returns a response object that looks successful until you try to parse JSON from an error message body, causing confusing downstream errors","It caches successful responses","It validates the JSON format"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"pi_multiprocess",title:"Multiprocessing â€” Parallel Scouting Data Pulls",est:"12 min",content:`## Fetching 60 Teams One at a Time Is Slow
A sequential loop fetching data for 60 teams at 200ms each takes 12 seconds. A parallel pool of 10 workers fetches all 60 in about 1.5 seconds â€” because each request waits on the network, not the CPU. Python's multiprocessing and concurrent.futures make this straightforward.

## ThreadPoolExecutor for Network Requests
\`\`\`python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed
import requests

TBA_KEY = "yourkey"
TBA_BASE = "https://www.thebluealliance.com/api/v3"

def fetch_team(team_key: str) -> dict:
    url = f"{TBA_BASE}/team/{team_key}/simple"
    resp = requests.get(url, headers={"X-TBA-Auth-Key": TBA_KEY}, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    data = resp.json()
    return {"key": team_key, "nickname": data["nickname"], "city": data.get("city", "")}

def fetch_all_teams(team_keys: list[str], max_workers: int = 10) -> list[dict]:
    results = []
    errors  = []

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=max_workers) as executor:
        future_to_key = {executor.submit(fetch_team, k): k for k in team_keys}

        for future in as_completed(future_to_key):
            key = future_to_key[future]
            try:
                results.append(future.result())
            except Exception as e:
                errors.append({"key": key, "error": str(e)})
                print(f"Warning: failed to fetch {key}: {e}")

    if errors:
        print(f"{len(errors)} teams failed to fetch")
    return sorted(results, key=lambda t: int(t["key"].replace("frc","")))

# Usage:
team_keys = [f"frc{n}" for n in [1234, 5678, 9012, 3456, 7890]]
teams = fetch_all_teams(team_keys)
\`\`\`

## When to Use Threads vs Processes
\`\`\`python
# Use ThreadPoolExecutor when:
#   â†’ I/O bound: waiting for network, files, databases
#   â†’ GIL doesn't matter (thread is sleeping while waiting for network)

# Use ProcessPoolExecutor when:
#   â†’ CPU bound: heavy computation, data processing
#   â†’ You want true parallelism that bypasses Python's GIL

from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

def compute_elo(team_data: dict) -> dict:
    # Expensive CPU calculation â€” process pool is appropriate
    # ... long computation ...
    return {"team": team_data["key"], "elo": result}

# For CPU work:
with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=4) as pool:
    futures = [pool.submit(compute_elo, t) for t in teams]
    elo_results = [f.result() for f in futures]
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is ThreadPoolExecutor appropriate for TBA API requests but ProcessPoolExecutor is better for heavy computation?",opts:["Threads are always faster","Network requests spend most of their time waiting for the server â€” threads release the GIL while waiting, so multiple threads genuinely run concurrently; heavy computation holds the GIL, preventing true thread parallelism â€” processes have separate GILs and achieve real CPU parallelism","ProcessPoolExecutor doesn't support I/O","Threads can't make HTTP requests"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does as_completed() do that iterating over the futures list directly cannot?",opts:["It sorts results by speed","as_completed() yields each future as it finishes, allowing results to be processed immediately without waiting for all requests to complete â€” iterating the list directly would wait for futures in submission order, blocking on slow requests even if faster ones already have results","as_completed filters errors","Direct iteration loses results"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

  {id:"pa_cli",title:"Building CLI Tools for Robot Analysis",est:"13 min",content:`## Give Your Analysis Tools a Professional Interface
A Python script that takes hardcoded variables and requires editing the source code to change parameters is a script. A script that uses argparse to accept command-line arguments is a tool â€” one anyone on the team can run without reading the code.

## Argparse Basics
\`\`\`python
import argparse

def make_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Analyze TBA event data and generate pick list",
        formatter_class=argparse.ArgumentDefaultsHelpFormatter
    )
    p.add_argument("event_key",
                   help="TBA event key (e.g. 2025casd)")
    p.add_argument("-t", "--top",
                   type=int, default=20,
                   help="Number of teams to display")
    p.add_argument("-s", "--sort-by",
                   choices=["avg", "max", "auto"],
                   default="avg",
                   help="Metric to sort by")
    p.add_argument("-o", "--output",
                   type=str, default=None,
                   help="Write results to this CSV file")
    p.add_argument("-v", "--verbose",
                   action="store_true",
                   help="Print extra debug information")
    return p

def main():
    args = make_parser().parse_args()

    if args.verbose:
        print(f"Fetching data for event: {args.event_key}")

    # Use args.event_key, args.top, args.sort_by, args.output
    # ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
\`\`\`

## Running and Getting Help
\`\`\`bash
# Positional argument required, rest are optional:
python analyze.py 2025casd
python analyze.py 2025casd --top 10 --sort-by auto
python analyze.py 2025casd -t 15 -s max -o picklist.csv
python analyze.py 2025casd --verbose

# Auto-generated help:
python analyze.py --help
# usage: analyze.py [-h] [-t TOP] [-s {avg,max,auto}] [-o OUTPUT] [-v] event_key
# Analyze TBA event data and generate pick list
# ...
\`\`\`

## Subcommands for Multi-Purpose Tools
\`\`\`python
p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Scouting tools")
sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

# 'scout' subcommand:
scout_p = sub.add_parser("scout", help="Record a match")
scout_p.add_argument("team", type=int)
scout_p.add_argument("match", type=int)

# 'report' subcommand:
report_p = sub.add_parser("report", help="Generate report")
report_p.add_argument("event_key")
report_p.add_argument("--format", choices=["csv","json","text"], default="text")

args = p.parse_args()
if args.command == "scout":
    run_scout(args.team, args.match)
elif args.command == "report":
    run_report(args.event_key, args.format)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What advantage does argparse provide over hardcoding parameters at the top of a script?",opts:["argparse is faster to execute","argparse generates a documented interface â€” any team member can run the tool with --help to understand all options without reading source code; parameters can be changed at runtime without editing the file, and invalid inputs produce clear error messages rather than cryptic runtime failures","argparse validates data types automatically","Hardcoded parameters are less readable"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does action='store_true' accomplish for a flag argument like --verbose?",opts:["It stores the string 'True'","It sets the argument's value to the boolean True when the flag is present and False when absent â€” no value needs to follow the flag; this creates an on/off toggle that controls behavior without requiring the user to type --verbose=True","It requires True or False after the flag","It makes the argument required"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"pa_testing",title:"Unit Testing Robot Analysis Code",est:"14 min",content:`## Code You Can't Test Is Code You Can't Trust
A scouting algorithm that calculates OPR wrong gives your strategy team incorrect data. Unit tests verify that your calculations are correct â€” and keep them correct when you change the code later. Writing tests before competition prevents the worst analysis bugs from reaching the pit.

## The unittest Framework
\`\`\`python
import unittest
from analysis import compute_team_avg, compute_opr, filter_by_climb

class TestTeamStats(unittest.TestCase):

    def setUp(self):
        # Runs before each test method:
        self.entries = [
            {"team": "1234", "total_pts": 40, "auto": 12, "climb": "L3"},
            {"team": "1234", "total_pts": 52, "auto": 15, "climb": "L3"},
            {"team": "1234", "total_pts": 38, "auto": 10, "climb": "L2"},
        ]

    def test_average_correct(self):
        avg = compute_team_avg(self.entries, metric="total_pts")
        self.assertAlmostEqual(avg, 43.33, places=1)

    def test_average_empty_list(self):
        result = compute_team_avg([], metric="total_pts")
        self.assertEqual(result, 0.0)

    def test_filter_by_climb_level(self):
        l3_entries = filter_by_climb(self.entries, min_level="L3")
        self.assertEqual(len(l3_entries), 2)
        for e in l3_entries:
            self.assertIn(e["climb"], ["L3", "L4"])

    def test_filter_no_match(self):
        l4_entries = filter_by_climb(self.entries, min_level="L4")
        self.assertEqual(l4_entries, [])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()
\`\`\`

## Running Tests
\`\`\`bash
# Run all tests in a file:
python -m unittest test_analysis.py -v

# Run all tests in the project:
python -m unittest discover -v

# Run a specific test:
python -m unittest test_analysis.TestTeamStats.test_average_correct

# Check test coverage:
pip install coverage
coverage run -m unittest discover
coverage report -m     # shows which lines are NOT tested
\`\`\`

## What to Test First (Highest Value)
\`\`\`
Test these before anything else:
  1. Edge cases: empty list, single entry, missing fields
  2. Known correct values: compute avg for [40, 52, 38] â†’ 43.33
  3. Boundary conditions: exactly-L3 climb should/shouldn't pass filter
  4. Data transformations: TBA JSON â†’ your dataclass â†’ correct fields

Don't test:
  â†’ Network calls (mock those instead)
  â†’ The exact format of print output
  â†’ Third-party library behavior (they test themselves)

Test naming: test_what_when_result
  â†’ test_average_empty_list_returns_zero
  â†’ test_filter_l3_excludes_l2_entries
  Clear names make failing tests self-documenting.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should edge cases (empty list, missing fields) be tested before typical cases?",opts:["Edge cases are more common","Edge cases are the most frequent source of production bugs â€” typical cases are usually thought through during development; an empty list passed to an average function, or a team with no recorded matches, are conditions that appear in real competition and cause crashes if untested","Edge cases are simpler to test","Typical cases don't need testing"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does setUp() in a unittest.TestCase class accomplish?",opts:["It imports test dependencies","It runs before every individual test method, creating fresh test data â€” this prevents tests from sharing state and affecting each other; a test that modifies the entries list won't corrupt the data for the next test because setUp rebuilds it fresh each time","It initializes the test file once","It defines which tests to run"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.electrical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"eb_connectors",title:"Connector Types â€” Choosing and Using Correctly",est:"11 min",content:`## The Right Connector for the Job
Using a 10A connector on a 40A motor circuit will melt it. Using a high-current connector on a 1A sensor is wasteful and makes a harder-to-service harness. Matching connector type to current requirement is fundamental electrical practice.

## Common FRC/FTC Connectors
\`\`\`
Anderson Powerpole (APP):
  â†’ Current ratings: 15A, 30A, 45A (color-coded housings)
  â†’ Use: battery connectors, PDH outputs, high-current circuits
  â†’ FRC: main battery connector uses 2Ã— 45A Powerpoles
  â†’ Assembly: crimp contact, slide into housing â€” no polarity key (CAUTION)
  â†’ Polarity: housing MUST be oriented correctly â€” check against known good connector
  â†’ Common error: reversed polarity â€” adds smoke

Anderson SB50 / SB120:
  â†’ Current ratings: 50A / 120A
  â†’ Use: very high current runs (main power, custom power supplies)
  â†’ Assembly: crimp or bolt terminal

XT30 / XT60 / XT90 (FTC and custom):
  â†’ XT30: 30A continuous  XT60: 60A  XT90: 90A
  â†’ Polarized by design: male and female shapes differ
  â†’ Assembly: solder (gold contacts)
  â†’ FTC: REV battery uses XT30; many FTC custom circuits use XT60

JST-PH / JST-XH (signal and low-current):
  â†’ JST-PH: 2A maximum â€” sensors, small servos, signal wiring
  â†’ JST-XH: similar, larger pitch â€” motor encoder connections
  â†’ Assembly: use the matching crimper (a wrong crimper damages the contacts)
  â†’ Polarity: keyed housing â€” physically impossible to reverse (usually)
\`\`\`

## Connector Assembly Best Practices
\`\`\`
Before assembling any connector:
  â†’ Verify you have the correct contact for the housing (same family, same gauge)
  â†’ Strip exactly the right length: too short â†’ weak crimp; too long â†’ short risk
  â†’ Crimp with the correct tool (each connector family needs its own tool)

After assembly:
  â†’ Tug test: pull the wire firmly â€” the contact should not pull back out
  â†’ Continuity test: multimeter beep across the assembled connector
  â†’ Check polarity before powering: probe with DVM

Documentation:
  â†’ Label each connector end with where it goes: "PDP CH4 ARM MOTOR"
  â†’ Use heat shrink over each crimp for strain relief and insulation
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is Anderson Powerpole polarity reversal a common and serious error?",opts:["Powerpoles are fragile","Powerpole housings have no keying â€” both polarities are physically identical; a reversed connection puts positive voltage on the ground pin of every connected device, destroying motor controllers and sensors instantly; always verify orientation against a known-good connector before connecting power","Powerpoles use non-standard polarity","Polarity reversal only affects batteries"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a tug test on a newly crimped connector verify?",opts:["It tests the connector rating","It confirms the contact is properly seated in the housing and the crimp is mechanically secure â€” a contact that pulls out during a tug test will fail in the field during vibration or cable movement, causing intermittent disconnection that's very difficult to diagnose","Tug tests check for polarity","It verifies the wire gauge"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"eb_sensors",title:"Sensor Types â€” Choosing the Right Sensor for the Job",est:"12 min",content:`## Every Sensing Task Has a Best-Fit Sensor
Teams often use the first sensor they have available rather than the best one for the task. A limit switch for position feedback bounces. An encoder for presence detection is overkill. Understanding sensor types and their tradeoffs prevents hours of debugging.

## Sensor Type Reference
\`\`\`
Limit switch / microswitch:
  â†’ Detects: physical contact (is the mechanism at this position?)
  â†’ Output: digital (closed/open)
  â†’ Strengths: simple, reliable, any microcontroller can read it
  â†’ Weaknesses: contact bounce (debounce required in code), wears out with millions of cycles
  â†’ Use for: home position detection, hard stop confirmation, game piece presence in a cradle

Photoelectric / beam break (IR):
  â†’ Detects: interruption of an IR beam
  â†’ Output: digital (beam clear / beam broken)
  â†’ Strengths: no contact, fast response, reliable presence detection
  â†’ Weaknesses: alignment required, reflective surfaces can fool it, ambient light sensitivity
  â†’ Use for: game piece presence in intake/shooter, counting pieces through a path

Encoder (quadrature):
  â†’ Detects: rotational position and velocity of a shaft
  â†’ Output: quadrature pulses (A and B channels, counts direction)
  â†’ Strengths: highly accurate, doesn't drift, fast update rate
  â†’ Weaknesses: measures rotation only, slip â†’ position error, expensive
  â†’ Use for: arm angle (absolute through full range), flywheel speed control, drivetrain odometry

Gyroscope (IMU):
  â†’ Detects: angular rate â†’ integrated to heading
  â†’ Output: degrees/radians of rotation
  â†’ Strengths: doesn't require contact with wheels, 360Â° range
  â†’ Weaknesses: drift over time, vibration sensitivity, must be initialized at rest
  â†’ Use for: drivetrain heading, auto turning, field-oriented drive

Distance sensor (ultrasonic or ToF):
  â†’ Detects: distance to nearest object in beam path
  â†’ Output: distance in mm/cm
  â†’ Strengths: non-contact distance measurement
  â†’ Weaknesses: narrow beam, reflective surfaces cause errors, min distance
  â†’ Use for: detecting game piece proximity, arm height above floor
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a beam break sensor preferable to a limit switch for detecting a game piece in an intake pathway?",opts:["Beam breaks are cheaper","A beam break requires no mechanical contact with the game piece â€” the piece interrupts the IR beam as it passes through; a limit switch requires physical contact and applies force to the game piece, which can deflect or slow it; beam breaks also have no contact bounce requiring debounce","Limit switches don't detect pieces","Beam breaks are more accurate"],ans:1},
      {q:"What causes an encoder to give incorrect position readings even when it's functioning correctly?",opts:["Encoder calibration drift","Mechanical slip between the encoder shaft and the mechanism â€” if a belt slips, a wheel skids, or the encoder gear skips, the encoder counts correctly but the actual mechanism is in a different position than the encoder reports; this is why absolute encoders at the joint are preferred over drive-side encoders for arm control","Encoders lose count at power cycles","Temperature affects encoder accuracy"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.electrical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ei_can2",title:"CAN Bus in FRC â€” Devices, IDs and Diagnostics",est:"13 min",content:`## CAN Lets One Wire Run the Whole Robot
A traditional PWM-wired robot runs a separate signal wire from the RoboRIO to every motor controller. A CAN-wired robot connects all motor controllers on a single two-wire loop â€” less wiring, richer data, and bidirectional communication that PWM can't provide.

## CAN Topology for FRC
\`\`\`
Single loop topology (required):
  RoboRIO â†’ PDP/PDH â†’ Spark MAX #1 â†’ Spark MAX #2 â†’ ... â†’ back to RoboRIO
  (120Î© termination resistors at both ends â€” usually built into RoboRIO and PDP)

Device addressing (CAN IDs):
  Each device has a unique ID (0-62 for most FRC devices)
  IDs must be unique across the entire bus â€” duplicates cause errors
  Convention for large robots:
    Drive motors:     1-6 (FL, FR, BL, BR, ML, MR)
    Arm/Elevator:     10-15
    Intake/Shooter:   20-25
    Sensors/PDH:      30+

Configuring IDs:
  CTRE (Falcon, Talon): Phoenix Tuner X â†’ device list â†’ set ID
  REV (Spark MAX): REV Hardware Client â†’ device list â†’ set ID
  PDH: Phoenix Tuner X (automatically ID 1 usually)

Check for duplicates:
  Open Phoenix Tuner X or REV Hardware Client with robot powered on
  All CAN devices should appear in the device list
  Two devices with the same ID = one or both won't appear â†’ ID conflict
\`\`\`

## CAN vs PWM â€” Capability Comparison
\`\`\`
CAN can do things PWM physically cannot:
  â†’ Read motor temperature â†’ prevent thermal failures
  â†’ Read supply voltage â†’ detect brownout risk in real time
  â†’ Read output current â†’ detect mechanism stalls before damage
  â†’ Configure velocity/position control loops ON the motor controller
     (runs at 1000Hz on the controller, not limited by RoboRIO loop rate)
  â†’ Firmware updates over the bus

CAN diagnostics at competition:
  Phoenix Tuner X â†’ CAN Utilization: should stay below 70%
  High utilization â†’ reduce telemetry update rates on less-critical devices
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What causes one or both CAN devices to disappear from the device list when two devices share the same CAN ID?",opts:["The devices power off","When two devices respond simultaneously to the same address, their signals collide on the bus â€” the collision corrupts both responses, making neither device recognizable to the network; only one device with a given ID can respond correctly","Device software crashes on ID conflict","Duplicate IDs require manual restart"],ans:1},
      {q:"What capability does CAN position/velocity control running on the motor controller itself provide that RoboRIO-side software control cannot?",opts:["CAN control is more accurate","Motor controller closed-loop control runs at 1000Hz â€” far faster than the RoboRIO's 50Hz robot loop; this enables tighter, more responsive control especially for fast mechanisms like flywheels where a 20ms RoboRIO loop is too slow to track rapid RPM changes","CAN control uses less power","RoboRIO can't run control loops"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ei_brownout",title:"Preventing and Diagnosing Brownouts",est:"12 min",content:`## A Brownout Can Lose a Match Instantly
When your robot's battery voltage drops below approximately 6.8V, the RoboRIO resets â€” robot disabled for 2-3 seconds mid-match. Brownouts are preventable with good electrical practice and controllable with code.

## Why Brownouts Happen
\`\`\`
V = E - I Ã— R_internal

Battery internal resistance (fresh 18Ah SLA): ~15mÎ©
At 80A total draw: V_drop = 80 Ã— 0.015 = 1.2V â†’ 12.6 - 1.2 = 11.4V (fine)
At 200A total draw: V_drop = 200 Ã— 0.015 = 3.0V â†’ 12.6 - 3.0 = 9.6V (brownout risk)

Conditions that spike current:
  â†’ 4 drive motors stalling simultaneously (pushing/being pushed)
  â†’ Multiple mechanisms activating at the same time
  â†’ Aged battery with higher internal resistance (> 30mÎ© â†’ 2Ã— the voltage drop)
  â†’ Low battery (12.0V nominal â†’ brownout occurs at lower current)
\`\`\`

## Prevention Strategies
\`\`\`
Hardware:
  â†’ Use fresh batteries (< 4 years, < 30mÎ© internal resistance)
  â†’ Track each battery's internal resistance with a battery analyzer
  â†’ Charge batteries to 12.6-12.8V before each match

Software (WPILib):
  â†’ Slew rate limiting on drive: ramp input from 0â†’1 over 0.2-0.4s
    â†’ Prevents 4 drive motors from demanding peak current simultaneously
  â†’ Current limiting on motor controllers:
    Spark MAX: setSmartCurrentLimit(40)   // 40A limit
    Talon FX: CurrentLimitsConfigs with stator and supply limits
  â†’ Voltage compensation: setVoltageCompensationNominalVoltage(10.0)
    â†’ Motor controllers reduce output proportionally to voltage â†’ consistent behavior

Dashboard monitoring:
  â†’ Log RobotController.getBatteryVoltage() continuously
  â†’ Alert when voltage drops below 11.0V during match
  â†’ Review voltage log after matches to see when spikes occurred
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does an aged battery with 30mÎ© internal resistance brown out at lower current than a fresh 15mÎ© battery?",opts:["Aged batteries have less charge","Higher internal resistance means more voltage is lost across the battery's internal impedance at any given current â€” at 100A, a 30mÎ© battery loses 3V (V=IR) while a 15mÎ© battery loses only 1.5V; the 30mÎ© battery hits the brownout threshold (6.8V) at half the current of the fresh battery","Aged batteries have weaker cells","Internal resistance increases voltage"],ans:1},
      {q:"How does slew rate limiting on the drivetrain reduce brownout risk?",opts:["It reduces maximum speed","It prevents all drive motors from demanding maximum current simultaneously by ramping the power command gradually â€” instead of 4 motors going from 0 to 100% in one loop cycle (instant large current spike), they ramp over 0.2-0.4 seconds, spreading the current demand over time and keeping peak current below the brownout threshold","Slew rate limits voltage","It disconnects motors during acceleration"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.electrical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ea_logging",title:"Electrical Data Logging for Post-Match Diagnosis",est:"12 min",content:`## The Robot Tells You What's Wrong â€” If You're Listening
A robot that browns out once during a match probably did so for a reason you can find in the data. A robot with an intermittent encoder drop-out leaves evidence in the voltage and current logs. Teams that record and review electrical telemetry diagnose problems in minutes; teams that guess debug for hours.

## What to Log
\`\`\`java
// In robotPeriodic() â€” log every 20ms:
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Battery/Voltage",
    RobotController.getBatteryVoltage());
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Battery/Current",
    m_pdh.getTotalCurrent());

// Per-motor current (Spark MAX):
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Drive/FL/Current",
    m_flMotor.getOutputCurrent());
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Drive/FL/Temp",
    m_flMotor.getMotorTemperature());

// Flag brownout events:
SmartDashboard.putBoolean("System/BrownoutOccurred",
    RobotController.isBrownedOut());
\`\`\`

## Using DataLog (WPILib Structured Logging)
\`\`\`java
import edu.wpi.first.util.datalog.*;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.DataLogManager;

// In robotInit():
DataLogManager.start();  // logs to /home/lvuser/logs/ on the RoboRIO

// Create log entries:
private final DataLog m_log = DataLogManager.getLog();
private final DoubleLogEntry m_voltageLog =
    new DoubleLogEntry(m_log, "/battery/voltage");
private final DoubleLogEntry m_currentLog =
    new DoubleLogEntry(m_log, "/battery/current");

// In robotPeriodic():
m_voltageLog.append(RobotController.getBatteryVoltage());
m_currentLog.append(m_pdh.getTotalCurrent());
\`\`\`

## Reading Logs After a Match
\`\`\`
Download logs:
  Driver Station â†’ USB drive (auto-logs to connected drive)
  OR sftp lvuser@10.12.34.2 â†’ /home/lvuser/logs/

Analyze with:
  AdvantageScope: drag .wpilog file â†’ view voltage/current vs time
  Look for:
    â†’ Voltage spike below 10V â†’ brownout risk moment
    â†’ Current spike > 200A total â†’ over-demand event
    â†’ Motor current spike > 80A â†’ stall detection
    â†’ Temperature above 60Â°C on any motor â†’ thermal throttling

After every competition match: review voltage graph.
Any dip below 10V â†’ investigate what caused the demand.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What specific information does logging per-motor current provide that total PDH current cannot?",opts:["Per-motor current is more accurate","Total PDH current shows how much the whole robot draws but not which mechanism caused a spike â€” per-motor current identifies the specific motor that stalled or drew excessive current, enabling targeted diagnosis of a mechanism fault rather than guessing across all systems","PDH current is less reliable","Motor current requires different hardware"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is reviewing voltage logs after every competition match recommended rather than only after apparent problems?",opts:["Constant review wastes time","Problems that didn't cause an obvious failure (a brief 10.5V dip that didn't quite brownout) still indicate an underlying risk â€” catching near-brownout events before they cause match losses allows preventive action; waiting for an actual failure means the fix happens after the damage is done","Logs are reviewed by FTA only","Voltage data is inaccurate during matches"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
