LESSONS.strategy.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"si_endgame",title:"Endgame Planning â€” Maximizing Last 30 Seconds",est:"12 min",content:`## The Endgame Is Worth Planning Specifically
Many games have climbing, parking, or endgame-specific actions worth 15-30% of total match score. Teams that treat endgame as an afterthought leave significant points behind. Teams that rehearse endgame routines â€” including starting position and exact timing â€” consistently score them.

## The Endgame Decision Framework
\`\`\`
30 seconds out, evaluate:
  1. Current score differential â€” are we winning or losing?
     â†’ Winning by > 15 pts: prioritize securing the endgame action
        (don't risk it for one more game piece)
     â†’ Losing by < 10 pts: score one more piece then endgame
     â†’ Losing by > 20 pts: consider skipping endgame for maximum scoring attempt

  2. Endgame RP threshold â€” are we at the boundary?
     â†’ If one more climb puts the alliance at the RP threshold â†’ prioritize it
     â†’ If RP is already secured â†’ standard endgame strategy

  3. Alliance coordination:
     â†’ Who climbs where? (Decide BEFORE the match, confirm pre-match)
     â†’ Which climb position is each robot targeting?
     â†’ Is there room for 3 robots? (Some games only allow 2 at the highest level)
\`\`\`

## The Endgame Clock
\`\`\`
Work backwards from the final buzzer:
  T-30s: last game piece released or abandoned
  T-28s: drive to climb position start zone
  T-22s: initiate climb sequence (first extension)
  T-8s: fully engaged in climb
  T-0s: buzzer â€” position locked

Practice this exact sequence in drive practice.
Time it with a stopwatch. Know your robot's actual climb time.

Common timing mistake: drivers assume they have "plenty of time"
Actual sequence from above: robot needs 22 seconds minimum for a 6-step sequence
Starting at T-25s leaves 3 seconds of margin â€” not "plenty"

Rule: if you're not in position by T-20s, you probably won't make it cleanly.
Practice the "late start" abort: when do you give up on endgame?
Attempting a partial climb that doesn't register = 0 pts for the risk taken.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should the endgame abort threshold (when to give up on climbing) be decided during practice rather than mid-match?",opts:["Abort rules vary by game","A mid-match decision under time pressure with an audience produces worse decisions than a pre-determined threshold â€” drivers who know 'if I'm not in position by T-20s, I abort and score instead' can make instant decisions that optimize expected points rather than attempting a risky partial climb","Drivers can always judge timing","Abort decisions don't affect score"],ans:1},
      {q:"When does scoring one more game piece before climbing make strategic sense despite the time risk?",opts:["Never â€” climbing always scores more","When the score differential is small enough that one game piece might change the outcome AND the robot has demonstrated reliable rapid climbs â€” the expected value of the piece plus reliable climb exceeds the expected value of conservative early climb; the calculation depends on specific point values and the team's climb reliability","Always â€” pieces score more","Only if the team is losing by exactly one game piece"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"si_data_driven",title:"Data-Driven Alliance Selection",est:"14 min",content:`## Gut Feelings Lose Alliances; Data Wins Them
At a competitive event, many alliance captains pick based on match impressions and reputation. Captains who have quantified data â€” average auto, teleop cycles, climb reliability, breakdown rate â€” make better decisions in the 30 seconds they have per pick.

## The Metrics That Predict Elimination Performance
\`\`\`
Most predictive for elimination alliance building:

1. Teleop consistency (std deviation of match scores)
   â†’ A team averaging 40pts with std dev 5 is more valuable than
     one averaging 45pts with std dev 20
   â†’ Eliminations are best-of-3: consistency wins series

2. Breakdown rate (% of matches with a significant breakdown)
   â†’ Any team with > 25% breakdown rate is a liability in elims
   â†’ Even if their ceiling score is highest

3. Complementary capability
   â†’ Your robot scores 3 pieces in auto and 8 cycles teleop
   â†’ Best partner: scores differently (amp vs speaker, different zone)
   â†’ Avoids: robot that needs the same field positions you do

4. Climb/endgame reliability (not just capability)
   â†’ A team that claims L3 climb but only achieves it 60% of matches
   â†’ Is worth less than a team that consistently achieves L2 (100%)
   â†’ Score: reliability_rate Ã— climb_pts = expected climb value

Computing expected points:
  Team A: L3 climb (6 pts) at 60% = 3.6 expected pts
  Team B: L2 climb (4 pts) at 95% = 3.8 expected pts â†’ pick Team B
\`\`\`

## Alliance Synergy Analysis
\`\`\`python
# Quick synergy check:
def expected_alliance_score(robots):
    total = 0
    for r in robots:
        total += r["avg_auto"]
        total += r["avg_cycles"] * r["pts_per_cycle"]
        total += r["avg_climb_pts"] * r["climb_reliability"]
    return total

# Compare alliance configurations:
config_1 = expected_alliance_score([us, team_a, team_b])  # 142 pts
config_2 = expected_alliance_score([us, team_a, team_c])  # 138 pts
config_3 = expected_alliance_score([us, team_b, team_c])  # 135 pts

# Config 1 has highest floor â€” pick team_a first if available
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is consistency (low score standard deviation) more valuable than peak performance in elimination alliances?",opts:["Consistency is easier to measure","Eliminations are played as best-of-3 series â€” an inconsistent team that occasionally scores 60pts but sometimes scores 15pts loses the series whenever they have a bad match; a consistent 40pt team wins all three matches against the same opponent; in a series format, floor performance matters more than ceiling","Consistent teams are better drivers","Standard deviation is the standard metric"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why might a team with L2 climb reliability of 95% be a better pick than one with L3 climb capability at 60%?",opts:["L2 climbs are faster","Expected value: 4pts Ã— 0.95 = 3.8 expected climb points vs 6pts Ã— 0.60 = 3.6 â€” the more reliable L2 climber produces slightly more expected points AND is more predictable; in elimination matches where you know what to count on, reliability is worth the tradeoff against higher ceiling capability","L2 climbs save time","The judges prefer consistent teams"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.strategy.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sa_film",title:"Film Study â€” Analyzing Match Video",est:"14 min",content:`## Watching Video Is How You Learn What Scouts Miss
A scout records cycle count; film study captures why cycles failed, how defense affected performance, and what the driver did in close situations. Alliance captains who watch video pick better; drive teams who watch themselves improve faster.

## What to Look For in Opponent Video
\`\`\`
For each team you're considering picking, watch 2-3 full match videos:

Intake reliability:
  â†’ Pickup success rate: count attempts vs successes
  â†’ Which field positions does the intake work from?
  â†’ Any game piece types the robot consistently struggles with?

Defense response:
  â†’ Does the robot's performance drop significantly when defended?
  â†’ Can the driver get around defense or do they get stuck?
  â†’ Any tendency to foul when frustrated by defense?

Endgame timing:
  â†’ Exactly when do they start their endgame sequence?
  â†’ What's their actual climb time (start climb â†’ fully engaged)?
  â†’ Have they ever failed to climb after attempting?

Breakdown tells:
  â†’ Robot stops moving and then restarts â†’ brownout or comms dropout
  â†’ Mechanism stops working mid-match â†’ specific subsystem failure
  â†’ Slow at end of match â†’ battery dying or thermal throttle
\`\`\`

## Using Film to Improve Your Own Team
\`\`\`
Weekly film review session (15-20 minutes, drive team only):
  Watch your last competition match. Identify:
    1. One moment where cycling speed was lost
       â†’ "We spent 8 seconds searching for the piece here â€” intake was misaligned"
    2. One decision that cost points
       â†’ "We went for the high-value score at T-25s instead of climbing"
    3. One thing that worked â€” reinforce it
       â†’ "The T-intersection auto routing worked perfectly all 3 matches"

Good film review culture:
  â†’ "Here's what I saw" not "you did this wrong"
  â†’ Find the systemic cause (intake alignment) not the personal failure
  â†’ Every session produces one specific practice goal for the next session
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do cycle count scouting data and film study provide different and complementary information?",opts:["Film is more accurate than scouts","Scouting counts what happened (6 cycles); film shows how it happened â€” whether cycles were fast or slow, what caused failures, how defense affected the robot, and when endgame started; the count validates the film and the film explains the count; together they produce a complete performance picture","Film study replaces scouting","Scouts are faster than film"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific electrical or mechanical issue does a robot that periodically stops and restarts mid-match most likely have?",opts:["Motor controller failure","Periodic stops followed by restarts are the characteristic signature of brownouts (voltage drop resets the RoboRIO causing 2-3 second disabled period) or communication dropouts â€” both cause the same symptom; this is distinguishable from a permanent mechanism failure because the robot recovers and continues functioning after each event","The driver is pressing stop","Random stops are normal behavior"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sa_captain_role",title:"Being an Effective Team Captain",est:"13 min",content:`## Captain Is Not the Loudest or Fastest Builder
The captain's job is to align the team around shared goals, make decisions under pressure, and represent the team in relationships with other teams. Technical skill is irrelevant to most of what captains do â€” communication, clarity, and composure are the core capabilities.

## The Captain's Responsibilities by Phase
\`\`\`
Before build season:
  â†’ Lead the goal-setting session
  â†’ Define decision authority clearly (who has final say on what)
  â†’ Set expectations for attendance and communication

During build season:
  â†’ Resolve inter-subteam conflicts (not technical disputes â€” those belong to leads)
  â†’ Make scope decisions when subteam leads disagree
  â†’ Manage the overall schedule (not each subteam's schedule)
  â†’ Communicate status to mentors and parents

At competition:
  â†’ Lead pre-match alliance strategy conversations
  â†’ Manage alliance relationships (respect and communication with other captains)
  â†’ Make mid-event adjustments when strategy needs to change
  â†’ Keep team composure after losses

Alliance selection:
  â†’ Know the pick list cold before selection starts
  â†’ Communicate clearly to captains you approach: "We'd like you as our first pick"
  â†’ Respond to offers from other captains promptly and graciously
\`\`\`

## Handling Pressure Situations
\`\`\`
Robot breaks in elimination:
  â†’ Your first words to the team set the tone
  â†’ "Okay. We have 12 minutes. Here's what we need to fix." â†’ team mobilizes
  â†’ Panic or blame â†’ team freezes

Alliance partner robot breaks:
  â†’ Offer help before they ask
  â†’ "What do you need? We have [tools/parts/people] available."
  â†’ This is GP and it builds relationships that matter in future seasons

Controversial referee call goes against you:
  â†’ Never argue with referees on the field
  â†’ Formal appeal process: Head Referee â†’ FTA (never the ref who made the call)
  â†’ Team sees you handle it calmly â†’ they model that composure

Losing a close match:
  â†’ Acknowledge the loss fully before analyzing
  â†’ "That was a tough one. Let's take 5 minutes, then figure out what we improve."
  â†’ Skipping the acknowledgment to jump to analysis makes people feel unheard
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a team captain avoid arguing with referees directly on the field after a contested call?",opts:["Referees can eject captains","Arguments with field referees are ineffective and create a negative impression â€” the formal appeal path (Head Referee, then FTA) is the correct procedure with the authority to change rulings; field-side arguing wastes time, rarely changes outcomes, and affects the team's composure for the next match","FIRST rules prohibit field arguments","Referees don't have authority on the field"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes a captain's first words after a major robot breakdown critical to team performance?",opts:["First words establish authority","The captain's initial response sets the team's emotional state â€” a calm, action-oriented response ('here's what we fix') activates the team's problem-solving mode; panic or blame freezes the team at the moment speed is most critical; composure is contagious in both directions","Teams always recover from breakdowns","Quick words prevent media attention"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ MECHANICAL +7 (76â†’83) â”€â”€
LESSONS.mechanical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"mi_fasteners2",title:"Thread Engagement & Bolt Preload",est:"12 min",content:`## Bolts That Fall Out Lose Matches
A loose bolt on a critical mechanism isn't a maintenance issue â€” it's a match-loss waiting to happen. Understanding thread engagement, preload, and locking methods prevents the class of failures where robots simply fall apart under competition stress.

## Thread Engagement Requirements
\`\`\`
Minimum engagement depth for full bolt strength:
  In steel:     1Ã— bolt diameter
  In aluminum:  1.5Ã— bolt diameter (aluminum threads strip easier)
  In plastics:  2-2.5Ã— bolt diameter (much softer than metal)

Examples (M5 bolt = 5mm diameter):
  Steel nut or insert:      5mm engagement minimum
  Aluminum tapped hole:     7.5mm minimum â†’ use M5 Ã— 10mm bolt in 7.5mm+ material
  PLA 3D print:             10-12mm minimum â†’ may need threaded insert

Why this matters:
  An M5 bolt in a 3mm aluminum bracket has inadequate engagement â†’
  first high-stress match load â†’ threads strip â†’ mechanism falls off

Common mistake on FTC GoBILDA channel:
  Channel wall is 3mm â†’ M5 tapped hole has only 3mm engagement
  â†’ Under load: threads pull out of channel
  Fix: use 2 bolts or a backing plate, or switch to through-bolt + nut
\`\`\`

## Bolt Preload and Locking
\`\`\`
Bolt preload: the clamping force created by tightening the bolt
  â†’ Preloaded joint stays closed because parts are compressed together
  â†’ Loosening = preload loss = vibration â†’ further loosening â†’ falls out

Fastener locking methods (in order of strength):
  1. Nylon insert locknut (Nylock):
     â†’ Best for most robot joints
     â†’ Nylon collar creates friction on the thread â†’ resists backout
     â†’ Torque to spec (hand tight + 1/4 turn for most robot applications)
     â†’ Single use: nylocks lose effectiveness after repeated removal

  2. Thread-locking compound (Loctite):
     â†’ Blue (removable): standard for robot mechanisms
     â†’ Red (permanent): drive shafts, set screws, never-remove fasteners
     â†’ Apply: clean threads, one drop, assemble within 15 minutes
     â†’ Cure time: 24h full strength (functional in 1h)

  3. Lock washer (spring or tooth):
     â†’ Least reliable of common methods â€” only adds friction, not locking
     â†’ Better than nothing; worse than Nylock or Loctite

Competition critical joints (use Nylock AND Loctite):
  â†’ Arm pivot bearing retention
  â†’ Drive gearbox output shaft set screw
  â†’ Any bolt that would cause immediate match failure if loose
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a bolt in a 3mm aluminum bracket have inadequate thread engagement even if fully tightened?",opts:["3mm brackets are too flexible","The 1.5Ã— bolt-diameter rule requires 7.5mm of engagement for an M5 bolt in aluminum â€” only 3mm of material means the threads will strip under load even though the bolt feels tight; full preload applied to inadequate engagement strip the aluminum threads, causing sudden joint failure","Thread engagement only matters in steel","3mm aluminum requires larger bolts"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why are nylon insert locknuts described as 'single use' for critical joints?",opts:["They are expensive to reuse","The nylon collar deforms during initial installation to grip the threads â€” each removal-and-reinstallation cycle reduces the amount of nylon remaining and the friction it creates; a locknut that's been removed and reinstalled multiple times may feel like it's engaging but provide significantly less locking force than a fresh one","Nylocks chemically bond to threads","Single use is a regulatory requirement"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"mi_belts",title:"Belt Drive Systems â€” Selection and Tensioning",est:"13 min",content:`## Belts Are Quiet, Efficient, and Easy to Break
A well-designed belt drive is one of the best power transmission methods for robots â€” lightweight, low maintenance, low backlash. A poorly tensioned belt skips under load, wears out in a match, or derails. Getting tension right is the critical skill.

## Belt Types in FRC/FTC
\`\`\`
HTD (High Torque Drive) â€” the FRC standard:
  â†’ Tooth profile: rounded arc shape
  â†’ Common pitches: 3mm (HTD3), 5mm (HTD5) â€” pitch = distance between teeth
  â†’ Higher torque capacity than older V-belt designs
  â†’ Used in: drivetrains, arm drives, most mechanism power transmission

GT2 / GT3 (Gates PowerGrip) â€” the FTC standard:
  â†’ Improved tooth profile vs HTD â†’ less backlash, more accurate positioning
  â†’ Common in FTC because GoBILDA and REV use GT2 throughout
  â†’ Pitch: 2mm (GT2) and 3mm (GT3)

Timing belt widths:
  â†’ Wider = more torque capacity
  â†’ FRC: 9mm, 12mm, 15mm widths common
  â†’ FTC: 6mm, 9mm standard
  â†’ Rule: select width such that belt load is < 50% of rated max (safety factor)
\`\`\`

## Center-to-Center Distance and Belt Length
\`\`\`
For two pulleys of different tooth counts, calculate C-to-C for a given belt:
  L = belt tooth count Ã— pitch
  C = (L - Ï€ Ã— (Dâ‚ + Dâ‚‚) / 2) / 2

  For standard values, use the WCP or REV belt calculator
  (much faster than manual calculation for iterating designs)

Tensioning methods:
  1. Fixed center-to-center (calculate exact belt length for given C-to-C)
     â†’ Cleanest design; requires precise C-to-C in CAD and manufacturing
     â†’ Belt must be stretched over pulleys; HTD5 and GT2 stretch slightly

  2. Adjustable tensioner (slot the motor or idler mount)
     â†’ Build a slot for the motor plate: Â±5mm adjustment
     â†’ Tighten slot fasteners when tension is correct
     â†’ Most forgiving; recommended for team-built mechanisms

  3. Idler pulley (adds a third contact point to tension the belt)
     â†’ Most controlled tensioning; good for long center-to-center spans
     â†’ Idler should contact the slack side of the belt

Correct tension (timing belt):
  Flick the belt; it should make a musical tone, not a thud or a twang.
  Thud = too loose (will skip) | Twang = too tight (will break or wear pulleys)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does belt width selection use a 50% load safety factor rather than specifying exactly the rated maximum width?",opts:["50% is the industry standard","Operating at 50% of rated load accounts for peak shock loads during robot operation that exceed average torques â€” a mechanism that averages 20Nm may spike to 40Nm during sudden direction changes or impacts; a belt selected at exactly its 20Nm rating will fail under these spikes; the 50% factor provides margin for transient overloads","Safety factors are required by FIRST","Belts fail at exactly rated capacity"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the 'musical tone' test for belt tension detect that visual inspection cannot?",opts:["Belt material quality","Belt tension determines natural frequency â€” too loose, the belt vibrates at a low frequency (thud) and will skip under load; too tight, it vibrates at a high frequency (twang) and stresses the pulley bearings; the correct tension produces a note in a specific range that's audible and repeatable without measuring tools","Tone tests are more accurate","Visual inspection is more reliable"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.mechanical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ma_linkages",title:"Four-Bar Linkages â€” Design and Analysis",est:"14 min",content:`## The Most Useful Mechanism You're Not Using Enough
A four-bar linkage converts rotation at a crank into a controlled, predictable path at the output link â€” without the complexity of a linear slide or the weight of a telescoping arm. Intakes, game piece manipulators, and arms that need a specific motion path are natural four-bar applications.

## Four-Bar Geometry
\`\`\`
The four links:
  Ground link (frame):  fixed, connects the two pivots on the robot
  Crank (input):        driven by motor, rotates at one end of ground
  Coupler:              connects crank to output (rocker)
  Rocker (output):      carries the end effector, pivots at other end of ground

Grashof condition (determines motion type):
  Let: s = shortest link, l = longest link, p and q = other two links
  If s + l < p + q: at least one full rotation is possible (crank-rocker)
  If s + l > p + q: only oscillating motion (double-rocker)
  For intake/arm: usually want crank-rocker configuration

Why it matters: the coupler traces a defined path through space â€”
  this path can be engineered to match your robot's needs.
  e.g., intake that stays parallel to the floor throughout its travel
  e.g., arm that moves forward while pivoting up (folds more compactly)
\`\`\`

## Designing a Parallel Four-Bar
\`\`\`
Parallel four-bar: all four links equal in pairs â†’ output stays parallel to crank

Ground link = Coupler link (same length)
Crank = Rocker (same length)

Result: the output link's orientation never changes â€” it stays horizontal
regardless of crank angle.

Use case: intake that must stay parallel to the floor:
  Ground link: 200mm (distance between pivot mounting points on frame)
  Crank: 150mm (driven by motor, sets intake height range)
  Coupler: 200mm (same as ground link â€” parallel constraint)
  Rocker: 150mm (same as crank)

CAD simulation check:
  Animate the four-bar through full crank range
  Verify output link stays horizontal Â±2Â° throughout range
  Check no link-on-link collision at any angle
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What specific motion quality does a parallel four-bar linkage provide that a simple pivoting arm cannot?",opts:["More speed reduction","The output link maintains a constant orientation throughout its travel â€” an intake that must always be parallel to the floor, or a gripper that must always face the same direction, achieves this automatically without any additional constraint or control; a simple pivot arm rotates the end effector's angle as the arm moves","Parallel linkages are stronger","Simple arms require more motors"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does a four-bar linkage allow a more compact retracted configuration than a simple arm with the same reach?",opts:["Four-bar links are shorter","The coupler traces a curved path that can extend further forward with less angular sweep than a simple arm â€” the designer chooses the coupler path by selecting link lengths; this can provide longer reach at lower pivot heights or fold more compactly into the robot frame than a direct pivot arm of equivalent reach","Four-bar mechanisms fold automatically","Simple arms can't fold"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ma_swerve",title:"Swerve Drive Mechanics â€” Module Design Principles",est:"15 min",content:`## Swerve Is Powerful and Unforgiving of Poor Design
A swerve module must accurately control both wheel direction and wheel speed independently, while surviving competition loads, being serviceable in a pit, and operating reliably for 150+ match cycles. Every module design tradeoff â€” steer ratio, drive ratio, encoder placement â€” affects all of these.

## Module Anatomy
\`\`\`
Two independent actuators per module:
  Drive motor:  controls wheel speed (forward/backward)
  Steer motor:  controls wheel direction (0-360Â°, usually controlled as 0-180Â° + direction)

Steer mechanism requirements:
  â†’ High gear reduction (typically 12-21:1) for precise angle control
  â†’ Absolute encoder for heading reference (doesn't reset on power cycle)
    â†’ REV Through Bore, CTRE CANcoder, or MA3 absolute encoder
  â†’ Steer motor current limit: 20-30A (much less load than drive)

Drive mechanism requirements:
  â†’ Gear reduction selected for target free speed:
    Common FRC target: 14-16 ft/s free speed (most competitive range)
    Falcons at 14 ft/s: roughly 6.5:1 reduction with 4" wheels
  â†’ Drive motor current limit: 40-60A (high current during defense/pushing)

Coupling (the hardest problem):
  â†’ Drive power must transmit from a stationary motor to a continuously-rotating module
  â†’ Solutions: bevel gear pair, belt over rotating tube, coaxial design
  â†’ Coaxial (motor inside the module): minimal external coupling needed â†’ most robust
\`\`\`

## Absolute Encoder â€” The Critical Component
\`\`\`
Without an absolute encoder:
  â†’ Robot powers on â†’ steer motor doesn't know current wheel angle
  â†’ First command â†’ wheels spin to random positions
  â†’ Robot lurches dangerously until encoder zeros

With absolute encoder:
  â†’ Power on â†’ immediately know exact wheel angle
  â†’ Can pre-position wheels before enabling
  â†’ Zero-crossing handled correctly (knows difference between 359Â° and 1Â°)

Encoder placement:
  â†’ On steer mechanism output shaft (after all gear reduction) â†’ most accurate
  â†’ On steer motor shaft (before reduction) â†’ less accurate (gear lash included)

Offset calibration:
  â†’ Zero each module with wheel pointing straight forward
  â†’ Record encoder reading â†’ this is the "offset" constant for that module
  â†’ In code: actual_angle = encoder_reading - offset
  â†’ Re-calibrate if the absolute encoder is replaced or the module is disassembled
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must swerve modules use absolute encoders for steer angle rather than incremental (relative) encoders?",opts:["Absolute encoders are more accurate","Incremental encoders only measure change from a reference point â€” when power is cycled, the reference is lost; the module doesn't know its current angle on startup; absolute encoders output the actual angle at all times regardless of power state, enabling immediate correct positioning from the first command after power-on","Incremental encoders are slower","Absolute encoders have more resolution"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does the steer motor require significantly lower current limiting than the drive motor?",opts:["Steer motors are smaller","The steer mechanism has a high gear reduction and low load â€” it only needs to overcome the friction of rotating a wheel module against the floor; the drive motor must overcome the full rolling friction of the wheel on carpet and push against defensive robots under peak loads; this load difference is typically 5-10Ã— between steer and drive","Steer motors have less torque","Current limiting is the same for all motors"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS +5 (25â†’30) â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Beginner.push(
  {id:"awb_imagery",title:"Imagery Award â€” What Judges Look For",est:"10 min",content:`## Imagery Is About Cohesion, Not Just Art
The Imagery Award recognizes teams whose visual identity â€” robot, team uniform, signage, and spirit materials â€” forms a unified, professional whole. Judges don't just look at the robot; they observe whether every element of your team's visual presence tells the same story.

## What Creates a Strong Imagery Identity
\`\`\`
The four surfaces judges evaluate:
  1. Robot: consistent color scheme applied to bumpers, panels, any accent pieces
  2. Uniform: student shirts/jackets that match the robot's color palette
  3. Pit: signage, banner, table setup that reflects the team theme
  4. Spirit materials: buttons, stickers, giveaways, spirit gear â€” consistent theme

What makes it cohesive:
  â†’ Same 2-3 colors used throughout (not different colors on each surface)
  â†’ Team logo applied consistently (same logo, same proportions everywhere)
  â†’ Robot panels/covers that look intentional, not functional-only
  â†’ Bumper numbers that match the uniform â€” same font/style

Common weaknesses:
  â†’ Robot is well-painted but uniform is unrelated generic shirts
  â†’ Pit banner is professional but robot is unpainted structural aluminum
  â†’ Three different logos used across materials
\`\`\`

## Applying Your Theme
\`\`\`
Budget-friendly approaches:
  â†’ Vinyl-cut stickers from a local shop: apply to robot panels and pit table
  â†’ Team shirts: one color, screen-printed logo â€” doesn't need to be expensive
  â†’ Pit banner: 24" Ã— 36" printed at Staples/FedEx â†’ $30-50

Design consistency rule:
  â†’ Pick one primary color, one accent color, one neutral
  â†’ Every element uses only those three colors
  â†’ Logo is the same file used everywhere (SVG format â†’ scales to any size)

If you have a mascot character:
  â†’ It should appear on: robot somewhere, shirts, pit banner, and spirit buttons
  â†’ Consistent art style (same illustration across everything)
  â†’ Not required â€” a strong geometric theme without a mascot also wins
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do judges evaluate the robot, uniform, pit, and spirit materials together rather than just the most visually impressive element?",opts:["Judges are required to view all elements","Imagery Award specifically recognizes a unified visual identity â€” a beautiful robot with unrelated team shirts shows artistic effort, not professional visual communication; cohesion across all surfaces demonstrates that the team's identity was intentionally designed, not just assembled from separate projects","Pit displays affect all awards","All awards consider multiple elements"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should a team's logo be stored as an SVG file for use across all materials?",opts:["SVG files are smaller","SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) scales to any size without quality loss â€” the same file produces a crisp logo on a business card and a 10-foot banner; raster formats (PNG, JPG) become pixelated when enlarged, making it impossible to maintain consistent quality across differently-sized applications","SVG is required by award judges","SVG files are easier to email"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_feedback",title:"Using Post-Award Feedback to Improve",est:"11 min",content:`## Judges Will Tell You Why You Didn't Win â€” If You Ask
Most events offer feedback sessions for award applicants after the award ceremony. Teams that attend, listen without defensiveness, and implement specific changes improve their award performance year over year. Teams that skip feedback wonder why they keep losing.

## How to Get and Use Feedback
\`\`\`
At the event:
  â†’ After award ceremony: find the award judge lead or head judge
  â†’ Ask specifically: "We submitted for Impact â€” could we have 15 minutes
    for feedback on how to improve our submission?"
  â†’ Most judges will say yes; a few won't have time

During the session:
  â†’ Bring a notebook (phone is fine)
  â†’ One person asks questions; one person writes everything down
  â†’ Don't defend your submission during the session
    â†’ Saying "but we did try to mention that" wastes the judge's time
    â†’ Your job is to understand THEIR perception, not to correct it
  â†’ Good questions:
    "What was missing from our submission compared to stronger submissions?"
    "Was there anything in our written submission that was unclear or unverifiable?"
    "What would the top submission in this award category have that ours didn't?"

After the session:
  â†’ Write up the feedback within 24 hours while it's fresh
  â†’ Identify 3 specific things to change for next season
  â†’ Review the feedback at the start of next build season BEFORE writing new submissions
\`\`\`

## The Most Common Judge Feedback (and What It Means)
\`\`\`
"We couldn't verify your numbers"
  â†’ You cited totals without showing how you got there
  â†’ Fix: include a summary table in your submission with event-level breakdown

"Your program sounded impressive but we didn't know the outcomes"
  â†’ You described activities, not impact
  â†’ Fix: for each program, explicitly state what changed because of it

"We wanted to hear more student voice"
  â†’ Mentors were too present in the interview; students were reading from a script
  â†’ Fix: students own specific sections; rehearse natural conversation, not recitation

"Strong on outreach but weak on technical"
  â†’ Relevant for combined-criteria awards (some evaluate both)
  â†’ Fix: add engineering highlights to your submission
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should team members avoid defending their submission during a judge feedback session?",opts:["Defense is disrespectful","The purpose of the feedback session is to understand the judge's perception â€” defending explains what you intended, which doesn't change their perception or help you improve; the gap between your intention and their understanding IS the problem to solve, and defending it closes the conversation that would reveal how to fix it","Judges can't be questioned","Defense wastes session time"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the feedback 'we couldn't verify your numbers' indicate about the submission's structure?",opts:["The numbers were incorrect","The submission cited totals without showing how they were derived â€” a judge who sees '847 students reached' but has no breakdown by event has no way to assess whether the number is accurate; including an event-by-event table makes the total checkable and increases credibility","Numbers require separate documentation","Judges don't verify during the event"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ FUNDRAISING +6 (24â†’30) â”€â”€
LESSONS.fundraising.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"fi_corporate",title:"Corporate Partnership Programs",est:"13 min",content:`## Moving Beyond One-Time Sponsors to Multi-Year Partners
A sponsor who writes a $500 check once and never hears from you again is a transaction. A company that considers your team part of their community investment portfolio and renews annually â€” increasing year over year â€” is a partner. The difference is how you treat the relationship.

## What Companies Actually Want from Sponsorship
\`\`\`
Companies sponsor teams for business reasons â€” even if they like the team:
  â†’ Talent pipeline: "These students might work for us someday"
  â†’ Community goodwill: "We invest in local education"
  â†’ Employee morale: "Our engineers love seeing students build robots"
  â†’ Brand visibility: "Our logo on a robot at a high-profile event"
  â†’ Tax benefit: charitable deduction (if your team has nonprofit status)

Understanding which motivation drives a specific company lets you:
  â†’ Pitch in the language that resonates for them
  â†’ Offer the right benefits package
  â†’ Report on the metrics they care about at year-end
\`\`\`

## The Partner Communication Calendar
\`\`\`
Month    Communication                      Purpose
--------+-----------------------------------+------------------------
October  Kickoff outreach + proposal sent   Establish relationship
January  Build season launch announcement   Keep them engaged
February Invite to competition              Event experience â†’ emotional connection
April    Post-competition report            Show ROI from their investment
May      Year-end impact summary            Show cumulative value
June     Early renewal conversation         Begin next year before they forget
August   Renewal confirmed + invoice        Lock in next season's funding

Total sponsor touches: 7 per year minimum for active sponsors
Most teams: 0-2 touches â†’ sponsors forget the team between seasons
\`\`\`

## The Year-End Report
\`\`\`
One page, to every sponsor, within 2 weeks of championship:

Team 1234 â€” 2025 Season Partner Report

Thank you: [Company name] invested $[amount] in Team 1234 this season.

Robot performance:
  â†’ Competed in 2 district events + State Championship
  â†’ Won Engineering Inspiration Award at Chesapeake District Week 3

Your investment enabled:
  â†’ [Specific item funded: 3 Falcon 500 motors, 3D printer filament, event travel]

Community impact (your logo was associated with):
  â†’ 847 students reached through 18 outreach events
  â†’ 4 FLL teams mentored through their season

Media:
  â†’ [link to newspaper article that mentions the team]
  â†’ [link to match video showing robot with sponsor logo]

Next season preview:
  â†’ We've already qualified for [next event]
  â†’ Partnership opportunities for 2026 season: [link to packet]
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does sending 7 communications per year to sponsors increase renewal rates compared to the 0-2 touches most teams send?",opts:["More emails are required","Sponsors make renewal decisions when they're reminded of the relationship â€” 7 purposeful touches through the year keep the team in the sponsor's memory and demonstrate active appreciation; companies that haven't heard from a team since January typically don't remember to renew in September","7 is the required number","Frequent contact builds obligation"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does including specific metrics in the year-end report (students reached, events attended, award won) accomplish beyond expressing gratitude?",opts:["Metrics are required by the IRS","Metrics demonstrate return on investment â€” a company that donated $1,500 can see that their investment contributed to reaching 847 students, winning an award, and competing at state; this converts the relationship from charity to business investment, making renewal a rational business decision rather than just goodwill","Gratitude is sufficient","Reports prevent legal issues"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fi_grant2",title:"Writing Competitive Grant Proposals",est:"14 min",content:`## Grant Writing Is a Learnable Skill
The same grant proposal template, submitted to three foundations, wins two and loses one â€” not because of the team's program, but because of how it's written for each audience. Understanding what grant reviewers look for and writing to those criteria separates funded teams from unfunded ones.

## Reading the RFP (Request for Proposals)
\`\`\`
Before writing a single word:
  â†’ Read the entire RFP twice
  â†’ Highlight the evaluation criteria (usually listed explicitly)
  â†’ Note any required sections, word/page limits, and format requirements
  â†’ Identify the funder's mission and values (match your language to theirs)

The funder's perspective:
  â†’ They receive 50-200 applications for limited funds
  â†’ Reviewers spend 10-20 minutes per application on average
  â†’ Clear, organized proposals score higher than comprehensive but dense ones
  â†’ Proposals that don't match the funder's stated priorities are eliminated early

Alignment check before writing:
  "Does our project actually fit this grant's purpose?"
  If you have to stretch significantly to make it fit â†’ don't apply
  A poor-fit application that's funded creates obligations you can't fulfill
\`\`\`

## Proposal Structure
\`\`\`
Executive summary (1 paragraph):
  â†’ Who you are + what you're requesting + what impact it produces
  â†’ This paragraph should stand alone as a complete description

Statement of need (1-2 paragraphs):
  â†’ Why does this problem exist in your community?
  â†’ Use local data where possible ("In [county], only 12% of students...")
  â†’ Connect the need to the funder's stated priorities

Project description (core of the proposal):
  â†’ What exactly will you do? (specific activities, not vague goals)
  â†’ Who will do it? (team members, mentors, number of people)
  â†’ When? (timeline with milestones)
  â†’ Where? (schools, community organizations, specific venues)

Evaluation / outcomes:
  â†’ How will you measure success?
  â†’ What are the specific, measurable targets?
  â†’ "At least 200 elementary students will receive 4+ hours of STEM instruction"
  â†’ Not: "We will positively impact many students in our community"

Budget:
  â†’ Itemized: each line is a specific cost with calculation
  â†’ "Laptop Ã— 1 @ $899 = $899" not "Technology: $900"
  â†’ Must add exactly to the requested amount
  â†’ Include any matching funds â€” funders like shared investment
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should teams not apply for grants where they need to significantly stretch their program to match the funder's stated priorities?",opts:["Stretch applications are rejected immediately","Being funded by a misaligned grant creates reporting obligations that require documenting activities the team didn't actually do â€” misrepresenting outcomes to satisfy reporting requirements is both unethical and a risk to future funding from that and other foundations","Funder priorities are just guidelines","Grant matching isn't required"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes an itemized budget ('Laptop Ã— 1 @ $899') more credible than a categorical budget line ('Technology: $900')?",opts:["Itemized budgets are required","Itemized budgets show the reviewer that the team knows exactly what it needs and has researched actual costs â€” a categorical estimate could mean anything; item-level detail demonstrates planning rigor and makes it easy for the reviewer to assess whether the request is reasonable","Itemized budgets must equal the request","Technology categories are flagged for review"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Advanced.push(
  {id:"fa_major_donor",title:"Cultivating Major Donors",est:"13 min",content:`## The Top 3 Donors Often Fund 50% of the Budget
In most nonprofits and sponsored programs, a small number of major donors contribute disproportionate amounts. A $5,000 gift from one relationship is worth 10Ã— more than fifty $100 donations in terms of donor-time ROI. Identifying and cultivating major donor prospects is advanced fundraising.

## Who Is a Major Donor Prospect?
\`\`\`
For a FIRST team, a major donor is typically:
  â†’ A technology company or engineering firm ($3,000-15,000)
  â†’ A wealthy individual with personal connection to STEM education
  â†’ A large local employer investing in talent pipeline
  â†’ A parent or alumnus in a senior professional role

Characteristics of strong prospects:
  â†’ Capacity: company or individual has the means to give at a major level
  â†’ Interest: clear connection to STEM, education, or workforce development
  â†’ Access: you have a relationship or introduction path to a decision-maker

Finding prospects:
  â†’ Parents of team members: what do they do professionally?
  â†’ Team alumni: where did they end up? Are they now in positions to give back?
  â†’ Local business leaders who attend FIRST events
  â†’ Companies that already donate to other STEM programs
\`\`\`

## The Major Gift Cultivation Process
\`\`\`
Step 1: Introduction (not an ask)
  â†’ Purpose: get the person interested and connected
  â†’ Invite to a competition as a guest (no agenda except watching)
  â†’ Let the robot and the students make the case without a pitch

Step 2: Relationship building (2-4 months)
  â†’ Personal follow-up from a student: "It was great meeting you at..."
  â†’ Updates on the team's progress (brief, not sales-y)
  â†’ One-on-one conversation: learn what they care about in STEM/education

Step 3: Ask (specific, after relationship is established)
  â†’ In person: "We're launching a 3-year STEM curriculum at three Title I schools.
    Would you consider a $5,000 gift to fund the first year?"
  â†’ Specific amount + specific use + specific timeframe
  â†’ Ask in person > phone > email â€” in that order of effectiveness

Step 4: Stewardship (after gift)
  â†’ Handwritten thank-you within 48 hours
  â†’ Named acknowledgment at next competition
  â†’ Quarterly updates on the program their gift funded
  â†’ Renewal conversation 10 months after first gift

Major gifts take 3-12 months to cultivate.
Skipping to the ask before the relationship exists
almost always gets a polite no.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does inviting a major donor prospect to a competition before making any ask constitute an effective first cultivation step?",opts:["Events are required for major gifts","Competition attendance creates an emotional connection that no pitch can replicate â€” the prospect sees real students working on real engineering problems in a real competitive environment; this experience creates the 'why this matters' motivation that makes a later ask resonate; trying to create that connection through words alone is far less effective","Prospects must be educated first","Competitions count as formal meetings"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does the major gift ask specify amount, use, and timeframe rather than making a general open-ended request?",opts:["General asks confuse donors","Specific requests are easier to evaluate and say yes to â€” 'Would you consider a $5,000 gift to fund year one of our school curriculum?' lets the prospect assess a concrete decision; 'Would you consider supporting our team?' requires them to invent what 'support' means, how much, and for what, creating friction that leads to vague non-commitments","Specific amounts are required","General asks seem greedy"],ans:1},
    ]},
);


// â”€â”€â”€ PACK 16 â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€

// â”€â”€ CAD +8 (24â†’32) â”€â”€
LESSONS.cad.Beginner.push(
  {id:"cadb_dimension",title:"Dimensioning Strategies â€” Fully Constraining a Sketch",est:"10 min",content:`## Under-Constrained Sketches Cause Unexpected Geometry
A sketch that's 90% constrained seems fine â€” until you drag a point and the whole profile moves. Fully constraining every sketch before extruding prevents geometry that shifts unexpectedly when you edit dimensions later.

## The Constraint Workflow
\`\`\`
In Onshape (or any parametric CAD):

Step 1: Start with geometry from an origin or existing feature
  â†’ First sketch entity should be constrained to the origin or a known edge
  â†’ "Fix" constraint as a last resort â€” it hard-codes position, prevents parametric editing

Step 2: Add geometric constraints first
  â†’ Horizontal/vertical for lines that should be exactly aligned
  â†’ Coincident for points that must touch
  â†’ Parallel/perpendicular for related edges

Step 3: Add dimension constraints
  â†’ Overall width and height first (bounding dimensions)
  â†’ Then hole positions, chamfer sizes, cutout widths
  â†’ Dimension from the datum corner/edge, not from other features

Step 4: Verify fully constrained
  â†’ All lines black (Onshape) or fully-constrained indicator
  â†’ Drag any point: nothing should move

Step 5: Test parametric behavior
  â†’ Change one dimension: does the rest of the sketch update correctly?
  â†’ If it does: your constraints are logically sound
  â†’ If it breaks: a constraint is wrong (common: parallel constraint prevents scaling)
\`\`\`

## Common Under-Constraint Sources
\`\`\`
1. Arc or circle with only one dimension (radius only, no position)
   Fix: add coincident constraint between arc center and a located point

2. Line that's horizontal but not positioned vertically
   Fix: dimension its Y-position from the datum edge

3. Two lines that are parallel but neither is fixed to a reference
   Fix: one of them must be coincident with a known edge or point

4. Closed polygon that can still translate as a unit
   Fix: at least one corner or midpoint must be coincident with the origin
        or a dimensioned offset from it
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should bounding dimensions (overall width and height) be added before hole position dimensions in a sketch?",opts:["Bounding dimensions are more important","Bounding dimensions establish the coordinate reference for the part â€” subsequent hole positions can then be dimensioned as fractions or offsets of those known extents; dimensioning holes first without established boundaries creates a sketch that can't be understood or edited logically","Onshape requires this order","Bounding dimensions must be added last"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does successfully dragging a point in a fully-constrained sketch verify?",opts:["The sketch is editable","That nothing moves â€” a truly fully-constrained sketch has zero degrees of freedom; if any element shifts when dragged, there's a remaining unconstrained degree of freedom somewhere that will cause unexpected geometry changes when dimensions are modified later","That the sketch exports correctly","Drag testing is not a verification method"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cadb_tubes",title:"Modeling Structural Tube in CAD",est:"10 min",content:`## Tubes Are the Foundation of Every Robot Frame
Every FRC robot is largely built from aluminum extrusion or structural tube. Modeling them correctly â€” with accurate wall thickness, correct hole patterns, and efficient assemblies â€” is the most-practiced CAD skill on most teams.

## Standard Tube Profiles in CAD
\`\`\`
1" Ã— 1" Ã— 1/8" wall aluminum square tube (most common FRC):
  Outer: 1.000" Ã— 1.000"
  Wall:  0.125" thick
  Inner: 0.750" Ã— 0.750"

In Onshape sketch:
  Draw outer 1"Ã—1" square centered on origin
  Offset â†’ inward 0.125" â†’ creates inner square
  Extrude: select region between inner and outer â†’ specify tube length
  Result: hollow square tube cross-section, extruded to length

For 1"Ã—2" (kickplate or horizontal member):
  Same approach: 1"Ã—2" outer, 0.125" offset inward

REV Ion 1"Ã—1" extrusion (FTC):
  Modeled same way but uses 25mm Ã— 25mm outer (metric)
  Slot features: add 6mm Ã— 3mm center slot on each face
  Use MKCAD library instead â€” saves 45 minutes of modeling

GoBILDA U-channel:
  Complex profile with internal webs â†’ use MKCAD library
\`\`\`

## Hole Pattern Best Practices
\`\`\`
FRC standard tube drilling (1" Ã— 1"):
  Center row: 0.196" (#10 clearance) holes at 0.5" spacing
  This matches most off-the-shelf brackets

Modeling a pattern efficiently:
  1. Model one hole at the correct position
  2. Linear pattern â†’ direction along tube length â†’ spacing 0.5" â†’ count = tube_length / 0.5 - 1
  3. If tube length changes: update one dimension â†’ pattern recalculates

Saved tube part template:
  Create a 12" tube with correct profile and hole pattern
  Vary length with a configuration (see Configurations skill)
  Every robot instance uses the same part, resized
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should GoBILDA U-channel and REV extrusion be sourced from the MKCAD library rather than modeled from scratch?",opts:["Library parts are more accurate","These profiles have complex cross-sections with internal webs, precise slot geometries, and specific hole patterns â€” modeling them from scratch takes 30-60 minutes and introduces dimensional errors; library parts are manufacturer-verified and insert in seconds","Library parts load faster","Custom models aren't allowed in CAD software"],ans:1},
      {q:"What allows a linear pattern of holes to automatically recalculate when the tube length changes?",opts:["Auto-recalculate is always on","Using a parametric count (tube_length / 0.5 - 1) or updating the pattern count as a dimension â€” linking the pattern count to the tube length dimension means changing the tube length propagates to the correct number of holes; a hard-coded count of 23 requires manual updating every time length changes","Patterns are always linked to dimensions","Tube length drives hole count automatically"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"cadi_configs",title:"Configurations â€” One Part, Multiple Sizes",est:"12 min",content:`## Stop Modeling the Same Bracket in 12 Lengths
If your team uses 1"Ã—1" tube in lengths from 4" to 24", modeling each length as a separate part wastes hours and creates a maintenance nightmare. Configurations let one part file produce every length â€” change one variable, get the right part.

## Creating Configurations in Onshape
\`\`\`
In the Part Studio:
  Configurations â†’ + Add configuration input

Type: List â†’ "Length" with options: 4in, 6in, 8in, 10in, 12in, 18in, 24in
Type: Variable â†’ "Length" with range 1in to 36in (more flexible)

Link to the extrude feature:
  Extrude depth: click the dimension field â†’ Configuration input â†’ "Length"
  Now changing the configuration changes the extrude depth

For hole patterns (count depends on length):
  Hole count: if-expression in pattern count field:
  = round(config_length / 0.5in) - 1
  This auto-calculates holes for any configured length
\`\`\`

## Using Configurations in Assembly
\`\`\`
Insert part â†’ select configuration from dropdown â†’ "12in tube"
  â†’ places that specific length

Change configuration after placement:
  Double-click the instance â†’ change configuration â†’ assembly updates

Bill of Materials:
  Each configuration appears as a separate line item in BOM
  "1x1 Tube 12in Ã— 4" + "1x1 Tube 18in Ã— 2"
  Accurate BOM automatically from one part file

Multi-parameter configurations (brackets with multiple hole spacings):
  Add second configuration for hole count or position
  Each unique combination = one BOM line item
\`\`\`

## When to Use Configurations vs Separate Parts
\`\`\`
Use configurations:
  â†’ Same geometry, different dimensions (tube lengths, plate thicknesses)
  â†’ Parts that differ only by a single feature (hole added/removed)
  â†’ Family of fasteners (M5 Ã— 8, 10, 12, 16mm â€” all same M5 thread)

Use separate parts:
  â†’ Different geometry (L-bracket vs flat plate)
  â†’ Different materials (same shape in aluminum and in plastic)
  â†’ Parts that share a name but differ in multiple ways
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What specific benefit does linking hole count to tube length as a formula provide over a fixed count?",opts:["Formulas are more precise","A formula automatically computes the correct hole count for any configured length â€” adding a 10in configuration doesn't require manually setting the hole count to 19; the formula recalculates correctly for every length, eliminating a common error source when adding new sizes","Formulas prevent extra holes","Fixed counts are harder to change"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does a configured part appear as multiple line items in the Bill of Materials rather than one?",opts:["CAD software separates instances","Each configuration represents a physically distinct part â€” a 12in tube and an 18in tube are ordered separately; the BOM correctly lists each unique configuration with its quantity so procurement can order exactly the right sizes and counts","Multi-line BOM is a software bug","Configurations require separate part numbers"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Advanced.push(
  {id:"cada_top_down",title:"Top-Down Design â€” Designing Robot from the Frame Out",est:"14 min",content:`## Design in Context, Not in Isolation
A mechanism designed in isolation often doesn't fit the robot. A mechanism designed top-down â€” inside the robot's master layout â€” respects packaging constraints from the first sketch. Top-down design is how professional engineering teams build complex assemblies.

## The Master Sketch Approach
\`\`\`
Step 1: Create a "Master Sketch" Part Studio
  â†’ This part studio defines the robot's key geometry:
    - Frame perimeter (with bumper zone)
    - Drivetrain centerlines
    - Maximum height at starting configuration
    - Key field interaction heights (intake floor clearance, speaker height)
    - Bumper zone (4.5" to 7.5" from floor)

Step 2: All mechanism assemblies reference the Master Sketch
  â†’ Insert Master Sketch into each mechanism assembly as a layout reference
  â†’ Mechanism designers see exactly where their mechanism must fit
  â†’ Frame perimeter line = hard constraint: mechanism can't cross it (unless extending)

Step 3: Mechanism sub-assemblies nest into the robot top assembly
  â†’ Top assembly: drivetrain + arm + intake + climber + electronics
  â†’ Check interference at top level: do all sub-assemblies fit simultaneously?
  â†’ Animation: does everything move without hitting each other?
\`\`\`

## Derived Geometry â€” Linking Dimensions Across Files
\`\`\`
Onshape: use "Derive" to pull geometry from the Master Sketch into a Part Studio
  Insert â†’ Derived â†’ select Master Sketch â†’ brings edges/faces in as reference

Use derived geometry to:
  â†’ Auto-size a bracket to match a frame feature that might change
  â†’ Ensure a pivot point lands exactly at a robot coordinate

Parametric constraint chain:
  Master Sketch (frame width = 26") â†’ Arm pivot position (26" - 4" offset = 22" from center)
  â†’ Arm length to reach scoring height â†’ Mechanism motor position relative to pivot

When the frame width changes to 27": update Master Sketch â†’ all downstream geometry updates
This is the power of top-down design over bottom-up isolation.
\`\`\`

## Pitfalls of Top-Down Design
\`\`\`
Circular references:
  â†’ Part A references Part B references Part A â†’ infinite loop â†’ rebuild failures
  â†’ Fix: Master Sketch references nothing; mechanisms reference Master Sketch only

Over-constraining across files:
  â†’ Linking too many dimensions across files creates fragile update chains
  â†’ Rule: link strategic (frame-level) dimensions top-down;
           detail (fastener position) dimensions stay local to the sub-assembly

File organization:
  ROBOT_2025/
    MasterSketch.onshape
    Frame/
      MainFrame.onshape
    Arm/
      ArmSubassembly.onshape
    RobotTopLevel.onshape
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What specific problem does a Master Sketch solve that designing mechanisms in isolation cannot?",opts:["Master Sketches are faster","Isolated mechanism design lacks spatial context â€” each mechanism designer doesn't know where the others' mechanisms land; a Master Sketch provides shared coordinates that all designers reference, preventing two mechanisms from occupying the same space or a mechanism from exceeding the robot's frame perimeter","Master Sketches are required for assemblies","Isolated design produces weaker parts"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should detail dimensions (fastener positions) remain local rather than being linked from the Master Sketch?",opts:["Fasteners are unimportant","Linking fine-grained details creates fragile update chains where a small master change cascades into unintended downstream changes â€” strategic dimensions (frame width, pivot height) are worth linking because they define the design space; fastener positions are local details that should adapt independently within the mechanism they serve","Detail dimensions can't be linked","Master Sketches have size limits"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"cada_sheet_metal",title:"Sheet Metal Design for Laser-Cut Brackets",est:"13 min",content:`## Flat Pattern to Finished Part â€” The Sheet Metal Workflow
Almost every custom robot bracket starts as a flat sheet of aluminum that gets cut by a laser or waterjet and bent into shape. Designing for this process â€” using sheet metal features instead of solid extrudes â€” gives you accurate flat patterns, correct bend radii, and automatic DXF export for the cutting service.

## Sheet Metal Part Studio in Onshape
\`\`\`
Instead of: Sketch â†’ Extrude (creates solid, incorrect for bending)
Use:        Sketch â†’ Flange or Base Flange (creates sheet metal features)

Base Flange:
  â†’ Sketch the flat outline of the part (the unbent footprint)
  â†’ Sheet Metal Flange feature: select sketch, set thickness (0.125" for 1/8" Al)
  â†’ Result: flat sheet with correct material assignment

Bend (Flange):
  â†’ Select an edge â†’ Flange feature
  â†’ Set: flange angle (90Â°), flange length, bend radius
  â†’ Onshape automatically calculates bend allowance (material stretches)
  â†’ Result: bent tab, correctly modeled for flat-pattern accuracy

Tab and slot connections:
  â†’ Design interlocking tabs that align two flat pieces before welding/riveting
  â†’ Tab: rectangular protrusion on one part
  â†’ Slot: matching rectangular cutout on the other
  â†’ When assembled: parts align perfectly with no separate fixturing
\`\`\`

## Flat Pattern Export for Fabrication
\`\`\`
In the sheet metal Part Studio:
  â†’ Onshape automatically creates a "Flat Pattern" view
  â†’ Flat pattern shows the exact shape to cut, including:
    - Bend lines (shown as dashed lines for the fabricator)
    - Correct blank size accounting for bend allowance
    - All holes in their correct flat-pattern positions

Export as DXF:
  Right-click Flat Pattern â†’ Export â†’ DXF
  â†’ Send to laser/waterjet cutter exactly as exported
  â†’ No manual flat-pattern calculation required

Bend radius selection:
  â†’ 1/8" aluminum: minimum bend radius = 0.125" (1Ã— thickness)
  â†’ Never go below minimum: part cracks at the bend
  â†’ Standard press brake tooling: 0.125", 0.250", 0.375"
  â†’ Design all bends to match one standard radius â†’ one tool setup at the shop
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does Onshape's sheet metal Flange feature produce a more accurate flat pattern than manually sketching the unbent shape?",opts:["Flange features are automated","The Flange feature automatically applies bend allowance â€” the material stretches during bending, so the flat blank must be shorter than the finished bent dimension; manually sketching the flat shape without this compensation produces a part that's dimensionally incorrect after bending","Flange features are required for sheet metal","Manual sketches can't be exported as DXF"],ans:1},
      {q:"What practical fabrication advantage do tab-and-slot connections provide when assembling a laser-cut sheet metal robot?",opts:["They eliminate the need for fasteners","Tabs that fit into slots create precise self-alignment â€” when two cut parts are assembled, they automatically locate correctly relative to each other without additional fixtures, rulers, or reference marks; this makes consistent assembly possible even for less experienced builders","Tab connections are faster to laser cut","Slots reduce material cost"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
