LESSONS.git.Beginner.push(
  {id:"gb_fork",title:"Forking & Contributing to Upstream Repos",est:"11 min",content:`## Your Code Could Help Other Teams
When you fix a bug in a library you use â€” WPILib, MKCAD scripts, or community scouting tools â€” submitting that fix upstream helps everyone. Understanding forks and pull requests lets you contribute rather than just consume open-source code.

## The Fork Workflow
\`\`\`
Scenario: you found a bug in an open-source scouting library.

Step 1: Fork the repo (GitHub UI):
  â†’ Go to github.com/original-team/scouting-lib
  â†’ Click "Fork" â†’ creates github.com/your-team/scouting-lib
  â†’ This is YOUR copy â€” you can modify it freely

Step 2: Clone your fork:
  git clone https://github.com/your-team/scouting-lib
  cd scouting-lib

Step 3: Add the original as "upstream" remote:
  git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-team/scouting-lib
  git remote -v
  # origin   â†’ your fork (push/pull)
  # upstream â†’ original (pull only â€” you don't have push access)

Step 4: Create a branch for your fix:
  git switch -c fix/csv-export-encoding

Step 5: Make the fix, commit, push to YOUR fork:
  git add .
  git commit -m "fix(export): correct UTF-8 encoding for team names with accents"
  git push origin fix/csv-export-encoding

Step 6: Open a Pull Request on GitHub:
  â†’ Your fork â†’ Compare & pull request â†’ to original-team/scouting-lib
  â†’ Describe what you fixed and why
\`\`\`

## Keeping Your Fork in Sync
\`\`\`bash
# When the original repo gets new commits:
git fetch upstream
git switch main
git merge upstream/main   # or: git rebase upstream/main
git push origin main      # update your fork's main

# Update your feature branch with upstream changes:
git switch fix/csv-export-encoding
git rebase upstream/main
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does adding the original repository as an 'upstream' remote accomplish?",opts:["It gives you push access","It creates a named reference to the original repository so you can fetch new commits from it â€” without 'upstream', your fork would diverge indefinitely as the original receives updates; with it, you can sync your fork to stay current with fixes and features from the original authors","Upstream remotes are required by GitHub","It enables you to merge to the original"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is a bug fix branch (fix/csv-export-encoding) created rather than fixing directly on main?",opts:["Branches are required for forks","The fix lives on a dedicated branch that can be submitted as a focused pull request containing only the bug fix â€” fixing on main would include any other work-in-progress, making it harder for maintainers to review and potentially mixing unrelated changes into the upstream repository","Branch naming is a GitHub requirement","Main branches can't be pushed to forks"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"gb_recover",title:"Recovering from Mistakes â€” Reset, Revert & Restore",est:"11 min",content:`## You Can Almost Always Undo It
New git users fear mistakes because they think they're permanent. Almost nothing in git is permanent before 30 days (git's garbage collection). Knowing which recovery command fits which situation is the skill.

## The Recovery Toolkit
\`\`\`bash
# Scenario 1: Staged files you don't want to commit yet
git restore --staged RobotContainer.java
# Unstages the file, leaves your edits on disk

# Scenario 2: Edits you want to throw away (not yet committed)
git restore RobotContainer.java
# WARNING: this permanently discards uncommitted changes â€” no undo for this one

# Scenario 3: Wrong commit message (not yet pushed)
git commit --amend -m "fix(arm): correct encoder scaling factor"
# Replaces the last commit message (and optionally adds staged changes)

# Scenario 4: One file from a specific old commit
git checkout a3f92b1 -- src/main/java/frc/robot/Constants.java
# Restores that file to its state at commit a3f92b1

# Scenario 5: Undo the last commit, keep changes staged
git reset --soft HEAD~1
# Commit is gone, changes are staged again â€” re-commit when ready

# Scenario 6: Undo the last commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1  # (mixed is the default)

# Scenario 7: Completely undo the last commit and discard changes
git reset --hard HEAD~1
# WARNING: changes are gone â€” only do this if you're sure
\`\`\`

## The Safe Undo (git revert â€” for pushed commits)
\`\`\`bash
# NEVER use reset --hard on commits already pushed to a shared branch
# It rewrites history â†’ everyone else's clone is now broken

# Safe alternative: revert creates a new commit that undoes the changes
git revert a3f92b1
# Creates: "Revert 'feat(vision): add AprilTag targeting'"
# History is preserved; the undo is visible in the log

# If the revert causes conflicts:
git revert --no-commit a3f92b1
# Applies the revert as staged changes â€” resolve conflicts, then commit manually
\`\`\`

## git reflog â€” The Safety Net
\`\`\`bash
# Even after a reset --hard, commits aren't immediately gone
git reflog
# Shows every HEAD position for the last 30 days:
# a3f92b1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~1
# 7c44d02 HEAD@{1}: commit: feat(vision): add AprilTag targeting

# Recover: checkout the commit you just reset away
git checkout 7c44d02
# Or restore the whole branch to where it was:
git reset --hard 7c44d02
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should 'git reset --hard' never be used on commits that have already been pushed to a shared branch?",opts:["Reset --hard is too destructive","Reset --hard rewrites history â€” it removes commits from the branch's history; team members who have already pulled those commits now have a diverged history that can't be reconciled with a normal push; using revert instead creates a new undo commit that preserves history for everyone","Shared branches are locked","Push access is required for reset"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'git reflog' allow you to recover that even 'git log' cannot show after a reset?",opts:["Deleted files","The history of every HEAD position including commits that were reset away â€” git log shows the current branch history; git reflog shows every state HEAD has been in for 30 days, including commits that are no longer reachable via any branch, allowing recovery of work that appeared to be lost","Merge conflicts","Remote branch history"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_squash",title:"Squashing Commits â€” Clean History Before Merging",est:"10 min",content:`## WIP Commits Should Never Reach Main
"wip", "more fixes", "asdf" â€” these are fine on a feature branch when you're in the middle of work. They shouldn't survive into main's history, where they obscure what actually changed. Squashing combines multiple messy commits into one clean, descriptive commit before merging.

## Interactive Rebase for Squashing
\`\`\`bash
# You have 5 commits on your branch since branching from main:
git log --oneline
# e7f2a11 actually working now
# c4b3d22 fix oops
# 9a8b7c6 more work
# 3f2e1d0 wip: arm working but oscillating
# 7c44d02 feat(arm): start position control (base commit â€” don't squash this)

# Squash the last 4 into the base commit:
git rebase -i HEAD~5

# Editor opens with:
# pick 7c44d02 feat(arm): start position control
# pick 3f2e1d0 wip: arm working but oscillating
# pick 9a8b7c6 more work
# pick c4b3d22 fix oops
# pick e7f2a11 actually working now

# Change to:
# pick 7c44d02 feat(arm): start position control
# squash 3f2e1d0 wip: arm working but oscillating
# squash 9a8b7c6 more work
# squash c4b3d22 fix oops
# squash e7f2a11 actually working now

# Save â†’ editor opens for new combined commit message
# Write: "feat(arm): add position control with PID, kP=0.008"
# Save â†’ squash complete

# Force push (required â€” history was rewritten):
git push --force-with-lease origin feature/arm-position
\`\`\`

## Squash Merge (GitHub approach â€” no interactive rebase)
\`\`\`
When merging a PR on GitHub:
  â†’ Merge pull request dropdown â†’ Squash and merge
  â†’ GitHub combines all PR commits into one + adds PR description as commit body
  â†’ Good default for teams that don't want to manage interactive rebase

Tradeoff:
  â†’ Individual commits on the branch are lost after squash merge
  â†’ The single squashed commit is clean on main
  â†’ Good for feature branches; less ideal if branch had multiple distinct features
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does squashing require a force push (git push --force-with-lease) rather than a normal push?",opts:["Force push is required for rebases","Interactive rebase rewrites history â€” the squashed branch has different commit hashes than the original; a normal push is rejected because the remote's history and the local history have diverged; force push overwrites the remote branch with the new history","Force push is always safer","GitHub requires force push for feature branches"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the practical difference between squash-merging via GitHub's UI and using interactive rebase locally?",opts:["GitHub's squash is more reliable","GitHub's squash merge happens automatically at merge time without requiring local commands, but uses the PR description for the commit message; local interactive rebase gives full control over the final commit message and allows choosing which commits to squash vs keep separate â€” more control at the cost of more steps","GitHub squash preserves individual commits","Local rebase requires admin access"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ga_secrets",title:"Managing Secrets in Robot Code Repos",est:"11 min",content:`## API Keys in Git History Are Permanent Security Risks
A TBA API key committed to a public GitHub repository is readable by anyone â€” and once committed, it's in git history even after you delete it. Removing secrets from git history is painful; never committing them is easy.

## The Secret Management Strategy
\`\`\`
Tiered by sensitivity:

Tier 1: Non-sensitive config (commit these):
  â†’ TBA event keys ("2025casd")
  â†’ Robot constants (motor IDs, gear ratios)
  â†’ Match schedule URLs without credentials
  â†’ team_config.json (robot settings, field dimensions)

Tier 2: Low-sensitivity (commit template, not values):
  â†’ API keys with rate-limited public access
  â†’ Practice field IP addresses

Tier 3: Never commit:
  â†’ API keys with write access
  â†’ Database passwords
  â†’ OAuth tokens
  â†’ Private SSH keys
\`\`\`

## Implementation Patterns
\`\`\`python
# Pattern 1: Environment variable (best for scripts)
import os
TBA_KEY = os.environ.get("TBA_KEY")
if not TBA_KEY:
    raise RuntimeError("TBA_KEY environment variable not set")

# Pattern 2: Config file not tracked by git (best for desktop tools)
# config_local.py â€” in .gitignore:
TBA_KEY = "your-actual-key-here"

# config_template.py â€” committed:
TBA_KEY = "REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_KEY"  # copy this file to config_local.py

# Pattern 3: .env file (best for team web apps)
# .env â€” in .gitignore:
TBA_KEY=your-actual-key-here
WEBHOOK_SECRET=another-secret

# In Python: use python-dotenv
from dotenv import load_dotenv
load_dotenv()
TBA_KEY = os.environ.get("TBA_KEY")
\`\`\`

## If You Accidentally Committed a Secret
\`\`\`bash
# Step 1: Immediately rotate/revoke the exposed credential
#   (Assume it's been seen â€” treat it as compromised)

# Step 2: Remove from history (complex â€” git filter-repo):
pip install git-filter-repo
git filter-repo --path secrets.py --invert-paths
# Rewrites entire history removing secrets.py from every commit

# Step 3: Force push ALL branches
git push --force --all origin

# Step 4: Inform all collaborators to re-clone
# (Their clones still have the old history)

# The lesson: rotation + prevention is easier than removal
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is rotating a compromised credential the first step even before removing it from git history?",opts:["Rotation is faster","The credential may have already been seen â€” bots scan public repos for secrets within seconds of a push; an attacker who found the key can use it regardless of whether you later remove it from history; rotating immediately invalidates the exposed credential, stopping any active misuse while you clean up history","History removal is complex","Rotation prevents future exposure"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a committed config_template.py file accomplish that a .gitignore entry alone cannot?",opts:["It documents the file structure","It documents what settings are required and in what format â€” a new team member can see exactly what config_local.py should look like by reading the template; .gitignore only prevents the actual secret file from being committed, providing no guidance on what should be in it","Templates are faster to load",".gitignore doesn't work for Python files"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ga_ci",title:"GitHub Actions â€” Automated Builds on Every Push",est:"13 min",content:`## Every Push Should Trigger a Build Check
A CI (Continuous Integration) pipeline automatically builds and tests your code every time someone pushes. If the build breaks, you know immediately â€” before the broken code reaches the robot and wastes drive practice time.

## FRC Robot Code CI Workflow
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/robot.yml
name: Robot Build & Check

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, "feature/**"]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    name: Gradle Build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Java 17
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '17'

      - name: Grant execute permission for gradlew
        run: chmod +x gradlew

      - name: Build robot code
        run: ./gradlew build

      - name: Run unit tests
        run: ./gradlew test

      - name: Upload test results
        if: always()   # run even if build fails
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: test-results
          path: build/reports/tests/
\`\`\`

## Python Scouting CI
\`\`\`yaml
# .github/workflows/scouting.yml
name: Scouting App Tests

on:
  push:
    paths: ['scouting/**']

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: scouting

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Run tests
        run: python -m unittest discover -v

      - name: Check formatting
        run: |
          pip install black
          black --check .
\`\`\`

## Reading CI Results
\`\`\`
GitHub â†’ repository â†’ Actions tab â†’ click any workflow run
  â†’ Green checkmark: build passed
  â†’ Red X: build failed â€” click to see which step failed and why

PR integration:
  â†’ Every PR shows CI status before merging
  â†’ Protected branch setting: require passing CI before merge is allowed
  â†’ "Squash and merge" stays grey until CI passes

Competition week tip:
  â†’ Add a badge to README.md:
  â†’ [![Build](https://github.com/team1234/robot2025/actions/workflows/robot.yml/badge.svg)]
  â†’ Visible pass/fail on the repo homepage
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What problem does requiring passing CI before a PR can be merged solve on a multi-member team?",opts:["It enforces code style","It prevents broken code from reaching the main branch â€” without this requirement, a reviewer might approve a PR that looks correct but fails to build; requiring CI pass means the code was actually compiled and tested before any human reviewed it, not just read for logical correctness","CI must run before code review","It prevents merge conflicts"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does the 'upload test results' step use 'if: always()' rather than the default behavior?",opts:["Test results are always needed","By default, a step only runs if all previous steps succeeded â€” if the build fails, the upload would be skipped; 'always()' ensures test results are uploaded even after a build failure, providing the specific test failure details that diagnose what broke","Always() is required for uploads","GitHub discards results without always()"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT +8 (25â†’33) â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Beginner.push(
  {id:"tmb_inclusive",title:"Building an Inclusive Team Culture",est:"11 min",content:`## Inclusion Is a Competitive Advantage
A team that only retains students who already look like engineers loses talent from day one. A team where every person â€” regardless of background, ability, or technical experience â€” feels genuinely valued builds a stronger, more creative team and runs more robust programs.

## What Inclusion Looks Like in Practice
\`\`\`
Visible inclusion:
  â†’ Leadership that reflects the team's demographics
    (if 40% of your team is female, 40% of leads should be female)
  â†’ Meeting structure where everyone speaks â€” not just the loudest
  â†’ Explicit space for quieter members:
    "We haven't heard from [name] yet â€” what do you think?"

Task inclusion:
  â†’ Every member has meaningful work on Day 1 (not "go watch")
  â†’ Non-technical roles valued explicitly: documentation, outreach, scouting
    are not "lesser" than building and coding
  â†’ Learning paths: a member with no coding experience has a clear path
    to contributing to code within 4-6 weeks

Language inclusion:
  â†’ No jargon without definition the first time (TLA, WPILib, subsystem)
  â†’ No "you should already know this" energy â€” explain without condescension
  â†’ Team language norms: "that's a dumb idea" â†’ never; "tell me more" â†’ default
\`\`\`

## The Belonging Check
\`\`\`
Once a month, every lead asks their subteam:
  "Is there anything that's making it hard for you to contribute?"
  "What's something about how we work that you'd change?"

Low-psychological-safety answer: "No, everything's fine"
This is the answer when people don't feel safe to say the real thing.

Building safety:
  â†’ Act on one piece of feedback publicly: "Last month [name] suggested X.
    We tried it and here's how it went."
  â†’ Even small responses to feedback build trust that speaking up matters
  â†’ Feedback that goes unacknowledged teaches people to stop giving it
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should leadership composition reflect the team's overall demographic composition?",opts:["Leadership quotas improve performance","When visible leadership looks like only a subset of the team, members outside that group receive an implicit signal that advancement isn't for them â€” this reduces engagement and increases attrition; leadership representation signals that all team members have real paths to impact and ownership","Leadership must be elected","Diverse leadership improves award scores"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a consistently 'No, everything's fine' response to inclusion check-ins most likely indicate?",opts:["The team has no inclusion problems","Low psychological safety â€” people don't feel it's safe to share genuine concerns; this response is a red flag, not reassurance; building safety requires demonstrating that feedback leads to visible action so members learn that speaking up produces change rather than being ignored or punished","The questions are too broad","Check-ins should be less frequent"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmb_expectations",title:"Setting and Managing Expectations",est:"10 min",content:`## Unclear Expectations Create Resentment
A member who doesn't know what's expected can't meet expectations. A lead who has expectations they never communicated can't fairly hold members to them. Almost every team conflict that feels personal is actually a failed expectations alignment.

## The Expectations Conversation at Onboarding
\`\`\`
Have this explicitly at the start of each season with every returning and new member:

Attendance:
  "Our expectation is 80% attendance during build season
   (that's 4 of every 5 sessions). If you need to miss, let us know by [channel]."

Communication:
  "If you can't make a session, we need to know by [time the day before].
   No-shows without notice affect the whole team's planning."

Ownership:
  "When you're assigned a task, you own it â€” that means either completing it
   or telling your lead why you can't before the deadline."

Learning:
  "You don't need to know everything â€” you do need to be willing to ask for help.
   Stuck for more than 20 minutes without asking is too long."

Write it down:
  â†’ Team handbook or onboarding doc
  â†’ Members who signed/acknowledged it can't later claim they didn't know
\`\`\`

## When Expectations Aren't Being Met
\`\`\`
Step 1: Assume good intent first
  "Is there something getting in the way I should know about?"
  â†’ School stress, family situation, health: real and valid
  â†’ Address the barrier, not the behavior

Step 2: Restate the expectation clearly
  "I need you to let me know by 6pm the day before you're missing a session.
   That's the specific part that makes it hard for the team when it doesn't happen."

Step 3: Agree on a specific behavior going forward
  "Can you commit to that? What would make it easier for you?"

Step 4: Follow up
  â†’ If improvement: acknowledge it specifically
  â†’ If no improvement: involve mentor, discuss role fit

Never: address expectations publicly in front of the group
Always: specific behavior, not character ("you don't communicate"
         â†’ "I need you to message before missing sessions")
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should unmet expectations be addressed with 'is there something getting in the way' before stating the expectation?",opts:["It avoids confrontation","Understanding context before asserting the expectation prevents addressing the symptom rather than the cause â€” a member missing sessions because of a family crisis needs support, not a lecture about attendance; addressing the barrier solves the problem while preserving the relationship","Good intent must be assumed always","Leading with questions is required"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does writing down team expectations in a handbook matter beyond verbal communication at onboarding?",opts:["Written rules are legally binding","A written document serves as shared reference â€” verbal-only expectations are remembered differently by different people and can be reinterpreted over time; a handbook means the expectation conversation was real, documented, and acknowledged rather than subject to 'I didn't know that was expected'","Handbooks are required for FIRST","Written expectations improve award scores"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"tmi_knowledge",title:"Knowledge Management â€” Preventing Institutional Memory Loss",est:"13 min",content:`## When Seniors Graduate, Knowledge Shouldn't Go With Them
A team that relies on three seniors knowing how to deploy code, order parts, and set up the field is three graduations away from starting over. Systematic knowledge capture keeps institutional memory alive regardless of who leaves.

## What Needs to Be Documented
\`\`\`
Critical knowledge (the team breaks without this):
  â†’ Deployment procedure: how to push code to the robot
  â†’ Part ordering: who has accounts, how to get approval, lead times
  â†’ Event logistics: hotel booking, trailer loading checklist, pit setup
  â†’ Robot setup: how to configure for a competition (battery, enabled, calibrated)
  â†’ Emergency contacts: who to call when X breaks at competition

Operational knowledge (the team works worse without this):
  â†’ Tuning procedures: how we tune our arm PID (step by step)
  â†’ Scouting system: how to run data collection at an event
  â†’ Awards: submission template, what's worked before, judge preferences
  â†’ Sponsor communication: who our contacts are and how we communicate

Institutional memory (the team learns from this):
  â†’ Season retrospectives: what worked, what didn't, why we made key decisions
  â†’ Design decisions: why we chose mechanism A over B (written in the notebook)
  â†’ Failed experiments: what we tried that didn't work (prevents repeating mistakes)
\`\`\`

## The Documentation System That Gets Used
\`\`\`
Google Drive folder structure:
  Team 1234/
    Playbooks/          â† How-to guides (one page each)
      deploy-code.md
      order-parts.md
      competition-setup.md
    Season 2025/        â† This season's documents
      Engineering Notebook/
      Outreach Log/
    History/            â† Prior seasons (don't delete)
      Season 2024/
      Season 2023/

Playbook format (one page, active voice):
  Title: How to Deploy Code to the Robot
  Author: [Name], Date: [date], Last reviewed: [date]
  Step 1: [specific action]
  Step 2: [specific action]
  ... (max 10 steps â€” if longer, split into sub-procedures)
  Troubleshooting: If [thing] happens, do [this]

Review cycle: once per season â€” assign one person to verify each playbook still works
  A playbook that's wrong is worse than no playbook
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a playbook that contains errors described as worse than no playbook?",opts:["Errors are embarrassing","Someone following an incorrect playbook confidently applies a wrong procedure, potentially causing additional problems or wasting more time than starting from scratch; a missing playbook signals that guidance must be sought; a wrong one appears authoritative and misleads the person following it","Playbooks must be perfect","Errors indicate poor documentation culture"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'institutional memory' (failed experiments, design decisions) valuable to document even though it's less urgent than operational procedures?",opts:["It impresses award judges","Teams that don't document failures repeat them â€” the next build season's designers spend weeks on the same approach that failed two years ago because no record of the failure and its root cause exists; documented history converts experience into durable team intelligence","Past decisions don't affect future seasons","Institutional memory is only for championship teams"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmi_succession",title:"Succession Planning â€” Preparing the Next Leadership Generation",est:"12 min",content:`## A Great Team Survives Its Leaders Graduating
Teams that plan succession have a smooth handoff when seniors leave. Teams that don't suddenly find that the student who built the elevator and the student who managed awards and the student who knew every sponsor relationship all graduated in June â€” and the team starts over.

## The Succession Timeline
\`\`\`
September (start of season):
  â†’ Identify 1-2 potential successors for each critical role
  â†’ These "apprentice leads" shadow the current lead all season
  â†’ They observe every important meeting and decision

November-January (build season):
  â†’ Apprentice leads take ownership of increasing responsibilities
  â†’ Lead: "You run today's subteam standup â€” I'll be here if you need me"
  â†’ Gradually remove scaffolding: "You run it, I'll just watch this time"

February-March (competition season):
  â†’ Apprentice leads visible at competition in a real capacity
  â†’ Current lead introduces them to sponsors, judges, other captains:
    "This is [name] â€” they'll be running [role] next year"

May-June (transition):
  â†’ Formal handoff meeting: current lead â†’ successor
  â†’ Transfer: account access, contacts, document ownership, relationship history
  â†’ One week of shadow (successor runs it, current lead watches) before full handoff

Fall:
  â†’ New lead runs it. Old lead = consultant, not manager.
    (The hardest part: letting go)
\`\`\`

## What to Transfer, Exactly
\`\`\`
Relationships:
  â†’ Sponsor contacts: name, role, what they care about, history with team
  â†’ Event contacts: local volunteers who help year after year
  â†’ Partner school teachers: names, what programs you run with them

Accounts:
  â†’ Team email addresses: who has access, what they're used for
  â†’ Sponsor portal logins: platforms where invoices and reporting happen
  â†’ Social media: credentials, posting guidelines
  â†’ Github org: admin access to the repository

Context:
  â†’ Current status of each active initiative
  â†’ What's working vs what's struggling
  â†’ One conversation with each mentor: "here's what you need to know about [new lead]"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should apprentice leads be introduced to sponsors and other captains at competitions rather than only during internal team activities?",opts:["Competition introductions are more formal","External relationships are built on personal familiarity â€” a sponsor who knows the current lead by name must rebuild trust with a new lead who is a stranger; introducing the successor in person during competitions, with the current lead vouching for them, transfers relationship credibility rather than requiring the new lead to start from zero","Competition contacts are most important","Sponsors prefer meeting new leads early"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the most common failure mode during leadership succession, and what does it prevent?",opts:["New leads change too much too fast","The outgoing leader failing to fully let go â€” continuing to make decisions, overriding the successor publicly, or being more available than necessary; this undermines the new leader's authority and prevents them from developing their own style and relationships, making the eventual full departure more disruptive","Succession always fails","New leads lack experience by definition"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Advanced.push(
  {id:"tma_crisis",title:"Crisis Management During Build Season",est:"13 min",content:`## Every Team Has at Least One Crisis Season
A critical mentor leaves in Week 3. A major sponsor cancels. The machine shop floods the day the frame needs to be cut. A team leadership conflict explodes. A student gets injured. How a team responds to crisis determines whether it recovers or collapses.

## The Crisis Response Framework
\`\`\`
The first 2 hours after a crisis is identified:
  1. Stabilize: stop the bleeding before solving the problem
     â†’ Injured student: get medical help first, robot work stops entirely
     â†’ Financial crisis: halt all non-essential spending immediately
     â†’ Technical crisis: freeze the robot in its last-known-good state

  2. Assess: what is actually true? (Separate fact from rumor)
     â†’ Who is affected?
     â†’ What is the minimum needed to continue the season?
     â†’ What are the real constraints?

  3. Communicate: to the people who need to know
     â†’ Leadership team: full information
     â†’ Full team: enough to stop speculation, not every detail
     â†’ Parents/mentors: what they need to know for their decisions
     â†’ Do NOT: let information vacuum fill with rumor

  4. Decide: one decision, by one accountable person
     â†’ Who is responsible for the response? (Name one person)
     â†’ What is the first action in the next 2 hours?
     â†’ What is the 48-hour plan?
\`\`\`

## Common Crises and Specific Responses
\`\`\`
Critical mentor departure:
  â†’ Identify which mentor skills are truly irreplaceable vs. learnable
  â†’ Reach out to sister teams immediately â€” community reciprocity is real
  â†’ Redistribute mentor load; identify senior students who can temporarily lead

Budget shortfall (>30% of season budget):
  â†’ Identify the minimum viable season (what costs can't be cut?)
  â†’ Emergency sponsor outreach: personal calls, not emails
  â†’ Scope robot to match budget: what can we build with what we have?

Robot catastrophe (destroyed, stolen, or major structural failure):
  â†’ Assess remaining time to competition
  â†’ < 2 weeks: simplified robot using available parts
  â†’ > 3 weeks: rebuild the critical subsystem, ship the robot
  â†’ Document the failure â€” some competitions accept extenuating circumstances

Team cohesion crisis:
  â†’ Leadership conflict must be resolved before robot work continues (or it gets worse)
  â†’ Separate parties; individual conversations first
  â†’ Mediated conversation with a trusted mentor
  â†’ Never: take sides publicly or allow the conflict to run while building continues
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the crisis response framework prioritize communication as step 3, before solving the problem?",opts:["Communication is faster than action","An information vacuum fills with rumors that are often worse than the truth â€” if the team doesn't know what happened, they invent explanations; communicating what is known (even 'we're still figuring this out, but here's what we know') stops speculation and keeps people from making decisions based on wrong assumptions","People must be informed before decisions","Communication is required by FIRST"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes naming one accountable person for the crisis response specifically important?",opts:["Accountability requires one name","When multiple people share crisis ownership, each assumes someone else is handling the critical pieces â€” naming one person creates a single point of contact who is responsible for the 48-hour plan and for escalating if it's not working; shared ownership without a named lead produces coordinated inaction","Crisis response requires hierarchy","One person has the most knowledge"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ OUTREACH +8 (25â†’33) â”€â”€
LESSONS.outreach.Beginner.push(
  {id:"orb_presentation",title:"Giving a Great Robot Presentation",est:"10 min",content:`## Five Minutes in Front of a Room
You've got a gym full of students, a robot, and five minutes to make them care about robotics. Most team presentations lose the audience in the first sixty seconds by explaining FIRST before showing anything cool. The structure below keeps audiences engaged.

## The Five-Minute Presentation Structure
\`\`\`
0:00-0:30 â€” The Hook (do something impressive immediately)
  â†’ Drive the robot fast and turn quickly (don't explain, just do it)
  â†’ Score a game piece from the other side of the room
  â†’ No words yet â€” let the action create curiosity

0:30-1:30 â€” Who We Are (brief)
  â†’ "We're Team [number] from [school] â€” we build competition robots."
  â†’ "Every year FIRST releases a new game in January and we have 6 weeks to build."
  â†’ That's it â€” don't explain the entire FIRST structure

1:30-3:00 â€” What We Built (the interesting part)
  â†’ Pick ONE mechanism, explain the problem it solves and how
  â†’ "This intake has to pick up a game piece from the floor while the robot is moving.
     The first version we tried [quick description of failure].
     We fixed it by [specific change]. Now it works [X]% of the time."
  â†’ Show it working during the explanation

3:00-4:00 â€” Let Them Drive
  â†’ Invite one student to try the controls (brief, supervised)
  â†’ Immediately creates personal connection to the robot
  â†’ Audience sees one of their peers succeeding at it

4:00-5:00 â€” How to Get Involved
  â†’ Specific: "We meet Tuesdays and Thursdays at 3:30 in [room]"
  â†’ Signup link/sheet: pass it around right now, not "find us online"
\`\`\`

## The #1 Presentation Mistake
\`\`\`
Presenting to the audience's back of the room rather than engaging them:
  â†’ Talking AT students rather than WITH them
  â†’ Reading from notes instead of knowing the content
  â†’ Going over time (every additional minute loses half the remaining attention)

Fix: practice the presentation 3 times before giving it
     Each practice: time it. If it runs over, cut content until it fits.
     Never add more information; cut down to what actually matters most.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the five-minute presentation structure start with robot action rather than explaining what FIRST is?",opts:["Action is more entertaining","Audiences form their attention decision in the first 30 seconds â€” impressive robot action immediately creates curiosity and emotional engagement before any explanation; context (what FIRST is, who the team is) is retained much better once the audience already cares about the robot","FIRST rules require demonstrations first","Explanations confuse younger students"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes handing one student the robot controls during a presentation effective for the whole audience?",opts:["It saves presentation time","Seeing a peer â€” someone from their own school or age group â€” succeed at controlling the robot eliminates the 'this is only for special/smart people' barrier; it creates social proof that the skill is learnable and approachable, making every audience member imagine themselves doing it","Student drivers are faster","Audience participation is required"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"orb_digital",title:"Digital Presence â€” Website and Social Media Basics",est:"10 min",content:`## Your Team Exists Online Whether You Manage It or Not
Sponsors Google your team name. Potential members look you up. Parents research before letting their student join. A team with no web presence or an outdated one creates doubt. A well-maintained presence reinforces credibility with everyone who finds you.

## The Minimum Viable Online Presence
\`\`\`
Website (must-have):
  â†’ Team number, school name, location â€” visible on the homepage
  â†’ What the team does â€” one clear paragraph
  â†’ Current season: at minimum, the game name and competition schedule
  â†’ How to join or contact â€” specific, not "reach out to us"
  â†’ Sponsors page â€” a reason for sponsors to care about visibility

Free hosting: GitHub Pages, Google Sites, Wix (free tier)
Free domain: teamXXXX.github.io works; custom domain costs $10-15/yr

Social media (choose ONE and maintain it):
  â†’ Instagram: best for photos, reels, visual team content
  â†’ Facebook: best for reaching parents and local community
  â†’ X/Twitter: best for following FIRST community, connecting with other teams
  â†’ TikTok: highest reach potential; requires consistent video content

The fatal mistake: multiple platforms, all rarely updated
The right choice: one platform, updated every build session
\`\`\`

## What to Post During Build Season
\`\`\`
Post cadence (Instagram example):
  â†’ Monday: "Week [X] of build season starts â€” here's what we're working on"
  â†’ Wednesday: "Here's how our [mechanism] works [video of it working]"
  â†’ Friday: "This week we [accomplishment] â€” one week closer to competition"

Content that performs:
  â†’ Video of mechanisms moving (stop motion, time lapse, slow-mo)
  â†’ Before/after: failed prototype â†’ final version
  â†’ Students explaining something they built in their own words
  â†’ Competition results (even if results were mixed â€” people respect honesty)

Content that doesn't work:
  â†’ Generic "we love robotics!" without anything specific
  â†’ Blurry photos of people standing around
  â†’ Posts with no description ("pic or it didn't happen" doesn't apply to robotics)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is maintaining one social platform consistently recommended over creating multiple accounts?",opts:["Multiple platforms cost money","Audience trust is built through consistency â€” a single frequently-updated account signals an active team; multiple accounts that each receive sporadic posts signal disorganization; new followers checking an account with posts from 8 months ago assume the team is inactive or disbanded","Multiple platforms are too complex","Platforms penalize multiple accounts from one team"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes 'before/after: failed prototype â†’ final version' effective content for a team's social media?",opts:["Failure content gets more views","It tells a complete story with tension and resolution â€” the audience experiences the engineering process, not just the outcome; this creates authentic connection and communicates that robotics involves real problem-solving rather than effortless success, which is both honest and more compelling than showing only polished results","Before/after satisfies FIRST requirements","Failed prototypes are more interesting than successful ones"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"orb_fll",title:"Supporting a Local FLL Team Through Their Season",est:"12 min",content:`## FLL Mentorship Is the Highest-ROI Outreach You Can Do
A single FLL team supported through their full season reaches 10 students with 40-80 hours of sustained STEM engagement. Compare that to a 2-hour demo reaching 100 students for 5 minutes each. Depth matters, and FLL gives you the structure to achieve it.

## The FLL Season Calendar
\`\`\`
September:  FLL Kickoff â€” team registers, gets their challenge kit
October:    Design and build phase â€” robots are built, research project starts
November:   Qualifier season â€” local tournaments (varies by region)
December:   State/regional championship (for qualifying teams)
January:    World Festival (for championship qualifiers)

Your involvement calendar:
  September:   Help with game manual review + brainstorming session
  October (early): Build skills session (driving, attachment building)
  October (mid):   Programming introduction (Scratch or EV3)
  October (late):  Mock qualifier practice run with your team as judges
  November:        Be present at their qualifier (not to coach â€” to support)
\`\`\`

## Running a Technical Skills Session
\`\`\`
Best single-session topic for new FLL teams: mission strategy

Session structure (90 minutes):
  0:00 â€” Review the mission map together: "Which missions are worth the most?"
  0:20 â€” Have them run the robot at 3 missions: record success rates
  0:40 â€” Discuss: "Is it better to run 5 missions at 60% or 3 missions at 90%?"
          Expected value math: 5 Ã— pts Ã— 0.6 vs 3 Ã— pts Ã— 0.9
  0:60 â€” They redesign their run order based on their own data
  1:15 â€” Run again and compare success rates
  1:30 â€” Debrief: what changed? why?

This session teaches:
  â†’ Data collection
  â†’ Expected value thinking
  â†’ Iterative improvement
  â†’ Decision-making under uncertainty
  All in 90 minutes on the FLL table.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does sustained FLL mentorship (40-80 hours with 10 students) produce more impact per hour than a 2-hour demo reaching 100 students?",opts:["FLL counts for more award points","Depth of engagement determines actual learning â€” 5 minutes with a robot creates curiosity at best; 40 hours of building, programming, and iterating creates genuine skill and lasting identity as someone who does engineering; breadth numbers look impressive in reports but depth changes students' trajectories","Demos are less effective with older students","FLL teams are more motivated"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should your team attend the FLL qualifier as a support presence rather than a coaching presence?",opts:["FLL rules prohibit coaching at events","The qualifier is the FLL team's moment â€” coaching from the sidelines removes their ownership of the outcome and signals that you don't trust them to perform independently; being a supportive presence (cheering, being available for emotional support) respects that the event is theirs, which is the goal of the mentorship relationship","FRC teams can't enter FLL venues","Coaching is provided by event staff"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_data",title:"Measuring Outreach Impact â€” Metrics That Matter",est:"11 min",content:`## 'We Reached 500 Students' Is a Starting Point, Not an Answer
Impact award judges ask follow-up questions about your numbers. "Reached" can mean a 2-minute robot demo or a 3-day camp. Tracking metrics that measure depth â€” not just breadth â€” differentiates a transformative program from a touring robot show.

## Output vs Outcome vs Impact
\`\`\`
Output (what you did):
  â†’ Number of events: 18
  â†’ Students present: 847
  â†’ Hours of programming: 240
  â†’ New FLL teams started: 3

Outputs are necessary to measure â€” but they don't prove anything changed.

Outcome (what immediately changed):
  â†’ Students who applied to join our FRC team after events: 12
  â†’ FLL teams that completed their full season: 3/3 (100%)
  â†’ Teachers who ran a robotics activity after our visit: 4/8 (50%)

Outcomes show your program produced an immediate change in behavior.

Impact (lasting change):
  â†’ FLL teams still running 2 years later without our support: 2/3
  â†’ Students who joined FRC who are now pursuing engineering degrees: 7
  â†’ Schools that now have standing robotics programs: 3

Impact is the hardest to measure and the most convincing.
\`\`\`

## Practical Metrics You Can Track Without a Research Budget
\`\`\`
Easy to track (start here):
  â†’ Event attendance (actual count, not estimate)
  â†’ New FRC team member applications attributed to outreach events
  â†’ FLL team season completion rate
  â†’ Teacher follow-up (email 6 weeks later: "Did you run a robotics activity?")

Medium effort:
  â†’ Pre/post surveys for multi-day camps
    "Before camp, I could [task]" â†’ "After camp, I can [task]"
  â†’ School program status check (annual: is the program still running?)

Long-term (invest early, pay off in 3+ years):
  â†’ Alumni tracking: where are former members now?
  â†’ Program independence: "how many programs run without us?"

Metric you should never lead with:
  "Impressions" or "social media reach" â€” these measure exposure, not impact
  A video that 10,000 people watched for 3 seconds changed nothing
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What makes outcome metrics (teachers who ran a robotics activity after your visit) more convincing than output metrics (number of school visits) for award submissions?",opts:["Outcomes are harder to fabricate","Outcomes demonstrate that something actually changed because of your work â€” a school visit that produced no follow-up activity is harder to distinguish from one that did; an outcome metric proves the visit had an effect beyond your presence, which is what 'impact' means","Outcomes are required by FIRST","Output metrics are less precise"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is 'programs that run without us' considered an impact metric rather than an outcome metric?",opts:["Independence takes longer to achieve","It measures lasting structural change â€” a program that continues operating after your support ends demonstrates that your intervention created something durable, not just a temporary effect dependent on your continued presence; this is the definition of sustainable impact vs. activity-dependent engagement","Independent programs are more valuable","Outcome metrics measure the wrong things"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ori_corporate2",title:"Corporate Partnership Events â€” Bringing Sponsors to You",est:"12 min",content:`## Sponsors Who Visit Become Champions
A company executive who has only written a check knows your team by a number on a report. A company executive who watched your students debug a robot for two hours and then nail an autonomous routine knows your team as real people doing real things. That person renews the sponsorship, introduces you to their network, and advocates for you internally.

## Planning a Sponsor Appreciation Event
\`\`\`
Goal: sponsors leave the event having seen students lead, not be led.

Format options:
  Option A: Robot demo + team presentation (1.5-2 hours)
    â†’ Students present competition strategy, then demo the robot
    â†’ Q&A with students (not mentors) answering questions
    â†’ Sponsors can try driving at the end

  Option B: Lab tour during build season (45-60 minutes)
    â†’ Students walk sponsors through each workstation
    â†’ "This is what we're building right now and here's the challenge"
    â†’ Shows the work in progress â€” more authentic than a polished event

  Option C: Competition day invitation
    â†’ Sponsors watch a real match from the stands
    â†’ Pit visit between matches (they see the team solve real problems)
    â†’ Most powerful but requires managing the unpredictability of competition

Logistics:
  â†’ Send calendar invitations 4 weeks out
  â†’ Confirm 3 days before ("We have 8 sponsors joining us Saturday at 2pm")
  â†’ Name tags for students and sponsors (facilitates introductions)
  â†’ Light refreshments (coffee + snacks minimum)
\`\`\`

## What Students Do at These Events
\`\`\`
Assign specific roles to specific students:
  â†’ Greeter: welcomes each arrival by name ("Mr. Chen, welcome â€” I'm Alex")
  â†’ Presenter 1: explains the game (3 minutes)
  â†’ Presenter 2: explains this season's robot design (5 minutes)
  â†’ Demo driver: runs the robot (no mentor on the controls)
  â†’ Pit guide: shows what a specific mechanism does (conversational)

What mentors do: stand at the back and observe
  â†’ Never correct a student in front of a sponsor
  â†’ Available for introductions, not as the primary communicator

After the event:
  â†’ Personal thank-you from one student to each sponsor contact (email or handwritten)
  â†’ Within 48 hours
  â†’ From the student who spent the most time with them during the event
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does a live competition visit have a stronger sponsor retention effect than a formal demo event, despite the unpredictability?",opts:["Competitions are more impressive","At a competition, sponsors witness authentic team behavior under genuine pressure â€” robots breaking and being fixed, alliance coordination, close matches; this unscripted reality creates deeper emotional investment than a rehearsed demo that's been polished to look easy","Competitions are free to attend","Demo events don't show the robot competing"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific protocol â€” mentors standing at the back â€” communicates to sponsors about the team?",opts:["Mentors have nothing to add","It demonstrates that students are the primary technical agents, not supervised performers â€” a sponsor who sees students independently explaining engineering decisions and running the robot forms a much stronger impression of student ownership and capability than one who sees mentors jump in to fill gaps or correct students","Mentor presence intimidates sponsors","FIRST requires student-led events"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.webdev.Beginner.push(
  {id:"wb_accessibility",title:"Web Accessibility â€” Building Apps Everyone Can Use",est:"10 min",content:`## Accessibility Is Good Engineering, Not Extra Work
An app that can't be used by a color-blind scout, or breaks when zoomed in for a student with low vision, has a bug â€” the same as a crashing button. Accessibility fixes are usually small; accessibility problems are always real.

## The Four Core Principles (POUR)
\`\`\`
Perceivable: information must be visible to all users
  â†’ Color alone never conveys meaning:
    âŒ Red = bad team, Green = good team
    âœ“ Red badge + "âš " icon + "Caution" label (3 cues, not just color)
  â†’ Images have alt text: <img src="robot.jpg" alt="Team 1234 robot at regionals">
  â†’ Text contrast: minimum 4.5:1 ratio (dark text on light background)

Operable: users can operate with keyboard + other inputs
  â†’ All clickable elements work with Tab key
  â†’ Buttons are buttons: <button>, not <div onclick="...">
  â†’ Touch targets: 44px minimum height (mobile)

Understandable: content is clear
  â†’ Form fields have labels: <label for="teamNum">Team Number</label>
  â†’ Error messages tell you what to fix: "Enter a 4-digit team number"
  â†’ Language declared: <html lang="en">

Robust: works across browsers and devices
  â†’ Use semantic HTML (<nav>, <main>, <header>, <section>)
  â†’ Test on a real phone, not just desktop DevTools
\`\`\`

## Quick Accessibility Wins
\`\`\`html
<!-- 1. Semantic button (keyboard-accessible by default): -->
<button onclick="submitScouting()">Submit Match</button>
<!-- NOT: <div onclick="..."> â€” not keyboard accessible -->

<!-- 2. Form label association: -->
<label for="teamNum">Team Number</label>
<input id="teamNum" type="number" min="1" max="9999">

<!-- 3. ARIA labels for icon-only buttons: -->
<button aria-label="Delete this entry">ðŸ—‘ï¸</button>

<!-- 4. Status announcements for screen readers: -->
<div role="status" aria-live="polite" id="saveStatus"></div>
<!-- JavaScript: document.getElementById("saveStatus").textContent = "Saved!"; -->
<!-- Screen reader announces "Saved!" when content changes -->
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should color never be the only indicator of status (good/bad team, pass/fail)?",opts:["Color is unreliable on all screens","Approximately 8% of males have color vision deficiency â€” red/green distinctions are the most common failure; an app that uses only color to convey status is unusable for that population; using color plus shape plus label ensures the information is perceivable regardless of color vision","WCAG requires multiple indicators","Color-only designs are illegal"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the functional difference between a <button> element and a <div> with an onclick handler for keyboard accessibility?",opts:["Buttons are styled differently","A native <button> is automatically focusable with Tab and activatable with Enter/Space â€” keyboard users can operate it without a mouse; a <div onclick> has no default keyboard behavior, so Tab doesn't focus it and keyboard users can't activate it, making the function inaccessible to anyone who can't use a mouse","Buttons have built-in styling","onclick handlers don't work on divs"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wb_fetch",title:"Fetch API â€” Loading Data Without Page Reloads",est:"11 min",content:`## Dynamic Data Without Refreshing\nA scouting dashboard that requires a full page reload to see new data wastes 2-3 seconds and loses scroll position. The Fetch API loads new data in the background and updates just the parts of the page that changed â€” keeping the interface responsive.\n\n## Basic Fetch\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// GET request:\nasync function loadRankings(eventKey) {\n  try {\n    const response = await fetch(\\\`/api/rankings/\\" + (eventKey) + "\\\`);\n\n    if (!response.ok) {\n      throw new Error(\\\`Server error: \\" + (response.status) + "\\\`);\n    }\n\n    const data = await response.json();\n    return data;          // parsed JSON object/array\n  } catch (error) {\n    console.error("Failed to load rankings:", error.message);\n    return null;\n  }\n}\n\n// POST request (sending scout data to your Python server):\nasync function submitMatch(matchData) {\n  const response = await fetch("/api/matches", {\n    method:  "POST",\n    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },\n    body:    JSON.stringify(matchData)\n  });\n\n  if (!response.ok) {\n    throw new Error("Submission failed");\n  }\n\n  return await response.json();  // usually: { success: true, id: 123 }\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Updating the DOM After Fetch\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Load and display without page reload:\nasync function refreshLeaderboard() {\n  const spinner = document.getElementById("spinner");\n  spinner.style.display = "block";           // show loading indicator\n\n  try {\n    const teams = await loadRankings("2025casd");\n    if (teams) {\n      renderTeamList(teams);                  // update just the table\n      document.getElementById("lastUpdated").textContent =\n        "Updated: " + new Date().toLocaleTimeString();\n    }\n  } finally {\n    spinner.style.display = "none";           // always hide spinner\n  }\n}\n\n// Auto-refresh every 30 seconds during an event:\nsetInterval(refreshLeaderboard, 30_000);\n\n// Also refresh on user request:\ndocument.getElementById("refreshBtn")\n  .addEventListener("click", refreshLeaderboard);\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the finally block hide the spinner rather than putting it inside the try block?",opts:["Finally always executes","The spinner must be hidden whether the fetch succeeds or fails â€” putting it inside try means an error leaves the spinner visible forever; finally executes in both success and error paths, ensuring the UI always returns to a usable state regardless of whether the network request succeeded","Finally blocks are faster","Spinners shouldn't be hidden on error"],ans:1},
      {q:"What user experience problem does using Fetch to refresh data solve compared to a full page reload?",opts:["Fetch is more secure","A full page reload resets scroll position, flashes blank white, and takes 2-3 seconds â€” jarring during active use; Fetch updates only the changed data in-place, preserving scroll position and filters, making the dashboard feel like a live application rather than a series of separate page loads","Full page reloads cause errors","Fetch works without internet connection"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"wi_auth",title:"Simple Authentication for Pit Apps",est:"12 min",content:`## Keep Your Scouting Data Private
A scouting dashboard visible to any team at the event gives away your strategy. Simple authentication â€” even just a shared password â€” prevents casual access without requiring complex user accounts.

## Password Protection with a Simple Token
\`\`\`javascript
// client-side: store a session token in sessionStorage (clears on tab close)
const AUTH_TOKEN = "team1234-scout-2025"; // change each event

function requireAuth() {
  const stored = sessionStorage.getItem("authToken");
  if (stored !== AUTH_TOKEN) {
    const entered = prompt("Enter event password:");
    if (entered !== AUTH_TOKEN) {
      document.body.innerHTML = "<h1>Access denied</h1>";
      return false;
    }
    sessionStorage.setItem("authToken", AUTH_TOKEN);
  }
  return true;
}

// Call on page load:
if (!requireAuth()) throw new Error("Unauthorized");
\`\`\`

## Flask Backend Authentication (Python Server)
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, session
import secrets

app = Flask(__name__)
app.secret_key = secrets.token_hex(32)  # random secret

EVENT_PASSWORD = "team1234-casd2025"    # change per event

@app.route("/api/login", methods=["POST"])
def login():
    data = request.get_json()
    if data.get("password") == EVENT_PASSWORD:
        session["authenticated"] = True
        return jsonify({"success": True})
    return jsonify({"error": "Wrong password"}), 401

def require_auth(f):
    """Decorator: reject requests without valid session."""
    from functools import wraps
    @wraps(f)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        if not session.get("authenticated"):
            return jsonify({"error": "Unauthorized"}), 401
        return f(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper

@app.route("/api/matches", methods=["GET"])
@require_auth
def get_matches():
    # Only authenticated scouts can get match data
    return jsonify(load_matches())
\`\`\`

## When Simple Auth Is Enough
\`\`\`
Simple shared password is appropriate when:
  â†’ The threat is casual â€” other teams at an event stumbling on your app
  â†’ The data isn't permanently sensitive (one-event scouting data)
  â†’ User management overhead isn't worth it (5-10 scouts)

NOT appropriate (need proper auth) when:
  â†’ The app handles personal student data
  â†’ Sponsor financial information is in the system
  â†’ The threat is someone motivated to bypass it
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is sessionStorage used instead of localStorage for the authentication token?",opts:["sessionStorage is more secure","sessionStorage clears automatically when the browser tab is closed â€” a scout's phone left unattended doesn't remain permanently authenticated; localStorage persists indefinitely, meaning anyone who picked up the unlocked phone hours later would still be authenticated without re-entering the password","sessionStorage is faster","localStorage doesn't work on mobile"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the Flask @require_auth decorator's mechanism for protecting API routes?",opts:["It encrypts the response","It wraps the route function with session validation â€” before the route function executes, the decorator checks for an authenticated session; if not authenticated, it returns a 401 response immediately without calling the actual route function; any route with the decorator is protected without repeating the check inside each function","Decorators modify the URL","It validates the request body"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wi_charts2",title:"Advanced Chart Types for Scouting Dashboards",est:"13 min",content:`## Different Data Questions Need Different Chart Types\nA bar chart comparing team averages works. The same bar chart comparing 60 teams becomes unreadable. Choosing the chart type that matches the analytical question makes data instantly interpretable.\n\n## Chart Type Selection Guide\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\nQuestion: "How do teams rank on a single metric?"\n  â†’ Horizontal bar chart (sorted) â€” easy to compare 20-30 teams\n  â†’ Best for: pick list ranking, auto score comparison\n\nQuestion: "Is there a relationship between two metrics?"\n  â†’ Scatter plot (X = auto score, Y = teleop cycles)\n  â†’ Best for: identifying well-rounded vs specialized robots\n\nQuestion: "How does a team perform across multiple metrics?"\n  â†’ Radar/spider chart â€” one team, 5-8 metrics as axes\n  â†’ Best for: individual team deep-dive card\n\nQuestion: "How consistent is a team\"s performance?"\n  â†’ Box plot (median, quartiles, outliers)\n  â†’ Best for: reliability comparison (prefer consistent 40pt avg vs 30/50 swings)\n\nQuestion: "How does performance trend over time?"\n  â†’ Line chart â€” match number on X, score on Y\n  â†’ Best for: "are they improving?" analysis\n\\"\\"\\"\n\n## Scatter Plot with Chart.js\n\\"\\"\\"javascript\nimport { Chart } from "chart.js/auto";\n\nfunction renderScatterPlot(teams) {\n  const ctx = document.getElementById("scatterChart").getContext("2d");\n\n  new Chart(ctx, {\n    type: "scatter",\n    data: {\n      datasets: [{\n        label: "Teams",\n        data: teams.map(t => ({\n          x: t.avgAuto,\n          y: t.avgCycles,\n          label: t.number     // custom property for tooltip\n        })),\n        backgroundColor: teams.map(t =>\n          t.avg >= 45 ? "#e63946" : t.avg >= 30 ? "#457b9d" : "#aaa"\n        ),\n        pointRadius: 8,\n        pointHoverRadius: 12,\n      }]\n    },\n    options: {\n      plugins: {\n        tooltip: {\n          callbacks: {\n            label: (ctx) => {\n              const pt = ctx.raw;\n              return \\\`Team \\" + (pt.label) + ": auto=\\" + (pt.x) + ", cycles=\\" + (pt.y) + "\\\`;\n            }\n          }\n        }\n      },\n      scales: {\n        x: { title: { display: true, text: "Avg Auto Points" }},\n        y: { title: { display: true, text: "Avg Teleop Cycles" }}\n      }\n    }\n  });\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a scatter plot more useful than a bar chart for identifying the relationship between auto score and teleop cycles?",opts:["Scatter plots hold more data","A bar chart shows one metric per team â€” comparing two metrics requires switching between two separate charts; a scatter plot encodes both metrics simultaneously as X and Y positions, revealing correlations and clusters (teams that are good at both, teams specialized in one, outliers) that no bar chart can show at a glance","Scatter plots are more colorful","Bar charts can't show two teams at once"],ans:1},
      {q:"What analytical question is a box plot specifically suited to answer that a bar chart of averages cannot?",opts:["Which team has the highest score","How consistent a team's performance is â€” a box plot shows the median, the interquartile range, and outlier matches, revealing whether a team's average comes from tight consistent scores or from wild swings between high and low matches; two teams with identical averages can have completely different box plots, revealing very different reliability profiles","Which team won the most matches","Box plots compare more teams simultaneously"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Advanced.push(
  {id:"wa_deploy",title:"Deploying a Scouting App to Production",est:"13 min",content:`## 'Works on My Machine' Isn't Good Enough at Competition
Your scouting app runs perfectly in development on your laptop. At the event, scouts connect from their phones on a different network, and the app fails silently. Deployment â€” running the app on a server that any device can reach â€” requires specific steps beyond local development.

## Competition Network Architecture
\`\`\`
Competition venue Wi-Fi: unreliable, congested, sometimes blocked
Best competition architecture:
  â†’ Bring your own access point (TP-Link travel router, ~$25)
  â†’ Connect it to venue internet OR run in AP-only mode (isolated LAN)
  â†’ All scouting devices connect to YOUR AP: 192.168.1.x
  â†’ Python server runs on the pit laptop: 192.168.1.100
  â†’ Scouts connect to: http://192.168.1.100:5000

This isolates your scouting from venue network issues.
\`\`\`

## Running Flask in Production Mode
\`\`\`python
# Development (DON'T use at competition):
app.run(debug=True)           # slow, single-threaded, not secure

# Production: use waitress (Windows-compatible) or gunicorn (Mac/Linux)
# pip install waitress
from waitress import serve
serve(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
# 0.0.0.0 = listen on all network interfaces (not just localhost)

# gunicorn (Mac/Linux):
# pip install gunicorn
# gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:5000 --workers 4 app:app
\`\`\`

## Pre-Event Deployment Checklist
\`\`\`
One week before competition:
  â–¡ App runs correctly on the pit laptop (not just your dev machine)
  â–¡ Tested on at least one phone on the same network
  â–¡ Database/storage initialized with current event data
  â–¡ API keys loaded via environment variables (not hardcoded)

Day before competition:
  â–¡ Run full end-to-end test: scout submits on phone â†’ appears on dashboard
  â–¡ Test offline mode: disconnect from AP â†’ does cached data still work?
  â–¡ Backup: export current database to a CSV file â†’ email to yourself
  â–¡ AP config saved: SSID and password written on a physical note

Competition day:
  â–¡ Start the server before scouts arrive
  â–¡ Verify all scout devices can load the app
  â–¡ Check the server URL is posted in your team communication channel
  â–¡ Have the CSV export command memorized for emergency manual fallback
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should the Flask server bind to '0.0.0.0' rather than 'localhost' or '127.0.0.1' when running at a competition?",opts:["0.0.0.0 is more secure","127.0.0.1 only accepts connections from the same computer â€” scouts' phones connecting from the same network are different devices; 0.0.0.0 tells the server to accept connections on all network interfaces including the Wi-Fi interface, making it reachable by any device on the local network","0.0.0.0 enables internet access","Localhost is deprecated"],ans:1},
      {q:"What problem does bringing your own access point solve compared to relying on the venue's Wi-Fi?",opts:["Venue Wi-Fi has data limits","Competition venue networks are often congested, filtered, or unreliable â€” your own AP creates an isolated local network where scouting traffic never touches the internet, eliminating dependency on venue infrastructure; scouts' devices communicate only with your pit laptop over a private network you control completely","Venue Wi-Fi is always blocked","Your AP is faster than venue networks"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wa_sqlite",title:"SQLite â€” A Real Database for Scouting Data",est:"14 min",content:`## JSON Files Are Fine Until They're Not
Scouting data stored in JSON files works for one event. By the third event, you're managing multiple files, merging them manually, and wondering which copy has the latest data. A SQLite database is a single file, queryable with SQL, and requires no server to run.

## Setting Up SQLite with Python
\`\`\`python
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

DB_PATH = Path("scouting.db")

def get_db():
    """Get a database connection with row_factory for dict-like access."""
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row   # rows behave like dicts
    conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    return conn

def init_db():
    """Create tables if they don't exist."""
    with get_db() as conn:
        conn.executescript("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS matches (
                id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                event_key   TEXT NOT NULL,
                team_number INTEGER NOT NULL,
                match_num   INTEGER NOT NULL,
                scout_name  TEXT NOT NULL,
                auto_pts    REAL DEFAULT 0,
                cycles      INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
                climb_level TEXT DEFAULT 'None',
                notes       TEXT DEFAULT '',
                created_at  DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
                UNIQUE(event_key, team_number, match_num)
            );

            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS teams (
                team_number INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
                nickname    TEXT,
                city        TEXT,
                updated_at  DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
            );
        """)

init_db()
\`\`\`

## CRUD Operations
\`\`\`python
def insert_match(entry: dict) -> int:
    """Insert a scouted match. Returns new row id."""
    with get_db() as conn:
        cur = conn.execute("""
            INSERT OR REPLACE INTO matches
              (event_key, team_number, match_num, scout_name, auto_pts, cycles, climb_level, notes)
            VALUES (:event_key, :team_number, :match_num, :scout_name,
                    :auto_pts, :cycles, :climb_level, :notes)
        """, entry)
        return cur.lastrowid

def get_team_stats(event_key: str) -> list[dict]:
    """Average stats per team for an event."""
    with get_db() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute("""
            SELECT
                team_number,
                COUNT(*)            AS matches_scouted,
                ROUND(AVG(auto_pts), 1)  AS avg_auto,
                ROUND(AVG(cycles), 1)    AS avg_cycles,
                MAX(climb_level)    AS best_climb
            FROM matches
            WHERE event_key = ?
            GROUP BY team_number
            ORDER BY avg_cycles DESC
        """, (event_key,)).fetchall()
        return [dict(r) for r in rows]
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does sqlite3.Row as the row_factory provide that default sqlite3 rows cannot?",opts:["Faster queries","Dict-like access by column name â€” default rows are accessed by integer index (row[0], row[2]) which is brittle if column order changes; sqlite3.Row allows row['team_number'] by name, making code more readable and resistant to schema changes","row_factory enables JSON output","Dict access is required for Flask"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'INSERT OR REPLACE' accomplish when a duplicate match is submitted by a scout?",opts:["It creates a second entry","It replaces the existing row with the new data if the UNIQUE constraint (event_key, team_number, match_num) would be violated â€” useful when a scout re-submits a corrected entry; without it, duplicate submissions would fail with an error and potentially lose corrected data","INSERT OR REPLACE skips duplicates","It merges the two rows"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
