LESSONS.safety.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sfb_noise",title:"Noise Safety in the Robot Shop",est:"9 min",content:`## Hearing Loss Is Permanent and Preventable
A shop with an angle grinder, a drill press, and 4 people talking runs at 90-100 decibels â€” the range where permanent hearing damage begins after 2 hours. Unlike most injuries, hearing loss accumulates silently over years before you notice it.

## Decibel Levels in Context
\`\`\`
Sound levels in a typical robot shop:
  Normal conversation:     60 dB
  Drill press:             85-95 dB
  Angle grinder:           95-105 dB
  Impact wrench:           100-105 dB
  Metal saw/band saw:      90-100 dB

OSHA permissible exposure (without hearing protection):
  90 dB â†’ 8 hours
  95 dB â†’ 4 hours
  100 dB â†’ 2 hours
  105 dB â†’ 1 hour
  110 dB â†’ 30 minutes

Rule: if you have to raise your voice to be heard by someone 3 feet away,
      the noise level likely requires hearing protection.
\`\`\`

## Hearing Protection Types
\`\`\`
Foam earplugs (NRR 29-33):
  â†’ Best protection available
  â†’ Must be properly inserted: roll thin, pull ear up and back, insert, let expand
  â†’ Improperly inserted = 50% of the rated protection
  â†’ Cost: pennies each â€” stock plenty in the shop

Earmuffs (NRR 22-33):
  â†’ Easier to put on correctly
  â†’ Can be worn over glasses
  â†’ Less effective if hair or glasses break the seal

When to wear:
  â†’ Angle grinder: always
  â†’ Drill press: for continuous drilling sessions > 15 minutes
  â†’ CNC router: always during operation
  â†’ Everyone in the room â€” not just the operator â€” needs protection
    when loud equipment runs

Hearing protection is not optional during angle grinder use.
This is a non-negotiable safety rule, same as safety glasses.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must everyone in the shop wear hearing protection during angle grinder use, not just the operator?",opts:["Operators are closer to the noise","Sound radiates in all directions â€” a grinder running at 100dB produces 95-97dB several feet away, still within the hearing-damage range; bystanders who think they're 'far enough away' are receiving damaging noise exposure without protection","Bystanders are required to leave","Operators control the noise level"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does improperly inserted foam earplugs provide only about 50% of their rated noise reduction?",opts:["Foam loses effectiveness quickly","Foam earplugs create a seal by conforming to the ear canal â€” if not rolled thin, fully inserted, and allowed to expand before the ear is released, they sit in the outer ear canal creating a partial seal that allows significant sound bypass; the rated NRR assumes a perfect fit achieved by the correct insertion technique","Foam degrades after one use","The NRR rating is inflated"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfb_wiring_safety",title:"Safe Wiring Practices â€” Prevention Before Connection",est:"10 min",content:`## Most Wiring Fires Are Caused by Mistakes Made Before Power-On
A reversed connector, an undersized wire, an unprotected terminal â€” these cause fires and damaged electronics when power is first applied. The right time to catch them is before the battery goes in, not after the smoke comes out.

## The Pre-Power Checklist
\`\`\`
Run this every time before connecting a battery to a modified robot:

Visual inspection:
  â–¡ All wire ends terminated â€” no bare copper exposed near any conductor
  â–¡ All connectors fully seated â€” no partially-inserted pins
  â–¡ Positive wires: red throughout; negative: black (check the whole run)
  â–¡ All fuses sized correctly for the wire gauge (not the device)
  â–¡ Main breaker: accessible, functional, not bypassed

Physical check:
  â–¡ Tug test every connector â€” no movement at either end
  â–¡ Wire routing doesn't cross a spinning mechanism or sharp edge
  â–¡ Battery secured and cannot shift when robot tilts or is bumped
  â–¡ No loose wires that could touch the battery terminals during a match

Polarity verification:
  â–¡ Motor controllers: verify + and - wires before powering
  â–¡ Anderson Powerpole: verify orientation against a known-good connector
  â–¡ All connectors with polarity: confirm with multimeter before first power-on
     Set multimeter to DC voltage, touch probes to + and - terminals of the connector:
       positive reading = correct polarity
       negative reading = REVERSED â€” fix before connecting power
\`\`\`

## The First Power-On Procedure
\`\`\`
First power-on after any major wiring change:
  1. Have a mentor or second person present
  2. Connect the battery while standing to the side (not directly over the robot)
  3. Watch and smell for: smoke, sparks, heat, burning smell
  4. If any: immediately disconnect the battery, investigate before re-powering
  5. If none: run for 30 seconds, then recheck all connectors for unexpected heat
     â†’ Any connector warmer than ambient after 30 seconds = undersized for the load
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should the tug test be performed on every connector rather than just the ones that were newly made?",opts:["Existing connectors are reliable","Connectors that were previously secure can work loose over build season vibration and handling â€” a connector that was fine last week may have developed a half-seated pin that creates intermittent connection or arcing; the pre-power check catches any connector regardless of age","New connectors need more testing","Tug tests damage existing connectors"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does a negative voltage reading on a multimeter indicate when checking connector polarity?",opts:["The multimeter battery is low","The polarity is reversed â€” the multimeter reads negative when the positive probe touches the negative terminal and the negative probe touches the positive terminal; this indicates the connector is wired backwards and must be corrected before connection to any device","The voltage is too low","The connector has no voltage"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"sfi_documentation2",title:"Safety Documentation â€” Incident Reports & Safety Plans",est:"11 min",content:`## Documentation Protects Everyone
An undocumented incident is an opportunity to prevent the next one that was missed. An undocumented safety plan is a plan nobody can reference when they need it. Good safety documentation takes 15 minutes and creates lasting protection.

## Incident Report Template
\`\`\`
Complete within 24 hours of any incident (injury, near-miss, property damage):

Incident Report â€” Team 1234

Date/Time:       [date] at [time]
Location:        [room, building, or competition venue]
People involved: [names â€” no need to blame, just document who was there]
What happened:   [factual description â€” what was being done, what occurred]
                 "Student was using the band saw to cut a piece of aluminum
                  channel when the blade deflected, contacting the index finger."
Severity:        [ ] Near-miss â€” no injury or damage
                 [ ] Minor injury (first aid only)
                 [ ] Significant injury (medical attention required)
                 [ ] Property damage only
Immediate response: [what was done immediately â€” first aid, shutdown, etc.]
Root cause:      [the underlying reason this happened]
                 "Workpiece was not clamped â€” student was holding by hand against
                  the blade guide."
Corrective action: [what will change to prevent recurrence]
                  "Reminder to all members: workpiece must be clamped or in a
                   miter guide before band saw use. Added clamping step to
                   machine-specific safety briefing."
Reported by:     [name, date]
Reviewed by:     [lead mentor, date]
\`\`\`

## Annual Safety Plan
\`\`\`
A one-page document, reviewed at the start of each season:
  1. Emergency contacts (mentor, first responder, school nurse)
  2. Emergency equipment locations (first aid kit, fire extinguisher, eyewash)
  3. Evacuation route and assembly point
  4. Machine-specific safety rules (one sentence each)
  5. PPE requirements by area/task
  6. Incident reporting process (brief â€” who to tell, where to log it)

Post physically in the shop â€” not just in a Google Drive folder.
Review it out loud on Day 1 of build season with every member present.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is the root cause section of an incident report more important than the description of what happened?",opts:["Root causes are required by FIRST","What happened describes the event; the root cause explains why it could happen â€” addressing the root cause prevents recurrence while documenting only the event leaves the underlying hazard unchanged; a student cutting without a clamp is the event, 'workpiece not clamped' is the immediate cause, 'no rule requiring clamping was established' is the root cause that the corrective action must address","Root causes are simpler to document","Root causes assign blame clearly"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should an emergency safety plan be posted physically in the shop rather than stored only in Google Drive?",opts:["Paper is more reliable than digital","In an emergency, accessing a digital document requires a device, a login, and an internet connection â€” all of which may be unavailable; a physical posted plan is accessible immediately in the moment it's needed, by anyone in the room including first responders who aren't team members","FIRST requires physical documentation","Physical documents can't be altered"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS +5 (27â†’32) â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Beginner.push(
  {id:"awb_deans_list",title:"Dean's List Nominee â€” Preparing a Student",est:"11 min",content:`## The Dean's List Recognizes Individuals, Not Teams
Every other major FIRST award recognizes the team. Dean's List recognizes one student â€” the student who best embodies FIRST's mission through personal leadership, community contribution, and STEM advocacy. Nominating the right student and preparing them well is a specific skill.

## Who Qualifies
\`\`\`
FIRST's Dean's List criteria (verify current year specifics):
  â†’ Significant and outstanding contributions to the team
  â†’ Exemplary leadership as a student mentor of other students
  â†’ Dedication to spreading FIRST's mission (outreach, advocacy)
  â†’ Strong academic background and pursuit of STEM education
  â†’ Typically: junior or senior (10th-12th grade in most regions)

Teams can nominate up to 2 students per event.

The profile of a strong nominee:
  â†’ A student other students go to when they're stuck (not just the most skilled)
  â†’ Has tangibly grown other members (who is better because of them?)
  â†’ Has represented the team externally (presentations, outreach, advocacy)
  â†’ Demonstrates FIRST values consistently, not just when judges are watching
\`\`\`

## The Nomination Essay
\`\`\`
Typically 100-250 words (verify current limits):
  â†’ Lead with a specific scene or story, not a list of accomplishments
  â†’ "When our new scouting lead was overwhelmed with the system in Week 4,
     [Name] sat with them for two hours on a Saturday afternoon â€” not because
     they were asked to, but because they noticed the struggle and showed up."

  â†’ Connect the specific story to the broader pattern
  â†’ Cite one external impact (a life they changed through outreach)
  â†’ End with a specific, credible claim about future contribution to STEM

What not to write:
  â†’ A list of things they did ("they led the programming team, built the vision
     system, managed outreach, and helped organize the engineering notebook")
  â†’ Generic superlatives ("an exceptional leader with outstanding dedication")
  â†’ Accomplishments without showing the person behind them
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the Dean's List nomination essay benefit from starting with a specific scene rather than listing accomplishments?",opts:["Scenes are easier to write","A specific scene makes the student real to the judge â€” it shows character through action rather than asserting it through adjectives; judges read many nominations claiming 'exceptional leadership'; a student who shows up on a Saturday afternoon to help a struggling teammate demonstrates it without claiming it","Scenes must be verified","Lists are not allowed in nominations"],ans:1},
      {q:"What distinguishes a Dean's List nominee from the student who simply has the highest technical skill on the team?",opts:["Dean's List is not for technical students","Dean's List specifically recognizes student leadership of other students â€” the student who elevates others through mentorship, who other members seek out when stuck, and who has built community beyond the team; technical skill that doesn't manifest as mentorship and outreach doesn't fulfill the award criteria","Technical students always qualify","The two qualities are identical"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_regional_vs_champs",title:"Award Strategy â€” Regional vs District vs Championship",est:"11 min",content:`## The Awards Path Differs by Competition System
FRC teams compete in either the Regional system or the District system â€” and the award strategy is different for each. Understanding which system your team is in, and how awards lead to championship eligibility, determines how to allocate your award preparation time.

## Regional System
\`\`\`
Teams attend 1-2 Regional events per season (standalone events, 40-50 teams each).
Awards at Regionals:
  â†’ Regional Chairman's Award (Impact): winner advances to Championship
  â†’ Engineering Inspiration: winner may advance to Championship
  â†’ Rookie All-Star, Rookie Inspiration: advancement varies by year

Strategy: submit your full award portfolio at every Regional you attend.
  â†’ Each Regional is independent â€” no cumulative advantage
  â†’ Missing a submission at Regional 1 = that slot is gone
  â†’ Treat each Regional as if it's the last opportunity
\`\`\`

## District System
\`\`\`
Teams attend 2 District events â†’ District Championship â†’ World Championship.
District events are smaller (30-40 teams each).
Awards accumulate via district points â€” different structure.

Impact Award path:
  â†’ Win at a District event â†’ present at District Championship
  â†’ Win at District Championship â†’ present at World Championship
  â†’ You must advance through the levels; there's no "skip to championship"

Strategy: build toward the District Championship.
  â†’ District event win = your submission is ready; refine for Champs
  â†’ Feedback from District event judges is actionable before Champs
  â†’ Losing at a District event does NOT mean no Impact at Champs
    (teams can still receive the award at Champs level through district points)

District award timing is more forgiving:
  â†’ More opportunities (2 district events + district champs) = more iterations
  â†’ Each event is a calibration: "which parts resonated with judges?"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should Regional teams treat every Regional event as their most important submission opportunity?",opts:["Regionals are more competitive","Regionals are independent events â€” missing or submitting a weak package at Regional 1 cannot be corrected or compensated at Regional 2; in the District system, district events build toward the Championship, but Regional events have no such accumulation mechanism","Regional judges are stricter","Championship awards are given at Regionals"],ans:1},
      {q:"What strategic advantage does the District system provide over the Regional system for award preparation?",opts:["Districts have easier judges","Multiple sequential events allow teams to receive feedback after each submission and refine for the next level â€” a district event loss comes with judge feedback that can be specifically addressed before the District Championship; this iterative improvement pathway doesn't exist in the single-opportunity Regional format","District awards are worth more points","Districts allow unlimited submissions"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awi_gp",title:"Demonstrating Gracious Professionalism All Event",est:"10 min",content:`## GP Is Observed, Not Performed on Command
Every award with a judging component includes "observed behavior" at the event. Judges watch the pits, the stands, the alliance queuing area, and the field. A team that is helpful and kind only during scheduled judging interactions and otherwise dismissive of other teams earns neither GP recognition nor the respect it implies.

## What Judges Actually Watch
\`\`\`
Pit area:
  â†’ Do you greet visitors and other teams warmly?
  â†’ If another team asks for help: do you actually help, or give a dismissive gesture?
  â†’ Is your pit welcoming to new/visiting students?

Alliance queuing:
  â†’ How do you treat your alliance partners during the 3-minute pre-match period?
  â†’ How do you treat the opposing alliance?
  â†’ If you're red and blue scores a great auto: do you acknowledge it?

Competition outcome:
  â†’ After a loss: do you congratulate the winning alliance genuinely?
  â†’ After a win where a partner struggled: do you acknowledge their contribution anyway?
  â†’ After a controversial call: does your team's behavior stay professional?

In the stands:
  â†’ Do you cheer for other teams' accomplishments?
  â†’ Do you avoid disparaging comments about other teams' robots or performance?
\`\`\`

## Building GP Into Team Culture
\`\`\`
Before competition, explicitly discuss:
  "One thing we do at every competition: if another team asks for help,
   we say yes first and figure out the details after."

  "We cheer when any robot does something impressive â€” including our opponents."

  "If we lose: shake every opposing alliance member's hand before leaving the field."

Make it a team norm, not a performance:
  â†’ Teams that are celebrated for GP culture are those where the behavior
     is consistent whether or not judges are present
  â†’ The best evidence: a team from another school complimenting your team's
    behavior to a judge, unprompted
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is unprompted positive feedback from other teams about your team's behavior considered the strongest GP evidence?",opts:["Third-party feedback is more credible to judges","A member of another team taking time to compliment your team to a judge is an unscripted, uncoached validation â€” it can only happen if your team's behavior genuinely impacted them; judges can discount your own team's GP claims as self-promotion, but can't discount a candid endorsement from a team with no incentive to provide it","Other teams observe more behavior","Judge feedback is less credible"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific behavior during alliance queuing demonstrates Gracious Professionalism beyond what most teams exhibit?",opts:["Arriving at queue on time","Engaging the opposing alliance members with genuine warmth â€” learning their names, asking about their robot, acknowledging impressive moments in previous matches; most teams only interact with their own alliance during queue; treating the opposing alliance as collaborators in a shared event distinguishes genuine GP from competitive politeness","Sharing technical information","Wearing team uniforms consistently"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ FUNDRAISING +5 (27â†’32) â”€â”€
LESSONS.fundraising.Beginner.push(
  {id:"fb_alumni",title:"Building an Alumni Giving Program",est:"11 min",content:`## Your Best Future Donors Are Students Who Already Love the Team
A team alumnus who went through the program, learned to code, won an award, and is now working as an engineer has two things: nostalgia for a formative experience and a paycheck. Annual alumni giving programs consistently outperform cold sponsor outreach in renewal rates and gift size growth.

## Starting an Alumni Database
\`\`\`
Immediately useful even if it's just 20 people:
  Spreadsheet columns:
  Name | Grad Year | Role on Team | Current City | Email | Employer | Last Contact | Last Gift

Building it:
  â†’ Start with current seniors: capture their email before graduation
  â†’ Ask existing alumni to connect you with others they know
  â†’ LinkedIn: search your school name + FIRST robotics
  â†’ Social media: "Looking for Team 1234 alumni! DM us"

What to capture at graduation:
  â†’ Personal email (not school email â€” those expire)
  â†’ What they plan to study
  â†’ Permission to add to the alumni mailing list (explicit opt-in)
\`\`\`

## The Annual Alumni Appeal
\`\`\`
Best timing: November-December (Giving Tuesday + year-end tax motivation)

Email structure (keep it short â€” alumni are busy):
  Subject: "Team 1234 â€” a lot has happened since your time here"

  Body:
    [1 paragraph: what the team accomplished this season]
    [1 paragraph: specific program that needs support â€” make it concrete]
    [1 sentence: the ask + link]
    "Your gift of $[50/100/250] directly funds [specific thing]."
    [1 sentence: the feeling â€” "because of people like you, the next
     generation of engineers is finding their path"]

  Link: donation form or PayPal (make it one click)

Response rate: 10-20% of alumni who receive a well-crafted appeal will give
Average first gift: $50-100
Average 5-year alumni gift: $150-250 (grows as careers advance)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a personal email address essential to capture at graduation rather than the student's school email?",opts:["Personal emails are more secure","School email addresses expire when the student leaves the institution â€” often within 6-12 months of graduation; without a personal address, alumni become permanently unreachable, eliminating any future giving or relationship opportunity for the entire tenure of that person","Personal emails are more reliable for deliverability","School emails block fundraising messages"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes Giving Tuesday in November a strategically effective time for an alumni appeal?",opts:["Alumni are home for holidays","Giving Tuesday is a nationally recognized giving moment that primes people for charitable action â€” many people plan year-end giving specifically around this date; combining it with year-end tax motivation (donations must be made by December 31) creates both social and financial reasons to give at the same time","Alumni have more time in November","Fundraising is prohibited at other times"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"fi_reporting",title:"Sponsor Reporting â€” Demonstrating ROI",est:"12 min",content:`## A Sponsor Who Doesn't Know What Their Money Did Won't Renew
Most teams send a thank-you letter when a sponsorship arrives and silence until the next ask. Sponsors who receive a meaningful report showing what their investment produced renew at dramatically higher rates â€” because the decision to renew feels justified, not charitable.

## The ROI Report Mindset
\`\`\`
Frame every sponsor communication from their perspective:
  "What did [Company] get from their $2,500 investment in Team 1234?"

Their return:
  â†’ Logo on robot and uniforms: "Your brand appeared in front of [N] spectators
    at [event names] and in [media mentions]."
  â†’ Community goodwill: "Your investment helped [N] students explore engineering
    careers in [City]."
  â†’ Talent pipeline: "2 of our graduating seniors are pursuing engineering degrees
    and are interested in internship opportunities."
  â†’ Employee pride: "[Engineer's name] at your company volunteered 4 hours at our
    competition â€” we hope they told you about it."

Different sponsors care about different returns:
  â†’ Tech company: talent pipeline + brand visibility
  â†’ Local business: community goodwill + visibility
  â†’ Nonprofit funder: student outcomes + equity metrics
  â†’ Individual donor: nostalgia + student success stories
\`\`\`

## Sponsor Report Contents
\`\`\`
One page + optional photo attachment:

Header: "[Company name] + Team 1234 â€” 2025 Partnership Report"

Section 1: Season Highlights (bullet points, 5 max)
  â†’ Best competitive result
  â†’ Most meaningful award
  â†’ Biggest outreach milestone

Section 2: Your Investment in Numbers
  â†’ Students reached through programs bearing your logo: [N]
  â†’ Events where your brand appeared: [N]
  â†’ [Unique metric that matters to THIS sponsor]

Section 3: A Story
  â†’ One student success story (name with permission)
  â†’ "Maria joined as a 9th grader with no coding experience. This year she led
     our autonomous programming and will study computer science at [school]."

Section 4: Thank You + What's Next
  â†’ Genuine thanks for the specific impact their gift enabled
  â†’ Brief preview of next season (creates anticipation, not obligation)
  â†’ Renewal path: "If you'd like to continue your investment in 2026, I'll
    reach out in September â€” or feel free to contact me at [email]."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does tailoring the ROI report to each sponsor's specific interests increase renewal rates?",opts:["Tailored reports take more work","Different sponsors have different motivations â€” a local business cares about community visibility while a tech company cares about talent pipeline; a generic report misses the return that actually mattered to each sponsor; a tailored report demonstrates that you understood their investment and measured the outcomes they valued, making renewal a rational continuation rather than an act of generosity","Sponsors prefer detailed reports","Generic reports appear more professional"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does including a specific student success story in a sponsor report accomplish that aggregate statistics cannot?",opts:["Stories are shorter than statistics","A single named student's journey from 'no coding experience' to 'accepted to computer science program' creates emotional resonance that abstract numbers cannot â€” the sponsor can imagine one real person their money helped; statistics prove scale while stories prove meaning; together they build a complete case for renewal","Stories replace the need for numbers","Sponsors prefer statistics only"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ MECHANICAL +5 (80â†’85) â”€â”€
LESSONS.mechanical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"mi_electronics_packaging",title:"Electronics Packaging â€” Protecting What Powers the Robot",est:"13 min",content:`## Electronics Live and Die by Their Mounting
A RoboRIO that vibrates loose mid-match and reboots the robot costs a match. An Ethernet cable that pulls out of the radio during alliance selection costs an event. Electronics packaging â€” the physical integration of boards, cables, and connectors into a robust robot assembly â€” is mechanical engineering at its quietest and highest stakes.

## The Electronics Layout Principles
\`\`\`
1. Serviceability first: you will work on this at 11pm at competition
   â†’ Every board accessible without removing other boards
   â†’ Every connector reachable with one hand
   â†’ Main breaker reachable without tools (inspection requirement)

2. Vibration isolation for sensitive electronics:
   â†’ RoboRIO: mount on rubber grommets (vibration isolators)
     REV provides these; 4Ã— per mounting hole
   â†’ Radio (OpenMesh, Vivid): mount away from high-vibration areas
     (not directly on the drivetrain bellypan)
   â†’ Vision coprocessor: rubber mount or 3D-printed vibration isolator

3. Thermal management:
   â†’ Motor controllers generate heat proportional to current
   â†’ Don't stack motor controllers directly on top of each other
   â†’ Provide airflow path if robot runs 150A+ continuous (e.g., intake fan)
   â†’ REV PDH has thermal shutdown protection â€” but thermal shutdown mid-match = problem

4. Cable management:
   â†’ Every cable routed against a frame member, not floating
   â†’ Strain relief at both ends: connector doesn't carry the cable weight
   â†’ Long cable runs: zip-tied every 6" to prevent snag on mechanisms
   â†’ Cable lengths: measure actual route, not straight-line distance
\`\`\`

## The Electronics Board
\`\`\`
Best practice: build all electronics on a removable board (lexan or aluminum plate):
  â†’ All electronics pre-wired to their board before mounting in robot
  â†’ Board mounts to robot via 4-6 quick-release standoffs
  â†’ To troubleshoot: pull the board out, work on a table with full access

Board material:
  â†’ 1/8" polycarbonate (lexan): clear (see wiring), lightweight, easy to drill
  â†’ 1/8" aluminum: stronger, heavier, conducts heat away from electronics

Layout on the board:
  â†’ PDP/PDH: center (it's the hub â€” everything connects to it)
  â†’ RoboRIO: adjacent to PDP â€” main CAN and PWM runs are short
  â†’ Motor controllers: grouped by subsystem on the edges
  â†’ Radio: mounted high and away from metal that could interfere
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should motor controllers not be stacked directly on top of each other on the electronics board?",opts:["Stacking causes short circuits","Motor controllers generate heat during operation â€” stacking them traps heat from the lower controller against the underside of the upper one, reducing cooling efficiency for both; sufficient thermal headroom prevents the mid-match thermal throttling or shutdown that causes robot performance issues","Stacking violates wiring standards","Motor controllers have mounting restrictions"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific maintenance advantage does a removable electronics board provide at competition?",opts:["It makes the robot lighter","The entire electronics assembly can be extracted from the robot and placed on a work table for full access from all sides â€” troubleshooting with the board inside the robot requires awkward access in a cramped space; a table gives technicians two hands and proper lighting, dramatically reducing repair time under competition pressure","Removable boards are inspection-required","Boards prevent vibration damage to electronics"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.mechanical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ma_weight",title:"Weight Reduction Strategies â€” From Heavy to Competition-Ready",est:"12 min",content:`## Every Gram Saved Is a Gram Available Elsewhere
FRC's 125 lb limit (with bumpers and battery) is a hard constraint. A robot that hits the scale at 140 lb must lose 15 lb â€” and every pound removed from structure is a pound that could become a more capable mechanism. Weight reduction is an engineering optimization problem with real tradeoffs.

## Weight Reduction Hierarchy (Best to Worst ROI)
\`\`\`
1. Remove it entirely (best â€” zero weight, zero complexity)
   â†’ Every mechanism that's not essential to the game plan: remove it
   â†’ A climber that scores 4 pts but weighs 8 lb: costs more than it gains
   â†’ Brackets that are 6" long but only use 1": cut to 2"

2. Use a lighter material
   â†’ Steel component â†’ aluminum equivalent: 65% weight reduction
   â†’ Aluminum plate â†’ aluminum hex beam or extrusion: 50-70% reduction
   â†’ Aluminum gearbox housing â†’ 3D printed PA-CF: 60-70% reduction for non-structural

3. Remove material from existing parts (lightening)
   â†’ Lightening holes in plate brackets: remove 30-50% of weight with <5% strength loss
   â†’ Pocket milling (CNC required): removes material from thick areas
   â†’ Topology: "what's the load path?" â€” remove material away from the load path

4. Optimize fasteners (small but adds up)
   â†’ Steel bolts â†’ aluminum or titanium: 65-70% lighter per fastener
   â†’ Reduce fastener count: 4 bolts where 2 suffice = unnecessary weight
   â†’ Socket head â†’ button head: slight reduction per fastener Ã— many fasteners
\`\`\`

## Lightening Hole Design
\`\`\`
Rule: holes should be away from the stress concentration areas

For a bracket in bending:
  â†’ Load enters at the bolt hole â†’ peak stress at the hole edge
  â†’ Lightening holes: place in the center span, not at the edges
  â†’ Hole diameter: max 1/3 of the narrowest span they're in

For a bracket in tension:
  â†’ Stress concentrates at the loaded edge
  â†’ Lightening holes safe in the middle of the bracket

Pattern for visual consistency + maximum weight removal:
  â†’ Hexagonal hole pattern: 40-50% material removal
  â†’ Circular holes in a grid: 30-40% material removal
  â†’ Swiss cheese (random): only for non-structural cosmetic parts

Weight reduction budget example:
  Raw bracket (3" Ã— 6" Ã— 0.125" aluminum): 180g
  After hex lightening pattern:             95g (47% reduction)
  After material switch to 0.090" wall:     80g (56% reduction from original)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'remove it entirely' ranked above 'use a lighter material' as a weight reduction strategy?",opts:["Removal is simpler","Removing a component eliminates its weight AND its failure modes, maintenance burden, and design complexity; a lighter version of the same component still requires manufacturing, assembly, and maintenance; if the mechanism doesn't contribute enough game value to justify its weight, removing it is always superior to optimizing it","Materials are harder to change","Removal changes robot function"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should lightening holes be placed in the center span of a bracket rather than near the loaded edges?",opts:["Center holes are easier to drill","Stress concentrations are highest at loaded edges and holes â€” adding a lightening hole near an existing stress concentration multiplies the local stress, potentially causing failure at a load well below design intent; center material is low-stress in bending, so removing it there costs almost no structural strength","Center holes save more weight","Edge holes cause interference with fasteners"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ STRATEGY +5 (66â†’71) â”€â”€
LESSONS.strategy.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sb_ranking_pts",title:"Understanding Ranking Points â€” How Placement Is Decided",est:"10 min",content:`## Ranking Points Drive Every Strategic Decision in Quals
Most teams optimize for match score. Top teams optimize for Ranking Points (RP). RP determines seeding â€” and the #1 seed picks their alliance first. Understanding what earns RP, and how to maximize it within a match, is the foundation of championship-level strategy.

## How Ranking Points Work (FRC)
\`\`\`
Standard RP structure (verify for current game year):
  Win:  2 RP
  Tie:  1 RP
  Loss: 0 RP

Bonus RP (game-specific thresholds â€” examples):
  Harmony RP: all three alliance robots climb at the highest level
  Auto RP:    alliance scores at least X points in autonomous
  Coop RP:    both alliances contribute to a shared objective

Why bonus RP matters more than match wins:
  Scenario A: Win every match 45-30 â†’ 12 RPs in 6 matches
  Scenario B: Win 4 matches, lose 2, but earn both bonus RPs every match â†’ 14 RPs
  â†’ Team B seeds higher despite more losses

The strategic implication:
  â†’ A match you're winning by 30 points is better spent chasing bonus RPs
    than running up the score
  â†’ A match you're losing might still earn you 2 bonus RPs
    (you lose = 0 match RP but earn 2 bonus RPs = net 2 RP vs 0)
\`\`\`

## Pre-Match RP Planning
\`\`\`
Before each qualification match:
  1. How close is this alliance to each RP threshold?
  2. What's the most efficient path to 4 RP in this match?
  3. Who runs auto? (If auto RP needs 3 pieces and we can do 2, can a partner do 1?)

Communicating in the pre-match meeting:
  "We're targeting both bonus RPs today.
   Auto RP needs [X] â€” we'll do 2, can one of you get the third?
   Harmony RP needs all three at L3 â€” are you climbing L3?"

Teams that play RP-optimized qualifications seed 2-4 spots higher on average
than teams of equivalent match-score performance.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why can a team that loses more matches still seed higher than a team with more wins?",opts:["Losses don't affect seeding","Ranking Points are cumulative across all matches â€” bonus RPs from game-specific thresholds can exceed the 2 RP from a win; a team that earns both bonus RPs in every match accumulates more total RPs per match than a team that wins without achieving the bonus thresholds","Only wins determine seeding","Loss penalty reduces RP in other categories"],ans:1},
      {q:"When your alliance is winning a qualification match by a large margin, what is the most strategically valuable use of remaining time?",opts:["Score as many additional points as possible","Pursue the bonus RP thresholds â€” running up the score beyond what's needed to win adds nothing to your ranking position while missing a bonus RP costs 1 ranking point; optimizing for bonus RPs rather than maximum match score produces higher seedings for equivalent robot performance","Defend to protect the lead","Help a partner robot who is struggling"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.strategy.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sa_meta",title:"Reading the Game Meta â€” What Wins Championships",est:"14 min",content:`## The Best Robot at the Event Is Not Always the Champion
At a regional with 60 robots, two robots at the top can outscore any other combination. At championship with 600 robots, 20 robots can win any given match. The meta â€” the emergent strategy that consistently wins at the highest level â€” determines what robot capabilities actually matter.

## What Creates a Game Meta
\`\`\`
A game meta emerges when the community figures out:
  â†’ Which mechanisms have the best scoring-to-weight/complexity ratio
  â†’ Which match segments (auto, teleop, endgame) have the highest RP leverage
  â†’ Which alliance compositions win elimination series consistently

Early season meta (Weeks 1-4):
  â†’ Teams playing what they built
  â†’ High variance: innovative robots outperform early
  â†’ Scouting this period: observe what's possible, not what's average

Mid-season meta (Weeks 4-8):
  â†’ Community converges on what works
  â†’ Most competitive robots look more similar
  â†’ Top teams have already made Week 6 changes based on this

Championship meta:
  â†’ Optimal alliance composition is known
  â†’ Match strategy is refined from thousands of matches
  â†’ Robots that excel at the meta's most valuable action dominate
\`\`\`

## Reverse-Engineering the Meta
\`\`\`
From championship data (TBA has this):
  1. Pull all elimination match data
  2. What do the winning alliance robots have in common?
  3. What scoring actions appear in every winning alliance match?
  4. Are there capabilities that appear in 90%+ of final 8 robots?

Example analysis:
  â†’ 80% of finalist robots had L3 or L4 climb
  â†’ 75% had at least 2 auto game pieces
  â†’ Average winning alliance total auto: 24+ points

Translation to design priorities for next season:
  â†’ L3/L4 climb is a requirement, not an option
  â†’ 2-piece auto is the minimum viable auto
  â†’ Teleop cycle speed is the differentiator above that floor

Using meta analysis before kickoff:
  â†’ Last year's championship data predicts what this year's top teams will prioritize
  â†’ Teams that enter kickoff already knowing "we will build X" based on meta
    analysis are more decisive in design and typically produce better-executed robots
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does the game meta converge toward similarity among top robots at the championship level?",opts:["Rules force similar designs","The community-wide learning process identifies which capabilities have the highest RP and match-win impact â€” teams with access to performance data and competition observation converge on the same conclusions about what's required to win; this produces similar robot profiles because the optimal solution space is narrow when constraints are well-understood","Manufacturers produce similar parts","Championship robots must meet higher standards"],ans:1},
      {q:"What specific analytical method converts championship elimination match data into design priorities for the following season?",opts:["Watching highlight videos","Pulling all elimination match data to identify which capabilities appear in winning alliance robots at statistically significant rates â€” capabilities present in 80%+ of finalists are requirements; the scoring actions appearing in every winning match define the minimum viable competitive profile for next season","Reading team disclosure reports","Following top team social media"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.cad.Beginner.push(
  {id:"cadb_planes",title:"Sketch Planes & Reference Geometry",est:"10 min",content:`## Where You Sketch Determines What You Build
Every sketch lives on a plane. The default planes (Top, Front, Right) work for simple parts. Complex parts â€” angled brackets, mechanism arms, parts that reference other geometry â€” need custom reference planes.

## Creating Custom Planes
\`\`\`
Onshape: Insert â†’ Plane

Types:
  Offset plane: parallel to an existing face, offset by a distance
    â†’ Use: sketch a hole pattern on the far face of a gearbox
    â†’ Input: select a face + distance

  Angle plane: tilted around an edge or axis
    â†’ Use: angled bracket face, mechanism that deploys at 45Â°
    â†’ Input: select an edge + angle

  Midplane: exactly between two parallel faces
    â†’ Use: symmetric parts where sketch origin should be at center
    â†’ Input: select two parallel faces

  Point + Normal: a plane through a point, perpendicular to a line
    â†’ Use: cut across a curved surface at a specific location
    â†’ Input: one point, one line/axis
\`\`\`

## Reference Axes and Points
\`\`\`
Axis: a line used for revolve features, circular patterns, or mate references
  â†’ Create from: two planes, a cylindrical face, or two points

Point: a 3D location for mate references or pattern origins
  â†’ Create from: intersection of edges, center of a circle, or typed coordinates

When to create these vs using default geometry:
  â†’ When the default top/front/right plane would create an awkward sketch angle
  â†’ When a revolve needs an axis that doesn't align with any default
  â†’ When circular pattern center isn't at the part origin
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"When should you use a midplane instead of an offset plane?",opts:["Always â€” midplanes are more accurate","When you want to sketch symmetrically about the center of a feature rather than relative to one face","Midplanes only work on cylindrical parts","When two faces are farther than 50mm apart"],ans:1},
      {q:"What input does an angle plane require?",opts:["A face and a distance","A cylindrical surface","An edge and a rotation angle","Two parallel faces"],ans:2},
    ]},
  {id:"cadb_mirror",title:"Mirror & Pattern Features",est:"9 min",content:`## Robots Are Symmetric â€” Use That
A drivetrain has a left and right side that are mirror images. An elevator has two identical rail faces. Building one side manually and mirroring it saves half the modeling time and guarantees the two sides are exactly identical.

## Mirror Feature
\`\`\`
Onshape: select a feature or body â†’ Mirror â†’ select the mirror plane

Mirror a single feature:
  â†’ Extrude a motor mount pocket on the left frame rail
  â†’ Mirror that extrude across the robot's center plane
  â†’ Result: identical pocket on the right rail
  â†’ If you change the left pocket: the mirror updates automatically

Mirror the entire body:
  â†’ Model one gearbox half
  â†’ Mirror â†’ select midplane
  â†’ Result: two halves, perfectly symmetric
  â†’ Merge if they should be one part, or keep as separate bodies
\`\`\`

## Linear and Circular Patterns
\`\`\`
Linear pattern:
  Feature: a single lightening hole
  Direction 1: along the bracket length, spacing 20mm, count 5
  Direction 2: (optional) perpendicular, spacing 20mm, count 3
  Result: 5Ã—3 grid of holes â€” all update if you change the first

Circular pattern:
  Feature: a single bolt hole around a flange
  Axis: center axis of the flange
  Count: 6 holes, 60Â° spacing
  Result: evenly spaced bolt circle â€” change one hole, all update

Combining patterns:
  First: linear pattern of holes along a tube face
  Then:  mirror the entire patterned face to the opposite face
  Result: matching holes on both sides from one sketch
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A circular pattern requires what input that a linear pattern does not?",opts:["A count","An axis of rotation","A sketch","A merge option"],ans:1},
      {q:"If you change the first hole in a linear pattern of 8 holes, what happens to the other 7?",opts:["Nothing â€” patterns are locked after creation","They update automatically to match","You must delete and re-create the pattern","Only adjacent holes update"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"cadi_mass",title:"Mass Properties & Weight Budget Tracking",est:"11 min",content:`## Weigh the Robot Before You Build It
FRC's 125 lb limit is absolute. A robot that reaches the scale at 132 lb must shed 7 lb of mechanism â€” usually by cutting parts that took weeks to build. Running mass properties weekly in CAD catches overweight trends before metal is cut.

## Setting Up Mass Properties
\`\`\`
In Onshape, right-click any part â†’ Assign Material
Common materials:
  6061-T6 aluminum:   2.70 g/cmÂ³
  1018 steel:         7.87 g/cmÂ³
  PLA (3D print):     1.24 g/cmÂ³
  Polycarbonate:      1.20 g/cmÂ³
  Carbon fiber tube:  ~1.55 g/cmÂ³ (varies)

For purchased components without models:
  â†’ Add a cube body with the correct material and density
  â†’ Scale the cube until its mass matches the spec sheet
  â†’ Label it "Mass Stand-in: REV Neo Motor"

Assembly mass properties:
  Right-click top-level assembly â†’ Mass Properties
  â†’ Total mass: compare to budget
  â†’ Center of mass: is it where you want it for stability?
\`\`\`

## The Weight Budget Spreadsheet
\`\`\`
Track alongside CAD (update weekly):

Subsystem      | CAD mass | Add'l components | Subsystem total | Budget
---------------+---------+-----------------+----------------+-------
Drivetrain     | 18.2 lb | 4 motors 2.4lb  |  20.6 lb       | 22 lb
Arm mechanism  |  8.4 lb | 1 motor 0.6lb   |   9.0 lb       | 10 lb
Electronics    |  3.1 lb | wiring ~2 lb    |   5.1 lb       |  6 lb
Bumpers        |  (estimated)              |  15.0 lb       | 15 lb
Frame          | 14.3 lb |                 |  14.3 lb       | 15 lb
Contingency    |                           |              |   5 lb
Total          |                           |  64.0 lb       | 73 lb

If total > 110 lb in Week 4: you will likely hit 125 lb with additional hardware
Flag it early â€” losing 15 lb in Week 5 requires removing real mechanisms.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a 'contingency' line in the weight budget important?",opts:["FIRST requires it","Robots always end up heavier than the CAD model â€” wiring, fasteners, zip ties, adhesives, and last-minute brackets add 5-10 lb that no CAD model tracks; without contingency margin you exceed the limit before competition","It prevents overbuilding","CAD models are always accurate"],ans:1},
      {q:"A robot hits the scale at 132 lb. What is the minimum the team must remove?",opts:["7 lb","12 lb","5 lb","Any amount over the limit"],ans:0},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Advanced.push(
  {id:"cada_api",title:"Onshape API â€” Automating Repetitive CAD Tasks",est:"13 min",content:`## CAD Work Computers Can Do for You
Onshape exposes a REST API. With Python and your API key, you can query assembly mass, list all parts and materials, check for un-materialed parts, and export flat patterns â€” without opening a browser.

## Getting an API Key
\`\`\`
Onshape â†’ Account â†’ Developer Tools â†’ API Keys â†’ Create API Key
Gives you: Access Key + Secret Key
Store them in environment variables, never in code.
\`\`\`

## Basic API Call: Assembly Mass Properties
\`\`\`python
import requests, os, base64

ACCESS = os.environ["ONSHAPE_ACCESS"]
SECRET = os.environ["ONSHAPE_SECRET"]
BASE   = "https://cad.onshape.com/api/v6"

def onshape_get(path):
    creds = base64.b64encode(f"{ACCESS}:{SECRET}".encode()).decode()
    r = requests.get(BASE + path,
                     headers={"Authorization": f"Basic {creds}",
                              "Accept": "application/json"})
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

# Get mass properties of an assembly:
doc_id = "your_document_id_from_url"
ws_id  = "your_workspace_id"
elem_id= "your_element_id"

data = onshape_get(
    f"/assemblies/d/{doc_id}/w/{ws_id}/e/{elem_id}/massproperties"
)
mass_kg = data["bodies"]["-all-"]["mass"][0]
print(f"Robot mass: {mass_kg:.2f} kg = {mass_kg * 2.205:.1f} lb")
\`\`\`

## Useful Automation: Check Un-Materialed Parts
\`\`\`python
# List all parts in the document:
parts = onshape_get(f"/parts/d/{doc_id}/w/{ws_id}")

unmaterialed = [p for p in parts
                if not p.get("material") or p["material"].get("id") == ""]

if unmaterialed:
    print("Parts without material (mass estimate invalid):")
    for p in unmaterialed:
        print(f"  - {p['name']} in {p.get('elementName', '?')}")
else:
    print("All parts have materials assigned.")
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must Onshape API keys be stored in environment variables rather than in the Python script?",opts:["Environment variables are faster","API keys in source code get committed to git and become public â€” rotating a leaked key is painful and a compromised key lets anyone access your CAD","Onshape requires environment variables","Python can't read keys from script files"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does the un-materialed parts check specifically protect against?",opts:["Incorrect part names","An inaccurate total mass â€” any part without a material has zero mass in the API response, making the assembly mass appear lighter than it really is","Missing part numbers","Incorrect BOM quantities"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
