LESSONS.git.Beginner.push(
  {id:"gb_config",title:"Git Configuration â€” Setting Up Your Environment",est:"8 min",content:`## Before You Commit Anything, Configure Git
An unconfigured git install assigns "unknown user" to every commit. On a team repo, commits from "unknown" at an email of "user@computer" are impossible to attribute or filter. Five minutes of setup prevents this for the lifetime of your machine.

## Essential Configuration
\`\`\`bash
# Identity (required â€” used in every commit):
git config --global user.name  "Alex Chen"
git config --global user.email "alex@team1234.org"

# Default editor (pick one you know):
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"   # VS Code
git config --global core.editor "nano"           # nano (easier for beginners)
git config --global core.editor "vim"            # vim (if you know it)

# Default branch name (modern convention):
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Line endings (prevent Windows/Mac conflicts):
# Windows:
git config --global core.autocrlf true
# Mac/Linux:
git config --global core.autocrlf input

# Verify all settings:
git config --global --list
\`\`\`

## Team-Specific .gitconfig
\`\`\`bash
# Add a conditional include for your team repos:
# In ~/.gitconfig:
[includeIf "gitdir:~/team1234/"]
    path = ~/.gitconfig-team1234

# In ~/.gitconfig-team1234:
[user]
    email = alex@team1234.org
    name  = Alex Chen (Team 1234)

# Now commits in ~/team1234/ use the team email;
# personal projects use your personal email.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What happens to commits made before git user.name is configured?",opts:["They fail with an error","They succeed but are attributed to the system username, making them impossible to filter by author and hard to attribute during code review","Git prompts for a name before each commit","The commits are unsigned only"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does Windows require 'core.autocrlf true' while Mac/Linux use 'input'?",opts:["Windows uses different git versions","Windows uses CRLF line endings and Mac/Linux use LF â€” 'true' converts to LF in the repo and back to CRLF on checkout; 'input' converts to LF on commit but never adds CRLF on checkout; without this, line ending differences appear as changes to every line in every file","Windows git is less reliable","autocrlf only affects text files"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_bisect",title:"git bisect â€” Finding Exactly Which Commit Broke Something",est:"11 min",content:`## Binary Search Your Bug to a Single Commit
"The arm worked at competition two weeks ago and doesn't now." You have 40 commits between then and now. Manually testing each one would take all evening. git bisect tests the midpoint, then the midpoint of the surviving half, finding the bad commit in ~6 steps regardless of how many commits there are.

## Running a Bisect
\`\`\`bash
git bisect start

# Mark known states:
git bisect bad HEAD                    # current code is broken
git bisect good competition-2025-02-22 # this tag is known-good

# Git checks out the midpoint commit automatically.
# Test the robot (or run your unit tests).

git bisect good   # if this commit works
git bisect bad    # if this commit is also broken

# Repeat 5-6 times. Git narrows down automatically.
# Final output: "a3f92b1 is the first bad commit"
# a3f92b1 feat(arm): increase kP from 0.007 to 0.012

# End the bisect (returns to HEAD):
git bisect reset
\`\`\`

## Automated Bisect with a Test Script
\`\`\`bash
# If you have a test that exits 0 (pass) or 1 (fail):
git bisect start
git bisect bad  HEAD
git bisect good competition-2025-02-22

git bisect run python test_arm_stability.py
# Git runs the script at each midpoint automatically.
# Finds the bad commit with no manual intervention.
\`\`\`

## When Bisect Helps Most
\`\`\`
Best case: clear pass/fail criterion + many commits between good and bad
  â†’ Auto routine fails to complete: bisect finds when it broke in ~6 steps
  â†’ Unit test that was passing now fails: automated bisect in 2 minutes

Harder case: intermittent failure or subjective "feels worse"
  â†’ Bisect is unreliable if the test result varies run-to-run
  â†’ Use manual log review instead (git log --oneline good..bad)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"How many commits does git bisect need to test to find the bad commit among 64 commits?",opts:["64","32","6","It depends on where the bug is"],ans:2},
      {q:"What does 'git bisect reset' do at the end of a bisect session?",opts:["Deletes the bad commit","Returns HEAD to where it was before bisect started","Marks the found commit as permanently bad","Resets the repository to the known-good state"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ga_worktree",title:"git worktree â€” Two Branches Checked Out at Once",est:"10 min",content:`## Fix a Competition Bug Without Disturbing Your Feature Work
You're mid-way through a large autonomous rewrite. A competition hotfix comes in and needs to be on main right now. Normally you'd stash, switch branches, fix, push, switch back, unstash. With worktrees, you check out main in a second folder while leaving your feature branch untouched.

## Adding a Worktree
\`\`\`bash
# From inside the repo, add a worktree for the main branch:
git worktree add ../robot-hotfix main

# Now you have two working directories:
#   ~/robot2025/          â†’ your feature branch (unchanged)
#   ~/robot-hotfix/       â†’ main branch checked out

# In robot-hotfix: make the fix, deploy, push
cd ../robot-hotfix
git commit -am "fix(auto): correct heading after crossing midfield"
git push

# Remove the worktree when done:
cd ~/robot2025
git worktree remove ../robot-hotfix
\`\`\`

## Rules and Limits
\`\`\`
One branch per worktree:
  â†’ You cannot check out the same branch in two worktrees simultaneously
  â†’ Different branches only: main in worktree 1, feature/vision in worktree 2

Each worktree is an independent working directory:
  â†’ It has its own unstaged changes, staged files, and HEAD
  â†’ Commits from one worktree appear immediately in the other (same repo)

List all worktrees:
  git worktree list
  # /home/alex/robot2025       a3f92b1 [feature/vision]
  # /home/alex/robot-hotfix    7c44d02 [main]

Prune stale worktrees (if the directory was deleted manually):
  git worktree prune
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the key limitation on which branches can be in different worktrees?",opts:["Only main can be in a worktree","Each branch can only appear in one worktree at a time â€” two worktrees cannot share the same branch because git would have two conflicting HEADs for it","Worktrees only support fast-forward branches","Feature branches can't be used in worktrees"],ans:1},
      {q:"After removing a worktree's directory, what command cleans up git's internal reference to it?",opts:["git gc","git worktree prune","git remote prune","git clean -fd"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ FUNDRAISING +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.fundraising.Beginner.push(
  {id:"fb_tax",title:"Tax Basics for Team Donations",est:"10 min",content:`## Sponsors Ask About Tax Deductions â€” Know the Answer
When a company donates $2,000 to your team, they often ask "is this tax deductible?" The answer depends entirely on your team's legal structure. Knowing this before the meeting â€” not during it â€” signals professionalism.

## Legal Structures and Deductibility
\`\`\`
School-based team (most common):
  â†’ The team is part of a public school district
  â†’ Donations go to the school/district, which is a government entity
  â†’ 100% tax deductible as a charitable contribution
  â†’ Donor gets a receipt from the school district

Independent 501(c)(3) nonprofit:
  â†’ Team is its own nonprofit organization
  â†’ Donations are fully tax deductible
  â†’ Team must issue IRS-compliant receipts for gifts â‰¥ $250

Fiscal sponsorship (team under a nonprofit umbrella):
  â†’ Team isn't its own nonprofit, but operates under one
  â†’ Donations go to the fiscal sponsor first, earmarked for your team
  â†’ Tax deductible through the fiscal sponsor's status

No legal structure (club, booster club without 501c3):
  â†’ Donations are NOT tax deductible
  â†’ Team has no legal identity to receive donations formally
  â†’ This limits what larger sponsors will give
\`\`\`

## What to Include in a Tax Receipt
\`\`\`
Required for any gift â‰¥ $250 (IRS rules):
  Organization name and address
  Donor name
  Date of contribution
  Amount (for cash gifts)
  Statement: "No goods or services were provided in exchange for this contribution"
    (or describe the fair market value of any benefits given)
  Signature of authorized representative

Template language:
  "Thank you for your donation of $[amount] on [date] to [Organization].
   This organization is a tax-exempt organization as described in
   Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code.
   No goods or services were provided in exchange for your contribution."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A school-based team's donations are tax deductible because:",opts:["FIRST teams are automatically nonprofits","School districts are government entities and donations to them qualify as charitable contributions","All student organizations qualify","The team files a 990 tax return"],ans:1},
      {q:"Below what dollar amount is a written receipt NOT required by the IRS?",opts:["$100","$500","$250","$1,000"],ans:2},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"fi_grant3",title:"STEM Foundation Grants â€” Finding and Targeting Them",est:"12 min",content:`## Grant Money Exists Specifically for Teams Like Yours
Hundreds of foundations fund STEM education specifically. Most teams don't apply because grant-finding feels overwhelming. A structured search process identifies the 5-10 grants your team is most likely to win â€” making applications a targeted investment rather than a lottery.

## Where to Find Grants
\`\`\`
FIRST-specific grants:
  â†’ FIRST website: grants.firstinspires.org (updated annually)
  â†’ Affiliate Partners: many regional FIRST affiliates have grant lists
  â†’ Other FIRST teams: ask at competitions "which grants did you win this year?"

Foundation databases:
  â†’ Candid/GuideStar (free basic search): search "STEM education" + your state
  â†’ Foundation Directory Online (library access): comprehensive, filterable
  â†’ Your state community foundation: most have grant search tools

Corporate foundation programs:
  â†’ Companies with robotics/engineering workforce often fund STEM grants
  â†’ Search: "[company name] foundation grants" + "education"
  â†’ Common: Boeing, Lockheed, Google, Texas Instruments, local utilities

Local sources often overlooked:
  â†’ Community foundations (every county has one)
  â†’ Local Rotary/Lions club grants (small but fast â€” often $500-2,000)
  â†’ Electric co-op education funds (if your area has a rural electric co-op)
\`\`\`

## Targeting: The 4-Question Filter
\`\`\`
Before investing time in an application, answer:

1. Geography match?
   â†’ Some grants are state-specific, county-specific, or city-specific
   â†’ A grant for "students in [your county]" is a stronger fit than a national one

2. Mission alignment?
   â†’ Does the funder care about STEM education, workforce development, or youth?
   â†’ If their portfolio is arts and environment: low match, skip

3. Organization eligibility?
   â†’ Many grants require 501(c)(3) status. Does your team qualify?
   â†’ Some accept school-based teams without 501(c)(3) â€” check carefully

4. Realistic funding range?
   â†’ A $500,000 foundation that gives $50,000 minimums: don't apply for $2,000
   â†’ A foundation that gives $1,000-5,000 grants: your size, worth applying

Only apply to grants where all four answers are yes.
One targeted application beats five misaligned ones every time.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do targeted grant applications outperform a high volume of misaligned ones?",opts:["Foundations prefer fewer applicants","Targeted applications address specific funder priorities with specific evidence of fit â€” misaligned applications are eliminated in the first screening; the effort spent on one strong fit application produces better outcomes than spreading the same effort across many weak-fit submissions","Grant reviewers prefer quality","Foundations track repeat applicants"],ans:1},
      {q:"Which of these sources is most commonly overlooked by FIRST teams?",opts:["FIRST's own grant database","Local county community foundations","Corporate foundations","State STEM funding"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Advanced.push(
  {id:"fa_board",title:"Building a Team Advisory Board",est:"12 min",content:`## An Advisory Board Opens Doors You Can't Open Alone
An advisory board of 6-8 adults â€” engineers, business leaders, educators â€” gives your team credibility, connections, and expertise on demand. A board member's introduction to a company is worth 10 cold emails. Their advice on grant applications is worth weeks of research.

## Who Belongs on an Advisory Board
\`\`\`
Ideal composition (6-8 people):
  â†’ 2 engineers from relevant industries (software, mechanical, electrical)
  â†’ 1 finance/accounting professional (budget review, tax questions)
  â†’ 1 marketing/communications professional (branding, sponsorship pitch review)
  â†’ 1 educator (connects you to school resources and grant opportunities)
  â†’ 1-2 community leaders (local recognition, civic connections)
  â†’ 1 team alumnus (understands the program; will be the most engaged)

What they're NOT:
  â†’ Day-to-day mentors (those are separate roles)
  â†’ Decision-makers (student leads decide; board advises)
  â†’ Checkwriters (though they often become donors â€” that's a side effect, not the purpose)
\`\`\`

## Structure and Expectations
\`\`\`
Commitment (keep it low or nobody stays):
  â†’ 2-3 meetings per year (1 hour each)
  â†’ Available for occasional email/call questions
  â†’ Optional: attend one competition per year

What you provide to board members:
  â†’ Season summary report (1 page, twice yearly)
  â†’ Recognition in team materials
  â†’ Concrete asks: "Can you review our Impact essay draft?"
     "Can you introduce us to someone at Boeing's Education Foundation?"

First meeting agenda:
  1. Introduce the team, the mission, the season (15 min)
  2. Each board member: who they are, what they can contribute (20 min)
  3. Season goals: where the team needs help (15 min)
  4. Agree on communication norms and next meeting date (10 min)

Recruiting the first board members:
  â†’ Start with mentors' professional networks
  â†’ Ask current sponsors if they'd serve in an advisory capacity
  â†’ One board member can recruit others ("I know someone who'd be great for this")
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What distinguishes an advisory board member from a mentor?",opts:["Board members have more expertise","Mentors are involved in day-to-day build operations; advisory board members provide strategic advice, connections, and expertise at a distance â€” typically 2-3 meetings per year rather than weekly sessions","Board members are paid","Advisory boards are for fundraising only"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should advisory board time commitments be kept minimal when recruiting?",opts:["Busy people shouldn't volunteer","High time demands deter exactly the experienced professionals you want â€” a quarterly 1-hour meeting is easy to say yes to; a weekly 3-hour commitment eliminates most candidates before you've made the case for why your team is worth it","Board members aren't reliable","Less commitment means less work"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Beginner.push(
  {id:"awb_notebook2",title:"Starting an Engineering Notebook From Day One",est:"10 min",content:`## The Notebook That's Built Daily Beats the One Filled In Overnight
Award judges can tell the difference. A notebook with entries timestamped consistently, handwriting that varies across authors, and genuinely messy first drafts looks authentic. One written in three colors of the same pen the week before the event does not.

## Notebook Basics
\`\`\`
Physical vs Digital:
  Physical spiral or bound notebook:
    â†’ Harder to falsify (pen, dates, handwriting)
    â†’ Easy to add photos, sketches
    â†’ Loses detail if the person who wrote it isn't there to explain

  Digital (Google Docs with timestamps, Notion):
    â†’ Revision history proves when entries were written
    â†’ Easier to search, add images, format
    â†’ Some judges are skeptical without a physical artifact

Best of both: physical daily log â†’ weekly digital summary
\`\`\`

## What to Record Each Session
\`\`\`
One entry per session, one author (rotate):
  Date: January 22
  Author: Sam Okafor
  Members present: 11

  Decisions made:
    Chose 4-bar linkage over linear slide for intake because
    it maintains orientation throughout travel (see Figure 1 sketch).

  Work completed:
    Built intake prototype #1. Tested on carpet.
    Success rate: 7/10 game pieces in 60 seconds.

  What we learned:
    Roller compliance is insufficient at current spring force.
    Plan: increase spring force and retest next session.

  Next session goal:
    Retest intake with stiffer springs. Target 9/10.

This is one page. Multiplied by 30 build sessions = 30 pages of evidence.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do rotating authors strengthen a physical notebook's credibility with judges?",opts:["It shows teamwork","Different handwriting makes it visually apparent that entries were written at different times by different people â€” a single author's handwriting throughout suggests one person summarized the season retroactively","Rotating is required","Judges prefer consistent formatting"],ans:1},
      {q:"What does 'Next session goal' at the bottom of each entry accomplish?",opts:["It fills space","It creates a direct link between sessions â€” readers can see what was planned and then verify in the next entry whether it happened, demonstrating genuine iterative engineering rather than post-hoc documentation","Goals are required entries","It keeps members accountable"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awb_control2",title:"Control Award â€” What Judges Evaluate",est:"10 min",content:`## The Control Award Is Won on Specificity
Judges reviewing Control Award submissions hear vague claims constantly: "we implemented sophisticated autonomous routines" and "our control systems are highly optimized." The submissions that win describe specific algorithms, name specific libraries, quantify specific improvements, and explain why specific design choices were made.

## What Control Award Judges Look For
\`\`\`
Technical depth:
  â†’ Not: "We use PID control on our arm"
  â†’ Yes: "We use a feedforward + PID cascade on our arm.
    The feedforward models gravity compensation (kG = 0.08) so the PID
    only corrects disturbances rather than fighting gravity on every cycle.
    This reduced arm oscillation from Â±4Â° to Â±0.8Â° at setpoint."

Innovation:
  â†’ Something the team designed or adapted beyond standard templates
  â†’ Could be: novel sensor fusion, custom state machine architecture,
    a particularly elegant autonomous path algorithm, vision pipeline

Student understanding:
  â†’ Students presenting must understand what they're describing
  â†’ Judge will ask: "why did you choose that value for kP?"
  â†’ Wrong: "that's what worked" â†’ better: "we tuned using Ziegler-Nichols method,
    then backed off to 80% of the ultimate gain for stability margin"

Documentation:
  â†’ Code comments that explain "why" not just "what"
  â†’ Control system block diagram in the engineering notebook
  â†’ Test data showing before/after improvement
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does the feedforward term in a feedforward+PID arm controller specifically reduce?",opts:["Integral windup","The load the PID must handle â€” by modeling gravity compensation, the feedforward provides the base torque needed to hold position, so the PID only corrects small disturbances rather than continuously fighting gravity","Oscillation frequency","Response time"],ans:1},
      {q:"A judge asks 'why did you choose that kP value?' What answer signals genuine understanding?",opts:["We used trial and error","We tuned using Ziegler-Nichols, found the ultimate gain, then used 80% of that for stability margin","Our mentor suggested it","That was the default"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_spirit",title:"Team Spirit Award â€” Culture Beyond Enthusiasm",est:"9 min",content:`## Spirit Is Observed, Not Performed on Command
Spirit Award judges don't watch for the loudest team. They watch for the team whose energy is consistent, inclusive, and infectious â€” the team that lifts the energy of the whole event and makes everyone around them want to participate more.

## What Judges Actually Observe
\`\`\`
In the stands during matches:
  â†’ Cheering for all alliances, not just your own
  â†’ Specific chants, traditions, or energy that's clearly been developed over time
  â†’ Members who are engaged the whole event, not just during your matches

In the pit:
  â†’ Spirit items distributed without being asked (buttons, stickers, trading cards)
  â†’ Welcoming energy toward teams who stop by
  â†’ Members who are clearly having fun while also working

In alliance queuing:
  â†’ Introducing your spirit traditions to partners
  â†’ Teaching your cheer to another team
  â†’ Visible enthusiasm that's not forced or performative

What disqualifies you:
  â†’ Spirit directed only toward your own alliance
  â†’ Performative spirit that visibly disappears when no judges are around
  â†’ A specific hype person while everyone else is disengaged
\`\`\`

## Building Genuine Spirit Culture
\`\`\`
Spirit traditions that travel:
  â†’ A team chant all members know (practiced at meetings, not just competition)
  â†’ A physical spirit item: button design, trading card, custom-made gift
  â†’ A team handshake or ritual at the start of each match

Spirit item design principles:
  â†’ Memorable: not generic FIRST stickers â€” something uniquely your team
  â†’ Tradeable: something another team would want to display
  â†’ Consistent year over year: recognition builds over seasons
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does spirit energy that disappears when judges aren't around hurt more than help?",opts:["Judges always watch","Judges specifically observe behavior in unscripted moments â€” authentic culture is consistent; performed culture drops when the audience leaves; a judge who sees the energy shift is more likely to note the inauthenticity than to credit the times it was on","Judges compare notes afterward","Consistency is a judging criterion"],ans:1},
      {q:"Which of these best demonstrates Spirit Award-worthy behavior?",opts:["Loudest cheering section at your own matches","Teaching your team chant to your alliance partners before a match","Custom pit banner and matching uniforms","Perfect robot presentation at judge visits"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ OUTREACH +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_higher_ed",title:"Partnering With Colleges and Universities",est:"11 min",content:`## Colleges Are the Most Underused FIRST Partner
A local community college or university has labs you can use, faculty who want industry partnerships, students who need service hours, and administrators who are already funded to do STEM outreach. Tapping this resource turns a single team into a regional STEM hub.

## Types of College Partnerships
\`\`\`
Facility use:
  â†’ Machine shop access for complex fabrication
  â†’ CNC routers, laser cutters, industrial 3D printers
  â†’ Testing space for field mock-ups
  â†’ Approach: department chairs in engineering or manufacturing

Volunteer pipeline:
  â†’ Engineering and education students need service hours
  â†’ STEM camps run by 4 team members + 8 college volunteers = very different
  â†’ Contact: service learning office or department coordinators

Curriculum collaboration:
  â†’ Community college dual enrollment: high school students get college credit
    for FIRST-related coursework taught by your mentors
  â†’ University outreach programs often want to co-brand STEM events
  â†’ Benefit: their funding pays for events you'd otherwise fund yourself

Mentorship source:
  â†’ Graduate engineering students make excellent technical mentors
  â†’ Motivated, recent knowledge, flexible schedules
  â†’ Contact: grad student association or department email lists
\`\`\`

## Making the First Contact
\`\`\`
Who to contact depends on what you want:
  Facility access â†’ department chair or lab coordinator
  Volunteers â†’ service learning office or student org coordinator
  Curriculum â†’ dean of workforce development or community education
  Mentors â†’ graduate program coordinator

Email template:
  "I'm [Name], student lead of Team 1234, a FIRST Robotics team from [school].
   We work with [N] students annually and run STEM programs at [N] local schools.

   We're looking for [specific thing: machine shop access / student volunteers / etc.].
   I'd love to schedule a 20-minute call to see if there's a fit.

   I'm available [times]."

This email is short, specific, and proposes a concrete next step.
A vague "we'd love to partner with you" produces vague responses.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a community college's service learning office a better first contact than a professor for finding student volunteers?",opts:["Service learning has more funding","The service learning office exists specifically to connect students needing service hours with community organizations â€” they have the infrastructure and the motivated student pool; a professor who forwards your request to students is a much weaker distribution mechanism","Professors are too busy","Service learning offices respond faster"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes the email template effective?",opts:["It's formal and professional","It's short, names a specific ask, and proposes a concrete next step â€” recipients can answer yes/no/maybe to a specific request; 'we'd love to partner' requires them to invent what that means before responding","It lists all programs","It includes a resume"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ori_peer",title:"Peer-to-Peer Mentoring Within Your Team",est:"10 min",content:`## The Most Scalable Outreach Is Inside Your Own Team
One mentor teaching fifteen students is a bottleneck. One mentor teaching three leads who each teach five members is a training multiplier. Teams that build peer teaching into their structure develop skills faster, retain members longer, and scale programs that would otherwise depend on adults.

## Structured Peer Teaching Formats
\`\`\`
Skill stations (30-minute rotation format):
  3-5 stations, each run by one experienced member:
    Station 1: Crimping Anderson connectors (electrical lead)
    Station 2: CAD sketch constraints (CAD lead)
    Station 3: Java for loop and array basics (programming lead)
    Station 4: Using a tap to thread aluminum (mechanical lead)
  Small groups rotate every 30 minutes.
  30 students learn 4 skills in 2 hours with one mentor supervising.

Buddy system:
  Every new member is paired with a member 1 year ahead, not a senior.
  Why not a senior: the skill gap is too large; explanation becomes lecture.
  Why 1 year ahead: they recently learned the same things and remember
  what was confusing; they're relatable; they're still present next season.

Documentation review pairs:
  Two members write documentation for their respective mechanisms.
  Then swap: each reads the other's doc and tries to follow the steps.
  Anything that's unclear comes back for revision.
  Result: both documents improve and both authors learn to explain clearly.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a buddy 1 year ahead more effective than a senior for new member mentoring?",opts:["Seniors are too busy","A peer 1 year ahead recently learned the same material and remembers what was confusing â€” they can explain from genuine recent experience; seniors often compress steps that seem obvious to them but aren't obvious to beginners, creating explanations that skip the parts new members most need","The skill gap is too small","Seniors prefer not to mentor"],ans:1},
      {q:"In the skill station format, what makes 30 minutes the appropriate rotation interval?",opts:["It matches class periods","Long enough to demonstrate a skill and practice it once; short enough that attention stays high and the group covers four stations in two hours â€” longer rotations allow over-teaching of detail that one session can't retain","30 minutes is a FIRST standard","Shorter intervals are more efficient"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ora_impact2",title:"Measuring Long-Term Program Impact",est:"12 min",content:`## The Real Question Is What Changed Three Years Later
A school that has a robotics program two years after your visit was genuinely impacted. A school that hosted you once and never again wasn't. Long-term impact measurement is harder than counting events â€” but it's what separates award-winning programs from award-claiming programs.

## Building a Longitudinal Tracking System
\`\`\`
Year 1 (when you start a program):
  Document the baseline:
  â†’ Does this school currently have robotics? (Y/N)
  â†’ How many students express interest?
  â†’ Teacher name and contact info
  â†’ What you provided (training, curriculum, equipment)

Year 2 follow-up (6-month and 12-month):
  â†’ Did they run robotics again?
  â†’ Did they register for FLL or similar?
  â†’ What support did they still need from you?

Year 3+ follow-up (annual):
  â†’ Is the program still running without your involvement?
  â†’ Has it grown (more students, more teams)?
  â†’ Have any students from that program joined FRC/FTC?

Spreadsheet structure:
  School | Start year | Program type | Year 2 status | Year 3 status | Notes
  Lincoln Elem | 2022 | FLL mentor | Active, 2 teams | Independent | Teacher: Ms. Garcia
\`\`\`

## The Impact Trajectory Narrative
\`\`\`
Strong award narrative uses trajectory data:
  "In 2022 we started a robotics club at Jefferson Elementary.
   In 2023 they registered independently for FLL for the first time.
   In 2024 they qualified for their state championship without any support from us.
   Their lead teacher now trains other schools in our district."

This is three data points across three years â€” each one a proof point.
No single-year snapshot can tell this story.

Collection strategy: annual May email to each partner contact
  "Just checking in â€” is the program still running? Any updates to share?"
  5-minute email. Most respond. Those who don't: note "no response" and try again.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does 'program independence' (running without your support) prove that 'program activity' (running with your support) cannot?",opts:["Independence is harder to achieve","Independence demonstrates that your intervention built lasting capacity rather than dependency â€” a program that only runs when you're there proves you're a good visitor; one that runs after you leave proves you taught them to do it themselves","Independent programs are better funded","Activity metrics are easier to fake"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is an annual May email the recommended collection method for long-term tracking data?",opts:["May is end of school year","It's timed to year-end when teachers know whether the program completed its season, requires minimal effort from both parties, and creates a consistent annual record without burdening anyone","Email has the best response rate","May is after competition season"],ans:2},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"tmi_remote",title:"Managing Remote and Hybrid Team Members",est:"11 min",content:`## Not Everyone Can Make Every In-Person Session
A strong programmer who lives 45 minutes away and can only attend half the sessions has more to contribute than the team's structure allows. Remote-friendly workflows capture that contribution instead of losing it.

## What Can Be Done Remotely
\`\`\`
Fully remote work:
  â†’ Code (commit and push from home)
  â†’ CAD (Onshape is browser-based â€” any machine, any location)
  â†’ Documentation (Google Docs, shared notebooks)
  â†’ Scouting data analysis (Python scripts, spreadsheets)
  â†’ Strategy research (TBA data, game manual analysis)
  â†’ Award essay drafts, notebook entries, sponsor communication

Requires in-person:
  â†’ Physical build (machining, assembly, wiring)
  â†’ Drive practice
  â†’ Robot testing and integration
  â†’ Safety-sensitive work (power tools, live robot)

The mistake: treating all members as either fully present or absent
The fix: assign remote-suitable tasks explicitly to members who can't attend
\`\`\`

## Communication for Hybrid Teams
\`\`\`
Asynchronous tools (members contribute on their own schedule):
  â†’ Slack/Discord: text-based updates that remote members can read later
  â†’ GitHub: code review that doesn't require being online at the same time
  â†’ Loom: 3-minute video walkthrough of "here's what I built today"
    â†’ Much faster to understand than a text explanation of code

Synchronous tools (everyone online at the same time):
  â†’ Weekly leads call (30 min, video): decisions that need real-time discussion
  â†’ Ad-hoc pair sessions: one in-person, one remote â€” screen share + Discord voice

Inclusion rules for hybrid:
  â†’ Build session standup: remote members join by video or read a written summary after
  â†’ Any decision made in-person: posted in Discord within 2 hours
  â†’ "We talked about it at the shop" is not communication â€” post it

Documentation is the bridge:
  â†’ A remote member who can read exactly what was decided and why
    can contribute intelligently the next day
  â†’ A remote member kept out of the loop becomes disengaged and leaves
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the most common reason remote team members become disengaged?",opts:["They have less motivation","They're kept out of the loop â€” decisions made in-person that aren't communicated to them make their contributions irrelevant and signal that their involvement doesn't matter","Remote work is less effective","They lack the skills for remote tasks"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is a Loom video walkthrough of code more effective than a text description for remote collaboration?",opts:["Video is higher quality","It shows the code running, the thought process, and the context simultaneously in 3 minutes â€” a text description of the same information takes longer to write, longer to read, and loses the visual component that makes code comprehensible","Loom is free","Text descriptions don't work for code"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"tmi_data",title:"Data-Driven Team Management",est:"11 min",content:`## Gut Feelings Run Teams Badly
"I feel like attendance is down" is less useful than "attendance this month is 68% vs 82% last month." Data doesn't replace judgment â€” it informs it. Teams that track a few key metrics make better decisions with less debate.

## Metrics Worth Tracking
\`\`\`
Attendance rate (weekly):
  â†’ Members present / members expected Ã— 100%
  â†’ Alert: below 75% for 2 consecutive weeks â†’ investigate root cause
  â†’ Segment by subteam: is the problem team-wide or in one area?

New member retention (season):
  â†’ Members who joined at start / members still active at competition
  â†’ Below 60%: onboarding or culture problem
  â†’ Track by cohort: does this year's cohort retain differently than last year's?

Task completion rate (per sprint/week):
  â†’ Tasks completed / tasks committed to Ã— 100%
  â†’ Below 70%: scope is too large, blockers aren't being resolved, or tasks aren't being taken seriously
  â†’ Trend matters: declining week over week = systemic issue

Subteam balance:
  â†’ Count of active members per subteam vs workload estimate
  â†’ One subteam with 2 people and 8 people-sessions of work: understaffed
  â†’ One subteam with 8 people and 2 people-sessions of work: overstaffed
\`\`\`

## Using Data Without Weaponizing It
\`\`\`
Data informs conversations; it doesn't replace them:
  "Attendance in programming this month is 62% â€” let's talk about what's going on"
  is different from "programming's attendance numbers are bad."

Don't publish individual attendance data to the whole team.
  â†’ Summary by subteam: yes
  â†’ Individual records visible to leads: yes
  â†’ Whole-team visibility: only if the team has explicitly agreed to this

When data shows a problem, act on the root cause:
  â†’ Low attendance could be: scheduling conflict, disengagement, outside pressure
  â†’ Low task completion could be: overpromising, blockers, clarity issues
  â†’ Each root cause has a different response â€” don't default to "try harder"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'below 70% task completion for 2+ weeks' more actionable than 'I feel like things are falling behind'?",opts:["Numbers are more convincing","A specific metric with a specific threshold gives the team something to investigate and respond to â€” vague feelings generate vague responses; a specific downward trend triggers specific questions: are tasks too large? are there blockers? is commitment unclear?","Data prevents conflict","Feelings are always inaccurate"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why should individual attendance records not be published team-wide?",opts:["Privacy laws prohibit it","Public individual data creates shame and comparison rather than support â€” the goal is to identify problems and help members, not rank them; subteam aggregate data gives leads what they need to act without the social dynamics of a public leaderboard","Individual data is unreliable","Teams don't track individuals"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Advanced.push(
  {id:"tma_alumni2",title:"Building an Alumni Network That Gives Back",est:"12 min",content:`## Alumni Who Stay Connected Become Your Best Resource
A team alumnus who is now a working engineer, university student, or professional has expertise, connections, and nostalgia â€” all potentially available to your current team. Teams that maintain alumni relationships tap this resource for mentorship, career advice, demonstrations, and donations for years after graduation.

## Staying Connected After Graduation
\`\`\`
The critical window: the first 3 months after graduation
  â†’ Send a personal email (not a mass email) within 30 days of graduation
  â†’ "Congrats on graduating. We'd love to stay in touch.
     Can I add you to our alumni list? We share updates about 4Ã— per year."
  â†’ Most alumni who lose connection in this window never reconnect

Annual alumni touchpoints:
  Season opener email:       September â€” "build season is coming"
  Mid-season update:         February â€” "here's what we built"
  End-of-season report:      April â€” "here's how it went"
  Career connection ask:     June â€” "any alumni want to speak at our STEM night?"

Alumni Discord/Slack channel:
  â†’ Low-maintenance, text-based, opt-in
  â†’ Current team can ask questions directly: "anyone have experience with CAN?"
  â†’ Alumni answer when they can â€” asynchronous, low commitment
\`\`\`

## Alumni Programming
\`\`\`
Career day:
  Alumni return (virtually or in-person) to describe their careers
  Best format: 3-4 alumni, 10 minutes each, 20 minutes Q&A
  Value: students see real-world paths from this team to this career

Mentorship matching:
  Senior students paired with college-age alumni for monthly check-ins
  Topics: college applications, major selection, internship navigation
  Time ask: 30 minutes per month â€” very manageable

Technical consultation:
  Current team has a hard technical problem â†’ post in alumni channel
  "We're trying to implement odometry with a swerve drive â€” anyone done this?"
  Alumni with industry experience often have immediately applicable answers
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is the first 3 months after graduation the critical window for alumni connection?",opts:["Alumni are most available then","New graduates are in transition and open to maintaining connections â€” the team identity is still fresh; after 6 months in college or work, a new identity forms and the team becomes a distant memory rather than an active part of self-concept; reaching out while the connection is warm costs almost nothing and preserves it","Alumni are required to respond","Graduation data is easiest to collect then"],ans:1},
      {q:"What makes an alumni Discord channel more sustainable than structured monthly meetings?",opts:["Discord is free","Asynchronous and opt-in â€” alumni contribute when they have time, not on a fixed schedule; structured meetings require everyone's calendar to align, which becomes impossible as alumni spread across time zones and careers; low-friction channels get used; high-friction commitments get abandoned","Discord has better search","Meeting fatigue is common"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ PYTHON +7 â”€â”€
LESSONS.python.Beginner.push(
  {id:"pyb_io",title:"File I/O â€” Reading and Writing Data Files",est:"10 min",content:`## Scouting Data That Isn't Saved Is Lost
A Python session ends and all variables disappear. File I/O persists data between runs â€” match results written to a file survive crashes, power outages, and session restarts.

## Reading and Writing Text Files
\`\`\`python
# Write a file (creates it if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does):
with open("matches.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Team 1234, Match 3, Auto: 12, Cycles: 6\\n")
    f.write("Team 5678, Match 3, Auto: 8,  Cycles: 4\\n")

# Append to an existing file (doesn't overwrite):
with open("matches.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Team 9012, Match 3, Auto: 15, Cycles: 7\\n")

# Read entire file:
with open("matches.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()       # entire file as one string

# Read line by line:
with open("matches.txt", "r") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())  # .strip() removes trailing newline
\`\`\`

## JSON Files for Structured Data
\`\`\`python
import json

# Write structured data:
matches = [
    {"team": 1234, "match": 3, "auto": 12, "cycles": 6},
    {"team": 5678, "match": 3, "auto": 8,  "cycles": 4},
]
with open("matches.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(matches, f, indent=2)  # indent=2 makes it human-readable

# Read it back:
with open("matches.json", "r") as f:
    loaded = json.load(f)

print(loaded[0]["team"])   # 1234
print(loaded[1]["auto"])   # 8

# Safe read (handle missing file gracefully):
from pathlib import Path
def load_matches(path="matches.json"):
    p = Path(path)
    if not p.exists():
        return []
    with open(p) as f:
        return json.load(f)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the difference between opening a file with 'w' vs 'a'?",opts:["'a' creates a new file","'w' overwrites the entire file from the start; 'a' appends to the end without erasing existing content â€” using 'w' to add a record destroys all previous records","'w' is write-protected","They are equivalent for new files only"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why use 'with open(...)' instead of calling open() and close() separately?",opts:["'with' is required in Python 3","The 'with' block automatically closes the file even if an error occurs â€” manually calling close() is skipped if an exception happens between open() and close(), leaving the file handle open and potentially corrupting data","'with' is shorter to type","File handles close automatically anyway"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.python.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"pi_oop",title:"Object-Oriented Design for Scouting Systems",est:"13 min",content:`## Classes Let You Think in Nouns, Not Procedures
A scouting system built with functions eventually becomes a pile of dictionaries passed between functions. A class-based design creates objects that know their own data and behavior â€” a Team object that can compute its own stats, a Match object that validates its own fields.

## From Dictionary to Class
\`\`\`python
# Before â€” data and logic are separate, easy to misuse:
def avg_score(matches: list[dict]) -> float:
    return sum(m["total"] for m in matches) / len(matches) if matches else 0.0

team_data = {"number": 1234, "matches": [...]}
avg = avg_score(team_data["matches"])  # what if "matches" is misspelled?

# After â€” the class owns its data and logic:
class Team:
    def __init__(self, number: int, nickname: str = ""):
        self.number   = number
        self.nickname = nickname
        self.matches: list[Match] = []

    def add_match(self, match: "Match") -> None:
        self.matches.append(match)

    @property
    def avg_score(self) -> float:
        if not self.matches:
            return 0.0
        return sum(m.total for m in self.matches) / len(self.matches)

    @property
    def best_climb(self) -> str:
        order = ["None", "L1", "L2", "L3", "L4"]
        return max((m.climb for m in self.matches),
                   key=lambda c: order.index(c),
                   default="None")

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"Team({self.number}, avg={self.avg_score:.1f})"


class Match:
    CLIMB_PTS = {"None": 0, "L1": 2, "L2": 4, "L3": 6, "L4": 10}

    def __init__(self, match_num: int, auto: float, cycles: int, climb: str):
        if climb not in self.CLIMB_PTS:
            raise ValueError(f"Invalid climb: {climb}")
        self.match_num = match_num
        self.auto      = auto
        self.cycles    = cycles
        self.climb     = climb

    @property
    def total(self) -> float:
        return self.auto + (self.cycles * 4) + self.CLIMB_PTS[self.climb]
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does the @property decorator accomplish for avg_score?",opts:["It caches the computed value","It lets you call team.avg_score like an attribute (no parentheses) while still running a computation each time â€” callers don't need to know whether avg_score is stored data or a calculated value","It makes the attribute read-only","Properties are required for class methods"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why does Match.__init__ raise ValueError for invalid climb strings rather than storing them silently?",opts:["Python requires this","Validation at creation time catches the error immediately where the bad data enters â€” silent storage propagates invalid data throughout the system, causing obscure failures later when CLIMB_PTS lookup fails on an unexpected key","ValueError is more informative","Strings can't be stored directly"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"pi_web_scrape",title:"Web Scraping With BeautifulSoup",est:"12 min",content:`## When There's No API, Parse the HTML
TBA has an API. Many other useful sites don't. BeautifulSoup parses HTML pages into a tree you can navigate to extract the data you need â€” event schedules, regional rankings, team lists from non-TBA sources.

## Basic Scraping Pattern
\`\`\`python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup  # pip install beautifulsoup4

def fetch_soup(url: str) -> BeautifulSoup:
    headers = {"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 Team1234 Scout Tool"}
    r = requests.get(url, headers=headers, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return BeautifulSoup(r.text, "html.parser")

# Example: scrape a team list table
soup = fetch_soup("https://example-regional.com/teams")

# Find a table with class "teams-table":
table = soup.find("table", class_="teams-table")
rows  = table.find_all("tr")[1:]  # skip header row

teams = []
for row in rows:
    cols = row.find_all("td")
    if len(cols) >= 2:
        teams.append({
            "number":   int(cols[0].text.strip()),
            "nickname": cols[1].text.strip(),
            "city":     cols[2].text.strip() if len(cols) > 2 else "",
        })
\`\`\`

## Finding Elements
\`\`\`python
# Find first match:
soup.find("h1")                          # first <h1>
soup.find("div", class_="team-card")    # div with class "team-card"
soup.find("a", href=True)               # first link with any href
soup.find(id="main-content")            # element with id="main-content"

# Find all matches:
soup.find_all("tr")                     # all table rows
soup.find_all("div", class_="match")   # all match divs
soup.select("table.results td.score")  # CSS selector: td.score inside table.results

# Getting data from elements:
el = soup.find("span", class_="rank")
el.text                    # text content
el.text.strip()            # without leading/trailing whitespace
el["href"]                 # attribute (raises KeyError if missing)
el.get("href", "")         # attribute with default (no error if missing)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should a User-Agent header be sent with scraping requests?",opts:["It speeds up the request","Without a User-Agent, requests use Python's default 'python-requests/x.x.x' which many servers block as a bot; a browser-like User-Agent reduces the chance of being blocked and also identifies your tool if the server logs show unexpected traffic","User-Agent is required by HTTP","It bypasses rate limiting"],ans:1},
      {q:"What is the difference between find() and find_all()?",opts:["find_all() is slower","find() returns the first matching element or None; find_all() returns a list of all matching elements (empty list if none found) â€” using find() when you expect multiple elements silently returns only the first one","find() requires a class argument","find_all() only works on tables"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.python.Advanced.push(
  {id:"pa_perf",title:"Performance Profiling Python Scouting Code",est:"12 min",content:`## Fast Enough Is Not Always Fast Enough
A pick-list computation that takes 4 seconds on your laptop might take 20 seconds on the pit laptop during alliance selection. Profiling identifies which functions actually consume time so you optimize the right things â€” not the things that feel slow.

## cProfile â€” Standard Library Profiler
\`\`\`python
import cProfile
import pstats

# Profile a function call:
with cProfile.Profile() as pr:
    result = compute_all_stats(matches)   # your function here

stats = pstats.Stats(pr)
stats.sort_stats("cumulative")
stats.print_stats(15)   # show top 15 most expensive functions

# Output (example):
# ncalls  tottime  percall  cumtime  percall filename:lineno(function)
#      1    0.001    0.001    4.231    4.231 analysis.py:42(compute_all_stats)
#  60000    3.980    0.000    4.218    0.000 analysis.py:18(_compute_opr)
#  60000    0.238    0.000    0.238    0.000 {built-in method sum}
#
# Conclusion: _compute_opr is called 60,000 times and dominates runtime
# Fix: cache its result or vectorize with numpy
\`\`\`

## timeit â€” Comparing Two Approaches
\`\`\`python
import timeit

# Compare two implementations:
slow_code = """
result = [compute_avg(team) for team in teams]
"""

fast_code = """
avgs = {t["number"]: sum(t["scores"]) / len(t["scores"]) for t in teams}
"""

setup = "from __main__ import compute_avg, teams"

slow = timeit.timeit(slow_code, setup=setup, number=1000)
fast = timeit.timeit(fast_code, setup=setup, number=1000)

print(f"Slow: {slow:.3f}s  Fast: {fast:.3f}s  Speedup: {slow/fast:.1f}x")
\`\`\`

## Common Python Performance Fixes
\`\`\`python
# 1. Avoid repeated lookups in loops â€” cache once
slow: [team for team in teams if team["number"] in set(get_picks())]
fast: picks = set(get_picks()); [t for t in teams if t["number"] in picks]

# 2. Use numpy for numerical operations on large arrays
import numpy as np
scores = np.array([m["total"] for m in matches])
avg    = scores.mean()     # ~50x faster than a Python loop for 10k+ items

# 3. sort() once, don't re-sort inside a loop
teams.sort(key=lambda t: t["avg"], reverse=True)  # once
# not: sorted(teams, ...) on every render call
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"cProfile shows _compute_opr is called 60,000 times. What are the two best fixes?",opts:["Rewrite it in C","Cache its result if the inputs haven't changed, or vectorize the computation with numpy to eliminate the Python loop overhead â€” reducing calls from 60,000 to a handful is more impactful than optimizing the function itself","Delete the function","Run the profiler on a faster machine"],ans:1},
      {q:"Why is 'picks = set(get_picks())' outside a list comprehension faster than calling get_picks() inside it?",opts:["set() is faster than list","get_picks() is called once instead of once per team â€” if the list comprehension evaluates 60 teams, get_picks() runs 60 times and creates 60 sets; caching outside creates one set and uses it for all 60 lookups","set lookup is O(1)","List comprehensions cache automatically"],ans:2},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€â”€ PACK 19 â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€

LESSONS.webdev.Beginner.push(
  {id:"wb_debug",title:"Browser DevTools for Web Debugging",est:"9 min",content:`## The Browser Already Has a Debugger Built In
F12 opens a full development environment in any browser. Most web bugs â€” layout problems, JavaScript errors, failed network requests â€” can be diagnosed without touching a single line of code.

## The Four Most Useful Panels
\`\`\`
Console:
  â†’ JavaScript errors appear here automatically
  â†’ console.log() output shows here
  â†’ You can run JS expressions interactively: type document.title, press Enter

Elements / Inspector:
  â†’ Live HTML tree â€” hover over any element to highlight it on the page
  â†’ Edit HTML or CSS directly in the browser (changes are temporary, for testing)
  â†’ Right-click any element on the page â†’ Inspect â†’ jumps to that element

Network:
  â†’ Every HTTP request: URL, method, status code, response time
  â†’ Click any request to see headers, request body, response body
  â†’ Red rows = failed requests (4xx, 5xx errors)
  â†’ Filter by "XHR" to see only your fetch() calls

Sources / Debugger:
  â†’ Open your JS file, click a line number â†’ sets a breakpoint
  â†’ Code pauses at that line during execution
  â†’ Inspect variable values at that exact moment
\`\`\`

## Quick Workflow for Common Problems
\`\`\`
Problem: page looks wrong
  â†’ Elements panel â†’ find the element â†’ look at computed styles
  â†’ Is the wrong CSS rule winning? Which stylesheet is it from?

Problem: fetch() is failing
  â†’ Network panel â†’ find the request â†’ check status code
  â†’ 404: wrong URL. 500: server error. CORS error: see response headers.

Problem: JS not running at all
  â†’ Console panel â†’ is there a SyntaxError or TypeError?
  â†’ Fix the error first â€” one error can stop all subsequent JS from running
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A fetch() call is failing silently. Which DevTools panel shows you why?",opts:["Console","Sources","Network","Elements"],ans:2},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"wi_testing",title:"Testing Your Scouting App Before Competition",est:"11 min",content:`## Bugs Found at Competition Cost Matches. Bugs Found at Home Cost Nothing.\nA test plan run two days before the event catches the issues that would otherwise appear during alliance selection. Systematic testing is faster than diagnosing the same bug under pressure.\n\n## The Pre-Competition Test Checklist\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\nData entry (run on a phone, not just desktop):\n  â–¡ Submit a complete match â€” does it save?\n  â–¡ Submit the same match twice â€” does it duplicate or handle gracefully?\n  â–¡ Submit with required fields empty â€” does it reject or crash?\n  â–¡ Tap the back button mid-entry â€” is data lost?\n\nData display:\n  â–¡ Load rankings with 0 matches scouted â€” does it show empty state or crash?\n  â–¡ Load rankings with 1 team â€” does math work (no divide-by-zero)?\n  â–¡ Load rankings with 60 teams â€” does the page scroll or overflow?\n\nNetwork resilience:\n  â–¡ Disconnect from Wi-Fi â€” does the app show an error or freeze?\n  â–¡ Reconnect â€” does it recover without a page reload?\n  â–¡ Slow connection (throttle in DevTools) â€” is there a loading indicator?\n\nDevice variety:\n  â–¡ Test on the oldest/slowest phone on your team â€” does it still work?\n  â–¡ Test in both portrait and landscape â€” does layout break?\n  â–¡ Test with large font size (accessibility setting) â€” does text overflow?\n\\\`\\\`\\\`\n\n## Writing a Simple Automated Test\n\\\`\\\`\\\`javascript\n// Basic test for your scoring calculation function:\nfunction runTests() {\n  const cases = [\n    { input: { auto: 12, cycles: 5, climb: "L3" }, expected: 38 },\n    { input: { auto: 0,  cycles: 0, climb: "None" }, expected: 0  },\n    { input: { auto: 15, cycles: 8, climb: "L4"  }, expected: 57 },\n  ];\n\n  let passed = 0;\n  cases.forEach(({ input, expected }, i) => {\n    const result = calculateScore(input);\n    if (result === expected) {\n      passed++;\n    } else {\n      console.error(\\\`Test \\" + (i+1) + " FAILED: expected \\" + (expected) + ", got \\" + (result) + "\\\`);\n    }\n  });\n  console.log(\\\`\\" + (passed) + "/\\" + (cases.length) + " tests passed\\\`);\n}\n\\\`\\\`\\\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why test with 0 matches scouted before adding any data?",opts:["To verify the database is empty","Empty state exposes divide-by-zero and undefined errors that won't appear once real data exists","It's the first logical state","To check the loading animation"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"wi_perf",title:"Frontend Performance â€” Making the App Feel Fast",est:"11 min",content:`## Slow Apps Get Abandoned During Stressful Matches
A scouting app that takes 3 seconds to load rankings after each match frustrates scouts. Performance problems compound on slower devices and congested event Wi-Fi. Most frontend slowness comes from a handful of fixable issues.

## Measuring Performance
\`\`\`
DevTools â†’ Lighthouse (Chrome):
  â†’ Run audit â†’ Performance score + specific recommendations
  â†’ First Contentful Paint: time until something appears
  â†’ Time to Interactive: time until the app responds to input

DevTools â†’ Performance tab:
  â†’ Record while doing the slow action
  â†’ Flame chart shows which JS functions consumed time
  â†’ Long yellow bars: JavaScript blocking the main thread
\`\`\`

## The Most Common Fixes
\`\`\`javascript
// 1. Don't re-render the whole list when one item changes
//    Bad: rebuild 60 team cards every time any state changes
//    Good: use React.memo to skip re-rendering unchanged cards
const TeamCard = React.memo(({ team }) => {
  return <div>{team.number}: {team.avg.toFixed(1)}</div>;
});

// 2. Virtualize long lists â€” only render visible rows
// Install: npm install react-window
import { FixedSizeList } from "react-window";
<FixedSizeList height={600} itemCount={teams.length} itemSize={48}>
  {({ index, style }) => (
    <div style={style}><TeamCard team={teams[index]} /></div>
  )}
</FixedSizeList>
// Renders ~15 rows at a time instead of 60 â€” massive speed improvement

// 3. Debounce filter inputs â€” don't re-filter on every keystroke
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";
const [query, setQuery] = useState("");
const filtered = useMemo(
  () => teams.filter(t => t.number.toString().includes(query)),
  [teams, query]  // only recomputes when teams or query changes
);
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does React.memo do for a component?",opts:["It stores the component in memory permanently","It prevents re-rendering if props haven't changed","It caches the component's network requests","It speeds up initial load time"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.webdev.Advanced.push(
  {id:"wa_realtime",title:"Real-Time Updates With Server-Sent Events",est:"12 min",content:`## Push Data to Scouts Without Them Refreshing
WebSockets are bidirectional and complex to set up. Server-Sent Events (SSE) are one-way (server â†’ browser) and require almost no setup â€” perfect for a scouting dashboard that needs live match result updates pushed to all tablets simultaneously.

## Flask SSE Endpoint
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, Response, stream_with_context
import json, time, threading

app = Flask(__name__)
clients = []          # list of active SSE connections
lock    = threading.Lock()

@app.route("/stream")
def stream():
    def generate():
        q = []
        with lock:
            clients.append(q)
        try:
            while True:
                if q:
                    data = q.pop(0)
                    yield f"data: {json.dumps(data)}\\n\\n"
                else:
                    yield ": heartbeat\\n\\n"   # keep connection alive
                time.sleep(0.5)
        finally:
            with lock:
                clients.remove(q)

    return Response(stream_with_context(generate()),
                    mimetype="text/event-stream",
                    headers={"Cache-Control": "no-cache",
                             "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"})

def broadcast(event_data: dict):
    with lock:
        for q in clients:
            q.append(event_data)

# Call broadcast() whenever new match data arrives:
@app.route("/api/matches", methods=["POST"])
def post_match():
    data = request.get_json()
    save_match(data)
    broadcast({"type": "new_match", "team": data["team"]})
    return {"ok": True}
\`\`\`

## Browser SSE Client
\`\`\`javascript
const es = new EventSource("/stream");

es.onmessage = (event) => {
  const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
  if (data.type === "new_match") {
    refreshTeamStats();    // re-fetch and re-render
  }
};

es.onerror = () => {
  console.warn("SSE connection lost â€” will auto-reconnect");
  // Browser reconnects automatically after a delay
};
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why choose SSE over WebSockets for a scouting dashboard?",opts:["SSE supports binary data","WebSockets require a different server setup and are bidirectional â€” SSE works over regular HTTP, the browser reconnects automatically on drop, and a dashboard only needs server-to-client updates","SSE is faster","WebSockets don't work on mobile"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

LESSONS.fundraising.Beginner.push(
  {id:"fb_ask",title:"Making the Ask â€” Directly Requesting a Sponsorship",est:"10 min",content:`## Sponsors Don't Volunteer Money. You Have to Ask.
Dozens of teams never get sponsorships because they send a packet and wait. The packet is not the ask. A phone call, a meeting, or a direct "will you sponsor us at the $1,500 level?" is the ask. Most professionals respect directness â€” vagueness makes decisions hard.

## The Sponsorship Conversation Structure
\`\`\`
Opening (30 seconds):
  Establish who you are and why you called.
  "Hi, I'm Alex Chen, student team lead for Team 1234 at Lincoln High.
   We're a FIRST Robotics team and I'm reaching out to local companies
   about partnering with us this season."

The pitch (90 seconds):
  â†’ What FIRST is (one sentence: "national robotics competition, 6-week build, 3,000 teams")
  â†’ What your team specifically does ("we run programs at 8 local schools, 800 students/year")
  â†’ Why their company is a fit ("we saw you're involved in local STEM education")

The ask (15 seconds):
  â†’ Specific level, specific amount
  "We'd love to have you as a Silver Partner at the $1,500 level.
   That includes your logo on our robot and uniforms for the season."

The close:
  â†’ "Is that something [Company] would consider?"
  â†’ Then stop talking. Let them respond.
\`\`\`

## Handling Common Responses
\`\`\`
"Send us some information first":
  â†’ "Absolutely â€” what email should I send it to? And should I follow up with you
     in about a week after you've had a chance to look it over?"

"Our budget decisions are made in [month]":
  â†’ "That's helpful to know. Can I reach back out in [month-1] to get on your radar
     before those decisions are made?"

"We're not interested":
  â†’ "I understand â€” thank you for your time. Is there a better fit elsewhere
     in your company, or should I check back next season?"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should you stop talking immediately after asking 'is that something you'd consider?'",opts:["It's polite","Silence prompts the other person to answer â€” filling the silence yourself lets them avoid committing","The ask must be exactly those words","Sponsors need time to calculate the amount"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"fi_crm",title:"Sponsor CRM â€” Tracking Relationships at Scale",est:"11 min",content:`## 15 Sponsors Means 15 Relationships to Manage
When does each renewal come up? Who's the right contact at each company? Who did you last speak with, and what did you promise to send? Without a system, things fall through. A simple spreadsheet CRM (Customer Relationship Management) tracks this without expensive software.

## The Sponsor CRM Spreadsheet
\`\`\`
Columns:
  Company | Contact Name | Title | Email | Phone
  Level | Amount | First Year | Renewal Month
  Last Contact Date | Last Contact Notes | Next Action | Next Action Date
  Logo received? | Listed on website? | Thank-you sent?

One row per sponsor. Update it after every interaction.

Example row:
  Acme Engineering | Sarah Cho | Marketing Dir | s.cho@acme.com | 555-1234
  Gold | $3,000 | 2022 | October
  2025-09-15 | "Call went well; she wants impact report first" | Send impact report | 2025-09-22
  âœ“ | âœ“ | âœ“
\`\`\`

## Weekly CRM Habits
\`\`\`
Every Monday, 10 minutes:
  â†’ Which sponsors have a Next Action Date this week?
  â†’ Make those contacts happen
  â†’ Update the row after each contact

Renewal pipeline view (filter by Renewal Month):
  September renewals: who needs contact now?
  October renewals:   who needs contact in 3 weeks?

Signals that a sponsor relationship is cooling:
  â†’ No response to two consecutive outreach attempts
  â†’ "Talk to [different person]" (your contact has changed)
  â†’ Changed company email domain (acquisition or reorganization)
  â†’ Last contact date > 5 months ago with no scheduled next action
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A sponsor hasn't responded to two outreach attempts. What should the CRM record reflect?",opts:["Mark them as lost and remove","Update Last Contact with the attempt dates, set Next Action to try a different contact method or person in 3 weeks, and note 'non-responsive' â€” don't remove until you've exhausted options","No update needed until they respond","Move them to a cold list"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"fi_matching",title:"Corporate Matching Gift Programs",est:"9 min",content:`## Your Sponsors' Employers May Double Their Gift
Thousands of companies have matching gift programs â€” they'll match employee donations to nonprofits dollar-for-dollar. A parent who donates $500 personally might trigger another $500 from their employer. Most families don't know to ask.

## How Matching Gifts Work
\`\`\`
Process:
  1. An employee (parent, alumni, supporter) makes a donation to your team
  2. They submit a matching gift request through their employer's HR portal
  3. The company verifies your eligibility (usually requires 501c3 or school status)
  4. The company sends a matching check directly to your team

Common matching ratios:
  1:1 (most common): $500 donation â†’ $500 match â†’ $1,000 total
  2:1 (more generous): $500 donation â†’ $1,000 match â†’ $1,500 total

Common matching gift companies:
  Microsoft, Google, Apple, Boeing, Lockheed, most major banks,
  most large healthcare systems, many law firms

Maximum match limits: usually $1,000-10,000/year per employee
\`\`\`

## Activating Matching Gifts on Your Team
\`\`\`
In every donation acknowledgment/thank-you:
  "If your employer offers matching gifts, your donation could be doubled.
   Check with your HR department or visit [company portal].
   Our EIN is [your EIN] for employer verification."

At parent meetings (September):
  â†’ "We'd like to ask: does anyone's employer offer matching gifts?
     If so, we can help you through the process."

Track matches in your CRM: add a column for "Matching Gift Potential"
When a donor says they work at Microsoft or Google â†’ flag immediately.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What information does an employer typically need to verify a matching gift request?",opts:["A copy of your engineering notebook","Your organization's EIN and proof of 501(c)(3) or school status","A letter from FIRST headquarters","A list of team members"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.fundraising.Advanced.push(
  {id:"fa_capital",title:"Capital Campaigns â€” Raising for Equipment or Facility",est:"12 min",content:`## One-Time Big Goals Need a Different Strategy
Annual fundraising pays for operations. A capital campaign raises money for something specific and significant â€” a new CNC router, a dedicated build space, a trailer. The goal is defined, the timeline is finite, and donors give because of the specific outcome.

## Capital Campaign Structure
\`\`\`
Pre-campaign (2-3 months before public launch):
  â†’ Define exactly what you're raising for and why
  â†’ Set a specific dollar goal with a specific deadline
  â†’ Secure 40-60% of the goal from major donors before going public
    (This is called the "quiet phase" â€” campaigns that launch publicly at 0%
     rarely reach goal; campaigns that launch at 50% almost always do)

Public launch:
  â†’ Announce the goal, what you've already raised, and what remains
  â†’ "We're raising $18,000 for a laser cutter. We've raised $9,500 so far."
  â†’ Momentum is visible â€” donors join something moving, not something static

Campaign close:
  â†’ Hard deadline creates urgency (December 31, end of summer)
  â†’ Final push: "48 hours left, $2,200 to go"
\`\`\`

## Why the Quiet Phase Works
\`\`\`
Psychology of giving to campaigns:
  â†’ People give to success, not to need
  â†’ "We're at $9,500 of $18,000" feels achievable; donors feel they're closing a gap
  â†’ "We're at $0 of $18,000" feels overwhelming; donors wonder if it'll succeed
  â†’ A campaign at 50% raised is 3-4Ã— more likely to reach goal than one at 0%

Quiet phase donors:
  â†’ Your most committed supporters (mentors, parents, alumni)
  â†’ Make the ask personally, not by mass email
  â†’ "I'm calling you first because I want you to be part of the founding group
     for this campaign before we announce it publicly."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What percentage of the goal should ideally be raised in the quiet phase before public launch?",opts:["10-20%","At least 40-60%","80-90%","Any amount"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ AWARDS +5 â”€â”€
LESSONS.awards.Beginner.push(
  {id:"awb_safety2",title:"Safety Award â€” What Actually Wins It",est:"9 min",content:`## Safety Award Is Not About Having Rules Posted on a Wall
Every team has safety glasses and a first aid kit. The Safety Award goes to teams with a safety culture â€” where members internalize why safety matters, not just what the rules say. Judges look for evidence of culture, not compliance theater.

## Safety Award Criteria
\`\`\`
What judges observe:
  â†’ Safety captain who explains the "why" behind each rule, not just the rule
  â†’ Members other than the safety captain who can answer safety questions
  â†’ Evidence of safety training: orientation records, signed acknowledgments
  â†’ Pit organization: PPE accessible, no tripping hazards, wires managed
  â†’ Robot on field: drive team with safety glasses, controlled power-down procedure

What judges are not impressed by:
  â†’ Safety poster (every team has one)
  â†’ Safety captain who clearly memorized a script
  â†’ Rules that are stated but visibly not followed in the pit

Strong safety award signals:
  â†’ A non-safety-captain member who demonstrates safety knowledge unprompted
  â†’ An incident log (shows the team takes near-misses seriously)
  â†’ A documented training process with records
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Which of these most impresses a Safety Award judge?",opts:["A laminated safety poster in the pit","A member who isn't the safety captain explaining why a rule exists","A complete first aid kit","Perfect PPE compliance during robot demos"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"awi_impact_data",title:"Quantifying Impact â€” Numbers That Mean Something",est:"11 min",content:`## Judges Can't Evaluate What They Can't Measure
"We reached hundreds of students" is meaningless. "We reached 847 students across 18 events with an average engagement of 90 minutes per student" is evidence. Impact Award submissions that win at championship level provide specific, verifiable numbers â€” and explain what those numbers mean.

## Metrics Hierarchy for Impact Submissions
\`\`\`
Tier 1 (strongest â€” outcome metrics):
  â†’ FLL teams still active 2 years after we started them: 3 of 3
  â†’ Teachers who continued robotics programs independently: 4
  â†’ Students who joined FRC/FTC through our outreach: 12

Tier 2 (solid â€” activity metrics with context):
  â†’ Students reached: 847 (across 18 events, average 47 students/event)
  â†’ Total contact hours: 1,200 (average 1.4 hours/student)
  â†’ Schools with active programs we supported: 6 of 8 contacted

Tier 3 (weak â€” breadth without depth):
  â†’ "Over 500 students"
  â†’ "Multiple events"
  â†’ "Significant community impact"
\`\`\`

## Connecting Numbers to Meaning
\`\`\`
Numbers alone don't make the case â€” interpretation does:

Weak: "We reached 847 students."

Strong: "We reached 847 students this season â€” 73% from Title I schools,
  representing communities historically underrepresented in engineering.
  Of the 18 events, 6 were sustained programs (3+ sessions) rather
  than one-time demonstrations, producing 340 students with 3+ hours
  of engagement â€” the threshold where interest becomes skill."

The second version uses the same number but tells a story of deliberate equity
focus and distinguishes meaningful engagement from passive attendance.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What makes 'contact hours' a better metric than 'students reached'?",opts:["Contact hours are easier to count","It captures depth â€” a student who attended a 3-hour camp and a student who watched a 5-minute demo both count as 'reached'; contact hours reveal whether engagement was substantive","Judges prefer time-based metrics","Students reached is inaccurate"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"awi_essays",title:"Writing the Impact Award Essay â€” Structure and Flow",est:"12 min",content:`## The Essay Is a Narrative, Not a List
Award essays that win tell a story with a beginning, a problem, an approach, and evidence of change. Submissions that don't win are formatted as bullet-point capability lists. Both contain the same information; only one is remembered.

## Impact Essay Structure (750-1000 words typical)
\`\`\`
Opening paragraph â€” The hook:
  Start with a specific scene, not a mission statement.
  "In February 2024, a 4th grader at Jefferson Elementary asked our student
   lead why she studied robotics. The answer she gave â€” and what happened
   when that student heard it â€” is the story of what Team 1234 is building."

Second section â€” The problem you're solving:
  â†’ What gap exists in your community?
  â†’ Why does it matter? (one specific data point)
  â†’ Why is your team positioned to address it?

Third section â€” What you do (programs):
  â†’ Name 2-3 flagship programs
  â†’ For each: name, scale, what specifically happens, one outcome
  â†’ Don't list every event â€” curate to the most impactful

Fourth section â€” Evidence of change:
  â†’ Outcome metrics (tier 1 and 2 from previous lesson)
  â†’ One specific person's story (with permission)
  â†’ Sustainability evidence: what continues without you?

Closing paragraph â€” Forward:
  â†’ Where is the program going next year? (one sentence)
  â†’ What does your team's continued work mean for the community?
  â†’ End with the same emotional register as the opening

What to cut:
  â†’ Team history that predates the last 2 seasons
  â†’ Robot performance and competition results
  â†’ Anything that's about the team, not about the community
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why should the essay open with a specific scene rather than a mission statement?",opts:["Mission statements are clichÃ©d","Specific scenes create emotional engagement before logical argument â€” readers who are invested in a story absorb evidence differently than readers who are evaluating claims; a 4th grader asking a question is remembered; 'we believe in inspiring the next generation' is not","Opening scenes are shorter","Mission statements are too formal"],ans:0},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.awards.Advanced.push(
  {id:"awa_multi2",title:"Managing Multiple Award Submissions at One Event",est:"10 min",content:`## Most Teams Undersubmit. Top Teams Enter Everything Relevant.
An Impact team that also has a Control-worthy programming system and a Safety-worthy culture should be submitting for all three. Awards don't conflict. Submitting for multiple awards isn't arrogant â€” judges evaluate each independently.

## Which Awards to Target
\`\`\`
Assess your team honestly against each award's criteria:

Always available (no submission required â€” observation only):
  â†’ Gracious Professionalism, Imagery, Spirit â€” judges observe all day

Submit if you have genuine program (written submission):
  â†’ Impact/Chairman's: strong outreach + advocacy program
  â†’ Engineering Inspiration: strong STEM outreach focus (different angle than Impact)
  â†’ Safety: documented safety culture
  â†’ Rookie awards (if eligible): competitive within rookies, not all teams

Robot-based (may require judges to see specific capability):
  â†’ Control Award: vision/autonomous/control system depth
  â†’ Innovation in Control: novel technical approach
  â†’ Excellence in Engineering: elegant design process

Dean's List: up to 2 nominees regardless of other submissions
\`\`\`

## Submission Logistics
\`\`\`
Most events:
  â†’ Submissions due before or early Day 1 (check event-specific rules)
  â†’ Digital: submit via FIRST's event system
  â†’ Physical: some events want printed copies â€” bring 3

Scheduling judge interviews:
  â†’ Impact interview: usually 10 minutes, scheduled Day 1
  â†’ Be at your pit, in uniform, all morning on Day 1
  â†’ Have 2-3 specific students assigned and briefed for each award type

Day-of coordination:
  â†’ One student owns the submission tracking list
  â†’ Check: "have we been visited for each award we submitted for?"
  â†’ If not visited by 2pm: ask the judge coordinator â€” not a complaint,
    just a check that your submission was received
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"If you haven't been visited for an award by mid-afternoon, what's the right action?",opts:["Assume you weren't selected and move on","Submit again","Ask the judge coordinator to confirm your submission was received","Send a student to find a judge"],ans:2},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ OUTREACH +5 â”€â”€
LESSONS.outreach.Beginner.push(
  {id:"orb_recruitment",title:"Converting Outreach Attendees Into Team Members",est:"10 min",content:`## A Demo That Doesn't Recruit Is Half a Demo
Every student who watches your robot and thinks "I want to do that" is a potential team member. Most teams let them walk away. A conversion-focused outreach event captures that moment with a specific, low-friction next step.

## The Conversion Funnel
\`\`\`
Interest â†’ Information â†’ Action â†’ Follow-through

Interest (they're already here â€” you caught it):
  â†’ They asked a question, stayed after the demo, or asked to try the controller

Information (give them exactly what they need):
  â†’ When do you meet? (specific day, time, room)
  â†’ Who do you contact? (name + contact, not just "find us")
  â†’ What happens at the first meeting? (answer "what am I walking into?")
  â†’ Cost? (honestly: "we try to keep participation free; some teams ask for a small fee")

Action (get a commitment before they leave):
  â†’ Sign-up sheet: name + phone/email right now
  â†’ QR code to a form they fill out on their phone while standing there
  â†’ NOT: "look us up online" â€” this rarely converts

Follow-through (you do the work):
  â†’ Contact every signup within 48 hours
