  â†’ "Hey [name], you signed up at [event]. We meet Thursdays at 3:30 in Room 214.
     Can we expect you this week?"
  â†’ Personal texts convert better than group announcements
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is 'look us up online' an ineffective call to action at outreach events?",opts:["Young people don't search online","It requires the student to take a self-directed action later, after the excitement of the event has faded â€” capturing contact info on-site converts the interest while it's present","Online searches don't find team pages","It's too vague"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ori_curriculum2",title:"Building a Reusable Curriculum",est:"11 min",content:`## A Curriculum You Built Once Gets Used 40 Times
A one-time robot demo requires prep every time. A curriculum package â€” activities, instructions, materials list, facilitator guide â€” can be run by any team member, handed to a teacher, or delivered at any event with 30 minutes of setup.

## Curriculum Package Components
\`\`\`
For a 60-minute robotics activity:

Student worksheet (1 page):
  â†’ Challenge statement: "Build a structure that holds a 250g weight using only..."
  â†’ Design constraint list
  â†’ Sketch box (they draw before they build)
  â†’ Test results table
  â†’ Reflection: "What would you change if you had 10 more minutes?"

Facilitator guide (2-3 pages):
  â†’ Learning objectives (what students should understand by the end)
  â†’ Materials per group
  â†’ Timing breakdown (build: 20 min, test: 10 min, present: 10 min, debrief: 10 min)
  â†’ Common questions and answers
  â†’ Safety notes
  â†’ How to debrief (what questions to ask the whole group)

Materials kit list:
  â†’ Exact quantities for a group of 20
  â†’ Sourcing: where to buy each item and cost
  â†’ Storage: how to pack it for reuse

What makes it reusable:
  â†’ Any team member can facilitate after reading the guide
  â†’ A teacher can run it without any team present
  â†’ Materials reset in 15 minutes for the next group
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What makes the facilitator guide the most important component of a reusable curriculum?",opts:["It contains the answer key","It lets anyone run the activity without prior knowledge â€” without it, the curriculum only works when a specific expert is present","It documents the learning outcomes","Facilitator guides are required for grants"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.outreach.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ora_ecosystem",title:"Building a Regional STEM Ecosystem",est:"13 min",content:`## The Best Teams Don't Just Run Programs â€” They Build Infrastructure
An ecosystem approach means every program you create builds capacity that outlasts you: trained teachers, seeded FLL teams, connected organizations, and a regional community where STEM programs help each other. This is what Judges' Award-level Impact programs look like.

## Ecosystem vs Program Thinking
\`\`\`
Program thinking: "We run a robotics camp."
  â†’ You deliver the program
  â†’ If your team doesn't show up, the program doesn't happen
  â†’ Impact scales with your team's capacity (bounded)

Ecosystem thinking: "We build robotics capacity in our region."
  â†’ You train others to run programs
  â†’ Programs continue and grow without your presence
  â†’ Impact scales with the capacity of everyone you've trained (unbounded)

Ecosystem markers:
  â†’ Teachers who train other teachers (you're two levels removed)
  â†’ FLL teams that mentor younger FLL teams
  â†’ A local robotics coordinator role at a school district, created partly
    because of your advocacy
  â†’ Programs at schools you've never visited, because someone you trained started them
\`\`\`

## The Ecosystem Investment Timeline
\`\`\`
Year 1: build your own programs (learn what works)
Year 2: document and systematize what works (curriculum, playbooks)
Year 3: start training others (hand off the playbooks, observe first runs)
Year 4: support others running it (consultant role, not operator)
Year 5: others are training others (you're two generations removed)

This is a multi-year commitment. Most teams don't get past Year 2.
Championship-level Impact teams are typically in Year 4-5.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What distinguishes ecosystem impact from program impact for award judges?",opts:["Ecosystem programs are larger","Ecosystem programs continue and multiply after the team stops running them â€” the test is whether removing your team from the region reduces STEM access; if trained teachers, independent FLL teams, and seeded organizations persist, the ecosystem is real","Ecosystem impact is easier to measure","Award judges don't distinguish them"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ SAFETY +4 â”€â”€
LESSONS.safety.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sfb_chemicals",title:"Chemical Safety in the Robot Shop",est:"9 min",content:`## Adhesives, Lubricants, and Solvents Are Hazardous
Loctite, WD-40, acetone, spray paint, and cutting fluid are all in most robot shops. Used correctly, they're safe. Used without ventilation, near ignition sources, or without understanding their hazards, they're serious risks.

## Common Shop Chemicals and Their Hazards
\`\`\`
Loctite threadlocker (cyanoacrylate base):
  Hazard: skin/eye irritant; bonds skin in seconds
  PPE: gloves; if eye contact, flush immediately and seek medical attention
  Never: apply near the face or with bare fingers

Acetone (nail polish remover, parts cleaner):
  Hazard: highly flammable; vapors heavier than air; can accumulate at floor level
  PPE: gloves, eye protection; use only in ventilated area
  Never: use near open flame, pilot lights, or sparks

Spray paint / primers:
  Hazard: flammable propellant; inhaled particles
  PPE: N95 mask minimum; use outdoors or in a spray booth
  Never: spray indoors without exhaust ventilation

Cutting fluid (used with metal working):
  Hazard: skin sensitizer with repeated exposure; slip hazard if spilled
  PPE: gloves for extended contact
  Storage: sealed container; keep away from electrical equipment

General rules for all chemicals:
  â†’ Read the SDS (Safety Data Sheet) before first use
  â†’ Store flammables away from ignition sources
  â†’ Never store chemicals in food/drink containers
  â†’ Dispose of chemical rags in a covered metal bin
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why are acetone vapors dangerous even when you're not directly inhaling from the container?",opts:["Acetone has a strong odor warning","Vapors are heavier than air and accumulate at floor level â€” an ignition source (power strip, motor) at floor level can ignite the accumulated vapor even if the open container is several feet away","Acetone evaporates very slowly","All solvents have the same vapor risk"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sfb_hand_tools",title:"Safe Use of Common Hand Tools",est:"9 min",content:`## Hand Tool Injuries Are the Most Common Shop Injuries
Cuts from slipping screwdrivers, crushed fingers from wrenches, punctures from improper knife use â€” these are the most frequent injuries in robotics shops. Most happen because the tool slips or the hand is in the path of the tool.

## Rule for Every Hand Tool: Control the Path of Failure
\`\`\`
Before using any hand tool, ask: if this tool slips, where does it go?
Your hand must not be in that path.

Screwdrivers:
  â†’ Work on a table, not in your lap
  â†’ Brace the workpiece â€” don't hold it in one hand and drive with the other
  â†’ If it slips: it goes forward into empty air, not into your palm

Box cutters / utility knives:
  â†’ Always cut away from your body
  â†’ Retract the blade immediately after each cut
  â†’ Change blades before they're dull â€” dull blades require more force and slip more

Wrenches:
  â†’ Pull toward you, don't push away â€” if it slips, your hand goes toward you, not into hardware
  â†’ Use the right size â€” an oversized wrench slips off at higher force
  â†’ Never use a wrench with worn jaws on a rounded fastener

Chisels and punches:
  â†’ Hold the workpiece in a vise, not your hand
  â†’ Strike straight â€” a glancing blow deflects the tool
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why do you pull a wrench toward you rather than push it away?",opts:["Pulling provides more torque","If it slips, your hand moves toward you rather than into sharp hardware on the other side","It's easier on your wrist","Pushing can strip the fastener"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"sfi_robot_ops",title:"Safe Robot Operation at Practice and Competition",est:"10 min",content:`## A 120lb Robot at Full Speed Is a Hazard
FRC robots weigh up to 125 lbs and can move at 15+ feet per second. At practice, familiarity breeds complacency. Most robot-related injuries happen to experienced team members who stopped treating the robot as a hazard.

## The Enable/Disable Protocol
\`\`\`
Before enabling the robot:
  â–¡ Call out: "Enabling!" â€” loud enough for everyone in the room to hear
  â–¡ Wait 3 seconds after calling out before pressing enable
  â–¡ Confirm all non-essential personnel are behind the robot's safety perimeter
  â–¡ Driver station operator is the only person who enables

While enabled:
  â†’ No one enters the robot's work envelope
  â†’ If someone must approach: disable first, then approach
  â†’ "Disabling!" is called before disabling, same as enabling

Never:
  â†’ Enable without calling out
  â†’ Enable while someone is adjusting or touching the robot
  â†’ Leave the robot enabled and unattended for any reason

Emergency stop:
  â†’ E-stop button on driver station disables immediately
  â†’ All team members should know where the E-stop is
  â†’ In doubt: E-stop, then investigate
\`\`\`

## Battery Safety at Practice
\`\`\`
Before connecting a battery:
  â†’ Inspect terminals â€” no corrosion, no cracks in housing
  â†’ Confirm main breaker is in the OFF position before connecting
  â†’ Secure the battery before connecting â€” it must not be able to shift

After disconnecting:
  â†’ Set aside to cool if it was under heavy load (warm battery = normal;
    hot battery = overloaded, needs inspection before reuse)
  â†’ Never leave a disconnected battery with terminals exposed â€” cover them
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is a 3-second wait required after calling 'Enabling!' before actually enabling?",opts:["It's an FRC rule","It gives everyone in the area time to clear the robot's path after hearing the warning â€” the call alone doesn't make anyone safe; the pause is what makes the call useful","The robot initializes during those 3 seconds","It prevents radio interference"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ GIT +5 â”€â”€
LESSONS.git.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"gi_rebase2",title:"Rebase vs Merge â€” When to Use Each",est:"11 min",content:`## Both Integrate Changes. The History They Leave Is Different.
Merge preserves the exact branching history â€” you can see exactly when a feature branch diverged and when it came back. Rebase replays your commits on top of the new base â€” the history looks linear, as if the feature was developed after the base changes.

## Side-by-Side Comparison
\`\`\`
Starting state:
  main:    A - B - C
  feature:     D - E (branched from B)

After: git merge main (from feature branch)
  main:    A - B - C
  feature:     D - E - M  â† merge commit M, preserves both histories

After: git rebase main (from feature branch)
  main:    A - B - C
  feature:         D'- E' â† D and E replayed on top of C, new hashes

\`\`\`

## When to Use Each
\`\`\`
Use merge:
  â†’ Merging a completed PR into main (keeps a clear record of the feature)
  â†’ Shared branches â€” never rebase commits others have already pulled
  â†’ When the branching history is meaningful to preserve

Use rebase:
  â†’ Updating a feature branch with main's latest changes before a PR
  â†’ Cleaning up local commits before pushing (not yet shared)
  â†’ Keeping history linear on a small team that prefers it

The Golden Rule of Rebase:
  Never rebase commits that exist on a remote branch others have pulled.
  Rebasing changes commit hashes â€” their clones diverge and can't reconcile normally.
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"After rebasing a feature branch, why do the commits get new hashes (D' and E') even if the code is identical?",opts:["Rebase compresses commits","A commit hash includes its parent's hash â€” D' has C as its parent instead of B, so even if the diff is identical, the hash is different","Hashes always change after merge","The rebase modifies the code slightly"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"gi_reflog",title:"git reflog â€” Recovering Anything",est:"9 min",content:`## Nothing Is Permanently Gone for 30 Days
git log shows your current branch's history. git reflog shows everywhere HEAD has been â€” including commits that were reset away, branches that were deleted, and stash pops that went wrong.

## Reading the Reflog
\`\`\`bash
git reflog
# Output:
# a3f92b1 HEAD@{0}: commit: fix(arm): correct encoder scaling
# 7c44d02 HEAD@{1}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
# 4f18e3a HEAD@{2}: commit: feat(vision): add AprilTag
# 9b2d5c1 HEAD@{3}: commit: wip: testing

# HEAD@{1} shows you moved HEAD via reset
# 4f18e3a and 9b2d5c1 are now "unreachable" â€” not in any branch
# But they're still in the object database
\`\`\`

## Recovery Patterns
\`\`\`bash
# Recover a commit that was reset away:
git checkout 4f18e3a        # detached HEAD at that commit
git switch -c recovered-vision  # make it a real branch

# Undo a bad reset (get back to before the reset):
# You did: git reset --hard HEAD~2 (lost commits 4f18e3a and 9b2d5c1)
# Reflog shows HEAD@{1} was at 4f18e3a before the reset
git reset --hard 4f18e3a   # go back to that state

# Recover a deleted branch:
git branch recovered-feature 7c44d02  # re-create branch at that commit
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does git reflog show that git log does not?",opts:["All commits across all branches","Every position HEAD has been, including commits no longer reachable from any branch","Remote branch history","Uncommitted changes"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.git.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ga_submodules",title:"Git Submodules for Shared Code Libraries",est:"11 min",content:`## One Repository Inside Another
Your FRC team has a vision library used by both the competition robot and the off-season practice bot. You want to develop it in one place and use it in multiple repos. Git submodules let you embed one repository inside another â€” the parent repo knows which commit of the submodule to use.

## Adding and Using a Submodule
\`\`\`bash
# Add the vision library as a submodule:
git submodule add https://github.com/team1234/vision-lib libs/vision
# Creates: libs/vision/ (checked out at the library's latest commit)
# Creates: .gitmodules file (records the mapping)

# Commit the submodule addition:
git add .gitmodules libs/vision
git commit -m "chore: add vision-lib as submodule"

# Cloning a repo with submodules:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/team1234/robot2025
# Without --recurse-submodules: libs/vision/ is empty

# Updating to the latest submodule commit:
cd libs/vision
git pull origin main
cd ../..
git add libs/vision
git commit -m "chore: update vision-lib to latest"
\`\`\`

## The Tradeoff
\`\`\`
Submodules work well when:
  â†’ The shared code changes infrequently
  â†’ You want an explicit, pinned version in each project

Submodules are painful when:
  â†’ The shared code changes frequently (constant update commits)
  â†’ Team members forget --recurse-submodules and get empty directories
  â†’ You need to make changes to the library from inside the parent repo

Alternatives to consider:
  â†’ Copy the code (simple, no submodule overhead, but duplicated)
  â†’ Python/npm package (if the library has its own release cycle)
  â†’ Git subtree (merges history, no empty directory problem)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What happens if you clone a repo with submodules without --recurse-submodules?",opts:["The clone fails","Submodule directories exist but are empty â€” the submodule code is not fetched","The latest submodule code is fetched automatically","Only the .gitmodules file is missing"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT +4 â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Beginner.push(
  {id:"tmb_conflict2",title:"Resolving Team Conflict Early",est:"10 min",content:`## Small Conflicts Ignored Become Big Ones
A disagreement about mechanism design that's talked through in 20 minutes doesn't become a two-week tension that splits the subteam. Conflict avoidance isn't professionalism â€” it's a time bomb. The skill is addressing issues while they're still small.

## The Conflict Conversation
\`\`\`
When you notice a conflict (between two others or involving you):

Step 1: Address it privately, not publicly
  â†’ "Can we talk after the session? I want to understand something."
  â†’ Never: raise the disagreement in front of the whole team

Step 2: Start with curiosity, not accusation
  â†’ "I noticed tension when we were discussing the intake. What's your read on what happened?"
  â†’ NOT: "You interrupted [name] three times."
  â†’ Accusation creates defense; curiosity creates conversation

Step 3: State your concern specifically
  â†’ "When design discussions get heated, people stop sharing ideas.
     I want to make sure we're not losing good input because of how we disagree."

Step 4: Find one agreement
  â†’ You don't have to resolve everything in one conversation
  â†’ One thing you both agree matters: "we both want the robot to work"
  â†’ One behavior you both can commit to: "let people finish before responding"
\`\`\`

## When to Escalate
\`\`\`
Handle yourself:
  â†’ Disagreements about technical approach
  â†’ Communication friction between two people
  â†’ Hurt feelings from a misunderstanding

Escalate to a mentor:
  â†’ The conflict involves someone in a position of authority over the other
  â†’ Two conversations haven't resolved it
  â†’ The conflict is affecting the rest of the team's ability to work
  â†’ Any concern involving personal safety
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why address conflict privately rather than in front of the team?",opts:["Group feedback is less accurate","Public conflict resolution puts someone on the defensive in front of peers, making resolution harder â€” private conversations allow both people to speak honestly without the audience effect","Private conversations aren't documented","Team conflicts should involve everyone"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.teammanagement.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"tmi_planning",title:"Build Season Planning â€” The 6-Week Sprint",est:"12 min",content:`## A Plan Isn't a Prediction. It's a Tool for Staying Coordinated.
The build season plan will be wrong by Week 2. That's fine. A plan that's updated weekly based on reality is still far more useful than no plan â€” it keeps the team coordinated, surfaces problems early, and makes explicit what has to happen for the robot to be competition-ready.

## The Build Season Timeline Structure
\`\`\`
Week 1: Game analysis + design decisions
  â†’ Game manual released Saturday
  â†’ Days 1-2: identify scoring opportunities, constraints, RP structure
  â†’ Days 3-4: mechanism concepts, prototype priorities
  â†’ Day 6: mechanism selections made + prototyping begins
  â†’ Milestone: "we know what robot we're building"

Week 2: Prototype and validate
  â†’ Critical mechanisms prototyped with real game pieces
  â†’ Don't build final robot until prototype validates the approach
  â†’ Milestone: "intake works at target success rate"

Week 3: Full CAD + order materials
  â†’ Frame fully designed in CAD
  â†’ All long-lead parts ordered by Day 17
  â†’ Milestone: "frame is being cut"

Week 4: Build
  â†’ Frame assembled
  â†’ Primary mechanisms installed
  â†’ Electronics on robot
  â†’ Milestone: "robot drives and does the primary mechanism"

Week 5: Integration + programming
  â†’ Full autonomous routines working
  â†’ Drive practice begins
  â†’ Milestone: "robot can play a full match, even if rough"

Week 6: Polish, driver practice, bag (if applicable)
  â†’ Fix top 3 reliability issues
  â†’ 3 hours of driver practice minimum
  â†’ Milestone: "we're confident going to competition"
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why start driver practice in Week 5 rather than Week 6?",opts:["Week 6 is too late","A robot first driven in Week 6 has one week of practice; one first driven in Week 5 has two â€” driver skill compounds quickly in the first hours and significantly affects match performance","Week 5 robot is usually more stable","Week 6 is reserved for fixes only"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ CAD +4 â”€â”€
LESSONS.cad.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"cadi_motion2",title:"Motion Studies â€” Simulating Mechanism Movement",est:"11 min",content:`## Catch Collisions Before Metal Gets Cut
A motion study animates your assembly through its range of motion. It catches interference â€” two parts occupying the same space â€” before you discover it physically when the mechanism jams on the robot.

## Running a Motion Study in Onshape
\`\`\`
Prerequisites: mates must correctly define the mechanism's degrees of freedom
  â†’ An arm that pivots: Revolute mate at the pivot
  â†’ An elevator: Slider mate along the travel direction

Animation view:
  Assemblies â†’ Animation â†’ Add animation
  â†’ Select the revolute mate â†’ input angle over time
  â†’ Play the animation: does the arm sweep its full range?

Interference detection:
  Assemblies â†’ Interference â†’ select all bodies â†’ Run
  â†’ Highlights any volumes where parts overlap
  â†’ Run at multiple positions: 0Â°, 45Â°, 90Â°, 135Â° of arm travel

Common interference sources:
  â†’ Chain/belt running into frame tube at full extension
  â†’ Motor body hitting a cross member at one extreme
  â†’ Bumper zone: mechanism descends into bumper zone at stowed position
\`\`\`

## Design for Range of Motion
\`\`\`
Add hard stop geometry:
  â†’ Model the physical hard stop (bolt, tab, or plate)
  â†’ The mechanism's range in the motion study should match the hard stop range
  â†’ If the motion study shows 180Â° range but the hard stop is at 120Â°:
    either the hard stop model is wrong or the mechanism will slam into it

Document the range:
  â†’ In assembly properties or a note on the drawing:
    "Arm range: -10Â° (below horizontal) to 135Â° (vertical + 45Â°)"
  â†’ Drive team needs this number; control software limit switches need this number
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why run interference detection at multiple arm positions rather than just the fully extended position?",opts:["Multiple positions are required by Onshape","Interference can occur at intermediate positions that aren't the extremes â€” a chain may clear at 0Â° and 90Â° but contact a frame tube at 45Â°; checking only the extremes misses mid-travel collisions","Full extension is the most dangerous","Onshape only checks one position at a time"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.cad.Advanced.push(
  {id:"cada_thermal",title:"Thermal Analysis in CAD â€” Predicting Heat Problems",est:"12 min",content:`## Electronics That Overheat Lose Matches
A motor controller running at 150A generates significant heat. Stacked in a tight electronics bay with no airflow, it can thermal-throttle mid-match. A basic thermal analysis in CAD â€” or even a back-of-envelope heat dissipation calculation â€” identifies these risks before competition.

## Heat Dissipation Basics
\`\`\`
Power dissipated as heat in a motor controller at current I:
  P = IÂ² Ã— R_internal
  Example: REV Spark MAX, R â‰ˆ 0.003 Î©, running 80A
  P = (80)Â² Ã— 0.003 = 19.2 W per controller

Heat must go somewhere:
  â†’ Convection to surrounding air (requires airflow)
  â†’ Conduction to mounting surface
  â†’ Radiation (minor at robot operating temperatures)

Temperature rise (simplified):
  Î”T = P / (h Ã— A)
  where: h = convective heat transfer coefficient (~5-10 W/mÂ²K for natural convection)
         A = controller surface area in mÂ²

REV Spark MAX surface area â‰ˆ 0.005 mÂ²
With no airflow: Î”T â‰ˆ 19.2 / (5 Ã— 0.005) = 768Â°C â€” clearly wrong
That means: natural convection alone cannot dissipate 19.2W
Forced airflow (fan): h â‰ˆ 50-100 W/mÂ²K â†’ Î”T â‰ˆ 38-77Â°C â†’ manageable
\`\`\`

## Practical Thermal Design Rules
\`\`\`
For motor controllers running > 60A sustained:
  â†’ Minimum 10mm gap between stacked controllers
  â†’ Mount with the label face (heat spreader side) toward airflow
  â†’ If multiple high-current controllers: add a 12V computer fan (REV Blinkin can control it)

CAD thermal check:
  â†’ In the assembly, add a "thermal envelope" box around the electronics bay
  â†’ Calculate total watts: sum all motor controller worst-case dissipations
  â†’ If total > 50W and bay volume < 3L with no fan: flag as thermal risk

FEA thermal simulation (Onshape Pro / Solidworks):
  â†’ Apply heat loads to controller bodies
  â†’ Apply convection boundary conditions (natural: 5 W/mÂ²K, forced: 50 W/mÂ²K)
  â†’ Run steady-state thermal â†’ temperature distribution
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why does natural convection alone fail to cool a motor controller at 19.2W?",opts:["19.2W is too much power","The convective heat transfer coefficient for still air (5 W/mÂ²K) is too low â€” with the controller's small surface area, the thermal resistance is high and the steady-state temperature rise would exceed safe limits; forced airflow increases the coefficient 10-20Ã— and brings temperatures into a manageable range","Natural convection requires vertical mounting","Motor controllers don't generate heat at 80A"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€â”€ PACK 20 â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€â”€
// 1 quiz per lesson. Correct answer position and length varies.

// â”€â”€ ELECTRICAL +8 â”€â”€
LESSONS.electrical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"eb_fuses",title:"Fuses and Circuit Protection â€” Sizing It Right",est:"9 min",content:`## The Fuse Protects the Wire, Not the Device
A common misconception: pick a fuse based on what the device draws. Wrong. Pick the fuse based on the wire gauge. The fuse's job is to blow before the wire overheats and catches fire. A 40A fuse on 18 AWG wire (rated 16A) means the wire melts before the fuse blows.

## Wire Gauge vs Fuse Size
\`\`\`
AWG | Max continuous current | Max fuse size
 6  |       75A              |    60A
 8  |       50A              |    40A
10  |       35A              |    30A
12  |       25A              |    20A
14  |       20A              |    15A
16  |       13A              |    10A
18  |        9A              |     5-7A

FRC-specific:
  40A breaker slot in PDP/PDH:   use 10 AWG or thicker
  30A breaker slot:               use 12 AWG or thicker
  20A breaker slot:               use 14 AWG or thicker
  Motor controller signal wires:  no fuse needed (signal only, no power)
\`\`\`

## Common Mistakes
\`\`\`
Too large a fuse:
  20 AWG wire with a 20A fuse â†’ wire is rated 11A â†’ fire risk
  Fix: use 10A fuse or upgrade wire to 14 AWG

Too small a fuse:
  Motor drawing 15A peaks with a 10A fuse â†’ nuisance tripping
  Fix: confirm motor's peak current draw, upsize fuse (not wire)

Fuse in the wrong location:
  Fuse must be within 18" of the power source (PDP/PDH or battery)
  A fuse at the device end doesn't protect the long wire run to it
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A motor controller is wired with 12 AWG wire. What is the maximum fuse it should use?",opts:["30A","10A","20A","40A"],ans:2},
    ]},
  {id:"eb_grounds",title:"Grounding â€” Why Every Ground Matters",est:"9 min",content:`## A Missing Ground Doesn't Just Fail â€” It Causes Weird Behavior
A sensor that reads garbage, a motor controller that randomly cuts out, a robot that behaves differently when picked up versus on the ground â€” these are often grounding problems. Ground is the reference everything else is measured against. Without it, measurements drift.

## Ground Loops and Star Grounding
\`\`\`
Ground loop: two grounds connected at different points in the wiring with
  different resistances â†’ small voltage difference between them
  â†’ sensor reads voltage difference instead of the signal
  â†’ ADC values drift, encoder counts jump, IMU goes crazy

Star grounding: all grounds connect to one central point
  â†’ PDP/PDH negative terminal is the star
  â†’ Every device's ground wire runs back to that star
  â†’ No two devices share a ground path (no loops)

In FRC:
  â†’ PDP/PDH negative bus: the star
  â†’ All motor controllers: ground to PDP negative terminal strip
  â†’ Signal ground (roboRIO SIG GND): separate from power ground
    â†’ Never use power ground for signal ground on sensors
    â†’ RoboRIO has separate SIG GND pins â€” use them
\`\`\`

## Diagnosing Grounding Problems
\`\`\`
Symptoms: sensor reads wrong when motor runs, values stable with robot lifted
Tool: multimeter, DC millivolt range

Measure between two "ground" points on the robot while running motors:
  â†’ 0 mV: grounds are truly equal, no loop
  â†’ > 50 mV: ground loop â€” current through the ground path creating voltage

Fix: find the shared path and re-route one ground wire to run directly to PDP
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must sensor signal ground connect to RoboRIO SIG GND pins rather than power ground?",opts:["SIG GND has lower resistance","Power ground carries motor return currents that create voltage fluctuations â€” a sensor referenced to fluctuating power ground sees those fluctuations as signal noise; SIG GND is isolated from high-current paths","SIG GND is required by FRC rules","Sensors require more current than power ground provides"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.electrical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"ei_encoders",title:"Encoder Wiring and Troubleshooting",est:"11 min",content:`## An Encoder That Skips Counts Ruins Closed-Loop Control
A PID controller fed wrong encoder data oscillates, overshoots, or does nothing. Most encoder problems are wiring â€” wrong pin assignment, missing pull-up, too-long signal wire picking up noise.

## Encoder Types and Wiring
\`\`\`
Quadrature encoder (most FRC use):
  Pins: A, B, Ground, [+5V or +3.3V]
  â†’ A and B are 90Â° out of phase â€” direction is determined by which leads which
  â†’ Both channels required â€” missing B gives position but not direction

Hall effect encoder (built into REV Neo, Falcon 500):
  â†’ Internal â€” wired through the motor controller, not separately
  â†’ Do not rewire; do not extend without understanding signal levels

Absolute encoder (e.g. Rev Through Bore, CTRE CANCoder):
  â†’ Outputs position 0-360Â° on power-on (no homing required)
  â†’ Wiring: power + ground + signal (PWM, analog, or CAN depending on model)
  â†’ Mount directly to the mechanism pivot â€” not to the motor shaft through a gearbox
\`\`\`

## Troubleshooting Encoder Problems
\`\`\`
Symptom: position doesn't change when mechanism moves
  â†’ Check: is the encoder actually turning? (watch the encoder body)
  â†’ Check: continuity on A and B wires end-to-end
  â†’ Check: supply voltage at the encoder (5V or 3.3V per spec)

Symptom: position jumps or counts in wrong direction
  â†’ Swap A and B wires to reverse direction
  â†’ Check: signal wire length > 24" without shielding â†’ add twisted pair or shielded cable
  â†’ Check: signal wire runs parallel to motor power wires â†’ re-route perpendicular

Symptom: works on bench, fails on robot under load
  â†’ Motor power wires inducing noise on signal wires (EMI)
  â†’ Fix: route signal and power wires separated by > 1", or use shielded cable
  â†’ Fix: add 100nF ceramic capacitor between signal and ground at the RoboRIO pin
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must absolute encoders mount to the mechanism pivot rather than the motor shaft?",opts:["They are too heavy for motor shafts","A gearbox between the motor and mechanism means the motor shaft spins at a different ratio than the mechanism â€” the absolute position at the motor shaft does not reflect the mechanism's actual angle; mounting at the pivot reads the mechanism's true position directly","Motor shafts spin too fast","Absolute encoders only work on slow-moving axes"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ei_radio",title:"Robot Radio Configuration and Troubleshooting",est:"10 min",content:`## Communication Loss Disables the Robot. Know Why.
An FRC robot communicates through a radio (OpenMesh OM5P-AN or similar). A misconfigured, overheating, or physically loose radio causes the most common competition communication failures â€” and most are preventable.

## Radio Configuration
\`\`\`
Required before every competition:
  â†’ Download FRC Radio Configuration Utility (FIRST website)
  â†’ Connect laptop to radio via Ethernet
  â†’ Select team number â†’ program radio
  â†’ Radio SSID becomes: [team number]_[robot name or year]

What programming sets:
  â†’ Team number (driver station only connects to your team's radio)
  â†’ Channel (competition field management sets this at the event)
  â†’ Bandwidth limits (prevents interference with other teams)

Common mistake: radio programmed for practice, not reprogrammed before competition
  â†’ Field management can't connect to improperly configured radio
  â†’ Robot is disabled during matches = eliminated from that match
\`\`\`

## Radio Mounting and Power
\`\`\`
Power: radio must be powered from the VRM (Voltage Regulator Module), not directly from PDP
  â†’ VRM provides regulated 12V even when battery voltage drops under load
  â†’ Radio brownout from direct PDP power = communication loss during defense

Mounting:
  â†’ NOT on metal (signal attenuation)
  â†’ NOT inside an enclosed metal box
  â†’ Mount on polycarbonate or wood, in an open area
  â†’ LEDs must be visible (inspection requirement)
  â†’ Secure against vibration â€” loose radio = intermittent connection

Heat:
  â†’ Radio runs warm â€” ensure airflow around it
  â†’ Prolonged matches in hot pits: place a small fan nearby between matches
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why power the radio from the VRM instead of the PDP directly?",opts:["VRM is the only legal option","The VRM provides stable regulated voltage even when battery voltage sags under heavy motor load â€” a radio powered from the PDP loses power during heavy defense, causing the exact communication dropouts that disable the robot at the worst moments","VRM has a higher current limit","PDP ports don't fit radio connectors"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.electrical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ea_can3",title:"CAN Bus Topology and Fault Isolation",est:"12 min",content:`## One Bad Node Takes Down the Whole Bus
CAN (Controller Area Network) is a shared bus â€” all devices talk on the same two wires. A broken terminator, a damaged wire, or a device with a marginal transceiver can corrupt every message on the bus simultaneously. Understanding topology helps isolate faults fast.

## CAN Topology in FRC
\`\`\`
Correct topology: daisy chain with terminators at both ends
  RoboRIO â†’ device1 â†’ device2 â†’ ... â†’ deviceN â†’ terminator (120Î©)
  The RoboRIO's CAN port is the other termination point (built in)

Incorrect topologies (cause bus errors):
  Star (multiple wires from one junction): reflections â†’ errors
  Stub longer than 12": also causes reflections
  Missing terminator: signal doesn't absorb at the end, reflects back

Checking termination:
  Disconnect all power (robot off)
  Multimeter across CAN H and CAN L at the far end of the bus:
  â†’ 60Î©: correct (two 120Î© resistors in parallel)
  â†’ 120Î©: one terminator missing (or only one device present)
  â†’ <50Î©: extra terminator somewhere, or a device is damaged
  â†’ Open (infinite): wiring break somewhere
\`\`\`

## Fault Isolation Procedure
\`\`\`
Problem: some or all CAN devices not appearing in Driver Station

Step 1: Measure termination resistance (above)
Step 2: Check CAN wire continuity end-to-end (both H and L)
Step 3: Disconnect devices one at a time from the far end
  â†’ If removing device X makes the rest appear: device X has a bad transceiver
Step 4: Check for shorts between CAN H and CAN L
  â†’ Should be ~60Î©, not 0Î©
  â†’ 0Î© = short, find the damaged wire or connector

Driver Station CAN utilization > 90%:
  â†’ Too many messages on the bus, too fast
  â†’ Fix: increase update period for non-critical devices
    motor_controller.setPeriodicFramePeriod(PeriodicFrame.kStatus1, 100); // 100ms instead of default
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A multimeter across CAN H and CAN L reads 120Î© with the robot powered off. What does this indicate?",opts:["Correct termination","A short circuit","One terminator is missing or only one endpoint is terminated","The CAN bus has no devices on it"],ans:2},
    ]},
  {id:"ea_current",title:"Current Monitoring and Brownout Prevention",est:"11 min",content:`## A Robot That Brownouts Loses the Match
A brownout occurs when battery voltage drops below ~6.8V â€” the RoboRIO resets, disabling the robot mid-match. It happens when total current draw exceeds what the battery can supply. Current monitoring in code lets you see it coming and act before it happens.

## Reading Current in WPILib
\`\`\`java
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.PowerDistribution;
import edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.PowerDistribution.ModuleType;

PowerDistribution pdh = new PowerDistribution(1, ModuleType.kRev);

// In periodic():
double totalCurrent  = pdh.getTotalCurrent();   // amps, all channels
double channel4Amps  = pdh.getCurrent(4);       // one channel
double batteryVolts  = pdh.getVoltage();        // battery voltage

// Log to SmartDashboard for monitoring:
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Total Current", totalCurrent);
SmartDashboard.putNumber("Battery Voltage", batteryVolts);
\`\`\`

## Brownout Prevention Strategies
\`\`\`java
// 1. Current limiting on motor controllers (SparkMAX example):
sparkMax.setSmartCurrentLimit(40);  // stall limit 40A
sparkMax.setSecondaryCurrentLimit(60, 10); // peak 60A for 10ms max

// 2. Ramp rate: slow acceleration reduces inrush current spikes
sparkMax.setOpenLoopRampRate(0.25);  // 0.25 seconds from 0 to full speed
// A drivetrain that ramps to full in 0.25s instead of instantly
// can cut peak current draw by 30-40%

// 3. Voltage compensation: normalize output to a reference voltage
sparkMax.enableVoltageCompensation(12.0);
// Motor output is now relative to 12V â€” consistent regardless of battery state

// 4. Auto-reduce output when voltage is low:
if (batteryVolts < 10.5) {
    driveSubsystem.setMaxOutput(0.7);  // cap drivetrain at 70%
}
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does enableVoltageCompensation(12.0) do on a motor controller?",opts:["Limits the motor to 12V supply","Scales output so the motor behaves consistently as if battery voltage were always 12V â€” at 11V battery, a 100% command delivers proportionally more PWM duty cycle to compensate","Enables brownout protection","Reduces maximum current draw"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ STRATEGY +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.strategy.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sb_penalties",title:"Understanding Penalties and Avoiding Them",est:"9 min",content:`## Penalties Score Points for the Other Team
A foul gives 5 points to your opponents. A tech foul gives 15. A match where your alliance commits 4 tech fouls has spotted 60 points to the other side before the game starts. Understanding what triggers fouls and communicating this to drivers prevents easily avoidable losses.

## Common Foul Categories (FRC)
\`\`\`
Verify specifics in the current year's game manual â€” categories vary by game.

Typical foul sources:
  Entering protected zones:
  â†’ Most games define areas opponents cannot enter
  â†’ Drivers must know the exact zone boundaries
  â†’ Cost: technical foul (15 pts) or worse

  Pinning:
  â†’ Holding a robot against a wall or obstacle for > 5 seconds
  â†’ Penalty clock resets if you release before 5 seconds
  â†’ Pinning under driver station: often higher penalty

  Extending beyond frame perimeter illegally:
  â†’ Some games allow extension in certain conditions only
  â†’ Mechanisms that extend when they shouldn't: foul per occurrence

  Possessing more game pieces than allowed:
  â†’ Know the possession limit for the current game
  â†’ "Inadvertent" possession still counts

Pre-match briefing for drivers:
  Name the 3 fouls most likely to occur in this year's game.
  Have drivers repeat the rules back.
  "If you pin someone, what do you do?" â†’ "Back away before 5 seconds."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A driver pins an opponent at 4 seconds. What is the correct action?",opts:["Hold the pin for 1 more second for strategic value","Back away immediately â€” releasing before 5 seconds resets the penalty clock","The referee will call it regardless","Ask the human player for guidance"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sb_endgame2",title:"Endgame Planning â€” The Last 30 Seconds",est:"10 min",content:`## More Matches Are Won and Lost in the Last 30 Seconds Than Any Other Period
Endgame scoring (climb, park, balance) typically concentrates 20-40% of total match points into 30 seconds. Teams that plan their endgame positioning â€” where they are on the field, how long the action takes, who does what â€” consistently outperform teams that play endgame ad hoc.

## Endgame Planning Framework
\`\`\`
Know your numbers:
  â†’ How many seconds does your climb take, start to secured?
  â†’ How many seconds to drive from your typical teleop position to the climb zone?
  â†’ Buffer: add 3-5 seconds for variability

Example calculation:
  Climb takes 8 seconds. Drive to zone: 4 seconds. Buffer: 4 seconds.
  Start endgame positioning at: 30 - 8 - 4 - 4 = 14 seconds
  â†’ Drivers begin positioning at 0:16 remaining on the match clock

Pre-match alliance conversation:
  "We need to be at the [zone] by [time]. We'll call 'going for climb' on radio.
   Can you give us space / cover us at that time?"

What ruins endgame plans:
  â†’ One more scoring cycle that runs long
  â†’ Getting pinned in teleop position
  â†’ Alliance partner needing the same space at the same time
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A climb takes 10 seconds and the drive to the zone takes 5 seconds. When should the driver begin moving toward the zone?",opts:["20 seconds remaining","15 seconds remaining","With a 4-second buffer: 19 seconds remaining","30 seconds remaining"],ans:2},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.strategy.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"si_picklist2",title:"Building a Picklist â€” Methodology",est:"12 min",content:`## Alliance Selection Determines Your Elimination Bracket Before It Starts
The team you pick as your second robot determines your alliance's ceiling. A fast picklist process built on real data â€” not reputation or prestige â€” consistently outperforms teams picking on name recognition.

## The Picklist Build Process
\`\`\`
48 hours before alliance selection (or as soon as data is available):

Step 1: Define what your robot needs from a partner
  â†’ "We score well in teleop but struggle in auto. We need a 2-piece auto."
  â†’ "We have no climb. We need a partner who can climb L3+."
  â†’ Be specific â€” vague needs produce vague picks.

Step 2: Pull scouting data and filter for minimum requirements
  â†’ Filter out teams you know can't meet your minimum need
  â†’ Don't pick a team hoping they'll figure out climb by eliminations. They won't.

Step 3: Rank remaining teams by overall value
  â†’ Expected Points Added (EPA): what does adding this team do to your alliance's expected score?
  â†’ Consistency (standard deviation): a 38 avg with std dev 5 beats a 42 avg with std dev 14

Step 4: Watch matches for teams near the top of your list
  â†’ Scouting data is accurate on average; match observation catches outliers
  â†’ "Their data says 40 avg but I just watched them score 12. What happened?"

Step 5: Build the list in tiers
  â†’ Tier 1 (teams you'd be thrilled to have): 3-5 teams
  â†’ Tier 2 (solid picks): next 5-8
  â†’ Tier 3 (acceptable if top tiers are taken): everyone else
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is standard deviation an important metric alongside average score?",opts:["It shows team ranking","A high standard deviation means performance is unpredictable â€” in elimination matches where one bad match can end your run, a consistent 38-point average beats an unpredictable 42-point average because you can plan around the 38","Standard deviation predicts auto score","Lower standard deviation teams are easier to drive"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"si_elim2",title:"Elimination Match Strategy â€” Playing to Win the Series",est:"11 min",content:`## Elimination Is Best-of-3. Single-Match Thinking Gets You Eliminated.
A team that plays their highest-variance strategy (risky auto, aggressive offense) in every elimination match optimizes for individual match ceiling, not series wins. Playing to win the series means managing risk across three potential matches.

## Series Strategy Framework
\`\`\`
Match 1: play your standard game
  â†’ No exotic strategies â€” establish what you can execute reliably
  â†’ Win: go up 1-0; now you can afford some risk in match 2
  â†’ Loss: must win matches 2 and 3; reduce risk, increase reliability

Match 2 (up 1-0):
  â†’ You have a cushion â€” can attempt a slightly higher-value risky element
  â†’ Win: series won; risk was worth it
  â†’ Loss: tied 1-1; reset to standard strategy for match 3

Match 2 (down 0-1):
  â†’ Must win â€” risky plays only if you're losing late; otherwise standard game
  â†’ The team that panics and "tries something new" in elimination match 2
    after losing match 1 rarely wins the series

Match 3 (tied 1-1):
  â†’ Both teams go for it â€” but go for it with your strongest, most practiced auto
  â†’ Not the one you planned on trying at some point; the one you've run 50 times
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"After winning elimination match 1, how should your strategy in match 2 change?",opts:["Play more conservatively since you have the lead","Play identically to match 1","You can afford modest additional risk since a match 2 loss doesn't end the series","Always attempt your riskiest auto in match 2"],ans:2},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.strategy.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sa_opr",title:"OPR and EPA â€” Understanding Contribution Metrics",est:"13 min",content:`## Average Score Doesn't Measure Your Contribution
Two teams that each average 40 points per match might contribute very differently to their alliance â€” one is doing the work, the other is a passenger. OPR (Offensive Power Rating) and EPA (Expected Points Added) attempt to disaggregate alliance scores into individual contributions.

## How OPR Works
\`\`\`
OPR solves a system of equations:
  For each match: robot_A_opr + robot_B_opr + robot_C_opr = alliance_total_score

  With N matches, you have N equations and one unknown per team.
  Solve via least-squares regression â†’ best-fit OPR for each team.

Interpretation:
  OPR 45 means: adding that robot to a zero-OPR alliance is expected to contribute 45 pts.

Limitations:
  â†’ Assumes contributions are additive (not always true â€” synergies exist)
  â†’ Garbage in, garbage out: if a team plays with consistently bad alliances,
    their OPR is underestimated
  â†’ 6-match qualification schedule: too few equations, high variance in estimates

OPR is a starting point, not a verdict.
A team with OPR 35 that you scouted at 42 average: investigate why.
\`\`\`

## EPA (Statbotics)
\`\`\`
EPA improves on OPR by:
  â†’ Using historical data to initialize priors (not starting from zero)
  â†’ Separating auto, teleop, and endgame components
  â†’ Updating as the season progresses across all events

Reading EPA on statbotics.io:
  Total EPA: 52.3 â€” expected contribution to total alliance score
  Auto EPA: 14.1 â€” contribution during autonomous
  Teleop EPA: 31.8 â€” contribution during driver control
  Endgame EPA: 6.4 â€” contribution during endgame

Use case: finding teams whose OPR looks low but EPA is high
  â†’ They may be contributing more than raw scores show
  â†’ Or they played weak alliance partners who hurt their OPR

Combined use: OPR for current-event estimate + EPA for season-wide context
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A team has OPR 33 but their match-by-match scouting shows an average of 45 points. What likely explains the gap?",opts:["OPR is always lower than average","Their alliance partners have been weak â€” alliance total scores were low even when they contributed well; OPR distributes credit based on total alliance scores, so weak partners pull their OPR down even if their actual contribution is high","The scouting data is wrong","OPR only counts autonomous"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"sa_alliance_coord",title:"Alliance Coordination â€” Pre-Match Communication",est:"11 min",content:`## Three Robots Playing Three Different Plans Lose to a Coordinated Alliance
The three-minute queuing period is the only time all three alliance members can align on strategy. Teams that use it effectively â€” specific roles, specific field positions, specific contingencies â€” outperform teams whose pre-match conversation is "good luck."

## The 3-Minute Alliance Meeting Structure
\`\`\`
Minute 1: Introductions + capability check
  â†’ Each team states their best auto: "We do 2-piece auto, north side."
  â†’ Each team states their teleop role: "We're a cycle bot â€” 4-5 cycles/match."
  â†’ Climb: "We do L3. How long does it take you? 8 seconds. Us too."

Minute 2: Plan coordination
  â†’ "Which side do you want for auto? We'll take the other."
  â†’ "Do you need us to feed game pieces or are you self-sufficient?"
  â†’ "When should we all go for climb? We need 12 seconds from the zone."
  â†’ "If one robot breaks down in auto, what do we adjust?"

Minute 3: Confirmation + roles
  â†’ Summarize the plan in two sentences
  â†’ Each driver repeats their one specific role
  â†’ Radio check: "We're on channel 3. You?"
  â†’ "Any questions? No? Let's go."
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why ask opponents' climb timing rather than just your own?",opts:["Courtesy","All three robots climbing simultaneously requires coordinating arrival at the climb zone â€” if two teams need the same space at the same time, they block each other; knowing everyone's timing lets the alliance stagger arrival and maximize successful climbs","Timing affects scoring value","Referees track climb timing"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ SAFETY +5 â”€â”€
LESSONS.safety.Beginner.push(
  {id:"sfb_lift",title:"Safe Lifting Technique for Heavy Robot Parts",est:"8 min",content:`## Back Injuries Don't Happen at Competition. They Happen at the Shop.
A drivetrain base weighs 20-30 lbs. A fully assembled robot weighs up to 125 lbs. Lifting these incorrectly â€” especially repeatedly across a build season â€” causes cumulative back injury that can sideline a student for weeks.

## Correct Lifting Technique
\`\`\`
For any lift > 30 lbs:
  1. Plan the lift before starting
     â†’ Where does it go? Is the path clear?
     â†’ Do you need a second person?

  2. Get close to the load
     â†’ Your feet should be on either side of or next to the object
     â†’ Long reaches from the waist = high injury risk

  3. Bend at the knees, not the waist
     â†’ Squat down to the load
     â†’ Keep your back straight (not necessarily vertical â€” just not rounded)

  4. Grip firmly before lifting
     â†’ Test the weight before committing: slight lift to check balance

  5. Lift with your legs, keep the load close
     â†’ Straighten your knees; let your legs do the work
     â†’ Load stays against your body â€” not extended away from you

  6. Pivot with your feet, don't twist your torso
     â†’ To turn: move your feet first, then your body

For the full robot (125 lbs):
  â†’ Minimum 2 people (ideally 4 for a balanced robot lift)
  â†’ Designate one person as the coordinator: "Ready? Lift on three. One, two, three."
  â†’ Never lift a robot by its wiring or mechanisms â€” only by the frame
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the most important difference between correct and incorrect heavy lifting?",opts:["Wearing a back brace","Bending at the knees and keeping your back straight instead of bending at the waist â€” leg muscles can handle much more load than spinal erectors; back-bending transfers the load to small muscles not designed for it","Wearing gloves","Using both hands"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"sfi_mental",title:"Mental Health and Team Culture During Build Season",est:"10 min",content:`## Build Season Stress Is Real. Ignoring It Makes It Worse.
Six weeks of intense work, late nights, high stakes, and close quarters push people past their limits. Teams that treat mental health as a priority have fewer conflicts, better output, and members who come back next year. Teams that ignore it burn people out.

## Recognizing Stress Signals
\`\`\`
Individual signals (watch for these in team members):
  â†’ Withdrawing from team interactions they previously enjoyed
  â†’ Snapping at small things; low frustration tolerance
  â†’ Declining quality of work without obvious reason
  â†’ "I don't care anymore" language â€” about the robot or the team
  â†’ Missing sessions without previous pattern of missing

Team signals:
  â†’ Conflict frequency increasing week over week
  â†’ Fewer people volunteering for tasks
  â†’ Conversations that are usually energetic become terse
  â†’ Gallows humor about the robot that crosses into genuine hopelessness

What to do:
  â†’ Address individual signals privately: "You seem tired â€” how are you doing?"
  â†’ Team signals: raise at a lead meeting, not publicly; small schedule adjustments
    help more than motivational speeches
  â†’ Know when to tell a mentor: if someone expresses that they're struggling
    significantly, connect them with a trusted adult â€” don't handle it alone
\`\`\`

## Sustainable Build Season Practices
\`\`\`
Non-negotiables:
  â†’ Minimum 1 non-build day per week (usually Sunday)
  â†’ Sessions don't run past [time agreed at season start] without explicit opt-in
  â†’ Food at sessions longer than 3 hours

Culture practices that help:
  â†’ Celebrate small wins publicly ("intake hit 90% success rate today")
  â†’ Normalize "I need help" â€” builds trust faster than "I've got it"
  â†’ End each session with one thing that went well â€” not just what's left to do
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What does 'I don't care anymore' language most likely signal in a build season context?",opts:["The student is lazy","Emotional exhaustion â€” the student has been caring a lot and has hit a wall; this is a signal to check in privately, not to increase expectations or make it a team example","They're planning to quit","Disinterest in the specific mechanism they mentioned"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.safety.Advanced.push(
  {id:"sfa_culture2",title:"Safety Culture vs Safety Compliance",est:"11 min",content:`## Compliance Is What You Do When Someone's Watching. Culture Is What You Do When No One Is.
A team with safety compliance has rules posted on the wall and members who wear glasses when a mentor is nearby. A team with safety culture has members who remind each other before anyone asks â€” because they believe the rules matter, not because they fear consequences.

## The Four Levels of Safety Maturity
\`\`\`
Level 1: Reactive
  â†’ Safety rules exist because something bad happened
  â†’ Incidents are handled but not systematically prevented
  â†’ PPE compliance is enforcement-dependent

Level 2: Dependent
  â†’ Rules exist and are enforced
  â†’ Members comply when supervised
  â†’ Safety captain carries the whole program

Level 3: Independent
  â†’ Members follow rules without being watched
  â†’ Each person takes responsibility for their own safety
  â†’ Safety captain has support, not sole ownership

Level 4: Interdependent
  â†’ Members watch out for each other
  â†’ New members are corrected by peers, not just leads
  â†’ Safety is embedded in how work gets done, not added on top of it
  â†’ "We don't do that here" is said naturally, not as a rule recitation

Level 4 markers on your team:
  â†’ A member corrects a peer's PPE without being asked
  â†’ A new member asks about the safety procedure before starting a machine
  â†’ A near-miss is reported voluntarily, not because it was discovered
\`\`\`

## Moving From Compliance to Culture
\`\`\`
What doesn't work:
  â†’ More rules
  â†’ Stricter enforcement
  â†’ Safety "events" that don't connect to daily work

What does work:
  â†’ Explaining why each rule exists, once, genuinely
  â†’ Praising safety behavior publicly (not just punishing violations)
  â†’ Making safety visible in non-crisis moments
  â†’ The safety captain who says "I do this because I've seen what happens when you don't"
    is more influential than any posted rule
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What distinguishes Level 3 (Independent) from Level 4 (Interdependent) safety culture?",opts:["Level 4 has more rules","At Level 3 each person takes responsibility for themselves; at Level 4 members actively watch out for each other â€” a peer corrects PPE before a lead notices, and new members absorb norms through observation of existing members rather than through formal enforcement","Level 4 requires more training","Level 3 teams have better compliance"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ MECHANICAL +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.mechanical.Beginner.push(
  {id:"mb_measuring",title:"Precision Measurement in the Robot Shop",est:"9 min",content:`## A Part Made to the Wrong Dimension Wastes Material and Time
A bracket designed at 3.750" that's cut at 3.875" doesn't fit. Measurement tools are only useful if you know how to read them and which one to use for the required precision.

## Tool Selection by Precision Needed
\`\`\`
Tape measure (Â±1/16" = Â±1.6mm):
  â†’ Use for: layout lines, rough positioning, long dimensions
  â†’ Not for: hole locations, tolerance-critical dimensions

Combination square (Â±1/32" = Â±0.8mm):
  â†’ Use for: squaring cuts, short layout dimensions, 90Â° checks
  â†’ The blade slides â€” lock it at the measured distance, then scribe

Digital calipers (Â±0.001" = Â±0.025mm):
  â†’ Use for: shaft diameters, bearing bore checks, tight-clearance dimensions
  â†’ Read: outer jaws = outside diameter; inner jaws = inside diameter; depth probe = pocket depth
  â†’ Zero with jaws closed before measuring; re-zero if reading drifts

Micrometer (Â±0.0001"):
  â†’ Use for: shaft diameters requiring close tolerance fits (press fits, slip fits)
  â†’ Most FRC teams don't need this â€” calipers are sufficient

Feeler gauge:
  â†’ Use for: checking gap dimensions (chain slack, gear mesh, roller clearances)
  â†’ A set of thin metal strips at known thicknesses
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Which tool is appropriate for checking that a bearing bore is exactly 1.1250\"?",opts:["Tape measure","Combination square","Digital calipers","Ruler"],ans:2},
    ]},
  {id:"mb_finishes",title:"Surface Finishes and Coatings for Robot Parts",est:"9 min",content:`## Bare Aluminum Corrodes. Finished Aluminum Lasts.
Anodizing, powder coating, paint, and raw aluminum all have different tradeoffs for robot parts. The choice affects corrosion resistance, friction, electrical conductivity, and appearance.

## Common Finishes and Their Properties
\`\`\`
Raw (unfinished) aluminum:
  â†’ Pros: no cost, electrically conductive, easy to machine after
  â†’ Cons: oxidizes to dull gray over time, higher friction surface

Anodized aluminum:
  â†’ Process: electrochemical â€” converts surface to aluminum oxide
  â†’ Pros: hard, wear-resistant, corrosion-resistant, can be colored
  â†’ Cons: electrically non-conductive (breaks ground paths through structure)
  â†’ FRC use: decorative parts, arm tubes, non-electrical contact surfaces
  â†’ Note: anodized parts cannot be welded

Powder coat:
  â†’ Process: electrostatic powder + oven cure
  â†’ Pros: tough, colorful, good corrosion resistance
  â†’ Cons: adds ~0.003-0.005" per surface (affects fit dimensions), must be stripped for machining
  â†’ FRC use: bumper hardware, frame members not requiring close tolerance

Spray paint (rattle can):
  â†’ Pros: cheap, easy, immediate
  â†’ Cons: chips under impact, thin, poor durability
  â†’ FRC use: cosmetic touch-ups, non-load-bearing covers

Bare steel (not recommended for robot use):
  â†’ Rusts rapidly in humid competition environments
  â†’ If steel: use black oxide or galvanized steel instead
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why can anodized aluminum not be used for structural ground paths?",opts:["Anodizing is too soft","The anodizing process converts the surface to aluminum oxide, which is an electrical insulator â€” two anodized surfaces bolted together have no electrical connection through the structure, breaking any ground path that relies on chassis continuity","Anodized parts corrode faster","Anodizing adds too much weight"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.mechanical.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"mi_chain2",title:"Chain Drive Design and Tensioning",est:"12 min",content:`## A Loose Chain Skips. A Too-Tight Chain Destroys Bearings.
Chain drives transmit power with near-zero slip (unlike belts). The tradeoff: they require precise tensioning and regular adjustment. A chain that's slightly loose skips under load; one that's too tight preloads the bearings and generates heat.

## Chain Drive Design
\`\`\`
Selecting chain pitch:
  #25 chain: lightweight, used for low-torque systems (< 50 lb-in at sprocket)
  #35 chain: standard FRC use, moderate torque
  #35 HD (heavy duty): high-torque applications, drivetrain
  ANSI roller chain â€” always match chain pitch to sprocket pitch

Center-to-center distance calculation:
  Given: driver sprocket N1 teeth, driven sprocket N2 teeth, chain pitch P
  Initial estimate: C â‰ˆ (N1 + N2) / 4 Ã— P  (approximation)
  Exact: use online chain length calculator (input C, N1, N2, get chain links needed)
  â†’ Chain length must be an even number of links (to avoid an offset link)

Wrap angle:
  â†’ Driven sprocket should wrap at least 120Â° of chain
  â†’ Less than 120Â°: chain can jump off under reverse load
  â†’ Fix: add an idler sprocket to increase wrap
\`\`\`

## Tensioning Methods
\`\`\`
Method 1: Adjustable center distance (best)
  â†’ Slot the mounting holes of one sprocket along the chain line
  â†’ Slide sprocket to take up slack, re-tighten
  â†’ Correct tension: 1/4" total deflection at midspan with light finger pressure

Method 2: Tensioner sprocket (idler)
  â†’ Spring-loaded sprocket on the slack side presses against the chain
  â†’ Automatically compensates for wear
  â†’ Adds complexity and weight; necessary for long chain runs

Method 3: Half-link
  â†’ When chain is slightly too long: add a half-link (odd number of links) to reduce by half a pitch
  â†’ Not adjustable â€” requires removing if more adjustment needed

Too tight: chain feels stiff, bearing housing runs warm after 30 seconds of operation
Too loose: chain makes a slapping sound under load, visible deflection > 3/8" at midspan
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why must chain length be an even number of links when possible?",opts:["Even links are stronger","An even count allows the standard connecting link (which needs matching inner plates) to close the loop â€” odd links require an offset link which is weaker and thicker than the chain itself, a common failure point","Chain calculators only work with even numbers","Odd link chains are not manufactured"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"mi_gearbox2",title:"Gearbox Selection â€” Matching Motor to Mechanism",est:"12 min",content:`## Wrong Gear Ratio = Wrong Speed or Wrong Torque
A drivetrain geared too fast can't push. A drivetrain geared too slow can't win a race to a game piece. An arm geared too fast oscillates; too slow means you wait for it. Gear ratio selection is one of the highest-leverage design decisions.

## The Gear Ratio Calculation
\`\`\`
Free speed of mechanism:
  mechanism_rpm = motor_free_rpm / total_gear_ratio
  wheel_speed_fps = (mechanism_rpm Ã— wheel_circumference_ft) / 60

Example (drivetrain):
  NEO motor free speed: 5820 rpm
  Desired top speed: 14 fps (fast but controllable)
  Wheel diameter: 4" â†’ circumference: 0.1047 ft
  Required mechanism rpm: 14 / 0.1047 Ã— 60 = 8,024 rpm ... wait
  â†’ That's faster than the motor. Error in thinking.
  Recalculate: 14 fps = ? rpm at 4" wheel
  rpm = (fps Ã— 60) / (Ï€ Ã— diameter_ft) = (14 Ã— 60) / (Ï€ Ã— 0.333) = 800 rpm
  Gear ratio = motor rpm / mechanism rpm = 5820 / 800 = 7.3:1

Verify stall torque at mechanism:
  NEO stall torque: 3.28 NÂ·m
  At 7.3:1 ratio: 3.28 Ã— 7.3 = 23.9 NÂ·m per gearbox
  Two gearboxes: 47.8 NÂ·m pushing force at the wheel = ~100 lbs of pushing force
\`\`\`

## Standard Gearboxes vs Custom
\`\`\`
Standard (West Coast Products, REV, Andymark):
  â†’ Pre-built ratios, tested designs, documentation available
  â†’ WCP Swerve, REV MAXSwerve, WCP SS Gearbox: common choices
  â†’ Faster to build, known reliability, replace if broken

Custom planetary:
  â†’ More compact for a given ratio and torque
  â†’ REV Max Planetary: stackable stages, multiple ratio options
  â†’ Use when packaging is constrained

Custom spur/chain gearbox:
  â†’ Full flexibility in ratio
  â†’ Takes longer to design and validate
  â†’ Use when standard options don't fit your constraints
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"A mechanism needs to move slower (more torque, less speed). Should the gear ratio increase or decrease?",opts:["Decrease","Increase â€” a higher ratio reduces output speed and multiplies torque proportionally","Stay the same and change the motor","Gear ratio doesn't affect torque"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.mechanical.Advanced.push(
  {id:"ma_swerve2",title:"Swerve Drive Maintenance and Failure Recovery",est:"13 min",content:`## Swerve Is Fast and Complex. Know How to Fix It Under Pressure.
Swerve drive is the dominant FRC drivetrain for competitive teams. It's also the most complex â€” 8 motors, 8 encoders, 4 steering mechanisms. At competition, the team that can diagnose and fix a module failure in 20 minutes keeps playing. The one that can't is watching from the stands.

## Pre-Competition Swerve Checklist
\`\`\`
Each module (run before every competition, between events):
  â–¡ Drive wheel: no flat spots, secure to drive shaft (hub locking screw)
  â–¡ Steering gear: no play, mesh gap appropriate (just barely no backlash)
  â–¡ Absolute encoder: reads correct offset angle when module is zeroed
  â–¡ Drive motor: spins freely by hand, no grinding
  â–¡ Steer motor: holds position when powered, no oscillation at setpoint
  â–¡ All fasteners: check with appropriate torque driver for looseness
  â–¡ Cable management: no cables touching rotating parts, no tension on connectors
\`\`\`

## Failure Modes and Field Fixes
\`\`\`
Module steering oscillates (bouncing):
  â†’ Cause: usually steering PID kP too high or encoder offset wrong
  â†’ Field fix: lock the module straight with a mechanical stop (zip tie through
    the frame, not ideal but functional), drive as a tank with that module fixed

Module drive motor stops responding:
  â†’ Cause: loose CAN connector, overcurrent trip, motor failure
  â†’ Field fix: disable that module in code (set drive power to 0), drive 3-module
  â†’ Code: set moduleStates[n] = new SwerveModuleState(0, currentAngle);

Absolute encoder reads wrong offset:
  â†’ Cause: module was physically rotated during collision, encoder lost position
  â†’ Field fix: re-zero module offset in constants â†’ re-deploy code
  â†’ Prevention: record encoder offset values â†’ write them on a label on the module

Complete module failure:
  â†’ If can't fix in pit time: remove the module, bolt in a dead wheel (castoring)
  â†’ Robot becomes 3-wheel swerve (works, just slightly asymmetric)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"An absolute encoder reads the wrong offset after a collision. What is the fastest field fix?",opts:["Replace the encoder","Re-zero the module to its correct forward position, record the new encoder reading, update the constant in code, and redeploy â€” takes 5-7 minutes and restores full function without any hardware replacement","Disable steering for that module","Re-wire the encoder connector"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"ma_intake3",title:"Compliant Roller Design for Game Piece Intake",est:"12 min",content:`## The Intake That Works Every Time Wins
Intake reliability â€” picking up game pieces consistently across different angles, speeds, and field conditions â€” determines match cycle count more than any other mechanism. Compliant rollers (flexible material that deforms around the game piece) are the most forgiving intake approach.

## Why Compliance Matters
\`\`\`
Rigid rollers:
  â†’ Game piece must be exactly the right size for the gap
  â†’ Works perfectly when aligned, fails when slightly off
  â†’ Tolerates no variation in game piece geometry or approach angle

Compliant rollers (rubber, foam, Flex Wheels, silicone tubing):
  â†’ Deform around the game piece â†’ wider effective intake range
  â†’ Grips irregularly shaped pieces (notes, cubes, cargo) better
  â†’ Forgives Â±0.5" approach variation and Â±10Â° angle variation

Materials:
  Flex Wheels (Andymark): standard FRC choice, sold in different durometers
    â†’ 40A durometer: very soft, maximum compliance
    â†’ 60A durometer: balanced compliance and durability
  Silicone tubing over hex shaft: cheap, effective, easy to replace
  Stealth wheels: good grip, moderate compliance
  Closed-cell foam tubing: maximum compliance, lowest durability
\`\`\`

## Intake Roller Geometry
\`\`\`
Gap between rollers (or roller and floor):
  â†’ Should be ~80% of game piece diameter
  â†’ Too tight: game piece won't enter, stalls motor
  â†’ Too loose: game piece falls through without gripping

Roller surface speed:
  â†’ Match surface speed to desired intake speed (not motor RPM)
  â†’ surface_speed = Ï€ Ã— roller_diameter Ã— RPM
  â†’ Intake RPM typically 1000-2500 RPM at the roller â†’ select gear ratio accordingly

Multiple roller stages:
  â†’ Single roller: works for low-speed intake
  â†’ Double roller (staged): second roller takes over as first passes the piece
  â†’ Reduces dead zones where piece has partially entered but isn't fully grabbed
  â†’ Most competitive intake designs use 2-4 rollers in sequence
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the recommended gap between intake rollers relative to game piece size?",opts:["100% of game piece diameter","80% â€” tight enough to grip and deform around the piece, with enough compliance to accept the piece from slightly different angles","50% of game piece diameter","Equal to roller diameter"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ PYTHON +6 â”€â”€
LESSONS.python.Beginner.push(
  {id:"pyb_errors",title:"Error Handling With Try/Except",est:"9 min",content:`## A Program That Crashes Loses Data
A scouting app that crashes when a scout submits bad data loses every match recorded in that session. Proper error handling catches problems, logs them, and keeps the program running.

## Basic Try/Except
\`\`\`python
# Without error handling â€” crashes on bad input:
team_num = int(input("Team number: "))  # crashes if scout types "abc"

# With error handling:
try:
    team_num = int(input("Team number: "))
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter a number.")
    team_num = None

# Multiple exception types:
try:
    data = json.load(open("matches.json"))
    total = data["total"] / data["count"]
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("No matches file found â€” starting fresh.")
    data = {}
except KeyError as e:
    print(f"Missing field in data: {e}")
    data = {}
except ZeroDivisionError:
    total = 0

# Catch everything (use sparingly):
try:
    risky_operation()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Unexpected error: {e}")
    # Log it, don't silently swallow it
\`\`\`

## Finally and Else
\`\`\`python
# finally: runs whether or not an error occurred
try:
    f = open("matches.json")
    data = json.load(f)
except FileNotFoundError:
    data = []
finally:
    f.close()  # always close the file
    # Better: use "with open(...)" and skip the finally

# else: runs only if no exception occurred
try:
    value = int(user_input)
except ValueError:
    print("Not a number")
else:
    process(value)   # only runs if int() succeeded
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"When should you use 'except Exception as e' vs a specific exception type?",opts:["Always use Exception â€” it's safer","Use specific types when you know what can go wrong and have a specific response for each; use bare Exception only as a catch-all of last resort, and always log the error rather than silently ignoring it","Specific exceptions are slower","Exception type only works in Python 3"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.python.Intermediate.push(
  {id:"pi_generators",title:"Generators and Lazy Evaluation",est:"11 min",content:`## Process Large Datasets Without Loading Them Into Memory
A scouting CSV with 10,000 match records doesn't need to be in memory all at once to compute averages. Generators process one item at a time â€” the memory footprint is constant regardless of dataset size.

## Generator Functions
\`\`\`python
# Regular function: builds the whole list in memory
def get_high_scorers(matches, threshold):
    result = []
    for m in matches:
        if m["total"] >= threshold:
            result.append(m)
    return result  # entire filtered list in memory

# Generator function: yields one at a time
def gen_high_scorers(matches, threshold):
    for m in matches:
        if m["total"] >= threshold:
            yield m   # pauses here, resumes on next()

# Usage â€” identical call syntax:
for match in gen_high_scorers(all_matches, 45):
    process(match)   # processes one at a time, no list built

# Generator expressions (inline):
totals = (m["total"] for m in matches)   # note: () not []
grand_total = sum(totals)                # streams through, no list
\`\`\`

## Reading a Large File with a Generator
\`\`\`python
def read_matches_csv(filepath):
    """Yield one match dict at a time â€” handles files of any size."""
    with open(filepath) as f:
        reader = csv.DictReader(f)
        for row in reader:
            yield {
                "team":   int(row["team"]),
                "match":  int(row["match"]),
                "total":  float(row["total"]),
                "climb":  row["climb"],
            }

# Process 50,000 rows with constant memory:
for match in read_matches_csv("season_data.csv"):
    update_stats(match)

# Pipeline: chain generators
raw      = read_matches_csv("season_data.csv")
filtered = (m for m in raw if m["total"] > 0)
high     = (m for m in filtered if m["climb"] in ("L3", "L4"))
for m in high:
    record_elite(m)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What is the key memory advantage of a generator over a list comprehension for large datasets?",opts:["Generators use compressed storage","A generator yields one item at a time and holds only the current item in memory â€” a list comprehension builds the entire result list before any processing begins; for 50,000 records, the generator uses kilobytes while the list uses megabytes","Generators are faster than lists","List comprehensions can't filter data"],ans:1},
    ]},
  {id:"pi_api2",title:"Building a REST API With Flask",est:"13 min",content:`## Your Scouting Data Deserves a Real API
A Python script that reads a CSV and prints results is fine for one user. A Flask REST API lets multiple scouts submit data simultaneously, lets a dashboard fetch it live, and lets any device on your network access it â€” without anyone installing Python.

## A Complete Mini Scouting API
\`\`\`python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, abort
from pathlib import Path
import json, threading

app  = Flask(__name__)
lock = threading.Lock()
DATA = Path("matches.json")

def load():
    if DATA.exists():
        return json.loads(DATA.read_text())
    return []

def save(matches):
    DATA.write_text(json.dumps(matches, indent=2))

# POST /api/matches â€” submit a scouted match
@app.route("/api/matches", methods=["POST"])
def post_match():
    body = request.get_json(silent=True)
    if not body:
        abort(400, "JSON body required")
    required = {"team", "match_num", "auto", "cycles", "climb"}
    if not required.issubset(body):
        abort(400, f"Missing fields: {required - body.keys()}")

    with lock:
        matches = load()
        matches.append(body)
        save(matches)
    return jsonify({"ok": True, "total": len(matches) + 1}), 201

# GET /api/teams â€” aggregate stats per team
@app.route("/api/teams")
def get_teams():
    with lock:
        matches = load()
    stats = {}
    for m in matches:
        t = m["team"]
        if t not in stats:
            stats[t] = {"team": t, "count": 0, "auto_sum": 0, "cycle_sum": 0}
        stats[t]["count"]     += 1
        stats[t]["auto_sum"]  += m.get("auto", 0)
        stats[t]["cycle_sum"] += m.get("cycles", 0)

    result = [
        {"team": v["team"],
         "avg_auto":   round(v["auto_sum"]  / v["count"], 1),
         "avg_cycles": round(v["cycle_sum"] / v["count"], 1),
         "matches":    v["count"]}
        for v in sorted(stats.values(), key=lambda x: -x["cycle_sum"] / x["count"])
    ]
    return jsonify(result)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    from waitress import serve
    serve(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=5000)
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"Why is the threading.Lock used around file reads and writes?",opts:["Flask requires locks for file access","Multiple scouts submitting simultaneously can cause two threads to read the file, both modify it, and overwrite each other's changes â€” the lock ensures only one thread accesses the file at a time, preventing data loss","Locks improve read performance","JSON files can't be read from two processes"],ans:1},
    ]},
);
LESSONS.python.Advanced.push(
  {id:"pa_packaging",title:"Packaging Python Tools for Your Team",est:"12 min",content:`## A Script Only You Can Run Helps Only You
A scouting tool that requires "install Python 3.11, then pip install these 8 packages, then set this environment variable" will be run by one person. A properly packaged tool installs in two steps and runs on any team member's computer.

## Option 1: requirements.txt + venv (simplest)
\`\`\`bash
# In your project:
python -m venv venv               # create virtual environment
source venv/bin/activate          # Mac/Linux
venv\\Scripts\\activate           # Windows

pip install flask requests pandas
pip freeze > requirements.txt     # capture exact versions

# Teammate setup (two commands):
python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
\`\`\`

## Option 2: PyInstaller â€” Single Executable
\`\`\`bash
# Package the app into a standalone executable:
pip install pyinstaller
pyinstaller --onefile --windowed scout_app.py

# Produces: dist/scout_app.exe (Windows) or dist/scout_app (Mac/Linux)
# Teammate runs: double-click scout_app.exe â€” no Python required

# Including data files:
pyinstaller --onefile --add-data "templates:templates" --add-data "static:static" app.py
\`\`\`

## Option 3: pyproject.toml Package (for reusable libraries)
\`\`\`toml
# pyproject.toml
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "team1234-scout"
version = "2025.1.0"
dependencies = ["flask>=3.0", "requests>=2.31", "pandas>=2.0"]

[project.scripts]
scout = "scout.cli:main"    # exposes 'scout' command after install
\`\`\`
\`\`\`bash
# Install the package in development mode:
pip install -e .
# Now 'scout' command is available anywhere in the venv
\`\`\``,quiz:[
      {q:"What advantage does PyInstaller provide over distributing a requirements.txt?",opts:["Smaller file size","The executable bundles Python and all dependencies â€” team members with no Python installation can run it with a double-click; requirements.txt still requires Python, a virtual environment, and pip install to be run first","PyInstaller is faster","requirements.txt doesn't work on Windows"],ans:1},
    ]},
);

// â”€â”€ TEAMMANAGEMENT +3 â”€â”€
LESSONS.teammanagement.Advanced.push(
